#### Where it breaks
| Layer | Failure | How the design handles it |
|---|---|---|
| A single hot key | One viral key saturates the one server that owns it while the rest idle | Replicated beyond the normal replication factor, reads round-robin, the coordinator coalesces concurrent misses into one fetch |
| Position count | Too few positions leave one server holding multiples of the average | Raise V for `1/sqrt(V)` returns, or allocate positions deliberately instead of randomly |
| Rebalance traffic | Streaming ~30GB into one node competes with the foreground load it also serves | Cap concurrent inbound streams at the recipient, not bytes per stream, since the recipient's own NIC is the true limit |
| Freshly joined server | It owns its arcs at the epoch bump but its cache is empty | Reads stay on the donor until the new owner's hit rate crosses a threshold, the warming state |
| Crash mid-rebalance | A joining server dies partway through the transfer | The donor deletes last, so nothing was given up; the join is simply abandoned rather than rolled back |
| Partition | Two halves of the fleet disagree on membership | A node never answers a request carrying a higher epoch than its own; it refreshes before it answers |
| Hash function drift | A binary upgrade silently changes the hash seed | The seed is pinned in config and checked against the cluster signature at boot |

#### What this design does not solve
**A hot key is a load problem the ring was never built to fix.** The ring distributes keys evenly, not per-key traffic, so one viral key can saturate its owning server while 999 others idle. Replicating it beyond the normal factor fixes hot reads and creates a hot write, because every write now fans out to every copy, or the copies drift apart. A hot write to a single key has no infrastructure answer at all: the key has to be split by the application into `key:0` through `key:9` and recombined by the caller.

**Membership stays eventually consistent, on purpose, rather than closing the gap with consensus.** Epoch tagging and dual reads narrow the window where two servers disagree about who owns what, but they do not eliminate it. Closing it fully means a linearizable membership check on every read, which puts a consensus round trip in front of a lookup deliberately built to cost about a hundred nanoseconds in local memory. That is not a fix, it is a different design. The actual choice made here is to refuse to serve once the last successful gossip exchange is older than thirty seconds, trading availability for the guarantee that nothing served is simply wrong.

**Rebalance pacing is a fixed number an operator picked, and the right value depends on load that varies by an order of magnitude across the day.** A closed loop that throttles from observed foreground latency sounds like the fix, but the loop tends to oscillate: throttling down improves latency, which raises the throttle, which degrades latency again, on a period set by the metric window. It also interacts badly with a large position count, since a rebuild at 200 positions per server touches nearly the whole cluster, making any pacing decision fleet-wide rather than local to two machines.

#### Final design
Read it back through the numbers. Modulo's 91% churn on a single join is what rules it out and forces a structure where ownership is a local property. That local property is what lets 1,000 servers agree on a placement without a lookup ever leaving one process. The `1/sqrt(V)` law is what turns "local property" into "fair local property", at V≈200 for about 7% spread, 3.2MB of metadata, and replica peers spanning nearly the whole cluster as the price. And the ~30GB moved per join, arriving from up to 200 donors, is what makes the donor-deletes-last ordering non-negotiable, because that ordering is the only thing that makes an aborted join free.

[The whole design](/diagram/consistent-hashing?focus=caller,hasher,ring-search,replica-walk,vnode-table,coordinator,serve-arcs,warming,arc-handoff,donors,failure-detector,gossip-view,epoch-issuer,snapshots)

> **The numbers to remember.** ~91% moved under modulo vs ~9% on a ring · V≈200 for ~7.1% spread, 4× the positions per halving · ~3.2MB ring metadata at 1,000 servers · ~30GB moved per join · epoch refresh replaces a stale-view bug with a latency blip.

#### Check your understanding
**Why does adding one server to a ten-server modulo fleet move 91% of keys, while a ring moves only about 9%?** Modulo ties every key's answer to N, a global quantity that changes for everyone the moment one server joins. A ring ties a key's answer to its nearest server in one direction, a local fact that a join only disturbs near the new boundary.

**Why does one position per server leave an uneven split, and why does V=200 fix it rather than V=1000?** A server's share is a sum of V random arcs, and the coefficient of variation of that sum falls as `1/sqrt(V)`. V=1 gives roughly 100% spread; V=200 gives about 7%; reaching 3.2% at V=1000 costs four times the positions for half the improvement.

**A key is served stale. What is the fastest way to localise the bug?** Compare the ring and its epoch across three points: the node that answered, a node that answers correctly, and the membership source of truth. The epoch difference tells you whether it is a stale view, a migration in progress, or buffered writes that have not replayed yet.

**Why does the donor delete its copy last, rather than as soon as the new owner starts receiving data?** Deleting last makes a join abortable for free. If the new owner dies mid-transfer, the donor never gave anything up, so recovery is deleting a partial copy on a dead machine rather than reconstructing lost data.

**Why would a cluster deliberately choose 16 positions per server over 200, when 200 gives a better spread?** At 200 random positions, a server's replica peers span nearly the whole cluster, so almost any three simultaneous failures lose some key's data. At 16, most random triples of failed servers never shared a replica set, trading some spread for real protection against correlated failure.
### 3. Design a Distributed Key-Value Store (Dynamo-style)
#### Understanding the problem
This store makes one refusal: no key has a leader. Any node can accept a write for any key, and the store stays writable even if most of the fleet is unreachable.

That refusal buys availability and creates a new problem in the same breath.

First, if no node is special, two different nodes can each accept a write to the same key at the same instant. Both succeed. The store now holds two answers to one question, and something has to decide which one is real, or whether both are.

Second, replicas fall behind constantly, not occasionally. A write that only needs two of three replicas to acknowledge leaves the third one stale by design, every single time. Convergence has to be a continuous background job, not a recovery procedure.

Third, the caller gets to choose, per request, how much of this it wants to deal with. One keyspace can serve a request that wants strict agreement and a request that wants speed, in the same second.

> **What this is not.** The closest question is a distributed object store, and both partition and replicate durable bytes with no single point of failure. They diverge on the payload. Objects there are immutable and megabytes to gigabytes; records here are mutable and about a kilobyte. Immutability deletes the conflict problem outright: an overwrite writes fresh bytes nobody has read yet and swaps one pointer in a small, strongly consistent index, so the bulk data never races. There is no equivalent move here, because the metadata *is* the value. A kilobyte record also breaks the durability arithmetic that makes erasure coding cheap on large objects: split a 1.2KB record with the same 6+3 scheme used on a 1MB blob and the per-fragment headers dominate the payload. Full replication is the right answer for small mutable state and the wrong one for a petabyte of blobs.

#### Requirements and the numbers
**Functional.** `get(key)`, `put(key, value)`, `delete(key)`. Replication factor and read and write quorum tunable per request.

**Non-functional.** No single point of failure across nodes, racks or regions. p99 under 10ms. 99.99% availability. Eventual consistency is an accepted answer, not a bug.

The whole design is decided by five numbers, so derive them before choosing anything.

**How big is one stored record?** A 1KB value plus a 32-byte key, a version vector of roughly three writer entries at 16 bytes each (~48B), and a version and TTL header (~16B), giving **~1.2KB per record**.

**How much data does the cluster actually hold?** 10¹⁰ keys × 1.2KB × a replication factor of 3 = 3.6 × 10¹³B, **~36TB logical**. Compaction keeps extra copies in flight at roughly 1.4×, so **~50TB physical**. That is tens of terabytes, not the petabytes this pattern is often described at; petabyte scale needs two more orders of magnitude of keys.

**How is 1M ops/s split, and what does each op actually cost the cluster?** At a 4:1 read to write ratio, that is **800k reads/s and 200k writes/s**. Every write fans to all N=3 replicas; every read sends one full read and two digest requests. So the cluster does roughly **3M replica operations/s**, three times the client-facing rate.

**How many nodes does that require, and which constraint actually binds?** By throughput, one tuned node sustains ~30k ops/s under compaction and repair: 3 × 10⁶ ÷ 3 × 10⁴ = 100 nodes. By capacity, keeping each node under ~1TB so a rebuild streams in hours: 50TB ÷ 1TB = 50 nodes. Throughput needs more nodes, so it binds: round to **128 nodes**, landing at ~400GB and ~23k replica ops/s per node, comfortably inside the 30k ceiling.

**What does a multi-hour outage cost in parked writes?** One node owns 3/128 of the keyspace, so it is a replica for 200k × 3 ÷ 128 ≈ 4.7k writes/s. A three-hour outage, the default hint lifetime, parks 4.7k × 10,800s ≈ **~60GB of hinted writes**, replayed as a burst the moment the node returns.

> **The numbers to carry.** ~1.2KB per record · ~36TB logical, ~50TB physical · 800k reads/s + 200k writes/s ≈ 3M replica ops/s · 128 nodes, throughput-bound · ~60GB of hints after a 3-hour outage.

#### Where the disagreement gets paid for
No key has a leader, so agreement about a key's current value has to happen somewhere else. This design pays for it in three separate places, each with a different cost.

- **Partitioning**: which N nodes own a key. Solved by a consistent hashing ring, a pure function of the key and the membership view, and the design does not repeat itself there.
- **Quorum**: how many of those N nodes must answer before a request completes. This is the caller's dial, chosen per request rather than fixed for the cluster.
- **Conflict resolution**: what happens when two writes to one key both succeeded. This is the part with no infrastructure-only answer, because the store can detect a conflict but someone still has to merge it.

The entities:

- **Record**: `(value, version_vector, ttl?)`, the unit stored per key per replica.
- **Coordinator**: any node handling a given request, a role every node can play, not a dedicated tier.
- **Version vector**: a small per-writer counter tuple, `{A:3, B:5}`, that detects whether one write happened after another or concurrently with it.
- **Tombstone**: a versioned delete marker, standing in for a row so the row cannot silently reappear.

The API is small; the interesting part is what it returns on conflict:

```
PUT /kv/{key}        body = value     opts: w_quorum
GET /kv/{key}                          opts: r_quorum
DELETE /kv/{key}
```

A read that finds concurrent siblings returns all of them with their vectors. The caller merges and writes back the result with the merged vector as its parent.

#### High-level design
Follow the numbered arrows. Every hop below the coordinator is inside the region the client was routed to.

[The hot path, request to acknowledged write](/diagram/distributed-kv-store?focus=client,geo-dns,ring-lookup,quorum,replicas,lsm,e1,e2,e3,e4,e7)

1. The **Client** sends `get` or `put`, and **Geo DNS + health checks** routes it to a healthy region, not to a specific node.
2. Any node in that region can serve as **Coordinator (any node)**; its **Ring lookup** hashes the key and finds the N=3 nodes that own it.
3. The **Quorum engine** fans the request to all three **Replica nodes** and waits for W acknowledgements on a write, or R responses on a read.
4. Each replica commits to its local **LSM storage engine**, a write-ahead log and an in-memory table flushed to disk in the background.
5. On a write, the coordinator answers the client once W replicas have acknowledged, without waiting for the third.
6. On a read that finds disagreement, the **Read repair** process pulls full values from all N, picks the winner by version, and writes it back to whoever was behind. The **Version vectors** step flags true concurrency and returns every sibling rather than guessing.

> **Why the flow is shaped this way.** The coordinator role and the storage role are separated on purpose. Any node can front any request, so there is no failover pause and no election, and background repair keeps replicas converging without ever making a request wait for all three.

#### Why any two of three is enough, and what that doesn't buy
With three replicas, waiting for all three to answer every request would make the whole store as available as its least reliable replica. Waiting for the fastest one gives up on correctness. What is the middle ground, and what does it actually guarantee?

[The quorum wait between coordinator and replicas](/diagram/distributed-kv-store?focus=quorum,replicas,e4)

**Bad: pick W and R independently, without a relationship between them.** Nothing stops a write acknowledged by two replicas from being read by a quorum that touches neither of them, so a fresh read can return a value from before the write ever happened.

**Good: require `W + R > N`.** With N=3, that means W plus R must be at least 4, and the cheapest pair satisfying it is W=2, R=2. Any set of two acknowledgers and any set of two responders, drawn from three replicas, must share at least one member, by the pigeonhole principle. A read is therefore guaranteed to reach at least one replica that holds the last acknowledged write.

**Great: state precisely what that overlap does and does not prove.** It is a set-intersection property, nothing more. It does not order concurrent writes. It does not make two successive reads agree, because the replica set answering a read can change between one read and the next. It does not make a read-modify-write safe at any setting of W and R, because nothing stops two clients from both reading the same value and both writing a successor.

Worked example, the counterexample worth carrying. A write to N=3 with W=2 reaches replica 1, and the coordinator dies before reaching replica 2, so the write is never actually acknowledged to the client. A later R=2 read hitting replicas 1 and 3 returns the new value. A read straight after that, hitting replicas 2 and 3, does not. Two reads, no write in between, two different answers, which a linearizable store forbids.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 358 253" role="img" aria-label="Any W=2 acknowledging set and any R=2 responding set out of 3 replicas must share a member; the shared member is what a read is guaranteed to see">
  <style>
    .set{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.12;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.5}
    .set2{fill:currentColor;fill-opacity:.08;stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.5;stroke-width:1.5}
    .dot{fill:currentColor}
    .hit{fill:var(--accent)}
    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    .sub{fill:currentColor;opacity:.8;font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    text{text-anchor:middle}
  </style>
  <ellipse class="set" cx="150" cy="130" rx="100" ry="65"/>
  <ellipse class="set2" cx="250" cy="130" rx="100" ry="65"/>
  <text class="sub" x="105" y="55">W=2 acknowledged</text>
  <text class="sub" x="295" y="55">R=2 responding</text>
  <circle class="dot" cx="115" cy="135" r="6"/><text class="sub" x="115" y="158">R1</text>
  <circle class="hit" cx="200" cy="135" r="7"/><text class="sub" x="200" y="160">R2, in both sets</text>
  <circle class="dot" cx="285" cy="135" r="6"/><text class="sub" x="285" y="158">R3</text>
  <text class="lbl" x="200" y="225">N=3, any 2-of-3 sets always overlap by</text>
  <text class="lbl" x="200" y="242">at least one replica</text>
</svg>
```

#### Divergence is the normal state
Every acknowledged write at W=2 leaves one replica behind, on purpose, every time. At 200k writes/s that is 200k newly stale copies a second before anything has gone wrong. What brings them back together?

[Read repair catching one stale replica mid-response](/diagram/distributed-kv-store?focus=quorum,read-repair,replicas,hints,anti-entropy,e5,e6,e8,e9,e14,e15)

**Bad: rely on one mechanism for the whole keyspace.** Nothing running at a single timescale covers both a key that is read constantly and a key that nobody has touched in months.

**Good: three mechanisms, but assume any one of them alone is enough.** Each covers a real gap, and each also leaves one open, which is why production runs all three together rather than picking a favourite.

**Great: run all three, and know exactly which gap each one closes.** **Read repair** fixes a stale replica the instant a read happens to notice it: the coordinator asks one replica for the value and the rest for a cheap digest, and a mismatch triggers a writeback to whoever was behind. Its hole is structural: it only touches keys somebody reads, so under the Zipfian skew every real workload has, a long tail can go unread and unrepaired for months. **Hinted handoff** covers an unreachable replica by parking its writes on a healthy neighbour, tagged with the intended owner, replayed the moment that owner returns. Its hole is the TTL: past three hours the hints are dropped, and the problem passes to the third mechanism. **Anti-entropy** sweeps everything, comparing Merkle trees, hashes of hashes, between replicas and recursing only into the branches that disagree. Its hole is cost: building the tree reads every key in the range regardless of how little diverged, about 1.1 hours per node at this size, whether one key was stale or a million.

[Read repair: two fast replicas satisfy R=2, the stale third catches up](/diagram/distributed-kv-store?figure=read-repair)

#### Deletes that refuse to delete
A delete cannot simply remove the row, because every repair mechanism above compares versions, and an absent row loses to a present row in every comparison. A replica that missed a delete would helpfully bring the data back.

[Where a delete lands, and what has to outrun it](/diagram/distributed-kv-store?focus=lsm,tombstones,anti-entropy,e12,e13)

**Bad: delete the row outright.** Any replica that missed the delete still holds the old value, and the next read repair or anti-entropy pass copies that old value back onto the replicas that correctly deleted it.

**Good: write a tombstone, a marker carrying a version that dominates the row it replaces.** The delete now wins every version comparison, so it propagates correctly through read repair and anti-entropy exactly like any other write. But the tombstone itself is a row, and it has to be removed eventually or it accumulates forever.

**Great: purge the tombstone only after `gc_grace_seconds` has passed, and hold that window to a stated invariant.** The invariant: the grace period, ten days by default, must exceed the worst realistic interval between anti-entropy repairs for any range, including the coldest one and including whatever an incident did to the repair schedule. A full repair pass here takes about 1.1 hours against a ten-day window, roughly two orders of magnitude of margin at this size.

Worked example. A row is deleted on day 0. Anti-entropy normally sweeps every range within 1.1 hours, so the tombstone reaches every replica the same day. If repair then falls behind for eleven days, past the ten-day grace window, a replica that was offline for the whole gap purges nothing because it never received the tombstone, and any replica that already purged its copy of the tombstone has no record the delete ever happened. The fix, when repair falls behind, is to raise the grace period. Running repair harder is not available, because repair is usually already the saturated resource.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 220" role="img" aria-label="A tombstone's grace period must outlast the worst-case gap between repair passes, or a replica that missed the delete can resurrect the row after purge">
  <style>
    .axis{stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.4;stroke-width:1.3}
    .safe{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.18;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.4}
    .danger{fill:currentColor;fill-opacity:.12;stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.6;stroke-width:1.4;stroke-dasharray:4 3}
    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    .sub{fill:currentColor;opacity:.8;font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
  </style>
  <text class="lbl" x="8" y="16">delete written, day 0</text>
  <line class="axis" x1="15" y1="140" x2="385" y2="140"/>
  <rect class="safe" x="20" y="60" width="290" height="50"/>
  <text class="sub" x="30" y="80">gc_grace_seconds: 10 days,</text>
  <text class="sub" x="30" y="96">repair passes every ~1.1h</text>
  <rect class="danger" x="310" y="60" width="65" height="50"/>
  <text class="lbl" x="20" y="40">grace window ends</text>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="180">repair falls behind past 10 days: purge happens</text>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="196">before every replica has seen the tombstone</text>
</svg>
```

#### When two writes disagree
Two clients write the same key within the same millisecond, both against different coordinators, both satisfying W=2. Both succeed. What does a later read return?

[Where concurrency is detected, and where it is resolved](/diagram/distributed-kv-store?focus=lsm,version-vectors,client,e10,e11)

**Bad: last write wins by wall-clock timestamp.** It is cheap and it returns exactly one value, but it is only safe when the gap between two writes to one key reliably exceeds the fleet's clock error. A live migration or an NTP step can move a clock by seconds, so a write that is actually earlier can carry a later timestamp, silently overwriting the real latest value with no trace it happened.

**Good: version vectors, a small counter per writer, incremented on every write.** `{A:3, B:5}` and `{A:4, B:5}` compare cleanly: the second dominates the first in every component, so it is strictly newer. But version vectors only detect. Faced with `{A:3, B:5}` and `{A:4, B:4}`, neither dominates the other, and the vector correctly reports the writes as concurrent, then stops.

**Great: return every concurrent sibling to the caller, or restrict the value to a type that merges itself.** For an arbitrary value, both siblings go back on the next read, and something above the store, application code or the client, merges them and writes back the result with the merged vector as its parent. For a value that only grows, a set, an add-only counter, a presence flag, the merge is a property of the type, and replicas converge with no code above the store ever seeing a conflict.

Worked example. Client A in New York writes `{"balance": 100}`. Client B in London writes `{"balance": 200}` in the same millisecond, against a different coordinator. Both satisfy W=2. Version vectors mark the two writes concurrent, because neither vector dominates the other, and a subsequent read returns both siblings with their vectors. Last-write-wins would have silently picked one by timestamp and discarded the other, and if New York's clock ran two seconds fast, it could discard the value that actually happened last.

[Version vectors: dominance versus concurrency](/diagram/distributed-kv-store?figure=version-vectors)

#### Sloppy quorum: available at the price of the guarantee it just gave you
During a partition, the coordinator cannot always reach the canonical replicas. What happens to `W + R > N` when the nodes that acknowledge a write are not the key's actual owners?

[Where a hint stands in for an unreachable replica](/diagram/distributed-kv-store?focus=quorum,hints,replicas,e5,e6)

**Bad: refuse writes whenever a replica is unreachable.** The store loses exactly the availability it exists to provide, the moment any single node has a bad network day.

**Good: park the write on a healthy neighbour instead, tagged with the intended owner.** That neighbour replays the buffered write once the real owner returns, within a bounded TTL, three hours by default. This is hinted handoff, and it is what keeps writes flowing during a partition.

**Great: be precise about what counting a hint toward W actually does to the guarantee.** A sloppy quorum counts hinted acknowledgements toward W, which is the whole point, since it is what lets the write succeed at all. But it means the acknowledging set can contain nodes that are not replicas of the key. `W + R > N` is a statement about the acknowledging set and the responding set of *replicas* sharing a member. If the acknowledgers were never replicas, that overlap argument has nothing to stand on, and a read during the same partition can miss the hinted write entirely.

The honest description is that a sloppy quorum has no consistency invariant during the partition it is covering for, only good odds that the network recovers before it matters. A strict quorum, refusing to use non-replica nodes, keeps the guarantee and gives up availability instead. Some deployments expose which mode a given acknowledgement came from, so a latency-tolerant caller can retry at strict quorum; most callers never check.

#### Where it breaks
| Layer | Failure | How the design handles it |
|---|---|---|
| Hot key | A viral key drives 100x traffic to its three owning replicas | Coordinator-side request coalescing serves one in-flight read per key to all waiters; the key is replicated beyond N if the burst persists |
| Compaction | LSM background rewrites compete with foreground reads for disk queue depth | Compaction bandwidth is throttled and, where possible, put on a separate device |
| Cross-region | A quorum spanning regions adds a full WAN round trip to every request | `LOCAL_QUORUM` satisfies the intersection property inside one region; cross-region replication runs asynchronously |
| Repair | A full Merkle-tree pass reads every key regardless of how little diverged | Subrange repair at finer granularity limits how much of the keyspace one pass touches |
| Tombstones | A queue-shaped workload deletes almost everything it writes, and scans still read every tombstone | Bucket by time and drop whole partitions as a metadata operation, rather than deleting rows one at a time |
| Version vectors | Many writers touching one key make the sibling set grow without bound | The vector is bounded by pruning the oldest entries, at the cost of occasionally over-reporting concurrency |
| Region outage | A whole datacenter goes offline | Geo DNS routes around it; the remaining regions keep serving from their own local quorum |

#### What this design does not solve
**There is no compare-and-set, and no quorum setting builds one.** Two clients can each read a value, each compute a successor, and each write it, and every setting of W and R accepts both writes. Version vectors correctly report the two as concurrent, but reporting is all they do. For a balance or a stock count, "here are two values, you decide" is not an answer. A consensus round per key fixes it at the cost of four round trips instead of one, and it still does not compose across two keys touched by the same transfer. The honest boundary is that this store is not the system of record for anything carrying an invariant; that value belongs behind a per-key leader instead.

**Sloppy quorum is on by default, and it quietly voids the guarantee the design leads with.** `W + R > N` is advertised as an overlap property, but during any partition the acknowledging nodes may not be replicas at all, and the caller has no built-in way to know the difference between an ordinary quorum write and a sloppy one. The guarantee is conditional on no partition being in progress, which is precisely the condition nobody can observe from outside.

**Repair cost scales with total data volume, not with how much actually diverged.** A cluster where a handful of keys are stale still reads the entire range to find them, because building a Merkle tree means reading every key regardless of the answer. At this size a full pass stays comfortably inside the grace window, but the coupling means the safe deletion window is tied to total bytes, not to anything about how many deletes actually happened, and it starts to bind hard around ten times this data on the same node count.

#### Final design
Read it back through the numbers. 3.6 × 10¹³ bytes of logical data, at 200k writes and 800k reads a second, is what makes N=3 replicas and W=R=2 the cheapest setting that still lets a read overlap an acknowledged write. That overlap is exactly what it sounds like and nothing more, which is why version vectors, read repair, hinted handoff and anti-entropy exist as separate mechanisms rather than one guarantee doing all the work. The ~60GB of hints after a three-hour outage is the number that justifies throttled, bursty replay rather than an immediate flood. And the fact that this store cannot refuse a second concurrent write, at any W or R, is the number that sends anything carrying an invariant to a different system entirely.

[The whole design](/diagram/distributed-kv-store?focus=client,geo-dns,coordinator,ring-lookup,quorum,read-repair,version-vectors,hints,replicas,lsm,remote-region,tombstones,anti-entropy,cas-store)

> **The numbers to remember.** N=3, W=R=2, the cheapest pair satisfying `W+R>N` · ~36TB logical / ~50TB physical · 3M replica ops/s from 1M client ops/s · ~60GB hints after 3h · gc_grace_seconds must exceed the worst repair gap, ten days against a ~1.1 hour pass.

#### Check your understanding
**Does `W + R > N` give you linearizability?** No. It only guarantees the acknowledging set and the responding set share a replica, so a read reaches at least one replica holding the last acknowledged write. A write that reached one replica before the coordinator died is never acknowledged, yet a later read can still see it; two reads with no write between them can then disagree, which linearizability forbids.

**Two clients write the same key in the same millisecond. What does the next reader see?** Both writes succeed, since neither coordinator knows about the other. Version vectors mark them concurrent because neither dominates, and the read returns both values as siblings for the application, or a self-merging type, to reconcile.

**Why can a delete not simply remove the row?** Every repair mechanism compares versions, and an absent row always loses to a present one. A replica that missed the delete would reintroduce the data at the next read repair or anti-entropy pass, so the delete has to win comparisons by writing a tombstone instead.

**Why does a sloppy quorum undermine the guarantee the design advertises?** `W + R > N` assumes the acknowledging nodes are replicas of the key. During a partition, hinted handoff lets non-replica neighbours count toward W, so the acknowledging set may share no member with the responding set at all, and the overlap argument has nothing to stand on until the partition heals.

**Why can this store not hold a bank balance?** Because nothing in it can refuse a second concurrent write. Two clients can both read 100, both write 90, and both writes are accepted at every setting of W and R; version vectors report the collision but never prevent it. A value with a real invariant needs a per-key leader and a consensus round, not a quorum store.
### 4. Design a Unique ID Generator (Snowflake)
#### Understanding the problem
Every row a database stores needs a primary key, and that key has to be unique across a fleet of machines with no single one of them in charge. It also has to sort roughly by creation time, so new rows land at the right edge of an index rather than scattering writes across it.

Three things make this harder than "generate a random number".

First, a duplicate is not a visible error. It is a second row silently sharing a key with the first, discovered months later when a foreign key points at the wrong record.

Second, the ID has to be produced on the hot path of every write in the system, so any network call or lock inside generation becomes the availability floor for everything that writes.

Third, the one thing this design has to trust, a machine's wall clock, is exactly the thing that occasionally lies.

> **What this is not.** The closest question is a Dynamo-style key-value store, and both refuse to coordinate on the write path. The difference is who owns the namespace. A key-value store cannot pre-partition its keyspace, because the keys belong to the client and any replica can be asked to write any key, so two writes to the same key during a partition are legitimate and the store detects the conflict after the fact and reconciles it. Here the namespace is entirely ours: nobody hands us the next ID, we mint it. So we spend a small amount of coordination once, at boot, to carve the space into private slices, and uniqueness follows from construction rather than from detecting a collision that already happened. Same refusal to coordinate per request, opposite mechanism, because one system owns its keys and the other does not.

#### Requirements and the numbers
**Functional.** A unique 64-bit ID per call. Ordered by creation time across milliseconds. Decodable back to a creation timestamp with no lookup.

**Non-functional.** No network call on the issue path. Sub-microsecond issuance. Zero duplicates as a hard bound, not a budget. Note what is not promised: within one millisecond, IDs from different workers carry no meaningful order between them.

The whole design is decided by four numbers, so derive them before choosing the bit layout.

**How many bits does a machine need to stay unique across the fleet?** A field of `b` bits gives `2^b` distinct values. At 10 bits, `2^10 = 1024` worker slots, comfortably above a fleet of roughly 700 to 1,000 live machines with headroom for a rolling deploy.

**How many IDs can one worker mint inside a single millisecond?** Whatever is left of the 64 bits after time and worker. At 12 bits, `2^12 = 4096` IDs per millisecond per worker, so **~4.096M IDs/s** is one worker's ceiling, aggregating to roughly 4M/s realistic steady state across a thousand workers running well below their individual ceiling.

**How long does a 41-bit millisecond field last?** `2^41` milliseconds ÷ (1000 × 86,400 × 365.25) ≈ **69.7 years**. Anchored at 1970 that runway expires in 2039; anchoring at a custom epoch set on launch day buys back the full span.

**What does the extra width of a 128-bit format actually cost, at scale?** A key is stored once per index it appears in. At 10¹⁰ rows across a primary key and three secondary indexes, an extra 8 bytes per key is `8B × 4 × 10¹⁰` ≈ **320GB of extra index**. At 10⁹ rows the same arithmetic gives ~32GB, which nobody notices. This one number decides the whole first fork below.

> **The numbers to carry.** 1024 worker slots (10 bits) · 4,096 IDs/ms/worker, ~4.1M/s ceiling (12 bits) · ~69.7 years of runway (41 bits) · ~320GB of extra index at 10¹⁰ rows if the ID were twice as wide.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 220" role="img" aria-label="A 64-bit id: unused sign bit, 41 bits of milliseconds since a custom epoch, 10 bits of worker id, 12 bits of sequence, high bits to low bits">
  <style>
    .box{fill:none;stroke:currentColor;stroke-width:1.5}
    .acc{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.15;stroke:var(--accent)}
    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    .sub{fill:currentColor;opacity:.8;font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
  </style>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="16">high bits → low bits, sorts as an integer</text>
  <rect class="box" x="20" y="24" width="360" height="26" rx="4"/><text class="lbl" x="30" y="41">sign, 1 bit</text>
  <rect class="acc" x="20" y="58" width="360" height="34" rx="4"/><text class="lbl" x="30" y="72">timestamp, 41 bits</text><text class="sub" x="30" y="87">~69.7 years from a custom epoch</text>
  <rect class="box" x="20" y="100" width="360" height="26" rx="4"/><text class="lbl" x="30" y="117">worker, 10 bits — 1024 slots</text>
  <rect class="box" x="20" y="134" width="360" height="26" rx="4"/><text class="lbl" x="30" y="151">sequence, 12 bits — 4096 / ms</text>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="185">packed as (timestamp &lt;&lt; 22) | (worker &lt;&lt; 12) | sequence</text>
</svg>
```

#### Two claims, coordinated once
Strip away the arithmetic and the design rests on exactly two claims. No two live processes hold the same worker id. Within one process, the pair `(timestamp, sequence)` never repeats. The first claim needs one coordinated act, at boot. The second needs nothing but local state, as long as the clock genuinely moves forward.

The entities:

- **ID**: the packed 64-bit integer, `(timestamp << 22) | (worker_id << 12) | sequence`.
- **Worker id**: a 10-bit slot, claimed exclusively once per process lifetime, never re-checked on the request path.
- **Sequence**: a 12-bit counter reset to zero every millisecond, incremented for each ID issued within it.
- **Watermark**: a small persisted promise, "I will not issue below this timestamp", covering a process restart.

The API is two calls, and only one of them runs at request volume:

```
next_id() -> int64      # in-process call, tens of nanoseconds, never blocks on the network
decode(id) -> (timestamp_ms, worker_id, sequence)
```

#### High-level design
Follow the numbered arrows. Only one of them runs at request volume; everything else happens once at boot or in the background.

[The hot path, entirely local](/diagram/unique-id-generator?focus=caller,guard,sequence,pack,sinks,e-call,e-clock,e-guard-seq,e-seq-pack,e-sinks)

1. The **Application process** calls `next_id()`, landing on the **Clock read + rewind guard**.
2. The guard reads the current time and compares it against the last timestamp this process used. If time moved forward normally, it resets the **Sequence counter** to zero; if the same millisecond is still current, it increments the counter.
3. **Pack 41 | 10 | 12** combines timestamp, the worker id fixed at boot, and the sequence into one 64-bit integer.
4. The packed ID goes to whatever **Downstream sinks** it become a key in, most often a BIGINT primary key with a uniqueness constraint as the backstop.

> **Why the flow is shaped this way.** Every one of those four steps reads only process-local memory. Nothing here can be slow, throttled, or unreachable, because nothing here leaves the process. All the coordination this design needs happens once, at boot, and everything downstream of it never has to ask permission again.

#### Why the hot path never touches the network
The obvious way to guarantee uniqueness across machines is to ask a shared authority for every ID. Why does this design refuse that, and what does refusing actually cost?

[Claiming a slot once, instead of asking for permission every time](/diagram/unique-id-generator?focus=worker-id-holder,lease-store,orchestrator,e-lease,e-ordinal,e-worker)

**Bad: ask a central counter for every ID.** One authority owns a single increasing number, which gives genuinely dense, sequential IDs with no clock involved at all. But that authority now has to be up for every write in the system, and it becomes the availability floor and the latency floor for everything downstream of it.

**Good: pre-partition the number space so machines never have to ask each other anything.** Give each worker an exclusive slice of the ID space at boot, and every subsequent ID is minted from purely local state. No two workers can produce the same value in the same instant, because their slices never overlap.

**Great: make the partitioning boundary the one and only place coordination happens, and make that boundary refuse to be ambiguous.** The **Worker-id holder** claims its slot with a create-if-absent operation against the **Worker-id lease store**, or, better where it is available, simply reads a stable ordinal the **Orchestrator ordinal** already assigns. Either way, the claim happens once per process lifetime, and a process that cannot get a slot refuses to start rather than guessing.

This is the same trade a wide, mostly-random ID makes from the opposite direction. Instead of partitioning a small space exactly, a 128-bit format like UUIDv7 makes the space so large that a collision becomes a probability argument rather than a structural impossibility. Both approaches share the same goal: remove the need for any machine to ask another machine "is this value taken" at issue time. They differ only in whether uniqueness is guaranteed by construction or made overwhelmingly unlikely by width.

#### When the clock lies
The uniqueness guarantee assumes `(timestamp, sequence)` never repeats within one process. That assumption is a statement about a hardware oscillator, and it is false more often than people expect.

[The one comparison standing between a rewind and a duplicate](/diagram/unique-id-generator?focus=ntp,clock,guard,e-ntp,e-clock,e-guard-seq)

**Bad: trust `now_ms()` and keep issuing.** Wall clocks step backwards for ordinary reasons: an NTP client correcting a large offset on a freshly started container, a virtual machine resuming after live migration with a stale clock, an unsmeared leap second re-running the same UTC second. A generator that keeps issuing through a rewind reissues IDs it already handed out.

**Good: compare against the last timestamp used, and halt on any rewind.** `if now < last_ts: halt and alert` costs nothing on the hot path, and it turns silent corruption into a visible, bounded outage on one node behind a load balancer. What it does not fix is which clock `now` reads: `CLOCK_REALTIME` is exactly the clock that steps.

**Great: derive the timestamp from a monotonic base, so most rewinds cannot reach it at all.** Read realtime once at startup, then compute every later timestamp as `base_realtime + (monotonic_now - base_monotonic)`. `CLOCK_MONOTONIC` cannot go backwards by contract, so an NTP step on the host no longer rewinds the field the generator emits. The field then drifts from true UTC at the host crystal's own rate, typically 10 to 50 parts per million, about 1 to 4 seconds a day, which matters only if something downstream treats the decoded value as an accurate event time rather than a sort key.

Worked example. A VM is live-migrated and its clock jumps back three seconds, from `1740000003000` to `1740000000000`. Under the bad version, the generator keeps issuing, and every ID it mints in the next three seconds duplicates one it already issued moments earlier. Under the great version, the guard sees `now < last_ts`, halts issuance, alerts, and rejoins only once the wall clock genuinely passes `last_ts` again, never overlapping its own earlier output.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 393 195" role="img" aria-label="Wall clock steps backward three seconds; the guard halts at the moment of the step and only resumes once real time passes the last timestamp used, never overlapping earlier output">
  <style>
    .axis{stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.4;stroke-width:1.3}
    .before{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.2;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.4}
    .halt{fill:currentColor;fill-opacity:.1;stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.6;stroke-width:1.4;stroke-dasharray:4 3}
    .after{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.2;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.4}
    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    .sub{fill:currentColor;opacity:.8;font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    text{text-anchor:middle}
  </style>
  <line class="axis" x1="15" y1="115" x2="385" y2="115"/>
  <rect class="before" x="20" y="85" width="105" height="30"/><text class="lbl" x="72" y="105">normal</text>
  <rect class="halt" x="135" y="85" width="130" height="30"/><text class="lbl" x="200" y="105">HALT</text>
  <rect class="after" x="275" y="85" width="105" height="30"/><text class="lbl" x="327" y="105">resume</text>
  <text class="lbl" x="200" y="70">clock steps back 3s here</text>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="150" style="text-anchor:start">normal: issuing, last_ts climbing</text>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="167" style="text-anchor:start">HALT: now &lt; last_ts → halt, refuse to issue</text>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="184" style="text-anchor:start">resume: once real time passes last_ts again</text>
</svg>
```

#### The hole in memory: process restart
The `now < last_ts` check works only as long as `last_ts` survives. What happens when the process holding it does not?

[Where the promise not to reissue actually lives](/diagram/unique-id-generator?focus=guard,watermark,e-watermark)

**Bad: keep `last_ts` in process memory only.** A generator that crashes and restarts in 200ms, right after a clock step of a few seconds, has no memory of what it just issued. It starts fresh, sees a clock that looks perfectly normal, and cheerfully reissues values it minted moments before.

**Good: persist `last_ts` to disk on every issue.** Correct, and unaffordable. An fsync costs tens to hundreds of microseconds, and this design issues at up to 4M IDs a second on a busy worker; syncing on every call would turn the one dependency-free step in the whole system into the slowest one.

**Great: reserve time forward instead of recording time already spent.** On startup, fsync a **Restart watermark** of `now + 10s` to local disk, refuse to issue any timestamp below it, and only fsync again once issuance actually crosses it. That is one fsync roughly every ten seconds instead of on every one of 4 × 10⁷ calls a second.

A crash restart inside the reserved window simply sleeps until the wall clock passes the watermark, so the cost lands entirely on restart latency, up to ten seconds, rather than on correctness. Tune the window against how often the process actually restarts, and log the sleep loudly, since a crash-looping process with this guard in front of it looks like a hang rather than a crash.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 393 193" role="img" aria-label="The watermark is fsynced ten seconds ahead of issuance; a crash restart inside that window sleeps until real time catches up, rather than reissuing anything">
  <style>
    .axis{stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.4;stroke-width:1.3}
    .issued{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.2;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.4}
    .reserved{fill:currentColor;fill-opacity:.08;stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.55;stroke-width:1.4;stroke-dasharray:4 3}
    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    .sub{fill:currentColor;opacity:.8;font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    text{text-anchor:middle}
  </style>
  <line class="axis" x1="15" y1="115" x2="385" y2="115"/>
  <rect class="issued" x="20" y="85" width="185" height="30"/><text class="lbl" x="112" y="105">issued</text>
  <rect class="reserved" x="205" y="85" width="175" height="30"/><text class="lbl" x="292" y="105">reserved</text>
  <text class="lbl" x="292" y="70">watermark: fsynced now+10s</text>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="150" style="text-anchor:start">issued: real issuance so far, real time</text>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="167" style="text-anchor:start">crash + restart: sleep until real time</text>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="182" style="text-anchor:start">passes the watermark, nothing reissued</text>
</svg>
```

#### Claiming a worker id, and losing it later
The worker id claim happens once, at boot, and is never re-checked. What holds that guarantee together for the rest of the process's life, and what happens if it quietly stops being true?

[The claim, and what watches it afterwards](/diagram/unique-id-generator?focus=lease-store,worker-id-holder,metrics,e-lease,e-telemetry,e-slots)

**Bad: assign worker ids by static configuration.** Baked-in values are simple and correct exactly as long as the fleet never exceeds the slot count and nothing ever restarts with a stale value. An autoscaling group of interchangeable instances guarantees neither, and once replacement churn passes roughly a hundred instances a day, two hosts eventually share an id.

**Good: claim an exclusive, expiring lease from a coordination service at boot.** Create-if-absent semantics against the **Worker-id lease store** mean two processes cannot both win the same slot, and a TTL returns a dead node's slot to the pool. The process refuses to start if it cannot get one, which is the correct trade: a pod that will not boot is a page, a guessed worker id is silent corruption.

**Great: prefer an orchestrator ordinal over a lease wherever one already exists.** A StatefulSet ordinal or an ECS task index is stronger than any lease this design could build, because the scheduler enforces exclusivity continuously, including during a network partition to the lease store, whereas an expiring lease does not. It also removes a boot-time dependency on a service that tends to be unhealthy at exactly the moment a fleet is trying to scale up.

Either way, the guarantee is asserted once and never re-verified. A generator that loses its lease through a long pause or a network partition, after its TTL has quietly expired and been reassigned, keeps issuing under a worker id someone else now also holds, and nothing on the request path would notice. The honest mitigation is a background watcher that kills issuance the moment it observes lease loss, which closes most of the window without closing it completely: the watcher is asynchronous, so the gap shrinks to its poll interval rather than disappearing. This is the concrete reason an orchestrator ordinal is the stronger answer wherever the scheduler can provide one.

#### What the bits cost you
A 64-bit Snowflake and a 128-bit UUIDv7 solve the same problem with the opposite trade. What does doubling the width actually buy, and when is it worth it?

[Where the bits go once they are packed](/diagram/unique-id-generator?focus=pack,sinks,boundary,e-sinks,e-opaque)

**Bad: assume width is free.** It is not: a key is stored once per index it participates in, so extra bytes multiply across every primary key, every secondary index, and every foreign key referencing it.

**Good: pick the format by what fits the schema today.** If every table is already BIGINT, a 64-bit Snowflake requires no migration. If the schema is greenfield, a 128-bit UUID is simpler on every other axis: no worker-id allocation, no boot-time claim, no clock-halt logic to write or operate.

**Great: pick by row count, because that is what the cost of width actually scales with.** At 10¹⁰ rows across four indexes, an extra 8 bytes per key is roughly 320GB of extra index, plus the memory pressure of keeping the hot part of that resident. At 10⁹ rows the same arithmetic gives about 32GB, which nobody will notice on a modern system. Below that threshold, UUIDv7 is not a close call: it removes an entire class of operational risk, standardised as RFC 9562 in 2024 and available as a native function in PostgreSQL 18, for a storage cost too small to matter.

| Format | Bits | Ordered by time | Coordination | Guessable |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Snowflake | 64 | yes, as an integer | worker-id claim at boot | yes |
| UUIDv7 | 128 | yes, as binary | none | partially |
| UUIDv4 | 128 | no | none | no |
| Ticket server | any | yes, and dense | one per block | yes |

Whichever format wins, its bits are also its weakness. Timestamp, worker and sequence are all decodable from a raw Snowflake, so two order IDs a day apart reveal daily volume, and consecutive IDs are trivially enumerable. That is why the **Public API boundary** carries a separate, opaque identifier rather than the raw value: the property that makes an ID cheap to sort by is the same property that makes it readable by anyone who receives it.

#### Where it breaks
| Layer | Failure | How the design handles it |
|---|---|---|
| Clock | Wall clock steps backward on NTP correction, live migration, or an unsmeared leap second | The guard halts issuance the moment `now < last_ts`, alerts, and rejoins only once real time passes it again |
| Process | A crash and restart loses `last_ts` from memory right after a rewind | The persisted watermark, reserved ten seconds forward, makes the restart sleep rather than reissue |
| Sequence | More than 4,096 IDs requested within one millisecond on one worker | The generator spins until the clock ticks over, turning the overflow into a microsecond stall rather than a duplicate |
| Worker id | Two processes end up holding the same slot | An exclusive create-if-absent lease, or better, an orchestrator ordinal the scheduler itself enforces |
| Lease | A process loses its lease silently through a pause or a partition, past its TTL | A background watcher kills issuance on observed lease loss; the window is narrowed to its poll interval, not closed |
| Deploy | A rolling deploy briefly holds more concurrent slots than the steady-state fleet size | The lease is released explicitly on SIGTERM rather than left to expire, and the free-slot gauge is alarmed directly |
| Boundary | A raw ID reaching an external party leaks creation time, worker and volume | A separate opaque identifier is issued at any boundary a customer or partner can see |

#### What this design does not solve
**Halting on a clock rewind is a real availability hole, and every alternative spends something else.** A five-second NTP step means that one node issues nothing for five seconds, a partial outage behind a load balancer and potentially a fleet-wide one during a shared time event. Deriving the timestamp from a monotonic base avoids most rewinds but lets the decoded value drift a few seconds a day from true UTC. Spending a sequence bit as a rewind-generation counter keeps issuance alive through a rewind at the cost of halving the per-millisecond ceiling and breaking strict ordering across the boundary. There is no version of this that keeps issuing correctly through an arbitrary backwards step; the actual mitigations are making the event rare and loud, a smearing time source, hardware clock synchronisation where available, and the forward watermark for restarts.

**The worker-id lease is checked once, at boot, and never again, so exclusivity is asserted rather than continuously enforced.** A generator that silently loses its lease, through a long pause or a partition to the lease store, keeps issuing under a worker id that may already belong to someone else. Fencing it properly would mean consulting something outside the process before every issue, which destroys the entire property this design exists to provide. A background watcher narrows the exposure window; it does not close it, because the watcher itself is asynchronous.

**These IDs leak information by construction, and removing the leak removes the property they were built for.** Timestamp, worker and sequence are all recoverable from the integer, so anyone holding two IDs a day apart can read off approximate daily volume. Hashing the value at a boundary destroys the ordering that makes cursor pagination work, so a hashed external identifier needs a separate sort field to replace what it lost. Carrying two identifiers per row, one internal and one opaque, is what actually happens in practice, and it introduces a recurring class of bug where the wrong one gets logged, returned, or joined on.

#### Final design
Read it back through the numbers. The 12-bit sequence field, 4,096 per millisecond per worker, is what makes local generation fast enough that no request ever needs to wait on another machine. The 10-bit worker field, 1,024 slots, is what makes the one coordinated step, the boot-time claim, cheap enough to do once and never repeat. The 41-bit timestamp, sitting in the high bits, is what turns a random-looking integer into something that sorts by creation time for free. And the 320GB gap between a 64-bit and a 128-bit key at ten billion rows is the number that decides, before any of the clock complexity is even relevant, whether this design is worth its cost at all.

[The whole design](/diagram/unique-id-generator?focus=ntp,clock,orchestrator,lease-store,caller,guard,sequence,pack,worker-id-holder,boundary,watermark,sinks,metrics)

> **The numbers to remember.** 1024 worker slots, 4,096 IDs/ms/worker, ~4.1M/s ceiling · ~69.7 years of runway from a custom epoch · ~320GB extra index at 10¹⁰ rows for a 128-bit key · one fsync per ~10s instead of per ID · a unique constraint on the sink is the only real duplicate detector.

#### Check your understanding
**Why does this design put the timestamp in the high bits rather than the worker id or sequence?** Sorting the packed integers as ordinary numbers then sorts them by creation time, since the highest-order bits dominate comparison. That keeps new rows landing at the right edge of a B-tree index instead of scattering inserts across it.

**A VM is live-migrated and its clock jumps back three seconds. What stops it from reissuing IDs?** The guard compares every new timestamp against the last one this process used and halts the moment `now < last_ts`. It refuses to issue anything until real time genuinely passes its previous high-water mark, so it never overlaps its own earlier output.

**Why can the generator not simply fsync `last_ts` to disk on every call?** An fsync costs tens to hundreds of microseconds, and a busy worker issues up to 4 million IDs a second. Persisting on every call would turn the one part of this design with no external dependency into its slowest step by several orders of magnitude.

**Why does an orchestrator ordinal beat a lease from a coordination service, when both give a worker id?** A scheduler enforces exclusivity continuously, including during a network partition to any external service, while a lease is only checked once at boot and expires on a timer that a paused or partitioned process cannot itself observe.

**Why can this ID never be shown to an external customer or partner, even though nothing about it is secret?** Timestamp, worker and sequence are all decodable from the raw integer, so consecutive IDs are enumerable and two IDs a day apart reveal approximate volume. The bits that make it cheap to sort by are exactly the bits that make it readable by anyone who receives it.
### 5. Design a URL Shortener (TinyURL, bit.ly)
#### Understanding the problem
A URL shortener takes a long link, hands back a short one, and redirects every future click on that short one to the original. Creation happens rarely. Redirecting happens constantly, on the same handful of bytes, forever.

Three things make that worth designing carefully rather than just building.

First, the mapping from short code to long URL never changes and reads identically for every single person who clicks it. That is a rare property, and it is the one fact the whole design leans on.

Second, the short code is time-ordered by construction if it comes from a simple counter, which quietly turns every write into a hotspot the moment you try to shard the table.

Third, once a code is public, someone can be handed the short link without ever being handed the long one, which turns "how guessable is this code" from a curiosity into a product or security decision.

> **What this is not.** The closest question is a unique ID generator, and this design consumes one rather than building its own. Say once that the code comes from a coordination-free generator, base62-encoded, with no collision check, and move on: that question is entirely inside the generator, this one starts after the code already exists. There is also an inversion worth naming. A generator's ids are internal, so being decodable and enumerable costs nothing. Here the code is handed to the public, so enumerability becomes exactly the kind of decision the generator question never had to make.

#### Requirements and the numbers
**Functional.** Shorten a URL, redirect a code, support a custom alias, support expiry, report basic click analytics.

**Non-functional.** Redirect p99 under 100ms. 99.99% availability on the redirect path specifically. Reads outweigh writes by roughly 100 to 1.

The whole design is decided by four numbers, so derive them before drawing anything.

**How many writes a day, and what does that average to?** 100M shortens a day ÷ 86,400s ≈ **~1.2k creates/s**, comparable to a top-tier public shortener.

**How many reads does that imply, given the ratio?** Each link averages 100 clicks over its life, so 1.2k × 100 = **~120k reads/s steady**, with diurnal concentration and the occasional simultaneously viral link pushing peak to roughly **~1M/s**.

**How much of that traffic actually reaches your servers, once caching does its job?** At a 95% CDN hit rate, origin sees 0.05 × 120k ≈ **~6k reads/s**. A memory cache in front of the backing store then serves about 99% of those, leaving 0.01 × 6k ≈ **~60 reads/s** hitting the alias store in steady state. That number, not the 120k it started from, is the one the whole architecture is built around.

**How much of the alias space does ten years of writes actually use?** Seven base62 characters gives `62^7 ≈ 3.5 × 10¹²` codes. A decade of creation at 100M/day is `100M × 365 × 10 ≈ 3.65 × 10¹¹` rows, about **10% of the space**, so there is ample headroom before an eighth character is ever needed.

> **The numbers to carry.** ~1.2k writes/s · ~120k reads/s steady, ~1M/s peak · ~6k/s at origin, ~60/s at the alias store · 3.5 trillion codes, ~10% used after ten years.

#### Two paths, one cacheable and one not
Split this into what can be cached to the edge and what cannot. **The redirect**: given a code, return the same bytes to everyone, forever, until someone explicitly changes them. This is the part that scales by disappearing from your servers entirely. **The click**: a record of who clicked, when, and from where. This is the part that has to be durable and analysable, and it must never be allowed to slow the redirect down.

The entities:

- **Alias**: the short code, mapped one-to-one to a long URL, immutable once created.
- **Redirect response**: the actual `Location` header and status code returned for an alias, byte-identical for every reader.
- **Click event**: `(alias, ts, country, referrer)`, written asynchronously, never on the request path.
- **Deletion marker**: a `deleted_at` timestamp, distinguishing "removed" (410) from "never existed" (404).

The two calls that matter are asymmetric on purpose:

```
POST /shorten
  body: { long_url, custom_alias?, ttl_sec? }
  -> { short_url, alias, expires_at }

GET /{alias}
  -> 302 Found, Location: <long_url>, Cache-Control: public, max-age=60
  -> 410 Gone if deleted_at is set
```

#### High-level design
Follow the numbered arrows. The redirect path is the one worth drawing carefully; the create path is a single insert.

[The hot path, a click resolving to a redirect](/diagram/url-shortener?focus=clicker,cdn,coalesce,resolve,cache,alias-store,emit,e6,e7,e8,e9,e10,e11,e14)

1. A **Clicker** requests `GET /{alias}`, and the **CDN edge** answers directly from cache for roughly 95% of all clicks, in around 10ms.
2. On a miss, the request reaches the **Single-flight gate**, which collapses simultaneous requests for the same alias into one in-flight lookup rather than issuing one per request.
3. **Resolve and redirect** checks the **In-memory cache** first, satisfying about 99% of what reaches it.
4. On a cache miss it falls through to the **Alias store**, the rare path, seeing only about 60 reads a second in steady state.
5. The answer flows back out, warming the memory cache on the way, while the **Click emitter** fires a click event off to the side without the redirect ever waiting on it.

> **Why the flow is shaped this way.** Every layer exists to stop a request before it reaches the next one. Writes are rare enough to afford a store hit every time; reads are hot enough that the system is built to terminate as early as possible, and analytics are split off asynchronously so a click log can never slow down a redirect.

#### Terminating the read as early as possible
Three caching layers sit between a click and the alias store. What does each one actually buy, and where does the arithmetic in the requirements section come from?

[The three layers, and the two fallback paths between them](/diagram/url-shortener?focus=cdn,cache,alias-store,e7,e8,e10,e11)

**Bad: serve every redirect from the origin database.** Correct, and it puts 120k reads a second, all for a static, unchanging answer, directly on a store that also has to absorb writes.

**Good: put a cache in front of the store.** A single memory cache tier catches the overwhelming majority of repeat lookups, and it is cheap because the working set is small: clicks concentrate on recent links, so roughly three days of creations, about 300MB of aliases at 250 bytes each, covers most of the traffic.

**Great: cache the response itself at the network edge, not just the data behind it.** The redirect for a given alias is byte-identical for every user on earth, which is the rare property that makes full edge caching possible at all. A 302 is not cacheable by default, so it must carry explicit freshness, `Cache-Control: public, max-age=60`. That single number does three jobs at once: it bounds origin load, since a link taking 100k requests a second across 200 points of presence generates at most 200 origin fetches a minute; it sets the granularity of click counting, since repeat clicks inside the window never reach origin and have to be recovered from CDN logs instead; and it caps how fast a takedown can propagate on its own, without an explicit purge.

Worked example. At 120k reads/s steady, a 95% CDN hit rate leaves 6k/s reaching the app tier. A 99% hit rate in the memory cache behind it leaves 60/s reaching the alias store. Two cache layers, each imperfect on its own, compound into a store that sees four orders of magnitude less traffic than the edge does, which is the entire reason the alias store can be a modestly sized, hash-partitioned cluster rather than the centre of the design.

[The redirect path terminating at each of the three layers](/diagram/url-shortener?focus=clicker,cdn,coalesce,resolve,cache,alias-store,e7,e8,e9,e10,e11)

#### A herd that coalesces, and a herd that can't
A link going from zero to 100,000 requests a second in two minutes hits every layer above at once, before any of them have a copy. What happens to the store during that first wave, and does the same fix work for every kind of miss?

[Where a stampede of identical requests gets collapsed to one](/diagram/url-shortener?focus=coalesce,resolve,cache,e8,e9,e10)

**Bad: let every miss issue its own read.** A hundred thousand simultaneous requests for one uncached alias produce a hundred thousand identical point queries against the same row, in the same second, on the same store partition.

**Good: coalesce identical requests at each app server.** The **Single-flight gate** keeps a map of alias to in-flight lookup; a request that finds one already running waits on its result instead of starting a new one. Across two hundred app servers that turns a hundred thousand reads into two hundred, one per server rather than one per request.

**Great: coalesce, and separately protect against requests that can never coalesce.** Single-flight only helps when many requests share one key. An enumeration scan walking the alias space produces a stream of distinct, guaranteed-nonexistent codes, each one a unique cache miss with nothing to coalesce against, and it lands directly on the store regardless. The fix for that case is different: a negative cache, a short-lived tombstone recorded for a code that does not exist, plus rate-limiting 404 responses per source IP at the edge. The negative TTL has to stay well below the positive one, or a code that gets probed moments before its real owner creates it will 404 for its own creator.

Layer a probabilistic early refresh on top of the positive cache, where an entry inside the last tenth of its TTL is refreshed by exactly one request while the rest keep serving the old value. Without it, the hottest keys resynchronise their expiry and recreate a smaller version of the same herd every sixty seconds.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 300" role="img" aria-label="A hundred thousand requests for one hot alias collapse to one read per app server through single-flight; a hundred thousand distinct enumeration probes do not, because there is nothing shared to coalesce">
  <style>
    .acc{stroke:var(--accent)}
    .miss{fill:currentColor;opacity:.3}
    .hit{fill:var(--accent)}
    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    .sub{fill:currentColor;opacity:.8;font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
```

#### A promise you cannot take back
Deletion has to reach every copy of a redirect for a takedown to actually work, and this design keeps copies in at least four different places, each with its own idea of how long it holds on.

[Where a deletion has to reach, and how fast it can](/diagram/url-shortener?focus=cdn,takedown,alias-store,e19,e20)

**Bad: rely on cache expiry alone.** Origin deletion is instant, but the CDN edge holds its copy for up to its TTL, and a browser that cached a permanent redirect holds it until the browser decides otherwise, which can mean indefinitely.

**Good: choose a short-lived redirect so nothing is ever cached for long.** A 302 with a sixty-second `max-age` bounds the edge's staleness to a minute, which is fast enough for most takedowns and keeps origin able to count clicks it would otherwise never see.

**Great: pair the short TTL with an explicit purge for anything time-critical.** **Takedown control** flips `deleted_at` at origin immediately, so the alias store and the app tier agree the link is gone within milliseconds, and it issues an explicit CDN purge that propagates across points of presence in seconds rather than waiting out the TTL. After deletion the alias answers 410 Gone, not 404, so a crawler or client can tell "deliberately removed" from "never existed".

The choice between 301 and 302 is really this same trade-off, stated once at creation time instead of once per takedown. A 301 lets the browser skip asking again entirely, which is the cheapest possible answer for a link that will never change and where nobody is paying for click data. It also means that browser can never be reached again by any mechanism this design controls: the redirect it cached is unreachable, permanently, the moment the destination needs to change. A 302 keeps every client re-checking on a short cycle, at the cost of that cycle's worth of continuous edge traffic, in exchange for keeping the ability to retract or redirect the link at all.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 388 179" role="img" aria-label="A deletion reaches four layers at different speeds: origin instantly, the memory cache on the same write, the CDN edge within its TTL or an explicit purge, and a browser holding a 301 not at all">

    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}

  <rect class="fast" x="140" y="8" width="30" height="22"/><text class="lbl" x="8" y="24">Origin</text><text class="sub" x="178" y="24">instant</text>
  <rect class="fast" x="140" y="42" width="38" height="22"/><text class="lbl" x="8" y="58">Memory cache</text><text class="sub" x="186" y="58">same write</text>
  <rect class="slow" x="140" y="76" width="150" height="22"/><text class="lbl" x="8" y="92">CDN edge</text>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="112">purge: seconds, else up to 60s TTL</text>
  <rect class="stuck" x="140" y="132" width="240" height="22"/><text class="lbl" x="8" y="148">Browser, 301 cached</text>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="168">not reachable at all, ever</text>
</svg>
```

#### Why every insert cannot land on one partition
Codes minted from a simple increasing generator sort by creation time. That sortability is what makes them cheap to encode, and it is also what breaks the most obvious way to shard the table that stores them.

[Where the write lands, and why it cannot be range-partitioned](/diagram/url-shortener?focus=write-api,alias-store,e4)

**Bad: partition the alias store by alphabetical or numeric range of the code.** Time-ordered codes mean every alias created this second sorts adjacent to every alias created the second before. A range partition scheme puts the entire write rate on whichever partition currently holds the newest range, and every other partition sits idle for writes.

**Good: notice the hotspot before it appears in production, not after.** Range partitioning is the natural first instinct for a key that already sorts usefully, which makes this an easy trap: it looks like exactly the property that should make sharding easy.

**Great: partition by `hash(alias)` instead.** Hashing scatters consecutive, time-adjacent codes uniformly across partitions, so a thousand creates a second spread across every shard rather than concentrating on one. The cost is that the store can no longer answer a cheap range scan, "give me every alias created this hour", but this workload never needed one: every read is an exact-match lookup by code.

At 1.2k writes/s spread across a partitioned cluster, no single partition sees more than a small fraction of create traffic, and the design-time choice costs nothing once made. Made the other way, it is expensive to undo, because undoing it means re-partitioning a table that is also serving 60 reads/s of live traffic.

#### How short is short enough
A public short code trades length for convenience. What does its length actually protect against, and when does that protection stop being enough?

[Where the code is minted, and what governs its length](/diagram/url-shortener?focus=write-api,alias-store,e1,e4)

**Bad: assume seven characters is short enough to be safe as well as convenient.** Seven base62 characters is `log2(62^7) ≈ 41.7` bits of space. At 10% occupancy after a decade of writes, roughly one random guess in ten resolves to a real link, which is a distributed scanner's dream rather than a meaningful barrier.

**Good: rate-limit and monitor the guessing rather than the guess itself.** Per-IP 404 rate limiting slows a scanner down and raises its cost, and a spike in 404s is a useful detection signal. It does not change the underlying arithmetic: the space is still walkable, just more slowly.

**Great: separate "short and convenient" from "long and effectively secret" as two different tiers.** A public marketing link wants seven characters and nothing more; a shared document or an invite link wants to function as a capability, unguessable rather than merely inconvenient to guess. A sixteen-character random code gives roughly 95 bits, large enough that scanning it is not a realistic strategy at any traffic volume this design will ever see.

Worked example. At 10% occupancy, an attacker sweeping the seven-character space at a modest rate finds a working code roughly every tenth attempt, cheap enough to run continuously. The same sweep against a sixteen-character space would need to enumerate a meaningful fraction of `2^95` codes before finding one, which is not a difference of degree, it is the difference between "public" and "actually private". Counter-derived codes make this worse in a way length cannot fix: knowing one code tells you roughly where its neighbours in time sit, so the walk does not even need to be random.

#### Where it breaks
| Layer | Failure | How the design handles it |
|---|---|---|
| Cold viral link | A hundred thousand identical requests for one uncached alias arrive together | Single-flight coalescing collapses them to one read per app server; probabilistic early refresh stops the herd reforming at each TTL boundary |
| Enumeration scan | A stream of distinct nonexistent codes, nothing for coalescing to share | Negative caching with a short TTL, plus per-IP 404 rate limiting at the edge |
| Write path | A centralised counter caps out and becomes a single point of failure | A coordination-free generator, or a leased block of ids, cuts counter traffic by orders of magnitude |
| Partitioning | Time-ordered codes concentrate every insert on one partition under range sharding | Partition on `hash(alias)`, chosen before the first row is written |
| Takedown | A phishing link keeps resolving after the destination is flagged | Origin deletion is instant; an explicit CDN purge propagates in seconds rather than waiting out the TTL; 410 replaces 404 |
| Analytics | A synchronous click write at peak load would serialise behind the redirect | Fire-and-forget onto a durable log; the redirect never waits, and the pipeline is allowed to degrade independently |
| Custom alias | Users squat on short, valuable, or trademarked paths | A reserved-word list, required authentication for custom aliases, and per-account rate limits |

#### What this design does not solve
**Deletion is best-effort, and no version of this design makes it otherwise.** A purge reaches the CDN in seconds and origin answers 410 immediately, but a browser holding a cached permanent redirect will not ask again until it decides to, and there is no protocol mechanism reaching into that cache. This is the real argument for defaulting to a short-lived redirect rather than a permanent one: it is the cost of retaining the ability to retract at all. Even a perfect purge only removes the redirect; anything that already copied the destination, a link preview, an archive crawler, keeps its own record regardless.

**Click counts are approximate, and the design cannot state the error bar.** Fire-and-forget delivery means a broker outage silently loses whatever a local buffer cannot hold. Edge-served clicks are recovered from CDN logs on a vendor-controlled delay and sampling policy, not counted directly. Bots, link unfurlers, and security scanners all fetch a link without a human ever seeing it, inflating counts by an amount that varies by referrer and cannot be fully filtered. Any customer billing on exact click counts needs a separate, reconciled counting path this design does not provide.

**A seven-character code is public by construction, and length alone cannot make it private.** Rate limiting a scanner raises the cost of walking the space; it does not close the space. The honest fix, a longer random tier for links meant to function as a capability, is a different product decision made at creation time, not a property that emerges from this architecture on its own.

#### Final design
Read it back through the numbers.
