The gap between 120k reads a second at the edge and 60 reads a second at the alias store, four orders of magnitude, is what makes the store a small, unremarkable piece of infrastructure rather than the centre of the design. The 3.5 trillion codes available at seven characters, only 10% used after a decade, is what makes collision-free base62 encoding the right default and what makes a longer capability tier a deliberate addition rather than a forced one. And the choice between a 60-second TTL and a permanent redirect is the single knob that decides whether this system can ever take back something it has already handed out.

[The whole design](/diagram/url-shortener?focus=creator,write-api,takedown,cache,alias-store,cold-archive,clicker,cdn,coalesce,resolve,emit,kafka,cdn-logs,warehouse)

> **The numbers to remember.** ~1.2k writes/s, ~120k reads/s steady, ~1M/s peak · 95% CDN hit, then 99% memory-cache hit, leaving ~60/s at the store · 3.5 trillion codes at seven characters, ~10% used after ten years · a purge propagates in seconds, a browser's cached 301 does not propagate at all.

#### Check your understanding
**Why does the alias store see only about 60 reads a second when the edge sees 120,000?** Two cache layers compound: a 95% CDN hit rate leaves 6,000 a second reaching the app tier, and a 99% memory-cache hit rate behind that leaves roughly 60 a second reaching the store, four orders of magnitude below where the traffic started.

**A link goes from zero to 100,000 requests a second in two minutes. What actually protects the store?** Single-flight coalescing collapses simultaneous requests for the same code into one in-flight lookup per app server, turning a hundred thousand identical reads into roughly one per server rather than one per request.

**Why does that same coalescing do nothing against an enumeration scan?** Coalescing only helps when many requests share one key. A scan produces a stream of distinct, nonexistent codes with nothing in common to share an in-flight slot, so it needs a different mechanism entirely: a negative cache plus per-IP rate limiting.

**Why can codes minted from a simple increasing counter not be range-partitioned?** They sort by creation time, so every code minted this second sits adjacent to every code minted the second before. Range partitioning would put the entire write rate onto whichever partition currently holds the newest range.

**Why is a 302 with a short TTL usually the safer default over a 301, even though it costs more traffic?** A 301 is cached by the browser indefinitely, so once handed out, that copy is permanently unreachable by anything this design controls. A 302 with a short `max-age` keeps every client re-checking on a bounded cycle, preserving the ability to retract or redirect the link later.
### 6. Design a Web Crawler
#### Understanding the problem
A web crawler starts from a handful of seed URLs, fetches each page, extracts its links, and feeds them back in so the crawl keeps expanding on its own. The output is a corpus for a search index, an archive, or a training set.

Downloading a page is easy. Three things make the rest of it a real design problem.

First, the graph of discoverable URLs is unbounded, and the fetch budget never is. A crawler is really a scheduler deciding which sliver of billions of known URLs a fixed rate of fetches gets spent on.

Second, "what is most worth fetching" and "which host am I currently allowed to touch" are two completely different questions, and the URLs that score highest on the first are usually on hosts that just got hit and are on the second's cooldown.

Third, some sites generate URLs without limit, a calendar page that emits a new address for every date into the far future, and none of them are actually duplicates, so ordinary deduplication cannot see the problem at all.

> **What this is not.** The closest question is a web search engine, and the boundary between them is worth stating precisely. A search engine takes a corpus as given and spends its budget at query time, ranking and serving in tens of milliseconds where every extra millisecond is visible to a user. Nothing in a crawler is latency sensitive: a fetch taking five seconds is fine, and the only clock that matters is a per-host cooldown measured in seconds. The corpus a search engine treats as an input is this design's entire output, and the two fail in opposite directions. A bad ranker returns bad results that can be measured and tested. A bad crawler silently omits pages, and because nothing was fetched, there is no record to compare against, which is why this design's honest gaps are all about loss nobody can observe.

#### Requirements and the numbers
**Functional.** Seed URLs, fetch, parse, extract links, enqueue, store. Respect `robots.txt`. Deduplicate both URLs and near-duplicate content.

**Non-functional.** Billions of pages. Per-domain politeness. Resumable after a crash. Extensible to new content types.

The whole design is decided by four numbers, so derive them before drawing anything.

**How many fetches a second does the target volume actually need?** 1 billion pages a month ÷ (30 × 86,400s) ≈ **~400 fetches/s average**, with catch-up windows pushing peak to roughly **~2,000/s**.

**How much of the known graph does that budget actually cover?** Roughly 10 billion URLs are known and held in active rotation. At 1B fetches a month against that, the crawl touches **under 10% of what it already knows about**, before counting the 50 to 500 billion URLs discoverable but not yet admitted. Admission order, not fetch speed, is the entire product.

**What does remembering every seen URL cost, exactly versus approximately?** An exact index over 10¹⁰ keys runs to roughly 240GB. A Bloom filter, a compact structure that answers "definitely not seen" or "probably seen" from a fixed bit array, needs about 10 bits per key at a 1% false-positive rate: 10¹⁰ × 10 bits ≈ **~12GB**, twenty times smaller, in exchange for occasionally saying "seen" to a URL that was never fetched.

**How much state does politeness itself require?** Roughly 10⁸ registrable domains are in active rotation, each needing a next-allowed-fetch timestamp and cached robots rules, about 2KB per domain. 10⁸ × 2KB ≈ **~200GB**, nearly all of it cold, with only currently-ready hosts needing to sit in memory.

> **The numbers to carry.** ~400 fetches/s average, ~2k/s peak · under 10% of ~10B known URLs actually fetched per month · ~12GB Bloom filter vs ~240GB exact index · ~200GB of politeness state across ~10⁸ domains.

#### Two questions the frontier has to answer
Everything downstream of "what to fetch next" is comparatively simple. That one decision splits into two sub-problems that share no data and pull in different directions.

- **Value**: which URL, of everything currently admitted, is worth fetching soonest. Built from domain authority, observed change rate, and how overdue a revisit is.
- **Availability**: which host, of everything currently admitted, am I allowed to touch right now. Built from a per-host cooldown and cached robots rules.

The entities:

- **URL**: normalised to a canonical form before anything else touches it, so the same page under two spellings dedupes correctly.
- **Frontier**: the two-tier structure holding every admitted URL, split into value order and host order.
- **Lease**: the contract between frontier and worker, a URL hidden for a bounded window rather than removed, so a crash never loses it.
- **Seen index**: the Bloom filter plus its exact backing store, answering whether a URL has already been admitted.

The interface is a job submission, not a per-page request:

```
enqueue(url, priority, depth)
get_status(crawl_id) -> {pages_done, errors, last_url}
```

#### High-level design
Follow the numbered arrows. This is a loop, not a pipeline with an end: the last step feeds the first.

[The crawl loop, one cycle](/diagram/web-crawler?focus=kafka,p-dedup,p-router,front-queues,back-queues,p-fetch,web,p-parse,p-normalise,object-store,e1,e8,e9,e11,e12,e15,e18,e20)

1. A discovered URL arrives on the **Kafka discovery bus**, partitioned so every URL lands on the shard that owns its domain, and passes through the **Seen check**.
2. Survivors reach the **Priority router**, which scores the URL and drops it into one of the **Front queues**, ten priority bands rather than a strict total order.
3. When a host's **Back queues** entry drains, it is refilled by pulling the next unassigned host from a front queue, so routing happens once per host rather than once per URL.
4. A worker picks up whichever back queue is off cooldown, leasing the URL, and **Fetch** issues the HTTP request against **The web**.
5. **Parse + extract** pulls text and outbound links from the response, **URL normalise** canonicalises each link, and the survivors go straight back onto the discovery bus, closing the loop.
6. The page itself lands in the **Page archive**, and only then is the lease acknowledged.

> **Why the flow is shaped this way.** The expensive part was never downloading; it is deciding what to fetch without duplicating work, getting banned, or falling into an infinite trap. That is why dedup, politeness and trap detection sit in the middle of the loop rather than being bolted onto its edges.

#### Two structures pretending to be one frontier
A single priority queue looks like the obvious way to decide what to fetch next. Why does this design insist on two separate structures instead?

[Front queues for value, back queues for politeness, meeting once per host](/diagram/web-crawler?focus=front-queues,back-queues,p-router,e8,e9)

**Bad: one priority queue, with a politeness check at the head.** High-value URLs concentrate on high-value hosts, and those are precisely the hosts most recently fetched from, so they are also the ones on cooldown. A single queue spends its time rejecting its own best candidates, and the crawler idles while holding a hundred million ready URLs.

**Good: separate the two concerns into two structures, checked independently.** A value-ordered structure decides what matters; a per-host structure decides what is currently allowed. That removes the rejection loop, but naively re-checking politeness at read time still means a worker can pick a URL only to discover its host is unavailable.

**Great: make politeness a property of storage, not a check.** Front queues, roughly ten priority bands rather than a total order, carry value. Back queues, one per host under the invariant that a host lives in exactly one queue, carry politeness. A worker only ever looks at back queues whose next-allowed time has passed, so any queue the scheduler can see is, by construction, one it is allowed to fetch from. Bands rather than a strict order matter here too: forcing a change-rate estimate and a domain-authority score onto one comparable scale hides the weights, and ten bands only need each score to be right to one significant figure, which is all those estimates are worth.

Worked example. A top-band URL sitting behind 40,000 other queued URLs on its own host, paced at one request a second, waits roughly 40,000 seconds, over eleven hours, whatever its score says. Priority in this design governs which hosts get admitted, not the order URLs are fetched within a host. A URL that genuinely must be fetched sooner needs a separate express path spending part of that host's own rate budget directly, capped so it cannot quietly become the whole crawl.

[Two-tier frontier: front queues for value, back queues for politeness](/diagram/web-crawler?figure=frontier)

#### A lease, not a dequeue
A worker that crashes mid-fetch cannot be allowed to lose the URL it was holding, and it cannot be allowed to duplicate the page if it merely appeared slow. What contract makes both true at once?

[Where a URL is held between the frontier and a worker](/diagram/web-crawler?focus=back-queues,p-fetch,p-fingerprint,e11,e22)

**Bad: dequeue the URL outright when a worker picks it up.** A crash between dequeue and completion loses the URL permanently, with nothing left to retry it.

**Good: hide the URL for a bounded window instead of removing it, and make it reappear if nobody confirms completion.** That recovers from a crash, but if the confirmation fires the moment the page is fetched, a crash between fetch and storage leaves a URL marked done with no page behind it, and nothing downstream will ever notice.

**Great: acknowledge only after the page is committed to storage, and key retry state to the host rather than the URL.** The lease window, sixty seconds against a ten-second fetch timeout, gives a worker room to fetch, parse and write before anything reclaims the URL. Tying retry state to the host matters too: a host returning errors to the whole fleet would otherwise pull every worker back on an identical schedule. Because retry state lives per host, a retry re-enters that host's own back queue and inherits its own cooldown, jittered so retries do not resynchronise.

This is also why restart and ordinary retry share one code path. Everything unacknowledged when a shard crashes simply reappears once its lease expires, exercised continuously rather than only during an incident.

[The full state machine a URL moves through](/diagram/web-crawler?focus=back-queues,p-fetch,p-parse,p-fingerprint,object-store,e11,e15,e20,e22)

[URL lifecycle: lease, retry, and dead-letter](/diagram/web-crawler?figure=lifecycle)

#### Catching a duplicate without remembering every URL
Ten billion URLs are too many to hold in an exact set cheaply. What does a crawler give up by remembering approximately instead, and where does that cost actually land?

[Where a discovered link is checked against everything seen before](/diagram/web-crawler?focus=p-dedup,seen,e2)

**Bad: an exact index of every seen URL.** Correct by definition, and roughly 240GB at this scale, which is affordable but wasteful for a check that runs on every single extracted link.

**Good: a Bloom filter, a fixed bit array where adding a URL flips a handful of bits and checking one asks whether those bits are all set.** At about 12GB for ten billion keys, it is twenty times smaller, and it can never produce a false negative: a URL it says "not seen" genuinely has not been seen. Its cost is a roughly 1% false-positive rate, saying "seen" for a URL that never actually was.

**Great: decide, deliberately, what to do about that 1%, rather than treating the filter as free.** A false positive means a genuinely new URL is silently never fetched, indistinguishable from one that simply does not exist. Confirming every positive against an exact backing store closes the gap, but on a mature crawl most extracted links are already known, so confirming every positive means a disk read on most checks, the exact read amplification the filter was bought to avoid. The practical answer confirms positives only from the highest-priority pages, and accepts the loss elsewhere.

Worked example. A page carries 300 outbound links; roughly three, at a 1% false-positive rate, are new URLs the filter wrongly calls "seen". Link-graph redundancy is the usual defence: a page reachable from three independent inbound links survives with probability `1 - 0.01^3`, about one in a million odds of total loss. That argument fails exactly where the loss matters. Popular, well-linked pages would have been found anyway; the pages actually lost are the singly-linked, long-tail content the crawl exists to find.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 220" role="img" aria-label="A Bloom filter bit array: adding a URL sets a few bits from independent hashes; checking a new URL that happens to hash onto bits already set by other URLs produces a false positive">
  <style>
    .cell{fill:none;stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.4;stroke-width:1.2}
    .set{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.3;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.4}
    .hit{fill:currentColor;fill-opacity:.15;stroke:currentColor;stroke-width:1.4}
    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    .sub{fill:currentColor;opacity:.8;font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
  </style>
  <text class="lbl" x="8" y="16">bit array, one row of a much larger structure</text>
  <g transform="translate(15,30)">
    <rect class="cell" x="0" y="0" width="24" height="30"/><rect class="cell" x="24" y="0" width="24" height="30"/><rect class="set" x="48" y="0" width="24" height="30"/><rect class="cell" x="72" y="0" width="24" height="30"/><rect class="set" x="96" y="0" width="24" height="30"/>
    <rect class="cell" x="120" y="0" width="24" height="30"/><rect class="set" x="144" y="0" width="24" height="30"/><rect class="cell" x="168" y="0" width="24" height="30"/><rect class="cell" x="192" y="0" width="24" height="30"/><rect class="set" x="216" y="0" width="24" height="30"/>
    <rect class="cell" x="240" y="0" width="24" height="30"/><rect class="cell" x="264" y="0" width="24" height="30"/><rect class="set" x="288" y="0" width="24" height="30"/><rect class="cell" x="312" y="0" width="24" height="30"/><rect class="cell" x="336" y="0" width="24" height="30"/>
  </g>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="80">shaded bits already set by earlier, unrelated URLs</text>
  <g transform="translate(15,92)">
    <rect class="hit" x="48" y="0" width="24" height="30"/><rect class="hit" x="144" y="0" width="24" height="30"/><rect class="hit" x="216" y="0" width="24" height="30"/>
  </g>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="145">a brand-new URL hashes onto three bits already</text>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="160">set: filter reports "seen", the URL is dropped</text>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="185">not a bug: the price of 12GB instead of 240GB</text>
</svg>
```

#### A trap that looks like real content
Some sites generate URLs without limit, one boilerplate page repeated under an endless series of distinct addresses. Neither URL dedup nor content dedup alone can see this, because every generated URL genuinely is new and every generated page genuinely is fetched successfully.

[Where novelty is measured against content, per domain](/diagram/web-crawler?focus=p-trap,robots,e6,e7)

**Bad: trust the URL dedup filter to catch runaway generation.** It cannot. A calendar emitting `/calendar?date=2026-01-01` through `/calendar?date=2099-12-31` produces genuinely distinct, never-before-seen URLs on every fetch, so the Bloom filter correctly says "new" every single time, and the frontier keeps admitting them forever.

**Good: cap crawl depth per domain.** A hard depth limit stops the worst runaway generation, but a shallow trap, many distinct query parameters hanging directly off a shallow path, sails straight past a depth cap untouched.

**Great: track novelty rate against content similarity, per domain, and throttle when they diverge.** A domain where nearly every extracted URL is new, and nearly every fetched page is a near-duplicate by content fingerprint, is a trap by definition: distinct addresses, indistinguishable content. Tracking the two signals together catches what neither catches alone, because a domain that is genuinely prolific has both new URLs and new content, while a trap has only the first.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 415 229" role="img" aria-label="Four domains plotted by URL novelty rate against content fingerprint diversity; only the quadrant with high novelty and low content diversity is a trap">
  <style>
    .axis{stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.45;stroke-width:1.3}
    .trap{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.18;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.4}
    .dot{fill:currentColor}
    .hitdot{fill:var(--accent)}
    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    .sub{fill:currentColor;opacity:.8;font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
  </style>
  <line class="axis" x1="40" y1="200" x2="380" y2="200"/>
  <line class="axis" x1="40" y1="200" x2="40" y2="20"/>
  <text class="sub" x="380" y="218" text-anchor="end">URL novelty rate →</text>
  <text class="sub" x="30" y="20" text-anchor="end" transform="rotate(-90 30 20)">content diversity →</text>
  <rect class="trap" x="220" y="20" width="160" height="65"/>
  <text class="lbl" x="230" y="38">trap: new URLs,</text>
  <text class="lbl" x="230" y="53">same content</text>
  <circle class="hitdot" cx="340" cy="45" r="6"/><text class="sub" x="340" y="65" text-anchor="middle">calendar domain</text>
  <circle class="dot" cx="320" cy="165" r="6"/><text class="sub" x="320" y="185" text-anchor="middle">prolific news site</text>
  <text class="sub" x="320" y="150" text-anchor="middle">high novelty, high diversity: fine</text>
  <circle class="dot" cx="90" cy="165" r="6"/><text class="sub" x="90" y="185" text-anchor="middle">static docs site</text>
  <text class="sub" x="90" y="150" text-anchor="middle">low novelty either way: fine</text>
</svg>
```

The two signals have to combine, because either alone punishes a real, high-value site. A novelty ceiling by itself would also suppress a domain legitimately publishing at high volume. Combined with agreeing content fingerprints, the throttle fires only on the pattern that is actually diagnostic: distinct URLs producing the same page over and over.

#### Sharding by domain, not by URL
The crawler runs across many machines, and the obvious way to split work is by hashing the URL itself. What goes wrong the instant politeness enters the picture?

[Where a discovered link crosses shard ownership](/diagram/web-crawler?focus=kafka,p-dedup,p-normalise,e1,e18)

**Bad: shard by `hash(url)`.** Work spreads perfectly evenly, which looks like the right answer until politeness is added. Every URL on one host scatters across every shard, so keeping one host under its rate limit now requires every shard to agree on that host's cooldown in real time, which turns a local counter into a distributed one.

**Good: shard by domain, and accept that a few very large domains land entirely on one shard.** Politeness state, robots cache, and the seen-set slice for a domain now all sit on the machine that owns it, so no politeness decision needs a lock or a remote read. A handful of mega-domains, a site with hundreds of millions of URLs, do concentrate on a single shard's worth of capacity.

**Great: shard by domain, and sub-shard the rare mega-domain by domain plus path prefix.** Ordinary sharding by `hash(registrable_domain)` handles the overwhelming majority of the graph with zero cross-shard coordination. The rare exception, a domain so large it saturates one shard on its own, is sub-sharded by `hash(domain + path_prefix)`, spreading its URLs across shards while the rate limiter itself stays keyed on the host through one leased token, so the sub-shards cannot exceed the domain's real politeness budget between them.

Worked example. At roughly 300 extracted links per page and 400 pages/s, cross-shard discovery traffic runs 300 × 400 = 120,000 URL messages a second, about 200 bytes each, so 24MB/s fleet-wide, negligible next to the ~40MB/s of page bytes being fetched. That gap is the justification for accepting a small cross-shard hop in exchange for never distributing a rate limit.

#### Where it breaks
| Layer | Failure | How the design handles it |
|---|---|---|
| DNS | Uncached resolution at ~50ms a lookup dominates wall-clock time at scale | An in-process resolver with an hour-scale TTL cache, warm hits sub-microsecond |
| Frontier | A domain returning errors to the whole fleet draws every worker back on the same retry schedule | Retry state lives per host, not per URL, with jittered backoff and a per-host circuit breaker |
| Content | JS-rendered single-page apps return near-empty HTML to a plain fetcher | Escalate selectively to a headless render pool only when extracted text is thin and script density is high, caching the verdict per domain |
| Sharding | A mega-domain saturates the single shard that owns it | Sub-shard by domain plus path prefix, while the rate limiter stays keyed on the host through one leased token |
| Robots | A site declares an unreasonable crawl-delay to discourage crawling | Treat very large values as a deprioritisation signal into the lowest band, not a literal day-long wait |
| Politeness | A slow-answering domain ties up a fetcher slot far longer than its fair share | A ten-second fetch timeout and a per-domain in-flight quota of one bound the damage |
| Dedup | A Bloom false positive silently drops a genuinely new URL | Confirm positives from high-priority pages against the exact index; run a sampled audit that estimates, without repairing, the rest |

#### What this design does not solve
**URL dedup silently drops pages, and the loss is unobservable by construction.** A false positive means a new URL is never fetched, never logged as skipped, and indistinguishable from one that never existed. Link-graph redundancy protects popular, well-linked pages, which the crawl would likely have found anyway; the pages actually lost are the singly-linked, long-tail content the crawl exists to find. Confirming every positive against the exact index fixes correctness but reverses the economics, since most checks on a mature crawl are positives. The honest state is that the seen-set is approximate and the corpus has a hole whose size can only be estimated, not repaired.

**Freshness cannot be measured without spending the very budget it is meant to save.** Observing whether a page changed requires fetching it, the same scarce resource as discovering something new. The change-rate model is therefore trained only on pages already chosen for recrawl, a closed loop: a deprioritised page is sampled rarely, looks unchanged when it finally is, and gets deprioritised further regardless of whether it is actually changing. A small slice of uniformly random recrawls, independent of score, bounds the drift without removing it; there is no honest staleness figure for the long tail the model rarely samples.

**Politeness is contracted with the wrong entity.** The rate limit is keyed on registrable domain, but the party that actually suffers from an impolite crawler is the origin server, and the two do not line up. Thousands of small domains sharing one hosting machine each receive their own full rate, so the machine sees the sum. A large domain behind a well-provisioned CDN could absorb far more than it is given, and gets crawled conservatively for no reason, at a direct cost to coverage of exactly the sites with the most content. The correct grouping key, the origin, is not reliably observable from where the crawler stands.

#### Final design
Read it back through the numbers. Fetching under 10% of a known graph of 10 billion URLs a month is what makes admission order, the frontier, the entire product rather than an optimisation on top of one. The gap between a 12GB Bloom filter and a 240GB exact index makes approximate dedup the only affordable choice, and that same approximation creates the unobservable loss the design cannot close. And 200GB of politeness state spread across a hundred million mostly-cold domains is what makes sharding by domain, rather than by URL, the difference between a local rate limiter and a distributed one.

[The whole design](/diagram/web-crawler?focus=kafka,p-dedup,p-robots,p-trap,p-router,seen,robots,front-queues,back-queues,p-fetch,p-parse,p-normalise,p-fingerprint,web,dns,render,object-store,metadata)

> **The numbers to remember.** ~400 fetches/s average, ~2k/s peak · under 10% of ~10B known URLs fetched monthly · ~12GB Bloom filter vs ~240GB exact index, ~1% false-positive rate · ~200GB politeness state across ~10⁸ domains · ~24MB/s cross-shard traffic against ~40MB/s of page bytes fetched.

#### Check your understanding
**Why can value and politeness not live in one priority queue?** High-value URLs concentrate on high-value hosts, which are also the hosts most recently fetched from and therefore on cooldown. A single queue with a politeness check at the head spends its time rejecting its own best candidates instead of making progress.

**A worker crashes between fetching a page and storing it. What happens to the URL?** Nothing is lost: the URL was leased rather than dequeued, and acknowledgement only fires after the storage write. The lease expires, the URL becomes visible again, and another worker retries it.

**Why does confirming every Bloom filter positive against the exact index defeat the filter's purpose?** On a mature crawl, most extracted links are already known, so most checks are positives. Confirming all of them means a disk read on most checks, which is exactly the cost the filter was built to avoid.

**Why does neither URL dedup nor content dedup alone catch a spider trap?** A trap generates genuinely distinct, never-seen URLs, so URL dedup correctly calls each one new. The pages behind them are also fetched and parsed successfully. Only tracking novelty rate against content similarity together reveals the pattern: many new addresses, one repeated page.

**Why does sharding by URL hash break politeness, even though it balances load perfectly?** A single host's URLs scatter across every shard, so keeping that host under its rate limit needs every shard to agree on its cooldown in real time. Sharding by domain instead keeps all of one host's state on one machine, making politeness a local decision rather than a distributed one.
### 7. Design a Notification System
#### Understanding the problem
A notification system accepts requests from every service in a company and delivers them to users over push, email, SMS and in-app. Whether to notify was already decided by the caller. This system's job is fan-out, delivery and restraint.

Three things make that harder than "call an API and forward the message".

First, a duplicate and a miss are both real failures, but they are not the same failure, and preventing one at every layer without a shared transaction to lean on takes several independent mechanisms.

Second, the providers underneath, Apple, Google, email and SMS relays, fail independently, throttle independently, and have different error vocabularies, so one provider's bad hour must never become every channel's outage.

Third, the volume here is small. The real constraint is not throughput, it is a human being's tolerance for interruption, and a system that delivers reliably and gets muted in settings has failed at its actual purpose.

> **What this is not.** The closest question by name is a stock price notification system, and the two share almost nothing else. There, the entire cost sits in deciding *whether* to notify: matching ten million standing rules against a quarter-million price ticks a second, with delivery reused as a thin dependency. Here the decision arrives with the request; nothing in this system evaluates a predicate. All the difficulty is on the other side, expanding one logical send into one message per user, channel and device, isolating channels, suppressing duplicates a retry would create, and refusing to send what a person does not want right now.

#### Requirements and the numbers
**Functional.** Accept sends from any internal service. Expand to the user's devices and channels. Apply preferences, quiet hours and a per-user cap. Retry per channel. Suppress duplicates. Expose delivery state.

**Non-functional.** 10M sends a day, with headroom for a full-base broadcast. No duplicate for one logical send. A channel outage must not stall the others. High-priority delivery p99 under 30 seconds.

The whole design is decided by four numbers, so derive them before choosing anything.

**How much steady traffic is this, really?** 10⁷ sends ÷ 86,400s ≈ **~120/s average**, rising to roughly **~220/s** across the ten hours a day when most activity happens. Both numbers are small; nothing here is a throughput problem.

**What does sending to the entire user base at once actually generate?** 10M users hold roughly 15M registered devices, so one broadcast call expands to **15M push sends**, about one and a half normal days of traffic arriving in a single instant.

**How fast can that broadcast be sent without breaking the provider?** Smeared over an hour, 15M ÷ 3,600s ≈ **~4,200/s**, plus the ~220/s of ordinary traffic underneath it, for **~4,400/s peak**. A published push ceiling of roughly 10,000/s per account leaves that at 44% of capacity, room enough for transactional sends to keep moving alongside it.

**Can every channel even carry a broadcast?** SMS caps out near 200 messages/s per account: 15M ÷ 200 ≈ 75,000s, **~20.8 hours**. That is not a policy choice, it is arithmetic. Broadcasts run over push and email only.

> **The numbers to carry.** ~120/s average, ~220/s daytime · a broadcast is ~15M sends, ~1.5 days of traffic at once · smeared to ~4,400/s against a ~10k/s push ceiling · SMS cannot carry a broadcast at all, ~20.8 hours to drain one.

#### Fan-out, delivery, and restraint
Three jobs, in the order a message actually passes through them. **Fan-out**: turn one accepted request into one message per user, channel and device. **Delivery**: get each of those messages to a provider, with a retry policy that knows the difference between "try again" and "never will work". **Restraint**: refuse or delay a send a person does not want right now, before it ever reaches a channel queue.

The entities:

- **Notification**: one logical send, identified by a caller-supplied idempotency key.
- **Outbox row**: a pending-publish record written in the same transaction as the notification, closing the gap between "database accepted it" and "queue received it".
- **Per-user gate**: preferences, quiet hours in local time, and a token bucket capping how many notifications one person receives per hour.
- **Delivery attempt**: one call to one provider for one message, classified by response and logged regardless of outcome.

The API accepts a logical send, never a physical one:

```
POST /notify
  body: { user_id | user_segment, template_id, params, channels: [push, email], priority, idempotency_key }
  -> { notification_id, status: queued }

GET /notifications/{id} -> { state, attempts, delivered_at }
```

#### High-level design
Follow the numbered arrows. Everything that can refuse a send happens before a message ever reaches a channel queue.

[The path from an accepted request to a queued, channel-specific message](/diagram/notification-system?focus=accept,gate,fanout,outbox,publisher,push-topic,push-workers,providers,e2,e4,e5,e6,e7,e10,e13)

1. A request lands on **Accept + dedupe**, which checks the caller's idempotency key against the cache before doing anything else.
2. The **Per-user gate** checks preferences, quiet hours and the hourly cap, holding or dropping anything that fails.
3. What survives reaches **Fan-out**, which expands one logical send into one row per user, channel and registered device.
4. Those rows commit alongside an unpublished row in the **Outbox table**, in one transaction, and the **Outbox publisher** moves them onto the **Push topic** and its siblings only after the broker acknowledges.
5. **Push workers** and their channel-specific counterparts drain their own topic independently and call **Providers and devices**.

> **Why the flow is shaped this way.** Every decision that can refuse a send sits above the queues, because a message already in a queue has only one question left: when to send it. Below the queues, each provider has its own limit, error vocabulary and outage schedule, so channel isolation keeps one bad provider from becoming a product-wide incident.

#### Four hops, four kinds of duplicate
There is no single transaction spanning caller, database, queue and provider. What stops a retry, a crash, or a redelivery from sending the same notification twice?

[Where a duplicate can be created, and what catches it at each point](/diagram/notification-system?focus=accept,cache,outbox,publisher,push-workers,providers,e1,e5,e6,e13)

**Bad: trust one mechanism to cover the whole path.** A client-supplied idempotency key stops a caller's own retry, but it says nothing about a crash between a database write and a queue publish, or a worker that dies after calling a provider but before recording that it did.

**Good: add a check at each place a duplicate can originate.** That closes most of the gap, but naively checking-then-writing at any one of these points still leaves a race: two concurrent retries can both miss a cache check and both create a notification.

**Great: name all four hops, and use a conditional write rather than a read-then-write at each one.** Caller to ingestion: a conditional insert on `(caller_id, key) -> notif_id`, so the loser of a race waits for the winner's id rather than creating its own row. Database to queue: the outbox, committing the notification and an unpublished marker in one transaction, so a crash before or after the publish always leaves something to replay. Queue to worker: a `sent:{notif_id}` key written after a successful provider call, narrowing, not closing, the window a redelivery can slip through. Worker to provider: passing the notification's own id as the provider's dedup identifier, so a redelivery that already succeeded is discarded on the provider's side instead of the sender's.

The honest description of the result is at-least-once with duplicate suppression at four hops, which is observably exactly-once and is a different claim from being exactly-once. One hop cannot be covered at all: provider to device. A 200 from APNs means Apple accepted the message, not that a handset received it or a person saw it, and there is no acknowledgement to wait for past that point.

[Four hops, four suppression mechanisms, one gap](/diagram/notification-system?figure=dedup-hops)

#### Whose bad hour becomes everyone's
Push, email and SMS have different rate limits, error codes and outage schedules. What happens if they share one backlog?

[Per-channel topics feeding independent worker pools](/diagram/notification-system?focus=push-topic,email-topic,sms-topic,push-workers,email-workers,sms-workers,e7,e8,e9)

**Bad: one shared queue for every channel.** A message for any channel sits behind every message ahead of it, regardless of channel. When APNs throttles or goes down for thirty minutes, push messages pile up at the head, and email and SMS behind them wait too, even though nothing is wrong with either.

**Good: separate queues per channel, still fed by one publisher.** Independent backlogs stop the head-of-line blocking. What is still shared is worker capacity if pools are not sized independently, so a channel with a slower provider can starve one with a faster one if they compete for the same fleet.

**Great: per-channel queues, each with its own worker pool sized to that provider's published limit.** Push workers stop consuming when APNs errors spike; the push topic simply backs up, safely, on durable retention. Email and SMS workers keep draining their own topics at their own pace, untouched. A circuit breaker per provider trips on sustained error rate and halts that pool alone, which turns a provider outage into a channel outage instead of a system outage.

The cost of this is real operational sprawl: one notification system is, underneath, several channel systems behind a shared front door, each with its own credentials, its own sending reputation, and its own way of signalling trouble. That cost buys the one property that actually matters here, which is that a bad APNs hour never touches a password reset email.

#### Classifying a failure instead of retrying blindly
A provider's response is not a boolean. What goes wrong if every failure gets the same retry treatment?

[The delivery state machine, driven entirely by response class](/diagram/notification-system?focus=push-workers,providers,status-store,e13,e19)

**Bad: retry every failure the same way.** Retrying a permanent failure, a pruned token, a malformed payload, spends the retry budget on something that will never succeed. Giving up on a transient one, a 5xx or a 429, discards a message that would have gone through on the next attempt.

**Good: split responses into retryable and terminal.** That stops the worst waste, but it still treats every retryable failure identically, which misses a provider that is explicitly telling you how long to wait.

**Great: classify by status code and act specifically.** A 429 requeues after the provider's own `Retry-After` interval, in preference to any self-chosen backoff curve, because ignoring the provider's stated wait time only extends the throttle. A 5xx gets jittered exponential backoff up to the attempt budget. A 410 or `UNREGISTERED` marks the message failed and prunes the device token, since retrying a dead token forever wastes every future broadcast too. A 403 marks failed and pages immediately, because an expired certificate silently fails every send on that channel until someone notices.

The retry budget itself has a reason to end: four attempts, roughly thirty seconds, five minutes and an hour apart, then the dead-letter queue. Past about an hour, a notification about something that already happened is worse than none at all, so the correct action stops being "try again" and becomes "record it and let a person look". Every interval is jittered, because an unjittered backoff synchronises: when a provider recovers from an outage, every message queued during it would otherwise retry in the same instant and re-trigger the exact throttle everyone was waiting out.

#### Restraint: the cap that protects the tail
Throughput here is nothing. What actually needs protecting is a person's patience, and averages are the wrong lens for sizing that protection.

[The gate, checked before anything reaches a channel queue](/diagram/notification-system?focus=gate,cache,e3,e4)

**Bad: size the rate limit against the average user.** The average user receives about 0.6 notifications a day, which makes almost any cap look generous and, by the same logic, look unnecessary.

**Good: notice the distribution is not flat.** Notification volume follows the same skew as everything else driven by user activity, so a cap set for the average protects nobody, because the average user was never going to be a problem.

**Great: size the cap against the tail, because the tail is who the limiter exists for.** The p99 user sits above 40 notifications a day, and that user is exactly who disables notifications entirely. A token bucket of five per hour per user, in front of the channel queues, holds anything over the cap and anything inside quiet hours, collapsing the excess into one digest delivered at the next allowed slot, rather than dropping it. Transactional and security categories carry a bypass flag so a two-factor code is never held for a digest.

The bypass flag is also the mechanism's weak point, and it has to be guarded on purpose. Once a category can skip the cap, every team has an incentive to mark its own traffic transactional, and the gate stops protecting anyone once enough traffic bypasses it. The usable rule: treat any category running above roughly 20% bypass volume as evidence its classification has drifted, and review it.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 196" role="img" aria-label="Notification volume per user is heavily skewed: the average user gets under one a day, while the p99 user is above forty; a cap sized for the average protects nobody">
  <style>
    .axis{stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.4;stroke-width:1.3}
    .bar{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.28;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.4}
    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    .sub{fill:currentColor;opacity:.8;font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    text{text-anchor:middle}
  </style>
  <text class="lbl" x="8" y="16" style="text-anchor:start">the cap is sized at the tail, not the median</text>
  <line class="axis" x1="15" y1="160" x2="385" y2="160"/>
  <rect class="bar" x="40" y="150" width="34" height="10"/><text class="sub" x="57" y="180">median: ~0.6/day</text>
  <rect class="bar" x="160" y="120" width="34" height="40"/><text class="sub" x="177" y="180">p90: a few/day</text>
  <rect class="bar" x="280" y="40" width="34" height="120"/><text class="sub" x="297" y="180">p99: 40+/day</text>
</svg>
```

#### The broadcast that could take down its own integration
A "send to everyone" call expands to 15M messages in one instant. Accepted the same way as a normal request, what happens?

[Fan-out and the outbox for a broadcast-scale write](/diagram/notification-system?focus=fanout,outbox,publisher,push-topic,e5,e6,e7)

**Bad: accept a broadcast synchronously, like any other request.** Fan-out hands push workers 15 million messages at once. They push at APNs as fast as the pool allows, APNs answers with 429, workers retry, the throttle persists, and the backlog grows faster than it can drain. The system has taken down its own integration, and the password resets stuck behind the marketing blast are now also delayed.

**Good: route broadcasts through a separate batch path.** That stops the synchronous API from being the trigger, but writing all 15M rows to the outbox at once still produces the same instantaneous spike one step later.

**Great: route through a batch path, and smear the write itself over a window sized to the provider ceiling.** 15M sends over sixty minutes lands at ~4,200/s, well under the ~10,000/s push ceiling, leaving headroom for the ~220/s of ordinary daytime traffic to keep moving underneath it. The window is chosen from the ceiling, not picked round: a thirty-minute smear would run at 8,400/s, 84% of capacity, too tight to also carry transactional sends safely.

Worked example. A batch endpoint that accepts up to 500 device tokens per call, with per-token errors returned in the response body, collapses the request count by 500x for the same message rate, which matters enormously at broadcast volume and not at all at 120/s. SMS is excluded from this path entirely: at its ~200/s ceiling, 15M messages would take nearly 21 hours to drain, so a broadcast is push and email only, by arithmetic rather than policy.

#### Where it breaks
| Layer | Failure | How the design handles it |
|---|---|---|
| Provider | APNs or SES is degraded or unreachable for tens of minutes | A per-provider circuit breaker stops that worker pool from consuming, so the queue backs up safely instead of burning the retry budget |
| Outbox | A stuck publisher leaves rows unpublished while the queue reads empty | Publisher lag is graphed as its own metric, since a stalled publisher looks exactly like a healthy, empty queue to any depth-based alert |
| Tokens | Uninstalled apps leave dead device tokens in the fan-out list forever | Prune on the first permanent-failure response, plus a weekly silent push to idle tokens to catch the ones that never get sent to again |
| Broadcast | A full-base send is accepted synchronously | The synchronous API rejects segment-wide targets outright; broadcasts route only through the batch path |
| Preferences | A user opts out after their notification is already queued | The worker re-checks preferences at dequeue as a second gate, one extra cache read per send, closing the propagation gap |
| Rendering | Per-notification template rendering adds tens of milliseconds at broadcast concurrency | The static shell is pre-rendered per template and locale at publish time; only per-user variables substitute at send time |
| Status store | Every attempt writes, against a store that is read almost never | Seven days hot for the status API, the rest archived to columnar storage; attempt writes batched per worker poll |

#### What this design does not solve
**Delivery and display are different things, and only the first can be measured.** A 200 from a provider means it was accepted, not that a device received it or a person saw it. A muted app looks identical, from here, to a successful delivery. Client-side receipts would help and bias the number hard, since they only report from users engaged enough to have the app open, which is precisely the population least at risk of disabling notifications. The honest position is to publish acceptance rate and open rate as two separate numbers rather than compute a delivery rate that implies more certainty than exists.

**The per-user cap counts logical sends, not the interruptions a person actually feels.** Five notifications an hour means five logical sends, but a user with two channels enabled and two devices experiences up to fifteen physical interruptions in that hour. Moving the cap after fan-out sounds like the fix and is not: the message is already persisted and enqueued by then, so refusing it there throws away guaranteed work and makes the outcome depend on which worker happens to dequeue first. What actually runs is a separate bucket per channel, which stops a marketing send from consuming a security notification's budget, at the cost of a guarantee that reads as "five of these and two of those" rather than one number a settings screen can show.

**Nothing coordinates across a user's own devices.** A phone, a tablet and a watch all buzz for the same event and all get dismissed separately. A client-side dismiss can trigger a silent withdrawal push to the user's other devices, but it is best-effort by construction: the other devices need to be online to act on it, the withdrawal is itself a push subject to the same acceptance-not-delivery gap, and some platforms cannot programmatically remove a notification once shown at all.

#### Final design
Read it back through the numbers. 120 sends a second is small enough that nothing about this design is a scaling problem, which is exactly why restraint, not throughput, gets the engineering attention. The gap between a 4,400/s smeared broadcast and a 10,000/s push ceiling is what makes staging broadcasts through a batch path non-negotiable rather than an optimisation. And the p99 user at forty-plus notifications a day, not the median at 0.6, is the number the entire per-user gate is sized against, because the median user was never the one at risk of disabling notifications.

[The whole design](/diagram/notification-system?focus=accept,gate,fanout,outbox,publisher,cache,push-topic,email-topic,sms-topic,push-workers,email-workers,sms-workers,providers,status-store)

> **The numbers to remember.** ~120/s average, ~4,400/s smeared broadcast peak against a ~10k/s push ceiling · SMS cannot carry a broadcast, ~20.8 hours to drain one · four dedup hops, one hop, provider to device, uncoverable · p99 user at 40+/day is what the five-per-hour cap protects against.

#### Check your understanding
**Why is "at-least-once with dedup at four hops" not the same claim as "exactly-once"?** Each hop narrows a specific duplicate window using a conditional write, but one hop, provider to device, has no acknowledgement to wait for at all. The guarantee holds up to what the provider accepted, and stops there by construction.

**Why can a shared queue across channels turn one provider's bad hour into a system-wide outage?** A message for any channel waits behind every message ahead of it in the same queue. If APNs throttles, push messages pile up at the head, and email and SMS behind them wait too, even though neither provider is degraded.

**Why does honouring a provider's `Retry-After` header matter more than a well-tuned backoff curve?** The provider knows exactly when its own throttle resets; a self-chosen backoff that ignores that hint can retry too early and extend the very throttle it is trying to wait out.

**Why is the per-user cap sized against the p99 user rather than the average?** The average user receives about 0.6 notifications a day and was never going to be a problem regardless of the cap. The p99 user, above 40 a day, is the one who actually disables notifications, so that is the population the cap exists to protect.

**Why does a full-base broadcast need its own batch path instead of just the normal accept flow?** Accepted synchronously, 15 million messages hit push workers at once, which push against APNs faster than its throttle allows, triggering retries that keep the backlog growing rather than draining, and stall transactional traffic queued behind it.
### 8. Design a News Feed System (Facebook, Twitter)
#### Understanding the problem
A news feed is a materialised join between two things: the posts table and the follow graph. Every user sees a ranked stream of posts from the accounts they follow, and the only real design question is when that join gets computed.

Three things make the answer harder than "pick a side".

First, the follow graph is a power law. The median account has a few hundred followers; the largest have a hundred million. Any single strategy that works at one end breaks badly at the other.

Second, ranking depends on signals, like engagement in the last hour, that do not exist until well after a post is written, so ranking cannot be precomputed the way delivery can.

Third, reads outnumber posts by roughly an order of magnitude, which decides which side of the system it is worth spending extra work on.

> **What this is not.** The closest question by name is a Twitter-style microblog, which runs this exact hybrid fan-out underneath. The two designs still diverge completely. There, fan-out is a small early piece and most of the design goes to what a microblog adds on top: a searchable index, trending counts, a repost graph, reply threads. The feed is one of several subsystems. Here it is the only one, so the fan-out decision has to carry the whole design: the threshold, its derivation, the crossing transition, the merge cap, hydration as the correctness boundary. Spending this question on search or trending answers the other question instead.

#### Requirements and the numbers
**Functional.** Post, follow, unfollow, fetch a feed, paginate, refresh.

**Non-functional.** Feed load under 200ms p95. Survives a celebrity-scale post. Eventually consistent. A delete becomes invisible within one hydration.

The whole design is decided by four numbers, so derive them before choosing a strategy.

**How many posts a second, steady and at peak?** 500M daily active users, a fifth of whom post roughly ten times a day, gives 1B posts a day. 10⁹ ÷ 86,400s ≈ **~12k posts/s**, with a major live event pushing that to roughly **~60k/s**.

**How many feed loads a second does that traffic generate?** 500M DAU at about five sessions a day and five loads a session is 12.5B loads a day, **~145k/s average**, rising to roughly **~220k/s** at diurnal peak. Against 1B posts a day, that is about 12.5 loads per post, the read-heaviness that justifies paying extra on the write side.

**What does pushing every post to every follower actually cost?** The average follower count of a posting account under the eventual threshold is around 500. 1B posts × 500 ≈ 500B inserts a day, **~5.8M cache writes/s sustained**. Filtering out followers with no session in the last 30 days, roughly 60% of any list, cuts that to **~2.3M/s**.

**What band does the threshold have to sit inside?** The read side sets a floor: a 200ms budget leaves roughly 30ms for merging pull sources, and each source costs about 5ms of ranking overhead per 500 candidates, capping the merge at **~25 sources**. The write side sets a ceiling: pushing accounts up to 100,000 followers would add roughly 7M writes/s on top of the 5.8M/s baseline against a ~15M/s cluster ceiling. The defensible band is **~1,000 to ~30,000**.

> **The numbers to carry.** ~12k posts/s, ~60k/s at a major event · ~145k feed loads/s average · fan-out write load ~5.8M/s, ~2.3M/s after filtering dormant followers · threshold band ~1,000 to ~30,000, read-bounded below and write-bounded above.

#### Push, pull, or both
Split the feed into what it costs to write and what it costs to read, because a single number does not capture either side alone.

- **Write cost**: what it takes to make a post available the moment it is created, if delivery is precomputed.
- **Read cost**: what it takes to assemble a feed at load time, if nothing was precomputed.

The entities:

- **Post**: canonical content, stored once, keyed by author.
- **Timeline**: a capped, time-sorted list of post ids, prebuilt per follower for pushed authors.
- **Author recent-posts list**: the mirror image, one list per large account, read by every one of its followers.
- **Threshold classification**: the single source of truth for whether an author is pushed, pulled, or both, read identically by both delivery paths.

The API separates a write from a read cleanly, because the two never share a code path:

```
POST /post            body: { content, media_ids }  -> { post_id }
POST /follow/{user}                                 -> { ok, backfill_queued }
GET  /feed?cursor=X&limit=20                        -> { posts: [...], next_cursor }
```

#### High-level design
Follow the numbered arrows. A post is acknowledged the instant it is durable; delivery happens afterwards and never blocks the caller.

[The write path and the read path](/diagram/news-feed?focus=client-write,post-service,fanout-bus,p-classify,p-push,timeline-cache,author-recent,client-read,p-merge,ranker,p-hydrate,follow-graph,posts-db,e1,e2,e3,e4,e6,e7,e10,e21,e22,e23,e24,e25,e26,e27,e28)

1. **Write.** A **Client · post** call reaches the **Post service**, which writes durably to the **Posts store** and returns success before anything else happens.
2. The post service then publishes a fan-out event onto the **Fan-out bus**, partitioned by author, and a worker runs **Classify author** against the threshold.
3. Under it, **Push fan-out** pages the follower list and inserts the post id into each follower's **Timeline cache** entry. Over it, the worker appends once to that author's own **Author recent posts** list and does nothing else.
4. **Read.** A **Client · feed** call reaches **Merge + dedupe**, which reads the reader's pushed timeline and, in parallel, the recent-posts lists of the large accounts they follow.
5. The merged candidate set passes through the **Ranking service** and then **Hydrate + visibility**, which turns surviving ids into posts and enforces deletes, blocks and region restrictions before the response returns.

> **Why the flow is shaped this way.** Reads outnumber posts more than ten to one, so the design spends work up front to make ordinary feed loads cheap. That trade inverts at the very top of the follow graph, where one post would otherwise cost a hundred million writes, so the largest accounts keep their posts in one place and readers come to them instead.

#### Why push and pull both break at the extremes
Two obvious strategies exist, compute on write or compute on read. Why does neither survive the actual shape of the follow graph?

[Push, pull, and the hybrid split between them](/diagram/news-feed?focus=post-service,p-classify,p-push,author-recent,e6,e7)

**Bad: push every post to every follower.** A feed load becomes a single cache read, which is the cheapest possible read. But the cost of a post is now set by how popular its author is rather than by how interesting the post is, and at a hundred million followers, one post becomes a hundred million writes landing on one cluster in one burst.

**Good: pull every post at read time instead.** A post costs exactly one write no matter the author's size, and there is no derived state to keep correct, so deletes and privacy changes are automatic. The cost moves to the read path: every load has to fetch and merge recent posts from every account a reader follows, paid again on every single refresh.

**Great: split the population by size, and run both.** Push for accounts under the threshold, so ordinary users get the cheap, prebuilt read. Pull for accounts over it, so the largest authors write once and let readers merge them in. This bounds the write burst at the top of the graph and the read fan-out at the bottom, at the cost of two delivery paths that have to agree on which authors belong to which.

[Hybrid fan-out: push below the threshold, pull above it](/diagram/news-feed?figure=hybrid)

The intuition that "push is expensive for celebrities" is not actually a cost argument. Amortised over a day, push costs `F × posts_per_day` writes and pull costs `F × active_fraction × loads_per_day` reads, and the follower count `F` cancels out of the ratio between them at every scale. What actually breaks is concentration: a push is a burst of `F` writes that must land inside a freshness window, all on one cluster, at one moment. A pull is one key read by many readers, which is the access pattern a cache is best at.

#### Deriving the threshold from both directions
The threshold is not a single number picked by instinct. It is the middle of a band bounded from opposite sides, and the design has to be able to say which bound it is closer to.

[Where the read-side merge and the write-side fan-out both spend their budget](/diagram/news-feed?focus=p-push,timeline-cache,ranker,p-merge,e10,e25)

**Bad: pick a round number.** "10,000" with no derivation is a memorised answer, and it cannot tell you what to do when either side of the system's capacity changes.

**Good: derive it from one side.** The read-side merge budget alone gives a floor: at roughly 5ms of ranking cost per 500 candidates, and only ~30ms available after ranking and hydration are subtracted from the 200ms total, the merge cannot afford more than about 25 pull sources. Below that many, the threshold has room to go lower.

**Great: derive it from both sides, and report the resulting band rather than a single figure.** The write side sets the ceiling independently: raising the threshold to 100,000 pulls the 10k-to-100k tier back onto the push path, adding roughly 7M writes/s on top of a 5.8M/s baseline against a ~15M/s cluster ceiling. The two bounds do not meet at one point, they overlap in a band, roughly 1,000 to 30,000, and 10,000 is simply the middle of it.

Worked example. At a 10,000 threshold, about 4% of follow edges point above the line, so a typical 200-follow reader carries roughly 8 pull sources, comfortably under the 25-source cap. Drop the threshold to 1,000 and that share rises to about 20%, pushing the same reader to roughly 40 sources, past the merge budget the read side allows. The threshold is a config value with a floor and a ceiling, not a constant, and it should move when either side of the capacity changes.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="-110 -4 499 183" role="img" aria-label="The threshold sits in a band: a read-side floor near 1,000 followers set by the merge budget, and a write-side ceiling near 30,000 set by cache write capacity">
  <style>
    .axis{stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.45;stroke-width:1.4}
    .band{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.16;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.4}
    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    .sub{fill:currentColor;opacity:.8;font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    text{text-anchor:middle}
  </style>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="16" text-anchor="start" style="text-anchor:start">floor: ~30ms merge budget</text>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="32" text-anchor="start" style="text-anchor:start">ceiling: ~15M/s cache write capacity</text>
  <line class="axis" x1="20" y1="110" x2="380" y2="110"/>
  <rect class="band" x="110" y="88" width="170" height="44"/>
  <text class="lbl" x="195" y="110">defensible band</text>
  <text class="sub" x="110" y="75">~1,000</text>
  <text class="sub" x="280" y="75">~30,000</text>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="152" text-anchor="start" style="text-anchor:start">10,000 sits near the middle of this band,</text>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="168" text-anchor="start" style="text-anchor:start">not derived from either bound alone</text>
</svg>
```

#### Crossing the line without vanishing
An account grows past the threshold. Both delivery paths need to agree on its new classification at the same moment, or something goes quietly wrong.

[Where classification is read by both the push and the pull path](/diagram/news-feed?focus=p-classify,classifier,follow-graph,e5,e18)

**Bad: let each path infer classification independently, at its own pace.** Fan-out reads it at write time; the feed service reads it at read time. If a nightly batch computes the classification and follows arrive continuously, the two reads can disagree during the gap.

**Good: read from one shared classification source.** That removes most disagreement, but a single instantaneous flip still creates a race the moment an account actually crosses: for a brief window, one path can believe the account is still small while the other already treats it as large.

**Great: run a dual-mode window around every crossing.** For 24 hours after an account crosses the threshold, it is both pushed and included in every follower's pull set. Posts arrive by both routes during that window, and the merge deduplicates by post id, so double delivery is invisible to the reader. The cost is one day of doubled writes for the handful of accounts crossing on any given day, which is negligible.

The failure this specifically prevents is worse than a duplicate. If the write path's counter is stale toward "still small" while the read path's counter is already stale toward "already large", the account is neither pushed nor pulled, and it disappears from every follower's feed for up to a day with no error anywhere in the system. Dual-mode turns that silent gap into an overlap instead, and the requirement it creates, that the merge must be idempotent by post id, has to hold at all times, not only during a known crossing window.

#### IDs, never bodies
Timelines hold post ids, not post content. What does that indirection actually buy, and where does it get paid for?

[Where an id becomes a post, and where correctness is actually enforced](/diagram/news-feed?focus=p-hydrate,posts-db,e27,e28)

**Bad: store the post body directly in every follower's timeline.** A feed load becomes a single read with nothing left to fetch, which sounds ideal until anything about the post changes. A delete, an edit, or a new block relationship now has to be found and rewritten across up to a hundred million cached copies.

**Good: store ids, and resolve them against the posts store at read time.** A delete is now one write to the source of truth. But if hydration only fetches content, it still has to separately check deletion, blocking, and region rules, each a further round trip.

**Great: make hydration the single place all of that is checked, in one pass.** **Hydrate + visibility** reads each candidate post and drops it if it has been deleted, if the author has since blocked the reader, if it is restricted in the reader's region, or if the account is suspended. A delete takes effect everywhere the moment it is written, because nothing downstream of it needs to be found and changed.

The real cost of this design is easy to skip over: hydration has to over-fetch, because some fraction of candidates will not survive the visibility check. A load whose candidates are 30% unhydratable fetches roughly seventy ids to return fifty posts, and occasionally still returns fewer than the target regardless. That over-fetch factor is tuned, not assumed, and it is the price of never having to rewrite a cached list.

#### The reader with too many big follows
The pull-side merge is capped at roughly 25 sources for the ranking budget's sake. What happens to a reader whose large-account follows exceed that cap?

[The pull set feeding the merge, capped before it reaches ranking](/diagram/news-feed?focus=follow-graph,p-merge,ranker,e24,e25)

**Bad: assume the cap is a rare edge case.** It disproportionately is not. A brand-new account's follow list, shaped by onboarding suggestions toward already-popular accounts, is almost entirely made up of large accounts from the very first day.

**Good: silently truncate to the cap and rank whatever made it through.** That keeps every load inside the latency budget, but the accounts ranked 26th and beyond are not merely deprioritised, they are entirely absent from the candidate pool. Two refreshes with no new posts anywhere can still show a different feed, purely from which 25 sources were sampled, which reads to a user as a bug.

**Great: rank the capped set by predicted engagement, rotate a portion of it between loads, and measure the resulting gap rather than hide it.** Ranking within the cap ensures the highest-value sources are represented consistently; rotating the remainder gives some coverage to sources that would otherwise never appear. Raising the cap itself is not free: every source added taxes every reader's ranking latency, not just the celebrity-heavy ones.

Worked example. The median reader carries about 8 pull sources, well inside the 25-source cap and effectively unaffected by it. The p99 reader, disproportionately a new account, carries 60 or more, so 35 of those sources contribute nothing to any single load. That is a measurable completeness gap this design accepts rather than closes, because closing it, either by raising the cap for everyone or by adding a per-reader dynamic cap, spends latency budget that the 200ms target does not have.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 -5 422 216" role="img" aria-label="Pull sources per reader by percentile: the median reader carries about 8, well under the 25-source cap, while the p99 reader carries 60 or more, well over it">
  <style>
    .axis{stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.4;stroke-width:1.3}
    .bar{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.28;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.4}
    .over{fill:currentColor;fill-opacity:.15;stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.6;stroke-width:1.4}
    .cap{stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.6;stroke-width:1.4;stroke-dasharray:5 4}
    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    .sub{fill:currentColor;opacity:.8;font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    text{text-anchor:middle}
  </style>
  <text class="lbl" x="200" y="16">above the cap line: absent, not deprioritised</text>
  <line class="axis" x1="20" y1="180" x2="380" y2="180"/>
  <line class="cap" x1="20" y1="95" x2="380" y2="95"/><text class="sub" x="370" y="85" text-anchor="end">cap: 25 sources</text>
  <rect class="bar" x="55" y="160" width="34" height="20"/><text class="sub" x="72" y="200">p50: ~8</text>
  <rect class="bar" x="175" y="130" width="34" height="50"/><text class="sub" x="192" y="200">p90: ~20</text>
  <rect class="over" x="295" y="40" width="34" height="140"/><text class="sub" x="312" y="200">p99: 60+</text>
</svg>
```

#### Where it breaks
| Layer | Failure | How the design handles it |
|---|---|---|
| Fan-out | A post from a hundred-million-follower account would saturate the cache cluster | The threshold routes it to pull instead, bounding read cost at roughly 25 merged sources per reader |
| Hot post | A single post's hydration load goes from ordinary traffic to spike traffic within minutes | An edge cache with a short TTL plus request coalescing collapses concurrent identical hydrations into one backend read |
| Classification | Push and pull paths briefly disagree on an author's size during a crossing | A 24-hour dual-mode window pushes and pulls simultaneously; the merge deduplicates by post id |
| Ranking | The read-time ranker degrades under load, threatening the latency budget | A timeout falls back to chronological order over the same candidate set instead of a blank feed |
| Cache economics | Holding push timelines in memory for the full active base is expensive at scale | The active working set stays in the fast cache tier; the cold tail moves to cheaper on-disk storage |
| Follow | A user follows someone new and their timeline has none of that author's history | Async backfill inserts the author's recent posts; until it lands, the new followee is treated as a one-shot pull source |
| Timeline | A reader's follows were mass-moderated, so most of a full timeline hydrates to almost nothing | Per-reader hydration yield is monitored, and a thin timeline is rebuilt offline from the pull path rather than inline |

#### What this design does not solve
**A celebrity-heavy reader gets a measurably worse feed, and there is no clean fix at this budget.** The merge cap exists because the ranking budget requires it, and the readers who exceed it, disproportionately new users guided by onboarding toward popular accounts, lose real coverage rather than mere ranking position. Rotating the excess between loads trades completeness for the appearance of freshness. The structurally clean answer, a third delivery mode that pushes large accounts selectively to their most engaged followers, has not been built.

**There is no ordering guarantee across different authors.** Fan-out is partitioned by author, so one author's own posts stay in order. Nothing orders posts between two different authors, so a reply can be delivered and ranked ahead of the post it replies to, and a timestamp-based score keeps it that way until the feed reorders for an unrelated reason. Hydrating an explicit parent inline fixes declared replies and quotes; it does nothing for the far more common implicit reference, and a real dependency check per candidate costs a second hydration round trip the latency budget cannot spare.

**Nothing notices when a timeline quietly degenerates.** Hydration silently drops deleted, blocked, suspended and region-restricted posts, so a reader whose follows were heavily moderated can hold a technically full, 1000-entry timeline that hydrates down to a handful of usable posts. The write path never sees this, because fan-out did exactly what it was asked to do: it delivered ids. The only remedy, rebuilding that timeline from the expensive pull path, is reserved for readers whose yield is already measurably low, which means those readers see a thin feed until the rebuild lands rather than a slow one.

#### Final design
Read it back through the numbers. The threshold band, bounded below by a ~30ms merge budget and above by a ~15M/s cache write ceiling, is what makes 10,000 a derived middle point rather than a memorised constant. The 60% of any follower list that has not opened the app in 30 days is what turns a 5.8M/s fan-out baseline into a 2.3M/s one, for free, before any harder optimisation is needed. And ids-never-bodies, paid for as an over-fetch at hydration time, is what lets a delete take effect everywhere at once instead of requiring a rewrite of up to a hundred million cached lists.

[The whole design](/diagram/news-feed?focus=client-write,post-service,posts-db,fanout-bus,p-classify,p-push,p-backfill,follow-graph,follow-service,timeline-cache,author-recent,classifier,p-merge,p-hydrate,ranker,client-read)

> **The numbers to remember.** ~12k posts/s, ~145k feed loads/s · fan-out threshold band ~1,000 to ~30,000, read-bounded below and write-bounded above · ~2.3M/s fan-out writes after dropping the ~60% dormant share · merge capped at ~25 pull sources, median reader needs ~8.

#### Check your understanding
**Why does neither pure push nor pure pull survive the actual follow graph?** Push turns one post from a huge account into a burst of writes that must land on one cluster inside a freshness window. Pull turns every feed load into work proportional to how many accounts a reader follows, paid again on every refresh. The graph's power law makes both extremes real at once.

**Why is the fan-out threshold described as a band rather than a single derived number?** It is bounded from two independent directions: a read-side latency budget sets a floor below which the merge gets too expensive, and a write-side cache capacity sets a ceiling above which fan-out writes overload the cluster. Any value inside that band is defensible; the chosen number is simply its middle.

**An account crosses the push-to-pull threshold. What stops it from vanishing from its followers' feeds?** A 24-hour dual-mode window pushes and pulls the account simultaneously, so a stale counter on either path cannot leave it uncovered by both. The merge deduplicates by post id, so the resulting double delivery is invisible to the reader.

**Why do timelines store post ids instead of post content?** A delete, edit, or new block relationship only has to change the posts store once, and it takes effect everywhere the next time that id is hydrated. Storing content directly would mean finding and rewriting the same fact across every cached copy that held it.

**Why does a brand-new user tend to get a worse feed than an established one, structurally rather than by bad luck?** Onboarding suggests popular accounts, so a new user's follow list is disproportionately made of large, pull-path accounts. The merge caps how many pull sources contribute to one load, so a reader following many large accounts loses real coverage, not just ranking position.
### 9. Design a Chat System (WhatsApp, Messenger)
#### Understanding the problem
A chat system delivers messages one-to-one and in groups, in under a second when both people are online, and without loss when they are not. Every device must be able to disappear for an arbitrary length of time and reconnect to exactly the conversation everyone else already sees.

Three things make that harder than "hold a socket open and push".

First, the socket is not the product, durability is. A message has to be safely stored before anyone is told it sent, because a tick that can later turn out to be wrong is worse than a slow tick.

Second, a device can vanish for a second, an hour, or three months, and the same mechanism has to cover all three without the client or server needing to know in advance which one is happening.

Third, whether the server can read the plaintext is a single decision that reshapes search, new-device history, group delivery and abuse detection all at once. It cannot be added later without rebuilding several subsystems.

> **What this is not.** The closest question by transport is Slack. Both hold a persistent connection per client and both push messages in real time, but the content policy is opposite and the whole design bends around that difference. Slack's organisation owns the messages, so the server holds plaintext by requirement, and the hard problem becomes read-side fan-in: a user in two hundred channels needs two hundred unread counts reconstructed the instant a cold client launches. A consumer messenger user has a handful of active conversations and a device that is almost always nearly caught up, so that fan-in problem never arises here. What does arise here, and barely troubles Slack, is connection count: phones, worldwide, at all hours, which is the number that actually sizes this fleet.

#### Requirements and the numbers
**Functional.** Send and receive one-to-one and group messages, capped at 1,024 members. Presence, typing, delivery and read receipts. Scrollable history. Offline delivery via push. Multi-device.

**Non-functional.** p99 end-to-end delivery under 300ms for two online users. Ordered within a conversation. At-least-once with idempotent client apply. A device offline for months converges correctly on reconnect.

The whole design is decided by four numbers, so derive them before choosing anything.
