**Good: recognise the failure mode and accept it as a known limitation.** Inserting even a few bytes at the start of a file shifts every later chunk boundary, so every subsequent hash changes even though almost none of the actual content did. Knowing this happens does not fix it.

**Great: switch to content-defined chunking wherever the corpus is genuinely edited in the middle.** A rolling hash over the bytes starts a new chunk whenever its fingerprint matches a chosen pattern, anchoring boundaries to content rather than position. An insert then perturbs only the one or two chunks it actually touches, and everything after it resynchronises on its own, at the cost of a second pass over every byte.

Worked example. A ten-byte insert at the very start of a one-gigabyte file, under fixed 4MB chunking, shifts all 256 chunk boundaries and re-uploads the entire gigabyte. The same insert under content-defined chunking perturbs roughly one or two chunks near the insertion point, costing on the order of a few megabytes, a difference of two orders of magnitude for what the user experienced as a trivial edit. Consumer Drive traffic sits at the low end of edit-in-the-middle behaviour, which is why fixed chunking is the right default here even though it is the wrong default for a backup product ingesting VM images or database files.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 210" role="img" aria-label="A 10-byte insert at the start of a file shifts every fixed chunk boundary after it, changing every hash; a content-defined boundary anchored to the bytes themselves resynchronises after one or two chunks">
  <style>
    .changed{fill:currentColor;fill-opacity:.15;stroke:currentColor;stroke-width:1.3}
    .same{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.18;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.3}
    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    .sub{fill:currentColor;opacity:.8;font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
  </style>
  <text class="lbl" x="8" y="16">Fixed offsets: insert shifts every boundary</text>
  <g transform="translate(20,26)">
    <rect class="changed" x="0" y="0" width="66" height="30"/><rect class="changed" x="70" y="0" width="66" height="30"/><rect class="changed" x="140" y="0" width="66" height="30"/><rect class="changed" x="210" y="0" width="66" height="30"/><rect class="changed" x="280" y="0" width="66" height="30"/>
  </g>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="76">every chunk after the insert re-hashes and re-uploads</text>
  <text class="lbl" x="8" y="112">Content-defined: boundary anchored to bytes</text>
  <g transform="translate(20,122)">
    <rect class="changed" x="0" y="0" width="66" height="30"/><rect class="same" x="70" y="0" width="66" height="30"/><rect class="same" x="140" y="0" width="66" height="30"/><rect class="same" x="210" y="0" width="66" height="30"/><rect class="same" x="280" y="0" width="66" height="30"/>
  </g>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="172">only the touched chunk changes; the rest</text>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="187">resynchronise unchanged</text>
</svg>
```

#### Namespaces, not user shards, for anything shared
A shared folder belongs to many users at once. Sharding metadata by owning user, the obvious choice for a private root, breaks down the moment a folder has real membership.

[Where a shared folder's own journal lives](/diagram/google-drive?focus=metadata-db,journal,devices,e11,e12,e16)

**Bad: shard metadata by user, and replicate a shared folder's state into every member's shard.** A single bulk edit inside a folder with many members then fans out to a write per file per member, and those writes must stay transactional across every one of those shards or members will observe different trees.

**Good: shard by user, and accept the fan-out for small folders.** Below a handful of members the write amplification is genuinely invisible, and per-user sharding keeps a private tree's internal moves cheap, since moving a file between two folders in one user's own tree is a single transaction either way.

**Great: make each shared folder its own namespace, mounted into every member's view, sharing one journal.** A bulk edit touching many files now produces exactly one journal entry per changed file, written once, regardless of how many people are watching that folder. Every member's device pulls the same range and applies it, rather than the system fanning writes out to each of them individually.

Worked example. A folder with five hundred members undergoes a ten-thousand-file bulk edit. Under per-user replication, that is five million metadata writes, needing to stay transactional across five hundred independently sharded stores. Under a namespace shared by all five hundred members, it is ten thousand writes to one journal, and each member simply pulls that range. The cost of the namespace choice shows up elsewhere: moving a file out of a shared folder into a private root now crosses two independently sequenced journals, which cannot be made atomic without a distributed transaction on the most common destructive operation in the product.

#### Where it breaks
| Layer | Failure | How the design handles it |
|---|---|---|
| Metadata | A folder of many small files produces one metadata write per file on every sync | Small files are packed into a single archive chunk with a manifest, cutting the write rate sharply at the cost of some read amplification |
| Upload | A very large file fails outright over an unreliable connection | Chunk-level acknowledgement lets the client resume from the last acknowledged chunk, and content addressing makes partial progress reusable even from a different device |
| Chunk store | A widely shared chunk is requested by many users simultaneously | Served from a CDN edge so origin sees effectively one fetch, with reference counts keeping the chunk alive as long as anything still points to it |
| Shared folder | One member's bulk change fans out as thousands of individual notifications | Notifications are debounced into one "namespace advanced to id N" message; each device pulls the range itself |
| Garbage collection | Reference counts on chunks drift from what metadata actually references | A nightly sweep removes refcount-zero chunks after a grace period, backed by a periodic mark-and-sweep that treats the counter as a fast path, not the truth |
| Privacy | Cross-user deduplication makes chunk existence observable, turning a hash into an oracle | Per-tenant keyspaces remove the cross-tenant leak while keeping most of the dedup value, since most of it is intra-tenant anyway |
| Journal | A device returns after longer than the retention window | It falls back to a full tree diff, the expensive path the journal exists specifically to avoid, refusing to run if the local tree looks suspiciously empty |

#### What this design does not solve
**Moves across a namespace boundary are not atomic, and that is a deliberate choice, not an oversight.** Dragging a large shared folder into a private root touches two independently sequenced journals with no transaction spanning them, so the system implements it as a copy followed by a delete: new file ids, reset version history, one namespace watching the folder disappear while the other gets a folder with no past. A two-phase commit between namespace owners would fix it and would put a distributed transaction on the interactive path of the most common destructive operation in the product, where a half-completed move is worse than today's deterministic, if unpleasant, behaviour.

**Rename detection is a best-effort heuristic, not a guarantee.** Filesystem watchers coalesce events under load, drop them outright, and never reliably deliver a rename as a rename, so a folder rename can surface as thousands of deletes followed by thousands of creates. Matching new files against recently deleted ones by content hash and size recovers a pure rename cheaply, but recovers nothing when an application also modified the file on save, which is exactly what many common "Save As" flows do, so the rename is lost and the bytes re-upload from scratch.

**Most conflict copies are probably not real conflicts, and there is no way to tell which ones are.** Conflict detection is a version compare-and-swap, so it fires whenever two devices commit against the same parent regardless of whether the actual content disagrees. Many applications rewrite an entire file on every save, embedding a fresh timestamp or re-serialising a container in a different byte order, so opening a document, changing nothing, and closing it on two devices produces a conflict copy of a file nobody actually edited. Quantifying how much of the roughly 100k daily conflicts are spurious this way would require understanding file formats, which is precisely the thing this design's whole approach refuses to do.

#### Final design
Read it back through the numbers. The gap between 10EB raw and 6EB distinct is what makes content-addressed chunking, not merely a nice deduplication feature, the thing that makes the storage bill payable at all. The fact that reconnection cost depends only on what changed, never on how large a namespace is, is what makes a ten-million-file enterprise tenant and a ten-file personal folder cost the same to resync after a week offline. And the roughly 100k conflict copies a day, tiny as a rate, is exactly why the mechanism handling them has to be a cheap, fully automatic write rather than anything requiring a human in the loop.

[The whole design](/diagram/google-drive?focus=watcher,three-tree,chunker,meta-svc,block-svc,chunk-index,metadata-db,object-store,journal,pubsub,notify,devices,cdn,gc)

> **The numbers to remember.** ~10EB raw, ~6EB distinct after dedup · reconnection cost is O(changes), never O(files) · ~100k conflict copies/day at roughly 1 in 10⁴ modifications · a 10-byte insert costs a whole file under fixed chunking, roughly two orders of magnitude less under content-defined chunking.

#### Check your understanding
**Why does the client need three trees instead of two to detect what changed?** With only local and server state, a file present locally but missing from the server is ambiguous: it could be a new local file or a file someone else deleted remotely. A third tree recording the last point of agreement resolves that ambiguity by letting the client diff each side against a shared reference point.

**Why must the server never trust a client's claim that it already holds a chunk?** If possession could simply be asserted, knowing a hash would be equivalent to holding the file, letting anyone who obtained or guessed a hash attach another user's chunk to their own file. The server either challenges for proof of possession or restricts deduplication to chunks that user has actually uploaded.

**Why is commit ordered as durability, then commit, then notification, and never any other order?** Committing before chunks are durable can publish a version pointing at bytes that do not exist. Notifying before the commit lands can tell a device about a version that is not real yet. The strict order guarantees anything a device is told about actually exists when it goes looking for it.

**Why does a failed compare-and-swap become a new file rather than an attempted merge?** The system cannot read file content, so it has no way to know whether merging two divergent byte sequences produces something sensible or something corrupted. Preserving the losing version as an ordinary new file is the only response that is always safe, regardless of what format the file happens to be.

**Why does a shared folder become its own namespace instead of being replicated into every member's personal shard?** A bulk edit in a folder with many members would otherwise fan out to one metadata write per file per member, needing to stay transactional across every member's shard. A shared namespace instead produces one journal entry per changed file, written once, that every member simply pulls independently.
### 13. Design a Proximity Service (Yelp, Find Nearby)
#### Understanding the problem
A proximity service answers "what is near this point" over a catalogue of roughly 200 million fixed places, in under 200ms, at hundreds of thousands of queries a second. No storage engine has a "near" operator, so the whole design starts from having to manufacture one.

Three things make that harder than an ordinary lookup.

First, any one-dimensional key built out of a latitude and longitude is necessarily lossy. A query is a circle; the structures that can be indexed cheaply are boxes, and a circle never aligns to a box's edges.

Second, population density varies by three orders of magnitude across those boxes. A downtown block and a rural county cannot use the same fixed assumptions about how many candidates a query will return.

Third, the places themselves do not move. Coordinate changes happen below one per second against tens of thousands of searches per second, which makes the index something fundamentally different from a live, continuously mutated structure.

> **What this is not.** The closest question by keyword is Nearby Friends, and the two answers diverge completely on one axis: whether the indexed points move. There, every entity rewrites its position every few seconds, so the write rate is the entity count divided by the reporting interval, the index must absorb writes rather than merely serve reads, and results cannot be cached at all because they are stale before the response even lands. Here the read-to-write ratio runs near 100,000 to 1, so the index is a file produced, diffed and promoted rather than a structure mutated in place, and caching is not just possible but does most of the load-bearing work. The word "geohash" appears in both answers and means something different each time: a mutable key rewritten on every heartbeat there, a column in an artifact rebuilt nightly here. Giving the moving-entity answer to this static question means building write-absorption machinery for data that changes once a year.

#### Requirements and the numbers
**Functional.** Find places within a given radius of a point. Filter by category and rating. Rank by a blend of distance and quality. Paginate.

**Non-functional.** Under 200ms p99. Correct in both dense and sparse regions. 200M-plus entities. The index must be rebuildable from source at any time.

The whole design is decided by four numbers, so derive them before choosing a structure.

**How many searches a second, and how skewed is the traffic?** 1B monthly active users at roughly five searches a day gives 5B searches a day, **~60k/s average**, with lunch and dinner in dense metros pushing peak to roughly **~300k/s**.

**How lopsided is reading against writing?** Roughly 0.6 coordinate changes a second against 60k reads a second is a **~100,000:1 read-to-write ratio**. That ratio, not any preference for simplicity, is what justifies building the index offline rather than mutating it live.

**How big does the index need to be, and does it fit in memory?** A packed 48-byte entry per place, 200M of them, is **~10GB**, small enough to memory-map whole on every serving node with room to spare.

**How much does density skew actually vary the candidate set?** A dense city block covering the search radius returns roughly 22,000 candidates; a rural county covering the same radius returns roughly 20. That is a **~1000x range**, and the design has to survive both ends without either dying on the dense end or silently truncating results on it.

> **The numbers to carry.** ~60k searches/s average, ~300k/s peak · ~100,000:1 read-to-write ratio · ~10GB index, memory-resident on every node · candidate count spans ~20 to ~22,000, a roughly 1000x range across density.

#### Two phases, one parameter
Split the search into a cheap approximate prune and an expensive exact test, because running the expensive test against the whole catalogue would never fit the latency budget.

- **Phase one, approximate**: cell membership. Which places fall inside the block of grid cells covering the search radius.
- **Phase two, exact**: true distance. Which of those candidates are actually inside the requested radius, computed precisely and only once the candidate set is small.

The entities:

- **Cell id**: a lossy one-dimensional key manufactured from a latitude and longitude, chosen so that a shared prefix implies geographic proximity.
- **Geo index entry**: a packed, self-contained record, roughly 48 bytes, carrying everything needed to filter and rank a candidate without a second fetch.
- **Card**: the small display projection returned to the client, fetched only for the handful of results actually shown.
- **Overlay**: a small in-memory map of coordinate changes since the last full build, consulted alongside the main artifact.

The hot path is entirely a function of one input, the requested radius, which decides everything downstream of it:

```
tier  = precision_for(radius)            // 3 tiers: 5km / 1km / 200m
block = cells_covering(lat, lng, radius, tier)
cand  = [e for c in block for e in index[c] if e.category & mask]
hits  = [e for e in cand if haversine(e, user) <= radius]
top   = nlargest(20, hits, key=score)    // distance blended with rating
page  = card_store.mget([e.id for e in top])
```

#### High-level design
Follow the numbered arrows. Everything above the cache probe is cheap; everything below it is a bounded scan over memory, never a database read per candidate.

[The path from a coordinate query to twenty ranked results](/diagram/proximity-service?focus=client,clamp,result-cache,block,scan,rank,geo-index,card-store,e1,e2,e3,e4,e5,e6,e8,e9)

1. A search reaches **Validate + clamp radius**, which bounds the requested radius into one of a small number of precision tiers before anything else runs.
2. It probes the **Result cache** first; a miss falls through to **Cell encode + block**, which computes the exact set of grid cells covering the requested circle.
3. **Block scan** reads every entry in those cells directly from the memory-resident **Geo index artifact**, filtering by category as it goes so nothing survives the scan that will not be returned.
4. **Haversine + rank** computes exact distance only over that already-filtered candidate set, keeps the top twenty, and only then fetches display data from the **Card store**.

> **Why the flow is shaped this way.** Raw geographic distance is expensive to compute globally; cell membership is nearly free. The index's job is narrowing the world down to a scannable set, and the ranking step's job is turning that set into something that reads as accurate to a human, without ever touching a database for a candidate that will be discarded.

#### Manufacturing a one-dimensional key out of two
A circle is defined by one centre and one radius. The structure being queried is made of rectangular cells. What does that mismatch actually cost, and how is it accounted for correctly?

[Where a radius becomes a block of cells, not one cell](/diagram/proximity-service?focus=block,geo-index,e4,e6)

**Bad: read only the cell the user is standing in.** Fast, and wrong the instant the search radius extends past that cell's own edges, which it almost always does.

**Good: read the target cell plus its eight immediate neighbours.** This is the standard folk answer, and it is only correct when the cell is at least as wide and as tall as the requested radius in both directions.

**Great: compute the exact block a radius requires, using the cell's shorter dimension.** For cells of width `w` and height `h`, covering radius `r` from anywhere inside the centre cell needs `(2·ceil(r/w) + 1) × (2·ceil(r/h) + 1)` cells. Many cell encodings are not square at every precision level; a common one alternates between roughly square and 2:1 rectangular depending on prefix length. At the rectangular lengths, comparing the radius only against the wider dimension silently under-covers the shorter one.

Worked example. At one common precision level a cell measures roughly 1.22km by 0.61km. For a 1km radius, columns needed each side round up to 1, but rows needed each side round up to 2, giving a block of 3 by 5, fifteen cells, not the folk answer's nine. Using nine loses every result between 610 metres and 1000 metres directly north or south of the searcher, a failure that never throws an error and shows up only as a place quietly missing from results. Too coarse a precision level over-fetches instead: one level up, the same 1km search reads a block covering roughly 68 times the area of the actual circle, turning a 22,000-candidate scan into hundreds of thousands.

[Geohash precision vs query cost](/diagram/proximity-service?figure=geohash-precision)

#### Why phase one has to cost nanoseconds, not microseconds
An index could store just enough to identify a candidate, leaving filtering and ranking to a second fetch. Why does this design pay to make every entry self-contained instead?

[Where filtering happens, before anything is fetched a second time](/diagram/proximity-service?focus=scan,geo-index,card-store,rank,e6,e8)

**Bad: index business ids only, and fetch full records for every candidate.** Simple, and it never goes stale on an attribute change, because there are no attributes to go stale. But at peak backend load, hydrating every candidate before filtering multiplies the query cost by roughly the mean candidate count, which is on the order of a hundred times the cost of hydrating only what gets returned.

**Good: filter using the ids, then fetch full records only for survivors.** Cheaper than hydrating everything, but a dense cell still forces fetching thousands of full records before the category and rating filters can even run.

**Great: pack coordinates, category, rating and everything filterable directly into a slim, self-contained index entry, and hydrate only the final twenty.** Scanning a packed entry costs a few nanoseconds; even a dense-city scan of 22,000 entries finishes in well under a fraction of a millisecond, a rounding error against a 200ms budget. Filtering and ranking happen entirely inside that scan, so hydration only ever touches the handful of rows actually returned to the client.

Worked example. At peak backend load, filtering-then-hydrating twenty results per query costs a modest multi-get per query. Hydrating every mean-sized candidate set before filtering, by contrast, would multiply that same query volume by roughly two thousand, the mean candidate count, which lands at close to a hundred times more backend reads for identical traffic. The price of this design is denormalisation: every attribute worth filtering on has to be copied into the index, so adding a new filter means rebuilding the whole ten-gigabyte structure rather than adding a column to a table.

#### A file you rebuild, not a structure you mutate
Coordinate writes are vanishingly rare against reads. What does that ratio let this design do that a live, continuously updated index cannot?

[Where a new index version is built, checked and released](/diagram/proximity-service?focus=catalogue,build-map,build-gate,build-promote,artifact-store,e16,e17,e18,e14)

**Bad: write through the index on every business edit, the way a moving-entity system must.** Correct, and it means every deploy, every schema change, and every bad edit is a live production incident happening to a structure serving hundreds of thousands of queries a second.

**Good: batch coordinate writes into periodic updates rather than writing through immediately.** That reduces write pressure, but the index is still a mutable structure that can be corrupted in place, with no clean way to compare a proposed change against what is currently serving traffic before it goes live.

**Great: build the whole index offline as an immutable, versioned artifact, verify it before anyone sees it, and promote it as a release rather than a write.** A nightly job maps over the full catalogue and produces a fresh, checksummed artifact. Before promotion, its entry count is checked against the previous version within a tight tolerance, and a recorded corpus of real queries is replayed against both versions to confirm the result sets agree. Only after a canary node has served real traffic against it does the rest of the fleet flip its pointer to the new file.

Worked example. A build job fails partway through and silently produces an artifact missing a large slice of one region's entries. Under a write-through design, the corruption is already live and searchers immediately see it. Under build-and-verify, the entry-count check catches the shortfall before the artifact is ever promoted, the previous known-good version keeps serving every query in the meantime, and the whole failed build costs nothing but a delayed release rather than an outage.

[Build, gate, canary, flip: nothing promoted blind](/diagram/proximity-service?figure=build-gate-canary)

#### The cache key that turns millions of coordinates into a few thousand hot ones
Two people standing metres apart send different coordinates for the same search. If the cache is keyed on raw location, it never gets a second hit on either of them.

[Where a result is stored, and what its key deliberately ignores](/diagram/proximity-service?focus=clamp,result-cache,e2)

**Bad: key the cache on exact latitude and longitude.** Every distinct coordinate pair is effectively unique, so the cache almost never hits, and the entire point of caching, absorbing repeated requests, never materialises.

**Good: round coordinates to a coarse grid before using them as a key.** That collapses many nearby searches onto the same key, but if the rounding grid does not match the same cell boundaries the index itself uses, two searches that would return identical results can still land on different cache keys for no good reason.

**Great: key the cache on the same cell id, category, radius bucket and page the index computation already uses.** Anyone searching from anywhere inside the same cell for the same thing shares one cache entry, because the key is built from exactly the same coarse geography the index already treats as equivalent. This is the difference between a key space with millions of practically distinct values and one with only a few thousand genuinely hot entries, and it is the entire reason a strong blended hit rate is achievable at all on the busiest cells.

Worked example. A thousand different people searching for coffee within a kilometre of roughly the same block in a dense downtown area, over the course of a minute, produce a thousand distinct latitude and longitude pairs but only one cell id. Keyed on raw coordinates, that traffic generates a thousand separate cache misses. Keyed on the cell, it generates one miss and nine hundred and ninety-nine hits, and the difference between those two outcomes is the difference between the backend serving a comfortable fraction of peak traffic and being asked to serve all of it.

#### A filter that changes without a single write
An "open now" filter depends on the current time, not on anything that was ever written to the catalogue. What does a filter with no corresponding write event do to a static index?

[Where a time-varying filter is evaluated inside a structure that never changes on its own](/diagram/proximity-service?focus=scan,geo-index,e6)

**Bad: apply the open-now filter after the scan, against freshly fetched full records.** Correct, and it reintroduces exactly the hydration cost the slim index entry exists to avoid, since every candidate now needs a full record fetch before it can even be filtered.

**Good: store a coarse open-hours representation inside the index entry itself, and evaluate it during the scan.** That keeps filtering cheap, but the cache built around this index was designed assuming a query's inputs alone determine its result, and open-now breaks that assumption without anyone touching a write path.

**Great: recognise that the result changes with wall-clock time even though nothing in the catalogue does, and adjust the cache key accordingly.** The cache key of cell, category, radius bucket and page is no longer a complete description of what determines the result once opening hours matter, because the same key now maps to different correct answers depending on when it is asked. The choice becomes explicit: add an hour bucket to the key, which is correct and reduces the hit rate for a filter most searches do not use, or exclude open-now queries from the result cache entirely and accept the extra backend load only when someone actually asks for it.

This is the sharpest illustration of what a genuinely static index still has to account for: not every input to a query is a write. Wall-clock time is a filter dimension with no corresponding catalogue edit, no journal entry, and no build trigger, and it is exactly the kind of dimension that a design built entirely around "the entities do not move" can quietly forget to account for.

#### Where it breaks
| Layer | Failure | How the design handles it |
|---|---|---|
| Radius | An unclamped, very wide radius forces a scan of millions of entries on one core | Radius is hard-clamped, and anything above a moderate threshold is routed to a coarser precision tier by design |
| Result cache | Thousands of concurrent misses hit the index the instant a hot cell's cached entry expires | Single-flight per cache key, plus jittered TTLs so hot cells do not all expire in the same instant |
| Index promotion | A bad build could take down search for the entire fleet at once, since the artifact is global | Promotion happens canary-first with a live result-set comparison, and the previous artifact stays resident for an instant rollback |
| Geometry | Cell arithmetic misbehaves near the antimeridian and degenerates near the poles | The block computation special-cases the wrap and clamps latitude away from the true poles |
| Ranking attributes | Rating and popularity live inside the index and drift between full rebuilds | Those fields refresh on a materially shorter cadence than geometry, since they are the attributes that actually move |
| Cache invalidation | A single business edit can touch an unenumerable set of cached result keys | The short TTL is the real mechanism; prefix-based invalidation is a best-effort optimisation layered on top, not depended on |
| Ingest | A malformed or spoofed coordinate silently pollutes a cell | Coordinates are sanity-checked and quarantined at write time, since a bad value gets baked permanently into the next build |

#### What this design does not solve
**Straight-line distance is not what a person means by "near".** The index answers "within a given radius as the crow flies," while users are really asking how easy something is to actually reach. A place slightly closer across a river with no nearby crossing can rank above one genuinely easier to get to, and nothing in a static geometric index can know that. Real travel-time isochrones depend on transport mode and time of day, so they cannot be baked into a static artifact at all, and a routing call per candidate costs milliseconds against the nanoseconds the scan budget assumes. The honest response is to ship straight-line distance labelled as exactly that, and accept the gap is worst precisely where users notice it most: waterfronts, cities cut by rail lines, and anywhere with real elevation change.

**Truncating a dense cell throws away results someone specifically wanted, and there is no capping rule that avoids it.** A cell holding tens of thousands of entries cannot return all of them, so some cap on candidates is unavoidable. Capping by distance discards a genuinely excellent place slightly further out in favour of many mediocre ones nearby; capping by rating discards a good, close option in favour of a famous one at the edge of the radius. A single blended score computed during a unified scan would resolve this, but the cells are scanned independently, so one cell's local top candidates are not necessarily the block's true global top candidates. The bias this creates is real, bounded, and measurable against an uncapped shadow query, but it is not eliminated.

**Cache invalidation is best-effort, and it is sometimes actively wrong in the expensive direction.** The result cache key fans out across category, radius bucket and page, so a single business edit touches a set of cached keys too large to enumerate directly. Invalidating by a coarser prefix instead over-invalidates badly: a large chain updating hours across thousands of locations at once can wipe the busiest cached cells across every major metro simultaneously, driving backend load up sharply for the time it takes the cache to refill. The short TTL, not the invalidation mechanism, is what actually bounds staleness; invalidation is an optimisation that occasionally makes things briefly worse rather than better.

#### Final design
Read it back through the numbers. The ~100,000-to-1 read-to-write ratio is what makes an offline, versioned, promotable artifact the right shape for this index, rather than a live structure absorbing writes the way a moving-entity system requires. The roughly hundredfold gap between scanning a slim self-contained entry and hydrating a full record for every candidate is what makes denormalising every filterable attribute into the index worth its rebuild cost. And the 1000x spread in candidate count across density, tiny in absolute time even at its worst, is what lets a single uniform precision-tiered grid outperform a more elaborate adaptive structure for this specific, static workload.

[The whole design](/diagram/proximity-service?focus=client,clamp,block,scan,rank,geo-index,overlay,result-cache,card-store,artifact-store,edit-stream,build-promote,build-gate,build-map,catalogue,ingest)

> **The numbers to remember.** ~60k/s average, ~300k/s peak · ~100,000:1 read-to-write ratio · ~10GB index, 48 bytes per entry, memory-resident · candidate count spans ~20 to ~22,000 across density, costing well under a millisecond even at its worst.

#### Check your understanding
**Why can a query never be answered by reading just the one cell a user is standing in?** A search radius almost always extends beyond the boundaries of whatever cell contains the searcher, so any answer confined to one cell would silently miss real results near the edges of that cell.

**Why is "target cell plus eight neighbours" sometimes wrong, even though it sounds intuitively complete?** It is only correct when a cell is at least as wide and as tall as the requested radius in both directions. Many cell encodings are rectangular rather than square at certain precision levels, so comparing the radius only against the longer dimension silently under-covers the shorter one.

**Why does packing every filterable attribute into the index entry pay for itself, given that it makes adding a new filter expensive?** Filtering inside a nanosecond-cost scan avoids fetching full records for candidates that will just be discarded, saving roughly a hundredfold in backend load at peak. Rebuilding the index to add a filter is a scheduled, offline job precisely because the underlying entities barely ever change.

**Why does a roughly 100,000-to-1 read-to-write ratio justify building the index offline instead of writing through it live?** At that ratio, the day's actual coordinate changes are small enough to sit entirely in a tiny in-memory overlay, so nothing about correctness depends on the main index being current to the second. A full rebuild becomes a scheduled release rather than a response to an emergency.

**Why can capping the number of candidates returned from a dense cell never be made fully fair?** Any cap has to choose what to discard using only local information about that one cell, but the true best results across the whole search radius can only be known by comparing candidates across every cell in the block together. A cell's own local top candidates are not guaranteed to be the block's actual best results.
### 14. Design Nearby Friends
#### Understanding the problem
Nearby Friends shows which of a user's friends are currently within a radius of them, keeping that answer fresh as everyone involved moves. Sharing is opt-in and revocable per friend, and the app runs on a phone whose battery is a binding constraint the design must respect.

Three things make this harder than an ordinary geo lookup.

First, every indexed point moves, so the number that actually shapes the design is the position write rate, not the query rate. A design that starts from "how do I search nearby points" has picked the wrong side of the problem.

Second, the read side is nearly trivial once seen correctly: nobody ever asks who in the world is near them, only which of roughly two hundred friends are near them, and two hundred is a list small enough to scan directly.

Third, privacy has to be structural rather than a checkbox. Sharing is bidirectional, permission has to be current to the millisecond it is checked, and the design has to survive the fact that "I stopped sharing" is itself information a viewer can infer from silence.

> **What this is not.** The sharper contrast is ride hailing, since it shares the property that actually makes this hard: both index continuously moving points at a comparable write rate, so the difference is not static against moving, it is the shape of the match. Ride hailing is bipartite and open: a rider is matched against drivers who are strangers, so the candidate set is genuinely everyone nearby, and a spatial index over all live supply is unavoidable. Nearby Friends is symmetric and closed: every participant is simultaneously a moving point and a subscriber, and the candidate set is pre-declared by a graph averaging two hundred entries that changes over days, not seconds. That closure deletes the read-side spatial index entirely. It also runs the other way: ride hailing chooses how many drivers to consider and can cap it low, whereas here fan-out is dictated by a social graph nobody controls, so crowd and hot-user cases are something to survive rather than tune away.

#### Requirements and the numbers
**Functional.** See which friends are currently in range. Be notified when one enters or leaves. Grant and revoke sharing per friend. History is a separate, opt-in product.

**Non-functional.** Map staleness under 10 seconds. Crossing notification under 5 seconds. No measurable battery regression. Correct within milliseconds on revoke.

The whole design is decided by four numbers, so derive them before choosing an architecture.

**How many position writes a second is this, really?** Roughly 500M users report at any given moment, split between foreground and background reporting at different adaptive rates. Summing both populations gives **~10M location writes/s peak**, the number the entire write path is sized against, not the query rate.

**How much of that traffic actually matters to anyone?** Most people are not near their friends most of the time. Only around 15% of writes have any online, permitted friend currently in range at all. Unconditional, that would still be **~4.5M would-be pushes/s** if every position update were simply streamed to interested parties, which is the number that makes streaming positions directly look expensive and makes a pre-filter worth building.

**How many genuine notifications does the system actually need to deliver?** A user enters or leaves a friend's radius roughly four times a day. Across the whole population that is **~46k crossing events/s**, roughly a hundred times smaller than the unfiltered push figure and two hundred times smaller than the raw write rate. The notification path is small enough to be structurally uninteresting, which is exactly the design's intent.

**What does polling the map cost instead of pushing every position?** A ten-second poll across roughly a hundred million foreground users, each checking around twenty online friends, comes to **~200M key reads/s**, needing on the order of **~400 cache nodes**. That is a real cost, but it buys away an entire class of stateful delivery infrastructure that pushing every position would require.

> **The numbers to carry.** ~10M writes/s, sized by device population and motion, not by query volume · only ~15% of writes have any interested party at all · ~46k crossing events/s, ~200x below the raw write rate · polling the map costs ~200M key reads/s, roughly 400 cache nodes, in exchange for zero delivery-side state.

#### Three attenuation stages
Every stage in this design exists to shed load before the next one has to pay for it, because nothing downstream can afford to see the full 10M writes/s.

- **Device sampling**: the phone decides its own report rate from on-device motion state, before a single byte leaves it.
- **The pre-filter**: every surviving write asks one cheap question, does this change anything for anyone, before it is allowed to cost anything more.
- **Crossing-only delivery**: what finally gets pushed is a verdict, not a stream of coordinates.

The entities:

- **Latest position**: one key per user, holding coordinates and a timestamp with a short expiry, with no history kept on this path by default.
- **Cell membership**: the same kind of geographic key a static proximity index would use for lookup, repurposed here as a write-side placement key deciding which shard a position lands on.
- **Crossing event**: `(subject, observer, entered or left, timestamp)`, deliberately carrying no coordinates at all.
- **Permission pair**: a bidirectional consent record, joined on every read that produces an answer, never cached at the point of delivery.

The write path and the read path are genuinely separate calls with different shapes:

```
cell = geohash(lat, lng, precision=5)
redis.set(f"loc:{user_id}", pack(lat, lng, ts), ex=300)
entered = crossings(user_id, cell, radius_km)   # local, uses this node's cell membership
for friend_id in entered:
    if permitted(user_id, friend_id):
        publish(f"user.crossing.{user_id}", friend_id, ts)
```

#### High-level design
Follow the numbered arrows. The write side and the read side barely touch, which is deliberate: one is sized by device population, the other by however many people currently have the map open.

[From a position report to a crossing pushed, and separately, a map polled](/diagram/nearby-friends?focus=device,ingest,latest-loc,prefilter,acl-gate,publisher,crossing-bus,subscription,friend-socket,map-client,nearby-api,e1,e2,e4,e5,e6,e8,e9,e10,e11,e12,e13)

1. A phone's **Write latest position** call lands on the **Latest-position store**, sharded by a coarse geographic cell so that anyone physically nearby is already resident on the same node.
2. **Pre-filter** intersects the writer's friend list against exactly that node's current cell membership, discarding roughly 85% of writes on the spot with no further cost.
3. Whatever survives passes **Permission check**, and only authorised pairs reach the **Crossing publisher**, which writes to a per-user topic on the **Crossing bus**.
4. **Subscription Service** routes surviving events to whichever friends currently hold an open socket, delivering a verdict with no coordinates attached.
5. Separately, a foreground **Map client** polls **GET /nearby** on its own timer, reading straight from the latest-position store and joining permission on that same read.

> **Why the flow is shaped this way.** The expensive direction is up, not down: ten million writes arrive whether or not anyone is watching, so every stage exists purely to shed load before the next one has to pay for what survives. The map's poll and the crossing push are two genuinely different mechanisms because they are paying for two genuinely different things.

#### Why the friend graph deletes the read-side index
A static proximity search has to narrow an entire world of candidates down to something scannable. Why does this design need no equivalent structure on its read path at all?

[Where the candidate set comes from, and where a spatial structure still shows up](/diagram/nearby-friends?focus=prefilter,cell-members,e5)

**Bad: build a spatial index over every user in the world, the way a static places search would.** Correct in shape, and catastrophically expensive here, because that index would need re-indexing roughly ten million times a second as every point in it moves continuously.

**Good: notice that a query never actually asks "who in the world is near me".** It asks which of a small, pre-declared set of friends are near, and evaluating two hundred distances directly is cheaper than maintaining any index that could answer a broader question nobody is asking.

**Great: let the friend graph itself be the candidate set, and confine the geographic structure to deciding write placement rather than read lookup.** A spatial cell scheme still exists in this design, but it is repurposed: it decides which shard a position write lands on, so that a pre-filter checking "does the writer have a friend nearby" can be answered as a local set intersection rather than a scatter-gather read across the whole fleet.

Worked example. A user in Tokyo whose entire friend list lives in London costs nothing extra to this system on a per-write basis: no shard holding that user's writes will ever contain any of their friends, so the pre-filter is answered by absence, instantly, with no lookup required at all. Compare that to a static proximity search's candidate set, which genuinely must consider every place within a physical radius regardless of any relationship, and therefore cannot shortcut in the same way.

#### The device decides its own report rate
A phone reporting its location every few seconds all day exhausts its battery well before evening. What decides how often to report, and why does that decision belong on the device rather than the server?

[Where motion state turns into a sampling interval](/diagram/nearby-friends?focus=device,ingest,e1)

**Bad: report at a fixed interval regardless of what the device is actually doing.** Simple, and it wastes enormous energy on a phone sitting still on a table, since republishing identical coordinates buys nothing for anyone watching.

**Good: let the server tell each device when to report next, based on who might currently be watching.** That targets the right kind of waste, but it needs a wake mechanism, adds a round trip whenever someone opens a map onto a sleeping device, and is unavailable outright on platforms that grant the app no background execution at all.

**Great: classify motion on the device itself, and set the sampling interval locally from that state.** The phone's sensor hub, not its main application processor, classifies whether the device is stationary, walking, or driving, and picks an interval accordingly: minutes when still, tens of seconds walking, single-digit seconds driving. Only the device knows its own motion state without a round trip, and the classifier itself draws a tiny fraction of the power a GPS fix does.

Worked example. A user who is still, which describes most users for most of a typical day, drops from a driving-rate fix every ten seconds to a stationary-rate fix every five minutes, roughly thirty times fewer writes for that period. The classification cost to achieve this is close to free, drawing single-digit milliamps on a dedicated low-power sensor coprocessor against the hundreds of milliamps a GPS fix requires, which is the entire reason this policy belongs on the device rather than anywhere it would need a network round trip to apply.

[Adaptive sampling: motion state sets the GPS interval](/diagram/nearby-friends?figure=motion-state)

#### Sharding by geography turns writes into local set intersections
The pre-filter has to answer, for every surviving write, whether any friend is nearby. Done naively, that question is itself a distributed lookup on every single write. What makes it cheap instead?

[Where a write lands, and why its candidates are already there](/diagram/nearby-friends?focus=ingest,latest-loc,cell-members,prefilter,e2,e4,e5)

**Bad: shard the latest-position store by user id, the obvious default.** A write lands wherever that user's id happens to hash to, with no relationship to where they physically are. Answering "is any friend nearby" then means fetching each of roughly twenty online friends' positions from potentially twenty different shards, a scatter-gather on every single write, whose tail latency is dominated by the slowest of those twenty reads.

**Good: cache friend positions locally to avoid repeated cross-shard reads.** That helps read-heavy patterns, but positions here change every few seconds to minutes for an active user, so a cache is stale again almost as soon as it is built.

**Great: shard by a coarse geographic cell instead of by user id.** A write from anywhere inside a given cell lands on the node that owns that cell, which means everyone physically near the writer is already resident on that same node. The pre-filter becomes a local set intersection, the writer's friend list against this node's current cell membership, with no network hop and no fan-in at all.

This trades one cost for a different, smaller one: users migrate between shards as they physically move between cells, but at realistic crossing rates that migration traffic is a small single-digit percentage of the write rate, cheap enough to treat as noise. The real cost surfaces where population itself concentrates: a quiet cell holds a few thousand reporters, but a stadium or festival cell can hold tens of thousands within a few hundred metres, which is exactly the geography-based sharding scheme's blind spot, since load now follows population directly rather than being spread evenly by a hash. The mitigation, splitting any cell above a threshold into a small, bounded number of hash sub-shards, bounds the worst case but also reintroduces, in precisely that crowd scenario, the cross-node scatter-gather geographic sharding exists to avoid.

[Sharding by cell keeps a write's candidates local](/diagram/nearby-friends?figure=cell-sharding)

#### Sending verdicts, not positions
Once a write survives the pre-filter, what actually gets sent to an interested friend? The answer is not the position that triggered the check.

[Where a surviving write becomes a delivered verdict, never coordinates](/diagram/nearby-friends?focus=prefilter,acl-gate,publisher,crossing-bus,subscription,friend-socket,e6,e8,e9,e10,e11)

**Bad: forward the triggering position itself to every interested friend.** A friend walking past generates one position update after another as they move through the radius, so the observer's client receives a stream of coordinates rather than a single fact, and every one of those coordinates sits in that client's memory whether or not it was ever displayed.

**Good: forward only positions that actually caused a crossing, filtering out the rest.** That cuts volume sharply, but the observer's client still ends up holding raw coordinates it did not strictly need, and a compromised or merely curious client can passively accumulate a track of a friend's movements over time.

**Great: publish a verdict, not a position, and let the observer's own client fetch fresh coordinates only when it is actively displaying a map.** A crossing event carries only who, which direction, and when, with no latitude or longitude in it at all. An observer who is not currently looking at a map never receives coordinates at all, and one who is gets them freshly from the poll path, never from something cached off a notification.

Crossings need hysteresis to avoid flapping at the boundary: entering and leaving thresholds set apart from each other, plus a cooldown before re-notifying the same pair, mean someone loitering near the edge of the radius produces one notification rather than dozens as ordinary GPS noise nudges them back and forth across a single boundary.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 210" role="img" aria-label="A position stream sends every coordinate as a friend walks through the radius; a verdict-only design sends one entered event and one left event, with no coordinates in either">
  <style>
    .acc{stroke:var(--accent);fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.15}
    .dot{fill:currentColor}
    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    .sub{fill:currentColor;opacity:.8;font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
  </style>
  <text class="lbl" x="8" y="16">Position stream: one message per fix</text>
  <g transform="translate(20,32)">
    <circle class="dot" cx="0" cy="10" r="5"/><circle class="dot" cx="42" cy="10" r="5"/><circle class="dot" cx="84" cy="10" r="5"/><circle class="dot" cx="126" cy="10" r="5"/><circle class="dot" cx="168" cy="10" r="5"/><circle class="dot" cx="210" cy="10" r="5"/><circle class="dot" cx="252" cy="10" r="5"/><circle class="dot" cx="294" cy="10" r="5"/><circle class="dot" cx="336" cy="10" r="5"/>
  </g>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="72">every fix while inside the radius reaches the client</text>
  <text class="lbl" x="8" y="115">Verdict only: two events, no coordinates</text>
  <g transform="translate(20,132)">
    <circle class="acc" cx="10" cy="10" r="6"/><text class="sub" x="10" y="33">entered</text>
    <circle class="acc" cx="330" cy="10" r="6"/><text class="sub" x="330" y="33">left</text>
  </g>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="180">only who, which direction, and when —</text>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="195">never latitude or longitude</text>
</svg>
```

#### Permission checked on the read, never cached at fan-out
A revoked friend should stop appearing on the very next answer, with no delay. What has to be true of where the permission check runs for that to actually hold?

[Where a permission decision is made, on the same path that produces an answer](/diagram/nearby-friends?focus=acl-gate,perm-cache,perm-db,nearby-api,e7,e14,e15,e16)

**Bad: check permission once, then cache the decision for delivery routing.** Fast on every subsequent lookup, and it means a revoked pair keeps being served for however long that cached decision survives, a real window during which private location data continues to leak.

**Good: shorten the cache lifetime to reduce the exposure window.** A shorter TTL genuinely narrows the gap, but it never closes it, and under load, invalidation itself can lag behind the TTL that was supposed to bound it.

**Great: join permission on the exact path that produces the answer, every single time, and never cache the decision for delivery.** Whether the answer comes from a poll response or a crossing evaluation, the permission pair is checked live on that path. The window this leaves is zero by construction on the next answer, because there is no separate cached decision that could be stale in the first place; there is only ever the current state of the permission record.

Worked example. A user revokes a friend's access. Under a fan-out cache with even a five-second lifetime, that friend can still receive a push carrying fresh location for up to five seconds, sometimes longer under load if the invalidation signal itself lags. Under a read-time check, the very next poll response or crossing evaluation, whichever the friend's client next triggers, joins against the permission record as it now stands, and the revoked pair simply cannot produce an answer anymore. The cost of this design is paid once, as one extra join on every read; the alternative pays nothing per read and instead accepts an unbounded worst case exactly where the consequence of being wrong is a privacy failure, not a slow response.

#### Where it breaks
| Layer | Failure | How the design handles it |
|---|---|---|
| Battery | A device stuck in high-frequency GPS mode drains far faster than expected | Motion-state sampling cuts the rate by an order of magnitude or more for a still device, with the classifier itself costing a fraction of a GPS fix |
| Hot cells | A crowd concentrates far more reporters onto one shard than an ordinary cell holds | Any cell above a threshold splits into a small, bounded number of hash sub-shards, trading load for reintroduced cross-node reads in exactly that case |
| Hot user | An account with an unusually large friend list degrades its own poll cost | The visible sharing set is capped, and that user's own read path degrades first rather than affecting anyone else's |
| Permission checks | Ten million reads a second against a permission store would be too slow if uncached | A read-through cache invalidated on write, not on a timer, so there is no window where a revoked pair is still served |
| Update storms | A misbehaving client build ships updates far faster than the design assumes | Client-side debouncing plus server-side coalescing within a short window per user, since the server cannot assume a well-behaved client |
| Network gaps | A device reconnects after a signal gap holding buffered samples | The pre-filter evaluates crossings against the whole buffered sequence, not only the newest point, so a friend passed during the gap is not silently missed |
| History storage | Naive per-user partitioning grows without bound over an account's lifetime | Partitioning by `(user_id, day_bucket)` plus movement-gated writes bounds each partition to roughly a day's worth of genuine movement |

#### What this design does not solve
**A silent pause is not actually silent, and pretending otherwise would be dishonest.** Every location product needs a way to stop sharing without announcing it, because the realistic threat here is not a stranger scraping a directory, it is someone who already has consent on file and is watching closely. But absence is itself a signal: a dot that stops moving at a specific moment can simply be asked about by whoever was watching it. Making a pause genuinely undetectable would mean fabricating plausible fake positions, which means lying to one user about another user's location, and that is not something this design is willing to build. The available mitigations, routine-looking expiry, never surfacing an explicit "paused" state, coarse last-seen rounding, narrow the inference without closing it.

**Revocation stops the next read and reaches nothing already delivered.** A read-time permission check gives a genuinely zero-length window on any answer produced after the revoke, the strongest guarantee the server side can offer. It says nothing about positions a friend's client already holds in memory or chose to retain, and a modified client logging every polled position since sharing began keeps all of it regardless. Capping client-side retention, quantising shared precision, and keeping a server-side access log help after the fact; none of it retroactively un-sends anything already delivered.

**Geographic sharding degrades exactly where the product matters most.** The pre-filter is cheap specifically because people physically near a writer are already on that writer's shard, and a crowd inverts that assumption completely. At a festival, precisely the situation where finding friends matters most, sub-sharding under load means notifications arrive far slower than target, and some do not arrive at all. The alternatives are all worse another way: a second index keyed by friendship roughly doubles the write path to cover well under a tenth of a percent of cells, and simply raising the sub-shard cap trades cross-node fan-in for a local scan that degrades just as badly at higher volume.

#### Final design
Read it back through the numbers. The gap between ~10M raw writes and ~46k actual crossing notifications, roughly two hundredfold, is what the three-stage pipeline, device sampling, the pre-filter, and verdict-only delivery, exists to produce, and no single stage alone gets there. A friend graph averaging two hundred entries being cheaper to scan directly than any spatial index could be maintained is what deletes an entire read-side subsystem a static proximity service would need. And a zero-length revocation window, bought by checking permission on the read rather than caching it at delivery, is the one guarantee this design refuses to compromise on, because for location data getting it wrong is a safety failure, not a latency one.

[The whole design](/diagram/nearby-friends?focus=device,ingest,latest-loc,cell-members,prefilter,acl-gate,publisher,crossing-bus,subscription,friend-socket,map-client,nearby-api,perm-cache,perm-db,history)

> **The numbers to remember.** ~10M writes/s, sized by device population · only ~15% of writes have any interested party, ~4.5M would-be pushes/s unfiltered · ~46k crossing events/s actually delivered, ~200x below raw writes · ~200M key reads/s to poll the map, versus a stateful routing table pushing would require instead.

#### Check your understanding
**Why does this design need no spatial index on its read path, when a static proximity search absolutely does?** A proximity search must narrow an entire world of candidates down to something scannable, because nothing pre-declares which places are worth considering. Here the candidate set is already given by a friend graph averaging two hundred entries, small enough to scan directly, so nothing needs to be indexed for reading at all.

**Why does the device decide its own reporting rate instead of the server deciding for it?** Only the device knows its current motion state without a network round trip, and classifying that state costs a small fraction of the power a GPS fix does. A server-directed schedule would need a wake mechanism and add latency exactly when someone opens a map onto a sleeping device.

**Why does sharding the latest-position store by geography rather than by user id make the pre-filter cheap?** A write lands on the node that owns the writer's current geographic cell, so anyone physically nearby, including any friends, is already resident on that same node. The pre-filter becomes a local set intersection instead of a scatter-gather read across potentially twenty different shards.

**Why does a crowd break exactly the mechanism that makes the ordinary case cheap?** Geographic sharding assumes population spreads roughly evenly across cells, but a festival or stadium concentrates tens of thousands of reporters into one small cell. Splitting that cell into sub-shards bounds the damage but reintroduces the cross-node reads the geographic scheme exists specifically to avoid.

**Why is checking permission on every read strictly better here than caching it at the point of delivery?** A read-time check is current by construction, giving a zero-length window between a revoke and it taking effect on the next answer produced. Any cache at the delivery layer has a window equal to however long invalidation takes to propagate, which for location data is a safety property, not merely a latency one.
### 15. Design Google Maps
#### Understanding the problem
Google Maps does three jobs that look like one product: it draws the map, it plans a route, and it narrates that route while you drive. The drawing is a static-asset problem, the narration is mostly a client concern, and the route is the one that is genuinely hard.

Two things make routing hard.

First, the scale of the search. A continental road graph has around 10 million intersections and 30 million road segments. A plain shortest-path search over that graph takes on the order of a second of CPU, and the product has to answer in under 100ms. Nothing about sharding the graph across machines fixes this, because a route that crosses a shard boundary needs both shards plus a way to join them, which is a smaller version of the same problem.

Second, the numbers that make the search fast go stale every five minutes. Live traffic replaces the travel-time weight on every road segment continuously, but the structure that makes a query fast is built by hours of preprocessing against one fixed set of weights. Freshness and precomputation pull in opposite directions, and the whole design is a position on that trade.

> **What this is not.** It looks like the ride-hailing question: both are geospatial, both use latitude and longitude, both ship a map to a phone. Underneath, ride hailing indexes points that move constantly and answers "who is near", where a second-best answer costs a few seconds of pickup time. This design indexes a graph that barely changes and answers "what is the shortest path", where a wrong answer sends someone down a closed road. Ride hailing calls a routing service like this one for its ETAs; this is the component, that is the system built around it.

#### Requirements and the numbers
**Functional.** Serve map tiles at every zoom level. Geocode a text query to a location. Plan a route between two points. Run turn-by-turn navigation with live re-planning. Fold live traffic into ETAs and route choice.

**Non-functional.** Tile fetch p99 under 500ms. Route compute under 100ms inside the routing pod, under 1s end to end. A verified road closure reflected in routing within 60 seconds. ETA error p50 under 10% of trip duration.

The whole design is decided by four numbers, so derive them before drawing anything.

**How much load hits the tile origin?** ~500M daily users, each panning through ~20 tiles a session, gives 500M × 20 = 10B tile requests a day, or 10B ÷ 86,400 ≈ 116k/s average and **~350k/s at commute peak**. Tile popularity is heavily skewed towards city centres, so a CDN absorbs measured hit rates above 95%. Origin load is the leftover 5%: 350k × 0.05 ≈ **17k/s at peak**, one modest fleet rather than the full number.

**What does one continent's road graph cost to hold in memory?** About 10 million nodes and 30 million edges. Contraction adds roughly one shortcut edge per original edge, so 60 million edges at 32 bytes each (two node ids, a weight, flags) is 60M × 32B ≈ **2GB resident per continent**.

**What does the query cost without preprocessing, and what does it cost with it?** At 10k route computes a second, an unguided search at roughly 0.5s of CPU per query needs 10,000 × 0.5 = **5,000 cores** running flat out against a 100ms budget. A preprocessed hierarchy answers in about 150 microseconds: 10,000 × 0.00015 = **1.5 cores**. That gap, roughly four orders of magnitude, is the entire argument for precomputing anything at all.

**How much of the road network actually has a live weight on it?** ~1M GPS probes a second over a 5-minute window is 1M × 300 = 300M probes. Probes follow the roads people already drive, so they concentrate: about 90% land on the busiest 3% of the roughly 150M global edges. The other 97% of edges never see enough samples in a window to trust, and fall back to a historical time-of-day profile.

> **The numbers to carry.** ~350k tile requests/s peak, 95%+ absorbed by a CDN · ~2GB per continent for a contracted road graph · 5,000 cores unguided vs 1.5 cores preprocessed at 10k route computes/s · only ~3% of edges carry a measured weight in any given window.

#### Three systems, one shared graph
It helps to say plainly that this is three subsystems sharing a road-graph source and very little else.

- **Tiles** are a static-asset problem: slice the world into a quadtree, render once, cache behind a CDN.
- **Traffic** is a stream-aggregation problem: snap GPS probes to road segments, reduce them per window, publish new edge weights.
- **Routing** is the hard one: a shortest-path query over a graph whose weights move faster than the structure built to search it quickly.

The entities:

- **Tile** `(zoom, x, y)`, geometry-only in the vector format, ~10 to 50KB.
- **Road graph**: nodes are intersections, edges are road segments carrying a travel-time weight plus restrictions (one-way, turn bans, vehicle class).
- **Hierarchy topology**: the contraction order and the shortcut edges it implies. Depends only on the shape of the graph.
- **Weight metric**: one float per edge. Depends on current travel times, rebuilt every 5 minutes.
- **Segment state**: a road's current traffic condition (free, slow, heavy, stopped, or closed), tracked with hysteresis.

The API is three request paths that never meet again after the client:

```
GET  /tiles/{z}/{x}/{y}.png            → image
GET  /vector_tiles/{z}/{x}/{y}.mvt     → vector data
POST /geocode          body: { query } → { lat, lng, address }
POST /route             body: { origin, dest, mode, prefs }
                                        → { polyline, steps, eta }
WS   /navigate                         ← turn-by-turn updates
```

#### High-level design
Follow the request path a single route computation takes.

[The hot path from request to polyline](/diagram/google-maps?focus=client,upward-search,shortcut-unpack,eta-model,cch-topology,weight-metric,e6,e7,e8,e9,e10,e11)

1. The **Client** sends `POST /route`, which lands on the **Upward search** step inside the resident **Routing pod**.
2. The search runs bidirectionally over the **Hierarchy topology**, climbing from both ends towards the motorway level, using the current **Weight metric** for every edge cost.
3. The winning path is a chain of shortcuts, so **Shortcut unpacking** recursively expands each one back into real road segments.
4. Those segments feed the **ETA model**, which adds a learned correction on top of the raw weight sum, then returns the polyline, turns and ETA to the **Client**.
5. Underneath, two arrows keep the pod's inputs current without the client ever seeing them: the **Hierarchy topology** is replaced weekly, and the **Weight metric** is swapped in every 5 minutes.

> **Why the flow is shaped this way.** Everything in this path is either a lookup or a bounded search against a structure someone else kept fresh. Nothing on the hot path scans the graph, joins a database, or waits on a rebuild; the rebuilds run on their own clocks and hand the pod a finished artefact.

#### Four orders of magnitude: making the query possible
How do you answer a shortest-path query over 10 million intersections inside a 100ms budget?

[The routing pod and the structure it searches](/diagram/google-maps?focus=routing-pod,upward-search,shortcut-unpack,cch-topology,e6,e7,e10)

**Bad: an unguided search from scratch.** A plain shortest-path algorithm settles nodes in increasing distance from the source, so a continental query settles most of the graph before it reaches the target: roughly 0.5s of CPU. At 10k queries a second that is 5,000 cores for a query with a 100ms budget, and sharding the graph does not help, because a route crossing a shard boundary needs both shards and a join.

**Good: guide the search with a lower bound.** Pick a few dozen landmark nodes scattered across the map, precompute each node's distance to every landmark, and use those distances as a lower bound on how far is left to go. The search then steers towards the target instead of expanding in every direction. Preprocessing is minutes, a few hundred bytes per node, and the bound stays valid when weights only get worse, which is what live traffic does. It buys roughly 10x over an unguided search, useful in a region whose weights just moved, but nowhere near enough on its own for a continent.

**Great: contract the graph once, then only ever search upward.** Rank every junction by importance. Working bottom-up, remove each junction and, wherever no equal-or-shorter alternative exists, add a direct shortcut edge between its neighbours that stands in for the path through it. A shortcut is exact: it represents a real path, not an approximation, so no optimal route is ever lost. The query then runs two searches at once, one from the origin and one from the destination, and each only ever relaxes edges towards higher-ranked nodes. The two searches meet somewhere near the motorway level instead of exploring the whole graph, settling hundreds of nodes rather than millions.

[Contraction: a shortcut skips a removed junction](/diagram/google-maps?figure=contraction)

Contraction hierarchies, introduced by Geisberger, Sanders, Schultes and Delling in 2008, are roughly four orders of magnitude faster than an unguided search: 150 microseconds against a second, exact rather than approximate. Landmark-guided search stays useful as a fallback for a region whose metric is mid-refresh, because its bound survives weight increases without needing a rebuild.

#### Two artefacts, two clocks
The hierarchy above assumed one fixed set of weights. Live traffic replaces every edge weight every five minutes. How does the structure stay correct?

[The topology and the metric that runs through it](/diagram/google-maps?focus=cch-topology,weight-metric,order-builder,customisation-pass,e12,e13,e14)

**Bad: rebuild the whole hierarchy overnight and paint traffic deltas on top.** Both the shortcut weights and the decision to add each shortcut in the first place were computed against one specific set of weights. When traffic changes sharply, a shortcut that used to summarise "go via the motorway" now summarises the wrong thing, and worse, a shortcut that was skipped because an alternative was shorter under the old weights may now be exactly what is needed and simply does not exist. Adjusting the numbers on top cannot repair a missing edge. The result is not merely stale, it can be silently wrong, and nothing at query time can detect it.

**Good: rebuild the entire hierarchy every time the metric changes.** Correct, but the rebuild is hours of work per continent against a traffic window of five minutes. It never catches up.

**Great: split contraction into a metric-independent order and a metric-dependent customisation pass.** Derive the contraction order from the graph's shape alone, typically by a technique called nested dissection, which repeatedly splits the graph along small separating cuts. Insert every shortcut the order implies, with no check against any particular set of weights. That topology is valid for any set of non-negative weights, forever, until the roads themselves change. Then, whenever the traffic metric updates, run one bottom-up sweep: visit contracted nodes in order and set each shortcut's weight to the minimum over its two possible paths. No search, one pass, parallel by rank level, about a second for a continent-sized graph.

Two artefacts now live on two clocks. The **Hierarchy topology** is rebuilt weekly, when roads physically change: about 2GB per continent. The **Weight metric** is rebuilt every 5 minutes, when travel times change: one float per edge, 60M × 4B = 240MB per continent, swapped into resident pods behind a pointer flip so a query never sees half a metric. Customisation costs roughly a second of work every 300 seconds, a 0.3% duty cycle, and the price for that freshness is a query that runs at about 1ms instead of 150 microseconds, because the metric-independent topology carries more shortcut edges than a metric-aware one would. Published as customizable route planning in 2011 and as customizable contraction hierarchies from 2014, this split is the single idea the whole routing design turns on.

> **Why the split, not a smarter overlay.** A shortcut is either implied by the order or it is not; there is no partial version of a missing edge. Making the order metric-independent is what makes "recompute the weights" a safe, total operation instead of a partial patch that can silently miss a now-necessary shortcut.

#### Turning probes into a trustworthy weight
Sketch workers aside, the weight metric above has to come from somewhere. How do a million noisy GPS pings a second become one number per road segment that a query can trust?

[Where the metric comes from: probes into segment state into the metric](/diagram/google-maps?focus=probe-bus,traffic-agg,map-match,window-reduce,segment-state,closure-gate,weight-metric,e15,e16,e17,e18,e21,e23,e24)

**Bad: use each probe's instantaneous speed as the segment weight.** A parked car with location sharing on and a motorcyclist filtering through traffic at high speed land in the same sample set as ordinary traffic. Every new probe would rewrite the weight, which would rewrite the metric, which would re-plan every navigation on that road.

**Good: reduce probes per segment with a trimmed mean over a window.** Snap each probe to a road segment by position, heading and recent trajectory, discard the top and bottom 10% of samples in a five-minute window, and average the rest. This filters single-probe noise, but a segment sitting right at a threshold can still flip state every window, and every flip invalidates cached routes and re-plans drivers who are already committed to that road.

**Great: a state machine with hysteresis, plus a separate channel for closures.** Each segment holds one of four traffic states, Free, Slow, Heavy or Stopped, and a state change requires the new trimmed mean to hold for two consecutive windows before it takes effect. A segment flickering around a boundary stays in its current state until the change is real. Closures get their own path entirely: a verified closure arrives on an override channel that skips the aggregation window and sets the edge impassable within seconds, because a closed road produces zero probes, which looks identical to a quiet one, and the state machine alone can never tell the two apart.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 300" role="img" aria-label="A raw probe stream flickers a single-sample weight; a trimmed mean over a window smooths it but still flips near a threshold; a two-window hysteresis state holds steady">
  <style>
    .ax{stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.3;stroke-width:1}
    .raw{fill:none;stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.45;stroke-width:1.3}
    .trim{fill:none;stroke:currentColor;stroke-width:1.6}
    .hyst{fill:none;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:2.2}
    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 12px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    .sub{fill:currentColor;opacity:.75;font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
  </style>
  <text class="lbl" x="8" y="16">raw probes, per-ping</text>
  <line class="ax" x1="8" y1="80" x2="392" y2="80"/>
  <path class="raw" d="M8,45 L48,68 L88,38 L128,72 L168,42 L208,70 L248,44 L288,66 L328,42 L368,68"/>
  <text class="lbl" x="8" y="118">trimmed mean, 5-min window</text>
  <line class="ax" x1="8" y1="178" x2="392" y2="178"/>
  <path class="trim" d="M8,168 L168,169 L208,138 L392,140"/>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="196">flips at every window crossing the threshold</text>
  <text class="lbl" x="8" y="234" fill="var(--accent)">hysteresis state</text>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="250">holds for 2 windows before it moves</text>
  <line class="ax" x1="8" y1="278" x2="392" y2="278"/>
  <path class="hyst" d="M8,268 L208,270 L208,270 L392,235"/>
</svg>
```

The single most important consequence: a route is exact only against the metric it was planned on, and that metric is up to five minutes old. Because the metric is a versioned, 240MB-per-continent artefact rather than a live overlay, a disputed route can be replanned against the exact array that produced it, which is the only honest way to answer why the system chose that road.

#### One geometry corpus for every style
The map on screen has to render as light mode, dark mode, satellite and whatever comes next, on phones, watches and car head units. How do you avoid paying for each style separately?

[The tile pipeline: source data into the tile origin, served through the client](/diagram/google-maps?focus=client,tile-origin,map-source,e-tiles,e-tilebuild)

**Bad: render a raster pixel pyramid per style.** Producing a PNG image per tile per zoom level per style is the obvious first build.
