3. **Rate plan resolver** finds the cheapest legal combination of nightly rates for the stay, as a pure read against a price snapshot.
4. **Saga orchestrator** issues one conditional decrement to **Inventory rows** through the **Inventory service**, all nights or none, roughly 2ms of lock hold time.
5. Only once inventory is committed does the saga call the **Payment provider** to authorise, not capture, the card.
6. Saga state is written to **Bookings + saga state** at every transition, so a crash mid-flow can resume from the last completed step.

> **Why the flow is shaped this way.** The inventory service owns the smallest possible critical section: one conditional decrement, committed before any external call happens. The booking service is a saga orchestrator rather than a monolithic transaction, because the payment leg is a network call to a third party and nothing that slow may sit inside a transaction holding inventory rows.

#### The number that isn't the room count
Rooms inside a class are interchangeable, and an unsold room-night is gone forever. What number should the booking path actually enforce?

[The row, and the two writers that touch it](/diagram/hotel-reservation?focus=inventory-svc,inventory-table,e10)

**Bad: track a single count of rooms remaining, equal to physical capacity.** This is the number everyone reaches for first, and it never oversells, which sounds safe until the arithmetic is done. A 120-room class with a 10% no-show rate leaves roughly 12 rooms empty every sold-out night, revenue that a comparable hotel down the road may capture instead, and that this hotel can never recover once the night has passed.

**Good: let one mutable count represent both physical capacity and how many are sold.** A single `available_count`, decremented by bookings and reset nightly by a forecast job, seems like it should work. It creates a read-modify-write race: the forecast job has to read how many are already sold in order to write a new remaining count, and a job that takes minutes to run across a large chain will occasionally overwrite a count that live bookings changed while it was thinking, silently resurrecting or destroying inventory.

**Great: split the row into two columns with two separate owners.** `sold` is written only by the booking path, incremented by confirmations and decremented only by compensations and cancellations. `allowance` is written only by the nightly forecast job, physical capacity plus a deliberate oversell, and it is simply overwritten, never read-modified. The booking path enforces `sold < allowance` and never looks at how that number was derived; the forecast job never looks at `sold` to decide what to write. Neither writer needs the other's value, so the race disappears by construction rather than by locking around it.

[One shared column races; two owned columns don't](/diagram/hotel-reservation?figure=sold-allowance)

#### One statement, ordered by date
A three-night stay must reserve every night or none. Two overlapping stays contend on the shared nights. How do you get both properties from one write?

[The write that checks and decrements together](/diagram/hotel-reservation?focus=bk-rates,bk-saga,inventory-svc,inventory-table,e8,e9,e10)

**Bad: read the availability, then decide, then write.** `SELECT` to check `sold < allowance`, then a separate `UPDATE` to increment it, is two round trips with a gap between them. Another booking can slip into that gap, both reads see room, both writes succeed, and the room-night is sold twice.

**Good: hold a lock across a read-then-write with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`.** This closes the race, at the cost of an extra round trip and locks held across an application hop, which lengthens the critical section for no benefit once a single statement can do the same job in one trip.

**Great: one conditional `UPDATE` that checks and writes atomically, visiting rows in date order.**

```sql
UPDATE inventory
   SET sold = sold + 1
 WHERE hotel_id = $1 AND room_type_id = $2
   AND date >= $3 AND date < $4
   AND sold < allowance
RETURNING date;
```

Fewer rows returned than nights requested means at least one night is unavailable, and the whole transaction rolls back, returning every lock it briefly held. The all-or-nothing property comes free from that rollback. Deadlock avoidance is a side effect of the primary key rather than a rule anyone has to remember: a range predicate over `(hotel_id, room_type_id, date)` forces an ascending index scan, so two overlapping stays, say the 10th to 12th and the 11th to 13th, both visit the shared nights of the 11th and 12th in the same order, and the second transaction simply waits rather than deadlocking.

```svg
  </style>

  <rect class="box acc" x="106" y="26" width="90" height="30" rx="5"/><text class="sub" x="151" y="41">11th</text>
  <rect class="box acc" x="204" y="26" width="90" height="30" rx="5"/><text class="sub" x="249" y="41">12th</text>
  <text class="lbl" x="8" y="88" style="text-anchor:start">Stay B: 11th, 12th, 13th</text>
  <rect class="box" x="106" y="98" width="90" height="30" rx="5"/><text class="sub" x="151" y="113">11th</text>
  <rect class="box" x="204" y="98" width="90" height="30" rx="5"/><text class="sub" x="249" y="113">12th</text>
  <rect class="box" x="302" y="98" width="90" height="30" rx="5"/><text class="sub" x="347" y="113">13th</text>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="156" style="text-anchor:start">both scans visit 11th before 12th:</text>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="172" style="text-anchor:start">A locks first, B waits, no deadlock</text>
</svg>
```

#### Payment outside the transaction
Card authorisation can take 30 seconds. Holding the inventory locks that long would sink throughput. Removing payment from the transaction opens a different problem: what if it fails afterwards?

[The saga, and what cleans up after it](/diagram/hotel-reservation?focus=bk-saga,payment,bookings-table,recovery-svc,resume-worker,sweeper,e12,e13,e19,e20,e21)

**Bad: hold the inventory transaction open across the payment call.** Correct in the sense that nothing is ever committed without payment. It drops a single row's throughput ceiling from roughly 500 attempts a second to about 5, because lock hold time now includes a call to a third party that can take 30 seconds, and it pins a database connection to every user staring at a card form.

**Good: wrap inventory and payment in a distributed transaction.** This would avoid the inconsistency window if it worked. It does not: payment providers do not participate in two-phase commit, and a coordinator that crashes after prepare holds inventory locks indefinitely with no way to resolve them.

**Great: commit inventory first, run payment as a saga step, and clean up if it fails.** **Saga orchestrator** decrements inventory and writes the booking as `InventoryReserved` in one fast transaction, then calls the **Payment provider** to authorise, not capture, the card. If authorisation fails, a compensation gives the room-nights back, keyed to `(booking_id, step_id)` so running it twice has the same effect as once. If the user simply abandons checkout, the **Expiry sweeper** releases any booking still `InventoryReserved` after 10 minutes; a **Resume worker** replays a crashed saga from its last completed step rather than restarting it.

The honest cost of this shape: there is a real window, up to 10 minutes, where a room-night is held by a booking that has not paid for anything, and it takes a dedicated, alarmed sweeper to bound it rather than letting it happen for free.

#### Guaranteeing a retry only books once
A user's connection drops after they click Book. Their client retries the same request. Nothing about that retry should produce a second reservation.

[Where the retry gets caught](/diagram/hotel-reservation?focus=client,bk-dedupe,e4,e6,e7)

**Bad: check for the idempotency key in a cache only.** Fast, and it fails exactly when it matters most: a cache failover during a traffic burst is precisely when clients are retrying most aggressively, and losing the cache's contents at that moment reopens the duplicate-booking window it was supposed to close.

**Good: check the key in application memory on the handling server.** This avoids the cache dependency and introduces a worse one: a retry that happens to land on a different server instance never sees the first attempt at all, so the guarantee only holds as long as retries are sticky to one process, which nothing about HTTP promises.

**Great: store the key under a unique database constraint, in the same transaction as the booking it protects, with a cache only as a fast path.** **Idempotency check** inserts `(idempotency_key, booking_id)` with a unique constraint. A duplicate insert fails the constraint and the handler returns the existing booking rather than starting again. The cache in front serves the common case quickly, but the durable row is what actually makes the guarantee true; the cache can disappear entirely and correctness survives, only latency suffers.

#### Search can be wrong for five seconds; booking cannot
Search has to answer tens of thousands of queries a second from a huge index. Booking has to be exactly right. Building one system that does both well is the wrong ambition. What should each one actually promise?

[Change capture feeding a deliberately stale index](/diagram/hotel-reservation?focus=inventory-table,inventory-svc,cdc,search-index,search-svc,e9,e10,e17,e18)

**Bad: query the transactional inventory table directly from search.** This gives search a perfectly fresh answer, and it puts search's enormous, cacheable read volume directly onto the same table that the booking path needs to serialise writes against, which is the one resource in this design that must stay cheap to lock.

**Good: cache search results and hope staleness stays low.** A time-based cache in front of a live query reduces load, and it does not remove the coupling: the underlying query still competes with booking writes whenever the cache misses, and there is no structural guarantee about how stale a hit can be.

**Great: feed a separate, denormalised index from change capture, and make booking the only reader that has to be right.** **Change capture** streams the write log off **Inventory rows** into the **Search index**, which never shares a resource with the booking path and is allowed to run a few seconds behind. **Search service** answers from that index, and when a result turns out to be stale, the booking path's own conditional decrement is the real check: the user sees a clear "no longer available" and searches again, which is friction, not a correctness failure.

The design deliberately puts the strictness where the cost of being wrong is high and none of it where the cost of being wrong is a few seconds of staleness. Search never gets to be a source of truth, and booking never gets to be fast.

#### Where it breaks
| Layer | Failure | How the design handles it |
|---|---|---|
| Inventory row | A popular date takes thousands of booking attempts in seconds | Admission control rejects excess attempts in milliseconds rather than queueing them; a faster lock would not help a genuinely saturated row |
| Forecast job | `allowance` is written from a stale or broken forecast | A hard clamp in the write path rejects any allowance above physical capacity times a policy ceiling, regardless of what the job computed |
| Saga orchestrator | Crash after payment authorisation, before the booking write completes | The resume worker replays from the last persisted step; forward-step idempotency keys make re-running safe |
| Expiry sweeper | The sweeper itself stops running | Bookings stuck in `InventoryReserved` past 10 minutes are counted and alerted on directly; the sweeper carries its own liveness alarm |
| Payment provider | Authorisation hangs or returns errors under load | A circuit breaker refuses new bookings rather than reserving inventory that cannot be paid for |
| Search index | Change-capture lag spikes during a large inventory push | Booking always re-checks at commit, so a stale search result costs one retry, never a wrong reservation |
| Idempotency cache | The cache in front of the durable table fails over | The unique constraint is the actual guarantee; losing the cache costs latency, not correctness |

#### What this design does not solve
**The feedback loop that justifies the oversell runs through a system this design does not own.** The allowance is computed from a forecast, but the walk cost it trades against happens at a front desk the platform typically cannot see, so the model is calibrated against an assumed number rather than a measured one, and it is most wrong on exactly the nights that matter, city-wide sold-out ones.

**First-come-first-served is not the right revenue policy, and this design ships it anyway.** A one-night booking on a peak Friday can block a more valuable four-night stay from ever being offered, and rejecting the smaller booking to protect the larger one would require a forecast inside the synchronous write path, which this design has not taken on.

**Modification is not a first-class operation.** Changing dates is reserve-new-then-release-old, the safe order, and when the new dates overlap the old ones the booking contends against itself, handled by computing a delta rather than by a clean model of what a modification actually is.

#### Final design
Read it back through the numbers. 182.5B inventory rows sharded by `hotel_id` is what makes the write path scale without any special hot-key handling, because one row is touched roughly once every 7,000 days on average. The 9% oversell on a 120-room class is the deliberate business number the transactional path enforces exactly, distinct from the physical room count it is not tracking. And the two-order-of-magnitude cost of holding a lock across payment is why the saga exists at all rather than one large transaction.

[The whole design](/diagram/hotel-reservation?focus=client,search-svc,search-index,cdc,bk-dedupe,bk-rates,bk-saga,idem-table,inventory-svc,inventory-table,bookings-table,payment,booking-events,recovery-svc,resume-worker,sweeper)

> **The numbers to remember.** 182.5B inventory rows, ~18.25TB, sharded by `hotel_id` · one row contended roughly once every 7,000 days, ~500 attempts/s available if needed · a 9% oversell on a 120-room class at a $200/$300 rate-to-walk-cost ratio · payment inside the lock drops throughput from ~500/s to ~5/s per row.

#### Check your understanding
**Why does splitting `sold` and `allowance` into separate columns remove a race that a single count could not?** Because each column has exactly one writer. The booking path only ever compares against `allowance` and increments `sold`; the forecast job only ever overwrites `allowance`. Neither has to read a value the other is actively changing.

**Why does one conditional `UPDATE` beat a `SELECT` followed by an `UPDATE`?** Because the check and the write happen in the same statement, so there is no gap between them for a second booking to slip into, and the lock is held for one round trip instead of two.

**Why does an ascending range predicate on `(hotel_id, room_type_id, date)` prevent deadlocks between overlapping stays?** Because every transaction visits shared rows in the same date order, so two overlapping bookings always contend in the same sequence; the second one waits instead of both transactions holding a lock the other needs.

**Why does authorising a card rather than capturing it matter for the saga's cost of failure?** An authorisation can be voided at zero cost if the booking fails afterwards. A capture moves money, and reversing it means an actual refund with a fee and accounting noise, which is a much more expensive way to undo the same mistake.

**Why is a stale search result acceptable but a stale inventory decrement is not?** Because the cost of being wrong differs by orders of magnitude. A stale search result costs one user one retry. A wrong inventory decrement is two guests holding the same room, which becomes a physical problem at a front desk.
### 20. Design a Distributed Email Service (Gmail)
#### Understanding the problem
An email service accepts mail from any host on the internet, decides inside a single SMTP transaction whether to take it, and then stores it durably and searchably for a billion users for years. The protocol is fixed by a specification from 1982 and cannot be changed.

Two things make this harder than an ordinary write path.

First, roughly half the inbound volume is hostile, and the interface belongs to nobody. Every other system in this space lets its owner define the write path: choose the API, authenticate the caller, version the protocol. Here any host on the internet is a legitimate caller, and the only vocabulary for declining is a three-digit code inside a connection that cannot be reopened.

Second, that decision is asymmetric and irreversible in one specific way. Once a message is refused, it is gone with no way to recall it. Once it is accepted, the acceptance cannot be withdrawn. So the real design question is not what to store, it is which signals are trustworthy enough to be allowed to refuse.

> **What this is not.** It looks like a workplace messaging system: years of history for a large population, per-tenant privacy, full-text search, files stored apart from metadata. There, every writer is an authenticated member of a known organisation, so the write path is a pass-or-fail authorisation check, and the hard problem moves downstream into tenancy and retention. Here nothing about the sender is known before the message arrives, authentication is voluntary, and the expensive decision has to happen inside a connection from a stranger who the system cannot vet in advance.

#### Requirements and the numbers
**Functional.** Accept and deliver SMTP in both directions. Classify and label, never silently discard. Search over the whole mailbox. Threading, labels, attachments.

**Non-functional.** Never silently drop an accepted message. False-positive rate on legitimate mail under 0.1%. Inbox list and search under 500ms p95. Outbound delivered or bounced within 72 hours.

The whole design is decided by four numbers, so derive them before drawing anything.

**How many SMTP transactions actually arrive, against how many are accepted?** At 1B active users and 100 accepted messages a day each, accepted mail is 1B × 100 = 100B/day, or **~1.16M/s average**. If roughly 30% of arrivals are refused at the door before reaching acceptance, total arrivals are 100B ÷ 0.7 ≈ 143B/day, **~1.65M/s average**, and around **6.6M/s at peak**.

**What does moving the classifier inside the SMTP transaction actually cost, against what it saves?** A production spam model runs near a 1-in-1,000 false-positive rate; a refusal authorised by the sending domain's own DMARC policy runs near 1-in-1,000,000, a three-order-of-magnitude gap. At 100B accepted messages a day, putting the model inside the transaction would destroy 0.001 × 100B = **100M legitimate messages daily**, permanently and invisibly.

**How much does content addressing actually save on storage?** Weighted average logical size per message is ~50KB. Content addressing deduplicates the attachment slice roughly 7x on real traffic, bringing stored bytes to roughly 10KB per message: 100B × 10KB = **~1PB/day stored**, against 100B × 50KB = **5PB/day logical**, a 5x gap.

**Why does the search index cost more than the mail it indexes?** The full corpus is roughly 2EB of bodies at around $5/TB-month, about $10M/month. The search index, covering only extracted text at roughly an eighth of the source bytes, still runs on fast storage at roughly $60/TB-month, landing near **$30M/month**: an eighth of the bytes and about three times the bill.

> **The numbers to carry.** ~1.16M/s accepted average, ~1.65M/s arriving, ~6.6M/s peak · a synchronous model at 1e-3 false positives destroys ~100M legitimate messages a day · content addressing cuts stored bytes 5x, from 5PB/day logical to 1PB/day stored · the search index is an eighth of the bytes and roughly three times the storage bill.

#### The boundary, the stores, and the API
It helps to say plainly what kind of decision this system is built around: one irreversible bit at the door, then everything else reversible behind it.

- **MX fleet**: the only place a refusal is possible, spending that power on three cheap-first checks.
- **Metadata row**: headers, labels, thread id, a body hash, roughly 250 bytes, sharded by `user_id`.
- **Body**: bytes keyed by content hash in object storage, shared across every mailbox that received the same content.
- **Change stream**: one log of accepted messages, consumed independently by the classifier, the indexer and the notifier.
- **Label**: `INBOX` or `SPAM`, written asynchronously, revisable in either direction.

The API:

```
SMTP (port 25/587)          inbound + outbound
IMAP / POP3                 client mailbox sync
GET  /folder/{name}?cursor  → [emails_summary]
GET  /email/{id}            → full email + thread
POST /email                 → send
GET  /search?q=...          → results
```

#### High-level design
Follow one message from an external server's connection to it landing in a mailbox.

[The hot path, connect to labelled row](/diagram/email-service?focus=external-senders,p-connect,p-rcpt,p-data,accept-writer,object-store,metadata-store,change-stream,classifier,clients,mailbox-api,e-arrive,e-connect-rcpt,e-rcpt-data,e-accept,e-body,e-row,e-event,e-cs-classifier,e-label,e-client-api,e-read-meta)

1. **on_connect** checks the peer IP against a reputation table before a byte of message crosses the wire.
2. **on_rcpt** refuses an unknown recipient immediately, never accepting and bouncing later.
3. **on_data_end** evaluates SPF, DKIM and DMARC, and returns `250` for everything not authorised to be refused.
4. **Acceptance writer** hashes the body, writes it once to **Body + attachment store**, and writes a small row to **Mailbox metadata**.
5. The same acceptance publishes to the **Change stream**, which the **Asynchronous classifier** reads to assign a label with no power to reject.
6. **Mailbox API + sync** answers a client's list or search request by paging **Mailbox metadata**, one shard, one user.

> **Why the flow is shaped this way.** Acceptance is a promise about storage, not about the inbox. Everything expensive and probabilistic happens after that promise, where a wrong verdict costs a mislabelled message rather than a permanently lost one.

#### The accept-or-refuse boundary
SMTP gives exactly one bit at the door, and it cannot be taken back either way. Which signals are trustworthy enough to spend that bit on?

[The three refusal points, cheapest first](/diagram/email-service?focus=p-connect,p-rcpt,p-data,external-senders,accept-writer,e-refuse-connect,e-connect-rcpt,e-refuse-rcpt,e-rcpt-data,e-refuse-data,e-accept)

**Bad: refuse on any signal that looks suspicious, including a probabilistic model score.** This disposes of junk before it is ever stored, which sounds efficient until the false-positive rate is priced against the volume. At 100B messages a day, a model running near its normal accuracy destroys roughly 100 million legitimate messages daily, silently, with no bounce the sender or recipient will ever see.

**Good: accept everything and sort it out later, with no refusals at all.** This protects every legitimate message and gives up a real defence: known-bad connections and forged senders now cost full storage and processing, and a portion of that traffic is trivially, cheaply identifiable before a single byte of the message body has even arrived.

**Great: refuse only on evidence with a near-certain false-positive rate, and accept everything else for asynchronous sorting.** **on_connect** drops known-bad IPs before any bytes cross the wire. **on_rcpt** refuses an address that does not resolve locally, because accepting for an unknown user and bouncing later sends that bounce to a forged return path, which turns the recipient into an abuser. **on_data_end** refuses only a DMARC failure against a policy the sending domain itself published, because that refusal is authorised by the party who can actually fix it. Everything else gets a `250` and an asynchronous, reversible verdict.

[A refusal is gone; an acceptance is reversible](/diagram/email-service?figure=accept-refuse)

Everything on the reversible side keeps a property the door cannot offer: a wrong verdict is recoverable, and the message itself becomes training data the next time a human corrects it.

#### What SPF, DKIM and DMARC each actually establish
Three protocols get recited as a stack. Only one of them produces a verdict this system is allowed to act on at the door. Why?

[Where the authentication check sits in the transaction](/diagram/email-service?focus=p-data,external-senders,e-refuse-data,e-accept)

**Bad: refuse on an SPF failure alone.** SPF checks whether the connecting IP is in the list the envelope sender's domain published, and it authenticates the invisible `Return-Path`, not the `From:` address a user actually sees. A message can fail SPF for entirely mundane reasons, a legitimate forward changes the connecting IP, and refusing on it alone would reject mail the visible sender never intended to be flagged.

**Good: refuse on a DKIM failure alone.** DKIM verifies a cryptographic signature over the body and a set of headers, and unlike SPF it travels with the message rather than the connection, so it survives a plain forward. It says nothing about which domain the recipient actually sees in `From:`, so a signature that verifies perfectly can still belong to a completely different, attacker-controlled domain than the one displayed.

**Great: refuse only on DMARC, which requires alignment and reads the sender's own published policy.** DMARC asks whether the visible `From:` domain matches whichever of SPF or DKIM passed, and then reads what that domain told receivers to do if it does not: `p=none`, `p=quarantine` or `p=reject`. A `5xx` here is not this system's judgement about the message. It is the sending domain instructing this system to refuse mail that fails its own authentication, which is what transfers the false-positive risk to the party that can actually fix the misconfiguration.

That is the entire reason the boundary sits where it does. Every other refusal a system might want to make is its own opinion, running at roughly a 1-in-1,000 error rate. A DMARC-authorised refusal runs roughly a thousand times more reliably, because the party bearing the risk chose it themselves.

#### Splitting metadata from body
A message looks like one object. Storing it as one object breaks the two things every mailbox has to do well. What has to be true of the split?

[Where an accepted message actually lands](/diagram/email-service?focus=accept-writer,object-store,metadata-store,e-body,e-row)

**Bad: store the whole message, headers and body together, in one row per recipient.** This is the obvious first design, and it fails the moment a mailbox has any real attachments in it: inlining a multi-megabyte body into the row that every inbox listing reads means a simple "show me my last 50 messages" query has to move gigabytes it never needed.

**Good: separate the body into its own store, but keep one copy per recipient.** This fixes the listing problem and misses the other one: the same corporate newsletter PDF landing in a million inboxes is stored a million times, even though every copy is byte-for-byte identical.

**Great: a small metadata row per recipient, and content-addressed bodies shared across every recipient.** **Mailbox metadata** holds only what a listing needs, roughly 250 bytes, sharded by `user_id` so every mailbox operation touches one partition. **Body + attachment store** keys bytes by their content hash, so the same newsletter PDF, however many mailboxes reference it, is stored exactly once.

The two stores exist because metadata and bodies are read completely differently: metadata is small, read on every inbox view, and needs strong consistency, since marking a message read has to show on every device at once; bodies are larger, typically read once, and deduplicate well. One store built to serve both would be wrong for one of them.

#### Dedup versus per-user erasure
Deduplication requires that identical content produce identical stored bytes. A user's right to have their mail become unreadable requires a key only they hold. Those two requirements contradict each other directly.

[The body, and the key that wraps it](/diagram/email-service?focus=object-store,accept-writer,e-body)

**Bad: encrypt each recipient's copy with an unrelated random key.** Erasure is trivial here, since discarding one user's key makes their copy unreadable. It also destroys deduplication completely: the same plaintext now produces different ciphertext for every recipient, because the key was never derived from the content, so there is nothing left to deduplicate against.

**Good: store one shared plaintext copy with no per-user key at all.** Deduplication works perfectly, since there is only ever one copy. Nobody can be individually revoked, because there is no separate key tied to any one user; erasure would mean deleting the only copy everyone else still needs.

**Great: derive the encryption key from the content itself, and wrap it separately per recipient.** **Acceptance writer** hashes the body, derives a data key from that hash, so the same content always produces the same key and therefore the same ciphertext, and content addressing still works. That data key is then wrapped separately under each recipient's own key-encryption key. Deduplication survives because the ciphertext is deterministic; per-user erasure survives because revoking one recipient's wrapping key ends their access without touching anyone else's copy.

[One ciphertext, wrapped separately per recipient](/diagram/email-service?figure=convergent-key)

The cost this concedes: because the data key is derived purely from content, anyone who can write to the store can test whether a specific plaintext already exists by computing its hash, a real weakness for low-entropy content like a template with one field changed.

#### One index per user, packed onto shared shards
Nobody searches anyone else's mail. That should make search easier than most search problems. What actually gets in the way at a billion users?

[The change stream feeding the search index](/diagram/email-service?focus=search-index,change-stream,mailbox-api,e-cs-search,e-search)

**Bad: one shared index across every user's mail.** This is the default shape for most search systems, and it is wrong here for a structural reason: nobody ever needs to rank one user's results against another's, so a shared index pays the cost of cross-corpus relevance and recall for a capability nothing in the product actually uses.

**Good: one fully isolated physical index per user.** This removes the shared-index problem cleanly and creates a different one at scale: a search-engine shard costs roughly 100MB resident and a slot in cluster state regardless of how much it holds, and a billion physical shards is four orders of magnitude past what any cluster can operate.

**Great: one logical index per user, packed many to a physical shard, sorted so a user's documents sit together.** **Per-user search index** packs roughly 50,000 users onto each physical shard, keeping the shard count in the tens of thousands rather than the billions. Sorting the index with `user_id` as the leading key means a common term's posting list, which now spans 50,000 users' worth of postings, can be skipped at the block level rather than scanned term by term, turning what would be a slow shared scan into a fast contiguous seek.

The packing cost is real and it is bounded: every query still pays something to skip past postings that belong to other users sharing the shard, and that cost is exactly what the sort order is there to minimise.

#### Where it breaks
| Layer | Failure | How the design handles it |
|---|---|---|
| Inbound MX | Backpressure from storage cascades into every MX deferring | An internal queue absorbs short bursts; sustained pressure returns 4xx so senders retry, never a silent drop and never a 5xx |
| Spam classifier | A bad model deploy silently moves legitimate mail to spam | Canary rollout with the "not spam" rate as the gating signal; auto-revert on a threshold breach |
| Outbound sending IP | One compromised account gets a shared address blocklisted | Reputation-tiered pools; a compromised account is demoted to quarantine before it burns the pool everyone else sends from |
| Mailbox shard | A multi-million-message mailbox saturates its partition | Rows older than a year tier into cold storage; cursor-based pagination bounds every read |
| Search index | One user's index outgrows affordable hot storage | Time-tiering, recent months hot, the rest warm or cold, fanning out to colder tiers only when the hot tier is sparse |
| Object store | Garbage collection removes a blob's last reference mid-read | A grace period between marking for delete and reclaiming; a read during that window aborts the delete |
| Authentication rollout | A domain enabling `p=reject` starts refusing its own legitimate senders | `pct=` staged enforcement and `rua` aggregate reports read at each step before enforcement widens |

#### What this design does not solve
**The false-positive rate the whole design is tuned around cannot actually be measured.** It is inferred from "not spam" clicks, which only counts errors a user happened to notice, and the messages most likely to be mis-filed, a one-off receipt, a stranger's reply, are exactly the ones nobody is watching for. Every claim about staying under a target rate inherits an unknown multiplier on top of it.

**Forwarding and mailing lists break authentication, and there is no protocol-level fix.** SPF fails on almost any forward because the connecting IP changes. DKIM survives an unmodified forward and breaks the moment a list rewrites the subject or appends a footer. The available remedy, an intermediary re-signing and asserting it authenticated the message, only works if that intermediary is already trusted, which converts a cryptographic question into a reputation question rather than answering it.

**Dedup and per-user erasure are reconciled by a compromise that leaks information.** Convergent encryption lets two requirements coexist that otherwise cannot, and it concedes that anyone able to write to the store can test whether specific content already exists by hashing it, a real weakness for predictable, low-entropy content.

#### Final design
Read it back through the numbers. ~1.65M SMTP transactions a second arriving, with only ~1.16M/s accepted, is why the door spends its one irreversible bit on nothing but near-certain evidence. The three-order-of-magnitude gap between a model's error rate and a DMARC-authorised refusal is why classification lives entirely on the reversible side of that door. And a search index that is an eighth of the bytes and three times the bill is why the index gets tiered and packed far more aggressively than the mail it describes.

[The whole design](/diagram/email-service?focus=external-senders,p-connect,p-rcpt,p-data,accept-writer,object-store,metadata-store,change-stream,classifier,search-index,mailbox-api,clients,outbound-queue,sending-workers)

> **The numbers to remember.** ~1.65M/s SMTP arrivals, ~1.16M/s accepted · a synchronous 1e-3 model would destroy ~100M legitimate messages a day, against a 1e-6 DMARC-authorised refusal · content addressing: 5PB/day logical to 1PB/day stored · the search index costs roughly three times the mail it indexes despite being an eighth of the bytes.

#### Check your understanding
**Why does a DMARC failure earn a 5xx refusal while a spam model's score never does?** Because DMARC's refusal is authorised by the sending domain's own published policy, running near a 1-in-1,000,000 error rate, while a model's opinion runs near 1-in-1,000, a thousand times less reliable to spend an irreversible action on.

**Why does SPF alone fail as a phishing defence even when it passes correctly?** Because SPF authenticates the invisible `Return-Path`, not the `From:` address a user actually sees, so a message can pass SPF while displaying a completely different, forged sender.

**Why can a metadata row and a message body never live in the same store without one of them suffering?** Because they are read completely differently: metadata is small and read on every inbox view, needing strong consistency; bodies are large and usually read once, and deduplicate well across unrelated users.

**Why does convergent encryption let deduplication and per-user erasure coexist, and what does it cost?** The data key is derived from the content hash, so identical content always encrypts to identical ciphertext, and that key is wrapped separately per recipient so one revocation does not touch anyone else's copy. The cost is that content existence becomes testable by anyone who can write to the store.

**Why is a shared search index across all users the wrong shape here, even though it works for other search problems?** Because nobody ever needs to rank one user's mail against another's, so a shared index would pay for cross-corpus ranking and recall that this product never uses, while still needing per-user isolation for privacy.
### 21. Design S3 (Distributed Object Storage)
#### Understanding the problem
An object store keeps an unbounded number of blobs under customer-chosen keys and serves them over HTTP, at a durability so high that losing one object is a news event. Objects run from 1KB config files to 5TB datasets, and the same fleet has to be cheap enough for a decade-old archive and fast enough to serve a website.

Two things make this harder than "a big key-value store".

First, nothing is ever modified in place. A change is new bytes plus a pointer swap, never an edit. That single rule is what turns the whole system into an index problem rather than a storage problem: once bytes are immutable, the only thing that can ever be wrong is which bytes a key currently points at.

Second, the two things being scaled grow on completely different axes. The data plane grows with bytes; the metadata plane grows with object count. A customer with a billion tiny objects costs almost nothing in bytes and everything in index, and a design that conflates the two axes prices one workload for the wrong resource.

> **What this is not.** It looks like a Dynamo-style key-value store: both partition and replicate durable bytes across a fleet with no single point of failure, and both answer how many copies and where. They diverge on the payload. Here every byte is immutable and the mean object is around 310KB; there every value is mutable and around 1.2KB. Immutability deletes the conflict problem entirely, so there is exactly one mutable cell in this whole system, the key-to-manifest pointer, and it lives in one small consensus-replicated index rather than needing quorums, version vectors or read repair anywhere.

#### Requirements and the numbers
**Functional.** PUT, GET, DELETE, LIST within a bucket. Versioning. Lifecycle transitions. Multipart upload for large objects. Server-side encryption.

**Non-functional.** 11 nines durability per object per year. 4 nines availability per region. Strong read-after-write on every in-region operation. GET p99 under 100ms.

The whole design is decided by four numbers, so derive them before drawing anything.

**How much physical storage does a tiered layout actually need against the logical bytes stored?** At ~40T objects and a mean size of ~310KB, logical bytes are roughly **12EB in region**. Weighting overhead by tier, 20% hot at 3x replication, 50% warm at 1.5x erasure coding, 30% archive at 1.4x, gives 0.2×3 + 0.5×1.5 + 0.3×1.4 ≈ **1.77x**, so physical storage is roughly **21EB**.

**Where does the durability number actually come from?** At a 1% annual failure rate per disk and a one-hour repair window, the chance of losing 3 more of the 8 surviving fragments before repair finishes is C(8,3) × (1.14×10⁻⁶)³ ≈ 8.3×10⁻¹⁷, times a 0.09 first-failure rate a year, giving roughly **seventeen nines** from independent failures alone. The published figure is **eleven**, a **six-order-of-magnitude gap** that independent disk failure cannot explain.

**Why does metadata scale on object count rather than on bytes?** An index record is roughly 300 bytes; 40T objects gives ~12PB of index. Sized by capacity, that needs 12PB ÷ 4TB per node ≈ 3,000 nodes; sized by throughput, 15M ops/s ÷ 200k ops/s per node ≈ **75 nodes**. Capacity binds by **40x**, so the real metadata fleet is sized by object count, not request rate.

**How many partitions does the metadata index actually need?** A range partition sustains roughly 5,500 GET/s before it must split. At 15M req/s fleet-wide, an evenly spread load needs 15M ÷ 5,500 ≈ **2,700 partitions**; real key skew pushes the working number into the tens of thousands, which is what forces automatic splitting rather than a fixed partition count.

> **The numbers to carry.** ~21EB physical against ~12EB logical, a 1.77x tiered overhead · independent-failure durability of ~seventeen nines against a published eleven, a six-order gap · metadata sized by object count (40x margin over throughput) not by request rate · ~2,700 partitions at even load, tens of thousands under real skew.

#### The pointer, the two planes, and the API
It helps to say plainly what is actually mutable in this design: one thing.

- **Manifest**: the immutable list of parts and fragments that make up one object version. Write-once.
- **Pointer**: `(bucket, key, version_id) → manifest_id`. The only mutable cell in the system, held in a consensus-replicated index.
- **Piece**: a fragment of a part, identified by `piece_id`, held on a storage node with no logic beyond bytes in, bytes out.
- **Storage class**: a per-object layout choice, whole replicas or an erasure code, recorded in the manifest and revised by lifecycle rules.

The API:

```
PUT    /{bucket}/{key}   body: bytes
GET    /{bucket}/{key}   [?versionId=] -> bytes
DELETE /{bucket}/{key}   [?versionId=]
GET    /{bucket}?prefix=&marker=&max-keys=   -> up to 1000 keys
POST   /{bucket}/{key}?uploads               -> upload_id
PUT    /{bucket}/{key}?partNumber=&uploadId= -> ETag
POST   /{bucket}/{key}?uploadId=             -> final ETag
```

#### High-level design
Follow one PUT from a client's request to a durable, discoverable object.

[The hot path, PUT to committed pointer](/diagram/object-storage?focus=client,frontend,metadata,ec,storage,manifest,e3,e5,e6,e7,e8,e9,e10)

1. **Client / SDK** sends the object bytes to the **API frontend**.
2. The **Erasure coder** splits the bytes into fragments according to the storage class and writes them fresh to **Storage nodes**, no coordination needed since nobody has read them yet.
3. The frontend asks the **Metadata service** to commit a new **Manifest store** entry describing those fragments.
4. **Metadata service** atomically swaps the `(bucket, key)` pointer to the new manifest.
5. Only after that commit does the client receive `200`.

> **Why the flow is shaped this way.** Nothing reads bytes without resolving through metadata first, the data plane never mutates anything, and a PUT acks only after the pointer commits. Consistency, versioning, overwrite and resumable upload collapse into one operation: build something immutable, then move a pointer.

#### Where eleven nines actually comes from
Every candidate answer starts with "Reed-Solomon 6+3, tolerates 3 losses". That is a fact about the code word. It is not where the published durability number comes from.

[Repair racing against the next failure](/diagram/object-storage?focus=storage,background-plane,repair,scrub,e15,e16,e17,e18)

**Bad: quote the code word as the durability guarantee.** RS(6,3) tolerates exactly 3 simultaneous fragment losses and says nothing about probability or time. Stopping here answers "what can this code survive," not "how often does an object actually die."

**Good: compute the probability from independent disk failures.** At a 1% annual failure rate and a one-hour repair window, the chance of losing 3 more of the 8 survivors before repair finishes, times the rate of the first failure, works out to roughly seventeen nines a year. This is a real calculation and it is not the number that governs the design: it is six orders of magnitude better than what gets published.

**Great: recognise that the gap between seventeen nines and eleven nines is the actual engineering problem.** Independent disk failure is not the binding term. Correlated failure, software defects and operator error are, by roughly a million times. That is why S3's storage layer was rewritten with an executable specification checked by property tests rather than given a wider code: widening the code improves a term that was never the bottleneck.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 210" role="img" aria-label="Independent disk failure gives roughly seventeen nines of durability; the published figure is eleven nines; the six orders of magnitude between them come from correlated failure, software defects and operator error, not from the code word">
  <style>
    .bar{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.28;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.5}
    .bar2{fill:currentColor;fill-opacity:.12;stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.5;stroke-width:1.5}
    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 12px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    .sub{fill:currentColor;opacity:.75;font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
  </style>
  <text class="lbl" x="8" y="16">Independent disk failure alone</text>
  <rect class="bar2" x="8" y="26" width="10" height="22" rx="3"/>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="66">~10⁻¹⁸ annual loss probability,</text>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="82">~seventeen nines</text>
  <text class="lbl" x="8" y="116">Published durability</text>
  <rect class="bar" x="8" y="126" width="384" height="22" rx="3"/>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="168">~10⁻¹¹ annual loss probability, eleven</text>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="184">nines: six orders of magnitude worse</text>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="204">gap = correlated failure + software + operator error, not the code word</text>
</svg>
```

The consequence for engineering effort: a team chasing more nines by widening the erasure code is spending budget on a term that is already irrelevant, while the term that actually limits durability sits in software correctness and operational discipline.

#### One pointer, and nothing else needs a lock
An object looks like it should need the same locking machinery as any mutable record. It does not. Why does nothing on the data plane ever race?

[The manifest and the pointer that resolves to it](/diagram/object-storage?focus=metadata,manifest,ec,frontend,e5,e6,e10)

**Bad: mutate bytes in place and lock around the write.** This is the obvious approach for "update an object", and it immediately creates every problem this design avoids: readers mid-fetch can observe a half-written object, and every write has to coordinate with every concurrent read of the same bytes.

**Good: version each write, but let the data plane and the index both participate in committing it.** This avoids in-place corruption and introduces a new coordination problem: now two systems, storage nodes and metadata, both have to agree that a write happened, which is exactly the kind of two-phase coordination that immutability was supposed to remove.

**Great: write fresh, immutable pieces that nobody has read yet, then commit a single pointer.** The **Erasure coder** writes new fragments to **Storage nodes** with no coordination required, because nothing has ever read them. Only then does the **Metadata service** atomically swap the `(bucket, key)` pointer in the **Manifest store** to point at the new manifest. An in-flight `GET` that already resolved the old manifest keeps reading valid bytes to completion, because that manifest is immutable and cannot be edited out from under it: snapshot isolation the design gets for free rather than one it has to implement.

[A reader keeps its manifest; a writer swaps the pointer](/diagram/object-storage?figure=pointer-swap)

This is also why S3 could add strong read-after-write consistency in December 2020 with no data-plane change: the bytes were already consistent, and only the pointer *read* had been served from a cache that could lag the commit.

#### Replicate or erasure-code
Both layouts keep an object durable. One of them costs far more in storage; the other costs far more per read. Where is the line, and can it be derived rather than guessed?

[Layout as a per-object property](/diagram/object-storage?focus=ec,storage,lifecycle,e9,e13,e14)

**Bad: pick one layout for everything.** Erasure-coding every object minimises the storage bill and turns every small, frequently read object into a multi-seek operation. Replicating every object minimises seeks and triples the storage bill on objects nobody reads twice a year.

**Good: split by object size alone.** Large objects get erasure coding, small ones get replicas. This is directionally right and misses the other half of the trade: a large object read constantly and a small object read once a decade have very different economics, and size alone does not capture that.

**Great: derive the crossover from cost, using both size and read frequency.** A disk seek costs roughly $1.9×10⁻⁸; an erasure-coded read costs 5 extra seeks over a replica read, roughly $9.5×10⁻⁸ per read. Erasure coding saves 1.5 × object size in GB, worth roughly $3.75×10⁻⁴ per GB per month. Setting the two equal gives a break-even of roughly 3,950 × size-in-GB reads per month: a 1MB object crosses over at about 4 reads a month, a 10KB object at about once every two years. **Storage lifecycle** records this as a per-object property, chosen at write time and revised as access patterns change.

The number this depends on is read frequency, not just size, which is exactly why the layout has to be a property lifecycle rules can revise rather than a fixed rule baked into the write path.

#### One index ordered for listing, hashed for placement
Customers who list objects by prefix need an ordered index. Customers who write sequential prefixes create the worst hotspots an ordered index can have. How does one system serve both?

[The metadata index and where it routes](/diagram/object-storage?focus=metadata,frontend,e5,e6)

**Bad: hash-partition the index on `hash(bucket, key)`.** This spreads every bucket uniformly and makes a hot sequential prefix structurally impossible on the index. It also makes a prefix `LIST` into a scatter-gather across every partition, since keys sharing a prefix are now scattered everywhere by design, turning a single ordered read into tens of thousands of small ones.

**Good: range-partition the index, and place fragments by the same key.** `LIST` becomes one ordered range scan again, which is correct. Coupling placement to the same ordering means a customer hammering one sequential prefix now concentrates both index load and disk load on the same narrow slice of the fleet, turning an index-tier problem into a disk-tier one.

**Great: range-partition the index for ordering, and hash fragment placement independently for load spreading.** **Metadata service** keeps `(bucket, key)` range-partitioned so a prefix `LIST` stays one ordered scan. Fragment placement is hashed separately, so a hot sequential prefix concentrates on one index partition, never on one set of disks. A partition split under pressure is an index-tier event lasting seconds to minutes, never a saturated disk.

The two orderings are deliberately different: the index is ordered by what customers query by, and placement is ordered by nothing at all, because placement's only job is to spread load evenly.

#### Multipart: independent retries and one atomic step
A 1TB upload on one long-lived connection is fragile: a load balancer recycle, a NAT timeout, a laptop closing its lid, and the whole transfer restarts from zero. How does a multi-hour upload survive that without losing everything on one dropped connection?

[Parts uploaded independently, committed once](/diagram/object-storage?focus=frontend,multipart,manifest,e11,e12)

**Bad: upload the whole object on one connection and retry the entire thing on failure.** A 1TB upload at typical bandwidth can take most of a day. Losing the connection at hour twenty means restarting from byte zero, and the probability of the connection surviving a full day only gets worse as the object grows.

**Good: split into parts, but make each part-plus-commit its own atomic operation.** This shortens the retry unit to one part, which helps, and it still leaves the object partially visible if a crash happens between committing individual parts, since there is no single moment where the whole object becomes real.

**Great: upload parts independently against an in-progress, unreachable manifest, and commit the whole object in one step.** **Multipart upload state** records each part's fragments as an ordinary row keyed by `(upload_id, part_num)`, invisible under the real key the whole time. A failed part is retried alone, at the cost of that part's transfer time, not the whole object's. `CompleteMultipartUpload` validates every part and only then writes the final entry to the **Manifest store**, the single atomic step in a transfer that may have run for hours.

One consequence catches almost everyone the first time: the ETag of a multipart object is the MD5 of the concatenated part MD5s, not the MD5 of the object itself, because the service never holds the whole object in one place to hash directly. Two byte-identical uploads split into different part sizes produce different ETags, which is why a real integrity check uses a dedicated whole-object checksum rather than comparing ETags.

#### Where it breaks
| Layer | Failure | How the design handles it |
|---|---|---|
| Storage node | A dead disk removes fragments from roughly 10⁸ erasure groups at once | Repair reconstructs from surviving fragments, prioritised so groups sitting at exactly the minimum jump the queue |
| Metadata partition | A sequential prefix saturates one range partition | Automatic split on rate and size, with pre-splitting on an observed trend rather than waiting for errors |
| Placement | Anti-affinity is violated, too many fragments land in one zone | The write is refused outright; any existing violation is rebalanced as background priority work |
| Multipart | A client crashes mid-upload and orphans parts | A lifecycle rule expires incomplete uploads after a set number of days; mark-and-sweep reclaims the pieces |
| Bit rot | Silent corruption flips bits on a spinning disk with no read error | Scrub's rolling re-read catches the checksum mismatch and reconstructs from surviving fragments |
| Metadata | A shard leader is lost mid-commit | Consensus re-elects in low seconds; an uncommitted PUT is simply unacknowledged, so the client retries safely |
| Garbage collection | The sweep falls behind and unreferenced bytes accumulate | Sweep cycle time is tracked directly, since a stalled sweep shows up as a cost anomaly long before anything else notices |

#### What this design does not solve
**A range-partitioned key index cannot become a query engine.** Every predicate beyond key order, a tag, a size, a modification time, requires a full scan, and the shipped answer is a periodic inventory report, a batch file standing in for an index customers keep wanting.

**Deletion can be proven unreachable, never proven physically erased.** A DELETE moves the pointer; the underlying blocks are reclaimed by mark-and-sweep and physically overwritten only whenever the drive next reuses them, which may be long after the delete. The honest claim for a compliance request is cryptographic erasure through key destruction, a genuinely weaker guarantee than physical erasure.

**An availability zone outage leaves an erasure-coded object with no margin at all.** RS(6,3) placed three fragments per zone across three zones leaves exactly the minimum needed for reconstruction the moment one zone goes dark, not one fragment more. Every warm object in the region is one more disk failure from unrecoverable for the outage's duration, and the mitigation, an emergency re-encode into the surviving zones, deliberately trades one kind of exposure for another rather than removing it.

#### Final design
Read it back through the numbers. The 1.77x tiered overhead, against 3x for pure replication, is what the per-tier layout decision buys. The six-order-of-magnitude gap between seventeen nines of independent-failure arithmetic and the published eleven nines is why durability engineering targets software correctness and operational discipline rather than a wider code. And metadata being sized by object count at a 40x margin over its throughput ceiling is why a customer's cost profile depends entirely on how many objects they have, not how many bytes.

[The whole design](/diagram/object-storage?focus=client,cdn,frontend,metadata,ec,storage,bucket,manifest,multipart,lifecycle,background-plane,repair,scrub,gc)

> **The numbers to remember.** ~21EB physical vs ~12EB logical, a 1.77x tiered overhead · ~seventeen nines from independent failure vs a published eleven, a six-order gap · metadata bound by object count at a 40x margin over throughput · ~2,700 partitions at even load, tens of thousands under real skew.

#### Check your understanding
**Why doesn't widening the erasure code from RS(6,3) to something like RS(17,5) meaningfully raise durability?** Because independent disk failure already accounts for roughly seventeen nines, far above the published eleven. The gap is correlated failure and software defects, which a wider code does nothing to close.

**Why can an in-flight GET keep returning correct bytes even while another client overwrites the same key?** Because the GET already resolved to an immutable manifest before the overwrite committed, and that manifest is never edited, only replaced by a new pointer value pointing elsewhere.

**Why does the right storage layout depend on both object size and read frequency, not size alone?** Because the cost of an erasure-coded read scales with extra seeks regardless of size, while the storage saved scales with size. A large object read constantly and a small object read rarely sit on opposite sides of the same crossover.

**Why can fragment placement be hashed while the metadata index stays ordered by key?** Because they solve different problems. Ordering serves `LIST`, which customers query by key. Hashing serves load spreading, which has no relationship to key order at all, so decoupling them lets a hot prefix concentrate index load without ever concentrating disk load.

**Why is the ETag of a multipart upload not simply the object's MD5?** Because the object is never assembled in one place to hash directly. The ETag is computed from the parts' individual MD5s instead, which means it depends on how the upload was split, not just on the bytes themselves.
### 22. Design a Real-Time Gaming Leaderboard
#### Understanding the problem
A real-time gaming leaderboard ranks 100M players across daily, weekly, all-time, regional and friends boards, with a finished match visible in the standings within seconds and rank reads under 100ms. Top-N sounds like the hard part. It is not.

Two things make this harder than "keep a sorted list".

First, the read that actually defines the problem is an arbitrary player, somewhere in the middle of 100 million, asking where they sit among everyone else. Top-N is trivial in almost anything with an index on score. Counting how many players sit above one specific player is a different query entirely, and it is the one that picks the data structure.

Second, the board is not the system of record. Scores are computed server-side from match events on a durable log, and the ranked structure is a derived, rebuildable index sitting on top of it. That is what makes it acceptable to keep the whole thing in memory.

> **What this is not.** It looks like Trending Topics: a firehose of events, a ranked list at the end. They diverge on the key space. Trending discovers its keys from the data, roughly 100 million distinct strings a day nobody enumerated in advance, so a sketch is the only option. A leaderboard's keys are player ids that already existed in a users table, so exact per-player state is simply affordable. And where trending only ever publishes the head, a leaderboard is asked about the tail by name, and the tail is most of the players.

#### Requirements and the numbers
**Functional.** Record a score. Top-N. An arbitrary player's rank. Neighbours around a rank. Multiple boards by period and segment.

**Non-functional.** Rank reads p99 under 100ms. A finished match visible within 5 seconds. Correct, deterministic ordering under ties. Survive the loss of any single node.

The whole design is decided by four numbers, so derive them before drawing anything.

**How close does the write burst come to a single primary's ceiling?** 10M DAU × 5 matches × 5 boards each gives 250M writes/day, ~2.9k/s average, and a contest close concentrates roughly **60k/s onto one key**. A single Redis primary handles roughly **100k `ZADD`/s**, so the burst is **60% of the ceiling**, comfortably inside one machine.

**How large does the read burst get, and can any of it be cached?** 600k concurrent players polling every 2 seconds is 600k ÷ 2 = **~300k rank reads/s**. Unlike top-N, a rank read is per-player and cannot be shared across users, so no cache collapses this the way it would collapse a shared top-100 request.

**How much memory does the whole system of boards actually need?** Each sorted-set entry costs roughly 90 bytes once skip-list pointers, the hash-table entry and the member string are counted. The all-time board alone is 100M × 90B ≈ **9GB**; every daily, weekly, regional board and their replicas together land around **~125GB**, comfortably inside a handful of commodity nodes.

**What does sharding actually do to the cost of a rank read?** Splitting one board into S score-band shards turns one rank lookup into 1 exact call plus S-1 count calls. At S=8 and 300k reads/s, that is **~2.4M ops/s** to answer a question a single bucketed array lookup already answers in one step.

> **The numbers to carry.** 60k/s contest burst against a ~100k/s single-primary ceiling · ~300k uncacheable rank reads/s at contest close · ~9GB for the all-time board, ~125GB resident across all boards and replicas · sharding multiplies rank reads by S, turning 300k/s into 2.4M ops/s at S=8.

#### The board, the log beneath it, and the API
It helps to say plainly what is derived and what is authoritative here.

- **Event log**: the durable, partitioned system of record for match results.
- **Sorted set**: an in-memory, ordered structure per board, rebuildable from the log, never the source of truth.
- **Board key**: a logical `(scope, period)` pair, `lb:daily:{date}`, resolved with a TTL so lifecycle is naming rather than migration.
- **Span**: the count of nodes a skip-list pointer jumps over, the property that makes rank a descent rather than a scan.

The API:

```
POST /score                { user_id, board_id, event_facts } -> 202
GET  /top/{board}?n=100                                        -> [{user_id, score, rank}]
GET  /rank/{board}/{user_id}                                   -> { rank | percentile, score, exact: bool }
```

#### High-level design
Follow a match result from a client to a rank another player can read.

[The hot path, match event to rank read](/diagram/gaming-leaderboard?focus=clients,leaderboard-svc,event-log,board-writer,zset-primary,read-replicas,e1,e2,e3,e4,e5,e6)

1. **Game clients** send match facts to the **Leaderboard Service**, which computes the score server-side rather than trusting a client-asserted number.
2. The scored result is appended to the **Match event log**, the durable system of record.
3. **Board writer** consumes the log in 50ms batch windows, so one round trip carries hundreds of updates.
4. Each batch issues one `ZADD` against the **Sorted set primary**, updating the board's ordering.
5. Rank and top-N reads go to **Read replicas** rather than the primary, since they are read-only.

> **Why the flow is shaped this way.** The board is a derived index, not a database, which is what makes an in-memory store acceptable: a crash costs the last second of writes plus a rebuild, not the game's history. Everything expensive lives on the write path in batches; everything read-heavy lives on replicas that never take a write.

#### Rank falls out of a descent, not a scan
An index on score makes top-100 trivial in almost any database. It does nothing for "where does this one player sit among 100 million." What structure answers both?

[The primary and the replicas that serve rank](/diagram/gaming-leaderboard?focus=leaderboard-svc,zset-primary,read-replicas,board-writer,e4,e6)

**Bad: an index on score, with rank computed by counting.** `ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 100` is a handful of index leaf reads and is genuinely fine. `COUNT(*) WHERE score > mine` has no rank stored anywhere, so it walks every entry above the player: roughly 50 million index tuples for a median player on a 100M board, hundreds of milliseconds against a 100ms budget.

**Good: a maintained rank column, recomputed on a schedule.** A periodic job walks the board and writes each player a rank number, so reads become a cheap lookup by primary key. The rank is only ever as fresh as the last pass, and at 60k writes a second the true ordering moves faster than a job running on any reasonable cadence can republish it.

**Great: a skip list that carries a count on every pointer.** The **Sorted set primary** stores each board as a skip list paired with a hash table. Every forward pointer in the skip list carries a span, the number of nodes it jumps over. Rank is computed by descending from the top level and accumulating spans on the way down, so it costs the same O(log N) as the lookup the structure was already doing, with no separate counting pass.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 183" role="img" aria-label="Descending a skip list tower accumulates the span at each level; the sum of spans passed on the way down is the player's rank, with no separate count of everyone above them">
  <style>
    .box{fill:none;stroke:currentColor;stroke-width:1.4}
    .acc{stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.8}
    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 12px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    .sub{fill:currentColor;opacity:.75;font:11px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    text{dominant-baseline:middle;text-anchor:middle}
  </style>
  <text class="lbl" x="8" y="14" style="text-anchor:start">Level 3</text>
  <rect class="box" x="62" y="6" width="352" height="22" rx="4"/><text class="sub" x="238" y="18">span 40 → target</text>
  <text class="lbl" x="8" y="58" style="text-anchor:start">Level 2</text>
  <rect class="box" x="62" y="50" width="170" height="22" rx="4"/><text class="sub" x="147" y="62">span 12</text>
  <rect class="box" x="244" y="50" width="170" height="22" rx="4"/><text class="sub" x="329" y="62">span 20</text>
  <text class="lbl" x="8" y="102" style="text-anchor:start">Level 1</text>
  <rect class="box" x="62" y="94" width="80" height="22" rx="4"/><text class="sub" x="102" y="106">4</text>
  <rect class="box" x="150" y="94" width="80" height="22" rx="4"/><text class="sub" x="190" y="106">3</text>
  <rect class="box acc" x="244" y="94" width="170" height="22" rx="4"/><text class="sub" x="329" y="106" fill="var(--accent)">span 5 → player</text>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="150" style="text-anchor:start">rank = 12 (level 2) + 5 (level 1)</text>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="166" style="text-anchor:start">= 17th, no scan of everyone above</text>
</svg>
```

The cost of this shows up on writes, not reads: an insert that changes rank has to fix span counts on every pointer that jumps over the new node, all the way up the tower, which is why writes are batched into 50ms windows rather than sent one at a time.

#### What sharding does to a question that used to be one call
A single board eventually outgrows one primary. Splitting it changes the cost of top-N and rank in opposite directions, and one of those changes is much worse than it looks.

[Sharded reads and the layer that collapses them](/diagram/gaming-leaderboard?focus=zset-primary,read-replicas,quantile-snapshots,e6,e7,e8)

**Bad: shard by hashing the player id.** This spreads write load evenly and destroys the ordering the whole board exists to provide: top-100 now has to fan out to every shard, pull 100 from each, and merge, and rank requires knowing which shard even holds a given player before anything else can happen.

**Good: shard by score band, and pay the round trips for rank.** Top-N becomes cheap and shard-invariant, since the top band alone always holds it. Rank becomes `Σ count(every band above the player) + rank inside their own band`, S round trips instead of one. They parallelise, so latency holds, but the operation count multiplies by S at exactly the moment read volume is highest.

**Great: keep the shards, and collapse the fan-out with a counter layer.** A coarse histogram, one counter per score bucket cut on the observed distribution's quantiles, sits alongside the shards. Every write increments the new bucket and decrements the old. Rank becomes a prefix sum over buckets above the player, held in a structure small enough to sit in the API process's own cache, plus one exact lookup inside the player's own shard.

The concession this requires: the histogram is fed asynchronously, so it lags, and the error is bounded by writes in flight, invisible at rank 4.2 million and potentially podium-changing in the top 100. So the counter layer serves only the tail; the head is always read directly off the top shard's exact structure, the same head-versus-tail boundary reached from the opposite direction.

#### Breaking ties without playing favourites
Two players finish with identical scores. Something has to order them, and the obvious default is worse than it looks.

[Where the tiebreaker has to live](/diagram/gaming-leaderboard?focus=zset-primary,board-writer,e4)

**Bad: let ties fall back to the structure's default ordering.** A sorted set with equal scores orders by member bytes, which is arbitrary and, worse, stable: the same player permanently wins every tie against the same opponent, forever, for no reason either of them could explain.

**Good: store a separate tiebreaker field and read both values on every comparison.** This produces a fair, deterministic order and doubles the read cost of every rank comparison, since the structure was never built to order by two fields at once, only by the one score it indexes.

**Great: encode the tiebreaker directly into the score.** `packed = points × 2³¹ + (2³¹ − 1 − t)`, where `t` is seconds since a fixed epoch. Points take 20 bits, the inverted time takes 31, for 51 bits total, inside the 53 bits of exact integer precision an IEEE-754 double carries. Earlier finishers at the same point total naturally rank higher, computed entirely within the one field the structure already sorts on.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="-117 -2 462 154" role="img" aria-label="A packed score fits 20 bits of points and 31 bits of inverted time into 51 bits, inside the 53 bits of exact integer precision a double carries; a third field would not fit">
  <style>
    .box{fill:none;stroke:currentColor;stroke-width:1.4}
    .acc{stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.8}
    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 12px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    .sub{fill:currentColor;opacity:.75;font:11px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    text{dominant-baseline:middle;text-anchor:middle}
  </style>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="14" text-anchor="start" style="text-anchor:start">53 bits of exact integer precision in a double</text>
  <rect class="box acc" x="8" y="24" width="116" height="30" rx="4"/><text class="sub" x="66" y="43" fill="var(--accent)">points, 20b</text>
  <rect class="box" x="124" y="24" width="180" height="30" rx="4"/><text class="sub" x="214" y="43">inverted time t, 31b</text>
  <rect class="box" x="304" y="24" width="32" height="30" rx="4" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><text class="sub" x="320" y="43">2b</text>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="82">51 bits used: earlier finishers at equal</text>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="98">points rank higher, no second field to read</text>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="122">a third tiebreak level does not fit; past 53</text>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="138">bits the encoding rounds silently</text>
</svg>
```

The bit budget is a hard constraint, not a detail: it caps how many tiebreak levels can ever be stacked into one score, and exceeding it makes ties reappear as ranks that silently flap between reads.

#### Rolling over the board at midnight without a race
The daily board resets at 00:00 UTC. Thousands of writes a second are landing on today's key in the final minutes. What happens at the boundary?

[The board key registry resolving today's key](/diagram/gaming-leaderboard?focus=board-keys,leaderboard-svc,zset-primary,e9,e4)

**Bad: create tomorrow's key lazily, on the first write after midnight.** Every service instance handling a write in that first moment races to create the same key simultaneously, and any read that lands in the gap hits a key that does not exist yet, returning a nonsensical empty rank for a board that should already be live.

**Good: create the key exactly at the boundary, in one coordinated step.** This avoids the race between writers, and it does nothing about the read side: a thundering herd of clients checking their rank right at midnight can still catch the key mid-creation, right when traffic is naturally highest.

**Great: pre-create tomorrow's key several minutes early with a sentinel member.** **Board key registry** resolves a logical board id to a concrete key by date, and the key for tomorrow already exists, already accepting writes, before the clock ticks. Rollover becomes a naming event, the service simply starts resolving "today" to a key that has been live for minutes, rather than a state change anything has to coordinate around.

The sentinel member matters as much as the early creation: an empty sorted set and a nonexistent key can behave identically to a careless read path, so a placeholder entry keeps the board unambiguously "exists and is empty" rather than "does not exist yet."

#### Rank reads at 300k/s: which knob actually helps
Contest close produces the read burst that defines this system's ceiling. Sharding writes does nothing for it. What does?

[Replicas serving read-only traffic](/diagram/gaming-leaderboard?focus=read-replicas,leaderboard-svc,zset-primary,e5,e6)

**Bad: shard the board to add more read capacity.** This is the reflexive answer, and it is backwards: sharding solves a write-throughput problem. Every shard still has to answer rank queries, and a rank read now has to touch several of them, multiplying the operation count while leaving total read capacity roughly where it started.

**Good: cache each rank read for a short window.** A cache helps enormously for a shared resource like top-100, where the same object serves every reader. Rank is per-player, so a cache in front of it only helps a player who asks twice inside the TTL, which a client polling every 2 seconds barely does.

**Great: scale reads with read replicas, independently of the write path.** Rank and top-N are read-only operations, so **Read replicas** absorb the 300k/s burst directly, sized from each instance's roughly 100k ops/s ceiling, 6 to 8 replicas on the contest board for headroom and failure tolerance. Writes stay on the **Sorted set primary** alone, on a completely separate axis from read capacity.

The deeper fix is to stop generating the burst at all: pushing a rank update over an existing connection only when a player's position actually changes removes most of the polling traffic rather than serving it faster.

#### Where it breaks
| Layer | Failure | How the design handles it |
|---|---|---|
| Primary | Process crash mid-contest | A replica is promoted, losing at most the last second of unflushed writes, replayed from the event log by sequence number |
| Write path | A write burst saturates the single event loop | Batching in 50ms windows amortises the per-command overhead across hundreds of updates in one round trip |
| Replica | Replication lag spikes during a snapshot | Snapshots run only from a dedicated, non-serving replica, never the primary, so the serving path never stalls for a fork |
| Counter layer | The histogram drifts from the sorted sets | A periodic sum comparison against the exact counts detects drift; the histogram is cheap to rebuild since it is derived |
| Band boundary | A cross-band score move leaves a member in two shards briefly | Add-then-remove ordering makes the failure a harmless double-count rather than a disappearance; a reconciler sweeps the duplicate |
| API tier | Rank reads exceed replica capacity | Shed to bucketed ranks for everyone outside the head; exact ranks stay available for the top of the board |
| Scoring | A client-trusted score reaches the board | Server-authoritative scoring computes the number itself; anomaly detection catches what still slips through after the fact |

#### What this design does not solve
**There is no consistency across the boards one match writes.** A single result updates five keys with no transaction spanning them, so a player can be visible on one board and briefly absent from another. Anything that pays out has to be computed from the event log at a sequence boundary, never read directly off a board.

**The board is called a derived index, and rebuilding the largest one is slower than that framing suggests.** Replaying the full event history for the all-time board is tens of minutes with no reads served during it, which means the hourly snapshot, nominally optional, is quietly load-bearing for any reasonable recovery time.

**Cheating is caught after the standings have already shown it.** Server-authoritative scoring stops a client from asserting a number it never earned. It does nothing about a bot playing convincingly or a collusion ring, and the correction is a retroactive removal the affected players see happen in public.

#### Final design
Read it back through the numbers. The 60k/s contest burst sitting at 60% of a single primary's ceiling is why this design does not shard by default. The 300k/s uncacheable read burst is why replicas, not shards, are the answer to read load. And the multiplication of rank reads by shard count, 300k/s becoming 2.4M ops/s at S=8, is exactly why the counter layer exists to collapse sharded rank back down before it ever gets that expensive.

[The whole design](/diagram/gaming-leaderboard?focus=clients,leaderboard-svc,event-log,board-writer,zset-primary,read-replicas,board-keys,score-history,aof-snapshots,quantile-snapshots)
