> **The numbers to remember.** 60k/s contest burst vs ~100k/s single-primary ceiling · ~300k/s uncacheable rank reads at contest close · ~9GB all-time board, ~125GB resident total · sharding turns 300k/s into 2.4M ops/s at S=8, which is what the counter layer exists to avoid.

#### Check your understanding
**Why does a database index solve top-N but not arbitrary rank?** An index on score gives ordered access from the top, which top-N needs. Rank needs a count of everyone above one player, and nothing in a plain index accumulates that count without scanning it.

**Why does span maintenance cost show up on writes rather than reads?** A span is fixed the moment a node's position changes, so an insert that shifts rank has to update every pointer that jumps over it. Reads only ever accumulate spans that are already correct.

**Why is sharding the wrong fix for a read-capacity problem?** Sharding distributes writes across more primaries. Every shard still has to be consulted for a rank read, so splitting the board multiplies the number of operations a single rank query needs rather than adding read capacity.

**Why can a tiebreaker be packed into the score instead of stored separately?** Because a double carries 53 bits of exact integer precision, more than points and an inverted timestamp need combined, so both values can be encoded into the one field the structure already sorts by.

**Why does the board need a sentinel member at rollover rather than just an early-created empty key?** Because an empty key and a nonexistent key can look identical to a careless read path, and the sentinel keeps the distinction between "this board exists and has no scores yet" and "this board is not ready" unambiguous.
### 23. Design a Payment System
#### Understanding the problem
A payment system takes a card payment end to end, authorize, capture, settle, refund, dispute, against an external processor nobody but the processor controls and nothing can roll back. It must never double-charge, never lose a payment it has acknowledged, and be able to prove years later where every unit of money went.

Two things make this harder than an ordinary write path.

First, the second participant will not cooperate with anything resembling a transaction. A card network exposes authorize, capture and void, nothing else. It will not hold a lock while a coordinator decides, and it will not tell a caller to come back later and finish. Whatever correctness this system has, it has to build without the other side's help.

Second, some failures are genuinely unknowable. A capture call times out, and there are three indistinguishable explanations: the request never arrived, it arrived and succeeded, or it arrived, succeeded, and the response was lost. Guessing wrong in either direction costs real money, in either direction.

> **What this is not.** It looks like a digital wallet transferring money between accounts: both move money, both need strong consistency, both fear double-spend. A wallet transfer moves money between two rows this system owns, so atomicity is genuinely achievable, same-shard as one transaction, cross-shard as a coordinated reservation over columns it controls. Here the second party is a card network reached through a processor that will not enlist in anything. A half-completed wallet transfer can be reversed with nobody the wiser; a half-completed card authorization has already put a hold on someone's account and may already be visible in their banking app.

#### Requirements and the numbers
**Functional.** Charge a card. Refund, including partial capture. Recurring subscriptions. Multi-currency. A durable ledger.

**Non-functional.** Strong consistency on money. Idempotent writes under at-least-once execution. PCI-compliant. A durable audit trail.

The whole design is decided by four numbers, so derive them before drawing anything.

**How much does peak volume actually exceed the average?** At 1B payments a year, average load is roughly 32/s. Black Friday runs at roughly 10x a normal day, compressed into a shorter window, and a flash-sale minute inside that runs another 3x, landing at roughly **2.3k payments/s**, provisioned to **3k/s**.

**How much latency budget is actually available for everything the system controls?** Checkout targets a 3-second p99 before abandonment climbs sharply. A PSP authorize call alone runs roughly 1.2 seconds at p99, leaving **~1.8 seconds** for risk scoring, the idempotency write, the ledger write and serialization combined.

**How big does the idempotency store actually get, and why 24 hours?** Sized on peak day rather than peak throughput held for a day, roughly 31.5M keys at ~1KB each is **~32GB**, doubled for replicas to **~64GB**. The 24-hour TTL is chosen to match what PSPs themselves honour for their own server-side deduplication, not an arbitrary round number.

**What does double-entry bookkeeping actually cost per payment?** Roughly 3 ledger entries per payment on average (2 for a plain charge, up to 6 through a refund chain) at ~500 bytes each is **~1.5KB of ledger per payment**, alongside a ~2KB charge record, for **~3.5TB/year** combined at 1B payments.

> **The numbers to carry.** ~2.3k payments/s peak, provisioned to 3k/s · ~1.8s of latency budget outside the PSP's own 1.2s · ~32GB idempotency store at a 24-hour TTL matching PSP-side dedupe · ~1.5KB of ledger writes per payment, ~3.5TB/year combined with charge records.

#### The workflow, the ledger, and the API
It helps to say plainly what each piece of state is actually for.

- **Idempotency key**: a client-generated UUID scoped to one purchase attempt, stored alongside a hash of the request body and a recovery point.
- **Recovery point**: the name of the last completed step in a charge's workflow, `started → risk_scored → psp_authorized → ledger_recorded → captured → finished`.
- **Ledger entry**: an immutable, paired debit and credit, append-only, never edited.
- **Charge**: the durable state machine record, holding `psp_charge_id`, the join key for reconciliation.

The API:

```
POST /charge
  headers: idempotency-key
  body: { customer_id, amount, currency, payment_method_token }
  → { charge_id, status: succeeded|requires_action|failed }
POST /charge/{id}/refund   body: { amount?, reason? }
```

#### High-level design
Follow one charge from a client's request to a committed ledger entry.

[The hot path, charge to ledger commit](/diagram/payment-system?focus=client,api,idem,orchestrator,psp,ledger,charges,e1,e2,e3,e4,e5,e6,e7)

1. **Payment API** validates the request and commits `(key, request_hash, recovery_point)` to the **Idempotency store** before any external call.
2. **Payment orchestrator** starts or resumes the saga from the stored recovery point.
3. The orchestrator calls the **PSP** to authorize, then capture, passing the client's own idempotency key through.
4. Successful steps write paired entries to the **Ledger** and advance the **Charges table**'s state.
5. Every recovery-point write lands in the same database transaction as the step it describes, so recorded progress can lag reality but never lead it.

> **Why the flow is shaped this way.** Gateways fail, webhooks retry, and money movement has to stay explainable when outside dependencies misbehave. Treating the ledger as the internal source of truth gives the design a stable centre that does not move when the processor does.

#### The recovery point that never lies
A crashed workflow needs to know exactly how far it got before it can safely resume. What state, recorded where, actually gives it that?

[Where the key and the recovery point commit](/diagram/payment-system?focus=api,idem,orchestrator,e2,e3,e6)

**Bad: store a binary `in_progress` / `done` flag.** A retry that finds `in_progress` learns only that somebody started, which leaves two bad options: replay every step and risk a second authorize, or poll the processor with no idea what to ask about.

**Good: store a named recovery point, but write it separately from the step's own work.** Naming the last completed step is real progress, and if the recovery-point write and the step's actual work commit in two different transactions, a crash between them leaves the recorded state ahead of reality, exactly the ambiguity a recovery point exists to remove.

**Great: commit each recovery point in the same transaction as the work it describes.** The **Idempotency store** row and the step's own effect land together or neither lands. A resumed workflow reading `risk_scored` knows risk scoring definitely ran and knows nothing about authorize, which is precisely the right amount of doubt: recorded progress can lag reality but can never lead it.

[The recovery point never lies ahead of the work](/diagram/payment-system?figure=recovery-point)

The gap this cannot close is the external call itself: the orchestrator can die between the PSP responding and the commit landing, which is why the client's own idempotency key is passed through to the PSP, so a repeated authorize returns the first result instead of creating a second hold.

#### The ambiguous timeout
Capture times out after 4 seconds. The request may never have arrived, may have succeeded, or may have succeeded with the response lost in transit. Nothing distinguishes these from where the caller sits.

[Verification before any compensation runs](/diagram/payment-system?focus=orchestrator,verifier,psp,e8,e9,e10)

**Bad: assume failure and void the authorization.** If the capture actually landed, this refunds money that was genuinely collected, a real loss dressed up as caution.

**Good: assume success and skip the retry.** If the capture never landed, this ships goods or services for a payment that never happened, a real loss dressed up as optimism. Neither guess is safer than the other; both are simply wrong in different directions.

**Great: move the charge to a genuine verification state, and ask the processor directly.** **Payment orchestrator** hands the charge to a **Verification worker**, which queries the **PSP** by the same idempotency key rather than guessing. Only once that answer comes back does the workflow confirm the charge or compensate it.

[One query replaces three guesses](/diagram/payment-system?figure=verification)

Running a compensation straight after a timeout, without this step, risks trying to void a charge the PSP already captured, which it rejects, leaving the workflow wedged with real money on one side and a permanently failing compensation on the other.

#### Why not two-phase commit
Two systems agreeing atomically on one outcome is exactly what two-phase commit is for. Why does this design reach for something else instead?

[The orchestrator against a participant that will not enlist](/diagram/payment-system?focus=orchestrator,psp,ledger,e4,e5)

**Bad: try to force the card network into a prepare-and-commit protocol.** No such API exists. Visa, Mastercard and every PSP layered on them expose authorize, capture and void, nothing that resembles holding a lock while a coordinator decides, so this option is not actually available.

**Good: call the PSP and retry blindly on any uncertainty, trusting it to sort out duplicates.** This depends entirely on the far side deduplicating, which not every rail does. Plenty of older acquirer APIs and domestic bank rails treat a resubmission as a brand-new instruction, so blind retrying against those creates a second real charge.

**Great: run the charge as a saga, and pass the client's own idempotency key to the PSP so it absorbs the repeat.** **Payment orchestrator** treats each step, risk score, authorize, ledger write, capture, as independently committed, with a compensating action for each. Passing the same client-generated key through to the **PSP** means a repeated authorize call returns the original result rather than creating a second hold, which is the far side doing the deduplication this design cannot force through a lock.

The honest limit: this only works because a modern PSP chooses to honour a caller-supplied key. Where a rail offers neither deduplication nor a queryable reference, exactly-once effect genuinely is not available, and the correct statement is at-most-once submission plus reconciliation by a human.

#### Ledger as an append-only journal, not a balance column
Every payment changes how much money is owed somewhere. The obvious way to store that is a number that goes up or down. That obvious way cannot answer the question a payments system gets asked years later.

[Where a payment's effect actually lands](/diagram/payment-system?focus=ledger,orchestrator,e5)

**Bad: one balance column per account, updated in place.** Fast to read, and it destroys history: once a balance is overwritten, there is no way to reconstruct what it was at any earlier moment, which is exactly the question a seven-year audit trail exists to answer.

**Good: a balance column plus a best-effort event log kept alongside it for support queries.** This adds a rough history back, and "best-effort" is doing real work in that sentence: nothing guarantees the log and the column stay in agreement, so the very discrepancy an auditor asks about can exist between the two records meant to explain it.

**Great: an append-only, double-entry ledger, with balances treated as a derived, checkpointed cache.** Every payment writes paired debit and credit entries to the **Ledger**, never edited, only ever added to. Reconstructing any account's balance at any past instant becomes a bounded scan over entries up to that point, not an impossible question. Refunds and compensations are new entries too, never edits to what already happened.

The price is concrete and small: roughly 3 entries per payment at ~500 bytes each, a few extra writes on the hot path, in exchange for a guarantee an in-place balance can never offer.

#### A hot merchant's ledger row under contention
One merchant taking thousands of charges a second means thousands of writes converging on the same account row. What actually breaks first, and how does the invariant survive the fix?

[The ledger under a concentrated write load](/diagram/payment-system?focus=ledger,e5)

**Bad: let every charge write straight to that merchant's single balance row.** Every write serialises on the same row lock, and throughput caps out at a few hundred transactions a second long before anything else in the system is under pressure.

**Good: batch writes and apply them periodically.** This reduces lock contention and introduces a lag between when money moved and when the balance reflects it, which is tolerable for some reads and not for anything gating a payout decision.

**Great: shard the hot account into N sub-accounts, and treat the true balance as their sum.** Each charge writes to a randomly chosen sub-account shard rather than one contended row. The global invariant, `sum(debits) == sum(credits)`, still holds exactly; it is simply computed as a sum across shards rather than a single row. A periodically materialised total serves ordinary balance reads.

The cost this shifts rather than removes: an exact, authoritative balance now needs all N shards available at once, so anything gating a payout has to wait for a complete checkpoint across every shard rather than trusting a partial sum, because stalling a payout is recoverable and paying out on a wrong number is not.

#### Where it breaks
| Layer | Failure | How the design handles it |
|---|---|---|
| PSP integration | A capture call times out with the outcome unknown | The charge moves to a verification state; a worker queries the PSP by idempotency key before anything is confirmed or compensated |
| Idempotency | The idempotency row is stuck `in_progress` after a crash | The recovery point resumes the workflow from its last committed step rather than replaying from the start |
| Ledger write | Authorization succeeds but the ledger write fails | The ledger sits on the success path; a failed write triggers a void compensation and an internal failure state |
| Webhook handling | Events arrive out of order or duplicated | Idempotent handlers dedupe on event id; the orchestrator's state machine rejects any illegal transition |
| Reconciliation | The daily PSP report disagrees with the ledger | Affected accounts freeze; a human investigates and corrects only through an explicit, audited adjustment entry |
| Ledger contention | A single merchant's balance row saturates under load | The account shards into sub-accounts; the debit-equals-credit invariant holds across the sum rather than one row |
| PCI boundary | Raw card data reaches a log or a backup | Tokenization at the client keeps raw card numbers off the backend entirely; CI blocks card-shaped fields in log emitters |

#### What this design does not solve
**Exactly-once holds per key, not per human intent.** A user who taps pay again after a cold app restart gets a fresh idempotency key, and two valid, correctly deduplicated authorizations result, both individually correct by every rule in this design and still two real charges for one purchase in the customer's mind.

**PSP failover and idempotency are in direct conflict.** An idempotency key is namespaced to one provider. Routing an in-flight charge to a backup PSP during an outage discards the only protection this design had for that charge, so a hard outage has to stop the in-flight set rather than gracefully degrade it.

**The idempotency window is far shorter than the liability window.** The key expires in 24 hours, matching what the PSP itself honours, while chargebacks can arrive up to 120 days later. Past the key's lifetime, the only handle on a payment is `psp_charge_id` and human judgement over the settlement archive.

#### Final design
Read it back through the numbers. A 1.8-second latency budget outside the PSP's own 1.2 seconds is why authorization stays synchronous while capture moves off the request path. A 24-hour idempotency window chosen to match the PSP's own deduplication is why that boundary, not a round number, sets the liability gap this design has to concede. And roughly 1.5KB of ledger writes per payment is the small, deliberate price of being able to answer, years later, exactly what happened to any unit of money.

[The whole design](/diagram/payment-system?focus=client,api,orchestrator,verifier,webhook-queue,recon,idem,psp,ledger,charges,settlement)

> **The numbers to remember.** ~2.3k payments/s peak, 3k/s provisioned · ~1.8s of latency budget outside the PSP's 1.2s · ~32GB idempotency store at a 24h TTL matching PSP-side dedupe · ~1.5KB of ledger writes per payment.

#### Check your understanding
**Why does a binary `in_progress` flag force a resumed workflow into replaying everything or guessing?** Because it records only that something started, not which step actually finished, so the resumer has no way to know what is safe to skip.

**Why must a recovery point commit in the same transaction as the step it names?** Because if the two could commit separately, a crash between them could leave the recorded state claiming progress that never actually happened, which is worse than recording no progress at all.

**Why is verifying with the PSP better than picking the statistically likelier outcome after a timeout?** Because either wrong guess costs real money in a different direction, refunding a real charge or shipping for free, and a direct query replaces both guesses with the actual answer.

**Why can a saga succeed here where two-phase commit cannot?** Because two-phase commit requires every participant to hold a lock until the coordinator decides, and the card network offers no such interface; a saga instead accepts visible intermediate states and undoes them with compensations if a later step fails.

**Why does sharding a hot merchant's ledger account not break the debit-equals-credit invariant?** Because the invariant was never about one row. It is a sum, and summing across shards produces the same total as summing one row would, just computed differently.
### 24. Design a Digital Wallet
#### Understanding the problem
A digital wallet holds balances for 100M users and moves money between them with no way to create or destroy value. Every transfer must be atomic, idempotent under retry, and reconstructible from an audit trail seven years later.

Two things make this harder than an ordinary balance update.

First, sender and receiver usually live on different database shards. A transfer that touches two rows on two machines cannot be one local transaction the way a single-account update can, and most transfers are exactly this kind: with accounts spread across shards, a random pair sharing one machine is rare.

Second, nothing about this problem lets a balance be authoritative. A number that can be overwritten cannot be proven correct months later, only trusted, and trust is not what a seven-year audit trail is for. The balance a user sees has to be a fast read of something else that is actually true.

> **What this is not.** It looks like a payment system authorizing a card: both move money, both fear double-spend, both need an audit trail. A card authorization crosses a boundary this system does not own; the card network will not hold a lock, cannot be rolled back, and may reverse the charge days later as a chargeback. Every account in a wallet transfer belongs to the same system, which means a reservation is genuinely available here: funds can be held, checked and released with nothing external to negotiate with. That is exactly why a compensating saga, correct for a card charge, is the wrong tool here when a cleaner reservation was available the whole time.

#### Requirements and the numbers
**Functional.** Deposit, withdraw, transfer between users, query balance, transaction history.

**Non-functional.** ACID on every transfer. No money created or lost, ever. Audit-grade history. Idempotent under retry.

The whole design is decided by four numbers, so derive them before drawing anything.

**How rare is it for a transfer to land on one shard?** With accounts sharded by `user_id % 128`, a random pair shares a shard with probability 1/128 ≈ 0.8%. Even generous co-location of predictable pairs still leaves **over 90% of transfers crossing shards**, which makes cross-shard the design, not the exception.

**How much load does the system actually carry?** 30M daily active users at roughly 8 money movements each gives 240M movements/day, **~2.8k/s average**, concentrating to **~10k/s at peak**.

**What does a single account row actually cost to write, and where does that break?** At roughly 1-2ms per committed transaction, one row absorbs **500 to 1,000 writes/s**. A popular merchant taking 3,000 credits/s at peak is **3 to 6x over that ceiling**, and the failure is not a graceful slowdown; optimistic retries thrash as offered load rises.

**How much does the append-only ledger actually cost to keep?** Double-entry writes 2 entries per movement: 240M × 2 = 480M entries/day, roughly **~435GB/day** on the hot store. At 7-year retention for audit and AML requirements, that is **~370TB raw**, compressing to **~75TB cold** once archived off the hot tier.

> **The numbers to carry.** Over 90% of transfers cross shards, so TCC is the default path, not the exception · ~10k/s peak against ~2.8k/s average · a single account row caps out around 500-1,000 writes/s · ~435GB/day of ledger writes, ~370TB raw over 7 years.

#### The ledger, the reservation, and the API
It helps to say plainly what is real and what is derived here.

- **Account row**: `(user_id, currency, balance, reserved, pending, version)`, sharded by `user_id`. Spendable balance is `balance - reserved`.
- **Ledger entry**: an append-only, paired debit and credit sharing one `reference`, never edited or deleted.
- **Reservation**: an application-level hold with a TTL and the orchestrator's lease id, the entire mechanism for cross-shard coordination.
- **Transfer**: `(transfer_id, from_user, to_user, amount, status, idempotency_key)`.

The API:

```
GET  /balance/{user_id}          → { available, pending, currency }
POST /transfer   headers: idempotency-key
     body: { from, to, amount, currency }
                                  → { transfer_id, status }
```

#### High-level design
Follow one transfer across two shards.

[The hot path, cross-shard transfer](/diagram/digital-wallet?focus=client,wallet-svc,orchestrator,shard-a,shard-b,ledger,e1,e3,e4,e5,e8,e9)

1. **Client** sends `POST /transfer` with an idempotency key to the **Wallet service**.
2. **Transfer orchestrator** determines whether sender and receiver share a shard; if not, it runs Try on both.
3. **Shard A** moves the amount from `available` into `reserved`, a single local transaction, writing no ledger entry yet.
4. **Shard B** adds the amount to `pending`, also writing no entry.
5. Once both Trys succeed, Confirm runs on each shard, clearing the hold and writing the paired entries to the **Ledger** in the same local transaction.

> **Why the flow is shaped this way.** Mutating a balance directly is easy to build and impossible to audit. Writing entries and deriving the balance makes every state change traceable, which is what a system needs the moment reversals, disputes or a regulator show up.

#### One statement, no window
Alice has $100 and fires two transfers for $80 and $70 at the same instant. Both requests read $100, both conclude she has enough, and she ends up overdrawn. What stops this without a lock?

[The account row under concurrent writes](/diagram/digital-wallet?focus=orchestrator,shard-a,e4)

**Bad: read the balance, decide, then write.** Two concurrent requests both read $100 before either has written anything, both correctly conclude the transfer is affordable, and both proceed. The check happened against a balance that changed underneath it before the write landed.

**Good: acquire an explicit lock before reading, then check and write.** `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` closes the race by serialising the two requests, at the cost of a lock held for the round trip between the read and the write, and every transfer on that account now queues behind whichever one got there first.

**Great: put the check inside the write itself, as one statement.** `UPDATE accounts SET available = available - 80, reserved = reserved + 80 WHERE user_id = alice AND available >= 80`. There is no gap between checking and deducting because there is only one statement. When the second transfer runs, `available` is already $20, the predicate fails, zero rows update, and the transfer fails cleanly with nothing to unwind.

[One conditional UPDATE, no gap to race into](/diagram/digital-wallet?figure=one-statement)

This needs no explicit lock and no coordination between the two requests, because the database engine itself guarantees the check and the deduction happen as one indivisible operation.

#### Coordinating money across shards without holding a lock
Sender and receiver live on different machines, so no local transaction spans both. What actually moves the money atomically without one side blocking the other for a network round trip?

[The orchestrator running Try against both shards](/diagram/digital-wallet?focus=orchestrator,shard-a,shard-b,e4,e5)

**Bad: hold a distributed lock across both shards until both sides agree.** This makes the transfer genuinely atomic, and it requires a coordinator holding row locks across a network round trip. Cross-region that round trip is 60 to 150ms, capping a hot account's throughput at roughly 16 transfers a second, and a coordinator that stalls holds both rows locked until an operator intervenes.

**Good: debit the sender, credit the receiver, and reverse the debit if the credit fails.** This is a plain compensating saga, and it creates a real window in which the money is in neither account. A balance query landing in that window returns a number that was never true, which a regulator does not accept as "briefly wrong."

**Great: reserve on both sides first, confirm only once both reservations succeed.** **Transfer orchestrator** runs Try against **Shard A**, moving funds from `available` into `reserved`, and Try against **Shard B**, adding to `pending`. Neither Try writes a ledger entry. Only once both succeed does Confirm run on each side, clearing the hold and writing the paired entry. Each reservation carries a TTL, so an orchestrator that dies leaves behind a row with a deadline rather than a permanently frozen account.

The property that makes this safe: nothing is ever locked between the two rounds, only marked, so recovery from a crash needs no human and no coordinator to be alive.

#### Where the entries land
Both sides of a transfer commit independently, in two rounds. If the ledger recorded a movement the moment either side started, what would reconciliation actually be checking?

[Try and Confirm against the ledger](/diagram/digital-wallet?focus=shard-a,shard-b,ledger,e4,e5,e8,e9)

**Bad: write the ledger entry at Try time, on both sides.** This records the movement as soon as it starts, and it creates entries for transfers that never complete: if the receiver's Try fails, the sender's entry already exists and has to be reversed, which is exactly the kind of correction an append-only ledger is supposed to avoid needing.

**Good: write the entry at Try, but mark it provisional until Confirm.** This avoids permanently recording a failed transfer, and it means the reconciliation invariant now has to account for a third category, provisional entries, alongside confirmed ones, which is exactly the kind of conditional logic a clean invariant exists to eliminate.

**Great: write no entry at Try, and let Confirm be the only place an entry is created.** Try only ever touches `reserved` and `pending` columns on **Shard A** and **Shard B**. **Ledger** entries are inserted exclusively inside Confirm, in the same local transaction that clears the hold. The reconciliation invariant stays exactly `sum(ledger entries) == accounts.balance`, never `balance + reserved`, because reserved money genuinely has no entries yet: it has not moved.

One consequence falls out cleanly: Confirm can only ever fail for infrastructure reasons, never business ones, because the funds were already checked and set aside at Try. That is what makes Confirm safe to retry blindly, something that would be dangerous at Try time.

#### A sweeper racing a late Confirm
An orchestrator stalls between Try and Confirm. The sweeper cancels the expired reservation at its TTL. Then the stalled orchestrator wakes up and tries to Confirm a reservation that no longer exists.

[The sweeper and the orchestrator's lease](/diagram/digital-wallet?focus=orchestrator,sweeper,shard-a,e6,e7)

**Bad: let the sweeper cancel purely on TTL, and let Confirm apply unconditionally.** Done naively, the recovered orchestrator's Confirm credits the receiver against money that has already been returned to the sender, creating value that was never there. The two processes have no way to know about each other's actions.

**Good: have the sweeper check the TTL carefully, but leave Confirm unguarded.** A careful sweeper still cannot prevent this failure alone, because the danger is not the sweeper acting wrongly, it is the orchestrator acting on stale information after the sweeper has already acted correctly.

**Great: tag every reservation with the orchestrator's lease id, and make Confirm conditional on it.** **Reservation sweeper** cancels only leases it can prove are expired. **Transfer orchestrator**'s Confirm runs `WHERE reservation_id = ? AND lease_id = ?`. If the sweeper already cancelled the reservation, that predicate matches zero rows, and the stale orchestrator's Confirm fails cleanly into the transfer's failure path instead of half-applying.

[A stale Confirm matches zero rows instead of half-applying](/diagram/digital-wallet?figure=lease-fencing)

The losing side of this race fails loudly by design. A Confirm that silently succeeds against a stale lease would be indistinguishable from a correct one until an audit found the extra money months later.

#### One row, thousands of writes
A merchant account takes 3,000 credits a second. A single row commits at most 1,000 writes a second. What happens, and what actually fixes it?

[A hot account under sustained credit load](/diagram/digital-wallet?focus=shard-b,hot-account,e10)

**Bad: let every credit write straight to the merchant's one balance row.** Under optimistic concurrency, each retry re-reads a version that has already moved again by the time it retries, so goodput falls as offered load rises rather than levelling off. Under a pessimistic lock, the queue in front of that row grows without bound at 3,000/s against a 500/s ceiling.

**Good: batch the account's credits in memory and flush periodically.** A write-behind aggregator collapsing 50ms of credits into one transaction genuinely reduces write pressure, and it now holds money the user has already been told they received inside one process's memory, a second write path with its own failure modes and its own risk of loss.

**Great: split the hot account into independent sub-balances, and sum them on read.** **Hot account sub-balances** hashes each credit onto one of 16 sub-rows, giving roughly 190 writes/s per row, comfortably inside the single-row ceiling. The ledger is unaffected: one entry per movement, still referencing the logical merchant account. A read sums 16 rows instead of one.

Debits are the part this does not solve cleanly: a single large payout can exceed any one sub-balance, so debits route through a designated sub-balance while a background rebalancer levels the sixteen with ordinary internal transfers between accounts the merchant already owns.

#### Where it breaks
| Layer | Failure | How the design handles it |
|---|---|---|
| Cross-shard reservation | Try succeeds on one side; the orchestrator dies before Confirm or Cancel | The reservation's TTL expires and the sweeper releases it automatically, with no human required |
| Sweeper vs orchestrator | A recovered orchestrator tries to Confirm a reservation the sweeper already cancelled | Lease-id fencing makes the stale Confirm match zero rows and fail cleanly rather than half-apply |
| Hot account | A popular merchant's balance row saturates under load | The account splits into sub-balances hashed by credit, keeping each row under its write ceiling |
| Ledger reconciliation | The materialised balance drifts from the sum of entries | The account freezes and pages a human; nothing auto-corrects a number with unreviewed write access to real money |
| Outbox relay | Balance changes commit but downstream event publication lags | Streaming from the write-ahead log via logical decoding bounds the delay by replication throughput, not poll interval |
| FX quote | A cross-currency reservation outlives the rate it locked | The reservation TTL is bound to the quote TTL, and Confirm revalidates freshness inline |
| Escrow | A transfer targets a recipient who has not registered yet | The funds live in a real escrow account with real entries, swept back to the sender if unclaimed after a deadline |

#### What this design does not solve
**The fast path is a rounding error, and co-location does not really fix that.** Hash placement puts under 1% of random pairs on the same shard, so the single-transaction path is not the common case despite reading like the simple one. Co-locating accounts by social graph helps only for pairs stable and high-volume enough to be worth pinning by hand; the long tail of transfers stays cross-shard permanently.

**Reconciliation can detect drift but cannot safely repair it.** Freezing and paging is the only defensible response to a mismatch, because an automatic corrector would be a background job with unreviewed write access to every balance in the system, a worse risk than the drift it exists to fix. That leaves a real person locked out of their own money for as long as the on-call response takes.

**Every guarantee here stops at the wallet's own boundary.** The invariant holds because both accounts in any transfer belong to the same system. The moment money crosses into a card or bank rail, that stops being true: the external leg is submitted, the bank's answer arrives hours or days later, and in between, the wallet's books and the bank's books disagree by construction.

#### Final design
Read it back through the numbers. Over 90% of transfers crossing shards is why TCC is the default path this design is built around, not a fallback for an edge case. A single row's 500-to-1,000 write ceiling against a hot merchant's 3,000/s is why sub-balances exist at all. And 480M ledger entries a day, kept for seven years, is the cost this design accepts in exchange for being able to prove, at any point in that window, exactly where every unit of money went.

[The whole design](/diagram/digital-wallet?focus=client,wallet-svc,idempotency,orchestrator,sweeper,shard-a,shard-b,ledger,hot-account,reconciler,event-log)

> **The numbers to remember.** Over 90% of transfers cross shards · ~10k/s peak against ~2.8k/s average · a single account row caps around 500-1,000 writes/s · ~435GB/day of ledger writes, ~370TB raw over 7 years.

#### Check your understanding
**Why does a read-then-write balance check fail under concurrency even with correct arithmetic?** Because two concurrent requests can both read the same starting balance before either writes, so both correctly conclude the transfer is affordable against a number that is about to become wrong.

**Why is a compensating saga the wrong tool inside a wallet even though it works for a payment system's card charge?** Because a saga's debit-then-credit ordering creates a real window where money sits in neither account, and every account in a wallet transfer belongs to the same system, so a reservation, which avoids that window entirely, is always available instead.

**Why does Try never write a ledger entry, only Confirm?** Because writing an entry at Try would record a movement that has not actually happened yet, and if the transfer later fails, that entry would need to be reversed, exactly the correction an append-only ledger is meant to make unnecessary.

**Why does a lease id on each reservation matter more than the sweeper simply checking the TTL correctly?** Because the danger is not the sweeper acting wrongly, it is the orchestrator acting on stale information afterward; the lease id is what lets Confirm detect that its own information is stale and fail instead of half-applying.

**Why does splitting a hot account into sub-balances leave the ledger's invariant untouched?** Because each sub-balance still writes one entry per movement referencing the same logical account; only the row being written changes, not the accounting.
### 25. Design a Stock Exchange (Matching Engine)
#### Understanding the problem
A stock exchange accepts orders from member firms, matches them into trades under published priority rules, and publishes the resulting market data to every subscriber at the same instant. Latency is measured in microseconds, and a wrong or unreproducible fill is a regulatory event rather than an ordinary bug.

Two things make this harder than a fast queue.

First, matching itself is the easy part. Everything genuinely hard follows from one earlier decision: where, exactly, the venue assigns the total order across every message it receives. Get that placement wrong and no amount of matching-engine cleverness fixes it, because the record of what happened first is now unprovable.

Second, the design has to survive being asked, years later, to prove exactly why a specific trade happened at a specific price. That requirement rules out anything that cannot be replayed byte-for-byte from a record, which is a far stricter bar than most systems that merely need to be correct right now.

> **What this is not.** It looks like a plain limit order book question: pick the data structure, walk the price levels, keep FIFO within a level. That question is bounded inside one instrument and one process. This one starts where that one stops: who assigns order across symbols and what that costs, what gets rejected before it ever enters the record, how identical bytes reach every subscriber at the same instant, and what a regulator can prove seven years later. Answering with just the book is answering a smaller question.

#### Requirements and the numbers
**Functional.** Place, cancel and modify orders. Match under the venue's priority rule. Publish market data. Report trades. Run opening and closing auctions.

**Non-functional.** Single-digit microseconds inside the engine. The total order provable years later. A complete audit trail. Sub-second failover. No unbounded pauses on the hot path.

The whole design is decided by four numbers, so derive them before drawing anything.

**How much headroom does the sequencer actually have?** A tuned single-threaded sequencer sustains 1M to 5M messages a second. Peak inbound across the venue runs at roughly **1M msgs/s**, sitting at the bottom of that band with **up to 5x headroom**, which is the number that decides whether one sequencer can carry the whole venue.

**How much does one trading day actually cost to keep, durably?** At roughly 80 bytes per message and ~4B inbound messages a day, the raw log is **~350GB/day**, replicated to **~1TB/day** across local and DR copies, comfortably one NVMe shelf.

**How much order-book state does the venue actually have to hold in memory?** Roughly 10,000 symbols at ~2MB of book state each, **~20GB total**, sharded by symbol so any single engine host holds its own slice with room to spare.

**How much market-data traffic does a busy open actually generate?** Each aggressive order touches roughly 10 price-level deltas on average. At 1M msgs/s peak, that is **~10M book-update events/s**, roughly **~500MB/s of multicast egress**, which fits comfortably on one 10GbE feed.

> **The numbers to carry.** ~1M msgs/s peak against a 1M-5M/s single-sequencer ceiling · ~350GB/day raw log, ~1TB/day replicated · ~20GB of total book state across ~10k symbols · ~500MB/s multicast egress at peak.

#### The sequenced log, the engines, and the API
It helps to say plainly what is authoritative here and what is derived from it.

- **Sequenced input log**: the single system of record, append-only, holding every accepted order in the exact order the venue assigned.
- **Matching engine**: one single-threaded process per symbol, a pure function of the log slice it reads.
- **Order book**: sorted price levels, each holding a FIFO queue, entirely in memory and entirely derivable from the log.
- **Output sequencer**: the single point where every symbol's outputs are reassembled into one globally ordered market-data stream.

The API:

```
NewOrder: { client_order_id, symbol, side, qty, price, type, tif }
Cancel:   { order_id }
Modify:   { order_id, new_qty, new_price }
Acks:
  ExecutionReport { order_id, status, filled_qty, avg_price }
  TradeReport     { trade_id, buy_order, sell_order, qty, price, ts }
```

#### High-level design
Follow one order from a member firm to a published trade.

[The hot path, order to published market data](/diagram/stock-exchange?focus=member-firms,gateway,sequencer,input-log,matching,order-book,output-seq,md-publisher,subscribers,e1,e3,e4,e5,e6,e10,e11,e12)

1. **Member firms** submit through the **Order gateway**, which authenticates, validates and runs pre-trade risk before anything else happens.
2. Survivors reach the **Sequencer**, a single pinned thread that assigns the next global sequence number.
3. The order is committed to the **Sequenced input log** before it becomes visible to anything downstream.
4. **Matching engines**, one single thread per symbol, read their symbol's slice of the log and update the **Order book, per symbol**.
5. Resulting fills and book deltas flow through the **Output sequencer** into the **Market data publisher**, reaching **Market data subscribers** at the same instant over reliable multicast.

> **Why the flow is shaped this way.** Everything above the sequencer exists to keep bad input out of the record; everything below it exists to derive state from that record. The sequencer is the only point where "what happened first" is decided, and once decided it is never revisited.

#### Why single-threaded per symbol is a correctness property, not a speed one
A matching engine handling one symbol at a time looks like it is leaving performance on the table. Adding threads seems like the obvious fix. Why does the design refuse that trade?

[One engine, reading only its own log slice](/diagram/stock-exchange?focus=matching,order-book,input-log,e5,e6)

**Bad: run multiple threads against one symbol's book, coordinated by locks.** This genuinely increases throughput on paper, and it introduces non-determinism the moment two threads can acquire a lock in different orders on different runs: identical input can produce different fills depending on scheduling, which makes replaying a day to verify a trade meaningless.

**Good: keep a single thread per symbol, but let it read live network input directly.** Single-threading alone removes the lock-ordering hazard. Reading live input still leaves the engine's behaviour dependent on exactly when packets arrived on this particular run, which is not something a regulator can reconstruct from a stored artefact months later.

**Great: a single thread per symbol, reading only a durable, sequenced log.** Each **Matching engine** consumes only its symbol's slice of the **Sequenced input log** and touches nothing else. Given the same log, it always produces the same **Order book** state and the same trades, because it is a pure function of its input. That single property is what makes a standby an extra reader instead of a replica to keep in sync, and what makes any trading day reproducible on demand.

The throughput this gives up is real and small: roughly 500,000 operations a second per symbol on current hardware, which comfortably exceeds what any single stock actually generates.

#### What determinism actually forbids
"The engine is a pure function of its log" sounds like a design principle. It is really a list of specific things the code must never do, and violating any one of them breaks replay in a way that stays invisible until the day someone needs it.

[The log as the engine's only input](/diagram/stock-exchange?focus=sequencer,input-log,matching,e4,e5)

**Bad: let the engine read the wall clock directly.** A timer-dependent rule, IOC expiry, a good-till-time cancel, an auction cutoff, that calls `now()` produces a different answer on replay than it did live, because replay does not happen at the same wall-clock speed as the original session.

**Good: remove the wall-clock reads, but leave randomness, allocation order and external config alone.** This closes the most obvious hole and leaves three quieter ones: a container whose iteration order depends on pointer values orders fills differently between runs; memory allocated on demand gives every run a different layout; and configuration changed by a live push outside the log makes two replays of the same log disagree about what rules were active.

**Great: push every time-dependent and external input through the sequenced log itself.** Time enters as sequenced tick events the **Sequencer** emits at a fixed cadence, so every timer-based rule reads those instead of a clock. Books use intrusive lists with explicit ordering rather than hash-map iteration. Memory pools are preallocated at startup so every run has identical layout. Reference data changes only via a sequenced control message on the same **Sequenced input log**, never a config push that bypasses it.

[Four inputs the engine must never read directly](/diagram/stock-exchange?figure=deterministic-inputs)

The consequence of getting this wrong is not a crash. It is an engine that appears to work correctly for months and then produces a replay that disagrees with what actually happened, at precisely the moment someone needed the two to match.

#### Durability before visibility
An order is sequenced. A moment later the matching engine sees it, matches it, and a trade happens. Where exactly does "durable" have to sit relative to "visible" for that trade to be unwindable if something crashes?

[The commit that has to land before any engine reads it](/diagram/stock-exchange?focus=sequencer,input-log,matching,e4,e5)

**Bad: publish the order to matching engines as soon as the sequencer assigns a number, and persist afterward.** This minimises the latency an order experiences, and it creates a genuinely unrecoverable case: if the process crashes after the engine has matched and emitted a trade but before that order reached durable storage, the trade exists in the market data feed and on a firm's blotter but not in the official record, with no clean way to unwind it.

**Good: persist to the primary's own disk before publishing, but skip synchronous replication.** This closes the single-process crash case and leaves a site-level one open: losing the machine holding the only durable copy loses orders that were acknowledged to firms as accepted.

**Great: commit synchronously to two local replicas before the order becomes visible to any engine.** The **Sequencer** writes the order into the **Sequenced input log**, fsyncs to NVMe, and replicates synchronously over RDMA to a second sequencer in the same rack, committing only once both hold it, roughly 5 to 10 microseconds. Only after that commit does any **Matching engine** ever see the order.

The ordering, not just the durability, is what matters: with commit strictly before visibility, the worst possible failure is an order that was never acknowledged, which a firm simply retries. Reversing the order turns the same failure into a trade nobody can prove happened, or can't un-happen.

#### Failover without a state migration
The primary matching engine for a symbol crashes mid-session. A standby needs to take over in under a second, with no data loss and no chance both processes believe they are primary at once.

[The standby reading the same log the primary reads](/diagram/stock-exchange?focus=input-log,standby,failover-ctl,matching,e7,e8,e9)

**Bad: restore the standby from a periodic snapshot of the primary's state.** This works only as well as the snapshot's age allows, and a snapshot taken minutes ago is missing every order since, which the standby would have to somehow recover from elsewhere before it could safely take over.

**Good: replicate the primary's internal state continuously to the standby.** This keeps the standby current, and it makes the standby a second copy that has to be kept synchronised with the primary's exact internal representation, a coordination problem with its own failure modes, rather than an independent computation of the same answer.

**Great: run the standby as a second reader of the same log, executing the same binary.** **Hot standby** reads the identical **Sequenced input log** the primary does and runs the same deterministic code at the same rate, so it stays within microseconds of the primary simply by doing the same work. Failover has no state-migration step at all: a **Failover controller** detects the primary's failure, fences its ability to publish, and only then promotes the standby.

The fencing step exists for one specific danger: two engines that both believe they are primary would each emit trades against the same sequence numbers with different order ids, which market data subscribers would both accept as real. A deliberate sub-second pause while the controller fences the old primary is the accepted cost of never risking that.

[Fencing revokes before the standby is promoted](/diagram/stock-exchange?figure=fencing)

#### Snapshots bound cold start, they are not durability
The venue keeps periodic snapshots of each order book. It would be easy to lean on them as the actual recovery mechanism. Why is that the wrong way to think about them?

[The log that has to stand alone](/diagram/stock-exchange?focus=input-log,matching,order-book,e5,e6)

**Bad: treat the latest snapshot as the source of truth for recovery.** This recovers quickly, and it quietly invites a snapshot to carry some field that is not actually derivable from the log, at which point the log alone is no longer sufficient to reconstruct the day, without anyone deciding that on purpose.

**Good: keep the log as the real source of truth, but never actually test recovering without a snapshot.** The intention is correct. Without the test, a snapshot can become silently load-bearing the first time someone adds a convenient field to it, and nobody notices until the day the snapshot is missing or wrong.

**Great: treat a snapshot purely as a bound on cold-start replay time, and prove it with a deliberate test.** A periodic serialisation of the **Order book** exists only so a restarting **Matching engine** does not have to replay an entire session from the open. The test is blunt and non-negotiable: delete every snapshot, and the venue must still reconstruct the day from the **Sequenced input log** alone.

This is the same discipline as the determinism rules above, applied to recovery rather than replay: anything that is allowed to matter has to be derivable from the log, or the log's claim to be the system of record stops being true in practice.

#### Where it breaks
| Layer | Failure | How the design handles it |
|---|---|---|
| Hot path | An unbounded pause, such as a garbage collection stop | Preallocated pools and no allocation on the hot path make the pause structurally impossible rather than merely rare |
| Hot symbol | One symbol's arrival rate spikes 100x during a news event | The per-symbol architecture already contains the blast radius; only that symbol's engine degrades |
| Sequencer | Cannot fsync at line rate or stalls | Gateways receive backpressure; matching never proceeds without durable sequence assignment |
| Hot standby | Falls materially behind the primary | Failover is blocked above a lag tolerance rather than promoting a standby that is not actually current |
| Market data | Subscribers miss multicast packets | A dedicated gap-fill channel serves recent sequence ranges from a ring buffer, rate-limited per subscriber |
| Gateway risk | Risk checks fail open under load | The gateway fails closed rather than letting unchecked orders reach the sequencer |
| Auction logic | The opening or closing auction price computation disagrees with a shadow implementation | The venue halts rather than publishing a price two independent computations do not agree on |

#### What this design does not solve
**There is no cross-symbol atomicity, only cross-symbol ordering.** A basket trade or a two-leg spread can fill on one leg and miss on the other, leaving the participant with unintended exposure. This design pushes that problem onto the member firm's own smart order router, which is a real gap rather than a clean boundary, and native multi-leg support would require a combined engine that reintroduces exactly the cross-book coupling the single-writer-per-symbol model exists to avoid.

**Fairness is provable per gateway, not per order.** Cable-length parity equalises the physical path inside the venue's own rack, but gateway queueing still contributes jitter ahead of the sequencer that is invisible to participants and not auditable. The honest claim is the absence of systematic advantage, not a provable ordering by wire arrival.

**Determinism stops at the edge of the deterministic core.** Replay reproduces the matching engine exactly. It does not reproduce the gateway's risk decisions, which read mutable per-firm state that changes with fills, so replaying a day against a different risk snapshot can produce different rejections and therefore a different input log entirely.

#### Final design
Read it back through the numbers. ~1M msgs/s peak against a 1M-to-5M ceiling is why one global sequencer carries the venue rather than a sharded one. ~350GB/day of raw log, replicated to ~1TB/day, is a cost this design accepts so that durability can sit strictly before visibility. And ~20GB of total book state across ten thousand symbols is why partitioning by symbol, not concurrency inside one engine, is where scale actually comes from.

[The whole design](/diagram/stock-exchange?focus=member-firms,gateway,risk-state,sequencer,input-log,matching,order-book,standby,failover-ctl,output-seq,md-publisher,subscribers)

> **The numbers to remember.** ~1M msgs/s peak against a 1M-5M/s sequencer ceiling · ~350GB/day raw log, ~1TB/day replicated · ~20GB total book state across ~10k symbols · ~500MB/s multicast egress at peak.

#### Check your understanding
**Why is single-threading per symbol described as a correctness property rather than a performance limitation?** Because a multi-threaded engine with locks can produce different fills from identical input depending on scheduling, which makes replaying a day to verify a trade meaningless; a single thread over a fixed log cannot.

**Why must timers inside the engine read sequenced tick events instead of the wall clock?** Because replay does not happen at the same speed as the original session, so a rule that calls the wall clock directly produces a different answer on replay than it did live.

**Why does durability have to be committed before an order becomes visible to the matching engine, not just before the acknowledgement is sent?** Because a trade that has already been matched and published but was never durably recorded cannot be cleanly unwound if a crash follows; an order that was simply never acknowledged can always be retried.

**Why does the hot standby need no state-migration step during failover?** Because it is already independently computing the same result from the same log at the same rate, so promoting it means only redirecting traffic, never transferring state it did not already have.

**Why is deleting every snapshot the actual test of whether the log is the true system of record?** Because a snapshot can silently pick up a field that is not derivable from the log without anyone intending that, and the only way to catch it is to prove recovery still works with no snapshot to fall back on.
### 26. Design Twitter / X
#### Understanding the problem
Twitter is a public microblogging service: short posts, a follow graph, a home timeline, replies and retweets, search over everything ever posted, and trending. Every post is world readable the moment it exists and searchable within seconds.

Two things make this harder than an ordinary feed.

First, the follower distribution spans six orders of magnitude, from accounts with twenty followers to accounts with a hundred million, and the middle of that distribution is thick. A single threshold on follower count sounds like a clean rule and turns out to leave a large share of an ordinary user's own follows on the expensive side of it.

Second, the corpus is public. Nothing here is delivered only to people who hold a relationship to the author, which is what makes real-time search and trending possible at all, and it turns deletion and blocking into filtering over copies that already exist rather than an access-control check that can simply refuse a read.

> **What this is not.** It looks like a generic news feed question, and answering it well gives most of the spine here: why precompute, what precomputation costs, where the crossover sits. Four things change the answer past that spine. The skew here runs orders of magnitude further than a generic feed's rare celebrity. The corpus is public rather than access-controlled. Search is a second architecture in its own right, not a feature bolted onto the first. And retweets are a reshare cascade that routes content back through the exact distribution path the design tried to exclude it from.

#### Requirements and the numbers
**Functional.** Post, follow, home timeline, profile timeline, replies and retweets, search over the public corpus, trending.

**Non-functional.** Timeline p99 under 300ms. A new tweet visible to an active follower within 5 seconds. Searchable within 10 seconds. The write path depends on nothing except the tweet store.

The whole design is decided by four numbers, so derive them before drawing anything.

**How much of an ordinary user's follow set actually sits above a flat threshold?** Follows are made by fame, so the followed distribution skews far harder than the account distribution. Roughly a quarter of a typical 150-account follow set sits above 10,000 followers, which is **~38 authors above a flat threshold**, not the handful a generic hybrid design assumes.

**How much work does precomputing the timeline actually save, given how the timeline is read?** Pure push produces roughly 100B timeline writes a day, the same order as the 100B daily impressions actually served. At this skew, **precomputation buys latency, not less total work**, because an 800-entry precomputed timeline still only has 20 entries read from it.

**How large a burst can one tweet's fan-out actually spend?** The fan-out worker pool can dedicate roughly 200k timeline appends a second to a single tweet. Against a 5-second freshness SLO, that is 200k × 5 = **1M entries**, which is the real ceiling one tweet's push can spend, not an arbitrary round number.

**How big does a retweet cascade actually get, compared to the celebrity write it was designed around?** A top-tier viral tweet takes roughly 500,000 retweets in about 20 minutes, from accounts averaging roughly 500 followers each: 500k × 500 = **250M pushed entries**, **2.5x** the 100M writes the celebrity exclusion rule existed to avoid, compressed into a fraction of the time.

> **The numbers to carry.** ~38 authors above a flat 10k threshold in a typical follow set, vs 2-4 above a per-edge 1M cut · precomputing 100B writes a day to serve 100B impressions, so it buys latency, not less work · a per-tweet push burst budget of ~1M entries, from 200k appends/s against a 5s SLO · a retweet cascade at 250M entries, 2.5x the celebrity write it was designed to avoid.

#### The event stream, the two caches, and the API
It helps to say plainly what is durable and what is derived here.

- **Tweet**: written once to a store partitioned by author, the only durable write in the system.
- **Timeline cache**: a packed block of up to 800 tweet ids per user, ordered by Snowflake id.
- **Author recent-tweets list**: one shared cache key per author, read on demand by anyone who follows an above-cut author.
- **Fetch-path set**: the small, denormalised set of above-cut authors a given user follows, maintained on follow and on cut crossings.

The API:

```
POST /tweet                 body: { text, media_ids? } → { tweet_id }
POST /follow/{user}
GET  /timeline/home?cursor  → [tweets]
GET  /search?q=...          → [tweets]
```

#### High-level design
Follow one tweet from a poster to a reader's timeline.

[The hot path, post to rendered timeline](/diagram/twitter?focus=poster,tweet-service,tweet-store,event-stream,fanout,timeline-caches,timeline-service,hydrator,reader,e1,e2,e4,e5,e7,e12,e14,e15,e17)

1. **Poster** sends `POST /tweet`; the **Tweet service** assigns a Snowflake id and writes durably to the **Tweet store**, acknowledging the poster immediately.
2. Only after that ack does the service publish to the **Tweet event stream**.
3. **Fan-out service** consumes the event, checks the author's active follower count against the cut, and appends the tweet id into the **Timeline + recent caches** of eligible followers.
4. On a read, **Timeline service** merges the reader's prebuilt block with any above-cut followees' recent lists, ranks the result, and hands the top 20 ids to **Hydration + counters**, which fetches bodies for the **Reader**.

> **Why the flow is shaped this way.** The tweet store answers "what did this author post" and nothing else. Every other question in the product is a different index over the same event stream, so search, trending and fan-out are all consumers rather than features of one database, and none of them sits in the write path.

#### Where to draw the push cut
A flat follower-count threshold is the standard answer. At this skew it puts a large share of an ordinary user's own follows above the line. What should the cut actually be measured against?

[The fan-out decision at write time](/diagram/twitter?focus=fanout,follow-graph,timeline-caches,e6,e7)

**Bad: a flat threshold on total follower count, applied to every follower regardless of activity.** This protects the write path cleanly, and a typical 150-account follow set holds roughly 38 authors above a 10,000-follower line, which turns every timeline read into 38 extra fetches to save writes the pool could largely have absorbed anyway.

**Good: raise the threshold, still measured per author, still applied to everyone who follows them.** A higher number reduces how many authors land above the cut, and it still pushes to every follower of a below-cut author regardless of whether they will ever read it, spending write capacity on readers who have not opened the app in weeks.

**Great: decide per relationship, on active follower count, filtered by recent reader activity.** **Fan-out service** checks `active_followers(author) < ~1M` and pushes only to followers who opened the app in the last 7 days. That combination lifts the effective cut by an order of magnitude, because the binding constraint is the fan-out pool's per-tweet burst budget, 200k appends/s against a 5-second SLO, which caps any single tweet's push at roughly 1M entries.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 175" role="img" aria-label="A tweet's push is bounded by the fan-out pool's burst rate times the freshness SLO: 200,000 appends a second for 5 seconds caps any single tweet's push at roughly 1 million entries, which is where the cut is derived from rather than picked">
  <style>
    .box{fill:none;stroke:currentColor;stroke-width:1.4}
    .acc{stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.8}
    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 12px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    .sub{fill:currentColor;opacity:.75;font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
  </style>
  <text class="lbl" x="8" y="16">200,000 appends/s burst budget</text>
  <rect class="box acc" x="8" y="26" width="384" height="24" rx="4"/>
  <text class="lbl" x="8" y="72">x 5s freshness SLO</text>
  <rect class="box" x="8" y="82" width="16" height="24" rx="4"/>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="130">= ~1,000,000 entries is the most one</text>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="146">tweet can push inside budget</text>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="166">the cut is derived from this ceiling, not a round number</text>
</svg>
```

The consequence lands on the read side: at a 1M cut a typical follow set holds 2 to 4 fetch-path authors instead of 38, which is the actual variable the read path pays for.

#### The cascade the celebrity rule doesn't touch
Excluding a 100M-follower account from fan-out saves 100M writes cleanly. Nothing about that rule touches what happens twenty minutes later, when 500,000 ordinary accounts each retweet it to their own followers.

[Where a retweet's fan-out decision is made](/diagram/twitter?focus=fanout,timeline-caches,follow-graph,e6,e7)

**Bad: fan out every retweet unconditionally, under the retweeter's own rules.** Each individual retweeter is far below the push cut, so each retweet looks like an ordinary tweet worth pushing. Multiplied across half a million retweeters averaging 500 followers each, that is 250M pushed entries at roughly 200k writes/s sustained for twenty minutes, more than double the celebrity write the exclusion rule was built to prevent.

**Good: exclude retweets of an above-cut original from fan-out entirely, always.** This caps the worst case completely, and it removes a real signal for the vast majority of tweets that never go viral: most retweets of most tweets are exactly the kind of low-volume activity the push path exists to serve cheaply.

**Great: fan out normally, but trigger a cutover once an original's retweet rate crosses a threshold.** Once an original exceeds roughly 1,000 retweets a minute, later retweets stop fanning out and instead append to a per-original retweeter index that the read-side merge already consults. Earlier retweets, from before the trigger fired, have already been pushed and cost nothing extra to keep.

The residual cost this accepts openly: a trigger with even a few seconds of measurement lag has already let a meaningful fraction of the peak through before it fires, so the cutover bounds the cascade without eliminating its early burst.

#### Why fan-in, not fan-out, is the number to control
A timeline read has to stay under a 300ms budget while merging content from a prebuilt cache and from any above-cut authors the reader follows. Which part of that actually scales with the size of the graph?

[The read path merging two sources](/diagram/twitter?focus=timeline-service,follow-graph,timeline-caches,hydrator,e11,e12,e14)

**Bad: store full tweet bodies in the timeline cache.** This avoids a second lookup at read time, and it makes every cache entry roughly 1KB instead of 8 bytes, multiplying the memory cost of the largest cache in the system by two orders of magnitude for content that is often edited, deleted or hidden before it is ever read.

**Good: store ids, but fetch each above-cut followee's recent list with a separate sequential round trip.** This keeps entries small, and it makes read latency a function of exactly how many famous accounts a reader happens to follow: 38 sequential fetches spread across shards can cost tens of milliseconds, turning a rare follow choice into a routine tail-latency problem.

**Great: store ids, fetch all above-cut followees in one pipelined multi-get, and merge sorted lists.** **Timeline service** reads the reader's prebuilt block from **Timeline + recent caches**, resolves the small **Follow graph**-maintained fetch-path set, and issues one pipelined multi-get for every above-cut followee at once rather than one call per author. Because both sources are already sorted by Snowflake id, merging them is a k-way merge of sorted integer lists, and duplicate `retweet_of` entries collapse during that same pass.

[The k-way merge dedupes a cascade in one pass](/diagram/twitter?figure=cascade-dedupe)

The step that scales with the graph is exactly that fan-in width. Everything else in the read path, the merge, the dedupe, the ranking, the hydration, is bounded by the page size and costs the same whether a reader follows five accounts or five thousand.

#### Two search indexes, not one
A search query has to include tweets posted seconds ago and also reach years of archive. A single search cluster with a fast refresh interval is the obvious way to build that. It does not survive contact with the ingest rate.

[Recency and archive as separate index shapes](/diagram/twitter?focus=event-stream,search,e9)

**Bad: one general-purpose cluster, time-partitioned, with a 1-second refresh interval.** This is the standard building block for search, and at 200M documents a day it means roughly 600GB of new index daily, with a tiered merge policy rewriting each document several times over as segments combine, concentrating write amplification exactly when ingest spikes and freshness matters most.

**Good: reduce merge frequency to lower write amplification.** This trades some freshness for less rewrite traffic, and it does not remove the underlying mismatch: any merge-based index still does work proportional to how much has already been indexed, which grows every day the corpus grows.

**Great: an append-only, time-ordered hot index for recency, and a separate batch-built archive for everything else.** **Search index tier** holds the last 7 days in memory with documents in descending id order and zero segment merging, because a document is written once and a sealed segment is never rewritten. Everything older moves into a relevance-ordered archive built in batch. Descending id order means a recency query can stop as soon as it has enough hits, rather than scoring every match in the index.

The trade this makes explicit: early termination only pays off for recency queries. A relevance-ranked query over the same hot index gets nothing from the ordering and has to score every match regardless, which is exactly why the archive uses the opposite ordering for the opposite query shape.

#### Rebuilding a cold mailbox from scratch
A user who has not opened the app in a month has an empty prebuilt timeline. Their next load has to produce a full timeline from nothing, inside the same 300ms budget everyone else gets.

[The read path with no prebuilt block to start from](/diagram/twitter?focus=timeline-service,follow-graph,timeline-caches,e11,e12)

**Bad: treat a missing prebuilt block as an error and return an empty or degraded timeline.** This is fast and it fails the user precisely at the moment they returned, showing them nothing when a full read from their actual follows was genuinely possible.

**Good: rebuild by looping over each followee's recent list sequentially.** This recovers a real timeline, and it does so one round trip at a time: 150 sequential reads at even a few milliseconds each adds up to seconds, on the single load a returning user is most likely to judge the product by.

**Great: treat every followee as a fetch-path author for this one rebuild, and pipeline the reads.** **Timeline service** runs the same pipelined-multi-get, k-way-merge machinery used for above-cut authors, but applies it to all 150 follows at once instead of just the 2 to 4 that would normally qualify. Done this way the rebuild costs roughly 50ms rather than seconds, using code that already exists for the fetch path rather than a separate cold-start mechanism.

The user is marked active again immediately afterward, so the very next tweet from anyone they follow reaches them through the ordinary push path. The first load back is still the slowest one this design will ever give them; the goal is keeping "slowest" inside the same order of magnitude as everyone else's.

#### Where it breaks
| Layer | Failure | How the design handles it |
|---|---|---|
| Fan-out | Tweet rate spikes far beyond the pool's steady-state capacity | The activity window narrows under load, shedding the least-recently-active readers to the cold-rebuild path rather than dropping any tweet |
| Retweet cascade | A viral original's retweets threaten to push far past the celebrity write it excluded | The rate-triggered cutover moves later retweets from fan-out into the retweeter index once the threshold fires |
| Hot tweet | Millions of concurrent engagement increments hit one logical counter | Counters shard across N keys per tweet, summed on read, approximate for a few hundred milliseconds |
| Search ingestion | The indexer falls behind during a breaking-news spike | The hot index is append-only with no merge amplification to fall behind on; low-value fields are dropped from tokenisation before any document is dropped |
| Mass-follow event | A fast-growing account gains millions of followers within an hour | The inverse index and fetch-path sets update asynchronously as a batch job rather than one event per follower |
| Timeline cache | A cache shard is lost, forcing many simultaneous rebuilds | Rebuilds happen lazily per user from author partitions rather than through a global backfill |
| Deletion | A deleted tweet must disappear from every timeline at once | Storing ids and hydrating late means a tombstone at hydration removes the tweet everywhere without rewriting any cached list |

#### What this design does not solve
**Deletion is fast for visibility and slow for erasure.** A tombstone at hydration time makes a deleted tweet vanish from every timeline instantly, and the append-only search index that makes 200M documents a day ingestible keeps that tweet's postings in a sealed segment until it ages out, so genuine erasure needs a batched segment rewrite that the hot index was specifically designed to avoid needing.

**The reply tree has no design that is both bounded and fair.** Ranking a bounded candidate window works for a timeline; a reply thread under a large account can hold hundreds of thousands of replies with no natural bound, and the interesting late reply competes against thousands of early ones for a handful of visible slots this design allocates by a score, not a guarantee.

**Correlated cold-rebuild demand arrives exactly when the system is least able to absorb it.** A major global event brings tens of millions of lapsed users back within minutes, each needing the expensive full rebuild path, at precisely the moment tweet rate is highest and the activity window has just been narrowed to shed load, widening the cold population on purpose.

#### Final design
Read it back through the numbers. ~38 authors above a flat threshold, against 2 to 4 above a per-edge active cut, is why the split runs per relationship rather than per author. A ~1M-entry per-tweet push budget, derived from the fan-out pool's burst rate against the freshness SLO, is what that cut is actually built from. And a 250M-entry retweet cascade, 2.5x the celebrity write the whole design was built to avoid, is why the real write burst in this system was never the famous account at all.

[The whole design](/diagram/twitter?focus=poster,tweet-service,tweet-store,event-stream,fanout,follow-graph,timeline-caches,timeline-service,hydrator,search,trending,reader)

> **The numbers to remember.** ~38 fetch-path authors at a flat 10k cut, vs 2-4 at a per-edge 1M cut · a ~1M-entry per-tweet push budget from 200k appends/s x 5s · a 250M-entry retweet cascade, 2.5x the celebrity write it replaces · precomputation costs roughly one write per impression ever served, buying latency rather than less total work.

#### Check your understanding
**Why does a flat follower-count threshold fail on the read side rather than the write side?** Because a typical follow set is stuffed with mid-tier accounts sitting just above whatever number gets picked, so a threshold chosen to protect writes turns every timeline read into dozens of extra fetches instead.

**Why does excluding a celebrity's original tweet from fan-out not protect the system from that tweet's retweets?** Because each individual retweeter sits far below the push cut on their own, so their retweet looks like an ordinary cheap push, and the aggregate across hundreds of thousands of retweeters can exceed the write volume the exclusion rule was built to prevent.

**Why does storing tweet ids instead of full bodies in the timeline cache matter for more than just memory?** Because it means a delete or an edit is resolved once at hydration time rather than requiring every cached list that references the tweet to be rewritten.

**Why does a pipelined multi-get change the shape of tail latency rather than just its average?** Because sequential fetches make latency proportional to how many above-cut authors a reader happens to follow, an arbitrary number outside anyone's control, while a single pipelined call keeps that cost close to constant.

**Why does the search index use two different orderings for two different query types instead of one?** Because descending id order lets a recency query stop early once it has enough hits, which only helps recency queries; a relevance-ranked query gains nothing from that order and has to score every match regardless.
### 27. Design Instagram
#### Understanding the problem
