The range is also taken all-or-nothing: if any row is not `available`, the whole transaction rolls back, because a guest left with three of their four requested nights has nothing usable, and the platform is left with an orphaned night in the middle of a week nobody else can now book either.

Worked example: guest A requests June 14 to 16, guest B requests June 15 to 17, arriving a few milliseconds apart. Both lock in ascending order, so both attempt June 14 or 15 first depending on their range, but crucially neither ever holds a later row while waiting for an earlier one. A simply waits for B, or B waits for A, and whichever is second sees `held` on the shared night and returns cleanly rather than deadlocking.

[Ascending lock order turns overlap into a queue, not a cycle](/diagram/booking-platform?figure=lock-order)

#### Payment outside the lock
Once the hold commits, the question is where the card authorisation happens, and it turns out that decision alone sets how many database connections the system needs.

[The escrow call sits after the hold commits, never inside it](/diagram/booking-platform?focus=booking-orch,calendar,e8)

**Bad: one transaction that locks, calls the payment provider, and commits around it.** Fewer moving parts, no `held` state, no reaper, no compensation logic. It also means the row locks and a database connection are held for however long the card network takes, 300ms at the median, up to 2 seconds at p99, sometimes 90 seconds if a 3-D Secure challenge fires.

**Good: a short timeout on the payment call inside the transaction.** Cap it at, say, 500ms and fail closed. This limits the damage but does not remove it, and it fails bookings that would have succeeded with a slightly slower but perfectly valid card check.

**Great: two short transactions with payment in between, holding no lock at all.** Transaction one flips the nights to `held` with a 15-minute expiry and commits in about 2ms. The card authorisation runs with zero locks held. Transaction two, on success, flips `held` to `booked`. On failure, a compare-and-set releases the hold.

Worked example: at 120 commits/s with payment inside a 2-second transaction, the connection pool needs roughly 240 concurrent connections doing nothing but waiting on a card network, and a slow afternoon at the payment provider becomes an outage in the booking database. Moving payment outside the lock cuts the time a lock is held by a factor of about 1,000, from 2 seconds to 2 milliseconds, and the pool never sees the payment provider at all. The price is a real `held` state, a night that looks taken but is not yet sold, which needs its own release mechanism.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 190" role="img" aria-label="A 2ms row lock compared to a 2 second payment authorisation drawn to the same timeline; the lock never spans the payment call">
  <style>
    .r{fill:none;stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.35;stroke-width:1.2}
    .lock{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.35;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.5}
    .pay{fill:currentColor;fill-opacity:.14;stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.6;stroke-width:1.5}
    .t{font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif;fill:currentColor;opacity:.8}
    .b{font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif;fill:currentColor}
    text{dominant-baseline:middle}
  </style>
  <text class="b" x="8" y="16">bad: payment inside the transaction</text>
  <rect class="r" x="8" y="28" width="368" height="26" rx="6"/>
  <rect class="lock" x="8" y="28" width="3" height="26"/>
  <rect class="pay" x="11" y="28" width="362" height="26"/>
  <text class="t" x="8" y="70">row lock + connection held for the full ~2s p99 call</text>
  <text class="b" x="8" y="104">great: two short transactions, payment between</text>
  <rect class="r" x="8" y="116" width="368" height="26" rx="6"/>
  <rect class="lock" x="8" y="116" width="3" height="26"/>
  <rect class="pay" x="11" y="116" width="362" height="26" fill-opacity="0"/>

```

#### The hold releases itself
A `held` night that nobody ever converts or cancels has to come back onto the market, and the question is who is responsible for noticing.

[The hold, and the two paths back to available](/diagram/booking-platform?focus=booking-orch,calendar,e8)

**Bad: nothing releases it automatically.** A guest who abandons checkout leaves the night `held` forever, or until a human intervenes. This obviously cannot ship, but it is worth naming because it is the default if the hold is treated as a database row with no lifecycle attached to it.

**Good: an operational job that scans for old holds and clears them.** This works, most of the time, but it is the only thing standing between an abandoned checkout and a permanently frozen night, and its failure mode is silent: a stopped job produces no errors, it just quietly stops releasing anything.

**Great: compensation as compare-and-set on the hold's own id, plus the scan as a backstop rather than the mechanism.** Every release, whether the payment failed, the guest cancelled, or a request timed out, is the same conditional write:

```sql
UPDATE calendar SET status='available', hold_id=NULL, hold_expires_at=NULL
 WHERE listing_id=$1 AND hold_id=$2 AND status='held';
```

The `hold_id` predicate is what makes it safe to run twice, and safe to run at the same time as a scheduled sweep. Without it, a release arriving late, after a retried request already succeeded, would release a night that is genuinely sold. A separate job then sweeps every 60 seconds for holds past their `hold_expires_at` using the identical predicate, purely as a backstop for an orchestrator that crashed mid-flow rather than the primary release path.

Worked example: an orchestrator process dies immediately after committing the hold transaction but before calling the payment provider. Nothing about the failed process's normal compensation path runs. The night sits `held` until the sweep finds `hold_expires_at` in the past, up to roughly 15 minutes plus a 60-second scan interval, then releases it with the same compare-and-set. At 0.1 bookings per listing per day that delay is invisible almost everywhere; on a listing with 200 attempts in a minute it is 15 minutes a lot of people notice, which is why the operational alert watches the count of stale `held` rows directly rather than trusting the sweep job's own heartbeat.

#### One home region per calendar shard
The calendar has to live somewhere, and where it lives decides both how fast a booking commits and how much an outage costs.

[Calendar rows, sharded by listing and pinned to one home region each](/diagram/booking-platform?focus=calendar,e8)

**Bad: a single global primary for the whole calendar.** Every booking commits in one place, which is simple and trivially consistent, and it means every guest outside that region pays a full round trip on every write, and the entire platform's booking path shares one failure domain.

**Good: shard by listing, no home region, any replica can propose a write.** Splits the load, but without a designated writer per shard, two regions can each believe they are allowed to commit against the same rows, and reconciling that after the fact is exactly the double-booking problem this whole design exists to prevent.

**Great: shard the calendar by `listing_id`, pin each shard to one home region, route every write there.** A synchronous in-region replica gives durability without a cross-region round trip on the common case. Cross-region copies are asynchronous and read-only. A home-region commit costs 5 to 10ms; a design that instead used a cross-region consensus store would cost roughly 60 to 100ms per commit, bounded by the round trip to the second-nearest voting region.

Worked example: at ~12 commits/s with a third of shards homed in one region, a 10-minute failover of that region loses roughly 12 × 600 × 0.33 ≈ 2,400 booking attempts, about 0.24% of one day's volume. That is the price paid for a 10ms commit on the other 99.76% of traffic. What does not rescue a global design here is the trick that works for fungible stock, giving each region a disjoint slice of inventory, because a single night cannot be split three ways between regions the way a batch of interchangeable seats can.

#### Whose calendar is the truth
A host can list the same property somewhere else, and that other system has its own idea of what is available.

[Channel sync feeds the calendar but never overrides a confirmed booking](/diagram/booking-platform?focus=host-app,channel-sync,calendar,e11,e14)

**Bad: treat the external channel manager as authoritative and check it synchronously at commit time.** This sounds correct, since it is genuinely the more up to date source in some cases, and it means the booking commit path now depends on the latency and uptime of every partner integration. With thousands of partner integrations, even each individually reliable, the combined probability that all of them answer in time is not a number worth publishing.

**Good: poll partners on a fixed schedule and treat their data as informational only, ignored at commit time.** Removes the dependency, but a fixed poll interval, once an hour, say, leaves the same exposure window for every listing regardless of how close its next check-in is, wasting freshness where it does not matter and under-delivering it where it does.

**Great: our calendar is the sole authority for anything we sell, external channels may only block nights, and polling interval adapts to near-term demand.** Ingestion from a channel can mark a night unavailable, but it can never release a night that carries one of our confirmed bookings; a conflict resolves in favour of the existing booking and raises a host-facing alert instead. Polling runs more often for listings with bookings in the next week and less often otherwise, which turns a flat, expensive poll into one sized to where it matters.

Worked example: a host sells a night on a rival site at 9am. The channel sync job for that listing, on a 15-minute adaptive interval because it has near-term demand, polls at 9:12am, sees the night gone, and marks the calendar row `blocked`. If a guest had already booked that night on this platform at 9:05am, the row was already `booked`, so the incoming update is rejected by the same rule and the host gets an alert about the conflict instead. The guest keeps a booking for a night that, on the rival site, no longer exists; that gap is a genuine exposure the design accepts rather than closes, because closing it would mean putting a partner's API inside the commit path.

#### Where it breaks
| Layer | Failure | How the design handles it |
|---|---|---|
| Calendar lock | A hot listing takes 200 attempts in a minute during an event | They serialise behind a 2ms transaction and drain in about 400ms; the design returns a fast, honest rejection rather than degrading, and can switch to a lottery-style entry window at extreme contention |
| Calendar lock | Overlapping ranges deadlock | Row locks always taken `ORDER BY date`; a bounded retry on serialisation failure catches anything the ordering does not |
| Booking orchestrator | A crashed process leaves a hold uncommitted or uncompensated | Compare-and-set compensation on `hold_id` handles the common case in milliseconds; a 60-second sweep is the backstop for a process that no longer exists |
| Search index | The CDC pipeline stalls and availability goes stale | The commit always re-validates, so a stale search hit costs one rejected booking rather than a wrong one |
| Channel sync | A partner returns a stale or empty calendar | Ingestion may only block nights, never release one carrying a confirmed booking; a partner whose conflict rate exceeds a threshold is quarantined |
| Calendar shard | The home region for a shard is lost | The synchronous in-region replica is promoted; bookings for that shard fail closed rather than being rerouted elsewhere, because rerouting is the double booking |
| Payment | A card authorisation expires before a distant check-in | A job re-authorises about five days before arrival; failure gives the guest a deadline, then releases the nights |

#### What this design does not solve
**A confirmed booking is not binding on the host, and nothing here makes it one.** Every mechanism above guarantees at most one guest per listing-night. None of them guarantees a guest actually gets the room, because the host is a person outside the system who can cancel the week before, and it looks identical to a double booking from the guest's side. The available tools are economic: a cancellation fee, blocking those nights so the host cannot relist at a higher price, and reduced ranking. None of them scale with the arbitrage a host might be chasing on a peak-demand weekend.

**The exposure window from unsynchronised external inventory is permanent, not a bug to be fixed.** A host selling the same night elsewhere will be seen only at the next poll, minutes later depending on how near-term the demand is. In that window, this design will happily confirm a booking against a night that is already gone. Closing that gap means putting a partner's availability check inside the commit path, and the traffic and reliability numbers rule that out. What remains is shrinking the window with adaptive polling and treating conflict frequency as a signal about the host, not eliminating it.

**Nothing in this system is atomic across more than one listing.** A trip stitched from several listings, or two units booked together from the same host, is several independent commits, and a guest can end up with some of them and not others. A coordinator that holds every leg before confirming any of them is buildable, but it means holding locks on inventory owned by different hosts, possibly homed in different regions, for as long as a human takes to check out. The design pushes this to the client instead: book sequentially, and cancel the earlier legs under the free-cancellation window if a later one fails, which stops working exactly for last-minute bookings with no such window.

#### Final design
Read it back through the numbers. ~120 bookings a second and 0.1 bookings per listing per day mean a plain row lock is nearly always uncontended, which is why the whole correctness story fits in one 2ms transaction. 12,000 search queries a second against 12 commits a second is four orders of magnitude, which is why search gets its own eventually consistent index rather than sharing the calendar's consistency model. A 2-second payment call against a 2ms lock, a factor of roughly 1,000, is why payment sits outside the transaction with its own hold-and-compensate lifecycle. And 2,400 lost attempts in a 10-minute regional failover, against 1M bookings a day, is why the calendar is sharded with one home region rather than replicated globally: the cost of the rare outage is smaller than the cost, paid on every single commit, of a cross-region consensus write.

[The whole design, search to confirmed stay](/diagram/booking-platform?focus=guest,search-svc,listing-svc,booking-orch,messaging,reviews,search-index,cdc,calendar,host-app,channel-sync)

> **The numbers to remember.** ~120 bookings/s peak · 0.1 bookings per listing per day · 12k search QPS vs ~12 commits/s · 2ms lock vs 2s payment call · ~2,400 attempts lost per 10-minute regional failover.

#### Check your understanding
**Why is the calendar a row per listing-night instead of a count per listing?** A count admits every trick that makes fungible inventory fast: decrement, reconcile, oversell against a known no-show rate. None of those survive here, because there is no second identical unit to hand a losing guest. A row means there is nothing to decrement and nothing to get wrong by one; two attempts on overlapping dates are contending for the same physical rows, not racing a shared number.

**Two overlapping date ranges are booked at nearly the same instant. Why doesn't this deadlock?** Because every transaction locks its rows in the same fixed order, ascending by date. A cycle needs two transactions each holding a row the other wants; with one global ordering, the second transaction always ends up waiting for the first rather than holding something the first needs, so the worst case is a clean rejection, not a deadlock.

**Why does the payment authorisation happen outside the row lock rather than inside it?** A card authorisation runs up to about 2 seconds at p99 against a lock that otherwise takes 2 milliseconds, a factor of roughly 1,000. Holding the lock across the payment call would tie a database connection pool's capacity to a third party's latency, so the design commits the hold first, calls payment with no lock held, and commits a second short transaction on success.

**A process crashes right after taking a hold but before charging the card. What happens to the night?** Nothing needs to notice immediately. The night stays `held` until a scheduled sweep finds its expiry has passed, roughly 15 minutes plus up to a 60-second scan delay, and releases it with the same compare-and-set every other release path uses. The operational alert watches the count of stale held rows directly, because a dead sweep produces no errors, only silently frozen inventory.

**A host sells the same night on another site. What does this design do about it, and what can it not do?** It finds out at the next poll, adaptively scheduled closer to check-in for listings with near-term demand, and marks the night blocked from that point on. It cannot prevent a booking confirmed in the gap before that poll, because closing that gap would mean putting a partner's API inside the commit path, which the traffic numbers rule out; the exposure window is accepted and shrunk, not eliminated.
### 31. Design Netflix (Video Streaming)
#### Understanding the problem
Netflix streams a curated catalogue of long-form video to hundreds of millions of subscribers, adapting quality to whatever connection each viewer has, starting playback in under a second with effectively no rebuffering. Stated like that it sounds like a networking problem. It is actually a placement problem, and seeing that is most of the question.

Two things make it distinctive.

First, the catalogue is finite and known weeks in advance. Tens of thousands of titles, not billions, licensed country by country, sitting in a system for months before anyone streams them. That single fact means nearly every byte a viewer will ever request can already be sitting inside their own internet provider before they press Play.

Second, the cost of moving bytes dominates every other cost in the system. At roughly 900 petabytes delivered a day, a fraction of a cent per gigabyte multiplies into hundreds of millions of dollars a year, so the entire design bends around minimising how far a byte has to travel.

> **What this is not.** It looks like YouTube, or any large-scale video platform, from a distance: encode, store, deliver, adapt bitrate. The resemblance stops at the corpus. YouTube's catalogue is user-generated, unbounded, and arriving continuously, hundreds of hours of new footage every minute, most of it watched by almost nobody. You cannot enumerate an unbounded, unpredictable corpus, so you cannot forecast it, so you cannot place it ahead of demand. That answer has to be a pull-through cache hierarchy that fills on first request and evicts the coldest content, with the hard engineering sitting in an ingest and transcode pipeline rather than a placement controller. A design that reaches for LRU eviction here has answered the wrong catalogue.

#### Requirements and the numbers
**Functional.** Browse the catalogue, play, pause and resume across devices, search, per-profile recommendations, offline downloads.

**Non-functional.** Playback start under 1 second at p99. Rebuffering under 0.5% of playback time. Global reach. The byte cost per delivered hour must not scale with subscriber growth.

The whole design is decided by five numbers, so derive them before drawing anything.

**How many streams are running at once?** ~500M viewing hours a day ÷ 24 ≈ **~21M average concurrent streams**. Timezones flatten the global curve, so peak runs about 1.5x average: 21M × 1.5 ≈ **~32M concurrent at peak**.

**What is the weighted average bitrate?** A delivered mix of roughly 55% at 1.5 Mbps, 35% at 5 Mbps and 10% at 15 Mbps: 0.55×1.5 + 0.35×5 + 0.10×15 = 0.825 + 1.75 + 1.5 ≈ **~4 Mbps average**.

**What does that mean for egress and daily volume?** 32M concurrent × 4 Mbps ≈ **~130 Tbps at peak**. Per day, 4 Mbps is 1.8 GB per viewing hour, so 500M hours × 1.8 GB ≈ **~900 PB/day**.

**How much of one country's catalogue fits on one storage box?** A country's regionally relevant renditions run to roughly 300 TB. A storage appliance holds 200 TB. **Two thirds of a country's catalogue is simply resident on one box**, which is the ratio that turns pre-positioning from a bet into an engineering plan.

**How much traffic does the nightly fill cost against what it enables?** About 500 GB pushed per appliance per night, across a fleet of roughly 18,000 appliances, is ~9 PB/day of fill against ~900 PB/day of delivery: a **100:1 amortisation**, every fill byte served roughly a hundred times over.

> **The numbers to carry.** ~32M concurrent streams at peak · ~4 Mbps average bitrate · ~900 PB/day delivered · two thirds of a country's catalogue resident on one 200 TB box · a 100:1 fill-to-delivery ratio.

#### Control plane and data plane, and why they never touch
It is worth saying plainly that this is two systems wearing one product. A control plane that decides what a viewer is allowed to watch and where to get it, costing a few kilobytes per session. A data plane that actually moves the video, costing petabytes a day. They meet only at a listing of appliance URLs, and video bytes never pass through the cloud at all.

The entities are:

- **Segment group**: the actual unit the placement system reasons about, a `(title, codec, rung, audio track)` tuple, not a title.
- **Appliance inventory**: which segment groups a given box holds, pinned or not.
- **Manifest**: a short-lived, per-session list of ranked appliance URLs plus the available rungs.
- **DRM licence**: a device-bound key that decrypts segments, issued per session.

The playback hot path is small:

```
POST /play -> auth + entitlement + geo
manifest_service.get(title_id, country, asn, device) -> ranked OCA URLs + rung list
drm.issue_key(device_id, content_key_id, country)
return {manifest, licence}
// client then:
GET {oca_url}/{title}/{codec}/{rung}/seg_00042.m4s
// OCA: pinned hit -> serve from SSD; miss -> peer OCA, then IXP, then origin
```

#### High-level design
Follow the numbered arrows. Everything on the control side happens once per session and costs kilobytes; everything on the data side happens continuously and costs petabytes.

[The hot path from Play to a delivered segment](/diagram/netflix?focus=client,playback-api,catalogue,manifest,drm,oca,e1,e2,e3,e4,e5,e6,e7,e8)

1. The client sends `POST /play` to the **Playback API**.
2. **Playback API** checks entitlement and country rights against **Catalogue + rights**.
3. **Playback API** asks **Manifest + steering** for a ranked list of appliance URLs for this viewer's network and device.
4. **Playback API** asks the **DRM licence server** for a short-lived, device-bound key.
5. The client fetches its first segment directly from an **Open Connect appliance**, never through the cloud.
6. On a miss, the appliance fills from a peer appliance, then an internet exchange, then the **Origin object store**, in that order.

> **Why the flow is shaped this way.** The encode and the placement both happen offline because they can: the catalogue is known in advance, so the expensive work moves ahead of the request. That leaves the runtime path doing something small: pick a rung, fetch a segment from a box that already has it. The control plane never touches a video byte, which is why it can run from a handful of cloud regions and still serve a system delivering 130 Tbps.

#### Segment groups, not titles
The placement controller's output looks, at first glance, like a list of popular shows. It is not, and the difference is the whole mechanism.

[What the placement controller actually decides for one appliance](/diagram/netflix?focus=forecast,placement,oca,e11,e13,e15)

**Bad: pre-position whole titles.** Rank titles by predicted popularity and push the top N until the appliance is full. This treats every rendition of a title as equally useful, which throws away most of the signal: a title has eight to twelve rungs across three codecs and several audio tracks, and most subscribers behind one appliance only ever need a handful of those combinations.

**Good: pre-position titles, but only the top rungs.** Slightly better, cuts obviously wasted 4K bytes where nobody has a 4K panel, but still treats every appliance in a country the same, when device and language mix vary sharply between one ISP's subscribers and the next.

**Great: pre-position segment groups, one `(title, codec, rung, audio track)` tuple at a time, per appliance.** An ISP whose subscribers are mostly smart TVs needs the high rungs in HEVC and AV1; one whose subscribers are mostly Android phones needs the low rungs in H.264 and VP9. Holding the wrong half of a ladder is functionally the same as holding nothing, because the player cannot use a rung the device cannot decode or a track in a language nobody selected.

Worked example: two appliances in the same country, one behind an ISP serving mostly connected TVs, one behind an ISP serving mostly prepaid mobile plans. Both hold the same top 400 titles by predicted popularity, but the TV-heavy appliance's segment groups skew toward 1080p and 4K HEVC, while the mobile-heavy appliance's skew toward 480p and 720p H.264. A title-level placement scheme would push identical bytes to both and waste roughly a third of each appliance's capacity on renditions its subscribers will never request.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 210" role="img" aria-label="Two appliances holding the same titles but different segment groups, split by the device mix behind each one">
  <style>
    .acc{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.3;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.5}
    .dim{fill:currentColor;fill-opacity:.12;stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.5;stroke-width:1.5}
    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    .sub{fill:currentColor;opacity:.75;font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
  </style>

  <rect class="dim" x="8" y="24" width="94" height="22" rx="4"/>
  <rect class="acc" x="106" y="24" width="286" height="22" rx="4"/>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="62">480p/720p H.264 — small slice</text>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="78">1080p/4K HEVC, AV1 — most of the box</text>

  <text class="sub" x="8" y="172">1080p/4K HEVC, AV1 — small slice</text>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="196">same top 400 titles; granularity is (title, codec, rung, track)</text>
```
