
#### Pinning versus LRU
The resident set the controller builds has to survive contact with an ordinary cache eviction policy, and that turns out to be its own decision.

[The pin, and why a plain cache undoes the placement](/diagram/netflix?focus=oca,e7,e10)

**Bad: treat the whole appliance as a plain LRU cache.** Whatever was requested most recently stays; whatever has not been touched in a while gets evicted to make room. This is the correct default for a cache with no forecast behind it, and it is exactly wrong here, because it evicts precisely when it matters most.

**Good: a larger cache with a longer eviction window.** Buys some slack, but the fundamental problem persists: a sudden spike in requests for anything, including a title deliberately being pre-positioned elsewhere, can still push out bytes the controller specifically placed.

**Great: pin the pre-positioned set, and run LRU only on the unpinned remainder of the disk.** Segments placed by the controller are marked pinned and are simply not eligible for eviction. Only the leftover space, whatever the forecast chose not to hold, behaves like an ordinary cache.

Worked example: a global launch sends tens of millions of plays at one title within an hour, all requesting segments that were pre-positioned days earlier. Under plain LRU, that flood of requests for other appliances' popular content could push the pre-positioned bytes for a less-hot title out of a shared cache; here, because the pre-positioned set is pinned, none of it moves, and the flood simply reads what was already there. The failure a plain cache would introduce is the pre-positioned set arriving late through the expensive peer-and-origin path, which is precisely the traffic the whole programme exists to avoid.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 190" role="img" aria-label="Plain LRU evicts pre-positioned bytes under a launch-day flood; pinning keeps the placed set and runs LRU only on the leftover space">
  <style>
    .r{fill:none;stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.35;stroke-width:1.2}
    .pin{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.32;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.5}
    .lru{fill:currentColor;fill-opacity:.12;stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.55;stroke-width:1.5}
    .gone{fill:none;stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.35;stroke-width:1.5;stroke-dasharray:4 3}
    .t{font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif;fill:currentColor;opacity:.8}
    .b{font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif;fill:currentColor}
    text{dominant-baseline:middle}
  </style>
  <text class="b" x="8" y="14">bad: plain LRU, 200 TB disk</text>
  <rect class="r" x="8" y="24" width="376" height="28" rx="6"/>
  <rect class="pin" x="8" y="24" width="242" height="28"/><text class="t" x="18" y="42" text-anchor="start" style="text-anchor:start">pre-positioned</text>
  <rect class="gone" x="252" y="24" width="132" height="28"/><text class="t" x="262" y="42" text-anchor="start" style="text-anchor:start">evicted</text>
  <text class="t" x="8" y="66" text-anchor="start" style="text-anchor:start">launch traffic pushes out bytes placed days earlier</text>
  <text class="b" x="8" y="100">great: pinned set, LRU only on the remainder</text>
  <rect class="r" x="8" y="110" width="376" height="28" rx="6"/>
  <rect class="pin" x="8" y="110" width="242" height="28"/><text class="t" x="18" y="128" text-anchor="start" style="text-anchor:start">pinned, never evicted</text>
  <rect class="lru" x="252" y="110" width="132" height="28"/><text class="t" x="262" y="128" text-anchor="start" style="text-anchor:start">ordinary LRU</text>
  <text class="t" x="8" y="152" text-anchor="start" style="text-anchor:start">the flood only ever competes for the unpinned remainder</text>
</svg>
```

#### Steering from the manifest, not DNS
Once an appliance holds the right bytes, the client still has to be told which appliance to ask, and that decision turns out not to belong to the network layer at all.

[Manifest issuance filters to appliances that are healthy, have headroom, and actually hold the title](/diagram/netflix?focus=playback-api,manifest,client,e3,e6)

**Bad: route with anycast, the way most commercial delivery does.** The network sends a client to the topologically nearest node. This is cheap and works well for a corpus small enough, or uniform enough, that any nearby node is likely to hold what is requested. It cannot see inventory, so it will happily route a client to a node that does not hold the object, turning what should have been a hit into a miss plus a fill.

**Good: route with DNS to a small set of known-good regional endpoints.** Slightly more control than anycast, still blind to what any specific box actually holds at this moment.

**Great: issue the manifest from the control plane, filtered on live inventory and health.** When a client requests a manifest, the service resolves the client to its network, looks up the appliances serving that network, filters to those that are healthy, have spare capacity, and actually hold the requested title's renditions, and returns three or four ranked URLs.

Worked example: a viewer's ASN is served by three appliances, one of which is at capacity and one of which does not hold the requested title's HEVC rungs because its device mix skews toward older hardware. Inventory-aware steering returns only the remaining appliance plus a fallback peer, so the client's first request is a hit. Anycast routing on the same network, blind to both facts, could have sent that request to either of the other two, each guaranteed to miss.

The price is worth stating plainly: manifest issuance becomes a stateful, uncacheable call on every single play, one that must know the health and contents of an entire fleet. If that service degrades, no new session can start anywhere, even though every appliance in the world is healthy and every already-running stream is untouched.

#### Own the hardware or rent delivery
The decision to build and place hardware at all is an economic one before it is a technical one, and the arithmetic is closer than it looks at a glance.

[Where the cost model actually lives: an appliance's fixed cost against a per-byte bill](/diagram/netflix?focus=oca,origin,e10,e12)

**Bad: own hardware everywhere, regardless of volume.** Place an appliance inside every network with any subscriber at all. This is the instinct once ownership has proven itself at the top of the distribution, and it is wrong at the bottom: a network with a handful of streaming households never generates enough delivered volume to repay the hardware, logistics and field support the box requires.

**Good: rent commercial delivery everywhere, and skip the hardware business entirely.** Removes the capital and operational cost of owning boxes, and it means the bill scales linearly with viewers forever, with no ceiling on it as volume grows.

**Great: compute the crossover volume per site, and own hardware above it, rent below it.** An appliance costs roughly $500 a month fully loaded with logistics and field support. At an aggressive bulk commercial rate of $0.002/GB, that budget buys about 250 TB a month of rented delivery, which is a few hundred concurrent streams' worth of sustained bandwidth. Any network clearing that easily justifies its own box; anything below it is cheaper to rent.

Worked example: globally, the same arithmetic gives roughly $650M a year of commercial delivery spend at that rate, against roughly $150M a year all-in for an owned fleet delivering the same volume, a real saving at scale. A service delivering only 1 petabyte a month pays about $2,000 a month for commercial delivery and would need a decade of that spend to justify funding one field engineer, so for it renting is simply correct, not a compromise.

#### Buffer occupancy over throughput for adaptive bitrate
Once a segment has landed, the player has to decide what quality to request next, and the signal it trusts changes everything about how stable playback feels.

[The player watches its own buffer, not the network](/diagram/netflix?focus=client,oca,e7,e8)

**Bad: pick a rung once, at session start, and keep it.** Simple, and wrong the moment the network changes mid-session, which it does constantly: wifi contention, a cellular handoff, someone else in the house starting a download.

**Good: re-estimate throughput from the last few segments and pick the highest rung that fits.** Adapts mid-session, but a per-segment throughput estimate is noisy, especially on cellular, and a noisy signal driving a rung decision every few seconds produces visible oscillation between quality levels.

**Great: choose the next rung from how full the playback buffer is.** Step up when the buffer exceeds roughly 40 seconds and is growing, step down immediately below about 10 seconds, never move more than one rung per segment. A VOD player holding 120 to 240 seconds of buffer, with four-second segments, is integrating 30 to 60 segments of history into that one number, which makes it far steadier than any single-segment throughput estimate.

Worked example: a viewer's wifi briefly saturates for 15 seconds while a housemate starts a large download. A throughput estimator sees a sharp drop and immediately drops several rungs, then sees the recovery and jumps back up, an oscillation the viewer notices as flicker. A buffer-occupancy player, holding two minutes of video, barely reacts, because 15 seconds of reduced throughput against 120 seconds of buffer is a small dent, not a cliff. The signal only fails where there is no buffer to read: the first few seconds of any session, and low-latency live with a two-to-four second target buffer, both of which fall back to a throughput estimate because the alternative simply does not exist yet.

#### Where it breaks
| Layer | Failure | How the design handles it |
|---|---|---|
| Appliance | A single Open Connect box inside an ISP fails mid-session | The manifest already lists three or four ranked appliances; the player fails over mid-stream, visible as a brief quality dip rather than a stall |
| Fill | An appliance falls back to origin during peak because the push missed it | Origin fill rate per appliance is a paged metric with a 5% threshold; the response is a targeted emergency push |
| Forecast | An unforecast title trends suddenly | The design accepts live-fill through peer and origin paths until the next push window, funded from a reserved egress budget |
| Manifest and steering | The steering service degrades or its inventory view goes stale | Active-active across regions plus a degraded mode returning a static per-network appliance list without the inventory filter, trading a higher miss rate for staying up |
| DRM licence server | A launch spike hits key issuance at the same instant as playback | Keys are cached per device for the session so a resume or seek does not re-issue; servers scale statelessly ahead of the launch calendar |
| Encoder fleet | The encode backlog threatens a scheduled launch | Priority ordered by fill deadline rather than launch date; a documented fallback ships a reduced ladder rather than an unpositioned title |
| Rights | A title's licence expires mid-session in a country | The manifest stops listing it and the licence server refuses new keys; sessions already playing continue until their current key expires |

#### What this design does not solve
**Live streaming is a genuinely different system, not a variant of this one.** Everything here depends on bytes existing before the request. A live event has zero warmth by definition, so pre-positioning is not merely unavailable, it is meaningless, and the fan-out problem this whole architecture was built to avoid, every appliance wanting the same segment in the same second, reappears in full. Live runs as a parallel pipeline on the same racks, with a deliberately narrower ladder and a rebuffer rate an order of magnitude worse than on-demand playback.

**The popularity forecast cannot see its own influence.** The strongest input to the model is the merchandising plan, and merchandising is itself informed by what is cheap to serve, so the forecast's accuracy metrics look excellent while quietly penalising anything never promoted: an unpositioned title starts slower on first play, depressing engagement, depressing its own next forecast. There is no clean way to measure the counterfactual without deliberately degrading real viewers to test it. A residency floor, holding a mid rung for every title regardless of forecast, bounds the worst case without removing the loop.

**There is no independent view of the last mile.** Every appliance sits inside a partner's building, on the partner's power and routing policy, and every measurement of that path comes either from the box itself or from clients on the far side of it. An ISP that quietly de-prioritises the appliance's ports during congestion looks, in the platform's own telemetry, identical to an ISP whose subscribers simply have slow lines, and there is no technical way to tell the two apart from inside the system.

#### Final design
Read it back through the numbers. ~32M concurrent streams at ~4 Mbps average is ~130 Tbps at peak and ~900 PB a day, a volume too large to buy on a commercial per-byte bill without the delivery cost overtaking every other cost in the business, which is why owning delivery hardware inside ISPs is the foundation rather than an optimisation. Two thirds of a country's catalogue fitting on one 200 TB box is what makes forecasting tractable: the model only has to be right about which third to leave off, not which sliver to guess at out of an unbounded corpus. And a 100:1 ratio between nightly fill and daily delivery is the number that justifies pre-positioning economically even when the forecast is imperfect, because every byte pushed off-peak is served roughly a hundred times during the day that follows.

[The whole design, forecast to delivered segment](/diagram/netflix?focus=client,playback-api,manifest,oca,telemetry,recs,catalogue,drm,placement,forecast,origin,encoder)

> **The numbers to remember.** ~32M concurrent streams at peak · ~4 Mbps average bitrate · ~900 PB/day delivered · two thirds of a country's catalogue resident on one 200 TB box · a 100:1 fill-to-delivery ratio.

#### Check your understanding
**Why does the placement controller reason about segment groups rather than titles?** A title is not one set of bytes, it is eight to twelve rungs across three codecs plus multiple audio tracks, and an appliance's subscribers only need the combinations their devices can decode and their language settings request. Holding the wrong half of a ladder wastes capacity as thoroughly as holding nothing, so the controller decides per `(title, codec, rung, audio track)` tuple, split by each appliance's own device and language mix.

**Why must the pre-positioned set be pinned rather than left to ordinary cache eviction?** A plain LRU policy evicts whatever has not been requested recently, which is exactly what a flood of launch-day traffic for other content would do to a pre-positioned but momentarily quiet title. Pinning removes the placed set from eviction entirely, so only the unpinned remainder of the disk behaves like an ordinary cache, and the placement survives the exact event it was built for.

**Why does the manifest service steer clients instead of using DNS or anycast?** Anycast and DNS route on network proximity and cannot see what any specific box currently holds, so they will happily send a client to a node that misses. Issuing the manifest from the control plane lets it filter to appliances that are healthy, have headroom, and actually hold the requested renditions, at the cost of making manifest issuance a stateful, uncacheable call on every single play.

**Why is the next segment's quality chosen from buffer occupancy rather than measured throughput?** A VOD player's buffer holds 120 to 240 seconds of video against four-second segments, so its fullness integrates 30 to 60 segments of history into one low-variance number. A per-segment throughput estimate is noisy, especially on cellular, and a noisy signal driving a rung decision every few seconds produces visible oscillation that viewers notice more than a stable, slightly lower quality level.

**When does it make more sense to rent delivery than to own an appliance?** Below the volume where an appliance's fixed monthly cost, roughly $500 fully loaded, is cheaper than buying the same delivery at a bulk commercial rate. That crossover works out to a few hundred concurrent streams' worth of sustained bandwidth per site; below it, and for any network where placing hardware is commercially or legally unavailable, renting delivery is the correct answer, not a fallback.
### 32. Design Slack (Workplace Messaging)
#### Understanding the problem
A workplace messaging platform runs channels, threads, direct messages, files and full-text search for hundreds of thousands of separate organisations at once. Each organisation's data has to be held as a distinct, auditable unit, because history is kept and searched by default rather than encrypted away. Organisational memory is the product.

Two things make that harder than an ordinary chat system.

First, customer size spans four orders of magnitude on the same code. A five-person startup and a 150,000-seat enterprise both send messages through the same channels, threads and search index, and any assumption that tenants are roughly the same size breaks at one end or the other.

Second, an enterprise buyer pays for guarantees expressed per organisation, not per user: delete our data within 30 days and prove it, keep it in one region, hold specific channels for litigation, revoke our encryption key and make us unreadable. Every one of those has to be a single operation somebody can point at, not a scan across everybody's rows with no way to demonstrate completeness.

> **What this is not.** It looks like a consumer chat system: sockets, channels, delivery, presence. A consumer chat system's population is uniform, every user is roughly the same size, so hashing conversations across a pool works forever, and there is no administrative entity above the user that can demand a set of conversations be exported or destroyed together. Content there is typically end-to-end encrypted, so the server holds ciphertext and search is a client-side problem over what one device already has. Here the opposite holds throughout: the server must hold plaintext because search, retention, legal hold and third-party integrations all need it, and the size distribution spans four orders of magnitude rather than being roughly flat. A design that adds a tenant column to a consumer chat schema has answered the easy half of a much harder question.

#### Requirements and the numbers
**Functional.** Public and private channels, direct messages, threads, mentions, file upload, full-text search over history, presence, third-party apps, cross-organisation shared channels.

**Non-functional.** Delivery under 200ms in region. Tenant isolation provable to an auditor. Search over five years in under a second. Per-customer retention, residency and key control. No message lost across a deploy.

The whole design is decided by five numbers, so derive them before drawing anything.

**How skewed is customer size?** Median workspace activity runs around 10 daily actives; the largest single customer runs around 150,000. 150,000 ÷ 10 = **a 15,000x spread** between the median and the largest tenant, on the same code.

**How many messages is that a day, and at peak?** ~35M daily active users sending roughly 20 messages each gives ~700M messages/day. Traffic concentrates into each region's working day rather than spreading flat: 700,000,000 ÷ 36,000 effective seconds ≈ **~19,000 messages/s at the busy hour**, with a top-of-hour spike pushing that to **~60,000/s at peak**.

**What does fan-out cost in a channel with 100,000 members?** A per-channel topic means one publish per message and one consume per gateway holding at least one subscriber to that channel, not one push per member. With subscribers spread across a fleet of gateway boxes, a 100,000-member channel costs roughly **300 pushes**, not 100,000, a **~300x reduction**.

**How many search shards does one index per tenant cost?** A search node holds on the order of 500 to 1,000 shards before cluster overhead dominates. One index per workspace across ~750,000 workspaces is **~750,000 shards**, needing roughly **1,000 dedicated nodes** holding a median of about 110MB each. A shard sized at 50 million documents corresponds to roughly **1,370 daily actives** over five years of history, which is close to the 98th percentile of workspace size.

**How big is the one thing that has to be global?** ~750,000 workspaces at roughly 200 bytes each is **~150MB**, small enough to cache in full, in memory, on every edge node.

> **The numbers to carry.** A 15,000x size spread between median and largest tenant · ~19,000 msgs/s busy hour, ~60,000/s peak · a 100,000-member channel costs ~300 pushes · ~750,000 search shards at one per tenant against ~1,000 available nodes · a 150MB directory cached in full at the edge.

#### The one global thing, and everything that isn't
It is worth saying plainly what this design refuses to let happen: almost nothing in the system is allowed to be globally scoped. One small table decides which physical bundle of infrastructure a workspace's data lives in, and everything downstream of that lookup, storage, search, sockets, keys, stays inside that bundle.

The entities are:

- **Workspace**: the tenant. The unit every enterprise guarantee is expressed against.
- **Shard**: a named bundle of a gateway pool, a database keyspace, a search index home, an object-store prefix and an encryption key alias, always moved and destroyed together.
- **Directory row**: `(workspace_id, shard_id, region, plan, key_alias, state)`, the only globally scoped record in the system.
- **Channel** and **message**: scoped entirely within one shard, except for the narrow, enumerated case of a channel shared across two workspaces.

The API resolves the tenant before it does anything else, and it is never a caller-supplied parameter:

```
WebSocket:
  →  { type: send_message, channel_id, text, thread_parent_id? }
  ←  { type: message, channel_id, message_id, user_id, text, ... }

REST:
  GET  /history/{channel_id}?cursor=      → range read from the cursor forward
  GET  /thread/{channel_id}/{parent_id}   → one partition read
  GET  /search?q=&from=&in=&before=       → tenant resolved from the token, never a parameter
```

#### High-level design
Follow the numbered arrows. Everything below the client sits inside one workspace's shard; the platform is a few hundred copies of this picture plus the directory that says which copy to use.

[The hot path from a connection to a delivered message](/diagram/slack?focus=client,edge,directory,gateway,messages,topics,e1,e2,e4,e5,e6,e7)

1. The client connects; the **Edge resolver** looks up the workspace in the **Tenant directory**.
2. The **Edge resolver** routes the connection to the **Gateway pool** for that workspace's shard.
3. The client sends a message; **Gateway pool** writes it to the **Message store** and acknowledges only once that write commits.
4. **Gateway pool** publishes once to **Per-channel topics** on the shard's bus.
5. Every other **Gateway pool** instance holding a subscriber to that channel consumes once and pushes to the sockets it owns locally.

> **Why the flow is shaped this way.** The message is durable before it is acknowledged, so a delivered tick means the record exists, not that one process accepted it. Everything that must never be lost, search indexing, notifications, compliance export, consumes the durable store's change stream rather than the bus, so a stalled topic degrades live delivery without losing data. The bus carries only what is being delivered right now, which is why a rollout that drops every socket in a pool is a reconnect event rather than a data event.

#### The workspace as the unit of placement
The single decision the rest of the design depends on is what a tenant boundary is made of: a column, or a physical bundle of infrastructure.

[Where a request stops being able to reach another tenant's data](/diagram/slack?focus=directory,edge,gateway,messages,e2,e4,e5)

**Bad: one pooled fleet, `workspace_id` as a column on every table.** Every query filters on it, capacity is generic, adding a customer costs a row. Utilisation is excellent and there is one deployment to operate. It also means every enterprise obligation, delete this customer, hold their data in one region, prove no one else can read it, becomes a scan across everybody's rows with no way to demonstrate completeness, and the only defence against a forgotten filter is code review.

**Good: a pooled fleet with stronger row-level enforcement.** Push the tenant filter into the database layer itself so a query cannot omit it. This closes the leakage risk somewhat, but a delete, a residency attestation or a key revocation is still a scan or a bulk operation across shared infrastructure, not something with a clean edge to point at.

**Great: home each workspace on a named shard, resolved at the edge before anything else runs.** A gateway pool, a database keyspace, a search index home, an object-store prefix and an encryption key alias, bundled together and moved or destroyed as one unit. A request physically cannot reach another tenant's storage, because the connection it holds was never given the ability to. Isolation becomes a routing decision made once rather than a predicate that has to be present in every query somebody ever writes.

Worked example: a customer terminates their contract and invokes deletion. On a pooled fleet this is a scan across every table filtering on that workspace's id, with no artifact proving the scan found everything. Homed, it is dropping one keyspace, deleting one object-store prefix, and destroying one encryption key, in minutes, with a tombstone recording exactly what was destroyed. Destroying the key last is what makes any backup nobody remembered to enumerate become unreadable ciphertext rather than a lingering copy, which is the difference between an attestation and a hope.

#### One index per tenant, or one index for thousands
Search inherits the same tenancy question, but its physical constraints push the answer in a different direction than storage did.

[Where the crossover between a shared index and a dedicated one sits](/diagram/slack?focus=messages,indexer,search,e10,e11,e12)

**Bad: one search index per workspace, uniformly.** Consistent with the physical-isolation story everywhere else, and it collides with a hard limit: a search node holds on the order of 500 to 1,000 shards before cluster state and heap overhead dominate. At ~750,000 workspaces, one index each is ~750,000 shards, needing roughly 1,000 dedicated nodes carrying a median of about 110MB each, almost entirely empty capacity.

**Good: one shared index for everyone, with a tenant routing key.** Solves the shard-count problem completely, and reintroduces the same query-time enforcement risk the storage layer was homed specifically to avoid: a missing or malformed tenant filter on a search query is a cross-tenant leak in a place that is much harder to test exhaustively than a row-level database predicate.

**Great: hybrid, split on document count.** Workspaces above roughly 50 million indexed documents, about 1,370 daily actives over five years, get a dedicated index; the top tier gets a dedicated cluster. Everyone below shares physical indices with the workspace id as a mandatory routing key, injected by a query builder that exposes no way to construct an unscoped query, plus a scheduled canary that plants a document in one tenant and asserts a search executed as another tenant never returns it.

Worked example: the top 2% of workspaces by size, roughly 15,000 of them, justify a dedicated index; the remaining 735,000 share physical indices behind the routing key. That threshold is not a policy choice, it falls directly out of the arithmetic: a shard is comfortable at around 50 million documents, and 20 messages a day for five years crosses that line at almost exactly the 98th percentile of workspace size, so the split tracks the size distribution rather than fighting it.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 180" role="img" aria-label="750,000 workspaces at one index each need about 1,000 mostly empty nodes; a hybrid splits the top 2% into dedicated indices and packs the rest onto shared ones">
  <style>
    .full{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.3;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.5}
    .empty{fill:currentColor;fill-opacity:.08;stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.4;stroke-width:1.5;stroke-dasharray:3 3}
    .t{font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif;fill:currentColor;opacity:.8}
    .b{font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif;fill:currentColor}
  </style>
  <text class="b" x="8" y="14">bad: 750,000 tenants, one index each</text>
  <g transform="translate(8,24)">
    <rect class="empty" x="0" y="0" width="56" height="26" rx="5"/><rect class="empty" x="62" y="0" width="56" height="26" rx="5"/>
    <rect class="empty" x="124" y="0" width="56" height="26" rx="5"/><rect class="empty" x="186" y="0" width="56" height="26" rx="5"/>
    <rect class="empty" x="248" y="0" width="56" height="26" rx="5"/><rect class="empty" x="310" y="0" width="56" height="26" rx="5"/>
  </g>
  <text class="t" x="8" y="68">~1,000 nodes, most holding ~110MB in a 15GB shard</text>
  <text class="b" x="8" y="98">great: top 2% dedicated, rest packed onto shared</text>
  <g transform="translate(8,108)">
    <rect class="full" x="0" y="0" width="66" height="28" rx="5"/>
    <rect class="full" x="74" y="0" width="302" height="28" rx="5"/>
  </g>
  <text class="t" x="8" y="154">left: dedicated index for a top-2% tenant, 50M+ docs</text>
  <text class="t" x="8" y="170">right: shared index, thousands of tenants</text>
</svg>
```

#### Fan-out without paying per member
Delivering one message to a channel with a hundred thousand members looks, at first glance, like it should cost a hundred thousand pushes.

[One publish, and one consume per gateway that actually needs it](/diagram/slack?focus=gateway,topics,e6,e7)

**Bad: push directly to every member's socket from the sending process.** Correct and simple to reason about, and it means the cost of one message scales with channel membership, so the largest channels become the most expensive thing in the system to use, exactly backwards from what a large, active channel should cost.

**Good: fan out through a single central dispatcher that holds every socket.** Removes the sender's own scaling problem, but now one process has to hold a fraction of every connection in the platform and push to all of them for every popular channel, which just moves the bottleneck rather than removing it.

**Great: a topic per channel, one publish, one consume per gateway holding at least one subscriber.** Sockets are spread across a fleet of gateway boxes. A message publishes once to its channel's topic; each gateway that owns at least one subscriber to that channel consumes once and pushes to the sockets it holds locally. The cost of delivering one message is the number of gateways involved, not the number of channel members.

Worked example: a 100,000-member channel has its subscribers spread across roughly 300 gateway boxes out of the fleet. One message costs one publish plus 300 consumes, not 100,000 pushes, a reduction of roughly 300x. What this does not fix is the receiving side: 100,000 clients still wake, render and update a badge for a message most of them will never read, which is why muted channels are suppressed at the gateway before a push ever leaves the building, rather than filtered client-side after delivery.

#### Threads without scanning the channel
Loading an 800-reply thread inside a channel holding four million messages looks like it should be expensive, and the data model decides whether it actually is.

[Two writes on send, one read on load](/diagram/slack?focus=gateway,messages,e5)

**Bad: store every message, including replies, in one timeline per channel.** Natural, since a thread reply is still a message in that channel. Finding a thread's replies means filtering that one partition for a matching parent id, which scans the whole channel's history, all four million rows, to return 800 of them.

**Good: index thread replies separately, updated asynchronously after the write.** Removes the scan from the read path, but introduces a lag window where a just-posted reply is in the channel timeline and not yet in the thread index, so a thread can appear to be missing its newest reply for a moment.

**Great: write every reply twice, synchronously, to two tables.** Once to the channel timeline, partitioned by channel and sorted by message id, for scrolling. Once to a second table partitioned by `(channel, thread_parent_id)` and sorted by message id, for threads. Both writes land in the same transaction against the same store, so there is no lag window to reason about.

Worked example: an 800-reply thread in a four-million-message channel loads as a single partition read on the second table, returning exactly its 800 rows regardless of how large the surrounding channel is. The extra write on send is nearly free, since it hits the same cluster and commit path as the first write, while the alternative, filtering the channel timeline for a parent id, degrades linearly as the channel grows and never gets better.

[Write once to the timeline, once to the thread's own partition](/diagram/slack?figure=thread-write)

#### One home for a channel two companies share
When two organisations share a channel, each has its own tenancy boundary, and the message log cannot obey both at once.

[The cross-shard write, and where it costs a hop](/diagram/slack?focus=gateway,messages,e15)

**Bad: replicate the channel's message log to both workspaces' shards.** Each side reads and writes locally, which looks like it preserves the isolation story on both sides. It requires a single ordering authority for the two copies anyway, or concurrent posts, edits and deletes on both sides interleave differently with no way to reconcile them afterwards, so it quietly reintroduces the coordination problem it was meant to avoid.

**Good: replicate, but elect one side as the ordering authority after the fact.** Slightly more defensible, but the two copies can still disagree during the window before reconciliation, and the visiting side's users can observe an inconsistent order that later silently changes.

**Great: exactly one home shard per shared channel, and a bridge row on the visiting side.** The workspace that created the channel owns the only copy of its message log. The visiting workspace holds a row carrying membership, a local channel name and local notification preferences, never messages. Reads and writes from the visiting side route to the home shard.

Worked example: a message sent from the visiting side crosses to the home shard, 20 to 80ms cross-region, on roughly 1% of total message volume, a cost accepted because it applies to a small fraction of traffic in exchange for never having two logs disagree about order. The subtler cost is identity: a visiting user's profile has to resolve for people on the home side, so it is cached per channel membership rather than per workspace, meaning an external user becomes visible only to the people who actually share a channel with them.

#### Moving a live tenant with no maintenance window
A workspace outgrows the shard it was placed on, or a placement forecast turns out wrong, and it has to move without users noticing.

[Snapshot, tail, and a directory flip](/diagram/slack?focus=placement,directory,messages,e17,e18)

**Bad: take the workspace offline, copy its data, bring it back up on the new shard.** Simple and correct, and it means every migration is a scheduled outage a customer has to be warned about, which does not scale once migration has to be routine maintenance rather than a rare event.

**Good: copy the data live, then do a single cutover write with a brief lock.** Reduces the downtime window somewhat, but a single large cutover step still blocks writes for as long as the remaining delta takes to apply, which grows with how active the workspace has been since the snapshot started.

**Great: snapshot, tail the change stream continuously, then flip the directory row only once the tail is nearly caught up.** Snapshot the keyspace to the target shard and continuously replay the change stream behind it. When the remaining tail lag drops under a second, flip the directory row to a migrating state so writes on the source fail with a retryable error rather than a user-visible one, drain the last of the tail, flip the row to the target, and let clients reconnect.

Worked example: measured write unavailability for a live move is 500ms to 2 seconds, not a maintenance window. Two choices make that survivable. Clients reconnect with a cursor, the last message id they hold, rather than a session, so a socket drop costs one range read per open channel rather than a full resync. And the search index moves separately and asynchronously, because search is already seconds behind by design, so a tenant's search stays stale-but-working throughout the move instead of sitting on the critical path of the cutover.

#### Where it breaks
| Layer | Failure | How the design handles it |
|---|---|---|
| Gateway pool | A rollout drops a large share of sockets at once, and reconnects overwhelm the survivors | Drain a fixed percentage of the pool at a time, never a whole workspace's pool; jittered client backoff over 30s; token-bucket admission on the receiving box |
| Channel | A hot channel with 100,000 mostly-connected members | Per-channel topics keep the cost at one publish per gateway with a subscriber, roughly 300 rather than 100,000; muted members are suppressed before the push leaves the gateway |
| Search index | A shared index absorbs an expensive, unbounded query from one tenant | Per-tenant query budgets and a circuit breaker; a tenant whose query cost crosses the threshold is promoted to a dedicated index using the same migration machinery |
| Consistency | An edit or delete lags between the message store, cached clients and the search index | Clients reconcile off a normal channel event; search hits are hydrated from the message store, so a stale index entry resolves to a miss rather than surfacing deleted content |
| Shard | One shard saturates because a tenant it holds grew past its forecast size | Live migration moves the heaviest tenant off; dedicated shards keep the largest customers out of shared failure domains entirely |
| Shared channel | The home shard for a cross-organisation channel is unavailable | Reads fall back to the bridge's cached tail; writes return retryable errors; the log is never replicated to work around the outage |
| Third-party app | An integration posts far faster than a human channel can absorb | Token bucket per app per workspace at the edge, 429 with a retry-after, plus an admin control to suspend an app's scopes without uninstalling it |

#### What this design does not solve
**A tenant can outgrow a single shard, and splitting one gives back the property the design exists to provide.** Every guarantee above rests on one workspace being one physical bundle. A dedicated shard and vertical scaling buy a great deal of room, but eventually a search index alone can exceed what one cluster should hold, and splitting a workspace by channel range breaks search relevance scoring, turns the cheap per-channel publish into a cross-shard one, and turns delete and legal hold back into distributed operations across the split pieces, which is precisely what homing a tenant was meant to avoid.

**Search results are only as correct as the membership they are filtered against at query time, not at index time.** Documents are indexed once; channel membership changes constantly. Filtering at query time against current membership is the right answer for never leaking a document to someone who has left a channel, and it means relevance is scored over a corpus that includes documents the searcher cannot see, so ranking is subtly off, and deep pagination degrades unpredictably once enough results are filtered out after the fact.

**Legal hold and retention pull in opposite directions, and there is no way to prove a negative.** Retention deletes on a schedule; legal hold has to override that deletion for an unbounded period, implemented as an exclusion list the deletion job consults. The correctness of a legal position then depends on that list staying accurate across renames, archival and tenant migration, and a bug in it is not an outage, it is a compliance failure that shows up in a courtroom rather than in monitoring. A tombstone log records what was deleted and under what policy, which answers what happened after the fact and does not prove nothing under hold was ever touched.

#### Final design
Read it back through the numbers. A 15,000x spread between the median and largest tenant is why the design is deliberately bimodal: pack tens of thousands of small workspaces onto shared shards and give the largest their own, because no single placement strategy serves both ends. ~60,000 messages a second at peak is comfortably absorbed because writes are partitioned per shard rather than shared globally. A 100,000-member channel costing roughly 300 pushes instead of 100,000 is what makes a large, busy channel affordable at all. ~750,000 potential search shards against roughly 1,000 available nodes is why search splits at the same 98th-percentile line that everything else does, dedicating an index only once a tenant's document count actually needs one. And a 150MB directory that fits in memory at every edge node is what makes tenant resolution a lookup rather than a network hop, which is the property the entire tenancy boundary is built on.

[The whole design, one workspace's shard plus the directory above it](/diagram/slack?focus=client,edge,directory,limiter,gateway,messages,topics,readstate,indexer,search,notifier,placement)

> **The numbers to remember.** A 15,000x size spread between median and largest tenant · ~60,000 msgs/s peak · ~300 pushes for a 100,000-member channel · ~750,000 potential search shards against ~1,000 nodes, split at ~1,370 daily actives · a 150MB directory cached in full at the edge.

#### Check your understanding
**Why is the tenancy boundary a physical shard rather than a `workspace_id` column?** A column depends on every query remembering to filter on it, and the only defence against a forgotten filter is review and testing, both probabilistic. A homed shard means a request's connection physically cannot reach another tenant's keyspace, index or object-store prefix, so tenant isolation becomes a routing decision made once at the edge rather than a predicate that has to be present everywhere, forever.

**Why does search split into shared and dedicated indices instead of one scheme for everyone?** A search node holds roughly 500 to 1,000 shards before overhead dominates, and one index per tenant across 750,000 workspaces would need about 1,000 mostly-empty nodes. The threshold for a dedicated index, around 50 million documents, falls out of the same arithmetic and lands near the 98th percentile of workspace size, so only the top 2% get one and everyone else shares physical indices behind a mandatory routing key.

**How does a message reach a channel with 100,000 members without 100,000 individual pushes?** It publishes once to that channel's topic. Every gateway box holding at least one subscriber to the channel consumes the publish once and pushes it to the sockets it owns locally, so the cost is the number of gateways involved, roughly 300 here, not the number of members.

**Why write a thread reply to two tables instead of filtering the channel's timeline?** The channel timeline is sorted by message id across the whole channel, so finding a thread's replies by filtering it scans the entire channel's history every time. Writing each reply once more to a table partitioned by `(channel, thread_parent)` makes loading a thread a single-partition read regardless of how large the surrounding channel is, at the cost of one extra, nearly free write.

**How does a live tenant move to a new shard without a maintenance window?** Its keyspace is snapshotted to the target shard while the change stream is continuously tailed behind it. Once the remaining tail lag drops under a second, the directory row flips to a migrating state so writes fail retryable rather than being lost, the last of the tail drains, and the row flips to the target. Measured write unavailability is 500ms to 2 seconds, not an outage, because clients reconnect from a cursor rather than a session.
### 33. Design Zoom (Video Conferencing)
#### Understanding the problem
A video conferencing platform runs multi-party audio and video calls with screen share, chat and recording, from two people talking to a thousand-person webinar. Every frame carries a deadline of roughly 150 milliseconds end to end, and a frame that misses it is thrown away rather than delayed.

Two things make that different from a normal distributed system.

First, the payload has an expiry. A video frame that arrives late is not late data, it is wrong data: the receiver discards it regardless, and every packet spent carrying it was taken from a frame that could still have made it. The question is not how to deliver everything, it is what to give up first, in what order, when the network cannot carry it all.

Second, the population fanning out from one sender is heterogeneous. One receiver is on a phone on hotel wifi, another is on a laptop on fibre, and both are watching the same speaker at the same instant. A single quality level is wrong for at least one of them, always.

> **What this is not.** It looks like a chat system from a distance: a persistent connection per client, a presence and control plane doing similar work, both marketed as real-time messaging. The payload inverts everything downstream of that resemblance. A chat message has no expiry, so that whole design is arranged so nothing is ever lost: persist before acknowledging, at-least-once delivery, a cursor on reconnect asking for everything since the last message seen. Losing one message there is a bug that surfaces as a support ticket weeks later. Here the identical instinct is a defect: a reconnecting client asks for a fresh keyframe and deliberately forgets everything it missed, because stale video is worse than no video. The transport question is the cleanest way to see it: a reliable ordered stream is correct for chat and disqualifying here, because a lost packet holds every later frame hostage behind the one being repaired.

#### Requirements and the numbers
**Functional.** Create a meeting, join, per-participant audio and video, screen share, chat, recording.

**Non-functional.** Under 150ms one-way latency. Support up to 1,000 participants in one meeting. Scale to millions of concurrent meetings.

The whole design is decided by five numbers, so derive them before drawing anything.

**At what participant count does a relay become mandatory rather than optional?** Direct mesh needs (N-1) uploads at roughly 1.5 Mbps each; a relay needs a flat ~2.5 Mbps regardless of N. Those cross at N=3, and by N=5 mesh needs 6 Mbps up against the relay's flat 2.5. Total flows in a mesh are N(N-1), so **8 people is 56 streams** and 7 simultaneous encoder instances per device.

**What does publishing three quality levels cost over publishing one?** Simulcast sends 180p, 480p and 720p together: 200 + 800 + 1,500 kbps ≈ **2.5 Mbps**, against 1.5 Mbps for 720p alone, a **1.67x upload cost** paid to avoid ever transcoding at the server.

**How many relay hosts does the whole fleet need?** ~3M concurrent meetings at roughly 12.5 Mbps ingress each is ~37.5 Tbps, and egress runs close to the same, so **~75 Tbps** across the fleet. A 16-core relay with no transcoding sustains roughly 20 Gbps, so 75 Tbps ÷ 20 Gbps ≈ **~4,000 relay hosts** before headroom.

**When does repairing a lost packet beat dropping it?** A retransmit costs one round trip plus turnaround. At 30ms RTT the repair lands about **40ms later**, comfortably inside a 50-100ms jitter buffer. At 140ms RTT it lands after the frame was due, so the only option left is forward error correction, at a **20 to 30% constant bitrate overhead**.

**How much does recording cost to keep?** Cloud recording touches roughly 5% of meetings, each producing a ~340MB composited file. That is ~1 PB/day, and at a 90-day default retention, **~90 PB hot**, the largest storage line in the system by two orders of magnitude.

> **The numbers to carry.** Mesh and relay uplink cross at N=3, hopeless by N=5 · simulcast costs 1.67x a single stream · ~75 Tbps and ~4,000 relay hosts at 3M concurrent meetings · retransmit under ~30ms RTT, FEC beyond ~70ms · ~90 PB hot recording storage at 90-day retention.

#### Signaling and media, and why they never share a transport
It helps to say plainly that this is two systems joined only by a meeting id. A control plane that is stateful, tiny and tolerant of 200ms of delay. A media plane that carries no state at all beyond a routing table and tolerates almost nothing.

The entities are:

- **Meeting**: the session, holding a participant list and a recording reference.
- **Participant**: one connection, publishing zero or more simulcast layers and subscribing to a per-receiver selection of others'.
- **Simulcast layer**: one of a sender's independently encoded quality streams, each with its own timeline and keyframes.
- **SFU relay**: the box in the middle that forwards packets between the two without ever decoding them.

The API surface is small, because almost everything interesting happens inside the media protocol rather than at it:

```
POST /meeting                  → { meeting_id, sfu_endpoint, jwt }
WS   sfu_endpoint              ← signaling: join, mute, layout, presence
WebRTC: media plane (UDP)      ← audio/video frames, never through signaling
```

#### High-level design
Follow the numbered arrows. This is the control loop that runs continuously for the life of a call, not a single request and response.

[The hot path from a published layer to a rendered frame](/diagram/zoom?focus=publisher,sfu,allocator,jitter,receiver,e-pub,e-egress,e-play,e-twcc,e-hint,e-decide)

1. The **Sending client** publishes all three simulcast layers to the **SFU relay**.
2. The **SFU relay** forwards exactly one chosen layer, through **Jitter buffer + repair**, to the **Receiving client**.
3. **Jitter buffer + repair** reports the arrival timing of every packet back to the **Per-receiver allocator**.
4. The **Receiving client** sends viewport and pin hints, active speaker, thumbnail, scrolled-off-screen, to the **Per-receiver allocator**.
5. The **Per-receiver allocator** decides, every few hundred milliseconds, which layer or none the **SFU relay** forwards to that receiver next.

> **Why the flow is shaped this way.** The relay never decodes a pixel, so its per-meeting cost is a routing table and a set of bandwidth estimates rather than a CPU-heavy transcode. That is what makes the loop affordable at millions of concurrent meetings: the expensive work, encoding, happens once at the sender using hardware that was already running, and the decision that varies per receiver is a cheap table lookup rather than a re-render.

#### Mesh, relay or mixer
The first fork in this design is not a detail, it is which of three fundamentally different topologies a given call needs, and the wrong default is expensive in a way that is easy to miss until the arithmetic is on the board.

[Where the relay sits between senders who never see each other directly and receivers who never see raw uploads](/diagram/zoom?focus=publisher,sfu,receiver,e-pub,e-egress,e-play)

**Bad: everyone sends to everyone, always.** No server in the media path, the lowest possible latency, no infrastructure to run. It costs upload bandwidth proportional to every other participant: a 720p mesh call needs (N-1) × 1.5 Mbps of uplink, which is fine for two people and unworkable by five, where it demands 6 Mbps up and down on connections where uplink is usually the scarce direction.

**Good: route every call of any size through one relay.** Removes the uplink-scaling problem entirely, a flat 2.5 Mbps regardless of participant count. Applied uniformly it wastes the one case where a relay actively hurts: a genuine two-person call pays a relay hop, 15 to 40ms, and loses the cheapest possible end-to-end encryption story, direct media that never touches shared infrastructure, for no benefit.

**Great: mesh for exactly two participants when a direct path exists, a relay above that, and a compositing mixer only for endpoints that can accept exactly one stream.** Roughly 80 to 85% of 1:1 calls find a direct path and use it; the rest fall back to a relay with the forwarding intelligence stripped out. From three participants up, the relay is mandatory, because the crossover in uplink cost happens exactly there. The mixer is reserved for dial-in phones, room systems and broadcast legs, the small set of receivers that are physically incapable of decoding more than one stream.

Worked example: an 8-person call under mesh needs 56 total streams and 7 simultaneous encoder instances per device, which is why phones overheat out of mesh calls before the network ever becomes the limiting factor. The same call under a relay costs each sender one 2.5 Mbps upload regardless of how many people are on the call, and the relay's own cost per meeting stays roughly a tenth of a CPU core, because it is forwarding packets, not compositing pixels.

```svg
    .relay{fill:currentColor;fill-opacity:.12;stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.55;stroke-width:1.5}
```

#### Three encodes instead of one
Given a relay, the next question is what a sender should actually upload, and the answer trades the sender's spare capacity against the server's.

[Three independent layers leave the sender and one is chosen per receiver](/diagram/zoom?focus=publisher,sfu,allocator,e-pub,e-decide)

**Bad: publish one quality level and let every receiver take it or leave it.** Simplest possible sender, and it forces a single bad choice for the whole call: send 720p and the participant on hotel wifi drops out, send 180p and everyone on a large monitor gets a soft picture.

**Good: publish one stream, and have the server transcode a version per receiver.** Solves the heterogeneity problem completely from the receiver's point of view, and it costs a decode plus an encode per distinct output, roughly a full CPU core per stream, which at millions of concurrent meetings is a fleet size nobody budgets for.

**Great: simulcast, three independently encoded layers published at once, and the relay forwards whichever one a receiver needs without touching the pixels.** 180p at 200 kbps, 480p at 800 kbps, 720p at 1.5 Mbps, three separate encode chains with their own keyframes. The relay treats them as three unrelated streams and copies packets from exactly one, per receiver, which is why it costs roughly a tenth of a core per meeting rather than a full core per output.

Worked example: three layers total 1.39 million pixels of encode work per frame against 921,000 for 720p alone, about 1.5x the encode cost and 1.67x the bitrate, paid entirely by the sender's hardware encoder, which was already running. At 3 million concurrent meetings, avoiding one decode-and-encode pass per output stream is the difference between roughly 4,000 relay hosts and a fleet an order of magnitude larger doing real transcoding work.

#### The keyframe tax
Choosing a layer is not free the instant it changes, and the cost of switching turns out to be the thing that actually shapes the mitigation.

[A receiver's upgrade request travels back to the sender before a new layer can start](/diagram/zoom?focus=sfu,publisher,e-pli)

**Bad: let every receiver's upgrade request reach the sender independently, answered immediately.** Correct in isolation. A decoder cannot start mid-stream, it needs a keyframe, so moving a receiver onto a new layer means either waiting for the sender's next scheduled keyframe, one to three seconds away, or asking for one now with a picture loss indication. Answering every request immediately means that when the active speaker changes in a busy call, dozens of receivers request an upgrade within the same 100 milliseconds, and a naive sender answers every one.

**Good: rate-limit keyframe requests per receiver.** Reduces one receiver's ability to hammer the sender, and it does nothing about the aggregate problem, because the storm comes from many different receivers each making one reasonable request at the same moment, not from one receiver making many.

**Great: coalesce keyframe requests per sender behind a floor, and always forward the bottom layer to every receiver regardless of their target.** One keyframe per 500 milliseconds per sender serves every pending upgrade waiting behind it. Keeping the lowest layer, 200 kbps, flowing to every receiver at all times means a downgrade never needs a keyframe at all, which matters precisely because downgrades happen when a link is already struggling and a keyframe, five to ten times the size of a normal frame, is the last thing that link needs.

Worked example: a 50-person call where the active speaker changes and dozens of receivers want the new speaker's 720p layer inside the same 100ms window. Without coalescing, each triggers its own picture loss indication and the sender answers every one, a burst of oversized keyframes that produces exactly the congestion the upgrade was meant to escape. With a 500ms floor, the sender emits one keyframe and every waiting receiver's upgrade is served from it, turning dozens of oversized frames into one.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 200" role="img" aria-label="Without coalescing, many receivers each trigger their own oversized keyframe within 100ms; coalesced behind a 500ms floor, one keyframe serves them all">
  <style>
    .big{fill:currentColor;fill-opacity:.16;stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.55;stroke-width:1.5}
    .one{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.32;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.5}
    .t{font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif;fill:currentColor;opacity:.8}
    .b{font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif;fill:currentColor}

    <rect class="big" x="280" y="0" width="46" height="28" rx="5"/>
  </g>
```
