#### Repair inside the deadline
Once a packet is actually lost, the design has to choose between asking for it again and never having lost it in the first place, and the right answer depends entirely on distance.

[Loss recovery sits between the relay and the receiving client's jitter buffer](/diagram/zoom?focus=sfu,jitter,receiver,e-egress,e-play)

**Bad: a reliable ordered transport for media, so nothing is ever lost.** Removes the entire loss-recovery problem by construction, and it introduces a worse one: a reliable stream holds every later frame behind the one it is repairing. One lost packet on a 140ms path freezes the picture for 280ms, and the frames queued up behind it then arrive as a burst the jitter buffer has to absorb or discard anyway.

**Good: retransmit every loss, unconditionally, over UDP.** Avoids head-of-line blocking since only the missing frame is affected, not everything after it. Unconditional retransmit ignores the deadline: a retransmit requested on a long path arrives after the frame was due to play, so the round trip was spent for nothing.

**Great: retransmit while there is time for it to arrive, forward error correction when there is not, and never delay playout to wait for either.** A NACK costs one round trip plus turnaround. Under roughly 30ms RTT the repair lands about 40ms later, comfortably inside a 50 to 100ms jitter buffer, and is cheaper than carrying constant redundancy. Beyond roughly 70ms RTT the repair would land after the deadline, so the sender carries forward error correction instead, redundant data that lets the receiver reconstruct a lost packet with no round trip at all, at a 20 to 30% constant bitrate cost.

Worked example: a participant inside one region sees occasional loss with a 30ms RTT to the relay; nearly every lost packet is repaired by a retransmit that lands with room to spare, so no permanent bandwidth is spent on redundancy. A transatlantic participant at 140ms RTT would see the same retransmit arrive 40ms after its playout deadline, so that link instead carries FEC continuously, paying a steady 20 to 30% overhead in exchange for zero added latency on the repair itself. Audio gets the stronger protection of the two, because a listener notices a 200ms gap far more readily than a viewer notices one soft frame.

#### Seeing congestion before it drops packets
The allocator needs to know how much bandwidth a receiver actually has before it can pick a layer, and waiting for loss to measure it turns out to be too slow.

[Arrival timing feeds the allocator before anything is actually lost](/diagram/zoom?focus=jitter,allocator,e-twcc)

**Bad: estimate available bandwidth from packet loss.** Loss is unambiguous once it happens, easy to measure, and it happens too late to be useful: by the time packets are dropping, a router queue has already filled and added upward of 100ms of delay, so the estimator is reacting to damage that already happened rather than avoiding it.

**Good: estimate from round-trip time alone.** Cheaper to compute than a full delay-gradient model, and RTT alone conflates a congested path with a merely long one, so it cannot distinguish a queue building from a link that was always going to take 140ms.

**Great: track the trend in inter-packet arrival delay against inter-packet departure delay.** The receiver reports the arrival timestamp of every packet by sequence number; the sender compares how far apart packets left against how far apart they arrived. A consistent, growing gap means a queue is building even though nothing has been lost yet, typically 200 to 500 milliseconds before loss would have shown it. The sender also probes upward deliberately, injecting padding to test for headroom, so a wrong guess wastes filler traffic rather than corrupting real media.

Worked example: a receiver's wifi begins to saturate. Packets are still arriving, none lost yet, but each one lands slightly later relative to when it was sent than the last, a trend the delay-gradient estimator catches within a few hundred milliseconds. A loss-based estimator would wait until the growing queue actually overflows and starts dropping packets, by which point the receiver has already accumulated over 100ms of extra delay on every frame in flight, degrading quality noticeably before any correction begins.

#### Keeping the first mile short
A meeting split across two continents cannot give every participant a short path to the relay unless there is more than one relay.

[One relay per region, joined over a dedicated backbone link](/diagram/zoom?focus=sfu,cascade,e-cascade)

**Bad: one relay cluster for the whole meeting, wherever it happens to be placed.** Simple to reason about, and it means half the participants, whichever half is far from the cluster, pay full transcontinental latency on every single packet rather than once.

**Good: place relay clusters regionally and have clients simply pick the nearest one, independently.** Shortens the first mile for everyone, and without any connection between clusters, participants in different regions cannot see or hear each other at all, which defeats the point of a shared meeting.

**Great: regional relay clusters that cascade, forwarding to each other over a dedicated backbone link.** Each participant connects to their nearest cluster and pays only that short first mile. The clusters forward each other's streams over Zoom's own backbone, adding exactly one extra hop, applied once for the whole group rather than once per participant.

Worked example: a meeting with half its participants in the EU and half in the US would, without cascading, force every EU participant's packets across the Atlantic individually. With cascading, EU participants connect to a EU relay and US participants to a US relay, and the two relays forward to each other over one dedicated backbone link that carries pre-applied forward error correction, so a single transatlantic hop is amortised across the whole group rather than paid by every packet from every participant.

#### Where it breaks
| Layer | Failure | How the design handles it |
|---|---|---|
| Huge meeting | A 1,000-participant call would need each receiver to decode hundreds of streams | Active-speaker selection forwards high resolution only to the top few speakers; beyond a size or view-only threshold, switch to a compositing mixer sending one stream per receiver |
| Network | A participant's link degrades mid-call | The delay-gradient estimator moves that receiver to a lower simulcast layer within a few hundred milliseconds; persistent loss falls back to audio-only with stronger redundancy |
| SFU relay | A relay pod crashes mid-meeting | Clients reconnect to a backup relay in the same cluster and re-publish; a brief quality dip while estimation re-converges, not a dropped call |
| Cascade backbone | The inter-region link between two relay clusters flaps | Per-hop retransmit budgets and pre-applied FEC on the cascade link stop transient loss from becoming a retransmit storm at the root |
| Signaling | Thousands of join attempts hit one meeting id | Rate limiting per IP and per meeting id, short-lived tokens bound to the invitee, and a waiting room that gates approval before any relay capacity is allocated |
| Recorder | The recording process crashes mid-meeting | Checkpointed buffers flushed to object storage every 5 to 10 seconds; the process restarts and resumes into the same chunked output, bounding the loss to one checkpoint interval |
| Region | A relay cluster's region has an outage | Ongoing meetings degrade or reconnect through the cascade to a healthy cluster; new meetings route around the affected region entirely |

#### What this design does not solve
**End-to-end encryption and per-receiver layer selection are in genuine conflict.** The relay still needs the layer id, keyframe flag and frame dependency structure in the clear to make its forwarding decision, even when it cannot see any pixel. That metadata is enough to infer who is speaking and how active a meeting is, a real leak rather than a technicality. Every feature that needs plaintext, cloud recording, live transcription, dial-in from the telephone network, server-side layouts, simply stops working in end-to-end mode, and there is no architecture that offers both fully encrypted and fully featured at once.

**Cascading confuses the bandwidth estimator's model of the path.** The estimator assumes it is measuring one link it can influence by sending less. With a cascade, a second-hop relay is estimating a path that includes a backbone link it does not control and does not share with the receiver. A congested backbone and a congested last mile produce an identical delay-gradient signal, so the relay sometimes degrades a receiver whose own link was never the problem, and doing so relieves nothing. Dedicated backbone capacity makes this rare rather than fixing it.

**A recording is not a faithful copy of what anyone in the meeting actually saw.** The recorder subscribes as just another receiver, with its own bandwidth estimate and its own losses, so it may hold a higher or lower layer than any human participant watched at that moment. Making it faithful would mean recording separately per receiver, multiplying storage by participant count, or buffering raw media durably, exactly the cost this design exists to avoid by dropping instead of storing. The result is a recording that is useful but not evidentiary, with a loss window bounded only by the checkpoint interval.

#### Final design
Read it back through the numbers. Mesh and relay uplink crossing at N=3 and going hopeless by N=5 is why a relay is mandatory for essentially every call above a direct pair. Simulcast's 1.67x upload cost is the price paid, entirely at the sender, to avoid a server-side transcode that would cost roughly a full core per output stream and turn ~4,000 relay hosts into a fleet many times larger. The retransmit-versus-FEC line at roughly 30 to 70ms of round-trip time is what decides, packet by packet, whether a repair is worth attempting or whether redundancy has to be carried the whole way. And ~90 petabytes of hot recording storage against a message-scale system elsewhere in the platform is the reminder that in this design, unlike almost any other, storing everything is never the default; discarding is.

[The whole design, publisher to recorded chunk](/diagram/zoom?focus=publisher,sfu,allocator,jitter,receiver,signalling,meeting-db,cascade,mcu,cdn,recorder,object-store)

> **The numbers to remember.** Mesh/relay crossover at N=3 · simulcast costs 1.67x a single stream · ~75 Tbps and ~4,000 relay hosts at 3M concurrent meetings · retransmit under ~30ms RTT, FEC beyond ~70ms · ~90 PB hot recording storage.

#### Check your understanding
**Why does a relay become mandatory above about four participants rather than being an optimisation?** Mesh uplink grows as (N-1) times a single stream's bitrate while a relay's uplink stays flat regardless of participant count. The two cross around N=3, and by N=5 mesh needs more than double the relay's flat cost in both directions, with total flows growing as N(N-1), which is why phones overheat out of large mesh calls before the network becomes the limiting factor.

**Why does the sender publish three quality levels instead of one, given that it costs more upload bandwidth?** Publishing one stream forces a single quality choice for a heterogeneous set of receivers, wrong for at least one of them always. Server-side transcoding fixes that but costs roughly a full CPU core per output stream. Simulcast pushes the extra encode work onto the sender's already-running hardware encoder for about 1.67x the bitrate, keeping the relay's cost near a tenth of a core per meeting.

**Why does switching a receiver to a higher simulcast layer take time, and how is the resulting request storm controlled?** A decoder cannot start mid-stream, so an upgrade needs a keyframe, five to ten times the size of a normal frame, requested from the sender if one is not already due. When many receivers want the same upgrade within the same window, requests are coalesced behind a floor of one keyframe per 500 milliseconds, so one oversized frame serves every pending upgrade instead of each receiver triggering its own.

**Why retransmit some lost packets but use forward error correction for others?** The choice depends on whether a retransmission can arrive before the packet's playout deadline. Under roughly 30ms round-trip time it can, and is cheaper than carrying constant redundancy. Beyond roughly 70ms it cannot, so the sender carries forward error correction instead, trading a steady 20 to 30% bitrate overhead for zero added latency on the actual repair.

**Why estimate bandwidth from the trend in packet arrival delay rather than from packet loss?** Loss only appears after a router queue has already filled and added significant delay, so a loss-based estimate reacts to damage that has already happened. Tracking how packet arrival spacing drifts from departure spacing catches a queue building 200 to 500 milliseconds earlier, while packets are still arriving, letting the allocator move a receiver to a lower layer before anything is actually lost.
### 34. Design a Distributed Cache (Memcached / Redis at scale)
#### Understanding the problem
A distributed cache puts an in-memory tier in front of a database or a computed result, so the common read never reaches the origin. It has to hold a working set measured in terabytes across many machines, answer in well under a millisecond, and stay useful while nodes are added, removed and lost.

Two things make it deceptively simple to draw and genuinely hard to get right.

First, nothing in it is authoritative. A cache may lose any value at any moment with no correctness consequence, because the origin still holds the truth. That is what makes it cheap to run, and it is also the fact that makes people underdesign it: if losing data is fine, it is tempting to assume everything about it is fine.

Second, it must not serve a wrong value for an unbounded time. Being allowed to be empty is not the same as being allowed to be stale forever. The actual work of this design is picking a staleness bound in seconds, per class of key, and choosing the cheapest mechanism that enforces it.

> **What this is not.** It looks like a distributed lock: both are shared mutable state sitting on the same Redis box, both get waved off as a small operational component rather than a system. They diverge entirely on what a lost write costs. If a cache loses a SET, a later reader takes a miss and reloads, and the price is one extra origin query. If a lock service loses a grant, two workers believe they hold the same lock, both write the protected resource, and the result is corrupted in a way no retry repairs. That single difference is why a lock needs consensus and a fencing token and pays tens of milliseconds for them, while a cache needs none of that and paying for it would destroy the only reason it exists. The trap is the case that looks like both: a per-key lock that stops thousands of requests stampeding the origin is correctly built with no consensus at all, because the worst outcome of losing it is a duplicate query, not corruption.

#### Requirements and the numbers
**Functional.** GET, SET with TTL, DELETE, bulk GET. Eviction under memory pressure. Optionally atomic counters and richer types.

**Non-functional.** Sub-millisecond p99 at the cache. A hit rate high enough that the origin stays inside its own capacity. A single node loss visible only as extra misses. Topology changes without a cluster-wide flush.

The whole design is decided by five numbers, so derive them before drawing anything.

**What is the read-to-write ratio?** ~10k app servers × 100 requests/s × 5 cache gets per request ≈ **5M gets/s**. Writes run at roughly 1% of that, ~50k/s, giving a **100:1 read-to-write ratio**, the number that decides whether the cache belongs in the write path at all.

**What hit rate does the origin actually require?** 50 read replicas at 2,000 QPS each is 100,000 QPS of origin capacity. Misses have to fit inside it: 5,000,000 × (1 − h) < 100,000 gives **h > 98%**. Hit rate is a capacity constraint, not a target to feel good about.

**How many shards does the working set need?** ~5 billion keys worth caching at ~2KB each is roughly 10TB. At 180GB usable per box, 10,000GB ÷ 180GB ≈ **60 primary shards**.

**What does one hot key cost?** A single key lives on a single shard. 1 million reads/s of a 2KB value is 1,000,000 × 2KB = 2GB/s, or **~16 Gbps arriving at one NIC**, while every other shard sits idle.

**How long does an unread key survive before it is evicted?** Admissions equal misses in steady state: 5,000,000 × 2% ≈ 100,000 admissions/s, or 200MB/s of churn. A 10TB cache turns over in 10,000GB ÷ 0.2GB/s ≈ 50,000 seconds, **~14 hours**, which is the number that decides whether TTLs matter more than eviction policy.

> **The numbers to carry.** 100:1 reads to writes · hit rate must clear 98% · 60 shards for a 10TB working set · one hot key can put 16 Gbps on one NIC · ~14 hours of residency before eviction reaches an unread key.

#### Two paths: trivial hits, and everything else
It is worth saying plainly that a cache has one easy path and one hard one, and almost none of the design effort belongs to the easy one. The hit path is a hash lookup and a network round trip. Everything interesting happens on the miss path and the invalidation path, because that is where a cache can go from a performance optimisation to a system that shows someone a wrong number.

The entities are:

- **Key**: an opaque string, always with a schema version embedded so a format change is a new key class rather than a reinterpretation of an old one.
- **Shard**: one node's slice of the keyspace, owning a set of keys with no authority over their correctness.
- **TTL**: the only expiry mechanism whose correctness does not depend on any other system being reachable.
- **Invalidation event**: a signal, from the write path or from a change log, that a key's cached value is no longer trustworthy.

The API is small, and the one addition worth noticing is `CAS`, which exists specifically to close the race the deep dives are about:

```
GET key                  -> value | NULL
MGET key...               -> values
SET key value [TTL]      -> OK
CAS key value version     -> OK | STALE
DEL key                  -> OK
```

#### High-level design
Follow the numbered arrows. A hit never reaches the origin; a miss becomes both a read and a write.

[The hot path from a request to a served value](/diagram/distributed-cache?focus=app,l1,proxy,ring,shard,loader,origin,e1,e2,e3,e4,e5,e6,e7,e8)

1. The **App server** checks its **In-process L1** for a small allowlist of known hot keys first.
2. Otherwise it routes through the **Proxy tier** to the **Consistent hash ring**, which resolves the key to its owning **Cache shard**.
3. On a hit, **Cache shard** returns the value directly to the app server.
4. On a miss, **Cache shard** hands off to the **Single-flight loader**.
5. **Single-flight loader** queries the **Origin database** once for the key, on behalf of every concurrent misser, and writes the result back to **Cache shard** with a jittered TTL.

> **Why the flow is shaped this way.** The cache absorbs read pressure and is deliberately not a second database reasoned about independently. The application, not the cache, knows which origin row a key came from and when it changed, so invalidation lives in the write path or in a consumer of the origin's change log, never inside the cache itself. That is what keeps the cache replaceable: nothing about its internal state is a source of truth anyone has to protect.

#### Write ordering: why delete beats update
There are two operations, writing the origin and mutating the cache, and two ways to mutate it. Three of the four combinations are broken, and it is worth seeing why before trusting the fourth.

[Where a write touches the origin and the cache, in order](/diagram/distributed-cache?focus=writer,origin,shard,e14,e15)

**Bad: delete the cache first, then write the origin.** Between the delete and the commit, any reader misses, reads the pre-write value from the still-unchanged origin, and caches it. The window is the duration of the origin write, single-digit milliseconds under load, and on a key read thousands of times a second that window is not a risk, it is a certainty.

**Bad: write the origin, then overwrite the cache with the new value.** Two concurrent writers can commit to the origin in one order and apply their cache SETs in the opposite order, leaving the cache holding the older value with nothing but the TTL left to dislodge it.

**Great: write the origin, then delete the cache key, never update it.** Deletes commute: any interleaving of two deletes leaves the key absent, and absent is always safe. A concurrent writer racing another delete cannot leave the cache in a worse state than before either write happened.

Worked example: two requests edit the same profile within milliseconds of each other. Under write-then-overwrite, request A's commit could land first in the origin but its cache SET could land second, after request B's, leaving the cache holding A's older value while the origin holds B's newer one, with only the TTL able to fix it. Under write-then-delete, both writers simply delete the same key, in either order, and the next reader repopulates it from whichever commit landed last in the origin, which is always the correct one.

```svg
    .box{fill:none;stroke:currentColor;stroke-width:1.5}
    .acc{stroke:var(--accent)}

  <rect class="box" x="8" y="90" width="376" height="24" rx="5"/><text class="sub" x="16" y="102">3. write origin commits</text>
```

#### The stale write race, and what closes it
Write-then-delete is correct against every ordinary interleaving, and there is still one race it does not fix, caused not by ordering but by time.

[The loader's SET landing after a delete that already happened](/diagram/distributed-cache?focus=loader,shard,writer,e8,e15)

**Bad: assume write-then-delete is sufficient and stop there.** A reader misses and reads v1 from the origin. It stalls: a garbage collection pause, a descheduled thread, a retried remote call. Meanwhile a writer commits v2 and deletes the cache key, which is a no-op because the key is already absent. The stalled reader wakes and SETs v1. The cache now holds a value the origin has already superseded, with nothing but the TTL to remove it, and the window is the reader's stall rather than the write's duration, unbounded in principle.

**Good: rely on the backstop TTL alone to bound the damage.** It works, in the sense that the stale value cannot survive forever. It does nothing to prevent the poisoning in the first place, and at high miss rates the arithmetic is unforgiving: at 100,000 misses/s, even a one-in-a-million race poisons a key roughly every ten seconds, and it tends to be a popular key, because popular keys miss most often in absolute terms.

**Great: reject the stale write directly, with versioned values or leases.** Versioned values store a version alongside the payload, taken from the origin's row version or commit sequence number, and reject any SET carrying a version lower than the one already resident, so the stalled reader's v1 SET simply loses to the resident v2. Leases go further: the cache issues a token on a miss and only accepts a SET carrying a live token, with a DELETE invalidating outstanding tokens so a stalled reader's write is rejected on arrival, which also happens to be a stampede defence, since only one lease is granted per key per interval.

Worked example: a version-carrying value adds 8 bytes per entry, 40GB fleet-wide at 5 billion keys, and turns SET into a compare-and-set. In exchange, the stalled reader's SET, carrying v1's version, is compared against the resident v2 and rejected outright, closing the race completely rather than merely bounding it. The one place this stops working is a value derived from more than one source row, which has no single version to compare against, and that gap carries through to what this design cannot solve.

#### Consistent hashing over hashing modulo N
Deciding which shard owns a key looks like a detail until the cluster needs to resize, at which point the choice decides whether resizing is routine or an incident.

[The ring resolving a key to its shard](/diagram/distributed-cache?focus=ring,shard,e4)

**Bad: hash the key modulo the current node count.** Simple, uniform, and catastrophic under change: adding one node to a 60-node cluster changes the modulus for nearly every key, reassigning roughly 98% of the keyspace at once. That empties the cache and sends the full read load at an origin sized for a fraction of it, at the exact moment capacity was being added to help.

**Good: consistent hashing with one position per shard on the ring.** Adding a shard now moves only the keys between its new position and its predecessor's, roughly 1/N of the keyspace rather than nearly all of it. With only one position per shard, though, placement luck produces meaningfully uneven load, 2x to 3x imbalance between shards is common.

**Great: consistent hashing with roughly 150 virtual positions per physical shard.** Each shard claims many scattered points on the ring instead of one, so the keys it owns are drawn from many small arcs rather than one large one, and the law of large numbers evens out the imbalance to a few percent.

Worked example: resizing a 60-shard cluster to 61 under modulo hashing reassigns close to 98% of a 10TB working set at once, a near-total flush that hands 5 million reads/s to a 100,000-QPS origin. Under consistent hashing with 150 virtual nodes, the same resize moves roughly 1/61 of the keyspace, about 164GB, which arrives at the origin as a manageable, temporary bump in misses rather than an outage.

#### One key, sixteen gigabits per second
A single popular key cannot be sharded further, because a key lives entirely on one shard by definition, so a viral key becomes a single-machine problem regardless of how large the cluster is.

[Hot key detection feeding either the in-process L1 or replication across the ring](/diagram/distributed-cache?focus=shard,hotkey,l1,ring,e11,e12,e13)

**Bad: do nothing until the shard falls over.** The default behaviour of a plain sharded cache. One key at a million reads a second saturates a NIC while 59 other shards idle, and the failure looks like a single-node outage rather than what it actually is, one object being read by everyone at once.

**Good: replicate the hot key across several shards under suffixed names, and pick a suffix at random on each read.** Divides the load: across 8 shards, 16 Gbps becomes 2 Gbps each. Deletes still work, because each suffix is deleted independently, at the cost of 8 SETs on every fill and 8 deletes on every invalidation.

**Great: an explicit allowlist of hot keys cached inside each application process, reserved for keys whose staleness budget can absorb it, with replication for the ones that cannot.** Reads reaching the cache tier for one key fall to P divided by T, the number of processes over the L1's TTL in seconds. At 10,000 processes and a 1-second TTL, that is 10,000/s instead of 1,000,000/s, a hundredfold cut, taking the key from 16 Gbps on one NIC to 160 Mbps.

Worked example: a trending list can sit behind an in-process L1 with a 1-second TTL, because being a second stale changes nothing anyone will notice. A price or an entitlement flag cannot, because a stale L1 has no path back to it, a delete simply cannot reach 10,000 process heaps, so it gets key-level replication instead, which keeps delete working at the cost of dividing rather than eliminating its load. The choice between the two is exactly the staleness budget for that key class, not a performance question.

```svg

  <style>
```
