#### Stopping a stampede before it starts
A popular key expiring is a routine event that becomes a crisis the moment thousands of requests notice it at the same instant.

[The single-flight loader turning many misses into one origin query](/diagram/distributed-cache?focus=shard,loader,origin,e6,e7,e8)

**Bad: let every request that misses query the origin independently.** Correct in isolation and catastrophic in aggregate: a popular key expiring sends every one of the requests that were about to hit it straight to the origin in the same millisecond, taking a key from 10 queries a second to 10,000.

**Good: a per-key lock that the first misser takes, queries the origin under, and releases.** This alone reduces the herd to one query, and it does nothing about the underlying cause, which is that many keys written together tend to expire together, so the next popular key to expire produces the same herd on a schedule.

**Great: three defences layered together, each covering a gap the others leave.** One loader per key limits the damage once an expiry has already happened. Refresh-before-expiry gives each read of a key nearing its TTL a small and rising chance of triggering a refresh, so the value is replaced while still being served and the expiry never actually arrives. Jittered TTLs, a base value plus a random offset, stop keys written in the same batch from expiring in the same millisecond in the first place.

Worked example: at a 300-second TTL with 10% jitter, keys written in the same deploy expire spread across a 30-second window rather than a single instant, which alone prevents most synchronised herds from forming. For the keys that do expire under load anyway, the single-flight loader turns whatever concurrent miss count arrives, ten or ten thousand, into exactly one origin query, with every other request waiting on the same in-flight fetch and reading what it produced.

#### LRU, or an admission policy in front of it
Once memory fills, something has to decide which keys survive, and the right answer depends entirely on whether the workload actually scans.

[Where eviction sits, and whether it is even the binding mechanism](/diagram/distributed-cache?focus=shard,eviction,e9)

**Bad: assume eviction policy always matters and optimise it first.** A natural instinct once memory fills, and it skips a cheaper question: compare the median TTL against the residency time the working set naturally achieves. At a 300-second TTL against roughly 14 hours of residency here, keys expire long before eviction ever reaches them, making the eviction policy nearly irrelevant regardless of which one is chosen.

**Good: plain least-recently-used with a backstop TTL.** The default in every cache server, and it is the right default for a workload whose popularity is stable, where the same keys stay hot and the same keys stay cold.

**Great: LRU as the default, replaced with an admission policy only once the workload is shown to scan.** Measure the share of admitted keys that get evicted having been read exactly once. Below roughly 20% one-hit wonders, LRU is fine and extra machinery buys nothing. Above roughly 50%, a large share of the cache is holding keys nobody will read again, and an admission policy, such as a small probationary queue that only promotes a key into the main cache after a second read, recovers that space directly.

Worked example: a search-results cache or a nightly analytics job that reads a table end to end sweeps a large key range exactly once, filling the cache with keys that will never be read again and evicting genuinely popular keys to make room. An admission policy refuses most of that sweep outright, since a key only earns a place in the main cache by being read a second time, leaving the space for keys with an actual pattern of repeated access. The concession is real: admission control cannot distinguish a scan from a genuine, sudden rise in popularity, so a newly popular key with no history is refused just as readily as a one-time sweep.

#### Where it breaks
| Layer | Failure | How the design handles it |
|---|---|---|
| Cache node | A shard's process crashes or is killed for memory | Replica promotion in roughly 10 seconds; the origin absorbs 1/N of read load as misses during the gap |
| Sharding | A topology change under naive hashing remaps nearly every key | Consistent hashing with ~150 virtual positions per shard moves only about 1/N of keys on resize |
| Stampede | A popular key expires and thousands of requests miss simultaneously | Single-flight loader, refresh-before-expiry, and jittered TTLs, each closing a different part of the gap |
| Invalidation race | A stalled reader writes back a value the origin has already superseded | Write-then-delete as the default ordering, backstop TTL always, versioned values or leases for tight-budget keys |
| Hot key | One key saturates a single shard's NIC | In-process L1 for staleness-tolerant keys, key-level replication across several shards for the rest |
| Connection mesh | Tens of thousands of app-server sockets exhaust a shard's descriptors and buffers | A proxy tier multiplexes many client connections onto a small pool per shard |
| Cold cache | A flush, failover or key-format change empties the cache | Rate-limited fill, load shedding, and staged key-format migrations so no large key class invalidates at once |

#### What this design does not solve
**A value derived from more than one source row cannot be invalidated by name.** Every mechanism above assumes a change event can name the cache keys it affects, which holds for a key that is one row and fails for a rendered fragment built from several. Nothing generates the reverse mapping from a changed row to the derived keys built from it, and maintaining one is a second cache with the same invalidation problem one level down. The practical answer is a short TTL and no real invalidation on that key class, which quietly makes derived keys, the ones users actually look at, the stalest thing in the system.

**A cold cache is not survivable on the capacity actually bought for the origin.** The whole design assumes a warm cache; the origin is sized for roughly 100,000 QPS against a peak read load fifty times larger. An empty cache, after a regional failover, an accidental flush, or a deploy that changed a key format, presents the origin with far more than it can serve, and it will saturate before the cache can refill. Rate-limited fill and load shedding turn that into a controlled degradation rather than a fix, and the uncomfortable consequence is that availability now depends on the cache staying warm, in direct tension with treating it as a pure performance optimisation.

**Hot key detection lags the hot key by design.** Exact per-key counters at millions of operations a second are not affordable, so detection runs on a sampled window, typically on the order of ten seconds to be trustworthy. A key can go from cold to a million reads a second well inside that window, so the first seconds of any new hot key are served with no mitigation engaged at all, and the owning shard can saturate before detection has a chance to act.

#### Final design
Read it back through the numbers. A 100:1 read-to-write ratio is why the cache sits outside the write path by default, deleting rather than updating on every write. The 98% hit-rate floor, forced by 5 million reads a second against 100,000 QPS of origin capacity, is why hit rate belongs on the same dashboard as origin load rather than being treated as a vanity metric. 60 shards for a 10TB working set, moved 1/N at a time by consistent hashing, is what makes adding capacity routine instead of an outage. One hot key's 16 Gbps is why per-key defences exist entirely separately from the sharding story, since no amount of resharding helps a single key. And roughly 14 hours of residency against a 300-second TTL is what makes the TTL, not the eviction policy, the thing actually governing what the cache holds at any moment.

[The whole design, from a request through the miss path to invalidation](/diagram/distributed-cache?focus=app,l1,proxy,ring,shard,eviction,replica,hotkey,loader,origin,writer,invalidator)

> **The numbers to remember.** 100:1 reads to writes · hit rate must clear 98% · 60 shards, moved ~1/N on resize · one hot key can reach 16 Gbps on a single NIC · ~14 hours of residency against a 300s TTL.

#### Check your understanding
**Why does a write commit to the origin and then delete the cache key, rather than updating it in place?** Deletes commute: any interleaving of two concurrent deletes on the same key leaves it absent, which is always safe. An in-place update can be applied out of order relative to two concurrent origin commits, leaving the cache holding an older value than the origin with nothing but the TTL able to correct it.

**What race does write-then-delete still leave open, and what closes it completely?** A reader can miss, read an old value, stall before writing it back, and by the time it resumes a writer has already committed a newer value and issued a now-useless delete against an absent key. The stalled reader's write then poisons the cache with a stale value until the TTL expires. Versioned values or leases close it by rejecting that stale write outright rather than merely bounding how long it survives.

**Why does consistent hashing move roughly 1/N of the keyspace on a resize instead of nearly all of it?** Hashing modulo the node count changes the modulus for almost every key the moment the count changes, since a key's owner is a function of the total. A hash ring assigns ownership by position instead, so adding one shard only reassigns the keys between its new position and its predecessor's, leaving everyone else's ownership untouched.

**A single key is suddenly read a million times a second. Why can't more shards fix it?** A key lives entirely on one shard by construction, so its load cannot spread across the cluster no matter how many shards exist. The fix is either an in-process cache at the application layer, which cuts load by the number of processes over the cache's TTL in seconds, or replicating the key itself across several shards under suffixed names, which divides its load by the replication factor while keeping deletes working.

**Why does a backstop TTL matter even after versioned values or leases are in place?** Both of those mechanisms depend on the invalidation pipeline actually running: a writer that forgets the delete, a stalled process, a dropped broadcast to another region. A TTL is the only enforcement that requires no other system to be reachable, which is why it sits underneath every other defence rather than being replaced by any of them.
### 35. Design a Distributed Lock
#### Understanding the problem
A distributed lock allows only one process at a time to act on a resource identified by a key, across machines that can crash, pause, or lose contact with each other. It has to release itself when a holder dies, and stay safe when a holder is merely slow rather than dead.

Two things make this harder than it first sounds.

First, safety means no two holders ever write, which is a stronger claim than no two holders believe they hold the lock. A lock service can behave perfectly at every step and still let two processes believe, at different moments, that they are the current owner.

Second, a distributed lock is actually two mechanisms, and most designs build only the first. A lock service grants time-bounded ownership of a key. The protected resource has to enforce that grant. Build only the service and the result is reduced contention, not safety.

> **What this is not.** It looks like a distributed cache: both put a small stateful cluster in front of a real system, and both have the same tempting first answer, an in-memory key-value store with a TTL. What differs is the price of being wrong. A cache is allowed to be wrong: a miss costs one extra database read, a stale entry costs one stale render, so the design is tuned around hit rate and stampedes because those are the failures that actually hurt. A lock that is wrong costs two concurrent writers and a record that no longer reconciles. So a cache question is answered by making the common path cheap and the worst path survivable, and this question is answered by deciding who verifies the grant, and conceding that the lock service is not that party.

#### Requirements and the numbers
**Functional.** Acquire a lock with a TTL, release it, optionally renew it.

**Non-functional.** Safety, no two holders act at once. Liveness, a lock is eventually granted. Low overhead on the common path.

The whole design is decided by five numbers, so derive them before drawing anything.

**How much of the traffic actually needs consensus?** Across a fleet where roughly ten services touch money movement or state-machine transitions at ~100 acquires/s each, that is **~1,000 correctness acquires/s**. The remaining traffic, cache refills, cron dedupe, stampede collapse, runs at roughly **~9,000 best-effort acquires/s**, a 9:1 split by volume that inverts by consequence.

**What does that look like at peak?** A fleet-wide deploy or a leader-election cascade restarts everything at once, and every holder reacquires within a few seconds: **~10,000/s correctness, ~90,000/s best-effort**. Each acquire pairs with a release, so correctness alone becomes **~20,000 writes/s** at the consensus store.

**How much headroom does a consensus cluster actually have?** A three-node consensus cluster's write ceiling sits around **10,000 to 30,000 writes/s**, bounded by the leader's disk fsync rather than by CPU. Peak correctness load of 20,000/s against a 30,000 ceiling is **~68%**, the number that decides whether one cluster is enough or the keyspace needs sharding.

**How much faster is the fast path?** A majority-commit acquire inside one datacentre costs **1 to 10ms**, p99 nearer 20 to 30ms under load. A single in-memory key with an expiry costs **under 1ms**. That **20x to 30x gap**, not safety, is what pushes latency-sensitive, non-critical work onto the fast path.

**How much slack does a lease actually need against a real pause?** A stop-the-world pause of 35 seconds is entirely plausible under load; a 20-second lease is not, because it expires mid-pause. Sizing a TTL at **3 to 5 times the measured p99.9 of the critical section** is what keeps healthy holders from losing their lease to ordinary latency variance.

> **The numbers to carry.** ~1,000 correctness acquires/s against ~9,000 best-effort/s · peak correctness load is ~68% of a single consensus cluster's ceiling · a 20x to 30x latency gap between consensus and a single in-memory store · a 35-second pause against a naively sized 20-second lease is exactly the failure this design exists to survive.

[A 35s pause outlasts a 20s lease: the fence catches the stale write](/diagram/distributed-lock?figure=lease-race)

#### Two mechanisms: the grant and the enforcement
It is worth separating, explicitly, the two jobs this design does, because conflating them is the single most common way a distributed lock ships unsafe. One mechanism decides who currently owns a key. A completely different mechanism decides whether a write from that owner is still allowed to land.

The entities are:

- **Lock key**: the resource identifier being protected, mapped to at most one current grant.
- **Grant**: a lease with a TTL, issued by the lock service, naming a holder.
- **Fencing token**: a number that strictly increases across successive grants of the same key, taken from the lock service's own agreed log position.
- **Protected resource**: the thing that actually enforces safety, by remembering the highest token it has accepted and rejecting anything lower.

The API surface is deliberately small; almost all of the design lives in what the resource does with the third field:

```
acquire(key, ttl_ms, owner_id?) → fence_token | null
release(key, fence_token)
renew(key, fence_token, ttl_ms)
```

#### High-level design
Follow the numbered arrows. A grant and a fenced write are two separate hops, and the second one is where safety actually lives.

[The hot path from an acquire to a fenced write](/diagram/distributed-lock?focus=worker-a,router,etcd,fence-token,fence-check,resource,e1,e2,e6,e7,e11,e12)

1. **Worker A, the holder** calls acquire against the **Lock class router**.
2. **Lock class router** sends correctness-critical acquires to the **etcd cluster, 3 nodes**.
3. **etcd cluster, 3 nodes** grants a lease and mints a **Fencing token** taken from its own Raft revision.
4. **Worker A, the holder** attaches that token to every write it makes, evaluated at **Fence check at the write**.
5. **Fence check at the write** compares the token against the **Protected resource**'s stored maximum, accepting or rejecting inside the same statement as the write.

> **Why the flow is shaped this way.** A lease expiring does not stop the process that held it; nothing tells a paused process that its lease has gone. The lock service can only ever know what it granted, not what a client currently believes, so the design puts the actual safety check at the last possible hop, the write itself, where both the old holder's stale write and the new holder's current one are visible to the same party.

#### Two backends, not one
The first fork is not a detail of implementation, it is which of two entirely different stores gets to answer any given acquire call.

[Correctness traffic routed to consensus, best-effort traffic routed around it](/diagram/distributed-lock?focus=router,etcd,redis,e2,e3)

**Bad: one backend for everything, a single in-memory key with an expiry.** Sub-millisecond, one hop, trivial to operate. Replication to a standby is asynchronous, so a failover can promote a replica that never heard about the most recent grant, handing the same key to a second caller with nothing anywhere noticing.

**Good: one backend for everything, a small consensus cluster.** Removes the failover gap entirely, since a grant is not acknowledged until a majority holds it durably. Applied uniformly it wastes the cluster's limited write ceiling, in the low tens of thousands per second, on traffic that never needed the guarantee: cache refills and cron dedupe where a duplicate holder costs nothing worse than a repeated no-op.

**Great: two lock classes, two backends, chosen per call site by what a duplicate holder actually costs.** Correctness-critical locks, money movement, ledger posting, state transitions, go to a consensus cluster and return a fencing token. Best-effort locks, cache refill, stampede collapse, deduplication, go to a sharded single-instance store and return nothing.

Worked example: correctness traffic runs ~1,000 acquires/s steady, ~10,000/s at peak, which paired with releases is ~20,000 writes/s against a consensus cluster's ceiling of roughly 30,000, about 68%, comfortably inside one cluster with room to spare. Best-effort traffic runs ~9,000/s steady, ~90,000/s at peak, well past what a single in-memory instance sustains at low latency, so it is sharded by key hash across several instances, each then carrying a fraction of that peak.

#### The token has to come from a log
A fencing token is only useful if it is genuinely monotonic, and where that number comes from turns out to matter more than the number itself.

[The token minted from the consensus cluster's own revision, not a separate counter](/diagram/distributed-lock?focus=etcd,fence-token,e6)

**Bad: mint the token from a separate counter service.** Looks reasonable, since a dedicated incrementing counter is simple and fast. It is a second consensus problem the moment more than one process can increment it, because two callers can race to read and increment the same counter, and now the token generator has exactly the correctness problem the token was meant to solve.

**Good: mint the token from a single, unsharded database sequence.** Genuinely monotonic as long as that one database is up, and it introduces a second store that has to be as available as the lock service itself, plus a second failure mode: a sequence that runs on a replica after a failover can hand out numbers already issued on the primary.

**Great: take the token directly from the lock service's own agreed log position.** etcd exposes the revision at which a lock key was created; ZooKeeper exposes the transaction id of the znode. Both are log positions, so monotonicity is a property of the log itself rather than a feature someone implemented and could get subtly wrong. No second system, no second failure mode, and no additional round trip.

Worked example: two grants of the same key, seconds apart after the first holder's lease expired, land at consensus log positions 33 and 34. Because both numbers came from the same single agreed order, there is no scenario, no failover, no partition, no retried write, in which a later grant produces a lower position than an earlier one. A counter minted by any system outside that log cannot make the same promise, because it has no way to observe where in the log its own increments actually landed relative to a concurrent one.

#### The check has to be one statement
Even with a correct token, the way the resource evaluates it can quietly reopen the exact gap fencing exists to close.

[Comparison and write, evaluated as a single atomic operation](/diagram/distributed-lock?focus=worker-a,fence-check,resource,e11,e12)

**Bad: read the resource's stored token, compare it in application code, then write if it passes.** Looks correct line by line, and it is not, because the process performing the check can pause between the read and the write, exactly the failure fencing was built to survive. A stalled process that read an old-but-then-current max token, then paused, can resume and write successfully even though a newer grant landed during the pause.

**Good: wrap the read, compare and write in a database transaction, still as separate statements inside it.** Better than application-level check-then-write, and still vulnerable depending on the isolation level: a transaction can itself be delayed at commit time by the same kind of pause that caused the original problem, and not every isolation level prevents a concurrent transaction from committing in between.

**Great: fold the comparison into the write's own predicate, as a single statement.** `UPDATE ... SET fence_token = :token WHERE id = ? AND fence_token < :token`. There is no separate read step to pause after, because the comparison and the write are the same atomic operation as far as the store is concerned; either it affects a row or it affects nothing.

Worked example: a worker's write carrying token 33 arrives after a resource has already accepted token 34. Under a single-statement compare-and-write, that write's predicate, `fence_token < 33`, does not match the row's stored value of 34, so zero rows are affected and the caller sees a clean rejection. Under a read-then-write split, the same worker could have read `max_seen_token = 34`, correctly concluded it was stale, and then paused before deciding not to write, but a differently timed worker performing the identical read-then-decide sequence with a slightly older snapshot could write successfully in the gap, which is precisely the race a single statement removes by construction.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 220" role="img" aria-label="Read-then-write leaves a pause window between the check and the write; a single compare-and-write statement has no such window">
  <style>
    .box{fill:none;stroke:currentColor;stroke-width:1.5}
    .acc{stroke:var(--accent)}
    .bad{fill:currentColor;fill-opacity:.14;stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.5;stroke-width:1.5}
    .t{font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif;fill:currentColor;opacity:.8}
    .b{font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif;fill:currentColor}
    text{dominant-baseline:middle}
  </style>
  <text class="b" x="8" y="14">bad: read, then decide, then write</text>
  <rect class="box" x="8" y="24" width="376" height="24" rx="5"/><text class="t" x="16" y="36">1. read max_seen</text>
  <rect class="bad" x="8" y="54" width="376" height="24" rx="5"/><text class="t" x="16" y="66">2. pause: a newer grant can land</text>
  <rect class="box" x="8" y="84" width="376" height="24" rx="5"/><text class="t" x="16" y="96">3. write, unguarded</text>
  <text class="b" x="8" y="128">great: compare and write, one statement</text>
  <rect class="box acc" x="8" y="138" width="376" height="24" rx="5"/><text class="t" x="16" y="150">UPDATE ... WHERE fence_token &lt; :token</text>
  <text class="t" x="8" y="180">no separate read to pause after: the store</text>
  <text class="t" x="8" y="196">evaluates the predicate and the write together</text>
</svg>
```

#### Renewal keeps the token
A holder still doing legitimate work has to extend its lease before it expires, and what that extension does to the token is easy to get backwards.

[A renewal touching the lease without touching the token the holder already carries](/diagram/distributed-lock?focus=worker-a,lease,fence-token,e7,e8)

**Bad: mint a fresh token on every renewal.** Seems consistent, a new lease period, a new number. It breaks the holder currently working correctly: an in-flight write carrying the token issued at acquisition time would be rejected by the resource's own fence the instant a renewal mints a newer one, because the resource only ever accepts the highest token it has seen.

**Good: keep the same token, but renew by re-acquiring the key from scratch.** Preserves the token during ordinary operation, and it briefly drops the lock in the middle of an active hold, opening a window where a different waiter could acquire it before the renewal completes.

**Great: extend the same lease in place, keeping the same token throughout.** A renewal is an extension of the same period of ownership, not a new one, so nothing about who is fenced changes: the resource still accepts exactly the token issued at the original acquisition, for as long as that holder keeps renewing successfully.

Worked example: a holder acquires with token 33, works for two minutes, renewing its 30-second lease every 10 seconds throughout. Every write it makes during those two minutes carries token 33, and every one is accepted, because the resource's fence never advances until a different acquisition happens. Only losing the lease, through a missed renewal or an explicit release, and then reacquiring produces a new token, which is exactly the boundary the resource needs to detect: a period of continuous ownership ending and a new one beginning, not the mere passage of time.

#### A lock, or a version column
Not every critical section needs a lock service at all, and the alternative turns out to be the same idea with the lock itself removed.

[Where the fence check sits when there is no separate grant step](/diagram/distributed-lock?focus=fence-check,resource,e12)

**Bad: reach for a distributed lock around every section that touches shared state.** Safe in every case, and it adds a lease to size, a renewal thread to run, and a lock service in the availability path for sections that never needed any of it.

**Good: skip the lock only when contention is provably near zero.** Reasonable instinct, and it is fragile in practice, because contention tends to rise exactly when it matters most, during a retry storm or a traffic spike, which is the worst moment to discover the assumption was wrong.

**Great: skip the lock specifically when the critical section ends in one conditional write to one store, using a version column instead.** Read the row with its version, do the work, then `UPDATE ... SET version = v+1 WHERE id = ? AND version = v`. Losers are told they lost and retry. There is no lease to size, nothing to renew, and no way to hold something already lost, because there was never anything held.

Worked example: below roughly 10% conflict rate, optimistic concurrency wins on every axis a lock would have cost something on. Above roughly 30%, the retry loop itself starts burning more work than a lock would have cost in lease overhead, and at that point a lock is genuinely the cheaper answer. The two are closer than they look: optimistic concurrency is the fencing token with the lock deleted, a version check happening at the exact same place, the write's own predicate, that a fenced write already checks.

#### Redlock: fast, and unsettled
A design that wants the low latency of a single in-memory store but the durability of several independent ones runs into a debate worth understanding rather than avoiding.

[The same fast path, but the question of whether several independent instances add up to safety](/diagram/distributed-lock?focus=redis,router,e3)

**Bad: dismiss the idea outright as obviously unsafe.** Understates a real benefit: acquiring a majority of several independent fast stores does genuinely improve availability over a single instance, since the lock survives one node failing outright.

**Good: adopt it uncritically as a safety mechanism because a majority of nodes agreed.** Overstates what a majority of independent instances can promise. They share no common log, so there is no value they can jointly guarantee is monotonic, and the reference protocol's validity calculation depends on a bounded clock drift allowance, a fraction of the TTL, that ordinary events like an NTP step or a resumed virtual machine can exceed on a subset of the nodes involved.

**Great: name exactly which of the two properties, availability or safety, is actually being bought, and route around the gap accordingly.** Where the workload is already best-effort and several independent fast instances are already in use, this genuinely improves survival of a single node dying, and it is a real upgrade over one uncoordinated instance. Where a fencing token is required, it cannot be retrofitted, because there is no shared log position to take it from.

Worked example: on a 30-second lease, the reference specification sets the drift allowance at roughly 1% of TTL, about 300 milliseconds. A forward clock step larger than that on a majority of the independent instances expires the lock on those nodes while a holder, checking against its own clock, still counts it as valid elsewhere, producing two callers who are each locally correct about owning the same key. That failure has no analogue in a single consensus log, where ownership is decided by log position rather than by comparing wall clocks across machines that do not share one.

#### Where it breaks
| Layer | Failure | How the design handles it |
|---|---|---|
| Consensus quorum | The lock service loses its majority | Correctness locks fail closed; existing holders keep their leases until natural expiry rather than being silently revoked |
| Holder process | A holder crashes mid-section and never releases | The TTL auto-releases the lock; any late write the crashed holder still manages to send is rejected by the resource's fence |
| Resource fence | The protected resource never enforces the token | Treated as part of the resource's contract rather than an optional client behaviour, verified by a chaos test that deliberately pauses a holder past its lease |
| Fast-path failover | A single in-memory store's primary dies before replicating a grant | Reserved for best-effort locks only, where a duplicate holder costs a repeated no-op rather than corruption |
| Hot lock | Thousands of workers contend for one key regardless of backend | Treated as a design defect: shard by sub-key, or replace the lock with optimistic concurrency on a version column |
| Renewal storm | Many holders renew on a synchronised schedule, spiking consensus writes | Jitter each holder's renewal interval so renewals spread rather than land together |
| Cross-region | A resource needs to be locked from more than one region | The resource and its lock service are homed in one region; acquires for it route there rather than running a stretched global quorum |

#### What this design does not solve
**Fencing makes each write safe, and it does not make a multi-step critical section atomic.** A holder that writes to one system, pauses past its lease, and gets fenced out before writing to a second system leaves the overall operation half done. The fence did exactly its job, no stale value overwrote a fresher one, but the invariant the lock was meant to protect spanned both writes and is now broken in a way no token check can see. Inside a single store this disappears entirely by putting both writes in one transaction; across two systems there is no equivalent fix at this layer, only idempotent, replayable steps or an explicit saga with compensations, both of which are a different design from taking a lock and doing the work.

**Some resources cannot be fenced at all.** The mechanism assumes a monotonic check can be added to the thing being written, which is true of a row in a database and increasingly true of object storage with conditional writes, and false of a third-party API, a partner's file drop, or an outbound message to a system nobody will modify. For those the lock is genuinely advisory, and the best available substitute is an idempotency key the receiver deduplicates, which depends entirely on their cooperation and their retention window rather than on anything this design controls.

**Cross-region locking with strong safety at usable latency is unsolved.** A single quorum stretched across regions pays a full round trip on every acquire, tens to hundreds of milliseconds, unusable on most hot paths; independent per-region quorums are fast and can each legitimately grant the same logical lock to a different region. The workaround actually in use is homing each resource in one region and routing every acquire for it there, which works but is not active-active: moving a resource's home is a coordinated procedure, not a failover, and during a regional outage the resources homed there are simply unavailable rather than served elsewhere.

#### Final design
Read it back through the numbers. Roughly 1,000 correctness acquires a second against 9,000 best-effort ones is why the design runs two backends rather than one, because forcing everything through consensus would waste its limited write ceiling on traffic that never needed the guarantee. Peak correctness load sitting at about 68% of a single consensus cluster's ceiling is the number that decides whether one cluster suffices or the correctness keyspace needs sharding before it grows further. The 20x to 30x latency gap between consensus and a single fast store is what makes that split worth the operational cost of running two systems rather than one. And a 35-second pause against a naively sized 20-second lease is the scenario the entire fencing mechanism exists to survive, which is why the resource, not the lock service, is where safety actually lives.

[The whole design, from an acquire through a fenced write](/diagram/distributed-lock?focus=worker-a,worker-b,router,etcd,lease,fence-token,redis,fence-check,resource)

> **The numbers to remember.** ~1,000 correctness acquires/s against ~9,000 best-effort/s · peak correctness load is ~68% of one consensus cluster's ceiling · a 20x to 30x latency gap between consensus and a single fast store · a 35-second pause against a 20-second lease is the failure fencing exists to survive.

#### Check your understanding
**Why is a lock service alone not sufficient for safety?** A lock service can only know what it granted, never what a client currently believes. A process paused long enough for its lease to expire resumes with no notification that anything changed, and any check it performs before writing can itself be followed by another pause. Only the resource, which sees every write from every holder, is positioned to catch a write from a holder that no longer legitimately holds the lock.

**Why must a fencing token come from the lock service's own consensus log rather than a separate counter?** A separate counter is a second system that itself needs to be correct under concurrency and failover, which is the exact problem the token was introduced to solve. A log position from the consensus store is monotonic as a property of the log itself, so no failover or retry can produce a lower value for a later grant than an earlier one.

**Why does the fence check have to be a single statement rather than a read followed by a write?** A process performing a separate read-then-write can pause between the two steps, which reopens the same unbounded window the fencing mechanism exists to close. Folding the comparison into the write's own predicate means the store evaluates both together as one atomic operation, so there is no gap for a pause to land in.

**Does renewing a lease produce a new fencing token, and why does it matter?** No. A renewal extends the same period of ownership, and minting a new token on renewal would cause the resource's own fence to reject the legitimate holder's in-flight writes, since it always accepts only the highest token seen. Only losing the lock and reacquiring it produces a new token, because that is the actual boundary between one period of ownership ending and another beginning.

**When is a distributed lock the wrong tool even though the workload has shared mutable state?** When the critical section ends in one conditional write to a single store, a version column with a compare-and-swap update gives the same exclusion at the write with no lease to size, nothing to renew, and no lock service sitting in the availability path. It stops being the better choice once conflict rates climb high enough that the retry loop costs more than a lock would have, or once the section spans more than one system with no single write to hang correctness on.
### 36. Design a Distributed Job Scheduler / Cron
#### Understanding the problem
A distributed job scheduler fires jobs at the times their owners asked for, one-shot and recurring, across a worker fleet that is constantly being restarted underneath it. Retries, dependencies and status history are part of the product, and so is the promise that a nightly batch scheduled for 02:00 either ran or someone was told it did not.

Two things make it harder than a queue with a delay attached.

First, the product is a decision about time, and that decision is the only thing in the system that can be made exactly-once. Everything downstream of it, executing a job, retrying it, writing its status, is ordinary at-least-once distributed work that any queue-and-worker system already knows how to do.

Second, nobody produces the input. A queue has a producer waiting for an acknowledgement, so a missing message is visible to someone. A scheduler manufactures its own input from a calendar, and time is not a well-behaved input: it drifts between hosts, it is not uniform across daylight-saving transitions, and its failure mode is silence. A run that never fires raises no error, consumes no capacity, and leaves no row anywhere.

> **What this is not.** It looks like a message queue: workers pulling records, leases, retries, dead-letter handling. A message queue's hard problems are throughput, per-partition ordering and consumer rebalancing, all problems of moving bytes that already exist without losing them. This design's hard problems are identity, what makes two fires the same fire, in a way that survives a leader change and a timezone; absence detection, proving something did not happen; and calendar semantics, since a naive implementation both skips and duplicates a run every year at the daylight-saving boundary. Throughput barely features here, a few hundred runs a second is a rounding error for any broker, and the queue is one component inside this design rather than the subject of it.

#### Requirements and the numbers
**Functional.** Schedule a one-shot job at a specific time, or a recurring one from a cron expression. Retries with backoff. DAG dependencies. Cancel. Status and history.

**Non-functional.** Millions of definitions. No single point of failure. At most one accepted completion per occurrence. A fire decision that survives any single host loss.

The whole design is decided by five numbers, so derive them before drawing anything.

**How much steady traffic is there really?** ~10M job definitions, averaging roughly 5 fires a day, is ~40M runs/day. 40,000,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ **~460 runs/s steady**, a volume any modern database handles without effort.

**What happens at round times?** ~840,000 hourly jobs and ~1.68M jobs set for midnight both come due in the same second, so 00:00:00 nominally brings **~2.5 million runs due at once**. Spread with a stable per-job jitter across a 600-second window, that becomes roughly **4,200 runs/s**, the number the queue and worker pool actually have to be sized for.

**What does the midnight window cost the jobs store?** Each fire is one run insert plus one `next_run_at` update, so 4,200 fires/s costs **~8,400 write operations/s**. A single database primary with batched commits handles 10,000 to 20,000 small writes/s, so this fits with under 2x headroom, which is the trigger for sharding, not the read query.

**How often does a run get interrupted mid-flight?** At peak, roughly 300,000 concurrent leases running continuously is ~336,000 worker-hours a day. At one unplanned worker termination per ~500 worker-hours, that is **~670 interrupted runs a day**, about **1 in 60,000**, the number that decides whether at-least-once execution is an acceptable default.

**At what dispatch rate does a plain claim table stop working?** A `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` claim table holds up to roughly **1,000 dispatches/s** and a couple of hundred pollers before empty polls and lock contention dominate. The midnight window's 4,200/s across a fleet of over 1,000 workers is well past that line.

> **The numbers to carry.** ~460 runs/s steady, ~4,200/s jittered peak · ~8,400 writes/s at the jobs store, near a single primary's ceiling · ~1 in 60,000 runs interrupted mid-flight · a plain claim table tops out around 1,000 dispatches/s.

#### Two guarantees: the decision and the execution
It is worth separating, precisely, what this design can promise exactly-once from what it can only promise at-least-once, because collapsing the two is the most common way a scheduler ships with a silent bug in it.

The entities are:

- **Job definition**: the cron expression or one-shot time, retry policy, DAG parents, and `next_run_at`, the source of truth for what should run.
- **Run record**: the materialised occurrence, identified by `(job_id, scheduled_at)` under a unique constraint, the one thing everything downstream keys on.
- **Lease**: a TTL'd claim a worker holds while executing a run, advisory rather than a true lock.
- **Idempotency ledger**: a row in the job's own domain, keyed on the same tuple, that is what actually prevents a duplicate side effect.

The API surface is deliberately small on the write side, because almost everything interesting is a background decision rather than a request:

```
POST /jobs           body: { cron|run_at, timezone, payload, max_retries,
                             catch_up, jitter_window, dependencies? }
                     -> { job_id }
GET  /jobs/{id}      -> definition, next_run, recent runs
POST /jobs/{id}/run  (manual trigger, allocates scheduled_at = now)
```

#### High-level design
Follow the numbered arrows. A run record exists before anything else in the system knows a fire happened, and that ordering is the entire design.

[The hot path from a due job to a completed run](/diagram/job-scheduler?focus=scheduler,jobs-db,runs-db,queue,workers,lease,target,e2,e4,e5,e6,e7,e8,e9)

1. The **Scheduler tick** reads due rows from the **Jobs store**.
2. For each due job, **Scheduler tick** inserts a row into **Run records + history** under a unique constraint and advances `next_run_at`, both in one transaction.
3. Only after that transaction commits, **Scheduler tick** publishes to the **Durable job queue**.
4. The **Worker pool** pulls a run record and takes a lease in the **Lease store**.
5. The **Worker pool** executes against **External systems** and writes a terminal status back to **Run records + history** with a compare-and-set.

> **Why the flow is shaped this way.** Mixing scheduling and execution leaves no artifact to attach a retry to. Materialising each due occurrence as its own record gives leases, retries, dependency resolution and audit a single thing to key on, and it is why coordination between multiple schedulers is a load optimisation rather than the correctness mechanism: the unique constraint on the run record already does correctness on its own.

#### Why identity comes from the calendar, not the clock
The single most consequential choice in this design is what value becomes the key for "this fire", and getting it wrong reintroduces every race the rest of the design exists to close.

[The run record's identity, computed once and never from the moment it fires](/diagram/job-scheduler?focus=scheduler,runs-db,e4)

**Bad: key the run on the wall-clock time it actually fired.** Intuitive, since that is genuinely when the work happened. Two schedulers ticking 50 milliseconds apart, or one scheduler retried after a timeout, would generate two different identities for what should be the same occurrence, and the unique constraint would accept both as distinct rows.

**Good: key the run on the time the scheduler intended to fire it, in local time.** Closer, and it inherits a second bug from the calendar itself: a naive local-time evaluation produces `02:30` twice on the autumn clock change, two genuinely different instants colliding on the same local-time key.

**Great: compute the occurrence in UTC from the cron expression against a current timezone database, and key on that UTC instant.** `scheduled_at` becomes a property of the calendar, never of `now()` at the moment of firing. That single choice is what makes the identity stable across a retried tick, a leader change, a clock running 400 milliseconds fast, and a worker redelivering an envelope four minutes late.

Worked example: a job scheduled for `02:00` local time on the day clocks fall back has two real UTC instants an hour apart that both map to the local label `02:00`. Keying on the UTC instant makes these two distinct, correctly generated occurrences rather than one ambiguous label; keying on the local string would collide them into a single row and silently drop one real fire. On the spring-forward day, `02:30` local time does not exist at all, and computing purely in UTC means that occurrence is simply never generated, rather than an implementation guessing at a nearby time.

#### One transaction, or two silent bugs
The scheduler does two things on every fire, insert a run row and advance the job's next fire time, and doing them separately produces failures with no error message anywhere.

[The insert and the advance, committed together or not at all](/diagram/job-scheduler?focus=scheduler,jobs-db,runs-db,e2,e4)

**Bad: advance `next_run_at` first, then insert the run row.** If the process crashes between the two, the job's next fire time has already moved forward, so the tick that should have produced this occurrence never runs again, and the occurrence is skipped forever. Nothing anywhere records an error, because from the job's perspective its schedule looks perfectly normal.

**Bad: insert the run row first, then advance `next_run_at`.** If the process crashes between the two, the next tick re-reads the same due row, attempts the same insert, hits the unique constraint, and does nothing, because the row already exists. The job fired exactly once and then appears to hang forever, with no further occurrences ever generated.

**Great: both operations inside one transaction, with a guard on the update.** Insert the run row with `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`, and advance `next_run_at` with a `WHERE next_run_at = :old_value` guard, committed together. Either both happen or neither does, so a crash between them is impossible by construction, and the guard on the update is what makes two concurrent schedulers safe: a second writer's update matches zero rows and it knows immediately that it lost.

Worked example: two scheduler processes both briefly believe they lead during a leadership handoff and both tick the same due job within milliseconds of each other. One's transaction commits first, inserting the run row and advancing `next_run_at`. The second's insert then conflicts with the existing row and its update's guard no longer matches the now-advanced value, so its entire transaction does nothing, cleanly, with the second scheduler aware it accomplished nothing rather than silently producing a duplicate.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 260" role="img" aria-label="Advancing next_run_at before inserting the run row can skip an occurrence forever; inserting first can wedge the job; one transaction with a guard closes both gaps at once">
  <style>
    .box{fill:none;stroke:currentColor;stroke-width:1.5}
    .acc{stroke:var(--accent)}
    .bad{fill:currentColor;fill-opacity:.14;stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.5;stroke-width:1.5}
    .t{font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif;fill:currentColor;opacity:.8}
    .b{font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif;fill:currentColor}
    text{dominant-baseline:middle}
  </style>
  <text class="b" x="8" y="14">bad: advance, then insert</text>
  <rect class="box" x="8" y="24" width="376" height="22" rx="5"/><text class="t" x="16" y="36">1. advance next_run_at</text>
  <rect class="bad" x="8" y="50" width="376" height="22" rx="5"/><text class="t" x="16" y="62">2. crash: occurrence skipped forever</text>
  <text class="b" x="8" y="100">bad: insert, then advance</text>
  <rect class="box" x="8" y="110" width="376" height="22" rx="5"/><text class="t" x="16" y="122">1. insert run row</text>
  <rect class="bad" x="8" y="136" width="376" height="22" rx="5"/><text class="t" x="16" y="148">2. crash: every retry conflicts, stalls</text>
  <text class="b" x="8" y="186">great: one transaction, both or neither</text>
  <rect class="box acc" x="8" y="196" width="376" height="22" rx="5"/><text class="t" x="16" y="208">insert + advance, guarded, COMMIT</text>
  <text class="t" x="8" y="234">a crash before commit leaves neither change;</text>
  <text class="t" x="8" y="250">the next tick simply retries cleanly</text>
</svg>
```

#### Leader election is a load optimisation
It is tempting to treat electing a single scheduler as the mechanism that prevents duplicate fires, and that framing is backwards.

[The coordination lease, existing to save work rather than to guarantee correctness](/diagram/job-scheduler?focus=scheduler,coordination,e3)

**Bad: assume duplicate fires are prevented because only one process is allowed to tick.** This is the natural mental model, one leader, one decision-maker, nothing can conflict. It quietly makes the coordination service load-bearing for correctness, so any bug in leader election, a stale lease, a split-brain window, becomes a data-corruption risk rather than a performance blip.

**Good: elect a leader, and also add the unique constraint as a backstop.** Better, and it undersells what is actually happening: with the constraint in place, the leader election is not really a backstop, it has become almost entirely unnecessary for correctness.

**Great: state plainly that the unique constraint provides correctness on its own, and leader election exists only to avoid wasted work.** With the constraint in place, two schedulers both ticking at once produce exactly one run record and one wasted transaction, nothing more. Leader election exists purely to avoid paying N times the write load and N-1 discarded queue messages per fire, which is a real cost worth avoiding, just not a safety one.

Worked example: a coordination lease expires during a garbage-collection pause and briefly grants leadership to two processes at once for a few seconds. Under the correct mental model, this produces a doubled load on the jobs store for those few seconds and nothing else, absorbed by the headroom already built into the write-rate sizing. Under the incorrect mental model, that same event would be treated as a data-integrity incident requiring investigation, when the unique constraint had already made it a non-event.

#### Commit before publish
Once a run row exists, it has to reach the workers, and the order in which the database write and the queue publish happen decides which of two very different failure shapes the system can have.

[The run row committing before the queue ever sees it](/diagram/job-scheduler?focus=scheduler,runs-db,queue,sweeper,e5,e10,e11)

**Bad: publish to the queue first, then commit the run row.** If the process crashes after publishing but before the database commit, a worker can pull a message describing a run that has no corresponding row, so its terminal status write has nothing to attach to, and there is no clean way to reconcile the gap after the fact.

**Good: commit the run row and publish in the same step, treated as best-effort together.** An improvement in spirit, and most infrastructure cannot actually make a database commit and a separate broker publish atomic without a distributed transaction, so this is really just the bad case with the two operations moved closer together in time rather than made indivisible.

**Great: commit the run row first, publish only after, and run a sweeper to cover the gap.** If the process crashes between commit and publish, the result is a row sitting in `QUEUED` with no queue message, a state that is easy to detect and cheap to fix. A sweeper scans for rows in that state older than 60 seconds and republishes them.

Worked example: the scheduler commits a run row and crashes before the publish call executes. Nothing is lost: the row exists, durably, in `QUEUED`. Sixty seconds later the sweeper finds it, republishes it to the queue, and a worker picks it up exactly as if the original publish had succeeded, with the only cost being roughly a minute of added latency on that one occurrence rather than a missing or unreconcilable run.

#### The lease is a hint, not a lock
A worker holding a lease looks, at first glance, like it guarantees exclusivity, and the gap between that appearance and reality is where duplicate execution actually comes from.

[Where a stalled worker and its replacement can both be alive at once](/diagram/job-scheduler?focus=workers,lease,target,runs-db,e7,e8,e9)

**Bad: assume the lease TTL prevents two workers from ever executing the same run.** True for the crashed-worker case, since a crashed process stops heartbeating and its lease genuinely expires with nobody left to contest it. False for the stalled-worker case: a garbage-collection pause, a blocked system call, or a network partition to the lease store can let the TTL expire while the process is still alive, still holding open connections, and still about to act.

**Good: shorten the TTL and heartbeat more aggressively to narrow the window.** Reduces how often the stall case actually triggers, and it cannot close the window completely, because any TTL short enough to matter also risks reclaiming perfectly healthy long-running jobs during ordinary latency variance.

**Great: accept that the lease is advisory, and put the real protection at the resource.** The terminal status write is a compare-and-set on `(run_id, attempt)`, so a stalled worker's late write is rejected and the run history stays coherent. Separately, and this is the part that actually matters, the job's own side effect is keyed on `(job_id, scheduled_at)` in a ledger row or an external idempotency key, so a stalled worker and its replacement collide there and only one of them takes effect in the real world.

Worked example: a four-hour backfill job renews its lease roughly 160 times over its run. A single 90-second network blip to the lease store during that window, well within normal operational variance, is enough to expire the lease while the job is perfectly healthy, letting a second worker claim and start the same occurrence. The compare-and-set keeps only one of the two workers' status writes accepted; the ledger row keyed on the occurrence tuple is what actually stops the underlying side effect, whatever it is, from happening twice.

#### A dedicated queue, or a claim table
Handing a due run from the scheduler to a worker can be built with an extra durable system in the middle, or without one, and the right choice is a question of scale rather than taste.

[The queue as the handoff between the scheduler's decision and a worker's execution](/diagram/job-scheduler?focus=scheduler,queue,workers,e5,e6)

**Bad: always add a dedicated queue, regardless of dispatch rate.** A second durable system that can disagree with the first, needing a sweeper solely to reconcile the two, which is real operational overhead for a scheduler that might never need it.

**Good: always skip the queue, using `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` against a claim table directly.** The run record and the claim become the same row in the same transaction, removing the entire class of "the record says queued but nothing is actually queued" bug and removing the sweeper outright. It works beautifully at moderate scale and starts to fail exactly where the claim table's own hot rows become a lock-contention point under enough concurrent pollers.

**Great: choose based on measured sustained dispatch rate and worker count.** A claim table holds up comfortably to roughly 1,000 dispatches/s and a couple of hundred pollers; past that, empty polls and lock contention dominate and a durable queue, despite its extra moving part, becomes the better answer.

Worked example: this design's midnight window runs at roughly 4,200 dispatches/s across a fleet that autoscales past a thousand workers, comfortably over the claim table's practical ceiling, which is why a durable queue and its sweeper are worth the added complexity here. A smaller internal scheduler running at a few hundred dispatches a second with a few dozen workers sits well under that line, where the claim table's single-datastore simplicity, easier consistent backups and complete absence of a commit-then-publish ordering hazard make it the genuinely better design, not merely the simpler one.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 190" role="img" aria-label="2.5 million runs nominally due in one second at midnight; a stable per-job jitter spreads them across a 600 second window instead">
  <style>
    .spike{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.32;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.5}
    .spread{fill:currentColor;fill-opacity:.14;stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.5;stroke-width:1.5}
    .t{font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif;fill:currentColor;opacity:.8}
  </style>
  <text class="t" x="8" y="16">2.5M at 00:00:00</text>
  <rect class="spike" x="40" y="24" width="14" height="110"/>
  <g transform="translate(110,118)">
    <rect class="spread" x="0" y="0" width="10" height="16"/><rect class="spread" x="16" y="0" width="10" height="16"/><rect class="spread" x="32" y="0" width="10" height="16"/>
    <rect class="spread" x="48" y="0" width="10" height="16"/><rect class="spread" x="64" y="0" width="10" height="16"/><rect class="spread" x="80" y="0" width="10" height="16"/>
    <rect class="spread" x="96" y="0" width="10" height="16"/><rect class="spread" x="112" y="0" width="10" height="16"/><rect class="spread" x="128" y="0" width="10" height="16"/>
    <rect class="spread" x="144" y="0" width="10" height="16"/><rect class="spread" x="160" y="0" width="10" height="16"/><rect class="spread" x="176" y="0" width="10" height="16"/>
  </g>
  <text class="t" x="8" y="160">jittered: ~4,200/s across a 600s window</text>
  <text class="t" x="8" y="176">cron line still reads "0 0 * * *"</text>
</svg>
```

#### Where it breaks
| Layer | Failure | How the design handles it |
|---|---|---|
| Jobs store write rate | The midnight window's write load approaches a single primary's ceiling | Shard the jobs store by `hash(job_id)` with one scheduler leader per shard, splitting both reads and writes |
| Round-time bursts | Millions of jobs set for the same round time fire in the same second | A stable per-job jitter derived from the job's own id spreads fires across a configurable window while the displayed cron line stays unchanged |
| Dead worker | A crashed worker holds a lease indefinitely | Heartbeat plus TTL reclaims the lease within a bounded window; dependent DAG tasks stall no longer than that window |
| Failed job | Repeated failures wedge a whole dependency graph | Bounded retries with backoff, then a dead-letter queue; dependents are marked skipped with a reason rather than queued indefinitely |
| Timezone transitions | Naive local-time evaluation skips or double-fires around daylight-saving changes | Occurrences computed in UTC against a current timezone database and keyed on the UTC instant, so the two boundary cases resolve to a defined policy rather than an accident |
| Scheduler and queue disagreement | The scheduler keeps emitting while workers are stalled, overrunning queue retention | The scheduler watches consumer lag and pauses emission above a threshold, relying on the same transactional guard to replay cleanly on resume |
| Coordination flap | Two schedulers briefly both believe they lead | The unique constraint collapses both attempts to one run record; the only cost is one wasted transaction and doubled load for the duration of the flap |

#### What this design does not solve
**A run that never fires produces no signal, and the natural watchdog shares the same blind spots.** The system can report that a run failed; it cannot report that a run was never created, because a missing run consumes nothing and touches no row. A watchdog checking for expected cadence helps, but if it depends on the same clock, the same timezone database and the same jobs store as the scheduler, exactly the class of bug most likely to cause a silent miss also blinds the detector. A genuinely independent check needs its own stack, its own data path, and its own externally verified liveness, which is a real gap rather than a rough edge.

**Catch-up assumes a job is parameterised by the period it covers, and most jobs are not.** Replaying every missed occurrence after an outage is correct only for a job that processes the specific window it was scheduled for. A job that simply reads current state at run time produces a different, silently wrong answer when replayed hours late, and nothing outside the job can detect that the answer differs from what would have been produced on time. The only real mitigation is making the scheduled time a mandatory argument the job must consume, enforced at registration rather than guaranteed by the system.

**Jitter spreads fires in time and has no concept of what those jobs actually contend for.** Two hundred jobs jittered evenly across a window can still all query the same downstream warehouse and queue behind each other there, even though the scheduler's own dispatch rate looks perfectly healthy throughout. The scheduler has no way to infer what a job's side effects actually touch, so protecting a shared downstream resource needs the job author to declare it explicitly, and a job that forgets to is invisible to any admission control built on top of that declaration.

#### Final design
Read it back through the numbers. ~460 runs/s steady is trivial for any component in this design, which is why the interesting engineering is entirely in the ~4,200/s jittered peak and the ~8,400 writes/s it produces at the jobs store, close enough to a single primary's ceiling to be the trigger for sharding. Roughly 1 in 60,000 runs being interrupted mid-flight is small enough that at-least-once execution with per-job idempotency is the right default everywhere except the small set of jobs whose side effects genuinely cannot tolerate a duplicate. And a plain claim table's ceiling near 1,000 dispatches a second is exactly why this design needs a durable queue and the sweeper that comes with it, while a smaller deployment running comfortably under that line would be better served without either.

[The whole design, from registration through execution to the missing-run watchdog](/diagram/job-scheduler?focus=registration,jobs-db,scheduler,coordination,runs-db,queue,sweeper,workers,lease,target,dlq,watchdog)

> **The numbers to remember.** ~460 runs/s steady, ~4,200/s jittered peak · ~8,400 writes/s near a single primary's ceiling · ~1 in 60,000 runs interrupted mid-flight · a claim table's ceiling near 1,000 dispatches/s.

#### Check your understanding
**Why is a run's identity computed from the calendar rather than from the moment it actually fires?** Two schedulers ticking milliseconds apart, or one tick retried after a timeout, would produce two different wall-clock moments for what should be the same occurrence, and a unique constraint keyed on that moment would happily accept both as distinct. Computing the occurrence from the cron expression in UTC against a timezone database gives every legitimate attempt at the same fire the identical key, so a unique constraint on that key does the deduplication regardless of how many times or how late the attempt happens.

**Why must inserting the run row and advancing `next_run_at` happen in one transaction?** Doing them separately creates two distinct silent failures depending on which one a crash lands between: advancing first can skip an occurrence forever with no error, and inserting first can wedge a job so every future tick conflicts and makes no progress. Wrapping both in one transaction with a guard on the update means a crash between them is impossible, and a second concurrent writer's guard simply fails to match, so it does no damage and knows it accomplished nothing.

**If leader election isn't what prevents duplicate fires, what is, and what does leader election actually buy?** The unique constraint on the run record's identity is what prevents duplicates; two schedulers ticking simultaneously produce one row and one wasted transaction regardless of coordination. Leader election exists purely to avoid paying that wasted load N times over and to avoid N-1 discarded downstream messages per fire, which is a real cost worth optimising away, just not a safety guarantee.

**A worker's lease has not expired, but a second worker is executing the same run. How?** The first worker stalled rather than crashed, held by a garbage-collection pause or a network partition to the lease store, and its TTL expired while the process was still alive and about to act. A TTL-based lease cannot prevent this by construction, because it has no way to know the difference between a dead process and a live one that simply stopped renewing in time; only a compare-and-set on the status record and an idempotency ledger keyed on the occurrence at the actual resource can stop the duplicate from taking effect.

**When does a dedicated queue between the scheduler and workers stop being worth its complexity?** Below roughly 1,000 sustained dispatches a second and a worker fleet of a few hundred, a claim table read directly with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` makes the run record and its claim the same row in the same transaction, removing an entire class of bug and the sweeper needed to catch it. Past that dispatch rate, lock contention on the claim table's hot rows and a flood of empty polls make a separate durable queue the better trade despite the second system it introduces.
### 37. Design Google Docs (Real-Time Collaborative Editor)
#### Understanding the problem
A real-time collaborative editor lets many people edit one rich-text document at once, each seeing the others' keystrokes within a couple of hundred milliseconds, with nobody waiting on a round trip to see their own typing appear. Concurrent edits to the same region must leave every client holding byte-identical text, and a client offline for hours must be able to rejoin and merge cleanly.

Two things make this genuinely different from an ordinary real-time system.

First, the document itself is never transmitted. What travels is a stream of small operations, each meaningful only relative to the state its author was looking at when they wrote it. An insert at position 5 is not a fact about the document, it is a function of one, and by the time it arrives that exact state may no longer exist anywhere.

Second, an operation that arrives late is not merely delayed, it is wrong. A chat message arriving out of order is a display problem, fixed by sorting on a timestamp, because its content is unaffected by anything that happened while it was in flight. An edit operation's positions point into a document that has since moved underneath them, so applying it unchanged corrupts the text rather than merely delaying its appearance.

> **What this is not.** It looks like a chat system at the transport layer: persistent sockets, a per-document ordering authority, durability before acknowledgement, offline clients catching up on reconnect. The resemblance stops the moment a message arrives late. A chat message is immutable and self-contained, so sorting it into place repairs everything a delay could break. An edit operation arriving late is not late data, it is data about a document that no longer exists, and sorting it does nothing, because the positions inside it are the problem. That single difference is why a chat system's ordering authority can be an id minted anywhere, while this design's authority has to be a single writer that also holds the document, because transforming an operation requires the history to transform it against.

#### Requirements and the numbers
**Functional.** Real-time collaborative editing, presence with cursors, comments, version history, offline editing with sync on reconnect.

**Non-functional.** Sub-200ms keystroke propagation. Eventual convergence. Conflict-free behaviour under concurrent edits.

The whole design is decided by five numbers, so derive them before drawing anything.

**How many editors can share one document before the machine, not the product, becomes the limit?** Fan-out from one owner is N² in editor count. At around 1,000 concurrent typists that is roughly **2 million frame-sends a second**, saturating several cores against a single-threaded owner. That is the hard ceiling; the useful ceiling is lower.

**Where does the 200ms latency budget actually go?** Roughly 40ms client to edge, 30ms edge to region, transform and log append near 15ms, 30ms back out, 40ms to the far client, leaving **~45ms of slack**. The append is the only part of that budget that is not simply physics, which is why it is the one worth optimising.

**How much does bounding replay actually save?** A document with 800,000 operations of raw history opens, with snapshotting, as one snapshot fetch plus a short tail rather than a full replay. Coalescing raw operations into named revisions for version history is roughly a **40x reduction**, turning 20TB/day of raw operations into about 500GB/day.

**How expensive is a long offline gap, really?** 200 local operations reconciled against 1,500 missed remote ones is **~300,000 pairwise transforms**, microseconds of total compute. The cost is never computational; it is that both parties may have rewritten the same section, producing a result that is provably consistent and reads like nonsense.

**What does ordering cost if every writer contends on the same log instead of one dedicated owner?** Ordering inside one process is a memory write, tens of nanoseconds. A conditional append to a replicated log costs 5 to 20ms, and its retry rate climbs sharply with concurrent writers: at 2 operations/s per editor, two editors collide on roughly **4% of appends**, twenty editors on roughly **50%**.

> **The numbers to carry.** ~1,000 concurrent typists saturates a single owner at ~2M frame-sends/s · ~45ms of slack inside a 200ms budget · snapshotting turns 800k operations of history into one fetch · a two-minute offline gap costs microseconds of compute and a readability problem, not a performance one · conditional-append retries reach ~50% at twenty concurrent editors.

#### Two halves: the server transform and the client rebase
It is worth separating the two places this design actually does its work, because most first drafts only build one of them and the missing half is where convergence quietly fails.

The entities are:

- **Operation**: a small edit, tagged with the revision its author was looking at when they wrote it.
- **Revision**: a monotonically increasing counter, one per accepted operation, owned entirely by the document's single owner.
- **Pending buffer**: the operations a client has applied locally and sent but not yet had acknowledged.
- **Transform function**: the rule that rewrites one operation so it means, against a different state, what its author meant against the state they actually saw.

The protocol is deliberately thin on the wire, because nearly all of the design lives in what each side does with these frames:

```
WebSocket per editing session:
  → { type: op, doc_id, ops: [...], rev: int }
  ← { type: ack, server_rev: int }
  ← { type: remote_op, ops, by, rev }
  ← { type: presence, user, cursor_pos }
```

#### High-level design
Follow the numbered arrows. A keystroke is applied locally before anything is sent, so typing never waits for the network; everything after that is about reconciling what every other screen believes.

[The hot path from a keystroke to a converged edit](/diagram/collaborative-editor?focus=client,socket-edge,owner,transform,oplog,broadcast,e1,e2,e3,e4,e5,e6)

1. The **Editor client** applies its own keystroke locally and sends the operation, tagged with its base revision, to the **WebSocket edge**.
2. **WebSocket edge** forwards operations to the **Document owner** in arrival order.
3. **Document owner** reads everything that happened since that base revision and hands the operation to **OT transform**.
4. **OT transform** rewrites the operation against that entire gap, and the result is appended to the **Op log**.
5. Only once that append commits, **Broadcast + ack** sends the transformed operation to every other client, and returns just the new revision number to the author.

> **Why the flow is shaped this way.** Funnelling every operation for one document through a single process turns a distributed concurrency problem into an ordered queue, which is the biggest simplification in the whole design. Applying edits locally first is what keeps typing from ever waiting on a round trip; the transform is what pulls those optimistic local states back into one shared document afterwards.

#### Two transforms, not one
The server half of this protocol is the half everyone describes. The client half is where an incomplete design silently produces wrong text that never self-corrects.

[A remote operation arriving while the client still has unacknowledged work of its own](/diagram/collaborative-editor?focus=client,socket-edge,broadcast,e1,e6)

**Bad: apply an incoming remote operation directly to the screen.** The remote operation was transformed against server state, and it is reasonable to assume that is exactly what the screen should reflect. It is not: the client's screen shows server state plus whatever is sitting unacknowledged in its own pending buffer, so applying the remote operation as received ignores work the user is currently looking at.

**Good: transform the remote operation against the pending buffer before applying it, and stop there.** This fixes what appears on screen immediately, correctly. It leaves the pending buffer itself untouched, still expressed against the old premise, so the next time the server transforms it, the two sides are working from different assumptions about what already happened.

**Great: transform in both directions.** `remote' = T(remote, pending)` produces the operation that is actually correct to apply to what the user is looking at right now. `pending' = T(pending, remote)` rewrites the buffer itself, so that when the server eventually processes it, both ends are transforming from the same shared premise.

Worked example: a client has one unacknowledged local insert sitting in its pending buffer when a remote delete arrives. Skipping the second transform means the buffer still refers to a position calculated before the delete happened; the client believes it is level with the server the moment its next acknowledgement lands, but the two documents actually differ by exactly the operations that were never rebased. The symptom reported by users is a single character sitting in the wrong place, permanently, with nothing anywhere that self-corrects it, because nothing in the protocol noticed the rebase was skipped.

```svg

    .acc{stroke:var(--accent)}

  <rect class="miss" x="8" y="52" width="376" height="24" rx="5"/><text class="t" x="16" y="64">pending buffer left unrebased</text>
  <text class="b" x="8" y="104">great: both directions transformed</text>
  <rect class="box acc" x="8" y="114" width="376" height="24" rx="5"/><text class="t" x="16" y="126">remote' = T(remote, pending) → screen</text>
  <rect class="box acc" x="8" y="142" width="376" height="24" rx="5"/><text class="t" x="16" y="154">pending' = T(pending, remote)</text>
```

#### Log before broadcast
The order in which the operation is written durably and shown to other clients decides which of two very different failures the system can have.

[The append that must complete before anyone else sees the edit](/diagram/collaborative-editor?focus=transform,oplog,broadcast,e4,e5)

**Bad: broadcast the transformed operation first, then append it to the durable log.** Removes any perceived delay before other clients see the edit. If the process crashes after broadcasting but before the append completes, the edit is now visible on every other open screen and exists nowhere durable, and there is no way to un-show it or reconstruct it for the replacement owner.

**Good: append and broadcast concurrently, treated as one best-effort step.** An improvement in spirit, and without a genuine distributed transaction across two separate systems, it collapses to the bad case under exactly the failure that matters, a crash landing between the two.

**Great: append to a majority before broadcasting, always, with no exceptions.** If the process crashes after the append but before the broadcast, the worst case is an operation nobody was told about yet, which the durable log still has, ready to be delivered to the new owner and from there to every client on reconnect.

Worked example: an owning process dies immediately after committing an operation to the log but before the broadcast call executes. Nothing is lost: the operation exists, durably, at its assigned revision. The replacement owner, once it acquires the lease, simply replays from that revision, and every client, reconnecting and reporting its own last-known revision, receives exactly the operations it missed, indistinguishable from a slightly slower broadcast rather than a lost edit.

#### One owner, one transform site
The entire correctness argument in this design rests on a property that sounds like an implementation detail and is actually the whole foundation.
