[Every operation transformed by exactly one process, never two](/diagram/collaborative-editor?focus=owner,transform,lease,e3,e7)

**Bad: assume the transform function works correctly under any amount of concurrency, because it is mathematically defined to converge.** A reasonable assumption from the outside, and it is false for the general case: convergence across three or more places where transforms actually happen requires a much stronger property than convergence between two clients and one server does, and several published algorithms claiming that stronger property were later shown, by formal model-checking, to violate it.

**Good: restrict transforms to happen in one place, and hope nothing ever needs a second.** Better, and stated this way it is fragile without anyone noticing, because the obvious scaling moves under load, sharding a hot document by section, or giving a distant region its own local owner, both quietly introduce a second place where transforms happen.

**Great: make single ownership an explicit, enforced architectural invariant, and treat every proposal that would violate it as a correctness question rather than a scaling one.** With exactly one process transforming every operation against a single linear history, the weaker convergence property is genuinely sufficient, and it holds by construction rather than by care.

Worked example: a hot document under heavy load is a natural candidate to shard by section for more throughput, giving each section its own owner and its own transform. Doing so creates a second transform site, and the stronger multi-site convergence property this design does not implement is now back in scope, with no known practical implementation to satisfy it. The design instead caps concurrent editors on a single document rather than sharding it, choosing a product limit over reintroducing a correctness risk that has no known fix at this scale.

#### Detecting a divergence you cannot prevent
Even with both transform directions correct and single ownership enforced, a bug, a dropped operation, or a doubly-applied one can still silently split one client from the rest, and nothing in the protocol so far notices.

[A periodic checksum comparing what every client believes against the owner's own state](/diagram/collaborative-editor?focus=broadcast,client,oplog,e5,e6)

**Bad: rely on the transform's correctness and add no verification.** If it is right, this costs nothing; if it is ever wrong, even briefly, a client can drift silently and stay drifted, because nothing anywhere is comparing states, and the symptom users report, a character in an odd place, is easy to dismiss as a rendering glitch.

**Good: log every operation with enough detail to manually reconstruct a client's state after a complaint.** Useful for investigating an incident after the fact, and it does nothing to catch a divergence while it is small and cheap to fix, so problems surface as unreproducible support tickets months later rather than as an alert.

**Great: broadcast a periodic hash of the document alongside its revision, and have clients compare when they can.** Every so many operations, the owner hashes its own document at that revision and broadcasts it. Any client sitting exactly at that revision with an empty pending buffer, a moment when its state should be provably identical to the server's, compares hashes.

Worked example: a subtle transform bug causes one client's document to silently diverge from everyone else's by a single misplaced character. Without a checksum, that divergence is invisible until a user notices and files a support ticket describing something impossible to reproduce weeks later. With a checksum broadcast regularly, the affected client detects the mismatch within one broadcast interval, discards its state, and reloads from the latest snapshot plus tail, costing it at most its last few hundred milliseconds of unacknowledged typing rather than an unbounded, undiagnosable drift.

#### A pinned owner, or a conditional-append log
Deciding how operations get their order, one dedicated process per document or a shared log any server can write to, turns out to be a question about the shape of contention rather than about elegance.

[Where ordering actually happens for one document](/diagram/collaborative-editor?focus=owner,lease,oplog,e7,e4)

**Bad: stateless collaboration servers writing to a shared log with an optimistic conditional append, uniformly for every document.** Removes the need for a coordination service and a lease entirely, since any server can serve any document. Under real concurrency it starts to fail exactly where collaboration is actually happening: a conditional append that loses its race has to re-read the gap, re-transform, and retry, and that retry rate climbs sharply with the number of concurrent writers on the same document.

**Good: the same stateless design, with a shorter retry window to reduce collision odds.** Helps somewhat, and it cannot remove the underlying arithmetic, because the collision probability is a function of how many editors are appending within the same short window, not of how quickly any single retry resolves.

**Great: lease each open document to exactly one process, and order everything for it in memory there.** Ordering inside one process is a plain memory write, tens of nanoseconds, with no contention to model at all. The cost is a coordination service on every document open and a bounded read-only window if the owning process dies before a replacement takes the lease.

Worked example: at 2 operations/s per editor, two concurrent editors collide on roughly 4% of conditional appends to a shared log, a tolerable retry rate. Twenty concurrent editors, this design's own p99 for a single document, collide on roughly half of all appends, and 50% retries at 5 to 20ms each destroys most of a 200ms latency budget precisely on the documents where real-time collaboration matters most. A pinned owner avoids that curve entirely, at the cost of needing a coordination service and accepting a brief read-only window during failover.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 215" role="img" aria-label="Conditional-append retry rate against a shared log climbs sharply with concurrent editors on one document, from about 4 percent at two editors to about 50 percent at twenty">
  <style>
    .bar{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.3;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.5}
    .t{font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif;fill:currentColor;opacity:.8}
    .b{font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif;fill:currentColor}
    text{dominant-baseline:middle;text-anchor:middle}
  </style>
  <text class="b" x="8" y="14" style="text-anchor:start">retry rate vs concurrent editors, one log</text>
  <rect class="bar" x="31" y="162" width="34" height="8"/>
  <rect class="bar" x="127" y="136" width="34" height="34"/>
  <rect class="bar" x="223" y="102" width="34" height="68"/>
  <rect class="bar" x="319" y="60" width="34" height="110"/>
  <text class="t" x="48" y="184">2 editors</text><text class="t" x="48" y="198">~4%</text>
  <text class="t" x="144" y="184">5 editors</text><text class="t" x="144" y="198">~15%</text>
  <text class="t" x="240" y="184">10 editors</text><text class="t" x="240" y="198">~30%</text>
  <text class="t" x="336" y="184">20 editors</text><text class="t" x="336" y="198">~50%</text>
</svg>
```

#### OT, or characters with identity
Stepping back from the mechanism itself, the whole approach of rewriting stale positions is one of two fundamentally different ways to make concurrent edits converge.

[Where the transform function lives, and what an alternative removes entirely](/diagram/collaborative-editor?focus=owner,transform,oplog,e3,e4)

**Bad: give every operation a position and rewrite positions as they go stale, with no central place doing the rewriting.** Without a single agreed authority, two clients rewriting the same operation independently can reach different, both locally reasonable, conclusions about where it now belongs, which is the exact multi-site correctness problem this design avoids by having only one transform site.

**Good: operational transformation with one server as the sole transform site, which is what this design builds.** No per-character bookkeeping, the stored document stays exactly the size of its text, and the difficult algorithm is concentrated in one function running in one process. The cost is that the whole approach depends on there always being a server on the edit path, and on that server always being the single owner.

**Great, for a different set of constraints: give every character a permanent identity instead of a position, so nothing ever needs rewriting.** A sequence CRDT expresses an insert as "between these two identities" rather than "at this offset". Merging two histories that diverged offline for days becomes a union operation with no authority required at all, because nothing refers to a position that could have moved.

Worked example: this design already needs a server on every operation regardless, for authorisation checks, durable append, and presence fan-out, so operational transformation costs nothing extra architecturally and keeps the stored document at exactly the size of its text. A product with no server on the edit path at all, or one built to tolerate offline gaps measured in days rather than minutes, would pay a real cost adopting operational transformation's single-owner requirement, and a sequence CRDT, despite its per-character bookkeeping, would be the more honest fit for that different set of constraints.

#### Where it breaks
| Layer | Failure | How the design handles it |
|---|---|---|
| Hot document | Fan-out from one owner grows as roughly the square of concurrent editors | Cap active editors and downgrade beyond it to suggestion or view mode, rather than sharding the document into a second transform site |
| Op log growth | A long-lived document accumulates millions of raw operations, slowing loads | Snapshot periodically so opening a document costs one snapshot fetch plus a short tail, independent of total history depth |
| Server crash mid-broadcast | Some clients received the newest operation, others did not | The operation was already durable before broadcast, so the new owner replays from each client's last known revision on reconnect |
| Transform correctness | A bug or a doubly-applied operation silently diverges one client | A periodic document hash lets an affected client detect the mismatch and force a clean reload rather than drift undetected |
| Comment anchors | The text a comment is anchored to is deleted by a concurrent edit | Anchors are resolved by range plus a text fingerprint, and an unresolvable anchor is surfaced explicitly rather than silently dropped or misattached |
| Authorisation | Access is revoked while a session is still open | Authorisation is re-checked on every operation, not only at connection time, so a revoked session cannot keep writing indefinitely |
| Presence channel | A buggy or hostile client floods cursor updates | Presence frames are throttled and excess dropped at the socket edge, before they ever reach the document's owning process |

#### What this design does not solve
**Convergence is not intention preservation, and no mechanism here closes that gap.** Two people rewriting the same sentence at the same time will converge on an interleaving of both rewrites that reads as neither, because every convergence guarantee here promises that everyone ends up looking at the same document, never that the document says what anyone meant. The available mitigation is a heuristic, nudging concurrent edits to the same region into a reviewable suggestion mode, which is a product patch on a problem no merge algorithm defines itself to solve.

**A single owner per document is a scaling wall this design has no plan to remove.** The entire correctness argument depends on exactly one process transforming every operation, and that forbids the two moves that would naturally be reached for under load: sharding a busy document across several owners, or giving a distant region its own local owner so far-away editors are not paying a full round trip on every keystroke. Editors far from a document's home region simply absorb that latency today, because the alternative requires either a fundamentally different convergence mechanism or a correctness property this design's transform function does not have.

**A long offline gap produces a merge result nobody can meaningfully review.** The compute cost of rebasing hours of divergent work is trivial, but the output is expressed as character-level operations, so the only preview available is a raw before-and-after of the merged text rather than a description of what actually changed structurally. Users are asked to accept or reject something they cannot really evaluate, and the honest long-term answer, treating a long offline gap as an explicit branch to merge deliberately, has not been built because the common case is short enough that the gap rarely matters in practice.

#### Final design
Read it back through the numbers. A single owner saturating near 1,000 concurrent typists is why the product caps active editors well below that machine limit rather than trying to push the ceiling higher, since the ceiling itself is a correctness boundary, not merely a performance one. The ~45ms of slack inside a 200ms budget is why the durable append is the one part of the pipeline worth optimising, everything else being close to physical limits already. Snapshotting turning 800,000 operations into one fetch is what keeps document open time independent of history depth. A two-minute offline gap costing microseconds of compute but a real readability problem is the reminder that this design's hardest failure is never computational. And conditional-append retries climbing to roughly 50% at twenty concurrent editors is exactly why ordering is pinned to one process rather than contested across many, on precisely the documents where collaboration is happening.

[The whole design, from a keystroke through convergence to history](/diagram/collaborative-editor?focus=client,socket-edge,owner,transform,broadcast,oplog,lease,presence,snapshotter,snapshots,history,offline)

> **The numbers to remember.** ~1,000 concurrent typists saturates a single owner · ~45ms of slack inside a 200ms budget · snapshotting bounds a document open to one fetch regardless of history depth · a two-minute offline gap is a readability problem, not a performance one · conditional-append retries reach ~50% at twenty concurrent editors.

#### Check your understanding
**Why does a remote operation have to be transformed against the client's own pending buffer, and the buffer transformed against it, rather than just applying the remote operation as received?** The screen reflects server state plus whatever the client has typed but not yet had acknowledged, so applying a remote operation transformed only against server state ignores the user's own unacknowledged work. Transforming in both directions keeps what appears on screen correct immediately, and keeps the buffer itself consistent with what the server will eventually see, so the two premises never silently diverge.

**Why must an operation be durably logged before it is broadcast, never the reverse?** A broadcast cannot be undone once other clients have applied it, while a missing acknowledgement can simply be retried. Logging first means the worst case of a crash is an operation nobody has been told about yet, safely recoverable from the log; broadcasting first means the worst case is an edit visible on other screens that exists nowhere durable and cannot be reconstructed.

**Why does this design require exactly one process to transform every operation for a given document?** The weaker convergence property this design relies on only holds between two participants and one transform site; correctness across three or more places where transforms happen requires a substantially stronger property that no practical implementation here satisfies. Sharding a document or giving a second region its own owner would each introduce a second transform site and reopen a correctness gap with no known fix at this scale.

**How does the system detect that a client has silently diverged from everyone else, given that the transform is assumed correct?** The owner periodically broadcasts a hash of its own document at a given revision. Any client sitting exactly at that revision with no unacknowledged operations pending can compare hashes with the server's; a mismatch has no incremental repair; the only correct response is discarding that client's state and reloading from the latest snapshot.

**Why is ordering pinned to a single leased process instead of resolved by a conditional append to a shared log?** Ordering inside one process is a plain memory write costing nanoseconds, while a conditional append that loses its race has to retry, and that retry rate grows sharply with concurrent writers on the same document, reaching roughly half of all attempts at this design's own p99 of twenty simultaneous editors. That retry cost lands hardest exactly on the busiest, most actively collaborative documents, which is precisely where a real-time editing product can least afford it.
### 38. Design Tinder (Dating / Match)
#### Understanding the problem
A dating app shows each user a stream of nearby candidates, records a swipe on every one, and opens a chat only when two people swipe right on each other. It looks like a recommendation feed with a geo filter attached, and treating it that way is the mistake the whole design exists to avoid.

Two properties make this fundamentally an inventory problem rather than a ranking one.

First, a candidate seen once is gone. Other ranked feeds can show the same item twice with no cost; here a swipe permanently spends a candidate, the pool is bounded by geography, and it shrinks every single day a user keeps swiping in one place. Ranking quality does not matter if the pool it draws from has already run out.

Second, nothing happens until both sides agree, and interest that is not reciprocated must never be visible to its target. The product's atom is mutual agreement, not a single user's preference, and the privacy rule protecting unreciprocated interest is not a separate feature bolted on afterward, it is the same mechanism that decides whether a match exists at all.

> **What this is not.** It looks like a proximity service: a radius query, a ranked list, a cache in front of it. A proximity service's answer is shared, so everyone standing in the same place searching for coffee gets the same list, a short cache absorbs most traffic, and a popular result being popular is a pure win, since the restaurant does not mind being returned a million times. Here geo is only the first of four narrowing stages, nothing caches, because the exclusion set, the preference predicate and the ranker are all specific to one person and change the moment that person swipes, and a person, unlike a restaurant, does mind being shown to a million people they will never meet. A design that stops at a geohash scheme and a distance refinement has answered the smaller question.

#### Requirements and the numbers
**Functional.** Profile, swipe left or right, match on mutual right, chat after a match, preference filters, ranked recommendations.

**Non-functional.** Feed p99 under 300ms. Reciprocity never lost. Unreciprocated interest never observable. Thin markets stay usable.

The whole design is decided by five numbers, so derive them before drawing anything.

**How much does the candidate pool shrink at each stage of the funnel?** A geo query in a dense city returns roughly **10,000 candidates**. Preference filters trim that to roughly **3,000**. Excluding everyone already swiped leaves roughly **1,500**, and only then does ranking run, inside a 300ms budget of which the ranker itself takes **100 to 150ms**.

**How exposed does a genuinely popular profile actually get?** A metro of 500,000 active users emits roughly 16 million impressions a day across 500,000 profiles, so the **mean profile is shown about 32 times a day**. A hard cap set at 50,000 impressions/day is roughly **1,500 times that mean**, which makes it a circuit breaker for one database partition, not a fairness mechanism.

**How long does a candidate pool actually last?** A dense metro's roughly 10,000 candidates, consumed at 32 swipes a day, gives a runway of about **10 months**, comfortably refilled by new arrivals. A small town's roughly 1,500 filtered candidates, at the same swipe rate, gives a runway of only about **7 weeks**.

**What does scoring every candidate against every other candidate actually cost?** A joint model run once per pair, at 1,500 candidates and roughly 2,800 feed requests a second at peak, is **~4.2 million model invocations a second**, not a system anyone builds. A factorised model computing one embedding per candidate offline needs only one user-side pass plus 1,500 dot products per request, on the order of **microseconds**.

**How concentrated does write traffic get on one popular profile?** Every right-swipe on a given profile writes a row keyed by that profile's id in the reverse index, so a viral profile can turn **one row into a target of thousands of writes a second**, while the primary swipe log, partitioned by the swiper instead, stays perfectly balanced throughout.

> **The numbers to carry.** Funnel narrows 10k to 3k to 1.5k to 20, inside a 300ms budget · a 50,000/day cap is ~1,500x the mean profile's exposure · pool runway ranges from ~10 months in a dense metro to ~7 weeks in a thin market · a joint ranker costs ~4.2M invocations/s against microseconds for a factorised one · one popular profile can drive thousands of reverse-index writes/s.

#### Two paths: the feed and the swipe
It helps to say plainly that this design is really two systems joined only by a user id, because they have almost opposite cost profiles. One path shows candidates and is expensive, approximate, and never authoritative about anything. The other records a decision and is cheap, exact, and the only place the product's one hard guarantee actually lives.

The entities are:

- **Candidate**: a user id surviving every stage of the funnel for a given viewer, never a stored object of its own.
- **Swipe**: `(swiper_id, target_id, direction, timestamp)`, written once and never observed by its target unless it becomes a match.
- **Match**: created only on a reciprocal right-swipe, keyed on the canonical ordered pair so two simultaneous swipes converge on one row.
- **Exposure budget**: a per-profile daily impression count that decays a profile's ranking score once it passes a market-relative threshold.

The API mirrors the split cleanly:

```
GET  /feed             → [{user_id, photos[], bio, distance_band, ...}]
POST /swipe            body: { target_id, direction }    → { matched: bool, match_id? }
GET  /matches          → list
```

#### High-level design
Follow the numbered arrows. The read path narrows and ranks; the write path does one cheap, exact lookup and a state change.

[The hot path from a feed request through a swipe to a possible match](/diagram/tinder?focus=client,feed,geo,bloom,ranker,embeddings,exposure,swipe-svc,swipes,reverse,match-svc,matches,e1,e2,e3,e4,e6,e7,e8,e9,e10,e13,e14,e15)

1. The **Client** requests a page from the **Feed Service** carrying its last known coordinates.
2. **Feed Service** queries the **Geo + attribute index** for everyone within radius.
3. **Feed Service** checks the **Exclusion filter** to drop everyone already swiped.
4. **Feed Service** hands the survivors to the **Two-tower ranker**, scored against **Candidate embeddings**.
5. **Exposure + diversify** applies a decaying multiplier and returns the top twenty to the **Client**.
6. The **Client** swipes; **Swipe Service** appends the swipe to the **Swipes table** and reads the **Reverse index** to check reciprocity.
7. On a reciprocal hit, **Swipe Service** hands off to **Match Service**, which inserts into the **Matches table** on the canonical pair and notifies both clients.

> **Why the flow is shaped this way.** Recommendation and matching are related but not the same problem, and they have opposite cost profiles. Showing good candidates is expensive and approximate; creating a match is cheap and must be exact, because it is the only irreversible thing the system does and the only one carrying a privacy guarantee. Keeping them as two separate paths means a ranker outage degrades the product without ever threatening that guarantee.

#### Exclusion before ranking, never after
The order the four funnel stages run in looks like an implementation detail and is actually the choice that keeps the whole design affordable as any one user's history grows.

[Exclusion narrowing the pool before the expensive stage ever sees it](/diagram/tinder?focus=feed,bloom,ranker,e3,e4)

**Bad: rank the full preference-filtered pool, then filter out already-swiped candidates afterward.** Looks equivalent, since the same candidates end up excluded either way. It forces over-fetching by the reciprocal of whatever fraction of the pool remains unswiped, and that fraction is not constant, it shrinks every day for a user who keeps swiping in one place.

**Good: rank a generously over-fetched pool to absorb the exclusion loss.** Works while the unswiped fraction is large, and it degrades exactly as a user becomes more engaged: someone 80% through their local market needs roughly 100 ranked results to yield 20 fresh ones, and someone at 95% needs roughly 400, so the expensive stage gets slower precisely for the most active users.

**Great: exclude first, rank only what survives.** Putting exclusion ahead of the model makes the model's cost independent of how depleted any given user's pool is, and it turns depletion into a single observable number, the cardinality surviving the exclusion stage, rather than a hidden multiplier buried inside an over-fetch factor.

Worked example: a new user with almost no swipe history and a three-year power user with tens of thousands of swipes both hit the ranker with the same fixed cardinality, roughly 1,500 candidates, because exclusion has already done its work before ranking starts. Under rank-then-exclude, the power user's request would need to fetch and score a far larger initial pool just to yield the same 20 usable results, silently making the most engaged users the most expensive ones to serve, exactly backwards from what a healthy system wants.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="-126 -6 489 203" role="img" aria-label="The funnel narrows from 10,000 candidates after geo to 3,000 after preferences to 1,500 after exclusion; only then does the expensive ranker run, over a fixed cardinality regardless of how depleted the user's pool is">
  <style>
    .bar{fill:currentColor;fill-opacity:.14;stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.5;stroke-width:1.5}
    .rank{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.32;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.5}
    .t{font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif;fill:currentColor;opacity:.8}
    .b{font:600 12px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif;fill:currentColor}
    text{text-anchor:middle}
  </style>
  <text class="b" x="8" y="14" text-anchor="start" style="text-anchor:start">funnel narrows before the ranker ever runs</text>
  <rect class="bar" x="8" y="30" width="70" height="140"/>
  <rect class="bar" x="100" y="128" width="70" height="42"/>
  <rect class="bar" x="192" y="149" width="70" height="21"/>
  <rect class="rank" x="284" y="149" width="70" height="21"/>
  <text class="t" x="43" y="186">geo: 10,000</text>
  <text class="t" x="135" y="186">prefs: 3,000</text>
  <text class="t" x="227" y="186">exclude: 1,500</text>
  <text class="t" x="319" y="186">ranker: 1,500</text>
</svg>
```

#### Two towers, not one joint model
Once the pool is down to roughly 1,500 candidates, scoring them still cannot be done the way a naive recommender would do it.

[The ranker computing one user embedding and 1,500 dot products, never a joint pass per pair](/diagram/tinder?focus=ranker,embeddings,e5,e6)

**Bad: score every candidate with a single joint network taking both the user and the candidate as input.** Gives the model the most expressive possible view of the pair, since every interaction between a user feature and a candidate feature is available to it. At 1,500 candidates per page and roughly 2,800 pages a second at peak, that is about 4.2 million model invocations a second, an infeasible amount of compute for what is ultimately a ranking pass.

**Good: score a small, cheaply pre-filtered shortlist with the joint network, skipping the rest.** Reduces the invocation count sharply, and choosing which candidates make the shortlist is itself a ranking problem, so this only relocates the original difficulty rather than resolving it.

**Great: factorise into two towers, one computed offline per candidate and one computed once per request.** A candidate tower produces a fixed-size embedding for every profile ahead of time, entirely offline. At request time, one pass through a user tower produces the current user's embedding, and scoring every candidate is a dot product against that single vector, cheap enough to run over the full 1,500 survivors on every request.

Worked example: the two-tower approach turns 4.2 million infeasible joint-network calls a second into roughly 1,500 dot products per request, each a handful of multiply-accumulates over a 128-dimensional vector, comfortably inside the ranker's share of a 300ms budget. The cost is expressivity: every interaction between a user feature and a candidate feature has to squeeze through a single inner product, which is why a design that needs more nuance reranks only the top 50 survivors with a joint model afterward, an expensive but entirely feasible 140,000 invocations a second rather than an impossible 4.2 million.

#### The reciprocity check is the privacy rule
Deciding whether two swipes constitute a match looks like an ordinary read-then-write, and the specific way it is built is what keeps unreciprocated interest genuinely invisible.

[One row read deciding both whether a match exists and what its target ever learns](/diagram/tinder?focus=swipe-svc,reverse,match-svc,matches,e10,e13,e14)

**Bad: notify a user whenever someone swipes right on them, then let them decide whether to swipe back.** Technically simpler and completely wrong for this product, because it exposes every one-sided interest to its target, turning a private signal into a public one and destroying the exact guarantee the product exists to make.

**Good: check for a match only, and store the check result somewhere the target could theoretically query.** An improvement in principle, and it leaves an exploitable seam: any surface, a support tool, an internal dashboard, a debugging endpoint, that lets someone read raw swipe rows for a target id defeats the privacy rule regardless of what the main product surface shows.

**Great: the only thing a right-swipe writes that is ever visible to its target is a match, created by an idempotent insert on the canonical ordered pair.** Recording a swipe writes one row, partitioned by the swiper for balanced write throughput; deciding whether that swipe became a match reads the reverse index by target id, and only a reciprocal hit produces anything either user can see. The privacy rule and the match rule collapse into a single mechanism rather than needing separate enforcement.

Worked example: two users swipe right on each other within milliseconds of each other, from different devices, hitting different servers. Each write independently checks the reverse index and finds a reciprocal hit, so both attempt to insert a match row keyed on `(min(a, b), max(a, b))`, the identical key regardless of which side wrote first. The first insert succeeds; the second is a no-op against the same row, so exactly one match exists and both users are notified exactly once, with neither ever having been shown that the other swiped first.

#### A hot profile turns one row into a bottleneck
A single very popular profile breaks the balanced-write story the swipe log otherwise enjoys, and the fix has to be narrow enough not to punish every other profile for one outlier's popularity.

[The reverse index, balanced everywhere except under one target](/diagram/tinder?focus=reverse,swipe-svc,e10)

**Bad: leave the reverse index as one row per target id, uniformly, regardless of popularity.** Correct and simple for the overwhelming majority of profiles, whose write rate is trivial. A viral profile receiving thousands of right-swipes a second turns its single row into a write hotspot capable of saturating a partition, while every other profile's row sits nowhere near that load.

**Good: sub-shard every target's reverse-index entry uniformly, regardless of popularity.** Removes the hotspot risk everywhere, and it pays the cost of extra reads on every single reciprocity check, the overwhelming majority of which never needed it, for a problem that only a small number of profiles actually have.

**Great: sub-shard only the targets that trip a hot-key threshold, on `(target_id, hash(swiper_id) % N)`.** The rare popular profile's writes fan out across N partitions instead of landing on one; its reciprocity check becomes N reads instead of one, applied only where the threshold is actually crossed, leaving the ordinary case exactly as cheap as it was.

Worked example: a profile that suddenly receives tens of thousands of right-swipes in an hour would otherwise concentrate every one of those writes on a single reverse-index row, a bottleneck with no relation to the swiper-partitioned primary log, which stays perfectly balanced throughout because it is keyed on the other side of each swipe. Once that profile trips the hot-key threshold, its writes spread across N sub-shards and its reciprocity checks become N reads instead of one, at the cost of slightly more read work only for the handful of profiles actually popular enough to need it.

#### The exposure cap is not the fairness mechanism
It is tempting to treat a single daily impression cap as the answer to popularity imbalance, and the arithmetic behind it says otherwise.

[Where the exposure control actually attaches, and at what threshold](/diagram/tinder?focus=ranker,exposure,e6,e7)

**Bad: set one hard daily impression cap and treat it as the fairness mechanism.** Sounds like it directly addresses popularity concentration, and the arithmetic reveals it is set far too high to touch ordinary fairness at all: a cap around 50,000 impressions a day sits roughly 1,500 times above the mean profile's actual daily exposure, so it only ever engages for the small number of profiles extreme enough to threaten a database partition.

**Good: lower the cap closer to the mean, applied as a hard cutoff.** Would genuinely engage more often, and a hard cutoff in a pool that has already been narrowed to roughly 1,500 candidates is dangerous: removing even a modest number of over-exposed profiles from a small pool can empty large parts of the feed for the exact users most likely to see those profiles.

**Great: keep the hard cap as a circuit breaker for extreme cases, and add a separate, smoothly decaying multiplier that engages far earlier, in the ranking stage rather than at retrieval.** A profile's score decays once its impressions cross roughly ten times the local mean, rather than being cut off outright, so exposure redistributes gradually rather than snapping a popular profile in or out of every feed.

Worked example: in a metro where the mean profile is shown roughly 32 times a day, a decaying multiplier beginning around 320 impressions a day, ten times that mean, gently reduces an increasingly popular profile's future ranking score well before it ever approaches the 50,000-impression circuit breaker. Applying the decay at the scoring stage rather than by removing budget-exhausted profiles from the candidate set entirely is what keeps a small pool from suddenly losing a chunk of its candidates the moment a popular profile crosses the threshold.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 233" role="img" aria-label="Mean profile exposure is about 32 impressions a day; the fairness multiplier begins decaying around 320, ten times the mean; the hard cap sits at 50,000, about 1,500 times the mean, and exists only to protect a database partition">
  <style>
    .mean{fill:currentColor;fill-opacity:.3;stroke:currentColor;stroke-width:1.5}
    .decay{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.32;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.5}
    .cap{fill:none;stroke:currentColor;stroke-width:1.5;stroke-dasharray:4 3}
    .t{font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif;fill:currentColor;opacity:.8}
    text{text-anchor:middle}
  </style>
  <text class="t" x="8" y="14" style="text-anchor:start">mean, decay start, and the hard cap</text>
  <rect class="mean" x="30" y="162" width="14" height="8"/>
  <rect class="decay" x="170" y="120" width="14" height="50"/>
  <rect class="cap" x="330" y="30" width="14" height="140"/>
  <text class="t" x="37" y="184">mean</text><text class="t" x="37" y="198">~32/day</text>
  <text class="t" x="177" y="184">decay starts</text><text class="t" x="177" y="198">~320/day (10x)</text>
  <text class="t" x="337" y="184">hard cap</text><text class="t" x="337" y="198">50,000/day</text>
  <text class="t" x="8" y="216" style="text-anchor:start">cap protects a partition; decay redistributes attention</text>
</svg>
```

#### Build the list live, or precompute it
Whether the whole funnel runs at request time or is assembled ahead of time in a batch job is a decision about how fast the defining predicate goes stale, more than one about compute cost.

[The funnel running fresh on every request rather than being read from a precomputed deck](/diagram/tinder?focus=feed,geo,ranker,e2,e4)

**Bad: precompute a ranked deck for every user overnight, uniformly, and read from it during the day.** The read path becomes a single lookup and the ranking model can be arbitrarily expensive since nothing waits on it live, a genuine quality win. The deck is anchored to wherever the user was when it was built, and location is exactly the predicate most likely to have changed by the time it is actually used.

**Good: precompute the deck, and repair it when location drifts too far from the origin it was built against.** Handles the common case reasonably, and it depends on location drift being rare enough to treat as an exception; measured on real mobile dating traffic, a large fraction of sessions start well outside the radius the previous session anchored on, closer to a third than to the small single-digit percentage that would make repair-by-exception workable.

**Great: run the full funnel at request time, for this product's traffic shape.** Costs a model pass inside the user's own latency budget, which is exactly why the funnel narrows to roughly 1,500 candidates before the model ever runs. In exchange, the location predicate, and every other predicate, is always evaluated against the truth at the moment of the request rather than against a snapshot from hours earlier.

Worked example: precomputing decks is actually somewhat cheaper on raw compute, since a nightly batch scores each candidate once rather than the online funnel scoring fresh every session, roughly a 40% saving by one estimate. That saving is irrelevant here, because a deck whose entire premise is a location that turns out stale by the time it is opened cannot be repaired, only rebuilt, at which point the batch design has quietly become an online one for the sessions that matter most.

#### Where it breaks
| Layer | Failure | How the design handles it |
|---|---|---|
| Hot target | A viral profile turns one reverse-index row into a write hotspot | Sub-shard on `(target_id, hash(swiper_id) % N)` for targets that trip a threshold; queue the reciprocity check under backpressure rather than dropping it |
| Match creation | Two simultaneous reciprocal swipes race to create a match | An idempotent insert keyed on the canonical ordered pair collapses both attempts to one row; both users are notified exactly once |
| Exclusion cache | A false positive drops a valid candidate at feed time | Tuned to roughly 1% loss out of ~1,500 candidates, imperceptible in the feed; an exact check runs at swipe-write time where a false positive would otherwise mask a duplicate |
| Geo skew | A fixed radius floods a dense city and empties a rural feed | Radius expands progressively until enough candidates are found; in sparse regions other filters relax before radius does |
| Fake and bot accounts | Commercially motivated fake profiles enter the pool | Layered defence cheapest first: verification at signup, a vision classifier on photos, behavioural anomaly detection, and shadow-banning confirmed-bad accounts |
| Stale embeddings | An overnight-only refresh misses same-day profile edits | Candidate embeddings re-embed incrementally on profile-edit events through a streaming pipeline |
| Thin markets | A small town's pool collapses toward everyone having seen everyone | Reserved exploration slots and progressive filter widening, tracked as an explicit SLO on candidates remaining per cohort |

#### What this design does not solve
**Distance bucketing raises the cost of trilateration and does not prevent it.** Rounding a displayed distance still leaks a band, and an attacker running several accounts with scriptable locations can narrow a target's position to the intersection of several such bands. Every genuine fix costs real product value: coarser bands destroy the proximity affordance that draws people to the app, per-viewer jitter is defeated by an attacker patient enough to average repeated observations, and rate-limiting location changes breaks legitimate travellers. Hysteresis on the displayed band and flagging accounts that repeatedly relocate around a fixed point raise the cost of an attack from minutes to days, which is a real improvement and still not a guarantee against a determined, patient adversary.

**The exposure budget and paid boosts are in direct tension, and the compromise satisfies neither fully.** A paid boost gives a profile a large temporary ranking multiplier; the exposure budget exists specifically to restrain multipliers on over-exposed profiles, and those two mechanisms collide precisely on the profiles most likely to purchase a boost, because popularity and paying customers overlap heavily. Exempting boosted profiles from the budget makes the fairness guarantee apply only to people who do not pay; applying the budget in full to a paid feature risks not delivering what was sold. The workaround, having a boost reallocate a profile's existing daily budget toward better-matched viewers rather than adding new impressions, is defensible and is a genuinely smaller product promise than the feature's marketing implies.

**Thin-market exhaustion cannot be reliably diagnosed, let alone fixed, by anything built here.** Widening the radius, relaxing filters and reserving exploration slots buy weeks against a pool that runs out in weeks; none of them creates new people to show. Worse, a user who has genuinely exhausted their market and one whose preferences are simply too narrow look identical from the one metric available, candidates remaining, though they need opposite responses. Telling the two apart needs a counterfactual estimate that cannot be validated, since the system never observes what a user would have done with candidates it chose not to show them.

#### Final design
Read it back through the numbers. The funnel narrowing from 10,000 to 3,000 to 1,500 candidates before ranking ever runs is what keeps the ranker's cost fixed regardless of how depleted any one user's pool has become, which is the property that makes the whole design affordable at scale. A 50,000-impression cap sitting some 1,500 times above the mean profile's actual exposure is why it functions as a circuit breaker rather than the fairness mechanism, which instead lives in a decaying multiplier engaging around ten times the mean. Pool runway swinging from roughly 10 months in a dense metro to roughly 7 weeks in a thin market is why thin-market health is tracked as a first-class SLO rather than an edge case. A joint ranker's 4.2 million infeasible invocations a second against a factorised model's microseconds is why candidates are scored through two towers and a dot product rather than one network per pair. And a hot profile's ability to concentrate thousands of writes a second on one reverse-index row is why that index is sub-sharded selectively rather than uniformly.

[The whole design, from a feed request to a chat unlocking](/diagram/tinder?focus=client,feed,ranker,exposure,geo,embeddings,bloom,swipe-svc,swipes,reverse,match-svc,matches)

> **The numbers to remember.** Funnel narrows 10k to 3k to 1.5k to 20 · a 50k/day cap is ~1,500x the mean profile's exposure · pool runway from ~10 months down to ~7 weeks in a thin market · a joint ranker costs ~4.2M invocations/s against microseconds for two towers · one hot profile can drive thousands of reverse-index writes/s.

#### Check your understanding
**Why must exclusion run before ranking rather than after?** The fraction of a pool a user has already swiped grows every day they keep swiping in one place, so filtering after ranking would force over-fetching by a factor that changes per user and gets worse the more engaged someone is. Filtering first keeps the ranker's workload at a fixed size regardless of how depleted a user's pool has become, and turns depletion into one observable number instead of a hidden multiplier.

**Why does the ranker compute two separate embeddings and a dot product instead of one joint model per candidate pair?** A joint model run once per pair, at this design's request volume, would need on the order of 4.2 million invocations a second, an infeasible amount of compute. Factorising into a candidate embedding computed offline and a user embedding computed once per request turns scoring 1,500 survivors into 1,500 cheap dot products, at the cost of expressivity that a top-tier rerank can partially buy back where it matters.

**Why is a hard daily impression cap not the mechanism that actually keeps one popular profile from dominating every feed in a city?** The mean profile in a typical metro is shown only a few dozen times a day, so a cap set high enough to protect a database partition sits over a thousand times above that mean and rarely engages at all. The mechanism that actually redistributes attention is a smoothly decaying ranking multiplier that begins around ten times the local mean, well below the hard cap, applied at scoring time rather than by removing candidates outright.

**Two users swipe right on each other at nearly the same instant, from different servers. How does exactly one match get created?** Both writes independently detect a reciprocal hit and attempt to insert a match row keyed on the same canonical ordered pair of user ids, regardless of which side technically wrote first. The first insert succeeds; the second is a no-op against the identical key, so exactly one match row exists and both users receive exactly one notification.

**Why does this design run the full candidate funnel on every request instead of precomputing a ranked deck overnight for each user?** A precomputed deck is anchored to wherever a user was located when it was built, and on real dating traffic a large share of sessions begin well outside that original radius, so the deck's central premise, location, is often stale by the time it is opened. Rebuilding a deck live for those sessions erases most of the batch approach's advantage, so running the funnel fresh against current location on every request is the option that actually matches how the traffic behaves.
### 39. Design GitHub (Source Code Hosting)
#### Understanding the problem
A source code hosting platform hosts tens of millions of git repositories with a web UI, pull requests, issues, code search and CI integration. The instinct is to treat this as a large file-storage problem, and that instinct is the trap the whole design exists to avoid.

Two things make the unit being stored different from an ordinary payload.

First, a repository is not a file or an object, it is already a content-addressed database: a Merkle DAG of objects plus a small mutable set of refs pointing into it. A push is a transaction over those refs, with its own consistency rules that already exist before any design decision gets made.

Second, a repository cannot be split. Every other storage system in this space gets to spread load by dividing the unit of storage: an object store shards by key, a database shards by row. A git operation walks an arbitrary reachable subgraph and needs every object it touches present on the machine doing the walk, so a repository must live whole on machines that hold it, however popular or large it becomes.

> **What this is not.** It looks like an object store: content-addressed data, replication, durability at scale. An object store's unit of durability is a single object, and a read touches exactly one of them, so objects can be placed independently and reassembled on read, erasure-coded across zones, and scaled by adding capacity to one pool. Here durability is per repository, not per object: a repository missing even one object it can reach is corrupt, not merely one object short, so the whole repository has to be placed, replicated and failed over as one stateful unit. A design that reaches for the object-storage playbook here will be asked, within minutes, what happens when two people push to the same branch at the same moment, a question that playbook has no answer to.

#### Requirements and the numbers
**Functional.** Git push, pull and clone over HTTPS and SSH. Web UI. Pull requests, issues, reviews. Org and team management. Code search.

**Non-functional.** No repository data loss. Clone and push latency acceptable across four orders of magnitude of repository size. 99.99% availability at the fleet level.

The whole design is decided by five numbers, so derive them before drawing anything.

**How much does local disk actually matter for a git operation?** A diff, blame or ancestry walk on a busy repository can touch on the order of 50,000 random reads scattered through a packfile. Local NVMe at roughly 80 microseconds per read costs **~4 seconds** of I/O; a network filesystem at 500 microseconds to a millisecond costs **25 to 50 seconds** for the identical walk.

**How much does sharing history across forks actually save?** A project with roughly 10,000 forks, each 5GB, would cost **50TB** as independent copies. Sharing one object pool per fork network costs roughly 5GB plus a small amount of per-fork divergence, **~1,000x less**, and this is the single largest storage decision in the whole design.

**How much write traffic does the push path actually see?** Roughly 175 pushes/s on average, ~900/s at peak. This is small; the write path here is never throughput-bound, it is bound by the fact that every push must land on one specific machine, regardless of how much capacity the rest of the fleet has.

**What does a cross-datacentre quorum cost per push?** Roughly 1 to 3 milliseconds within a metro area, 30 milliseconds or more across a continent. That gap is why replicas are spread across a metro rather than the globe.

**When does building a search index actually pay for itself over grep?** An unscoped query against a roughly 50TB deduplicated corpus costs on the order of **50,000 core-seconds** run as a plain search; a single repository-scoped query over a warm checkout costs about **1 core-second**. The index only pays for itself above roughly 10,000 repositories in scope for a single query.

> **The numbers to carry.** Local NVMe is roughly 10x faster than a network filesystem on the exact access pattern git uses most · fork pooling saves ~1,000x storage on a heavily forked project · pushes run at only ~175/s average, bound by one machine per repository, not by throughput · a cross-DC quorum costs 1 to 3ms in-metro · an unscoped search costs ~50,000x a single repository-scoped one.

#### The repository as shard, and everything that hangs off it
It is worth saying plainly that once the repository is accepted as the unit of placement, almost every other decision in this design follows directly from that acceptance rather than needing its own justification.

The entities are:

- **Repository**: the shard itself, a bare git repository assigned to a fixed replica set of machines.
- **Object**: a piece of git's content-addressed graph, named by the hash of its own contents, immutable once written.
- **Ref**: a small, mutable pointer, such as `refs/heads/main`, into the object graph; the only thing a push actually changes.
- **Push**: a two-phase transaction, objects streamed first, then a single ref update as the commit point.

The API surface reflects the split between git's own protocol and everything built on top of it:

```
git protocol over HTTPS + SSH                  (upload-pack, receive-pack)
REST + GraphQL:
  GET  /repos/{owner}/{repo}
  POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{n}/merge   → 409 if head_sha moved
  GET  /search/code?q=...
```

#### High-level design
Follow the numbered arrows. Everything before the ref update is provisional and safe to abandon; everything after it is committed history, including its consequences.

[The hot path from a push to its asynchronous fan-out](/diagram/github?focus=client,git-proxy,primary,replicas,event-queue,e1,e4,e5,e7)

1. The **Git client + browser** sends a push to the **Git proxy fleet**.
2. **Git proxy fleet** resolves the owner and repository name to a repo id and forwards the git stream to the **Primary file server**.
3. **Primary file server** verifies and writes the incoming objects, then replicates the packfile to **Two replicas, other DCs**.
4. Only once a quorum of replicas has fsynced does **Primary file server** compare-and-swap the ref and acknowledge the client.
5. After the acknowledgement, **Primary file server** publishes to the **Push event queue**, which fans out asynchronously to CI, webhooks and search.

> **Why the flow is shaped this way.** The product surface looks unified, but the workloads underneath it are not: git storage is stateful and indivisible, metadata is small and transactional, search is a large derived index, and CI is untrusted compute. Keeping them separate means the hardest of the four, the stateful git layer, never has to accommodate the requirements of the other three, and a failure in search or CI can never stop a push from landing.

#### A repository is a database, not a payload
The single decision the rest of this design depends on is whether repositories live as stateful shards on local disk or float over a shared, interchangeable storage layer.

[Where a repository's data actually sits](/diagram/github?focus=primary,replicas,git-proxy,e4,e5)

**Bad: a shared distributed filesystem or object store under stateless, interchangeable git servers.** Any server can serve any repository, capacity is one pool, and a failure is a restart rather than a failover, which is a genuinely appealing operational story. It pays a latency tax on every object read, the single most common thing a git operation does, and that tax cannot be cached away, because a busy repository's working set does not fit in a shared cache tier.

**Good: stateful replica sets, but sized generously enough to hide the read pattern behind aggressive caching.** Reduces how often the latency gap actually bites, and it does not remove the gap itself; the difference between local NVMe and a network filesystem on a 50,000-random-read walk is roughly a factor of ten, and no amount of cache tuning changes what happens on a genuine cache miss against a large repository.

**Great: each repository assigned a fixed, small replica set of machines holding a real bare git repository on local disk, with a stateful routing table treated as first-class infrastructure.** This accepts placement, rebalancing and per-repository failover as real ongoing work, in exchange for git's access pattern, which is dominated by small random reads, running against a local page cache rather than a network hop on every single one.

Worked example: a diff, blame or merge on a large, busy repository can touch roughly 50,000 objects scattered through a packfile. On local NVMe that is about 4 seconds of I/O; on a network filesystem at 500 microseconds to a millisecond per read, the identical operation costs 25 to 50 seconds, a gap that stays roughly constant regardless of how much caching sits in front of it, because the working set of a genuinely busy repository does not fit in any shared cache tier that also has to serve everyone else's repositories.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 214" role="img" aria-label="50,000 random reads for one git operation cost about 4 seconds on local NVMe against 25 to 50 seconds on a network filesystem, a gap caching cannot close">
  <style>
    .fast{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.32;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.5}
    .slow{fill:currentColor;fill-opacity:.14;stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.5;stroke-width:1.5}
    .t{font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif;fill:currentColor;opacity:.8}
    .b{font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif;fill:currentColor}
    text{text-anchor:middle}
  </style>
  <text class="b" x="8" y="14" text-anchor="start" style="text-anchor:start">50,000 random reads, one busy-repo operation</text>
  <rect class="fast" x="40" y="140" width="60" height="20"/>
  <rect class="slow" x="180" y="40" width="60" height="120"/>
  <text class="t" x="70" y="176">local NVMe, ~4s</text>
  <text class="t" x="210" y="176">network FS, 25-50s</text>
  <text class="t" x="8" y="196" text-anchor="start" style="text-anchor:start">not closable by caching: working set exceeds any cache tier</text>
</svg>
```

#### Objects first, ref second
A push moves bytes and changes state, and the order those two things happen in decides whether a crash mid-push corrupts anything.

[Objects streamed before the one ref update that actually commits anything](/diagram/github?focus=primary,e4)

**Bad: update the ref as soon as any object has been received, streaming the rest afterward.** Makes the operation appear to complete sooner from the ref's perspective. If the connection drops partway through, the ref now points at a commit whose object graph is incomplete, so the repository is genuinely broken, not merely behind, and every future operation touching that history fails.

**Good: buffer the entire incoming packfile in memory before writing anything to disk, then update the ref.** Avoids partially writing objects to disk, and it does nothing to change what happens if the process crashes before the buffer is flushed, which loses the whole push rather than making a partial one safe.

**Great: write and verify every object first, and treat the ref update as the sole commit point.** Objects are written and hash-verified before any ref is touched. An object written but not yet referenced by anything is simply unreachable, and unreachable objects are garbage for the next collection cycle, not corruption. Nothing about the repository is visible or changed until the ref update itself succeeds.

Worked example: a client's connection drops midway through uploading a large packfile. Under this design, the repository is left exactly as valid as it was before the push started, with some now-unreachable objects sitting on disk waiting for garbage collection. The client's retry re-sends only the objects the negotiation determines are still missing, at near-zero additional byte cost, because everything already durably written is recognised and skipped rather than resent.

#### The ref update is a compare-and-swap
Two developers pushing to the same branch from the same starting point is an ordinary occurrence, and how the server resolves it decides whether it ever has to understand what either push actually contains.

[The ref update accepted or rejected based on what the client expected to find](/diagram/github?focus=primary,client,e4)

**Bad: apply every incoming ref update unconditionally, last write wins.** Simple, and it silently discards one developer's work whenever two pushes race, with no signal to either party that anything was lost.

**Good: lock the ref for the duration of each push, serialising all writers.** Prevents concurrent writers from ever racing, and it does so by making every push wait behind whichever one got there first, turning ordinary contention on a busy branch into a queue rather than a fast rejection the losing client can act on immediately.

**Great: accept a client-supplied expected previous value, and update only if the ref still holds it.** Every push carries the SHA the client believed the ref pointed to when it started. The server applies the update only if that is still true; otherwise it rejects the push outright, and the client is expected to fetch and reconcile before trying again.

Worked example: two developers both start from the same commit and push to `main` moments apart. The first push's compare-and-swap finds the ref exactly where it expected and succeeds. The second arrives with an `old_sha` the ref no longer holds, so the server rejects it as a non-fast-forward, the client sees the rejection immediately, and no merge decision or conflict resolution happens on the server at all, because that responsibility sits entirely with the client that lost the race.

#### Quorum before the CAS, not after
Durability and the ref update both have to happen on every push, and the order between them decides what a crash at the worst possible moment actually costs.

[Waiting for replicas to confirm before the ref ever moves](/diagram/github?focus=primary,replicas,e5)

**Bad: update the ref immediately, then replicate to other machines afterward.** Makes the client-visible commit point as fast as possible. If the primary dies before replication completes, a promoted replica can have a ref history the fleet disagrees about, with objects it cannot actually reach, because the thing that was supposed to make that ref meaningful never arrived.

**Good: replicate first, but ack the client as soon as any single replica confirms.** An improvement, and a single confirming replica is not enough to survive that replica's own subsequent failure without losing the durability the ack implied.

**Great: replicate to all replicas, wait for a majority to confirm durability, and only then perform the ref update.** If a crash happens before quorum is reached, the worst case is a set of unreachable objects on some subset of replicas, cleaned up by the next garbage collection, exactly the same safe failure mode as an ordinary dropped connection.

Worked example: a primary streams a packfile to two other replicas and dies immediately after two of the three, including itself, have durably written it but before it performs the ref update. Nothing user-visible has happened yet; the replacement primary, once elected, simply completes the sequence its predecessor was partway through, and the client's retry either finds the ref already where it wanted it, a safe no-op, or completes the push cleanly. Reversing the order, ref first and replication after, would instead leave a promoted replica with a ref pointing at history it may not fully hold, which is a much harder state to safely recover from.

#### A fork is not a copy
Millions of forks of the same popular project is the case that decides whether fork-heavy hosting is affordable at all.

[One shared history behind thousands of independent sets of refs](/diagram/github?focus=primary,object-pool,e6)

**Bad: give every fork its own complete, independent copy of the full object graph.** Simple to reason about and trivially isolated from every other fork. A popular project with thousands of forks multiplies its entire history by that many, turning a single 5GB repository into tens of terabytes of near-identical, mostly redundant storage.

**Good: deduplicate at the object level across all repositories globally, regardless of fork relationship.** Would recover most of the same saving. Doing it as a general-purpose, unbounded cross-repository deduplication scheme is a much larger and riskier system to build and reason about than deduplication scoped to a known, bounded relationship.

**Great: one shared object pool per fork network, mounted as a git alternate, with each fork owning only its own refs and whatever objects it has uniquely added.** A fork costs a new namespace of refs pointed into history it does not have to copy, plus storage only for the commits it actually adds beyond what the network already shares.

Worked example: a project with roughly 10,000 forks, each notionally a full 5GB repository, would cost roughly 50TB stored independently. Sharing one object pool across the whole fork network costs roughly 5GB for the shared history plus a small amount of storage per fork for its own unique commits, on the order of a thousandfold reduction, concentrated on precisely the largest and most-forked repositories where storage pressure is highest.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 180" role="img" aria-label="10,000 independent fork copies of a 5GB project cost 50TB; one shared object pool with per-fork refs costs about 5GB plus small per-fork divergence">
  <style>
    .acc{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.3;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.5}
    .dim{fill:currentColor;fill-opacity:.12;stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.5;stroke-width:1.5}
    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    .sub{fill:currentColor;opacity:.75;font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    text{dominant-baseline:middle}
  </style>
  <text class="lbl" x="8" y="14">bad: 10,000 independent copies</text>
  <rect class="dim" x="8" y="24" width="376" height="28" rx="5"/><text class="sub" x="196" y="38" text-anchor="middle">10,000 x 5GB = ~50TB</text>
  <text class="lbl" x="8" y="76">great: one shared pool</text>
  <rect class="acc" x="8" y="86" width="376" height="28" rx="5"/><text class="sub" x="196" y="100" text-anchor="middle">~5GB shared + per-fork divergence</text>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="134">each fork owns only its own refs + unique objects</text>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="150">shared history mounted once, as a git alternate</text>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="166">roughly 1,000x reduction on the most-forked repos</text>
</svg>
```

#### An index, or grep
Code search across millions of repositories looks like it obviously needs a dedicated index, and the arithmetic behind that assumption only holds above a specific scale.

[Search served from a purpose-built index rather than reading git repositories directly](/diagram/github?focus=search,event-queue,e13)

**Bad: build and maintain a global search index unconditionally, for every deployment regardless of scope.** Guarantees fast search at any scale, and it is genuinely wasteful for a small, self-hosted deployment scoped to one organisation's repositories, where the entire indexable corpus might fit comfortably in a warm checkout already sitting on disk.

**Good: index only the largest or most-queried repositories, falling back to a direct search for everything else.** Reduces index size and update cost somewhat, and it introduces an inconsistent experience, where search quality and latency depend on an internal threshold the user cannot see or reason about.

**Great: decide based on the actual product of corpus size and query rate, building a global index only where that product is large enough to matter.** A direct search against a single repository's warm checkout costs on the order of one CPU-second; an unscoped search against a large deduplicated corpus costs tens of thousands of CPU-seconds for a single query, a gap that only a purpose-built index can close.

Worked example: a repository-scoped search box, even inside a platform that maintains a global index for cross-repository search, correctly runs a direct search over that one repository's checkout rather than querying the index, because a single-repository query costs about one CPU-second either way and a direct search is never stale and needs no reindex after a push. The global index earns its cost, roughly 150 to 200TB and a continuous update pipeline, only for the genuinely cross-repository case, where an unindexed search would cost tens of thousands of times more per query.

#### Where it breaks
| Layer | Failure | How the design handles it |
|---|---|---|
| Hot repository | A megaproject's fetch and clone traffic saturates its primary | Additional read-only replicas absorb fetch load; the write side stays on one primary regardless, because that limit is structural, not a capacity shortfall |
| Very large repository | A tens-of-gigabyte clone is slow to transfer and enumerate | Partial clone defers blob download, sparse checkout limits what materialises, and multi-pack reachability bitmaps make enumeration near-constant time |
| CI fan-out | One push triggers thousands of workflow jobs, each cloning | Per-org concurrency caps, priority queues, and dedup on SHA so repeated triggers collapse into one run |
| Split-brain risk | A demoted primary comes back online and still believes it leads | A generation number fences it; a write stamped with a stale generation is rejected regardless of how convincing the demoted primary otherwise looks |
| Repack pressure | Many repositories repacking at once saturate one file server's disk | Concurrent repacks capped per server and prioritised by activity rather than run on a fixed schedule |
| Unauthenticated clone traffic | Anonymous, bandwidth-heavy clones are cheap to request and easy to abuse | Rate-limit buckets per IP and per authenticated user, with authentication required for expensive operations under load |
| Search index | A shard falls behind or serves from stale data | Rebuild a stale shard directly from the git store; degrade to an explicit "search unavailable" rather than silently return stale results |

#### What this design does not solve
**A shared fork network leaks objects across visibility boundaries, and every mitigation is partial.** Because a pool means an object pushed to any member is physically present for every member, git will serve any object by its raw hash whether or not a ref in that specific fork points at it, so a commit pushed to a private fork and later force-removed can still be fetched through the public parent by anyone who learns its hash. Partitioning pools by visibility class stops private objects from ever entering a public pool, and it does nothing for the public-to-public case, where a deleted commit remains fetchable by hash indefinitely. Full isolation is available, at the cost of the thousand-fold storage saving forking exists to provide.

**There is no transaction spanning the git store and the metadata database.** A merge writes a ref on a file server and a state change in a relational database as two separate operations with nothing making them atomic, so a crash between them can leave a branch that is merged with a pull request record that still says open. A force-push compounds this by moving a branch's head out from under an open review with no coordination at all. A background reconciler that treats git as the sole authority repairs metadata after the fact, which means the product's own UI is only eventually consistent with the repository, on a horizon of seconds to minutes.

**Fleet-level availability numbers hide outages that are entirely per-repository.** Because each repository's data lives on a specific, fixed set of three machines, that repository's actual availability is independent of the other tens of millions the platform hosts, so a headline 99.99% fleet figure can coexist with a specific customer being fully unable to reach their repository while two of its three replicas re-replicate a large working set. Re-replication itself competes for the same disk bandwidth the surviving replica needs to serve reads, so recovery and availability draw from the same limited resource during exactly the window that matters most.

#### Final design
Read it back through the numbers. Local NVMe's roughly tenfold latency advantage over a network filesystem on git's dominant access pattern, tens of thousands of small random reads per operation, is why repositories are placed as stateful shards on local disk rather than floated over shared storage. Fork pooling's roughly thousandfold storage saving on a heavily forked project is why a fork costs a namespace of refs rather than a copy of history. Pushes running at only a few hundred a second on average, bound by one machine per repository rather than by throughput, is why the write path's hard limit is structural rather than a capacity problem more hardware could solve. A cross-datacentre quorum's few-millisecond cost within a metro is why replicas spread across a metro rather than the globe. And search's roughly fifty-thousandfold cost gap between a scoped and an unscoped query is why a global index exists only where that gap is actually paid, not by default.

[The whole design, from a push through storage, metadata, search and CI](/diagram/github?focus=client,git-proxy,primary,replicas,diff-service,event-queue,ci,web-app,metadata,object-pool,search,webhooks)

> **The numbers to remember.** Local NVMe beats a network filesystem by roughly 10x on git's dominant read pattern · fork pooling saves ~1,000x storage on a heavily forked project · pushes run at only ~175/s average, bound by one machine per repository · a cross-DC quorum costs 1 to 3ms in-metro · an unscoped search costs roughly 50,000x a repository-scoped one.

#### Check your understanding
**Why can a git repository not be sharded the way an object store shards its keys?** A git operation walks an arbitrary reachable subgraph and needs every object it touches present on the machine performing the walk, so durability applies to the whole reachability closure rather than to any individual object. Spreading a repository's objects across the fleet would turn every clone or diff into a distributed graph traversal, which is exactly the cost an object store's per-key placement never has to pay.

**Why are objects written and verified before the ref is ever updated, rather than the other way around?** An object written but not yet pointed to by any ref is simply unreachable garbage, safely collected later, not corruption. Updating the ref first and streaming objects afterward would leave a ref pointing at an incomplete history if the push were interrupted, which is a genuinely broken repository rather than one that merely rejects a retry.

**How does the server resolve two developers pushing to the same branch at nearly the same time?** Each push carries the SHA the client expected the ref to hold. The server applies the update only if the ref still matches that expectation; the first push to arrive succeeds, and the second is rejected outright as a non-fast-forward, with all merge and conflict resolution left entirely to the client rather than attempted on the server.

**Why does replication have to complete before the ref update, rather than after it?** If the ref moved first and the primary failed before replication finished, a promoted replica could hold a ref pointing at history it does not fully have, a state with no safe automatic recovery. Requiring a quorum of replicas to confirm durability first means the worst case of any crash is a set of unreachable objects, cleaned up by ordinary garbage collection, never a ref pointing at something that does not exist.

**Why does forking a public repository into a private one cost a full copy of history, when public forks share storage for free?** A shared object pool makes every object physically present for every member of that pool, retrievable by anyone who learns its hash regardless of which fork's refs point to it. A private fork sharing a pool with its public parent would mean anything pushed to the private fork sits in storage the public parent can also serve, so visibility boundaries force a fork crossing them to be detached into fully independent storage, at the cost of the deduplication forking normally provides.
### 40. Design Spotify (Music Streaming + Recommendations)
#### Understanding the problem
A music streaming platform serves a catalogue of around 100 million tracks to hundreds of millions of listeners, decides what plays next, and pays rights holders for every qualifying stream. It looks like a smaller, simpler cousin of video streaming, and that resemblance hides the two facts that actually decide the design.

First, a track is tiny. A four-minute file at a normal bitrate is a few megabytes rather than a few gigabytes, so the entire popular catalogue fits comfortably at the edge. Delivery stops being a chunking and adaptive-bitrate problem and becomes a caching problem instead.

Second, people replay what they already love. The overwhelming majority of plays are of a track the listener has heard before, which inverts the recommender a normal ranked feed would need: what a listener has already consumed is not something to exclude, it is the single best predictor of what they want next.

A third fact sits underneath both: every qualifying play is money. Rights holders are paid a fractional split per stream, which means one path through this system has to behave like a ledger, provably correct, rather than like an ordinary analytics pipeline.

> **What this is not.** It looks like TikTok: embeddings, an approximate-nearest-neighbour index, cheap retrieval feeding an expensive ranker. The two systems diverge on one word, "again". TikTok never intentionally serves the same video twice, so its candidate set is the whole corpus and every impression is spent on something unproven, with roughly 100 million new videos a day each needing hundreds of impressions just to be measured, a genuine scarcity of inventory. Here the catalogue grows by tens of thousands of tracks a day, two orders of magnitude smaller, and the scarce resource is never inventory, it is the listener's tolerance for a song they did not ask for. TikTok's hardest question is how something with zero observations reaches anyone; this design's hardest question is how anything unfamiliar ever wins a slot against a track the listener already loves, when the familiar choice scores higher on every metric a two-week experiment can see.

#### Requirements and the numbers
**Functional.** Play, pause, skip, queue. Library and playlists. Search. Discovery surfaces. Offline download. Per-stream royalty accounting.

**Non-functional.** Under 300ms tap-to-first-audio at p99. Under one rebuffer per 10 minutes of play. Discovery surfaces present at 99.9% on Monday morning. Royalty ledger reproducible to the cent from the event log.

The whole design is decided by five numbers, so derive them before drawing anything.
