**How much of the catalogue actually fits at the edge?** The top 10 million tracks at two mainstream quality rungs is roughly **144TB**, comfortably one storage node, and covers roughly 90% of all plays. A four-minute track itself is only about **4.8MB** at a normal streaming bitrate.

**How much of listening is actually repeat?** First hears arrive at roughly 200 a month per active listener against roughly 1,050 monthly plays, which is **~19% first hear, ~81% repeat**. That single ratio is the reason this design differs fundamentally from a video feed.

**At what object size does whole-file delivery stop making sense?** A 4.8MB track on a 5Mbps connection finishes downloading in under 8 seconds, well inside the first few percent of playback. The threshold where speculative whole-object download stops paying off sits around **25MB**, well above any lossy music track and well below a video file.

**How does the retrieval index scale compare to a video feed's?** 100 million track vectors at a normal embedding size is roughly **100GB**, comfortably fitting an in-memory graph index. The equivalent index for a corpus like TikTok's, at roughly 10 billion vectors, is **~10TB**, which forces a fundamentally different, lossier indexing approach that this design never needs.

**How late can a legitimate royalty-bearing event legally arrive?** Offline licences run for **30 days**, so a play that happened on the 3rd of a month can legitimately be uploaded to the server on the 30th, a lateness window wide enough to decide the entire shape of the royalty pipeline.

> **The numbers to carry.** Top 10M tracks at two rungs fits one 144TB storage node · ~81% of plays are repeats · whole-object delivery holds up to roughly 25MB · a 100M-vector index fits comfortably in RAM against a 10TB index for a corpus two orders of magnitude larger · offline events can legitimately arrive up to 30 days late.

#### Three paths, one log: playback, recommendation, royalty
It helps to say plainly that this is three businesses sharing one front door, joined only by a single shared event log, because they have almost nothing else in common. One path moves audio bytes as cheaply as possible. One path decides what to play next. One path counts money and must never be wrong.

The entities are:

- **Track**: an immutable audio object encoded once at upload into several bitrate rungs, plus its metadata.
- **Play event**: a `start`, a `qualified` marker at the 30-second royalty threshold, and a terminal event, each stamped with the time it actually happened rather than when it arrived.
- **Discovery list**: a fixed, precomputed set of tracks written for a listener on a schedule, read as a single key lookup.
- **Royalty statement**: one row per rights holder per period, produced by a deterministic recomputation over the immutable archived events.

The API mirrors the three-way split directly:

```
GET  /track/{id}                  -> metadata + entitlement + per-rung edge URLs
GET  /track/{id}/audio?rung=160   -> whole object (range-able); HLS manifest above 25MB
GET  /discovery/{surface}         -> precomputed list, key read
POST /events                      body: [{ track_id, type, played_at, position_ms, ... }]
```

#### High-level design
Follow the numbered arrows. Fetching audio, deciding what plays next, and counting a stream for royalties are three separate concerns that only ever meet at the shared event log.

[The hot path from a play request to a delivered track](/diagram/spotify?focus=client,play-api,catalogue,edge,origin,events,e1,e2,e3,e4,e5,e6,e7)

1. The **Listener client** requests track metadata and entitlement from the **Play API**.
2. **Play API** reads **Catalogue + rights** for rung pointers and returns signed edge URLs.
3. The **Listener client** issues one GET against the **Edge audio cache** for the whole object at its chosen rung.
4. On a miss, **Edge audio cache** fills from **Audio origin**, once, and serves every subsequent listener from that fill.
5. As playback proceeds, the **Listener client** emits `start`, `qualified` and terminal events to the **Play-event log**.

> **Why the flow is shaped this way.** Roughly 20 seconds before a track ends, the client has already fetched the entire next track in the queue, so the gap between songs is zero and the following track's start never depends on the network. Splitting the design into three paths that only share the event log means playback may lose an occasional event with nobody noticing, while the royalty path treats the identical log as an immutable, fully auditable source of truth, and neither has to compromise for the other.

#### Whole objects, not chunks
The decision to fetch a track as one file rather than as adaptive segments looks like an implementation detail borrowed from video streaming, and the object sizes involved make it a different decision entirely.

[A track fetched whole, never adapted mid-play](/diagram/spotify?focus=client,edge,origin,e4,e5,e6)

**Bad: chunked adaptive streaming throughout, exactly as video does it.** Segmenting into short chunks with mid-stream bitrate switching handles arbitrarily large objects gracefully and is the correct default for anything measured in gigabytes. Applied to a five-megabyte track, it adds segmenting and manifest overhead to solve a problem that never actually occurs at this size.

**Good: whole-object delivery only for the most common lossy rungs, chunked everywhere else on a case-by-case basis.** A reasonable instinct, and deciding per format rather than per object size misses the cases that actually matter, such as a long podcast episode encoded at a normally lossy bitrate but running well past the point where whole-object download makes sense.

**Great: pick a rung once at track start, fetch the whole object, and set delivery mode by an explicit size threshold in the manifest rather than by format.** A track under roughly 25MB downloads inside the first few percent of playback on any reasonable connection, so there is nothing left to adapt to mid-track; anything larger, lossless audio or a long podcast, gets chunked delivery from the same client.

Worked example: a 160kbps four-minute track is 4.8MB, and on a 5Mbps connection the whole file lands in under 8 seconds, comfortably inside the first 15 seconds of playback that follows first audio at around 120 milliseconds. A two-hour video title at 5 to 15GB has no equivalent moment where the whole object could reasonably be pre-fetched, which is precisely why the two products' delivery designs diverge despite looking superficially similar.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="-135 -7 439 218" role="img" aria-label="A 4.8MB track downloads whole in under 8 seconds on a 5 Mbps connection; a 5 to 15GB video file has no equivalent moment where downloading the whole object is reasonable">
  <style>
    .track{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.32;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.5}
    .video{fill:currentColor;fill-opacity:.14;stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.5;stroke-width:1.5}
    .t{font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif;fill:currentColor;opacity:.8}
    .b{font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif;fill:currentColor}
    text{text-anchor:middle}
  </style>
  <text class="b" x="8" y="14" text-anchor="start" style="text-anchor:start">object size, drawn to a compressed scale</text>
  <rect class="track" x="40" y="150" width="20" height="10"/>
  <rect class="video" x="220" y="40" width="20" height="120"/>
  <text class="t" x="50" y="176">track, ~4.8MB, &lt;8s</text>
  <text class="t" x="230" y="176">video, 5-15GB, chunked</text>
  <text class="t" x="8" y="200" text-anchor="start" style="text-anchor:start">threshold ~25MB: above a track, below any video</text>
</svg>
```

#### The exclusion filter becomes the candidate pool
Every ranked feed a candidate has built treats a listener's history as something to filter out. Here that instinct is exactly backwards, and seeing why reshapes almost everything downstream of it.

[A listener's own history as the dominant source of candidates](/diagram/spotify?focus=queue,library,e14)

**Bad: exclude everything the listener has already played, and rank only unfamiliar candidates.** This is the correct default for a video or short-form feed, where showing the same item twice is a bug. Applied here it discards the single strongest signal available, since the overwhelming majority of what a listener actually wants to hear next is something they have already heard and loved.

**Good: rank a blend of familiar and unfamiliar candidates with no particular weighting rule.** Acknowledges that repeats matter without giving the design anything concrete to build around, so the balance between familiar and unfamiliar ends up decided implicitly by whatever a ranking model happens to learn, which biases toward familiarity anyway for reasons covered below.

**Great: treat a listener's own library, playlists and followed artists, almost always under 10,000 tracks, as the default candidate pool for most listening, with unfamiliar tracks rationed separately.** Ranking that pool is a scan with a scoring function over recency, play count, time of day and the current queue, needing no vector index, no candidate generation and no accelerator fleet at all.

Worked example: for the large majority of listeners, their realistic universe of saved library, playlists and followed artists' recent releases is a few hundred kilobytes of rows, comfortably scanned and scored directly rather than requiring anything resembling a retrieval pipeline. That single sizing decision is what keeps the bulk of the recommendation tier at a few hundred hosts rather than the few thousand a full retrieval-and-ranking funnel over the entire catalogue would need, because that heavier funnel only ever needs to run for the roughly one-fifth of plays that are genuinely unfamiliar.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 120" role="img" aria-label="Roughly 81 percent of plays are repeats served from a listener's own under-10,000-track history with no model; roughly 19 percent are first hears served from a small set of dedicated discovery surfaces">
  <style>
    .repeat{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.3;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.5}
    .novel{fill:currentColor;fill-opacity:.14;stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.55;stroke-width:1.5}
    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    .sub{fill:currentColor;opacity:.75;font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    text{dominant-baseline:middle}
  </style>
  <rect class="repeat" x="8" y="20" width="305" height="36" rx="5"/><text class="lbl" x="160" y="42" text-anchor="middle">~81% repeat: scan &lt;10k tracks, no model</text>
  <rect class="novel" x="313" y="20" width="71" height="36" rx="5"/>
  <text class="sub" x="348" y="72" text-anchor="middle">~19% first hear</text>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="100" text-anchor="start" style="text-anchor:start">the funnel most candidates use only decides this slice</text>
</svg>
```

#### Completion is not a label here
Training a ranker needs a target, and the obvious target from video recommendation systems turns out to measure almost nothing useful in this product.

[Where the training signal actually comes from](/diagram/spotify?focus=events,labels,e11,e12)

**Bad: predict play-completion probability, the standard objective from video recommendation.** A completed play is a reasonable proxy for satisfaction in a feed where every item is unfamiliar. Here a familiar track completes over 95% of the time regardless of quality, so the blended completion rate sits close to that ceiling and carries almost no useful variance, because the vast majority of impressions are already familiar and predictably satisfying.

**Good: predict completion, but only on surfaces where every candidate is unfamiliar.** Correctly identifies that completion still carries real signal in a narrower context. Applied as the sole objective everywhere, it wastes model capacity learning to predict familiarity, which a listener's own history already reveals for free and far more cheaply than a trained model.

**Great: train on skip-before-30-seconds as the negative and repeat-play-within-7-days as the positive, reserving completion as the objective only on surfaces that are unfamiliar by construction.** A skip inside the royalty-qualifying window is already computed on the money path at essentially no extra cost, and it carries real variance because it is rare enough, roughly one in seven impressions, to actually distinguish good recommendations from bad ones.

Worked example: a model trained purely on completion, given that 80% of impressions are familiar tracks completing at over 95%, spends nearly all its learning capacity modelling the 20% of impressions that are first hears, while nominally optimising a metric dominated by data that tells it nothing new. Switching the primary objective to skip-before-30-seconds keeps the signal concentrated where it actually varies, while a discovery surface built entirely from unfamiliar tracks correctly keeps completion as its objective, because on that surface, and only that surface, completion is the sharpest signal available.

#### The ledger is a batch, not a stream
Every stream of 30 seconds or more is money owed to a rights holder, and the mechanism computing that number has to handle a kind of lateness an ordinary streaming pipeline is not built for.

[The immutable archive, recomputed deterministically rather than aggregated live](/diagram/spotify?focus=events,archive,royalty,e8,e9)

**Bad: one exactly-once streaming pipeline whose live aggregated output is the payable ledger.** Gives fast, continuously updated numbers, appealing for a business that wants near-real-time payable figures. It assumes events arrive close to when they happened, and offline playback breaks that assumption directly: a device can legitimately upload three weeks of backdated events at once, which a streaming aggregator has to either hold state open for far longer than is practical or simply get wrong.

**Good: a streaming pipeline for the ledger, with a generous late-arrival window built in.** Handles moderate lateness, and holding streaming operator state open for the full 30 days a legitimate offline licence permits costs more in operational complexity than the alternative it is trying to avoid, without actually removing the risk of a genuinely late event arriving after even that generous window closes.

**Great: the streaming aggregation exists only for dashboards and alerts, at-least-once and explicitly labelled provisional; the payable ledger is a separate, deterministic batch recomputation over the immutable archived events, keyed on event time and deduplicated on a stable key.** A period's ledger can be recomputed exactly, at any time, from the archive alone, which is what makes it something a rights holder can audit years later rather than something anyone has to simply trust.

Worked example: a listener's device stays offline for three weeks on a trip and then uploads a backlog of events all at once. Because the ledger keys strictly on each event's own recorded playback time rather than on when it happened to arrive at the server, those three-week-old plays land correctly in whichever period they actually occurred in, recomputed if that period is still open or credited forward with an explanatory note if it has already been paid. A streaming pipeline attempting the same correctness would need to hold that listener's partial state open for the entire month on the chance of exactly this scenario, for every listener, which is why the batch is cheaper as well as more correct.

#### Novelty is a budget, not an optimisation
Every measurable online signal rewards playing the same familiar tracks forever, which means the decision to play anything unfamiliar at all has to be made deliberately rather than learned.

[Where the deliberately unfamiliar tracks actually get spent](/diagram/spotify?focus=labels,discovery,e12)

**Bad: let a ranker trained on engagement metrics decide the novelty rate implicitly.** Sounds reasonable, since the model is optimising the metrics the business cares about. Every one of those metrics prefers familiarity inside any experiment window short enough to run, so a model left to decide converges toward playing an ever-smaller rotation of tracks the listener already loves, and the listener does not complain until they quietly disengage months later for a reason nobody's dashboard captured.

**Good: set a novelty rate and spend it uniformly across every surface, including playlists the listener built themselves.** Guarantees a fixed amount of exposure to unfamiliar tracks. Spreading it evenly means an unrequested track shows up inside a playlist the listener deliberately curated, which is one of the more reliable ways to make someone abandon that playlist entirely.

**Great: fix the novelty rate as an explicit policy constant, and concentrate its spend into a small number of surfaces that announce themselves as discovery, so exposure to the unfamiliar always comes with the listener's implicit consent.** The listener who opens a weekly discovery surface has already accepted the risk that not everything on it will land, in a way nobody consents to inside a playlist they built themselves.

Worked example: spending roughly 15 to 20% of impressions on unfamiliar tracks produces the identical total volume of first hears whether that spend is spread uniformly across every surface or concentrated into a handful of dedicated discovery lists, because the arithmetic is the same either way. The difference is entirely in expectation: a listener who opens a surface explicitly labelled as discovery tolerates a miss there in a way they never would inside a playlist they built and returned to specifically because it already sounded right.

#### Retrieval without the hard index problem
Recommendation systems at this scale usually have to fight a genuinely hard trade-off between index accuracy and memory, and this product's specific numbers mean that fight simply does not happen.

[The scale at which retrieval stops being the hard part](/diagram/spotify?focus=discovery,catalogue,e2)

**Bad: assume any large-scale recommendation system needs the same lossy, quantised vector index a huge corpus would require.** A reasonable assumption if the comparison is drawn from feeds with corpora in the billions of items, where memory pressure genuinely forces a trade-off between recall and index size that has to be actively managed and tuned.

**Good: build a full-precision index and accept whatever memory cost that implies, without checking whether the constraint actually applies here.** Works, and it is solving a problem that was never actually present at this catalogue size, spending engineering effort on a trade-off that a corpus two orders of magnitude smaller never forces.

**Great: check the actual numbers before assuming the hard version of the problem applies.** At roughly 100 million tracks and a normal embedding size, the full index is on the order of 100 gigabytes, comfortably fitting in memory with room to spare, so the graph-based index simply keeps its full recall with no quantisation trade-off to make at all.

Worked example: a corpus of 100 million tracks needs an index of roughly 100 gigabytes at full precision, small enough to sit entirely in memory across a handful of shards with no accuracy compromise. A corpus like TikTok's, at roughly 10 billion items, needs an index two orders of magnitude larger, around 10 terabytes, which genuinely forces quantisation and the recall loss that comes with it. The two systems can look identical in outline, embeddings feeding an approximate index feeding a ranker, while one of them is fighting a real memory constraint and the other, at this catalogue's actual size, is not.

#### Where it breaks
| Layer | Failure | How the design handles it |
|---|---|---|
| Coordinated release | Every active listener requests the same new object within minutes | Pre-push the whole object to every edge from the release calendar; even without it, each edge fills once per rung and serves everyone after |
| Shuffle | Random playback order defeats prefetch, collapsing the device cache's hit rate | The shuffle order is resolved server-side ahead of time and shipped with the queue, so the client always knows what to prefetch next |
| Royalty archive | A rerun of a closed period produces a different total than the original | Rate and rights tables are versioned and effective-dated, passed as explicit inputs to the batch, so a rerun reproduces exactly what was originally paid |
| Long-tail storage | Eagerly encoding every upload into every rung grows storage faster than most of it is ever played | Only the default rung is generated eagerly for unplayed tracks; other rungs transcode on first request |
| Vector index freshness | New uploads must become retrievable quickly for release-day discovery surfaces | Incremental inserts into the live graph within minutes, with a periodic full rebuild to control degradation |
| New listener | No history exists for either the repeat path or collaborative filtering | Onboarding preferences seed a coarse profile blended with regional popularity priors until enough real plays accumulate |
| Offline lateness | A device offline for weeks uploads a large backlog of old events at once | The batch ledger costs nothing extra structurally, since every event carries its own true playback time regardless of arrival time |

#### What this design does not solve
**The novelty rate cannot be optimised by any experiment this design can afford to run.** A skip is measurable within a session; the value of having introduced a listener to an artist they will still love in three years is not attributable to that session and lands far outside any practical test window. Every online metric available penalises novelty because its cost is inside the measurement window and its benefit is outside it, so the exploration rate is held as a fixed policy constant precisely because it cannot be honestly tuned, defended only by argument and by underpowered long-horizon holdouts rather than by the experiment framework everything else in the product uses.

**Royalty correctness is bounded by what the client reports, not by anything the pipeline itself can verify.** Everything downstream of ingest is fully reconcilable, since the log is immutable and the batch is deterministic and reproducible, but none of that can confirm whether a reported play actually happened. A play farm running on real accounts with real subscriptions generates events indistinguishable, at the event level, from a genuine listener, so detection is necessarily statistical, catches the crude and misses the careful, and the fraction that gets away is unknown by construction, because there is no ground truth to measure a false-negative rate against.

**The stream count is exact and the payout split is not, and the split is where the actual money sits.** Recording ownership is generally clean, but composition ownership is asserted by publishers and collecting societies, frequently arrives incomplete, and gets revised retroactively, sometimes years later and sometimes as the outcome of litigation the platform is not even party to. A reserve held against unmatched compositions, trued up as claims eventually resolve, means the platform's own books carry a liability of genuinely unknown size against streams that were counted with perfect precision, and no amount of exactly-once machinery anywhere in the pipeline touches that particular gap.

#### Final design
Read it back through the numbers. The top 10 million tracks fitting in 144TB on a single storage node is what makes delivery a caching problem rather than a chunking one, and it is why whole-object fetching, holding up cleanly to roughly 25MB, is the right default rather than an approximation borrowed from video. Roughly 81% of plays being repeats is the fact that turns a listener's own under-10,000-track history into the dominant candidate pool, needing no model at all for the large majority of listening, and it is why completion, which barely varies across that majority, gets replaced as a training signal by skip-before-30-seconds and repeat-within-7-days. A 100-million-vector index fitting comfortably in memory, against a 10-terabyte index for a corpus two orders of magnitude larger, is why retrieval here never fights the accuracy-versus-memory trade-off a much bigger catalogue would force. And a 30-day legitimate lateness window on offline events is why the payable ledger is a deterministic batch over an immutable archive rather than a live streaming aggregate.

[The whole design, from a play request through recommendation to the royalty ledger](/diagram/spotify?focus=client,play-api,edge,origin,catalogue,library,queue,events,labels,discovery,archive,royalty)

> **The numbers to remember.** Top 10M tracks at two rungs fits one 144TB storage node · ~81% of plays are repeats · whole-object delivery holds up to ~25MB · a 100M-vector index fits in RAM against a 10TB index at TikTok's scale · offline events can legitimately arrive up to 30 days late.

#### Check your understanding
**Why does this design fetch a whole track object instead of using chunked, adaptive-bitrate delivery the way video streaming does?** A four-minute track at a normal bitrate is a few megabytes, small enough to download entirely in under 8 seconds on an ordinary connection, well inside the first few percent of playback. There is nothing left to adapt to mid-track by the time the file has already arrived, which is why the delivery mode is set by an explicit size threshold in the manifest rather than by a blanket protocol choice, with only lossless audio and long-form podcasts crossing into chunked delivery.

**Why does a listener's own play history become the primary candidate pool instead of being excluded from it?** Roughly four out of five plays are of a track the listener has heard before, so what they have already played is the strongest available predictor of what they want next, the exact reverse of a feed where repeating an item is a bug. That pool is almost always under 10,000 tracks, small enough to rank with a plain scoring scan rather than any retrieval infrastructure.

**Why is play-completion probability not used as the primary training label here?** A familiar track completes over 95% of the time regardless of quality, and since the large majority of impressions are familiar, a completion-trained model spends nearly all its capacity learning to predict familiarity, something a listener's own history already reveals for free. Skip-before-30-seconds carries far more variance because it is comparatively rare, making it a sharper signal for what actually distinguishes a good recommendation from a bad one.

**Why is the royalty ledger computed as a batch over an archive rather than as a live streaming total?** Offline licences legitimately allow events to arrive up to 30 days after they happened, and a streaming pipeline would need to hold state open for that entire window for every listener to handle it correctly. A deterministic batch keyed on each event's own recorded playback time can be recomputed exactly at any point from an immutable archive, which is what lets a rights holder audit a payment years later rather than simply trust a number nobody can reproduce.

**Why is the novelty rate a fixed policy constant instead of a value tuned by experimentation?** Every online engagement metric rewards playing familiar tracks within the timeframe any affordable experiment can measure, while the benefit of introducing a listener to something they will love for years shows up, if at all, far outside that window. Since no practical test can honestly weigh that trade-off, the rate is set deliberately as policy rather than learned, and its value is defended by argument rather than by the same experimentation framework the rest of the product relies on.
### 41. Design a Stock Price Notification System
#### Understanding the problem
A stock price notification system lets users subscribe to price rules on financial instruments, "AAPL crosses above $200", "BTC drops 5% in an hour", and delivers a push or email alert within seconds of the condition firing. At broker scale that means millions of standing rules, tens of thousands of instruments, and up to a quarter of a million price ticks a second.

Two things make this a matching problem rather than a delivery problem.

First, the volumes are backwards from what they look like. Ten million rules sit almost still while ticks arrive constantly, so the real question is never how to notify someone, it is how a single price change finds the handful of rules it could possibly trigger without touching the other 9,999,990.

Second, a rule is a crossing, not a level. A threshold like `price >= 200` describes a state that stays true for the rest of the session; a correct rule fires exactly once, at the moment the price passes through the boundary, which is a subtly different and easy to get wrong condition.

> **What this is not.** It looks like a notification/delivery system: push tokens, provider retries, quiet hours, per-channel fan-out. In a delivery system, the input already is a decision, one notification per recipient, arriving because a producer created it, and the hard problems are fan-out and reliable delivery of something that already exists. Here nothing has decided anything yet; the decision is the entire design. Ten million rules produce only around twenty notifications a second in ordinary markets, small enough that delivery is a dependency to reuse rather than something to design. A candidate who spends the first ten minutes on push providers and quiet hours has answered a different, easier question, and the design that results, a beautifully isolated delivery tier fed by an evaluator that cannot keep up with a volatile stock, fails in exactly the way this question is built to expose.

#### Requirements and the numbers
**Functional.** Users create, read and delete price rules on any instrument. Rule types include threshold cross, percent change over a window, and volume spike. Fire within seconds of the triggering tick. Fire once then disarm, with an optional re-arm cooldown. Respect notification preferences and quiet hours. Maintain an audit trail of every fire.

**Non-functional.** p99 tick-to-push latency under 5 seconds. Handle 10M active rules, 50k instruments, up to 1M ticks/s at peak. 99.9% of alerts delivered within SLA, with no duplicate alert for the same crossing. Survive a market-data feed disconnect without losing armed state.

The whole design is decided by five numbers, so derive them before drawing anything.

**What does the naive approach actually cost?** Polling all 10M rules once a minute means roughly **167,000 price lookups/s**, and the poll interval itself becomes a hard **60-second floor** under how quickly any alert can possibly fire, regardless of how fast the lookups run.

**Do 10 million rules actually fit in memory next to the ticks that evaluate them?** At roughly 500 bytes per loaded rule, 10M rules total about **5GB**, spread across 16 evaluator shards at roughly 310MB each, comfortably inside a single process's memory alongside its window buffers.

**How expensive is a genuinely hot instrument without an index?** A flat scan of 500,000 rules parked on one popular stock, against a sustained 200 ticks/s, is **100 million comparisons a second**, a fully saturated CPU core doing nothing but comparisons, before any deserialisation or state update, and roughly five times that during an actual earnings surprise.

**How much does a sharp market move actually burst the fire rate by?** An index dropping 3% in ten seconds can trip roughly 100,000 rules at once, **~10,000 fires/s**, against a normal average of only about 17 fires/s, a burst of roughly **600x**.

**Does the wire format actually matter at this scale?** At 250,000 ticks/s, even 100 wasted bytes per tick from a verbose format like JSON is **25MB/s of pure overhead**, which is why a compact binary encoding is not an optional optimisation here but a baseline requirement.

> **The numbers to carry.** Naive polling floors latency at 60 seconds · all 10M rules fit in ~5GB across 16 shards · a hot instrument's flat scan saturates a full core at 100M compares/s · a sharp move bursts fire rate roughly 600x above average · binary encoding saves 25MB/s of pure overhead at peak tick rate.

#### Matching and delivery: the hard half and the easy half
It is worth separating, explicitly, the two problems this design solves, because one of them is genuinely hard and the other is a solved problem this design simply reuses.

The entities are:

- **Rule**: a standing predicate on one instrument, holding a threshold or window definition, a state, and an arm epoch.
- **Tick**: a single price update from an exchange feed, the event stream this design's cost is actually built around.
- **Fired event**: emitted the instant a tick's crossing satisfies an armed rule, carrying the rule's arm epoch for downstream deduplication.
- **Arm epoch**: a counter on each rule that increments every time it re-arms, turning "the same fire replayed" into something a downstream consumer can recognise and discard.

The API and the one internal event carrying the arm epoch reflect the split between the hard matching problem and the reused delivery problem:

```
POST   /alerts
  body: { instrument_id, rule: { type, value, window_sec? }, channels: [...], cooldown_sec? }
  → { alert_id, state: "armed" }

Internal event: alerts.fired
  { alert_id, arm_epoch, user_id, instrument_id, triggered_at, trigger_price, exchange_seq_no }
```

#### High-level design
Follow the numbered arrows. Everything before the fired event is the matching problem; everything after it is an ordinary, reused notification pipeline.

[The hot path from a raw tick to a fired alert](/diagram/price-alerts?focus=exchanges,gateway,tick-log,evaluator,threshold-idx,fired-stream,dispatcher,notify,e1,e2,e3,e4,e6,e10,e13)

1. **Exchanges and vendors** publish raw ticks to the **Market data gateway**.
2. **Market data gateway** deduplicates, normalises to a compact binary format, and publishes onto the **Partitioned tick log**, keyed by instrument.
3. The **Rule evaluator**, partitioned by that same instrument key, receives the tick and looks it up in the **Threshold index** it already holds in local memory.
4. A crossing produces a write to the **Fired-alerts stream**.
5. The **Alert dispatcher** checks idempotency, applies user preferences and quiet hours, and hands the alert off to the **Notification service**.

> **Why the flow is shaped this way.** Routing ticks and rules by the identical instrument key means the process handling an instrument's price updates already holds that instrument's rules in local memory, so evaluation is a pure in-process operation with no network hop on the hot path. Everything downstream of a fired event is an ordinary at-least-once notification pipeline that this design deliberately treats as a dependency rather than a problem to redesign.

#### Invert the loop: iterate ticks, not rules
The single decision the rest of this design depends on is which side of the matching problem drives the loop, rules polling prices or prices finding rules.

[Ticks and rules meeting on the same worker, keyed the same way](/diagram/price-alerts?focus=tick-log,evaluator,rule-store,rule-cdc,e3,e9)

**Bad: iterate rules, polling each one's current price on a timer.** Simple to build and genuinely correct at small scale, when there are only tens of thousands of rules and a latency tolerance measured in minutes. Its cost scales with the number of rules rather than with how often prices actually change, which becomes backwards the moment rules outnumber the ticks that could ever move them, and the poll interval sets a hard floor under how fast any alert can possibly fire.

**Good: iterate rules more frequently, and query a shared low-latency store per rule for the current price.** Reduces the latency floor substantially, and it turns every evaluation into a network round trip; at high enough rule counts, the aggregate wait time for those round trips becomes its own throughput ceiling, needing a large fleet purely to absorb network latency rather than to do useful comparison work.

**Great: route ticks and rule-change events by the same instrument key, so the process consuming an instrument's ticks already holds that instrument's rules in local memory.** Cost now scales with ticks and with rules genuinely crossed, never with the total number of rules sitting quietly on an instrument that has not moved.

Worked example: with 10 million rules co-partitioned across 16 evaluator shards, each shard holds roughly 310MB of rule state entirely in RAM, small enough that evaluating a tick against its shard's rules never leaves the process. Polling the same 10 million rules once a minute, by contrast, needs roughly 167,000 lookups every second regardless of how many prices actually changed in that minute, and no amount of added polling frequency can push the latency floor below the interval itself.

#### A threshold index turns a scan into a sliver
Once ticks and rules share a process, the next question is how that process avoids comparing every tick against every rule it holds for a given instrument.

[Rules sorted by trigger price, range-scanned rather than fully scanned](/diagram/price-alerts?focus=evaluator,threshold-idx,e4)

**Bad: a flat list of rules, scanned in full on every tick.** No structure to build or maintain when a rule is created, deleted or re-armed, and it handles every rule type uniformly, including ones with no fixed point on the price axis. At the average of a couple hundred rules per instrument this costs almost nothing, and on a genuinely popular name carrying hundreds of thousands of rules it turns into tens of millions of comparisons a second, saturating a core that a partitioning scheme by design cannot split further.

**Good: a flat list, with an early exit once the price move is known to be small.** Helps somewhat on quiet ticks, and it does nothing for the case that actually matters, a large sudden move on a heavily subscribed instrument, which is precisely when the full list still has to be walked in its entirety to find the handful of rules that matter.

**Great: keep rules with a fixed numeric trigger sorted by that trigger price, and range-scan only the interval between the previous and current tick.** A tick that nudges a price by a fraction of a percent touches only the handful of rules whose thresholds sit inside that narrow sliver, regardless of how many thousands of other rules the instrument carries outside it.

Worked example: 500,000 rules parked on one instrument during an earnings surprise, scanned as a flat list against a burst of 1,000 ticks/s, would need roughly 500 million comparisons a second, several fully saturated cores doing nothing but comparing thresholds. The same rules held in a threshold-sorted index mean an 8% jump touches only the rules whose thresholds actually sit inside that 8% band, typically a tiny fraction of the half million, turning an unworkable scan into single-digit-millisecond evaluation.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 180" role="img" aria-label="A flat scan of 500,000 rules against a 1,000 ticks per second burst needs roughly 500 million comparisons a second; a threshold-sorted index touches only the rules whose trigger sits inside the moved price interval">
  <style>
    .bad{fill:currentColor;fill-opacity:.14;stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.5;stroke-width:1.5}
    .good{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.32;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.5}
    .t{font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif;fill:currentColor;opacity:.8}
    .b{font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif;fill:currentColor}
    text{text-anchor:middle}
  </style>
  <text class="b" x="8" y="14" style="text-anchor:start">bad: flat scan, all 500,000 rules, every tick</text>
  <rect class="bad" x="8" y="24" width="376" height="28" rx="5"/><text class="t" x="196" y="42">~500M comparisons/s during an earnings burst</text>
  <text class="b" x="8" y="90" style="text-anchor:start">great: threshold index, only the moved interval</text>

  <rect class="good" x="185" y="106" width="18" height="28"/>

  <text class="t" x="8" y="162" style="text-anchor:start">never touched</text>
```
