
#### When one instrument is too hot for one process
Even with a threshold index, a single instrument's rules live entirely on one partition by construction, and that partition has a hard ceiling no amount of indexing removes.

[Splitting one instrument's rules across several processes, at a real cost](/diagram/price-alerts?focus=evaluator,threshold-idx,windowed,e4,e5)

**Bad: accept the single-partition ceiling as fixed, and let consumer lag build during an extreme event.** Keeps the "one owner per instrument" invariant perfectly intact, which is what made the whole design simple in the first place. During a genuine event, tick rate on that one instrument can climb five times its ordinary rate, needing more processing capacity than one core, however well indexed, can supply, and alerts land minutes late on exactly the move users most wanted to know about immediately.

**Good: give the hottest few instruments a permanently larger, dedicated shard.** Buys headroom for known hot names ahead of time, and it cannot anticipate which name will spike next, since the instruments that actually saturate under load are often driven by unscheduled news rather than by their everyday popularity ranking.

**Great: split a genuinely hot instrument across N sub-shards by hashing the alert id, publishing every tick for that instrument to all N.** Each sub-shard holds only 1/N of the rules, so CPU work spreads across N cores instead of saturating one, engaged only for instruments that actually trip a lag threshold rather than applied universally.

Worked example: splitting a hot instrument three ways means its tick is now written and read three times instead of once, and each sub-shard has to maintain its own copy of `last_price` independently, which can drift slightly out of step with its siblings if one sub-shard lags behind the others. That is a real, worthwhile cost paid specifically on the instruments where it is needed, in exchange for CPU capacity that the single-owner-per-instrument model, by its own construction, could never otherwise supply.

#### Fire on the crossing, not the level
Deciding exactly when a rule has been satisfied looks trivial and is the single most common place a first attempt at this design goes quietly wrong.

[The comparison that fires exactly once, not on every subsequent tick](/diagram/price-alerts?focus=evaluator,threshold-idx,e4)

**Bad: `price >= threshold`.** Reads naturally as "the price crossed the level", and it is actually a state test, true for every tick from the moment the threshold is first reached onward. A user who wanted to know the instant AAPL crossed $200 instead gets an alert on every single tick above $200 for the rest of the session.

**Good: fire once, then remember that it already fired, checked separately from the comparison itself.** Prevents the flood of repeat alerts, and bolting a separate "already notified" flag onto a level test is fragile in exactly the cases that matter, a restart or a replay that loses track of whether the flag was ever set correctly in the first place.

**Great: define the rule as a crossing of the interval between two consecutive ticks, `prev < threshold <= price`.** The comparison itself only evaluates true at the single tick where the boundary is actually crossed, so there is no separate flag to lose track of, and the same comparison correctly fires even when a tick jumps clean over the threshold with no tick ever landing exactly on it.

Worked example: a gap-open move from $199.00 straight to $201.00, with no tick ever touching exactly $200, still correctly fires a rule set at $200, because the crossing condition evaluates against the interval between the two consecutive prices rather than requiring any single tick to land precisely on the threshold. A level test would either miss this crossing entirely, since no tick ever equalled $200, or require a separate range check bolted on as a special case, which is exactly the kind of extra correctness surface the interval-based definition avoids needing at all.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 194" role="img" aria-label="A level test price greater than or equal to 200 fires on every tick above 200; a crossing test prev less than 200 less than or equal to price fires exactly once, and still fires when a tick jumps clean over the threshold with none landing on it">
  <style>
    .bad{fill:currentColor;fill-opacity:.14;stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.5;stroke-width:1.5}
    .good{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.32;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.5}
    .t{font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif;fill:currentColor;opacity:.8}
    .b{font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif;fill:currentColor}
  </style>
  <text class="b" x="8" y="14">bad: price &gt;= 200, refires on every tick after</text>
  <rect class="bad" x="8" y="24" width="56" height="28" rx="4"/><rect class="bad" x="72" y="24" width="56" height="28" rx="4"/>
  <rect class="bad" x="136" y="24" width="56" height="28" rx="4"/><rect class="bad" x="200" y="24" width="56" height="28" rx="4"/>
  <text class="t" x="8" y="68">every one of these fires again</text>
  <text class="b" x="8" y="100">great: prev &lt; 200 &lt;= price, fires exactly once</text>
  <line x1="8" y1="140" x2="384" y2="140" stroke="currentColor" stroke-opacity=".35"/>
  <rect class="good" x="180" y="126" width="20" height="28" rx="4"/>
  <text class="t" x="8" y="168">fires here only, even on a gap</text>
  <text class="t" x="8" y="182">from 199 to 201</text>
</svg>
```

#### The gap guard: do not invent a crossing
A checkpoint restore or a feed outage leaves the evaluator with a stale idea of "the previous price", and the naive interval definition turns that staleness into a serious correctness bug.

[The first tick after any gap treated as a reseed, never a crossing](/diagram/price-alerts?focus=gateway,tick-log,evaluator,e2,e3)

**Bad: treat the first tick after any restart or feed gap exactly like an ordinary tick.** Requires no special handling at all, and it silently invents an enormous, entirely fictional price move: if the last known price before a ten-minute gap was $190 and the first tick on resumption is $210, the interval definition sees that as one single crossing of every threshold between the two, firing every rule in that band simultaneously, none of which reflects anything that actually happened tick by tick in the market.

**Good: cap how large an interval a single tick is allowed to imply, silently truncating anything larger.** Bounds the damage somewhat, and choosing an arbitrary cap either still fires rules that should not have fired within that capped range, or arbitrarily suppresses ones that genuinely should have, with no principled way to know which.

**Great: explicitly treat the first tick after any gap beyond a few seconds as a reseed rather than a crossing, updating the stored price with no evaluation at all.** Accepts that any real crossings that happened during the blind window are simply missed rather than guessed at, which is the correct direction of error for a regulated system: never inventing an event that did not provably happen.

Worked example: an evaluator restores from a ten-minute-old checkpoint and the first tick it receives shows a price ten dollars higher than what the checkpoint recorded. Without the gap guard, every rule with a threshold in that ten-dollar band fires at once, alerting users to a crossing computed from a stale price rather than an actual sequence of market moves. With the guard, that first tick simply re-seeds the stored price with no evaluation, and only genuine crossings from that point forward, based on real consecutive ticks, ever fire a rule.

#### The epoch makes a replay harmless
An evaluator crash and restart can replay ticks it already processed, which means the same genuine crossing can be detected and emitted twice, and the fix has to work without a distributed transaction across systems that do not share one.

[A stable identity for one specific arming of one rule, surviving a replay](/diagram/price-alerts?focus=fired-stream,dispatcher,e10,e13)

**Bad: build a fully transactional, exactly-once pipeline from ingest through to the notification provider.** Would genuinely remove an entire class of duplicate-alert incidents if it were achievable end to end. Push and email providers are plain HTTP endpoints with nothing to enlist in a distributed transaction, so even a perfectly exactly-once pipeline up to that point can still hand a provider two identical send requests, and paying for transactional commits earlier in the pipeline pushes checkpoint latency from tens of milliseconds into the hundreds against a five-second end-to-end budget.

**Good: deduplicate on the alert's id alone at the dispatcher.** Catches an ordinary replayed fire of a rule that has not re-armed since, and it fails the far more important case: a rule that legitimately fires, re-arms, and fires again within the same session produces two events sharing the same alert id, and naive deduplication on that id alone would wrongly suppress the second, genuine alert.

**Great: deduplicate on the pair of alert id and arm epoch, where the epoch increments only on a genuine re-arm.** A replayed fire from before a crash carries the same epoch as the original and is correctly recognised and dropped; a legitimate second fire after a real re-arm carries a new epoch and correctly passes through.

Worked example: an evaluator crashes, restores a checkpoint taken slightly before a rule fired, and replays the tick log from that offset, re-detecting and re-emitting the identical crossing with the same arm epoch it had the first time. The dispatcher's idempotency check finds that epoch's key already recorded and silently drops the duplicate, at the cost of one cache lookup per fire, roughly seventeen a second on average and ten thousand at the worst burst, which is a trivial price for correctness on a hot path measured in single-digit milliseconds elsewhere.

#### Where it breaks
| Layer | Failure | How the design handles it |
|---|---|---|
| Hot instrument | A single popular stock's tick rate multiplies during a major event | The threshold index absorbs ordinary moves; a hash-based sub-shard split by alert id spreads extreme, sustained bursts across several cores |
| Sharp market move | A fast index drop trips a large fraction of rules within seconds | The dispatcher rate-limits and smears delivery per downstream channel rather than attempting to send everything at once |
| Windowed rules | Percent-change rules have no fixed threshold to index and are scanned in full every tick | They are the actual ceiling on a hot instrument even with an index in place, isolated in their own scan path rather than allowed to degrade threshold evaluation |
| Cold start | Rebuilding 10 million rules from a change-stream replay after a full outage takes minutes | Periodic state snapshots combined with delta replay bring restore time down to well under a minute |
| Vendor discrepancy | A primary feed briefly reports a wrong price, risking a phantom crossing | Cross-checking against a secondary vendor suppresses crossing fires while the two sources meaningfully diverge |
| Rule abuse | A single account or script creates an excessive number of rules | Per-user and per-instrument quotas enforced at the API layer, with anomaly detection on accounts whose fan-out looks scripted |
| DST and exchange calendars | A jurisdiction's clock change shifts session open and close relative to a stored schedule | Hours are stored against a maintained timezone database and alerts flag if a session's first tick lands significantly off the expected open |

#### What this design does not solve
**Windowed rules have no good index, and on a hot instrument they become the real ceiling.** A percent-change rule's implied trigger price moves continuously as its reference window rolls forward, so it has no fixed point on the price axis a sorted structure can hold, and every one of these rules is scanned in full on every tick regardless of how well threshold rules are indexed. On an instrument carrying hundreds of thousands of such rules, the threshold index makes the comparison worse rather than better, because the windowed scan is now the visible bottleneck sitting right beside an otherwise fast path.

**Corporate actions have no correct automatic behaviour.** A stock split makes an existing price threshold instantly meaningless, and there is no response that is both automatic and honest: silently rescaling every affected threshold changes what the user actually asked for without their knowledge, while leaving thresholds unrescaled fires every affected rule simultaneously against a price that moved for a reason entirely unrelated to what the user cared about. Suspending affected rules and prompting the user is the least dishonest option available, and it still leaves people believing an alert is live when it has quietly been paused.

**The alert is structurally too late for anyone actually trying to trade the move it describes.** Getting a notification to a phone within five seconds of the triggering tick says nothing about how long it then takes a human to notice it, unlock their phone, open the app, and place an order, by which point the price has often moved again. No amount of added evaluation capacity closes that human-reaction gap, because it was never a capacity problem; the honest product answer for anyone who actually needs to act at the moment of the crossing is a conditional order sitting directly at the broker, a different system with fundamentally different guarantees than a notification.

#### Final design
Read it back through the numbers. A naive poll's 60-second latency floor is why the whole design inverts the loop, iterating ticks against rules instead of rules against prices, since nothing about polling faster ever removes that floor. All 10 million rules fitting in roughly 5GB across 16 shards is what makes co-partitioning rules with the ticks that evaluate them a genuinely affordable choice rather than a theoretical one. A hot instrument's flat scan saturating a full core at 100 million comparisons a second is exactly why the threshold index exists, and why even that index needs a sub-sharding escape hatch for the rare instrument that outgrows one process entirely. A sharp move's roughly 600-fold burst above average fire rate is why the dispatcher, not the evaluator, is where delivery smearing happens. And binary encoding's 25MB/s saving at peak tick rate is a reminder that at this volume, format choices that look like premature optimisation anywhere else are simply required here.

[The whole design, from raw ticks through matching to delivered alerts](/diagram/price-alerts?focus=exchanges,gateway,tick-log,evaluator,threshold-idx,windowed,rule-store,rule-cdc,fired-stream,dispatcher,notify,audit)

> **The numbers to remember.** Naive polling floors latency at 60 seconds · all 10M rules fit in ~5GB across 16 shards · a hot instrument's flat scan saturates a full core · a sharp move bursts fire rate roughly 600x above average · binary encoding saves 25MB/s of overhead at peak tick rate.

#### Check your understanding
**Why does this design route ticks and rules by the same instrument key instead of having rules poll for the current price?** Polling scales with the number of rules regardless of how often prices actually move, and the poll interval itself sets a hard floor under how fast any alert can fire. Co-partitioning means the process that sees an instrument's ticks already holds that instrument's rules in local memory, so cost scales with actual price movement and matched rules rather than with total rule count.

**Why is a threshold-sorted index needed even though rules and ticks already share a process?** Sharing a process only removes the network hop; it does nothing about how many rules on that instrument a single tick has to be compared against. A flat scan against hundreds of thousands of rules on one popular instrument can saturate an entire CPU core, while a threshold-sorted index touches only the rules whose trigger price actually sits inside the interval a tick just moved through.

**Why does a rule fire on `prev < threshold <= price` instead of `price >= threshold`?** The second form is a state test that stays true for every tick after the threshold is first reached, so it fires again and again for the rest of the session. The first form only evaluates true at the exact tick where the boundary is crossed, and it correctly handles a price that jumps clean over the threshold with no tick ever landing precisely on it.

**Why does the first tick after a checkpoint restore or a feed outage get treated specially?** The stored "previous price" after a gap can be many minutes stale, so treating the next tick as an ordinary crossing would compute an enormous, entirely fictional price move and fire every rule with a threshold inside that fabricated interval. Treating that first tick as a reseed instead means any real crossings during the gap are missed rather than invented, which is the safer direction of error for a regulated system.

**Why deduplicate fired events on the pair of alert id and arm epoch rather than on the alert id alone?** A rule that legitimately fires, re-arms, and fires again within the same session produces two genuine events sharing the same alert id, and deduplicating on that id alone would wrongly discard the second real alert. The arm epoch increments only on an actual re-arm, so a replayed fire from before a crash carries the same epoch as the original and is correctly dropped, while a genuinely new fire after re-arming carries a new epoch and correctly passes through.
### 42. Design a Matching Engine / Limit Order Book
#### Understanding the problem
A matching engine processes a continuous stream of new orders, cancels, and cancel/replaces for a set of financial instruments, matching buys against sells in strict price-time priority at microsecond latency. The output is a stream of fills and execution reports plus a published top-of-book, and the same ordered input has to produce byte-identical output on every replay.

Two things make this a memory-layout problem rather than an algorithm problem.

First, the matching logic itself is trivial, a while loop with a minimum in it. What separates a working prototype from a production engine is entirely how the order book is laid out in memory, because access is extremely skewed: nearly every event touches the best price or one level in from it, and cancels outnumber fills by ten to twenty to one.

Second, determinism is not a nice-to-have here, it is the product. Trades are money, and regulators, participants and the venue's own recovery process all replay the same log and must arrive at exactly the same result, to the byte. That single requirement rules out the one optimisation most engineers reach for instinctively: adding threads to a hot book.

> **What this is not.** It looks like the venue described by a stock exchange design: member gateways, pre-trade risk checks, an organisation-wide sequencer, multicast market data, halts and circuit breakers. That design is everything around the engine; this one is the box in the middle of that diagram, opened up. A stock exchange design can be answered well without ever mentioning a cache line. This question starts where that one stops and asks what the book is actually made of: how a cancel finds its order in one memory load, why the best-price pointer never searches, and what a tick-indexed array costs in megabytes. Answering this question with that design's architecture is the classic miss, everything said is true, and none of it touches what is actually being asked.

#### Requirements and the numbers
**Functional.** Accept new orders (market, limit, IOC, FOK), cancels, and cancel/replace for each instrument. Match in strict price-time priority, generating fills and execution reports. Maintain and publish top-of-book and incremental updates. Enforce self-trade prevention. Deterministically rebuild book state from the ordered input log.

**Non-functional.** Single-digit to low-tens-of-microseconds internal matching latency at p99. Bit-for-bit reproducible output for a given ordered input. Throughput of roughly 1 to 3 million messages a second at peak. No hot-path allocation or locks inside a book. Recovery in seconds with zero data loss on anything acknowledged.

The whole design is decided by five numbers, so derive them before drawing anything.

**How much of the traffic is actually cancels?** At a 15:1 cancel-to-fill ratio against a 2 million message-a-second peak, fills run at only about 125,000/s while cancel-type messages run at roughly **1.875 million/s**, close to 90% of all traffic. The cancel path, not the fill path, is what the layout has to be built around.

**How much does the choice between an array lookup and a hash lookup actually cost?** A predictable array load costs around **4 nanoseconds**; a hash lookup, typically two dependent cache misses at roughly 100 nanoseconds each, costs around **200 nanoseconds**, which is 2 to 4% of a 5-microsecond p99 budget on its own, before accounting for its far less predictable tail.

**How much memory does a dense, tick-indexed price array actually cost?** A $190 equity on a one-cent tick, banded at plus or minus 20% around a reference price, spans roughly 7,600 ticks. At 64 bytes per level header, that is **~486KB per book**. Dense-banding the top 500 symbols costs roughly 243MB; dense-banding all 10,000 listed instruments would cost roughly **4.9GB**, mostly empty.

**How many cache lines does a typical marketable order actually touch?** A marketable order sweeping two price levels touches roughly **four cache lines** total: two level headers and two order records, which is the entire justification for padding a level header to exactly one 64-byte cache line.

**Does one core actually need help to hit the throughput target?** A lean in-memory book achieves roughly 1 to 5 million matches a second on a single core, so the full 2 million message-a-second venue-wide peak needs only a handful of cores for raw throughput; running 16 to 64 shards exists to isolate hot instruments and leave headroom, not because one core is too slow.

> **The numbers to carry.** Cancels are ~90% of traffic at ~1.875M/s · an array load costs ~4ns against ~200ns for a hash lookup · a dense tick array costs ~486KB per book, ~4.9GB for the whole venue done densely · a marketable order touches roughly 4 cache lines · one core alone handles 1 to 5M matches/s, far above what raw throughput requires.

#### One writer per book, and why nothing else needs a lock
It is worth stating the invariant this entire design rests on before anything else, because every other decision either follows from it or exists to protect it.

The entities are:

- **Order**: a resting or incoming instruction, holding price, quantity, side and its own list pointers.
- **Price level**: one discrete price point, holding a FIFO queue of resting orders in arrival order.
- **Fill**: the result of matching an incoming order against a resting one, printed at the resting order's price.
- **Sequence number**: a gap-free, monotonically increasing stamp applied to every inbound event before it reaches any book.

The API surface is small, and the asynchronous execution report is where the actual state changes are visible:

```
submit_order(instrument_id, participant_id, side, type, price?, quantity, tif, client_order_id) ->
  { status: ACCEPTED | REJECTED, order_id, seq, reason? }

cancel_order(instrument_id, order_id | client_order_id, participant_id) ->
  { status: CANCELLED | TOO_LATE | UNKNOWN, seq }
```

#### High-level design
Follow the numbered arrows. Every event is validated and sequenced exactly once before it ever reaches a book, and from there it touches exactly one thread for its entire life.

[The hot path from a sequenced event to a printed fill](/diagram/matching-engine?focus=inbound,dispatch,match-loop,best-ptr,level-array,fifo,stp,outputs,e1,e4,e5,e6,e7,e8,e9)

1. The **Per-shard ring buffer** delivers a sequenced event, single writer, to **Event dispatch**.
2. **Event dispatch** routes a new order to the **Matching loop**.
3. **Matching loop** reads the **Best-price pointer** for the opposite side of the book.
4. **Best-price pointer** resolves directly to an entry in **Price levels by tick**, a subscript rather than a search.
5. **Price levels by tick** hands off to the **Intrusive FIFO per level**, whose head is the oldest resting order.
6. **Self-trade prevention** checks the pair before **Fills + book deltas** emits the fill at the resting order's price.

> **Why the flow is shaped this way.** Sequencing happens before matching so the log, not the in-memory book, is the actual source of truth, and matching becomes a pure function of that ordered log. Routing every event for one instrument to the same fixed worker is what makes this lock-free: the loop above mutates shared state with no synchronisation at all, and that is only sound because nothing else can ever be inside it at the same time.

#### A price is a subscript, not a search
Deciding how price levels are stored looks like a routine data-structure choice, and the actual tick range involved decides it far more sharply than intuition would suggest.

[Levels addressed directly by tick, with a tree reserved for the sparse tail](/diagram/matching-engine?focus=level-array,tree-tail,e13)

**Bad: a general-purpose sorted map for every instrument, uniformly.** Correct by construction for any price range, costs nothing for an instrument nobody trades, and is genuinely what most venues outside the very top tier ship. Even a logarithmic lookup over a few hundred distinct levels involves real comparison work and pointer chasing on a path where every operation is measured in nanoseconds.

**Good: a dense array for every instrument, uniformly, sized to its full tradable band.** Removes comparison entirely for every book, and applied without discrimination it allocates memory proportional to the price range whether or not anyone ever trades near most of it, which becomes wasteful fast on a venue listing thousands of thinly traded names or wide-ranging instruments like options.

**Great: a dense tick-indexed array for the instruments with a bounded price range, a tree for everything wide or sparse.** A price becomes a plain array subscript with no comparison at all for the names that carry the overwhelming majority of traffic, while the long tail of thinly traded or wide-ranging instruments keeps the tree's property of allocating only levels that actually hold an order.

Worked example: a $190 equity on a penny tick, banded at plus or minus 20%, needs roughly 7,600 levels, about 486KB, cheap enough to keep dense for the top 500 symbols at roughly 243MB total. An options contract on a $0.0001 tick over a $0 to $500 range needs roughly 5 million levels, around 320MB for that single contract alone, which makes the identical dense scheme unaffordable the moment the tick range widens, and is exactly why the rule of thumb sits at roughly 100,000 ticks per book as the crossover point.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 217" role="img" aria-label="A dense array costs about 486KB per book for a normal equity; dense-banding the top 500 symbols costs about 243MB; dense-banding all 10,000 listed instruments would cost about 4.9GB, mostly empty">
  <style>
    .small{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.32;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.5}
    .big{fill:currentColor;fill-opacity:.14;stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.5;stroke-width:1.5}
    .t{font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif;fill:currentColor;opacity:.8}
    .b{font:600 12px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif;fill:currentColor}
    text{text-anchor:middle}
  </style>
  <text class="b" x="8" y="14" style="text-anchor:start">density pays off for the hot list;</text>
  <text class="b" x="8" y="30" style="text-anchor:start">the tree covers the tail</text>
  <rect class="small" x="40" y="174" width="30" height="10"/>
  <rect class="small" x="170" y="134" width="30" height="50"/>
  <rect class="big" x="300" y="44" width="30" height="140"/>
  <text class="t" x="55" y="200">one book, ~486KB</text>
  <text class="t" x="185" y="200">top 500, ~243MB</text>
  <text class="t" x="315" y="200">10,000, ~4.9GB</text>
</svg>
```

#### A cancel is one load, not a hash probe
Cancels dominate the traffic this engine actually processes, which means the mechanism for finding an order to remove matters more than the mechanism for finding one to insert.

[Finding a resting order to remove in a single memory access](/diagram/matching-engine?focus=slot-table,fifo,e2,e3)

**Bad: a hash map from order id to node.** The natural first implementation, requiring no separate id-translation scheme, since it accepts whatever identifier arrives at the edge directly. A hash lookup is typically two dependent cache misses, and worse, its probe length is data-dependent, so it surfaces as unpredictable tail latency rather than a fixed, budgetable cost on a path carrying roughly 90% of all traffic.

**Good: a hash map, tuned aggressively for cache locality.** Reduces the average cost meaningfully, and it cannot remove the fundamental dependency chain a hash lookup requires, nor make its worst case as predictable as a direct memory access.

**Great: a dense internal id assigned at admission, held in a flat slot table indexed directly by that id.** A cancel becomes one array subscript to find the node, plus an O(1) unlink from an intrusive list that requires no further lookup at all, turning the dominant traffic type into the cheapest possible operation on the entire path.

Worked example: at roughly 1.875 million cancels a second, the difference between a 4-nanosecond array load and a 200-nanosecond hash lookup is not a rounding error, it is the difference between the cancel path consuming a small, predictable slice of a 5-microsecond budget and consuming several percent of it with unpredictable tail variance layered on top, on the single message type that arrives nine times out of ten.

#### FIFO at the head, or pro-rata across the level
Deciding how an incoming order is allocated against multiple resting orders at the same price is stated as a venue rule, and its engineering cost is what actually decides whether it is affordable.

[The head of the queue as the only order touched per fill](/diagram/matching-engine?focus=fifo,match-loop,e7)

**Bad: allocate strictly by arrival time, with no accommodation for size.** Gives an unambiguous, O(1) tie-break, since the fill is always simply the list head, and it is a real venue rule with a real economic consequence: on instruments where a handful of large participants would otherwise dominate the front of every queue, quoting can collapse entirely, since nobody smaller can meaningfully compete for priority.

**Good: pro-rata allocation, giving every resting order at a level a share proportional to its size, with no special case for the first order.** Solves the domination problem directly, and without any bias toward the order that arrived first, it removes the incentive to post early at all, which is precisely the behaviour that keeps a book liquid in normal, uncontested conditions.

**Great: choose per venue rule, understanding the engineering cost is asymmetric.** Strict FIFO touches only the list head per fill, an O(1) operation regardless of how many orders sit behind it. Pro-rata has to touch every order at the level to compute each one's proportional share, so a level holding thousands of resting orders costs thousands of pointer chases per fill instead of one, and needs rounding rules that are byte-stable enough to survive a deterministic replay.

Worked example: a price level holding 2,000 resting orders costs a strict-FIFO engine exactly one pointer dereference per fill, regardless of how deep the queue behind the head grows. The identical level under pro-rata allocation costs roughly 2,000 pointer chases for that same single fill, which is why most listed short-term interest-rate futures, where large participants genuinely would otherwise monopolise the queue, accept that cost deliberately as a pro-rata or hybrid rule, while the overwhelming majority of instruments correctly default to the far cheaper strict FIFO.

#### Fires exactly at the crossing, never on a level
An incoming order does not simply "match" a price, it walks a sequence of levels, filling what it can and stopping the instant it no longer crosses, and getting the stopping condition wrong corrupts every trade after it.

[The walk from the touch, filling the FIFO head at each level until the order no longer crosses](/diagram/matching-engine?focus=match-loop,best-ptr,level-array,fifo,remainder,e5,e6,e7,e10,e11,e12)

**Bad: walk the opposite side and fill against every resting order regardless of price, stopping only when the incoming quantity is exhausted.** Ignores the incoming order's own limit price entirely, which means a limit order can trade through prices its owner never agreed to, a direct violation of the entire purpose of setting a limit in the first place.

**Good: check the limit price once, before the walk begins, and then fill everything the walk touches.** Prevents trading beyond the stated limit at the moment of the check, and a single check taken before the loop starts does not account for the fact that the incoming order's remaining quantity, and therefore whether it should keep walking to the next level at all, changes with every single fill inside that same loop.

**Great: re-check whether the order still crosses the opposite side's best price before advancing to each successive level, stopping the instant it does not.** The walk fills `min(incoming, resting)` at the current best level, advances only if quantity remains and the next level still crosses the incoming order's limit, and stops the moment either the order is exhausted or the next level no longer qualifies.

Worked example: a buy limit at $190.05 walking down a thin ask side fills fully against the best ask at $190.00, partially against the next level at $190.03, and then finds the level at $190.06 does not cross its own limit price at all, so the walk stops there with a remainder. That remainder, if the order is a day limit, becomes new resting liquidity on the bid side at $190.05; if the order was IOC, FOK, or market, the identical remainder is simply cancelled rather than left resting, with the crossing check itself being what decides where that boundary falls, not a separate quantity check bolted on afterward.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 200" role="img" aria-label="A marketable order sweeping two price levels touches four cache lines total: two level headers and the two order records at their heads">
  <style>
    .touch{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.3;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.5}
    .t{font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif;fill:currentColor;opacity:.8}
    .b{font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif;fill:currentColor}
  </style>
  <text class="b" x="8" y="14">two levels swept, four 64-byte cache lines</text>
  <rect class="touch" x="8" y="24" width="376" height="24" rx="5"/><text class="t" x="16" y="40">1. level header, best</text>
  <rect class="touch" x="8" y="52" width="376" height="24" rx="5"/><text class="t" x="16" y="68">2. order record, head</text>
  <rect class="touch" x="8" y="80" width="376" height="24" rx="5"/><text class="t" x="16" y="96">3. level header, next</text>
  <rect class="touch" x="8" y="108" width="376" height="24" rx="5"/><text class="t" x="16" y="124">4. order record, head</text>
  <text class="t" x="8" y="152">nothing else in the book is read; the rest</text>
  <text class="t" x="8" y="168">of both levels stays untouched, already</text>
  <text class="t" x="8" y="184">resident in L1/L2 on an active symbol</text>
</svg>
```

#### Self-trade prevention sits inside the loop, not after it
Preventing a participant from trading against their own resting order looks like a check that could run anywhere convenient, and where it actually runs decides whether it can see what it needs to.

[The check evaluated against the specific pair about to trade](/diagram/matching-engine?focus=fifo,stp,outputs,e8,e9)

**Bad: scan for self-trades after a batch of fills has already been emitted, and reverse any that violate the policy.** Simple to reason about as a separate pass, and reversing an already-emitted fill means retracting a trade that participants, market data subscribers and downstream systems may already have observed and acted on, which is a far more damaging correction than never emitting it in the first place.

**Good: check self-trade eligibility once, at order entry, before the order enters the matching loop at all.** Catches the case where a participant's own resting order happens to already be at the best price when the incoming order arrives, and it cannot catch the case where the incoming order's own walk reaches a different one of that same participant's resting orders several levels deeper into the book.

**Great: check immediately before each individual fill is emitted, comparing the specific incoming order against the specific resting order about to trade.** Because the check runs inside the same loop, against the exact pair that is about to be matched, it catches self-trades at every level the walk reaches, not only the first, and the chosen policy, cancelling the incoming order, cancelling the resting one, or decrementing both, is applied before anything is ever emitted rather than corrected afterward.

Worked example: a participant's incoming order walks three price levels deep into the book, where the first two resting orders belong to other participants and the third happens to belong to the same firm. A check performed only once at order entry, against the best price at arrival, never inspects that third level and lets the self-trade through; the in-loop check evaluates every candidate resting order immediately before it would be filled, catching the collision at exactly the level where it occurs and applying the venue's policy before any fill involving that pair is ever emitted.

#### Where it breaks
| Layer | Failure | How the design handles it |
|---|---|---|
| Hot book | A single very active symbol cannot be sped up by adding threads, by design | A dedicated shard and pinned core with local memory, plus zero hot-path allocation, buy a bounded constant-factor improvement rather than parallelism |
| Input queue | Producers outrun the matcher during a burst | A bounded ring buffer with explicit rejection, never silent drops, so overload degrades predictably instead of growing without limit |
| Hot-path allocation | Object churn per event risks a garbage-collection pause inside the latency budget | Pre-allocated order slots and reused objects keep steady-state allocation at zero |
| Durable journal | Writing every event before acknowledging risks dominating latency | Sequential append with group commit on its own device, so the journal never contends with book memory access |
| Cross-instrument events | A basket order touching multiple books breaks the one-writer-per-book model | Handled on a separate coordinating boundary with two-phase reservation, never by taking a lock inside a single book |
| Market-data fanout | Thousands of subscribers on a hot tick can back up the publisher | Latest-wins conflated snapshot fanout on a separate tier, so a slow subscriber never backpressures the matcher itself |
| Book integrity | A bug leaves the book crossed, with the best bid at or above the best ask | An invariant check asserted after every apply treats any violation as a correctness incident, halting the instrument rather than continuing |

#### What this design does not solve
**A single symbol that genuinely outgrows one core has no fix inside this design.** Splitting a book across threads is a correctness bug rather than a scaling lever, because concurrent matching reorders fills and destroys the time priority the entire product depends on. Every available escape hatch, a dedicated shard, core pinning, a lower-overhead runtime, zero allocation, is a constant-factor improvement, realistically three to five times, never the order-of-magnitude gain true parallelism would offer, and past that limit the only honest answer changes the product itself: listing the instrument across two independent books with a router splitting flow, which means there is no longer a single price-time queue and participants must reconcile two feeds themselves.

**The dense tick array has no graceful response to a price move outside the band it was sized for.** A limit-up move, a corporate action, or a resumption after a long halt can put the market entirely outside a book's allocated tick range. Rebasing that array mid-session is precisely the kind of hot-path allocation the rest of the design specifically forbids, so the only available response today is pausing the instrument, rebuilding the band, and resuming, which forces a brief halt at exactly the moment of highest volatility, the worst possible time for one to happen.

**Auctions are a second matching algorithm sharing the same structure, not a variant of the continuous one.** The open and close uncross maximises executed volume at a single clearing price through a scan across the whole band, with its own tie-break rules for imbalance, which is a fundamentally different operation from a walk starting at the touch. It runs on the identical thread and data as continuous matching, but it is a genuinely separate implementation, and the mode transitions between continuous and auction phases are where the sharpest, hardest-to-reproduce bugs in a real exchange tend to live.

#### Final design
Read it back through the numbers. Cancels making up roughly 90% of all traffic is why the entire layout is built around removing an order in a single memory access rather than around inserting one. The roughly 50x gap between a 4-nanosecond array load and a 200-nanosecond hash lookup is why that removal is a flat slot-table subscript rather than any form of hashing, on a path where every nanosecond is a real fraction of the total budget. A dense tick array costing under 500KB for a typical liquid book, but nearly 5GB if applied indiscriminately across every listed instrument, is exactly why the design runs two storage strategies rather than one, dense for the hot list, a tree for the tail. A marketable order touching only about four cache lines is the entire justification for padding every level header to exactly one cache line's width. And one core alone comfortably clearing several times the venue's raw throughput requirement is the reason sharding exists to isolate hot instruments and provide headroom, not because a single thread is somehow too slow to keep up.

[The whole design, from a sequenced event to a printed fill and its invariant checks](/diagram/matching-engine?focus=inbound,dispatch,match-loop,stp,remainder,outputs,slot-table,best-ptr,level-array,fifo,tree-tail,invariants)

> **The numbers to remember.** Cancels are ~90% of traffic · an array load beats a hash lookup by roughly 50x · a dense tick array costs ~486KB per book, ~4.9GB done venue-wide · a marketable order touches roughly 4 cache lines · one core alone clears several times the raw throughput target.

#### Check your understanding
**Why is price stored as a direct array subscript instead of in a sorted tree, for the instruments that matter most?** A tree needs real comparison work and pointer chasing even at a modest number of distinct price levels, on a path measured in nanoseconds. A tick-indexed array turns finding a price level into a single, predictable memory access with no comparison at all, at the cost of memory proportional to the tradable price range rather than to the number of orders actually resting in it.

**Why does a cancel use a dense slot table instead of a hash map keyed on order id?** Cancels make up roughly 90% of all traffic, so whatever mechanism finds an order to remove is paid on nine messages out of every ten. A hash lookup costs on the order of 200 nanoseconds with unpredictable tail variance from its probe length, while a dense internal id in a flat slot table costs a single, predictable array load of a few nanoseconds.

**Why does strict FIFO cost less than pro-rata allocation at a price level?** A FIFO fill only ever needs to touch the list head, an O(1) operation no matter how many orders sit behind it in the queue. Pro-rata allocation has to compute a proportional share for every resting order at that level to fill even one incoming order, so a level with thousands of resting orders costs thousands of pointer chases for a single fill instead of one.

**Why is self-trade prevention checked immediately before each individual fill rather than once at order entry?** A check performed only at entry sees only the best price at that instant and cannot see a resting order belonging to the same participant several price levels deeper into the book that the incoming order's walk will reach later in the same match. Checking against the exact pair about to trade, inside the loop, catches a self-trade at whatever level it actually occurs and applies the venue's policy before anything is emitted, rather than needing to retract an already-visible trade afterward.

**Why can a single hot instrument never be sped up by adding more threads to its book?** Concurrent matching against the same book would let fills be applied out of the strict arrival order that defines time priority, and because trades represent real money that must replay to an identical byte-for-byte result, any reordering is a correctness failure rather than a performance trade-off. The only safe way to add capacity to a genuinely saturated instrument is a constant-factor improvement to the single thread already serving it, never a second thread touching the same book.
### 43. Design a High-Throughput Market Data Ingest Pipeline
#### Understanding the problem
An exchange publishes a firehose: price ticks on every quote and trade, plus the orders and cancels traders send back. The job is to take many of these streams at once, agree on one order for everything that happened, and hand each instrument's slice of that order to the engine that matches its book.

Three things make it hard.

First, the order has to be a single, deterministic decision. Two venues can quote the same instrument microseconds apart, and something downstream has to say, without ambiguity, which one came first. Wall clocks on different machines cannot settle that.

Second, the edge cannot stall. A socket reader that blocks on anything downstream lets the kernel's receive buffer fill, and on a multicast feed that is silent packet loss at the worst possible moment.

Third, not every message is allowed to be dropped the same way. A price tick is a snapshot you can overwrite. An order is money someone is trying to move, and it can never vanish without telling anyone.

> **What this is not.** It looks like ad click aggregation: many streams, a fan-in, a fan-out, millions of events a second. The difference is what a mistake costs. Ad click aggregation publishes an approximate number and corrects it overnight from raw events kept in storage, so a click counted twice becomes correct later. Here the consumer is a matching engine, and its output is an executed trade. A message dropped or reordered is not an estimate that gets fixed, it is a wrong trade, so the design spends its complexity on gap-free sequencing and byte-identical replay instead of on watermarks and a batch correction.

#### Requirements and the numbers
**Functional.** Ingest many concurrent venue streams across different wire protocols and normalise them into one canonical event. Stamp every event into a single gap-free sequence. Fan out to per-instrument consumers, preserving each instrument's order. Conflate price ticks under load; never silently drop an order or a cancel. Expose a data-plane subscribe stream and a control-plane order API.

**Non-functional.** Millions of messages a second at peak. Ingest-to-dispatch latency in the tens of microseconds at p99. Zero order-flow loss. Bounded, predictable memory even under sustained overload. Deterministic ordering, so a crash can be replayed exactly.

The whole design is decided by four numbers, so derive them before drawing anything.

**What is the peak we design for?** Market data plus order flow, combined across the venue, at the open, the close, and on news. Take **2M messages a second** as the planning peak.

**How is that peak spread across instruments?** About 10,000 instruments trade. 2,000,000 ÷ 10,000 = **200 messages a second per instrument on average**, but the top 10 symbols alone carry 30 to 40% of all traffic. Average load is not the number that decides shard sizing; skew is.

**What does the wire format cost?** 2,000,000 × 32 bytes ≈ **64MB/s** as packed binary. The same event as JSON runs 150 to 250 bytes, so 2,000,000 × 150 to 2,000,000 × 250 ≈ **300 to 500MB/s**, five to eight times more for identical information.

**How much headroom does a single writer need?** A stage that only assigns a number and writes a slot has been benchmarked past 6M messages a second on one core. Against a 2M peak that is roughly **3x headroom** (6,000,000 ÷ 2,000,000 = 3).

> **The numbers to carry.** 2M msg/s peak · ~10k instruments, top 10 take 30 to 40% · 64MB/s packed binary vs 300 to 500MB/s JSON · ~3x sequencer headroom · p99 tens of microseconds.

#### Two rules, one pipeline
The pipeline looks like one problem and is really two, with different rhythms. **Ordering** is a single decision made once, cheaply, at one point in the pipeline. **Shedding** runs continuously, at every stage, and the answer depends on what kind of message is in front of it.

The entities:

- **Event** `{seq, instrument_id, kind, venue, side, price, quantity, source_ts, ingest_ts}`, the canonical shape every venue protocol decodes into, roughly 32 bytes packed.
- **Venue sequence**: the feed's own per-message counter, published by the exchange. It can have holes.
- **Internal sequence**: the number our pipeline assigns. Gap-free by construction, because one writer assigns it.
- **Instrument**: the partition key. A book's events must keep their relative order; books are independent of one another.
- **Conflation slot**: one per instrument, holding only the freshest tick a shard has not yet consumed.

The API is a streaming read and a small request-response control surface:

```
subscribe(instrument_id | instrument_set, from_seq?) -> stream<Event>
  # server-streaming or a multicast group join; from_seq resumes after a gap

submit_order(instrument_id, participant_id, side, type, price?, quantity, tif,
             client_order_id) -> { status: ACCEPTED | REJECTED | BUSY, seq, reason? }
cancel_order(instrument_id, order_id, participant_id) -> { status, seq }

Event {
  seq, instrument_id, kind: TICK | ORDER | CANCEL | TRADE,
  venue, side, price, quantity,
  source_ts,   # the venue's clock
  ingest_ts    # ours
}
```

#### High-level design
Follow the numbered arrows. Every message crosses the same seven stages, whatever venue or protocol it started as.

[The hot path, feeds to matching](/diagram/market-data-ingest?focus=venue-feeds,feed-handlers,normaliser,sequencer,ordered-ring,dispatch,shards,matching-cores,e1,e6,e8,e9,e11,e14,e18)

1. **Venue feeds** publish a tick firehose as two identical multicast copies over separate paths, each message carrying the venue's own sequence number.
2. **Feed handlers**, one thin process per stream, do nothing but drain the socket and decode the venue's frame.
3. The **Normaliser** turns FIX, an ITCH-style binary and a proprietary frame into one canonical event, decoded into a pre-allocated struct.
4. The **Sequencer**, a single writer, assigns the next monotonic number and claims a slot in the **Ordered ring**.
5. **Fan-out** batch-drains the ring and routes each event by `hash(instrumentId)`.
6. **Per-instrument shards** each own a set of books and apply events strictly in the sequence they were stamped.
7. **Matching cores** take the ordered, per-instrument stream and turn it into executed trades. This pipeline's job ends there.

> **Why the flow is shaped this way.** Every stage that could stall the socket has been moved off the drain path. The Sequencer is deliberately given almost nothing to do, because every microsecond spent there comes straight off the venue's throughput ceiling. Fan-out hashes on the instrument, not the arrival order, because ordering only has to hold within a book, and books do not need to agree with each other.

#### One writer, one total order
How do you decide, with no lock, which of two near-simultaneous events happened first?

[The sequencer's claim](/diagram/market-data-ingest?focus=normaliser,sequencer,ordered-ring,e8,e9)

**Bad: stamp each event with the wall clock of the machine that received it.** Two venues quoting the same instrument within microseconds now race to be first in the queue, and two machines' clocks are never close enough to settle it. Worse, the stamp is assigned by whichever thread happens to run first, so replaying the same captured traffic twice can produce two different orders.

**Good: let each feed handler assign its own local counter, independently.** That fixes ordering within one feed, but nothing tells you how feed A's counter relates to feed B's. Merging two feeds still needs an arbitrary decision at merge time, and a consumer asking "what happened first, globally" has no answer.

**Great: one thread, the Sequencer, is the only writer that ever assigns a sequence number.** It does exactly three things: increment a counter, write the event into a claimed **Ordered ring** slot, and append it to the journal. Nothing else runs on that thread, no parsing, no risk checks, no logging, because every microsecond there is a microsecond off the pipeline's ceiling. Because only one thread ever writes, there is no lock and no compare-and-swap contention: the next slot is simply the next slot.

The arithmetic is what makes this affordable rather than a bottleneck. A stage that only assigns a number and writes a slot has been benchmarked past 6M events a second on a single core. Against a 2M planning peak that is 6,000,000 ÷ 2,000,000 ≈ 3x headroom, so a global total order across every instrument is close to free. Below roughly 2x headroom the design stops trusting it and shards the whole pipeline by instrument range instead, accepting that a global order is no longer available.

That single decision is made exactly once and inherited as fact by every consumer, every replay and every audit downstream. There is no second pass that could catch a mistake here.

#### Partition by book, never by turn
Once events are in one order, how do you spread them across consumers without breaking that order?

[Fan-out and the shards](/diagram/market-data-ingest?focus=ordered-ring,dispatch,shards,e11,e14)

**Bad: round-robin across N consumers, spreading load evenly.** Evenly spread is the wrong goal. Instrument A's first event lands on consumer 0, its second on consumer 1, its third back on consumer 0. Nothing downstream can reconstruct A's true order without collecting every consumer's output and merging it again, which defeats the point of sequencing in the first place.

**Good: route by venue or feed instead of by instrument.** This keeps one feed's messages together, but a feed still carries thousands of instruments on one queue, so a quiet symbol waits behind a busy one on the same shard, and the granularity is far coarser than the actual unit of correctness, which is one book.

**Great: partition by `hash(instrumentId)`.** The same instrument always lands on the same shard, in the sequence order it was stamped with. Ordering only has to hold inside a book, and books are independent of each other, so this turns one global guarantee into many small ones that can run in parallel with zero coordination between shards.

The figure below shows why the difference matters, not just that it does.

[Round-robin scatters a book; hashing keeps it on one shard](/diagram/market-data-ingest?figure=shard-by-book)

Skew is the residual problem, and it is solved by placement, not by dispatch. The top 10 instruments carry 30 to 40% of all traffic, and one hot book cannot be split without breaking its order. Shards are assigned by measured load rather than an even hash bucket count, so a whale instrument gets a dedicated core with memory local to it, while an average instrument at 200 messages a second shares comfortably.

#### What you are allowed to drop
Under sustained overload, a shard falls behind. What happens to the message waiting for it?

[The overload split](/diagram/market-data-ingest?focus=dispatch,conflation,order-gateway,shards,e12,e13,e15)

**Bad: treat every message the same and drop the oldest once the queue is full.** This discards whichever message has waited longest, tick or order alike. For an order, that is a trade that silently never happened. For a tick, it keeps a stale price and throws away the fresh one behind it, which is exactly backwards.

**Good: bound every queue and apply backpressure uniformly, dropping nothing.** This is correct for order flow: slow the producer or reject explicitly, and nobody's trade vanishes without a trace. Applied to ticks, though, it is wrong in a different way. A tick queued behind a backlog is delivered milliseconds late, and nobody needs the price from three milliseconds ago once a fresher one exists.

**Great: classify by message kind before deciding what happens.** A **Conflation map** holds one slot per instrument, the freshest unconsumed tick. A new tick simply overwrites the previous one in that slot; nothing is queued, nothing grows. An order or a cancel can never go anywhere near that map. It is state that accumulates, so the **Order entry gateway** either lets it through, slows the sending participant, or answers with an explicit busy status. Never a silent drop.

Why this is safe: a tick is a fact about right now, and the old value is worthless the moment a new one exists. An order is a fact about intent, and intent does not expire just because the system is busy.

[A tick overwrites its slot; an order queues, then backs off](/diagram/market-data-ingest?figure=tick-vs-order)

#### Filling a hole nobody reported
Multicast never tells you a packet went missing. How do you even find out, and what do you do while you wait?

[Arbitration and gap detection](/diagram/market-data-ingest?focus=venue-feeds,edge-group,gap-arb,e1,e2,e3,e4,e5)

**Bad: trust the transport and assume every packet arrives.** Nothing detects the hole, so the book silently drifts from the true one. A consumer trades against a price that is wrong and has no way to know it.

**Good: subscribe to one copy, watch the venue's own sequence number, and request a retransmit the instant a gap appears.** This finds the hole, which is real progress, but it is slow and trigger-happy. A retransmit round trip plus the venue's recovery queue costs 5 to 50 milliseconds every single time, and firing on the first out-of-order message also means requesting packets that were merely reordered and about to arrive anyway. A venue-wide burst then means every participant requests at once, exactly when the recovery service is slowest.

**Great: subscribe to both of the venue's redundant multicast copies and arbitrate.** Keep whichever copy of a given sequence number lands first, discard the duplicate. Loss confined to one network path now costs nothing: it is repaired within the arrival spread between the two copies, typically tens of microseconds, with no request at all. Only a hole in both copies escalates, and even then a short timer waits before firing, because most apparent gaps are just reordering.

The recovery ladder runs fastest first: the B copy in tens of microseconds, retransmit at 5 to 50 milliseconds for a bounded hole, then a periodic snapshot refresh, 1 to 30 seconds, for anything larger. Meanwhile, every affected instrument is marked stale and stops publishing its book, because a book known to be missing messages is worse than no book at all.


#### Replay that reproduces the day
After a crash, how do you rebuild a shard's state without lying about what actually happened?

[Journal, snapshot, replay](/diagram/market-data-ingest?focus=sequencer,ordered-ring,journal,shards,e9,e10,e17)

**Bad: restart cold and rebuild only from new traffic.** Everything the shard knew before the crash is gone. The book resumes from an empty state and disagrees with reality until enough fresh messages arrive to catch it up, if they ever fully do.

**Good: take a full snapshot of consumer state periodically and restore the latest one on restart.** This recovers most of the state cheaply, but anything that happened between the last snapshot and the crash is still lost unless the raw events were kept somewhere too, and snapshotting often enough to close that gap competes with the hot path for time.

**Great: append every sequenced event to the Journal + snapshots store, and snapshot consumer state every 30 seconds.** A crash costs at most 30 seconds of replay: load the newest snapshot, then replay the log forward from its sequence number. The replay reads sequentially and mostly from a warm cache, so it runs far faster than line rate.

Replay is only trustworthy if it is deterministic, and that has to be enforced deliberately rather than assumed. No wall-clock reads on the processing path, only the timestamps carried in the event itself. No iteration over a hash map whose order depends on insertion history. No branching on which thread happened to run first. The test that matters is that replaying a captured session twice produces byte-identical output both times, and a hot standby runs exactly this replay continuously, so promoting it on failure is instant rather than a rebuild from nothing.

#### Where it breaks
| Layer | Failure | How the design handles it |
|---|---|---|
| Feed handler | One process dies, a whole feed goes dark | Per-feed heartbeat catches the zero rate; restart and rejoin the multicast group; gap detection replays the missed range |
| Sequencer | The single writer crashes | A hot standby replaying the same journal in lockstep is promoted; it resumes from the last durable sequence |
| Shard | A consumer falls behind | Its ticks conflate to latest; its order flow backpressures at the producer; the gap between producer and consumer cursors is alarmed on |
| Transport | A multicast packet is lost | The recovery ladder runs: the B copy, then a retransmit, then a snapshot refresh; nothing is ever silently skipped |
| Ring buffer | A bounded ring fills under a burst | Conflate ticks, backpressure or reject order flow; the ring stays bounded on purpose so overload has a defined outcome |
| Standby link | Replication to the hot standby drops | The primary continues unaffected within its RPO budget; the standby catches up by replaying the journal once reconnected |

#### What this design does not solve
**Cross-instrument events have no home.** A basket order or a portfolio-level risk check needs a consistent view across several books, and partitioning by instrument gives it none once the pipeline shards. The honest answer is a separate, far slower coordinating path with its own sequencer, running at millisecond latency rather than microsecond, so the venue ends up with two latency tiers and callers have to know which one they are using.

**The sequence number is arrival order, not market order.** Events are stamped in the order our own network hardware happened to see them, which reflects the path length from each venue to us, not the order the markets actually moved. Any consumer reasoning about cross-venue causality will sometimes be wrong. Carrying both `source_ts` and `ingest_ts` on every event, and timestamping at the network card, narrows the error but never removes it, because the total order is ours, not the market's.

**Sustained order-flow overload has no graceful answer.** Conflation only helps the traffic class this pipeline is allowed to lose, and order flow is never that class. If order flow alone exceeds what a shard can absorb, the only correct responses are backpressure, which penalises every client sharing that connection, or an explicit reject, which is a visible failure. Per-participant credit quotas at the **Order entry gateway** ration the damage to the one client whose burst caused it, but rationing is not extra capacity.

#### Final design
Read it back through the numbers. A 2M message peak spread thin across 10,000 instruments, but concentrated 30 to 40% into 10 symbols, is what forces partitioning by instrument rather than by turn. A single writer with 3x headroom over that peak is what makes one global order affordable rather than a bottleneck. A 5 to 8 times bandwidth gap between packed binary and JSON is what keeps the firehose off any format with human-readable fields. And the choice between overwriting a tick and accumulating an order is what lets the whole pipeline survive a burst without an out-of-memory failure or a lost trade.

[The whole design](/diagram/market-data-ingest?focus=venue-feeds,order-gateway,edge-group,feed-handlers,gap-arb,normaliser,sequencer,ordered-ring,journal,dispatch,conflation,shards,matching-cores)

> **The numbers to remember.** 2M msg/s peak · top 10 instruments carry 30 to 40% of it · ~3x sequencer headroom over peak · 64MB/s packed binary vs 300 to 500MB/s JSON · 30 second snapshot cadence bounds replay to 30 seconds.

#### Check your understanding
**Why can't the Sequencer use wall clocks to order two near-simultaneous events?** Two machines' clocks are never close enough to settle microsecond-scale ties, and replaying the same traffic could then produce a different order each time. One writer assigning one counter removes the ambiguity entirely, with no lock required.

**A round-robin dispatcher spreads load evenly across shards. What breaks?** One instrument's events land on different shards depending on arrival position, so no single shard ever holds that book's true order. Hashing on the instrument keeps every event for one book on one shard, in the order it was stamped.

**A shard falls behind under load. What happens to a queued tick versus a queued order?** The tick is conflated: a fresh one simply overwrites the stale one in its per-instrument slot, and nothing is ever queued. The order is never touched by conflation; it backpressures the producer or returns an explicit busy status instead.

**Multicast drops a packet silently. How does the pipeline even find out?** The venue's own per-feed sequence number is the only signal, since the transport itself reports nothing. A message above the expected counter starts a timer, and the redundant B copy usually fills the hole within tens of microseconds before a retransmit is ever needed.

**The Sequencer sits at 80% of one core doing only its three jobs. What do you do?** There is no incremental fix, since it is a single-writer ceiling by design. The only lever left is sharding the whole pipeline by instrument range, which costs the ability to answer what the venue looked like at any single sequence number.
### 44. Design Strava (Fitness Activity Tracking)
#### Understanding the problem
An athlete finishes a ride. The phone has a GPS track. The product has to turn that track into a distance, a moving time and a climb figure, work out which of roughly 35 million user-drawn segments the ride actually covered, time each one, update a leaderboard, and publish the ride to a feed. All without revealing where the athlete lives.

Three things make this hard.

First, the expensive comparison is against a corpus, not against the request. One upload has to be checked against 35 million stored segments, and the corpus is thousands of times bigger than anything in the request itself.

Second, "matched" is an ordering question, not a distance one. A road crossed at a junction is close to a segment for an instant. A ride on the opposite carriageway is close to it for the entire length. Neither traversed it.

Third, the same route ridden most mornings is a location, whether or not anyone meant it to be. Hiding a radius around the house is not the same as hiding the house.

> **What this is not.** It looks like a proximity service: index a corpus by location, answer what is nearby. The resemblance stops at the index. A proximity service asks a single point plus a radius, on read, against a corpus that barely changes, so the cell index genuinely is the whole answer. Here the query is itself a 3,600-point ordered track, it runs once per upload rather than being cached, the predicate is contiguous directional traversal rather than distance, and the corpus mutates retroactively: a segment created today has to reach back and find efforts in rides recorded years earlier.

#### Requirements and the numbers
**Functional.** Record GPS and sensor data offline. Upload and parse FIT, GPX or TCX. Clean the track and derive distance, moving time and elevation gain. Match against user-created segments to produce timed efforts and leaderboards. Publish to a social feed. Enforce privacy zones. Render aggregate heatmaps.

**Non-functional.** Zero activity loss once the upload is acknowledged. Upload-to-feed p95 under 30 seconds, upload-to-efforts p95 under 90 seconds. Feed reads p99 under 200ms, leaderboard reads p99 under 100ms. A privacy-zone endpoint must never be fittable back to a true home location.

The whole design is decided by four numbers, so derive them before drawing anything.

**What does the naive match cost?** One comparison per segment, at roughly 1 microsecond each: 35,000,000 × 1µs ≈ **35 seconds of CPU per upload**.

**How many uploads a second?** Roughly 2.5 billion activities a year. 2,500,000,000 ÷ 31,500,000 seconds ≈ **80 uploads a second steady**, and a predictable weekend-morning spike takes that to **~800 a second**.

**What does the naive cost become at scale?** 35 seconds × 80/s ≈ **2,800 cores steady**, and 35 seconds × 800/s ≈ **28,000 cores at peak**, just to keep pace with matching alone.

**How big is the corpus in memory?** ~35,000,000 segments at ~500 bytes each ≈ **18GB**, small enough to sit resident in RAM on every matcher, rather than behind a network call.

> **The numbers to carry.** 80 uploads/s steady, ~800/s peak · 35M segments, ~18GB RAM-resident · naive match ~35s CPU/upload vs a funnel at ~100ms · ~2KB feed summary against a ~30KB detail stream, 15x apart.

#### The upload path and the matching join
The pipeline is really two problems wearing one name. The **upload path** is deliberately dumb: get bytes durable and acknowledge fast. The **matching join** is where all the real cost and all the real risk live, run once per activity against a corpus that never stops growing.

The entities:

- **Activity**: one recorded track, split at storage time into a small **summary** (feed) and a large **stream** (detail, fetched on tap).
- **Segment**: a user-drawn stretch of road or trail, stored as a polyline with a start point, a bounding box and a direction.
- **Effort**: one timed traversal of one segment by one activity, the highest-row-count table in the system.
- **S2 cell**: a fixed tile of the Earth's surface, keyed to a 64-bit id; a coarser prefix means a larger, containing tile.

The control surface is small; the volume is in the events behind it:

```
POST /uploads/init                → { upload_id, put_url }
PUT  <put_url>       body: bytes  → 200
POST /uploads/{id}/commit         → { status: "processing" }
GET  /activities/{id}             → { summary, polyline, efforts[] }
GET  /activities/{id}/streams     → { streams: {...} }
GET  /segments/{id}/leaderboard   → [{ rank, athlete, elapsed }]
```

#### High-level design
Follow the flow from a phone finishing a ride to a leaderboard entry and a feed card.

[The hot path, upload to efforts](/diagram/strava?focus=upload-api,kafka,workers,matcher,seg-index,efforts,e3,e4,e9,e10,e11)

1. The **Mobile app** buffers every sample to disk, then PUTs the finished file straight to the **Raw upload store** and calls the **Upload API** to commit.
2. The **Upload API** records the intent and publishes to **Kafka: activity.uploaded**, returning `202` in about 150ms.
3. **Processing workers** consume the event, parse the file, clean the GPS and derive distance, moving time and elevation gain.
4. Workers hand the cleaned track to the **Segment matcher**, which narrows candidates against the **Segments + S2 cell index**.
5. Surviving matches are written to the **Efforts store**, and each triggers a conditional write into **Leaderboards**.
6. Workers also write a summary to the **Activity summary store**, and **Feed fan-out** pushes it into followers' timelines.
7. The **Mobile app** reads the feed directly, and only fetches the **Activity stream store** when the athlete taps into an activity's detail view.

> **Why the flow is shaped this way.** The user-perceived cost of an upload and the actual cost of processing it are unrelated, so a queue sits between them. The matcher is the only stage whose cost scales with the size of the whole global corpus rather than with one activity, which is why its index sits in memory beside it rather than behind a database call.

#### Sizing the join by the corpus, not the request
How do you check one track against 35 million stored segments without burning 2,800 cores just to keep up?

[The funnel](/diagram/strava?focus=matcher,seg-index,e9,e10,e11)

**Bad: compare the track to every segment.** Correct and simple, and 35,000,000 × 1µs ≈ 35 seconds of CPU per upload. At 80 uploads a second that is 2,800 cores running continuously, and 28,000 at the Saturday peak, to answer a question the athlete expects settled before they have put the bike away.

**Good: push the join into a spatially indexed database.** Ask, per upload, which segments lie within some distance of the track. Nothing has to be replicated, and a brand-new segment matches immediately. It falls over on request rate: at 80 to 800 proximity queries a second against one shared store, each returning thousands of rows that still need filtering by hand, the database becomes the ceiling and the real matching work still has to run afterwards, in the application.

**Great: a narrowing funnel, cheapest test first, each stage allowed false positives but never a false negative.** Cover the track with level-13 S2 cells and look up segments whose start point falls in one, taking 35,000,000 down to about 9,800 as a pure hash lookup, roughly 3ms. Reject on bounding box, to about 1,200, roughly 1ms. Test a 15m corridor against the track's own points, to about 50, roughly 20ms. Only then run the expensive ordered match on the survivors, down to about 22 confirmed efforts, roughly 30ms.

The stage 1 correctness argument is short and it is the whole reason this is safe to run sloppy-first: a real effort requires a complete traversal, a complete traversal necessarily passes through the segment's start point, and the start point therefore falls within the corridor width of some track point. So the cell index can shrink 35 million to 9,800 candidates without ever discarding a genuine match.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="-4 -7 409 268" role="img" aria-label="The funnel narrows 35 million segments to 22 confirmed efforts across four stages, each cheaper than the last">
  <style>
    .bar{fill:none;stroke:currentColor;stroke-width:1.2}
    .fill{fill:currentColor;fill-opacity:.10}
    .fillacc{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.22;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.4}
    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    .sub{fill:currentColor;opacity:.8;font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
  </style>
  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="14">Candidates surviving each stage (log scale)</text>

  <text class="sub" x="4" y="34">Stage 0 · every segment</text><text class="sub" x="396" y="34" text-anchor="end">35,000,000</text>
  <rect class="bar fill" x="4" y="40" width="384" height="14" rx="4"/>

  <text class="sub" x="4" y="74">Stage 1 · S2 cell prefilter, ~3ms</text><text class="sub" x="396" y="74" text-anchor="end">~9,800</text>
  <rect class="bar fill" x="4" y="80" width="110" height="14" rx="4"/>

  <text class="sub" x="4" y="114">Stage 2 · bbox reject, ~1ms</text><text class="sub" x="396" y="114" text-anchor="end">~1,200</text>
  <rect class="bar fill" x="4" y="120" width="44" height="14" rx="4"/>

  <text class="sub" x="4" y="154">Stage 3 · corridor test, ~20ms</text><text class="sub" x="396" y="154" text-anchor="end">~50</text>
  <rect class="bar fill" x="4" y="160" width="17" height="14" rx="4"/>

  <text class="sub" x="4" y="194">Stage 4 · map-match, ~30ms</text><text class="sub" x="396" y="194" text-anchor="end">22 efforts</text>
  <rect class="bar fillacc" x="4" y="200" width="9" height="14" rx="4"/>

  <text class="sub" x="4" y="234">Total ~55ms p50 per upload,</text>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="250">against ~35s for a full scan: a ~640x reduction</text>
</svg>
```

The corpus mutates under this design in one uncomfortable way. A segment created today was never in the index when a five-year-old ride was processed, so it earns no efforts from that ride until a bounded backfill sweep re-checks it.

#### Matching is ordering, not proximity
Once a segment is a candidate, what actually decides whether the athlete traversed it?

[The corridor and the cursor](/diagram/strava?focus=matcher,e9,e11)

**Bad: does the track pass near the segment?** A ride on the opposite carriageway of a dual carriageway, roughly 11 metres away, is well inside any generous proximity radius for the segment's entire length. So is a ride that crosses the segment once at a junction and carries on somewhere else entirely. Proximity alone gives both a match, and neither is one.

**Good: require every segment point to be near some track point, in any order.** This is the corridor test, and it is a genuine improvement: it demands coverage, not one lucky close pass. It still cannot tell a through-traversal from a crossing, because a track that touches every part of a segment out of sequence, doubling back and criss-crossing, still passes.

**Great: walk the segment's vertices in order against a cursor into the track that only ever advances.** For each vertex, scan forward from the cursor for the nearest track point within the corridor; if none appears within a bounded look-ahead, the candidate fails outright. Direction falls out for free: a ride on the opposite carriageway generates matching points in descending index order, so the cursor never advances and the walk simply fails, with no separate heading calculation needed. A maximum gap between consecutive matched positions kills the junction case, because a track that crosses the segment, leaves, and returns twenty minutes later cannot be stitched into one contiguous effort.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 300" role="img" aria-label="A junction crossing and an opposite-carriageway ride are both near the segment but neither advances the ordered cursor">
```
