```svg
  <defs><marker id="ahm" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z" fill="currentColor"/></marker></defs>
  <style>
    .seg{fill:none;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:3}
    .trk{fill:none;stroke:currentColor;stroke-width:1.5;marker-end:url(#ahm)}
    .dot{fill:currentColor}
    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    .sub{fill:currentColor;opacity:.8;font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
  </style>

  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="14">A: crosses at a junction, never matches</text>
  <line class="seg" x1="20" y1="50" x2="280" y2="50"/>
  <path class="trk" d="M150,20 L150,48"/>
  <path class="trk" d="M150,52 L150,80"/>
  <text class="sub" x="290" y="53">segment</text>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="96">cursor never sees consecutive segment vertices near the track</text>

  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="122">B: opposite carriageway, close but reversed</text>
  <line class="seg" x1="20" y1="155" x2="280" y2="155"/>
  <path class="trk" d="M280,172 L20,172"/>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="196">track runs right to left; segment vertices run left to right</text>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="212">cursor index would need to go backwards: walk fails</text>

  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="238">C: a real effort, cursor only ever advances</text>
  <line class="seg" x1="20" y1="270" x2="280" y2="270"/>
  <path class="trk" d="M20,268 L280,268"/>
  <circle class="dot" cx="60" cy="269" r="3"/><circle class="dot" cx="120" cy="269" r="3"/><circle class="dot" cx="180" cy="269" r="3"/><circle class="dot" cx="240" cy="269" r="3"/>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="292">each vertex matched at a higher track index than the last</text>
</svg>
```

Worked example: a criterium on a 1km circuit legitimately produces 40 efforts on the same segment in one activity, because the walk restarts from the position after each success rather than stopping at the first match.

#### Two objects per activity
A feed page shows 20 activities at once. A detail view shows one, in full. Should they read the same record?

[The storage split](/diagram/strava?focus=workers,summary-store,stream-store,e7,e8,e13,e15)

**Bad: one record per activity, holding the full point stream.** Simple, and every read gets everything. A feed page of 20 activities at ~30KB each is 600KB on a mobile connection, and roughly 99% of feed impressions never open the detail view at all, so almost all of that is wasted every single time.

**Good: cache the feed's fields separately, but still fetch from the same big record.** This helps hit rates but does not change what crosses the network on a cache miss, and a feed under load still occasionally pays the full 30KB cost per row it was trying to avoid.

**Great: two objects, written once, read by different paths.** A ~2KB **Activity summary store** row, including a polyline simplified from 3,600 points down to about 300, serves every feed impression. A ~30KB **Activity stream store** blob, the full per-channel columnar data, sits in object storage and is fetched only when the athlete taps through, roughly 1% of the time.

The ratio is 15x, and it is the single most consequential storage decision in the system. Twenty summary rows are about 40KB; the same page from the unified record would be about 600KB. That is the difference between a feed that loads on a train and one that does not, multiplied across tens of millions of monthly readers.

#### Ack fast, match slow
Should the upload request wait for matching to finish, or return before it starts?

[The seam between ack and processing](/diagram/strava?focus=upload-api,kafka,workers,e3,e4)

**Bad: match everything inside the upload request.** On a median activity this is nearly free: about 55ms to parse, clean and derive, plus about 55ms to match, turning a 150ms ack into roughly 260ms. Nobody notices that on a Tuesday afternoon.

**Good: match asynchronously, but size capacity for the steady rate.** This removes the median-case cost from the request, which is progress, but it under-provisions for the one moment that actually matters: the weekend morning spike.

**Great: ack in ~150ms once bytes are durable, and let a queue absorb the 10x weekend spike as depth rather than latency.** At 800 uploads a second, a ~100ms mean matching cost is roughly 80 cores that must already be warm, with an 18GB index already loaded, at the exact minute the spike lands. Doing that inside the request means every one of those uploads carries the cost live, and the dense-metro tail of 300 to 600ms lands directly in the athlete's own request. Asynchronous processing turns the same spike into tens of seconds of queue lag against a 90-second budget instead.

The trade is real and worth naming: efforts and feed entries become eventually consistent, so an athlete can see their own ride in the feed seconds before their crown notification arrives, and the interface has to say so honestly rather than pretend everything finished at once.

#### Hiding where you live
An athlete wants their morning ride visible without revealing their front door. What actually leaks it?

[Where the truncation has to hold](/diagram/strava?focus=workers,summary-store,e8)

**Bad: hide every point within some radius of home.** This looks safe and is not. Every visible endpoint of every ride now sits on the edge of a circle of that radius, centred on the house. Three points determine a circle, and a dozen published rides fit that centre to within metres.

**Good: randomise the radius per activity.** This does not close the gap, it just changes its shape. The endpoints now fill an annulus rather than a circle, and the annulus has exactly the same centre the circle had.

**Great: truncate by distance travelled along the path, add a uniform random extra distance, and snap the cut point to a road junction other athletes also use.** No visible endpoint carries a fixed radial relationship to the house any more, and the cut lands somewhere plausibly shared rather than somewhere unique to one address.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 320" role="img" aria-label="A fixed radius leaves every endpoint on a circle around home; path truncation to a shared junction does not">
  <style>
    .home{fill:var(--accent)}
    .pt{fill:currentColor}
    .ring{fill:none;stroke:currentColor;stroke-width:1.2;stroke-dasharray:4 3;opacity:.6}
    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    .sub{fill:currentColor;opacity:.8;font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
  </style>
  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="14">Fixed radius: every endpoint on one circle</text>
  <circle class="home" cx="150" cy="95" r="4"/>
  <circle class="ring" cx="150" cy="95" r="60"/>
  <circle class="pt" cx="210" cy="95" r="3"/><circle class="pt" cx="115" cy="42" r="3"/><circle class="pt" cx="105" cy="148" r="3"/><circle class="pt" cx="195" cy="52" r="3"/>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="172">three points fit the circle; the circle's centre is home</text>

  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="204">Path truncation to a shared junction</text>
  <circle class="home" cx="150" cy="255" r="4"/>
  <circle class="pt" cx="230" cy="240" r="3"/><circle class="pt" cx="232" cy="238" r="3"/>
  <circle class="pt" cx="228" cy="268" r="3"/><circle class="pt" cx="234" cy="242" r="3"/>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="300">endpoints cluster at a junction many athletes share, not at home</text>
</svg>
```

That is a reduction, not a guarantee, and worth being honest about rather than presenting as solved. Junction snapping can still narrow home to the handful of dwellings reachable from that junction, which in a rural setting can be exactly one. And correlation from outside the zone entirely defeats it: a training partner whose own activity starts at the same address, or the truncated start happening at the same time every weekday morning.

#### Where it breaks
| Layer | Failure | How the design handles it |
|---|---|---|
| Matcher | A matcher starts with a stale segment index; recent segments never match | The index version is stamped on every effort; a node too far behind the segments watermark refuses to consume, turning a silent gap into a visible lag alarm |
| Matcher | A dense metro cell holds thousands of segment starts, stage 1 returns ~80k instead of ~10k | Crowded cells adaptively descend to a smaller S2 level, identically on every matcher, so two nodes never derive different efforts from one activity |
| Leaderboards | A famous segment concentrates writes on one sorted set and one efforts partition | Reads are served from a short-TTL cache of the top ranks; writes are buffered and batched, and the athlete's own new time is merged client-side for read-your-writes |
| Leaderboards | A Redis node loss wipes the sorted sets for its slots | The sorted set is a cache, not the source of truth: any segment's board rebuilds from a single-partition read against the efforts store |
| Backfill | One new segment on a busy road can enqueue millions of stream fetches | Backfill runs on its own low-priority consumer group with a hard rate limit and is shed before the live pipeline is touched |
| Privacy | A privacy-zone lookup fails and a worker is about to publish an untruncated polyline | Fail closed: the activity publishes with no map at all rather than risk a leaked one, and is reprocessed once the service recovers |

#### What this design does not solve
**Privacy zones reduce the leak; they do not close it.** Junction snapping still narrows a home to the dwellings reachable from that junction, which can be one house in a rural area. Correlation from entirely outside the zone, a training partner's own activity, a shared club photo, a start that always happens at 07:02, defeats it regardless of how the truncation itself is tuned.

**The system cannot measure its own false-negative rate.** The funnel's whole contract is that no stage drops a real match, but nothing in production verifies that. A false positive is loud, because another athlete disputes a crown. A false negative is silent: nobody reports an effort they never knew they were owed, and there is no ground truth to check against.

**The corpus mutates under its own derived data, and backfill only partly follows.** Backfill is capped, commonly at 24 months, to protect the live pipeline, so a board labelled all-time is provably not all-time, and the athlete holding the fastest ever recorded ride can simply be absent from it.

#### Final design
Read it back through the numbers. A 35-second naive match at 80 to 800 uploads a second is what forces the funnel; an 18GB corpus is what makes holding it in every matcher's memory cheaper than querying it over a network. A 15x gap between a 2KB summary and a 30KB stream is what keeps the feed off the analysis path entirely. And an ordering predicate that no spatial index expresses on its own is what turns matching into a four-stage funnel rather than a single proximity query.

[The whole design](/diagram/strava?focus=mobile,raw-store,upload-api,kafka,workers,matcher,seg-index,efforts,leaderboards,summary-store,stream-store,feed)

> **The numbers to remember.** 35M segments, ~18GB RAM-resident · funnel 35M to ~9,800 to ~1,200 to ~50 to ~22 · ~55ms p50 matching against ~35s naive · ~2KB summary vs ~30KB stream, 15x · 80 uploads/s steady, ~800/s at weekend peak.

#### Check your understanding
**Why can a matcher hold 35 million segments in memory rather than querying a database per upload?** The full corpus at roughly 500 bytes each is about 18GB, small enough to replicate on every node. A database round trip would instead mean 80 to 800 proximity queries a second against one shared store, each returning rows that still need the same filtering done afterwards.

**A ride crosses a segment once at a road junction. Why doesn't that count as an effort?** The ordered cursor never sees consecutive segment vertices matched at rising track indices; it sees one crossing point and nothing before or after it within the allowed gap, so the walk fails outright.

**Why can't a fixed-radius privacy zone actually hide a home address?** Every visible endpoint then sits on the edge of a circle of that radius centred on the house, and three points are enough to fit a circle. Truncating along the path instead, with a random extra distance and a shared junction snap, removes the fixed radial relationship.

**A segment is created today over a road ridden for a decade. How does it acquire old efforts?** A bounded backfill sweep, driven by a coarse activity-cell index built at processing time, re-reads candidate historical streams and reruns only the corridor and ordered-match stages against the new segment, capped to protect the live pipeline.

**Why does the feed never read the same object as the activity detail view?** A feed page is 20 activities; at the full stream's size that is roughly 600KB, and about 99% of impressions never open the detail view at all. A separate ~2KB summary keeps a page to about 40KB, which is the difference between usable and not on a mobile connection.
### 45. Design Goodreads (Book Catalog, Shelves & Reviews)
#### Understanding the problem
Goodreads has to hold every book ever published, let members shelve and rate the editions they actually own, aggregate those ratings per creative work, and recommend what to read next. Nobody hands it a clean catalogue. Publisher feeds, library records and member submissions arrive disagreeing on title, author spelling, page count and year, so deciding which records describe the same book is something the system has to work out, not a key it can look up.

Two things make it hard.

First, that inference has to run at a scale no pairwise comparison survives. Roughly 300 million edition records means checking every pair is impossible before any tuning even starts.

Second, the two ways to get it wrong are not the same size. Splitting one book's ratings across two pages is annoying. Merging two different books puts one novel's reviews on an unrelated book's page, in public, within minutes.

> **What this is not.** It looks like the music streaming design: a huge media catalogue, a user library, ratings, an offline recommender, a CDN out front. The resemblance stops at the surface. Music arrives from a few hundred rights holders under contract, with an authoritative identifier already attached, so when two records disagree someone emails the label. Identity is given, and the whole design is spent downstream of that on delivering bytes and honouring licences. Here there are no bytes worth delivering, identity is never given, and the entire problem sits upstream of serving a single page.

#### Requirements and the numbers
**Functional.** Serve a book page combining work, editions, aggregate rating and reviews. Let members shelve an edition, track reading progress, rate and review it. Search by title, author or ISBN. Merge and unmerge catalogue entries with a full audit trail.

**Non-functional.** Book page p99 under 200ms server-side, under 30ms on a CDN hit. Shelf write p99 under 150ms. A new rating reflected in the work average within 60 seconds. Every merge reversible in one operation. Duplicate-work rate at or below 1% among the top 100,000 works.

The whole design is decided by four numbers, so derive them before drawing anything.

**What does comparing every record against every other cost?** 300,000,000² ÷ 2 ≈ **4.5 × 10¹⁶ comparisons**. Not a tuning problem, an impossibility.

**What does grouping first bring that down to?** Records sharing a cheap key fall into roughly 80 million blocks averaging about 4 records each. Summed, that is roughly **500 million pairs**, eight orders of magnitude fewer, and minutes of wall clock.

**How skewed is the shelving data?** The most-shelved book carries roughly 5 million shelvings, while a typical shelf holds a few hundred books. That is a difference of **six orders of magnitude** between the two sides of the same table.

**What is the read-to-write ratio?** Roughly 250 million page views a day against roughly 16 million writes: 250,000,000 ÷ 16,000,000 ≈ **16 to 1** at the request level, closer to 100 to 1 once one page's fan-out is counted.

> **The numbers to carry.** 300M editions, ~90M distinct works · naive 4.5 × 10¹⁶ comparisons vs ~500M after blocking · 92% CDN hit rate at ~9k views/s peak · ~750/s peak writes, ~16:1 reads to writes.

#### Inference and serving: two different problems
The system is really two pipelines sharing a name. **Inference** decides, offline and under uncertainty, which edition records describe the same book. **Serving** answers a page request that is, for 90% of viewers, byte-identical to every other viewer's. They run on entirely different clocks: inference can take an hour, serving has a 30ms budget.

The entities:

- **Work**: the abstract creative thing, Dune by Frank Herbert, 1965.
- **Edition**: one physical or digital manifestation, the 2021 paperback, the audiobook, the Polish translation, each with its own page count and cover.
- **Identifier**: an ISBN or ASIN, mapping to a *list* of editions, never one, because publishers reuse and misassign them.
- **Cluster**: the pointer structure a merge writes. `edition_id -> cluster_id -> work_id`.
- **Merge log**: an append-only record of every merge, its evidence, and the full pre-merge membership of both sides.

User content stores `edition_id` and nothing else:

```
GET  /work/{id}                          -> { work, editions[], aggregate, top_reviews[] }
GET  /me/shelf-state?work_id={id}        -> { shelf, progress_pct, my_rating }
PUT  /me/shelves/{shelf_id}/{edition_id} -> { status }
POST /me/ratings/{edition_id} body:{stars} -> { status }
GET  /resolve?isbn={isbn13}              -> { edition_ids[], ambiguous? }
```

#### High-level design
Follow the numbered arrows. A read and a write both cross this same spine, in different directions.

[The hot path, a page view and a shelf write](/diagram/goodreads?focus=client,cdn,catalog-svc,shelf-svc,shelvings,kafka,aggregates,e1,e2,e7,e8,e9,e10)

1. A **Reader / search crawler** requests a book page and hits the **CDN edge** first.
2. On a miss, about 8% of the time, the **CDN edge** calls the **Catalog Service**, which reads the work, its editions and its aggregate.
3. When a logged-in reader acts, the **Reader / search crawler** calls the **Shelf + Review Service** directly, never through the cache.
4. The **Shelf + Review Service** writes one small row into **Shelves & reviews**, a single-partition append.
5. It also emits an event onto **Kafka**.
6. **Kafka** carries that event to **work_aggregates**, folding it into the work's running average within seconds.

> **Why the flow is shaped this way.** The catalogue changes rarely and is read enormously, so it is cached hard and rebuilt offline. Shelvings and ratings change per user, cannot be shared between viewers, and are individually cheap, so they are served live from a store partitioned by user and deliberately kept out of the cacheable page.

#### Deciding two records are the same book
How do you check one record against 300 million others without an impossible number of comparisons?

[Blocking before scoring](/diagram/goodreads?focus=catalog-store,er-pipeline,clusters,e12,e13)

**Bad: compare every record to every other record.** 300,000,000² ÷ 2 ≈ 4.5 × 10¹⁶ comparisons. Even at a wildly optimistic microsecond each, that is over a million CPU-years. No cluster of any realistic size fixes this; it has to be avoided rather than sped up.

**Good: trust the identifier already printed on the cover.** Group by ISBN, ship. It costs almost nothing and is correct for well-behaved sources. It fails on everything else: books printed before ISBNs existed, self-published records, translations with no link back to the original, and most feeds simply not populating a work identifier at all.

**Great: group cheaply on a shared key, then score only within a group.** Records sharing a normalised key, the first three title tokens, a folded author surname, a language, fall into a block. Within a block of typically four records, score every pair on weighted evidence: a shared ISBN, title similarity after normalisation, author match after transliteration folding, page count and year within tolerance. Above 0.92, auto-merge. Between 0.75 and 0.92, a human moderator decides. Below that, a new work.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="-4 -7 400 226" role="img" aria-label="Blocking groups 300 million records into roughly 80 million small blocks, cutting comparisons from 4.5 times 10 to the 16 down to about 500 million">
  <style>
    .bar{fill:none;stroke:currentColor;stroke-width:1.2}
    .fill{fill:currentColor;fill-opacity:.1}
    .fillacc{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.22;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.4}
    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    .sub{fill:currentColor;opacity:.8;font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
  </style>
  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="14">300M records, ungrouped</text>
  <rect class="bar fill" x="4" y="22" width="384" height="24" rx="4"/>
  <text class="sub" x="12" y="38">every record vs every other: 4.5 × 10¹⁶ pairs</text>

  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="80">Blocked by (title tokens, author surname, language)</text>
  <rect class="bar" x="4" y="90" width="34" height="22" rx="4"/><text class="sub" x="21" y="105" text-anchor="middle">4</text>
  <rect class="bar" x="44" y="90" width="34" height="22" rx="4"/><text class="sub" x="61" y="105" text-anchor="middle">3</text>
  <rect class="bar" x="84" y="90" width="34" height="22" rx="4"/><text class="sub" x="101" y="105" text-anchor="middle">5</text>
  <rect class="bar" x="124" y="90" width="34" height="22" rx="4"/><text class="sub" x="141" y="105" text-anchor="middle">2</text>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="130">~80M blocks like these, most with 3-5 members</text>

  <rect class="bar fillacc" x="4" y="150" width="22" height="22" rx="4"/>
  <text class="lbl" x="34" y="165">Only pairs inside a block scored: ~500M total</text>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="192">eight orders of magnitude fewer than the</text>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="208">ungrouped count; minutes of wall clock</text>
</svg>
```

The cost is real: blocking guarantees some false negatives, since a typo inside the first three title tokens lands a record in the wrong block forever. A second pass with an independent key, an ISBN prefix instead of title tokens, catches most of what the first misses, because the two keys fail for unrelated reasons.

#### A merge that can be taken back
Two clusters turn out to be the same book. How do you combine them without making the mistake permanent?

[Pointers, not rewrites](/diagram/goodreads?focus=clusters,er-pipeline,e13,e14,e15)

**Bad: rewrite every rating, review and shelving row to the surviving work.** On a heavily reviewed work that is millions of row updates spread across several stores. It is slow, it is not atomic, and it half-applies if the job dies partway. Worse, it is irreversible: once the old `work_id` is gone from a row, undoing it means a restore from backup, and every review written since the merge has no correct home in that backup.

**Good: soft-delete the losing work and redirect its page.** This avoids touching millions of rows, but review and rating content still has to be reattributed somewhere for the aggregate to be correct, which quietly reintroduces the same rewrite under a different name.

**Great: a merge touches only the cluster table.** `edition_id -> cluster_id -> work_id` is one indirection layer. A merge points one cluster's editions at another, appends the evidence and the full pre-merge membership to an append-only log, and enqueues an aggregate recompute. Nothing that a member wrote is ever touched, because every review and rating already stores `edition_id`, never `work_id`, and the work is resolved through the cluster table only at read time.

Worked example: someone merges a children's picture book called *The Gift* into a horror novel of the same name. Nine hundred horror reviews appear on the picture book's page within minutes, someone screenshots it, a moderator hits unmerge. Because the log holds the full pre-merge membership rather than a single parent pointer, unmerge restores both clusters exactly and both pages are correct within about two minutes, including the reviews written during the merge window, since each recorded the edition its author was actually looking at.

Reversibility has a real limit worth naming plainly. Merges compose: A folds into B on Monday, B folds into C on Wednesday, and undoing Monday needs the shape of the tree before Wednesday flattened it. The system's rule is to require unwinding newer merges first, which is exactly backwards from how bad merges are actually discovered, oldest ones surfacing last.

#### Splitting the cacheable from the personal
A book page looks the same to almost everyone. One reader's shelf status does not. How do both live on one page?

[The shell and the splice](/diagram/goodreads?focus=client,cdn,catalog-svc,shelf-svc,e1,e2,e7)

**Bad: render the whole page per request, personalised state and all.** Correct, and it means the origin renders every one of roughly 9,000 requests a second at peak, none of them cacheable, because each one differs by the one field that matters least to the page's actual content.

**Good: cache the page per logged-in user.** This caches something, but the cache key space now grows with the number of readers rather than the number of books, so hit rate collapses and the cache buys almost nothing.

**Great: split the page into an anonymous shell and a tiny personalised splice.** The shell, work metadata, edition list, aggregate rating, top reviews, is identical for 90% of viewers and sits at the CDN edge on a five-minute TTL. A logged-in reader's shelf, progress and own rating come from a separate call, roughly 5ms, that the client splices onto the cached shell locally.

At a 92% hit rate the edge answers most requests in about 20ms and the origin never wakes up. This is the single biggest lever in the whole design: the personalisation, not the content, is what would have made the page uncacheable, so only the personalisation leaves the cache.

#### One store, two shapes of skew
Shelvings has to answer "what are my shelves" and, more rarely, "who shelved this book". Why does one store serve both badly if built the same way?

[Where the skew lives](/diagram/goodreads?focus=shelvings,e8)

**Bad: one table, read by whichever side asks.** A partition keyed by book works for a rare title and fails for a popular one, and the reverse holds for a partition keyed by user. Neither shape survives both access patterns at once.

**Good: partition by `edition_id`, since "who shelved this" looks like the harder query.** This looks reasonable until the data shows up. The most-shelved book carries roughly 5 million shelvings, a partition of hundreds of megabytes that no wide-column store handles gracefully, and almost nothing on the product actually reads that full list anyway.

**Great: partition by `user_id`, and keep the book side as counters only.** Even a reader with 30,000 books produces a partition of a few megabytes, comfortably small. The book side gets a per-edition counter for "1.2 million people want to read this", not a member list. Anything that genuinely needs the book-side view, co-occurrence for the recommender, a bulk export, reads a nightly columnar dump instead of the live serving path.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 190" role="img" aria-label="A user partition stays a few megabytes even at 30,000 books; a book partition can reach hundreds of megabytes at 5 million shelvings">
  <style>
    .bar{fill:none;stroke:currentColor;stroke-width:1.2}
    .fillacc{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.22;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.4}
    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    .sub{fill:currentColor;opacity:.8;font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
  </style>
  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="16">Partitioned by user_id: a 30,000-book reader</text>
  <rect class="bar" x="4" y="26" width="4" height="22" rx="2"/>
  <text class="sub" x="14" y="41">~3.6MB, one partition, comfortably small</text>

  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="80">Partitioned by edition_id: the most-shelved book</text>
  <rect class="bar fillacc" x="4" y="90" width="384" height="22" rx="2"/>
  <text class="sub" x="10" y="105">~5,000,000 shelvings, ~600MB, nothing reads it whole</text>

  <text class="sub" x="4" y="146">six orders of magnitude apart on the same table,</text>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="162">solved by choosing one side, holding the other as counters</text>
</svg>
```

#### Work-level averages without summing a billion rows
A rating landing on one edition has to move a work-level average that roughly 1.8 billion ratings feed into. How, without scanning them?

[The fold, not the scan](/diagram/goodreads?focus=shelf-svc,kafka,aggregates,e9,e10)

**Bad: recompute the average from every rating on every page render.** Correct and far too slow: summing even a fraction of a busy work's ratings blows a 30ms serving budget on every single view.

**Good: cache the computed average with a short TTL.** Faster to read, but a stampede of readers on a TTL expiry all recompute the same expensive sum at once, and the number is still stale for however long the TTL runs.

**Great: fold each rating in once, incrementally, as an atomic update.** A new rating emits an event onto **Kafka**; a stream processor applies it to `work_aggregates`, `(sum_stars, count, histogram[5])`, as an atomic increment rather than a read-modify-write. Concurrent raters commute, because addition does not care about order, and the displayed average moves within about 30 seconds of the event.

Two safety nets make this durable rather than merely fast. Events carry an idempotent id, so at-least-once delivery from Kafka never double-counts a rating. And a nightly reconciliation pass recomputes every work touched in the last 24 hours directly from the ratings table, catching any drift the incremental fold missed.

#### Where it breaks
| Layer | Failure | How the design handles it |
|---|---|---|
| Entity resolution | A model change causes a wave of false merges; reviews appear under the wrong books | Cap auto-merges per hour; require human sign-off when both sides already carry over 1,000 ratings; bulk unmerge by replaying the merge log for a time range |
| Identifier index | A feed reuses an ISBN that already belongs to a different book | Identifiers map to a list, never a single edition; a shared ISBN is capped evidence requiring corroboration before a merge |
| Blocking | A generic title like "Selected Poems" produces a block of 50,000+ members | Hard-cap block size by appending a sub-block key, publisher or decade; the lost recall lands on the safest side, since these are also the riskiest titles to auto-merge |
| CDN | An edge purge storm or a cold cache after a deploy sends full read volume to origin | Request coalescing per point of presence, stale-while-revalidate, staggered purges, and origin autoscaling with a fallback that serves the last-good shell |
| Aggregate stream | Consumer lag or a lost event leaves a work's average wrong | Idempotent event ids with dedupe; nightly recomputation of every work touched in the last 24 hours from the ratings table |
| Search index | A partially built index gets swapped in and serves wrong results | Build into a parallel index, gate the swap on a document-count and smoke-query check, and keep instant rollback to the previous index |

#### What this design does not solve
**Undo is last-in-first-out, and bad merges surface out of order.** A merge from a year ago sitting under two later merges cannot be cleanly reversed, because the later merges were decided against a cluster that included editions the old undo would remove. The honest fix, a versioned cluster history addressable at any point, has not been built, and today this is a manual reconstruction from the log.

**Nobody has actually decided what a work is.** Is a translation the same work as the original? An abridgement? A three-novel omnibus? The scoring function has an opinion about each, expressed as a number, and it was never a deliberate product choice. An omnibus edition, in particular, contaminates whichever single work it clustered into with an opinion about three separate books.

**The published duplicate-rate figure is measured where the pipeline is strongest.** It is reported against the top 100,000 works, where dense metadata and moderator attention both help. The cold tail, where blocking loses the most recall and the ambiguous band quietly expires as "keep separate" after 30 days, is unmeasured and almost certainly far worse.

#### Final design
Read it back through the numbers. A 4.5 × 10¹⁶-comparison impossibility is what forces blocking before scoring, and the asymmetry between a missed merge and a wrong one is what forces a reversible pointer write instead of a rewrite. A 92% CDN hit rate at 9,000 views a second is what makes splitting the personalised splice from the cacheable shell the biggest single lever available. And a six-order-of-magnitude skew between a reader's shelf and a bestseller's shelvers is what decides which side of one table gets to be a full list and which becomes a counter.

[The whole design](/diagram/goodreads?focus=client,cdn,catalog-svc,shelf-svc,catalog-store,clusters,search,shelvings,aggregates,kafka,er-pipeline,recommender)

> **The numbers to remember.** 300M editions, ~90M works · 4.5 × 10¹⁶ naive comparisons vs ~500M after blocking · 0.92 auto-merge cut, 0.75 human band · 92% CDN hit, ~9k views/s peak · six orders of magnitude between a reader's shelf and a bestseller's shelvers.

#### Check your understanding
**Why does a review store `edition_id` and never `work_id`?** The work is an inference, revised as evidence arrives; the edition is a fact fixed at ingest. Keeping user content keyed on the fact means a bad merge is undone by rewriting a few cluster pointers, never millions of review rows.

**Why is the auto-merge threshold set well above the point that maximises accuracy?** The two errors are not the same size. A missed merge splits a book's ratings, which is annoying and recoverable. A wrong merge publishes one novel's reviews on an unrelated book, which is what gets screenshotted, so precision on an auto-merge has to clear roughly 99.5% before it runs unattended.

**Why does the book page's cache never include a reader's own shelf status?** Because that one field would be the only thing making an otherwise identical page uncacheable for 90% of viewers. Splitting it out onto a separate, tiny, uncached call is what lets the rest of the page live at the CDN edge.

**Why is the shelvings table partitioned by reader rather than by book?** A reader's shelf tops out at a few megabytes even at 30,000 books. The most-shelved book runs to roughly 600MB of rows that almost nothing reads in full, so that side is served as a counter instead, with a nightly dump covering the rare bulk read.

**A rating lands while a thousand others are landing at the same instant. How does the average stay correct?** Each rating is an atomic increment into `work_aggregates` off an idempotent event, so concurrent writers commute regardless of order. A nightly reconciliation pass recomputes every recently touched work from the ratings table as a backstop against any drift.
### 46. Design an LLM Inference & Serving Platform
#### Understanding the problem
An LLM serving platform takes a prompt, runs it through a transformer, and streams back tokens, at high throughput, at a predictable per-token pace, and at a cost per million tokens someone can defend to a finance team.

Two things make this hard, and neither is the model itself.

First, inference is two workloads wearing one name. Reading a prompt is fast and parallel. Producing each output token afterwards is slow and sequential, one step at a time, and a single stream alone uses a sliver of the machine's capacity.

Second, the thing that actually runs out is memory, not arithmetic. Every sequence in flight holds a growing key-value tensor for its whole context, for as long as it lives, and nothing in a parameter-count or FLOPs calculation shows that cost at all.

> **What this is not.** It looks like the RAG system design: a model behind an API, a fixed-seeming latency, a black box you call and wait on. Here the model is not a black box, it is the entire problem. A RAG design spends its complexity upstream, on chunking and retrieval quality, and treats generation as a fixed cost. This design spends nothing upstream and everything on a memory budget that has to balance every single step.

#### Requirements and the numbers
**Functional.** Streaming and non-streaming completions. Per-tenant quotas and usage accounting. Multiple model versions with safe rollout. Request cancellation. Deterministic sampling on request.

**Non-functional.** Time-to-first-token p95 under 400ms, inter-token latency p95 under 30ms, at 2,000 requests a second peak. 99.9% availability. Cost at or below roughly $0.50 per million blended tokens.

The whole design is decided by four numbers, so derive them before drawing anything.

**What does one token of context cost in memory?** With 80 layers, 8 grouped-query KV heads, a head dimension of 128, in bf16: 2 × 80 × 8 × 128 × 2 bytes = 327,680 bytes, call it **~320KB per token**, held for the life of the sequence.

**What does that mean for concurrency?** A 1,100-token conversation costs 1,100 × 320KB ≈ **350MB**. On a ~452GB pool, 452,000MB ÷ 350MB ≈ **1,290 concurrent sequences**. At 32k tokens the same request costs ~10.5GB, so the pool holds only **~43**, thirty times fewer, from context length alone.

**What does one decode step cost?** Reading every weight, 17.5GB per GPU at ~2.3TB/s achieved ≈ 7.6ms, plus the KV cache for the running batch ≈ 4.4ms, plus an all-reduce ≈ 2ms. **~14ms per step**, producing one token for the whole batch at once: ~71 tokens/s per stream, ~18,000 tokens/s per replica.

**What does an allocator change buy?** Contiguous pre-allocation to an 8k ceiling gives 452GB ÷ 2.6GB ≈ 173 slots at every context length. Paged allocation at true length gives 452GB ÷ 350MB ≈ 1,290. That is **~7x concurrency from an allocator alone**.

> **The numbers to carry.** ~320KB of KV per token · 350MB per 1.1k-token sequence, ~10.5GB at 32k · ~14ms per decode step, ~71 tok/s per stream, ~18k tok/s per replica · paging: ~173 to ~1,290 slots, roughly 7x.

#### Prefill and decode: two machines sharing weights
The platform solves two problems that only look like one because they share a model. **Prefill** pushes a whole prompt through in one pass and runs near the arithmetic roofline: compute-bound. **Decode** emits one token per sequence per step, re-reading every weight each time: bandwidth-bound. A single scheduling rule cannot serve both well, which is why almost every mechanism in this design exists to keep the two apart while sharing one pool of GPUs.

The entities:

- **Sequence**: one request in flight, holding a growing key-value tensor for every token it has generated so far.
- **KV block**: a fixed 16-token chunk of that tensor, the unit the pool actually allocates.
- **Replica**: 8 GPUs, tensor-parallel inside one NVLink domain, holding one full copy of the weights.
- **Prefix cache**: refcounted KV blocks shared across requests whose leading tokens are byte-identical.

The control surface is one endpoint carrying most of the complexity behind it:

```
POST /v1/completions
  body: { model, prompt, max_tokens, temperature, stream }
stream=true  -> SSE: { token, finish_reason? }
stream=false -> { text, usage: { prompt_tokens, completion_tokens }, finish_reason }
```

#### High-level design
Follow a request from the wire to its first streamed token.

[The hot path, request to first token](/diagram/llm-serving?focus=client,gateway,queue,router,scheduler,prefill,decode,kv-pool,e1,e3,e4,e5,e8,e9,e11,e17)

1. The **Client** posts a completion request over SSE to the **API gateway**.
2. The **API gateway** authenticates it and pushes it onto the **Priority queue**, never onto a GPU directly.
3. The **Priority queue** hands it to the **Router + autoscaler**, deadline-aware, when a replica has room.
4. The **Router + autoscaler** offers it to a replica's **Scheduler**.
5. The **Scheduler** admits it only if the **Paged KV pool** has the free blocks to afford it, and hands it to **Prefill**.
6. **Prefill** runs the prompt through the model in one pass and joins the request to the running **Decode** batch.
7. **Decode** reads the **Paged KV pool** every step to produce one token for every sequence in the batch at once.
8. **Decode** streams each token back to the **Client** over SSE as it is produced.

> **Why the flow is shaped this way.** Admission has to sit next to the memory it spends. A generic load balancer sees request counts, not free KV blocks, and would happily route a 32k-token prompt to a replica with 12MB left. Putting the **Scheduler** beside the **Paged KV pool** is the whole trick.

#### The number that decides everything
Why does a fleet sized from parameter count and FLOPs run out of capacity at a twentieth of the planned batch?

[Where the memory goes](/diagram/llm-serving?focus=decode,kv-pool,e11)

**Bad: size the fleet from FLOPs and parameter count.** This treats the model as arithmetic-bound everywhere. It is true for prefill and false for decode, where each step re-reads the entire weight set to produce one token per sequence, so a lone stream uses roughly a fifth of a percent of the machine's peak throughput.

**Good: size the fleet with a memory safety margin, in general terms.** An improvement, but "some headroom" is not a number, and the actual constraint scales with context length in a way a flat margin cannot track.

**Great: compute bytes of KV per token exactly, and treat concurrency as a division.** 2 × layers × KV heads × head dimension × dtype size gives ~320KB per token on this model. A request's KV footprint is that number times its context length, and the pool's concurrency ceiling is simply its size divided by that footprint.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 200" role="img" aria-label="KV memory per sequence grows with context length, so concurrency on a fixed pool falls thirty-fold from 1.1k to 32k tokens">
  <style>
    .bar{fill:none;stroke:currentColor;stroke-width:1.2}
    .fillacc{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.22;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.4}
    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    .sub{fill:currentColor;opacity:.8;font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
  </style>
  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="14">KV cost per sequence, concurrency on a ~452GB pool</text>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="34">1.1k tokens: ~350MB → ~1,290 sequences</text>
  <rect class="bar" x="4" y="40" width="6" height="20" rx="3"/>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="72">8k tokens: ~2.6GB → ~173 sequences</text>
  <rect class="bar" x="4" y="78" width="40" height="20" rx="3"/>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="110">32k tokens: ~10.5GB → ~43 sequences</text>
  <rect class="bar fillacc" x="4" y="116" width="160" height="20" rx="3"/>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="164">same 8 GPUs, same weights, thirty times fewer</text>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="180">concurrent users, purely because requests got longer</text>
</svg>
```

A fleet planned from FLOPs alone would confidently forecast headroom that the memory ceiling never allows it to use.

#### Paging the KV cache
The naive allocator reserves a flat buffer per sequence up front. Why does that waste most of the pool?

[Blocks instead of one flat buffer](/diagram/llm-serving?focus=prefill,kv-pool,e10)

**Bad: reserve `max_tokens` worth of contiguous memory per sequence at admission.** A request declaring 8,192 tokens that stops after 40 holds 2.6GB to use 13MB. Add external fragmentation, where a 2.6GB hole cannot serve a 2.7GB request, and a naive server leaves 60 to 80% of its pool idle while reporting itself out of memory at a batch of 20.

**Good: shrink the reservation to a tighter estimate of expected length.** This helps on average and fails exactly when it matters, on the request that runs unexpectedly long, because the buffer still has to be contiguous and cannot grow past its estimate without a costly reallocation.

**Great: split KV into fixed 16-token blocks with a per-sequence block table, and let the attention kernel gather across them.** This is PagedAttention: virtual memory for attention. A sequence holds only the blocks it has actually generated, rounded up to 16 tokens, so external fragmentation disappears because every block is the same size, and internal fragmentation is bounded at 15 wasted tokens, under 1.5% of a typical sequence.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="-4 -7 396 186" role="img" aria-label="A contiguous reservation wastes most of its space and cannot fill a fragmented hole; fixed blocks are allocated only as needed and never fragment externally">
  <style>
    .used{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.3;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.2}
    .waste{fill:currentColor;fill-opacity:.06;stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.4;stroke-width:1;stroke-dasharray:4 3}
    .block{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.3;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.2}
    .free{fill:none;stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.4;stroke-width:1}
    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    .sub{fill:currentColor;opacity:.8;font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
  </style>
  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="14">Contiguous reservation: max_tokens=8192, 40 generated</text>
  <rect class="used" x="4" y="24" width="2" height="24"/><rect class="waste" x="6" y="24" width="378" height="24"/>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="66">2.6GB reserved, 13MB used, unusable by anyone else</text>

  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="100">Paged: 16-token blocks, allocated as generated</text>
  <rect class="block" x="4" y="110" width="20" height="24" rx="3"/>
  <rect class="block" x="28" y="110" width="20" height="24" rx="3"/>
  <rect class="block" x="52" y="110" width="20" height="24" rx="3"/>
  <rect class="free" x="76" y="110" width="308" height="24" rx="3" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="152">3 blocks held (48 tokens of room for 40 used),</text>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="168">the rest free for any sequence</text>
</svg>
```

The same pool that holds ~173 sequences under contiguous pre-allocation holds ~1,290 paged, roughly a 7x concurrency gain from the allocator alone. Two further properties fall out for free: a shared prefix becomes a block run with a refcount above one, and parallel sampling forks cheaply because candidates share the prompt's blocks until they diverge.

#### Admission without knowing the finish line
The scheduler knows a request's prompt length exactly. It never knows how long the output will run. How does it admit safely anyway?

[The reserve and the preemption path](/diagram/llm-serving?focus=scheduler,kv-pool,preempt,e12,e15,e16)

**Bad: reserve `max_tokens` of memory at admission, just in case.** This is the contiguous mistake again, wearing different clothes. It is safe against running out mid-generation and catastrophic for utilisation, because almost every reservation is far larger than the sequence ever actually uses.

**Good: refuse any request whose declared `max_tokens` would not fit if fully realised.** This protects the pool completely and rejects a large share of requests that would, in practice, have finished long before hitting their stated ceiling.

**Great: admit optimistically, charging only for the blocks the prompt actually needs, and hold back a fixed reserve so every running sequence can grow by one block next step.** Preemption becomes the safety valve rather than an error path. When free blocks hit zero mid-step, the scheduler evicts the newest, lowest-priority sequence and either recomputes its prefill on readmission, roughly 43ms, or swaps its KV to host memory, roughly 22ms each way.

Newest-first eviction matters as much as the mechanism itself: preempting the oldest sequence discards the most accumulated work and produces a convoy where the same nearly finished requests are evicted repeatedly. Aging a sequence into eviction-immunity after two preemptions stops newest-first from starving late arrivals under sustained pressure. Tuning the reserve so preemption stays under roughly 1% of steps keeps the mechanism a safety valve; above roughly 5%, the pool is thrashing, and every instantaneous gauge still looks healthy because the free-block count reads fine immediately after each eviction.

#### Continuous batching, not static
Throughput lives in batching decode. What shape should that batch take?

[Batch membership, re-decided every step](/diagram/llm-serving?focus=queue,router,scheduler,e4,e5,e8)

**Bad: give each request the whole machine, one generation at a time.** The latency a request sees never changes because of a stranger's arrival, which is genuinely valuable. It also means the entire memory bandwidth of the hardware produces one token at a time, roughly a hundredth of what the machine can do.

**Good: fill a fixed batch at the door and run it to completion.** Batching is where throughput comes from, and a fixed shape is simple to optimise. It fails on the variance in output length: with lengths spread over more than an order of magnitude, a batch only retires when its longest member finishes, so most slots spend most of their life producing padding nobody reads.

**Great: re-decide batch membership every step.** The **Scheduler** evicts a sequence the step it finishes and admits a queued one from the **Priority queue** into the vacated slot immediately, rather than waiting for the whole cohort to retire. Occupancy tracks offered load instead of collapsing to the slowest member in the batch, worth several times the throughput of a fixed cohort.

The cost is real and worth naming: every sequence admitted lengthens the step for every sequence already running, so a stream's own per-token latency moves with strangers' arrivals, roughly 9ms at a batch of 64 and 22ms at a batch of 512. A published p95 latency is a fleet statistic, not a promise about any one request.

#### Sharing a prompt nobody typed twice
A tenant sends the same 600-token system prompt on every one of 40,000 requests today. Must the model read it 40,000 times?

[The prefix cache](/diagram/llm-serving?focus=prefix-cache,scheduler,e13,e14)

**Bad: recompute every prompt from scratch, every time.** Correct, and it means a shared instruction block that never changes still burns a full compute pass on every single request that carries it.

**Good: cache the whole rendered response for identical prompts.** This works only when a request is fully deterministic and repeated verbatim, which excludes almost everything, since the variable tail of a prompt, the actual user question, differs on every call.

**Great: key KV blocks by a rolling hash of the token prefix, and refcount them.** A request whose first 600 tokens exactly match a cached run reuses those blocks directly; only the new tail needs computing. The cache key must include the model version, or a rollout would serve KV computed by weights that no longer exist.

Pinning the top handful of tenant prompts by observed frequency keeps them resident against eviction. At a ~75% hit rate on a workload where 600 of 800 prompt tokens are shared, effective prefill work per request drops from 800 tokens to roughly 350, which is worth close to a third of the whole prefill fleet.

#### Where it breaks
| Layer | Failure | How the design handles it |
|---|---|---|
| GPU / replica | A GPU faults mid-step; the whole tensor-parallel group and every in-flight generation are lost | The replica is failed out of the routing table immediately; clients retry with an idempotency key, since KV is unrecoverable and partial output is discarded rather than resumed |
| KV pool | Preemption rate spikes and throughput collapses into thrash | The free-block gauge and preemptions-per-step are watched together; the reserve is raised and the admission ceiling lowered, since occupancy alone reads healthy mid-thrash |
| Scheduler | The scheduler process wedges; GPUs sit idle with a full queue | Step-rate is watched, never GPU utilisation, which stays high while wedged; a watchdog restarts the replica and treats the loss of in-flight KV as a replica failure |
| Interconnect | An all-reduce hangs and the tensor-parallel group deadlocks silently | NCCL timeouts set well below the client deadline turn a hang into a crash; the node is drained and checked for a degraded link before returning to service |
| Prefix cache | Stale blocks are served after a model-version change | The model version is part of the cache key; a rollout flushes the cache and any mismatched hit is alarmed on |
| Gateway | A client disconnects mid-stream and generation keeps running, holding blocks and billing | The TCP close is propagated as an abort on the next step; a server-side generation deadline and heartbeat frame bound the worst case |

#### What this design does not solve
**The allocator has no stable equilibrium under sustained overload.** Preemption is not free work: a preempted sequence's recompute competes for the same compute budget that would otherwise retire the sequences still running, so under genuine oversubscription the loop can feed itself. The reserve that bounds it is a tuned constant with no principled derivation, and it silently goes wrong whenever a large tenant's prompt mix shifts.

**No individual request has a latency contract.** Continuous batching makes a stream's inter-token latency a function of who else happens to be running, moving more than two-fold between a light batch and a full one. The published p95 is a fleet statistic. Isolating one tenant's tail latency inside a shared batch is not possible, because sharing the batch is the entire economic argument for the platform.

**The fleet is sized on two ratios nobody controls.** The prefill-to-decode split comes from customer behaviour, and a shift toward long-prompt, short-output traffic inverts it within a week. The prefix cache hit rate, worth roughly a third of the fleet, is a property of how many distinct system prompts tenants happen to run, not of anything the platform builds.

#### Final design
Read it back through the numbers. ~320KB of KV per token is what turns concurrency into a division rather than a tuning knob, and it is what a FLOPs-based capacity model never shows. A 7x gap between contiguous and paged allocation is what makes the block table the platform's real unit of work. A step cost of ~14ms, almost entirely bandwidth rather than arithmetic, is why batching decode is close to free throughput while running one stream alone wastes the machine. And an unknown output length is what forces admission to be optimistic and preemption to be routine rather than exceptional.

[The whole design](/diagram/llm-serving?focus=client,gateway,queue,router,registry,scheduler,prefill,decode,preempt,kv-pool,prefix-cache,usage-ledger)

> **The numbers to remember.** ~320KB KV per token · ~350MB at 1.1k tokens vs ~10.5GB at 32k · paging ~173 to ~1,290 slots, ~7x · ~14ms per decode step, ~18k tok/s per replica · prefix cache worth roughly a third of the prefill fleet at a 75% hit rate.

#### Check your understanding
**Why does a fleet sized from parameter count and FLOPs run out of capacity early?** Decode re-reads every weight from memory each step to produce one token, so it is bandwidth-bound, not compute-bound. The binding constraint is bytes of KV per token, invisible to a FLOPs-based model, and concurrency is simply the pool's size divided by that cost.

**Why does reserving `max_tokens` per sequence waste most of a KV pool?** Output length is unknown at admission, so a flat reservation sized for the worst case holds far more than almost any request ever uses, and a naive contiguous allocator cannot serve that leftover space to anyone else.

**What does paged allocation actually change?** It replaces one flat buffer per sequence with fixed 16-token blocks and a per-sequence block table, so a sequence holds only what it has generated. External fragmentation disappears because every block is the same size.

**Why is preemption a routine mechanism here rather than a failure mode?** Admission is optimistic because output length cannot be known in advance, so the pool sometimes runs out mid-step. Evicting the newest, lowest-priority sequence and recomputing it later is the planned response, not an emergency one.

**Why can't the platform promise one request a fixed inter-token latency?** Continuous batching re-forms the running batch every step, so a stream's latency depends on how many other sequences are running alongside it at that moment, which changes constantly with the arrival of unrelated requests.
### 47. Design a Web Search Engine
#### Understanding the problem
A web search engine takes a free-text query and returns the ten best pages, with a snippet each, out of roughly 50 billion documents, in a few hundred milliseconds. Acquiring those documents is somebody else's job; this system starts once a stream of fetched pages arrives.

Two things make it hard.

First, the answer cannot be precomputed. The space of possible queries is combinatorial, so ten results for `coffee shops brooklyn` have to be produced at request time out of however many documents contain those words, and there is no shortcut around looking at real candidates.

Second, that request-time work has to be bounded twice over: bounded across machines, so one query does not require reading the whole corpus on one box, and bounded within a machine, so a matching document does not have to be individually scored just because it matched.

> **What this is not.** It looks like search autocomplete: type a few characters, get ranked suggestions back fast. Autocomplete's answer space is enumerable, finitely many prefixes, each with one correct top ten, computable offline and shipped as a lookup table. That single fact lets it partition by key and serve from a CDN. Free-text search cannot precompute an answer for every possible query, so it must partition by document instead, which forces a fan-out to every shard, which creates the tail-latency problem that is the actual subject of this design.

#### Requirements and the numbers
**Functional.** Ingest a document stream. Build a positional inverted index. Serve ranked free-text queries with phrase support. Generate snippets. Keep newly published content findable within minutes.

**Non-functional.** p99 under 300ms server-side at 100,000 queries a second peak. Freshness within 5 minutes via a real-time tier, within an hour for a published segment. 99.95% query availability. No single shard failure may fail a query.

The whole design is decided by four numbers, so derive them before drawing anything.

**How many documents does one query actually touch on a shard?** A term at 1% corpus frequency across ~50M documents per shard is roughly 500,000 postings locally. Three such terms union to about **750,000 documents on a single shard**.

**What does scoring all of them cost?** Scoring one document is a random read, about 175ns. 750,000 × 175ns ≈ **130ms of CPU**, against a per-query budget of roughly 30ms if a shard is to sustain its share of load. **Roughly 4x over budget** on a three-word query alone.

**What does document partitioning cost in raw fan-out?** 100,000 queries a second × 1,000 shards = **100 million leaf calls a second** with a cold cache, more like 50 million at a 50% cache hit rate. At a sustainable ~2,000 queries a second per leaf, that needs on the order of **25,000 leaf nodes**.

**What does the tail cost at 1,000 shards?** If a single leaf has a 1-in-100 chance of a slow response, a query touching 100 leaves has roughly a **63% chance of hitting at least one slow one**; at 1,000 leaves that rises to **roughly 99.99%**. The service's p99 is close to a single leaf's p99.9.

> **The numbers to carry.** ~50B documents, ~1,000 shards, ~50M docs each · union ~750k candidates per shard, ~5,000 fully scored · ~130ms naive CPU vs a ~30ms budget · service p99 ≈ leaf p99.9 across 1,000 shards.

#### Retrieval and ranking: two different jobs
The engine is really two problems sharing one corpus. **Retrieval** is cheap per document and has to consider billions of them, so it runs pushed down, on a thousand machines each looking at a fraction of the whole. **Ranking** is expensive per document and only ever needs to consider hundreds, so it runs pulled up, on one central tier with a GPU. Every shape in this design follows from keeping those two apart.

The entities:

- **Document**: one indexed page, reduced to roughly 500 postings across its title, body and anchor text.
- **Term**: one indexed word, mapping through a dictionary to a posting list of every document that contains it.
- **Posting**: `(doc_id, term_frequency, field_weights, positions[])`, one entry per document a term appears in.
- **Segment**: an immutable, self-contained mini-index built offline and published by a pointer swap.
- **Shard**: one of roughly 1,000 machines, each holding a complete index for its own slice of documents.

The read surface is a single call carrying the whole funnel behind it:

```
GET /search?q=coffee+shops+brooklyn&locale=en-US
  -> { as_of, partial, results: [{ doc_id, title, url, snippet, score }] }
```

#### High-level design
Follow one query from the wire down to a scored candidate set and back.

[The hot path, query to reranked results](/diagram/web-search?focus=query-service,fanout,leaf,retrieval,merge,reranker,snippets,e2,e3,e4,e7,e8,e9)

1. The **Query service** normalises the query, checks the **Query result cache**, and on a miss hands it to the **Root + mid-tier mergers**.
2. The **Root + mid-tier mergers** fan the request out to all roughly 1,000 **Leaf query server** instances.
3. Each **Leaf query server** hands the query to its local **Block-max WAND** retrieval stage against its own slice of the index.
4. **Block-max WAND** returns its shard's top 20 candidates up to the **Candidate merge + GBDT** tier, which collapses 20,000 candidates to a global top 500.
5. **Candidate merge + GBDT** passes those 500 to the **Cross-encoder rerank** stage.
6. **Cross-encoder rerank** narrows to the winning 10, and the **Snippet service** fetches and highlights their text before the response returns.

> **Why the flow is shaped this way.** Retrieval is cheap per document and has to see billions of them, so it runs on a thousand machines that each see a fraction. Ranking is expensive per document and only ever needs hundreds, so it runs once, centrally, with a GPU. Neither tier could do the other's job at the other's scale.

#### Splitting the index
Fifty billion documents will never fit on one machine. What is the actual axis to split on?

[Document partitioning versus the alternative](/diagram/web-search?focus=fanout,leaf-group,leaf,e2,e3)

**Bad: keep one flat index on one machine.** Trivially correct at small scale, and it stops being an option once the corpus outgrows a single box's memory and CPU, which happens long before 50 billion documents.

**Good: split by term, so each shard owns a slice of the vocabulary.** A three-word query then wakes only three machines instead of a thousand, which looks like an obvious win. It fails on what a query actually has to do next: the lists for those three terms now live on different machines and have to be combined. The smallest of them can still be tens or hundreds of megabytes, and at tens of thousands of queries a second that is terabytes of network traffic a second, a number that ends the design rather than merely constraining it. Term popularity is Zipf-distributed too, so the shard holding common words becomes a permanent hotspot no amount of resharding relieves.

**Great: split by document, so each shard owns a slice of the corpus and the complete index for it.** Every query goes to every shard, but each one answers entirely locally and returns only its own top 20, roughly 800 bytes. Load is uniform because documents are assigned by hash, and a new document touches exactly one shard at index time.

The price of document partitioning is fan-out itself: every machine in the fleet participates in every query, so capacity scales with queries-per-second times shard count, not with queries-per-second alone. That is a real, bounded cost. The network cost of term partitioning is not bounded at all; it grows with the size of the lists a query happens to need combined, and the worst lists are the most common words in the language.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="-4 -7 400 182" role="img" aria-label="Term partitioning ships a huge posting list across the network per query; document partitioning ships only a small results list, but from every shard">
  <style>
    .bar{fill:none;stroke:currentColor;stroke-width:1.2}
    .fillacc{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.22;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.4}
    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    .sub{fill:currentColor;opacity:.8;font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
  </style>
  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="14">Term partitioning: ship the posting list, ~180MB</text>
  <rect class="bar" x="4" y="22" width="384" height="22" rx="4"/>

  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="82">Document partitioning: top 20 from every shard</text>
```
