
#### Skipping documents you don't have to score
750,000 candidate documents on a shard, a 30ms budget, and only 20 results wanted. How do you avoid scoring almost all of them?

[Retrieval against a segment](/diagram/web-search?focus=retrieval,segments,e4,e5)

**Bad: score every document that matches any query term.** Correct and complete, and 750,000 documents at roughly 175ns each is about 130ms of CPU, four times the available budget on a short query and far worse on a longer one.

**Good: require every query term to be present, and score only that intersection.** Fast, roughly 1ms for the few thousand documents that satisfy all three terms, using skip pointers to jump cursors forward without scanning. It answers a different question than the one asked. A page titled "Brooklyn Coffee" that says "cafés" instead of "shops" is dropped outright, and on a six-term query strict intersection drops nearly everything.

**Great: keep the disjunctive candidate set, but prove most of it cannot win before scoring it.** At index time, store each term's maximum possible score contribution to any document. At query time, track the current 20th-best score as a threshold and walk cursors sorted by document id, summing upper bounds; the first document where that running sum could still beat the threshold becomes a pivot, and everything before it is provably unable to win and is skipped without being read. This is WAND, refined by block-max scoring at 128-posting granularity so the bound is tight locally rather than over an entire list.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="-4 -7 400 190" role="img" aria-label="Cursors advance by document id; documents before the pivot cannot beat the current threshold and are skipped without being scored">
  <style>
    .lane{fill:none;stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.35;stroke-width:1.2}
    .doc{fill:currentColor;fill-opacity:.15;stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.5;stroke-width:1.2}
    .skip{fill:currentColor;fill-opacity:.04;stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.25;stroke-width:1;stroke-dasharray:3 3}
    .pivot{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.28;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.6}
    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    .sub{fill:currentColor;opacity:.8;font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
  </style>
  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="14">coffee, shops, brooklyn cursors, sorted by doc id</text>
  <rect class="lane" x="4" y="26" width="384" height="26" rx="5"/>
  <rect class="skip" x="6" y="26" width="200" height="26" rx="4"/>
  <rect class="pivot" x="212" y="23" width="34" height="32" rx="5"/>
  <rect class="doc" x="252" y="26" width="130" height="26" rx="4"/>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="70">skipped: summed upper bounds here can never reach θ</text>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="86">pivot doc, then fully scored: ~5,000 of 750,000</text>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="116">θ = current 20th-best score, updated as documents are scored</text>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="140">result: same count as strict intersection, but drawn from</text>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="156">the whole union, so strong two-term matches survive and</text>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="172">weak three-term ones are dropped</text>
</svg>
```

This holds only while every scoring signal decomposes into per-term contributions with a known ceiling. That is why a transformer reranker, which reads the whole query and document together and produces no such bound, cannot participate in retrieval at all and has to sit above it, scoring a candidate set someone else already narrowed.

#### Taming the tail
A leaf answering in 20ms sounds fine. With 1,000 of them in every query, why does the service feel much slower?

[Where the wait comes from](/diagram/web-search?focus=fanout,leaf,e3)

**Bad: wait for every one of a thousand shards, every time.** The service's latency becomes the maximum of a thousand independent draws, not the average of one. A leaf with a 1-in-100 chance of a slow response gives a query touching all 1,000 of them a roughly 99.99% chance of hitting at least one slow leaf.

**Good: apply a uniform timeout and retry whatever is slow.** This bounds the worst case somewhat, but a blind retry after the fact re-sends the whole request from scratch and does not use the time already spent productively.

**Great: hedge, deadline, and accept partial coverage.** After the p95 elapses, send the same request to a second replica and take whichever answers first, costing roughly 5% extra load in exchange for a large cut to the tail. Enforce a hard deadline, around 40ms, on every leaf. Return once 99% of shards have answered rather than waiting for the last one, flagged as a partial response.

The quality cost of returning early is small enough to be worth stating precisely: dropping 10 of 1,000 shards loses about 0.1% of candidates, and since documents are hashed onto shards uniformly, the chance any one member of the true top 10 lived on a dropped shard is roughly 1%. That is a fraction of one perturbed result, almost always at position 8, 9 or 10, traded against not waiting for the genuine maximum of a thousand draws from a fat-tailed distribution.

#### Publishing an index without ever locking it
The index has to keep growing while it keeps answering queries. How does a write never block a read?

[Segments, generations, and the real-time gap](/diagram/web-search?focus=indexer,segments,rt-index,e11,e12,e13,e6)

**Bad: update postings in place as documents change.** Every write now contends with every concurrent read for the same structure, and a crash mid-update can leave a posting list in a state nothing can safely serve.

**Good: rebuild the whole index from scratch on a schedule and swap it in.** Correct and simple, but rebuilding roughly 165TB takes days, so freshness is bounded by the rebuild cycle, and a story published minutes ago is invisible until the next one completes.

**Great: build immutable segments offline, publish by a pointer swap, and cover the gap with a small in-memory tier.** The **Index build** stage runs as a batch job over the crawl stream, sorting postings by term and writing self-contained **Immutable segments**. Publishing a new segment is a pointer update, nothing is ever mutated, and a bad build rolls back in seconds by pointing back at the previous generation. Deletions are a bitmap overlay rather than a rewrite. The **Real-time tier** holds only what has arrived since the last hourly publish, small enough, roughly 234MB per leaf, to stay resident in memory and be unioned with the base segments at query time.

The seam between the two tiers is a real cost, not a free lunch: a document in the real-time tier has no PageRank yet, because the link graph has not seen it, and no click history, because nobody has clicked it. Those signals are missing by definition, so a page's rank can shift for reasons unrelated to the page itself the moment it graduates into the base index.

#### Where it breaks
| Layer | Failure | How the design handles it |
|---|---|---|
| Leaf shard | All replicas of one shard are unavailable, hiding a slice of the corpus | Return with `partial:true` set; re-replicate the shard's segments from object storage onto spare capacity |
| Leaf shard | One slow replica drags the tail without failing health checks | Hedged and tied requests route around it automatically; sustained deviation puts it on probation and out of rotation |
| Query cache | The cache cluster fails or is cold after a deploy | The fleet is provisioned with cache-miss headroom rather than assuming a full doubling; rerank depth and deadlines widen to shed load while the cache rewarms |
| Index publish | A bad segment ships corrupt postings or a tokeniser bug | Segments are immutable and generation-tagged; a pointer swap rolls back in seconds, and a new build canaries on a small slice of shards first |
| Real-time tier | The crawl stream stalls and breaking content stops appearing | The base index keeps serving everything older; freshness degrades but correctness does not, since the tier is purely additive |
| Merge tier | A mid-tier merger dies mid-query, silently losing a subtree of shards | Shard coverage is computed per query rather than assumed; below the 99% threshold the root retries the missing subtree against a second merger |

#### What this design does not solve
**Word matching cannot retrieve a document that never uses the query's words.** Every mechanism in this design, from the inverted index through the score ceilings that make early termination safe, assumes relevance is a function of term overlap. The best possible answer in the world is not merely ranked low if it phrases everything differently; it is never a candidate, and no amount of reranking downstream can rescue it. A dense retrieval path run alongside word matching narrows this gap without closing it, and introduces its own staleness and a fusion weight nobody has a clean answer for.

**Spam is managed, not solved, because the opponent adapts.** Every other subsystem here faces a fixed adversary: hardware limits, physics, load. This one faces someone actively probing the ranking function, so any signal strong enough to move rankings is strong enough to be worth attacking. The realistic target is a tolerated spam rate in what is actually shown, sampled by human review, not a clean corpus verified by any classifier's own confidence.

**The base index and the real-time tier will never score by the same function.** A freshly indexed document is missing PageRank and click signals structurally, not by an oversight that could be fixed. Breaking-news results are measurably noisier than steady-state ones as a direct consequence, and the honest response is to bound how many real-time results can enter a top 10 rather than pretend the two tiers are equivalent.

#### Final design
Read it back through the numbers. A 750,000-document union against a 30ms budget is what forces early termination rather than exhaustive scoring. An unbounded network cost for term partitioning against a bounded fan-out cost for document partitioning is what settles the split. A leaf p99.9 becoming the service's effective p99 across 1,000 shards is what makes hedging and a hard deadline load-bearing rather than optional. And a days-long full rebuild against a minutes-fresh product requirement is what forces immutable segments plus a small real-time tier rather than one mutable index.

[The whole design](/diagram/web-search?focus=query-service,query-cache,fanout,leaf,retrieval,crawl-stream,indexer,segments,rt-index,merge,reranker,snippets)

> **The numbers to remember.** ~50B documents, ~1,000 shards · union ~750k candidates per shard, ~5,000 fully scored · service p99 ≈ leaf p99.9 · 40ms hard deadline, return at 99% shard coverage · real-time tier ~234MB per leaf, base rebuild in days.

#### Check your understanding
**Why does the service's p99 look so much worse than any single leaf's p99?** A query touches all 1,000 shards, so the service latency is the maximum of 1,000 independent draws rather than the average of one. A leaf with even a small chance of a slow response makes hitting at least one slow leaf almost certain at that fan-out.

**Why does document partitioning win over term partitioning at web scale?** Term partitioning has to move a posting list, sometimes hundreds of megabytes, across the network on every query, and that cost is unbounded as lists grow. Document partitioning bounds the network cost to a small results list from every shard, trading it for a bounded, engineerable fan-out cost instead.

**A shard fully scores only 5,000 of 750,000 candidate documents. Does that change the top 20?** No, as long as every scoring signal decomposes into per-term contributions with a known upper bound. The documents skipped are provably unable to beat the current 20th-best score, so the result is identical to scoring everything, just far cheaper to reach.

**Why can't a cross-encoder reranker run at the retrieval stage instead of after it?** It reads the query and a document together and produces no per-term score bound, so nothing about it can be proven to fall below a threshold in advance. Early termination needs that bound to skip documents safely, so the reranker has to sit above retrieval, scoring a set someone else already narrowed.

**Why does a document indexed one minute ago rank differently once it enters the base index the next day?** The real-time tier serves it before it has any PageRank or click history, because neither signal can exist yet. Those signals become available only once the link graph and click logs catch up, which happens when the document graduates into the base index, not because anything about the document itself changed.
### 48. Design an E-Commerce Platform (Catalog, Cart & Flash Sales)
#### Understanding the problem
An e-commerce platform serves a catalogue of roughly 200 million products, holds a shopper's cart, and turns a checkout into an order that correctly decrements inventory. Almost all of that is easy. The hard case is a flash sale, where half a million people try to buy the same item in the same sixty seconds while everyone else keeps browsing normally.

Two things make this hard.

First, browsing and buying are different problems wearing one product. Roughly 1,600 page views happen for every order placed, so the read side is a caching problem and the write side is a contention problem, and designing them as one system fails both.

Second, the last unit of a popular item is one database row that thousands of buyers want to decrement at once. Neither of the two textbook answers, optimistic retry or a row lock, survives that load, and each fails in its own distinct way.

> **What this is not.** It looks like Ticketmaster: a catalogue, contention for scarce inventory, a checkout flow. The resemblance inverts almost everywhere it matters. Ticketmaster's inventory is tens of thousands of individually named seats, so contention spreads naturally across many keys and there is no single counter to protect. Here inventory is one undated counter per SKU, and tens of thousands of buyers can converge on that one row. Ticketmaster's on-sale moment is printed on a poster and provisioned for in advance; here a sale can start because a post went viral, with no warning at all.

#### Requirements and the numbers
**Functional.** Browse and search a 200M-SKU catalogue. A cart that works for guests and signed-in shoppers. Checkout with inventory reservation, order placement, cancellation and refund initiation.

**Non-functional.** Product page p99 under 200ms at the edge. Checkout p99 under 1.5 seconds including payment. Zero double-charges. Oversell at or below 0.1% of units on replenishable stock, and zero on limited drops. Browsing stays available at 100 times normal checkout load.

The whole design is decided by four numbers, so derive them before drawing anything.

**What is the ratio of browsing to buying?** Roughly 240 million product-page views a day against roughly 150,000 orders: 240,000,000 ÷ 150,000 ≈ **1,600 views for every order**.

**What does the last unit of a doorbuster actually face?** At the peak second of a drop, roughly **8,000 reserve attempts a second** land on one SKU's row.

**What can a locked row actually sustain?** At roughly 3ms per critical section, one row processes about **330 decrements a second**. Against 8,000 arriving, the wait queue grows by **~7,670 requests every second**.

**How big is the whole inventory table, and is it ever a capacity problem?** 200 million SKUs across roughly 3 stocking locations is 600 million rows at ~64 bytes each: 600,000,000 × 64B ≈ **~40GB**, small enough to sit resident in memory on one large node.

> **The numbers to carry.** ~1,600 page views per order · ~8,000 reserve attempts/s on one hot row · a locked row sustains ~330/s against that · ~40GB of inventory, entirely in RAM.

#### Browsing and buying: two systems sharing a gateway
The platform is really two products that happen to share a storefront. **Browsing** is enormous in volume and tolerant of staleness, so it is solved by caching aggressively. **Buying** is tiny in volume and intolerant of the wrong answer, so it is solved by controlling contention precisely. They share only the entry point.

The entities:

- **Product**: one catalogue entry, split into a near-static shell and a volatile price and stock fragment.
- **Cart**: a durable, server-side list of lines with a price snapshot, never a reservation.
- **Hold**: a reservation with a TTL, the one artefact all three inventory lanes produce.
- **Order**: the durable, idempotent record a checkout produces once payment succeeds.

```
GET  /p/{sku}                    -> cached shell + live price/stock fragment
POST /cart/items                 -> { cart_id, lines[] }
POST /checkout/session           -> { hold_ids[], quoted_total }
POST /orders   (Idempotency-Key) -> { status, order_id }
```

#### High-level design
Follow a shopper from add-to-cart through to a confirmed order.

[The hot path, cart to payment](/diagram/ecommerce?focus=gateway,cart,saga,pricing,cold,warm,hot,orders,payment,e3,e4,e5,e7,e8,e9,e14,e15)

1. The **Gateway + waiting room** admits the request and hands it to the **Cart service**.
2. The **Cart service** hands the cart to the **Checkout saga** to open a checkout session.
3. The **Checkout saga** asks **Pricing + promotions** for an authoritative re-quote.
4. For a cold SKU, the **Checkout saga** issues one conditional update against the **Cold lane**.
5. For a warm SKU, it grants stock from one of 32 bucket rows in the **Warm lane**.
6. For a hot SKU, it appends a ticket to the per-SKU log in the **Hot lane** and waits for an SSE answer.
7. Once every line holds, the **Checkout saga** writes the **Order store** row under its idempotency key.
8. The **Checkout saga** calls **Payment service** to capture the charge, then converts holds into a confirmed order.

> **Why the flow is shaped this way.** The two columns of the diagram share only the gateway on purpose. Browsing must survive a checkout meltdown, because a saturated inventory row cannot be allowed to exhaust anything the read path depends on.

#### Two systems sharing a gateway
Why can a single hot SKU not be allowed to slow down anyone reading a product page?

[Where the read and write paths split](/diagram/ecommerce?focus=cdn,gateway,catalog,cart,e1,e2,e3)

**Bad: serve the whole product page from one origin call, cached as one object.** Simple, and it fails the moment price or stock changes, because invalidating one field invalidates the entire cached page, and price and stock change constantly on a popular item.

**Good: cache the whole page for a short TTL and accept some staleness everywhere.** This helps, but it forces an uncomfortable choice: a TTL long enough to make caching worthwhile is too stale for price and stock, and a TTL short enough for price and stock defeats the caching of everything else on the page.

**Great: split the page where volatility actually changes.** A near-static shell, title, media, description, sits at the **CDN + edge KV** for minutes. A small volatile fragment, price, stock band and promo, is served separately from the same edge tier for seconds. Nothing on this path is authoritative; **Checkout saga** re-prices and re-reserves against the source of truth regardless of what the cache showed.

That last property is what makes the whole split safe rather than merely fast. A stale cache costs a shopper a re-quote at checkout, never a wrong charge, because the read path is never the thing that decides what actually happens to inventory or price.

#### One counter, eight thousand writers a second
The textbook answers to contended writes both exist for a reason. Why do both fail here?

[Where a naive mechanism collapses](/diagram/ecommerce?focus=cold,warm,hot,holds,e7,e8,e9)

**Bad: optimistic retry, read the count and version, then update only if unchanged.** One writer succeeds per round and the other 7,999 retry immediately. Those retries land on top of fresh arrivals, so the contended set grows faster than it drains. Throughput falls as load rises: a livelock, not a slowdown.

**Good: pessimistic locking, take the row lock and queue everyone else behind it.** Correct and orderly in isolation. At roughly 3ms per critical section the row sustains about 330 decrements a second against 8,000 arriving, so the wait queue grows by roughly 7,670 requests every second, connections pin, and unrelated traffic sharing that connection pool starves behind it.

**Great: classify each SKU by measured heat and route it to a matching lane.** A conditional update handles the cold 99.99% of the catalogue with no read-then-write step at all, so there is nothing to livelock. Stock split across 32 bucket rows handles the warm middle. A per-SKU log with one consumer handles the genuinely hot handful, serialising writers without making any of them wait on a lock.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 200" role="img" aria-label="A cold conditional update, a warm 32-bucket split, and a hot single-consumer log each match their lane's write rate; only the log keeps up at 8,000 a second">
  <style>
    .bar{fill:none;stroke:currentColor;stroke-width:1.2}
    .fillacc{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.22;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.4}
    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    .sub{fill:currentColor;opacity:.8;font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
  </style>
  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="16">Cold: one row, &lt;50 reserves/s, one conditional update</text>
  <rect class="bar" x="4" y="24" width="7" height="20" rx="3"/>

  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="76">Warm: 50-1,000/s, split 32 ways, ~31/s per bucket</text>
  <rect class="bar" x="4" y="84" width="48" height="20" rx="3"/>

  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="136">Hot: &gt;1,000/s, single consumer at ~50,000/s</text>
  <rect class="bar fillacc" x="4" y="144" width="384" height="20" rx="3"/>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="180">arrival rate at T+0, ~8,000/s, sits well inside this ceiling</text>
</svg>
```

The lane a SKU sits in is not a permanent property; it is a live classification revisited every ten seconds, because the same item can move from cold to hot within a single afternoon.

#### Splitting a counter without losing the tail
Splitting one hot row into 32 bucket rows fixes contention. What does it break as stock runs low?

[The bucket endgame](/diagram/ecommerce?focus=warm,holds,e11,e12)

**Bad: keep buckets forever, however little stock remains.** Contention is gone, and a new failure appears at the tail: with 5 units spread across 32 buckets, 27 buckets are empty. Most buyers hashed into an empty bucket are told the item is sold out while stock genuinely exists elsewhere in the row.

**Good: probe a neighbouring bucket, then steal from the fullest one, when the first bucket is empty.** This buys real headroom and delays the failure, but it does not remove it; as the total shrinks further, the fallback chain itself starts failing the same way the single bucket did.

**Great: merge the buckets back into one row once the total falls below a threshold, and promote the SKU to the hot lane.** When `total_remaining < 2N`, a coordinator takes a brief exclusive window across all 32 rows, sums them into one row, and hands the SKU to serialised handling for its final units.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="-4 -7 388 140" role="img" aria-label="With 5 units spread across 32 buckets, 27 are empty; most buyers land on an empty bucket while stock still exists elsewhere in the row">
  <style>
    .full{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.3;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.2}
    .empty{fill:none;stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.3;stroke-width:1}
    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
```

The merge itself is a real, measured stall, tens of milliseconds under an exclusive lock across all 32 rows. That cost is worth stating plainly: it is the price of not underselling stock that genuinely exists, which the design treats as the more expensive of the two errors.

#### Serialisation without waiting
The hot lane still serialises every writer. How is that different from the lock that just failed?

[The log and its consumer](/diagram/ecommerce?focus=hot,holds,e9,e13,e17)

**Bad: a lock queue, walked one critical section at a time.** Correct, and it has to be walked. Once the counter reaches zero, every remaining waiter still has to be processed in turn just to be told the item is gone.

**Good: an asynchronous queue with many consumers applying decrements concurrently.** Faster to drain on paper, but it reopens the exact problem the queue was meant to close: concurrent writers against one shared count need their own concurrency control, and the lane is back to needing a lock.

**Great: a per-SKU log with exactly one consumer.** Every reserve attempt is appended, cheaply, roughly 0.3ms, without ever blocking. The single consumer applies decrements against an in-memory counter at tens of thousands a second, far faster than any plausible arrival rate. Once the counter hits zero, the consumer stops decrementing and rejects the entire remaining backlog at memory speed, a single pass rather than a walk.

That last property is the whole argument for the lane over a lock: a lock queue must be processed request by request even after the answer is already known, while a log can simply be truncated once the outcome is certain. Durability rides along for free: the consumer batch-persists the counter and its log offset together, so a standby taking over replays only from the last persisted point, and a `hold_id` on every grant makes any duplicate replay harmless rather than a double reservation.

#### Pricing the mistake, not just preventing it
An oversell and an undersell are both wrong answers. Are they the same kind of wrong?

[Where the policy is set](/diagram/ecommerce?focus=pricing,saga,e5)

**Bad: pick one concurrency mechanism and let whatever it does become the business outcome.** A strict lock undersells, because it turns buyers away in favour of not risking a mistake. Bucketing undersells too, for a different reason, in its endgame. Neither of these was a decision anyone made on purpose; it fell out of the mechanism.

**Good: set one global oversell tolerance and apply it everywhere.** An improvement, since at least someone decided a number. It is still wrong for either end of the catalogue, because a replenishable T-shirt and a numbered concert seat do not carry anything like the same cost when the platform gets it wrong.

**Great: set the policy per SKU class, in money.** An oversell on replenishable stock costs roughly a cancellation email and a goodwill credit, call it £15, and the unit restocks next week regardless. An undersell costs the entire margin on a unit that existed, plus the acquisition spend already made on that session, plus a shopper who buys from a competitor instead. On a typical item that runs to roughly 1.7 times the cost of an oversell, which is why replenishable stock deliberately tolerates a small oversell buffer while limited drops run strict zero-oversell through the queue lane.

The concurrency control is not allowed to make this call by accident. **Pricing + promotions** and the **Checkout saga** enforce whichever policy the SKU class carries; the lane a SKU runs in decides how contention is resolved, never whether an oversell is acceptable.

#### Where it breaks
| Layer | Failure | How the design handles it |
|---|---|---|
| CDN | A drop page not yet cached produces a stampede of simultaneous origin misses | Pages and images are pre-rendered and pushed to every edge point of presence ahead of a scheduled drop; concurrent misses for the same key coalesce into one origin fetch |
| Inventory hot lane | The single consumer for a hot SKU dies mid-drop | A standby takes over the partition and replays from the last persisted offset; every grant's `hold_id` makes re-application harmless |
| Inventory buckets | Skewed hashing empties some buckets while stock remains elsewhere | Next-bucket probing, then stealing from the fullest bucket, then a forced merge and promotion to the hot lane below the threshold |
| Holds | A hold expires while payment is still in flight | The TTL is extended before the charge step; on failure, an immediate re-reserve, or a full refund plus an alert if that also fails |
| Checkout saga | The orchestrator crashes between payment success and hold confirmation | Durable workflow state resumes from the last completed step rather than restarting; a reconciler confirms or compensates against the payment provider by idempotency key |
| Payment provider | The provider rate-limits or degrades during the spike | The payment step runs behind its own bounded concurrency budget, with failover to a secondary provider; browsing and any in-flight checkout are never shed |

#### What this design does not solve
**A cart that mixes a hot line with ordinary ones cannot be reserved as a single unit.** The ordinary lines reserve in milliseconds; the hot line returns a ticket that can take seconds behind a deep queue, and there is no transaction spanning both. The design holds the ordinary lines while the hot one is queued and biases toward shipping a partial order if the hot line comes back sold out, because a partial order recovers most of the basket value and a full release recovers none. That is a policy choice covering a missing guarantee, not a fix for it.

**The price a shopper saw on the page is never a promise.** Promotions depend on the whole cart and tax depends on an address, so the product page can never hold the authoritative number, and re-pricing at checkout is structural. The mitigation is entirely presentational, an explained delta and an accepted total the shopper confirms, and a genuine price lock for the session would mean a write to the pricing engine on every page view, which has not been built.

**The heat classifier is reactive, so the first seconds of an unannounced spike run in the wrong lane.** A rolling ten-second window means a sudden, unscheduled surge hits the cold lane before the classifier catches up, and one row absorbs thousands of conditional updates for those few seconds. It fails safely, as lost sales rather than an oversell, but those are the seconds that mattered most, and shortening the window risks flapping during a bucket merge, which is the one transition that can actually lose count.

#### Final design
Read it back through the numbers. A 1,600-to-1 ratio of views to orders is what makes the CDN the dominant lever on the read side and lets it be built without touching inventory at all. Eight thousand reserve attempts a second against a row that a lock sustains at 330 is what rules out both textbook concurrency controls and forces heat-classified lanes. And a 40GB inventory table sitting entirely in memory is what confirms this was never a storage problem, only a contention one, freeing the whole design to focus on how writers are ordered rather than where data lives.

[The whole design](/diagram/ecommerce?focus=cdn,catalog,gateway,cart,saga,pricing,cold,warm,hot,holds,orders,payment)

> **The numbers to remember.** ~1,600 views per order · ~8,000 reserve attempts/s on one hot row at T+0 · a locked row sustains ~330/s · hot lane consumer at tens of thousands of decrements/s · inventory ~40GB, entirely in memory.

#### Check your understanding
**Why does optimistic retry fail on a hot SKU specifically, rather than just run slowly?** Every failed retry lands back on top of fresh arrivals, so the contended set grows faster than any single writer can drain it. Throughput falls as load rises, which is a livelock, not merely a slowdown.

**Why does a row lock make unrelated SKUs slower during a flash sale?** A lock sustains only a few hundred decrements a second against thousands arriving, so the wait queue grows every second and pins database connections, and traffic sharing that same connection pool starves behind it regardless of which SKU it touches.

**With 5 units left across 32 buckets, why does the site say sold out while stock exists?** Most of the 32 buckets are empty at that point, so a buyer hashed into an empty one is told there is nothing left even though other buckets still hold units, which is why the design merges buckets back into one row before the count gets that low.

**Why is an oversell treated as the cheaper mistake on replenishable stock?** An oversell costs roughly a cancellation email and a goodwill credit, and the unit restocks regardless. An undersell forfeits margin on a unit that existed, plus acquisition spend already made, plus a shopper who may buy elsewhere instead, which runs well above the oversell's cost.

**Why can the hot lane reject a sold-out backlog instantly, while a lock queue cannot?** A lock queue has to be walked one critical section at a time even after the outcome is known. A log-backed lane can simply be truncated once its single consumer's counter reaches zero, rejecting everything still queued in one pass rather than processing each request in turn.
### 49. Design Ticketmaster (High-Demand Ticket Booking)
#### Understanding the problem
Ticketmaster sells specific numbered seats for a live event to more than a million people who all press buy at the same publicly announced second. No seat may ever be sold twice, and organised, funded resale operations must not be allowed to beat real fans to the good seats.

Two things make this hard, and neither is the part most people expect.

First, deciding who wins a contested seat is trivial: one conditional write settles two buyers in a microsecond. The actual load is on the read side. A million and a half browsers all want a live picture of sixty thousand seats, and naive versions of that read collapse the system before a single seat is sold.

Second, whichever rule decides who gets served first is not a UX detail, it is a security control. Any ordering rule based on arrival time becomes an auction on network latency, which is a rule an organised bot can win every time.

> **What this is not.** It looks like the e-commerce flash sale: an announced instant, a spike orders of magnitude above baseline, bots. The difference is what the inventory is. A flash sale's inventory is a count of interchangeable units, so it can be split across shards, oversold slightly and reconciled with a refund, and a buyer who wanted the third unit does not care which one they get. A seat has no substitute; a buyer who wants row 5 centre will not accept row 40 and will say so. So the flash sale spends its budget on write-path sharding while this design spends its budget keeping the crowd away from the write path entirely.

#### Requirements and the numbers
**Functional.** Browse events, view a live seat map, join a queue, be admitted, hold specific seats, check out, and receive transferable tickets. Enforce purchase limits. Release expired holds automatically.

**Non-functional.** Zero double-sold seats, ever. Seat-map staleness at or under 1 second. Queue-position updates at or under 5 seconds. Hold acquisition p99 under 100ms. The system must absorb roughly 150,000 arrivals a second for about 10 seconds with no origin saturation.

The whole design is decided by four numbers, so derive them before drawing anything.

**How many buyers compete for one seat?** 1,500,000 arrivals against 60,000 seats: 1,500,000 ÷ 60,000 = **25 buyers per seat**, closer to **60 to 1** once average order size is counted.

**What does a naive position query cost?** 1.5 million clients polling their own position every 5 seconds is 1,500,000 ÷ 5 ≈ **300,000 queries a second** of pure per-user overhead, before a single seat is touched.

**What admission rate does the inventory itself imply?** Cap in-flow buyers at 25,000, one venue's worth at an average order of 2.4 seats. A mean session of 240 seconds gives, by Little's law, 25,000 ÷ 240 ≈ **~100 admissions a second**.

**How much of the crowd is ever actually admitted?** Clearing the inventory needs roughly 42,000 admissions, which at 100 a second takes about 7 minutes. Draining the whole 1.5 million-person queue at that rate would take over 4 hours, so roughly **97% of the queue is never admitted at all**.

> **The numbers to carry.** 25 buyers per seat, ~60 per ticket · naive per-user reads ~300k QPS vs a shared object at ~50 origin req/s · admission rate ~100/s from Little's law · ~97% of the queue told sold out, never admitted.

#### The seat lock and the crowd: two different sizes of problem
The write race that decides who gets a contested seat is small and fast: one conditional set, settled in microseconds. Everything expensive in this design exists to stop that write from ever seeing the full crowd. The read side, a live picture of scarce inventory watched by everyone at once, is the actual system.

The entities:

- **Queue token**: one per arriving user, carrying a random sort key rather than an arrival timestamp.
- **Seat**: one numbered, individually identified unit of inventory, with no substitute.
- **Hold**: a time-limited lease on a seat, acquired by a conditional write and released by a TTL or a checkout.
- **Session**: a purchase window granted by admission, the only context in which a hold can be taken.

```
GET  /event/{id}/queue                 -> { token_id, sort_key }
GET  /q/{id}/serving                   -> { now_serving }          (shared, 2s TTL)
GET  /event/{id}/status.bin            -> 2-bit-per-seat bitmap    (shared, 1s TTL)
POST /event/{id}/admit                 -> { session_id, expires_at }
POST /event/{id}/hold  body:{seat_ids} -> { hold_id, expires_at } | 409 CONFLICT
```

#### High-level design
Follow one buyer from arrival through to a held seat.

[The hot path, arrival to hold](/diagram/ticketmaster?focus=clients,cdn,token-svc,queue-tokens,admission,purchase-api,seat-state,checkout,e1,e2,e3,e5,e7,e8,e14)

1. **1.5M clients** call the **Queue token service** to join the queue.
2. The **Queue token service** writes a random sort key into the **Queue token store**.
3. From then on, **1.5M clients** poll the **CDN edge** for shared, cacheable status objects, never the origin.
4. The **Queue token store** hands the **Admission controller** the lowest sort key first.
5. The **Admission controller** grants a purchase session to the **Purchase API**.
6. The **Purchase API** attempts an atomic hold against **Seat state**.
7. On success, the **Purchase API** hands the session to **Checkout** to run payment.

> **Why the flow is shaped this way.** The arrival rate and the sustainable service rate differ by three orders of magnitude, so something has to buffer that gap. Putting the buffer in front of the application, as tokens and shared read objects, rather than inside it, as threads, connections and database locks, means the expensive tier is sized for the sustainable rate rather than the peak.

#### Inverting the position query
1.5 million people want to know their place in line. Answering that per person is a service whose only output is the word "wait". What replaces it?

[The watermark, not a lookup](/diagram/ticketmaster?focus=clients,cdn,admission,e1,e5)

**Bad: an endpoint that returns each caller's own position.** Correct, and 1.5 million clients polling every 5 seconds is roughly 300,000 queries a second against a service that exists purely to say not yet.

**Good: push updates over a persistent connection to every waiting client.** This removes the polling overhead per request, but 1.5 million TLS handshakes inside ten seconds is a connection-establishment stampede that exhausts load-balancer accept queues before a single seat sells, and every surviving connection pins memory in exactly the tier meant to stay empty.

**Great: publish one shared global watermark, and let the client compute its own position.** The **Admission controller** publishes `now_serving`, roughly 20 bytes, as one cacheable object with a short TTL. Every client already knows its own sort key from its token, so it subtracts locally. Origin load falls to roughly 50 requests a second, and that number does not grow with audience size, because a million extra arrivals still read the same one object.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 180" role="img" aria-label="A per-user position endpoint scales with audience size to 300,000 requests a second; one shared watermark stays flat at about 50 origin requests a second regardless of crowd size">
  <style>
    .bar{fill:none;stroke:currentColor;stroke-width:1.2}
    .fillacc{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.22;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.4}
    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    .sub{fill:currentColor;opacity:.8;font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
  </style>
  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="16">Per-user position lookup: scales with audience</text>
  <rect class="bar" x="4" y="24" width="384" height="22" rx="4"/>
  <text class="sub" x="10" y="40">1.5M clients ÷ 5s poll ≈ 300,000 origin req/s</text>

  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="84">One shared watermark: origin load is flat</text>
  <rect class="bar fillacc" x="4" y="92" width="2" height="22" rx="2"/>
  <text class="sub" x="10" y="132">~100 edge PoPs ÷ 2s TTL ≈ 50 origin req/s,</text>
  <text class="sub" x="10" y="148">the same whether 150k or 15M people are waiting</text>
</svg>
```

The client cannot cheat by claiming a better position, because the sort key is signed into the token and re-verified at admission.

#### A shared, stale map instead of a live query
The seat map actually changes constantly, unlike a rank. How do 1.5 million viewers see roughly current status without querying inventory directly?

[The bitmap and its staleness](/diagram/ticketmaster?focus=seat-state,edge-publisher,cdn,e9,e13)

**Bad: query the seat table directly on every client refresh.** Correct at the instant of the query, and it melts the database on reads before a single hold is even attempted, since the read volume dwarfs every write in the system combined.

**Good: push seat-taken events to connected clients.** Accurate and immediate, and it inherits the same connection-stampede problem push has everywhere outside the admission gate: it is the wrong tool before a client has a session, and the right one only after.

**Great: encode every seat's status in 2 bits and republish one shared bitmap once a second.** Sixty thousand seats compress to roughly 5KB gzipped. Every viewer receives identical bytes, so 1.5 million clients polling at 1Hz reach the origin as roughly 100 requests a second rather than millions. Splitting the immutable venue geometry out of this object, cached forever behind a versioned URL, keeps the per-tick payload tiny.

The price of the tick is that every client acts on state up to a second old. That is handled in the response to a hold attempt, not prevented at read time: a `409 CONFLICT` carries the seat's current status inline, and the client greys the seat immediately rather than waiting for the next publish. Conflict is resolved where it is cheap to resolve, not avoided where it would be expensive to avoid.

#### Fairness as a security control
Whoever decides the ordering rule is deciding who wins. What happens when that rule is arrival time?

[The random sort key](/diagram/ticketmaster?focus=clients,token-svc,queue-tokens,e2,e3)

**Bad: strict first-come-first-served by arrival timestamp.** Legible, and exactly what users assume they are getting. It is also an auction on network latency rather than on anything a human controls: inventory here is nominally exhausted within the first fraction of a second of arrivals, a window in which only network position varies and human reaction time never enters at all. A bot on a cloud instance milliseconds from the edge beats a home broadband user by tens of milliseconds, worth thousands of queue positions at this arrival rate.

**Good: a monotonic sequence number, assigned in strict arrival order.** This is the mechanism FCFS actually needs, and it tops out at roughly the same rate as peak arrivals, with zero headroom and a livelock risk the moment retries begin, on top of still rewarding exactly the latency advantage that made FCFS the wrong rule.

**Great: a random 64-bit sort key drawn at token issue.** Every arrival in the opening window enters one randomised pool, served in ascending key order. The latency advantage money can buy becomes worthless, because the key was never a function of when the request arrived. It also shards with no coordination at all, since there is no shared counter to increment, only independent random draws written to sharded storage.

A random draw does not stop an attacker holding more tokens; it only removes the value of arriving fastest. That gap is a genuine, acknowledged limit, not a hidden one, and it reappears later as the reason identity binding still matters.

#### Sizing the gate with Little's law
How many buyers should the purchase flow admit at once, and how fast should it let new ones in?

[The admission cap and its refill](/diagram/ticketmaster?focus=admission,purchase-api,checkout,e7,e17)

**Bad: guess a concurrency limit that feels safe.** Arbitrary, and either too tight, wasting throughput the inventory could support, or too loose, letting more buyers in than the venue has seats for.

**Good: admit on a fixed schedule, a constant number of users every few seconds.** An improvement over guessing, but it ignores how long sessions actually take. If checkout slows down, for any reason, admissions keep arriving on schedule regardless, and the number of buyers actually in flight silently climbs past what the inventory can support.

**Great: derive the cap from inventory with Little's law, and refill it only from completions.** Cap concurrent buyers at 25,000, sized so the worst case is exactly one venue's seats held and nothing oversubscribed. A 240-second mean session then gives an admission rate of roughly 100 a second. Crucially, the **Admission controller**'s bucket refills from **Checkout**'s completions, abandonments and hold expiries, never from a clock.

That refill rule matters more than it looks. If admission ran on a fixed schedule while sessions ran long, say because the payment provider slowed down, the in-flow count would drift past the cap, every remaining seat would end up held by someone, and newly admitted buyers would arrive to a fully grey map, having spent the scarcest resource in the system, an admission slot, on someone who cannot buy anything. Refilling from completions makes the rate self-correct downward exactly when the funnel slows.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 170" role="img" aria-label="Little's law: a 25,000-buyer cap over a 240-second mean session gives roughly 100 admissions a second, refilled only as sessions complete">
  <style>.box{fill:none;stroke:currentColor;stroke-width:1.2}.fillacc{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.2;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.4}.lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}.sub{fill:currentColor;opacity:.8;font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}</style>
  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="16">C = 25,000 concurrent buyers (one venue's worth)</text>
  <rect class="box" x="4" y="24" width="384" height="22" rx="4"/>
  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="76">mean session = 240s</text>
  <rect class="fillacc" x="4" y="84" width="96" height="22" rx="4"/>
  <text class="sub" x="108" y="99">admission rate = 25,000 ÷ 240 ≈ 100/s</text>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="140">refilled by checkout completions, abandonments</text>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="156">and TTL expiry, never by a timer</text>
</svg>
```

#### Telling 97% of the crowd the truth
The queue cannot serve everyone, and it never will. What is the queue's actual job, then?

[Projecting the ending, not waiting for it](/diagram/ticketmaster?focus=exhaustion,edge-publisher,e11,e12)

**Bad: let the queue drain naturally and let people find out when they reach the front.** Technically honest and practically cruel. Draining the full queue at 100 admissions a second would take over four hours, while the inventory itself is gone in about seven minutes, so almost everyone waiting would sit through hours of a countdown toward nothing.

**Good: cut the queue off at a fixed position once the last seat is known to be sold.** Better, but it reacts only after the fact, and it ignores that roughly 40% of holds never convert, so seats keep trickling back after most of the queue has already been told no.

**Great: continuously project the exhaustion point from observed sell-through, and terminate the queue well ahead of it, with margin for returns.** The **Exhaustion projector** tracks sell-through velocity from **Seat state** and computes a live projected rank at which inventory runs out. Everyone beyond roughly twice that rank is told sold out within about 90 seconds of the on-sale opening, long before they would otherwise have found out by waiting.

The 2x margin, not 1x, exists specifically for the seats that come back. Roughly 40% of holds do not convert, and those seats need buyers who are still present in the queue rather than already dismissed. A countdown that quietly stalls generates more complaints and worse press than an early, honest no, which is why the design treats getting to "sold out" fast as a feature rather than an afterthought.

#### Where it breaks
| Layer | Failure | How the design handles it |
|---|---|---|
| Queue token service | A shard fails during the spike, leaving some arrivals without a token | Clients retry against a different shard by client-side hash; a lost token simply means drawing a new random key, which stays fair since order was never meaningful |
| Admission controller | The leader for an event dies mid-on-sale, and admissions stop | Leader election with a short lease; the new leader resumes from the persisted watermark, and slightly over-admitting on handover is safe while under-admitting is not |
| Seat state store | The Redis shard for an event fails, with the async replica milliseconds behind | Freeze the event, promote the replica, rebuild from durable `sold` rows plus the ordered hold log, and reopen within roughly a minute |
| Payment provider | An authorisation succeeds after a hold was already released and the seat resold | Never capture before the seat flip commits; auto-void any late authorisation; treat a slipped-through capture as an oversell incident with an automatic refund |
| Risk engine | The engine becomes unavailable, or a rule starts challenging real users | Fail open rather than blocking the sale outright, while automatically tightening per-identity purchase caps to bound the damage |
| Bot wave | A residential-proxy pool defeats fingerprinting and consumes admission slots | Dynamically raise proof-of-work difficulty, shadow-deny the suspect cohort rather than giving clean feedback, and tighten identity-graph caps |

#### What this design does not solve
**A fair draw per token is not a fair draw per person, and identity checks arrive too late to fix it.** A random sort key removes the latency advantage, and an attacker's answer is simply to hold more tokens. Anything that binds a token to something expensive to duplicate can only be checked at admission or checkout, by which point a bot has already consumed admission slots a genuine buyer could have used. Checking identity earlier, at the token gate itself, would mean demanding a verified payment method before anyone is even allowed to queue, which suppresses real demand at a rate high enough to be a commercial decision rather than an engineering one.

**Seats that return from expired holds make "sold out" temporarily untrue, and there is no clean fix.** Around 40% of holds do not convert, so several thousand seats return to the pool after most of the queue has already been told to leave. Retaining a margin of waiting users and drip-feeding returns to them is arbitrary in size: too small and returns leak to whoever refreshes at the right moment, too large and it keeps many people waiting for inventory that may never appear. A second randomised draw among opted-in latecomers is the principled fix and it recreates a second on-sale spike against a dispersed crowd, which measurably performs worse.

**The read tick that makes browsing survivable is the same thing that makes the final minutes brutal.** One second of staleness costs nothing while seats are plentiful. With a few thousand seats left against tens of thousands of buyers still in flow, nearly every click lands on a seat someone else already took, and the conflict rate on hold attempts approaches total. Publishing faster only multiplies edge egress without addressing the actual cause, which is far more buyers than seats. The honest response is a UI change, switching to a server-chosen best-available seat below a remaining-inventory threshold, not a technical fix.

#### Final design
Read it back through the numbers. Twenty-five buyers per seat is what makes the write race itself trivial and the read fan-out the entire problem. A 300,000-query-a-second naive position check collapsing to roughly 50 origin requests a second is what makes one shared, cacheable object the load-bearing idea across the whole read path. An admission rate of roughly 100 a second, derived from the inventory rather than guessed, is what keeps the purchase flow's concurrency bounded to exactly what 60,000 seats can support. And a queue where 97% of arrivals will never be admitted is what makes an honest, fast sold-out message as important as the purchase flow itself.

[The whole design](/diagram/ticketmaster?focus=clients,cdn,token-svc,queue-tokens,admission,purchase-api,seat-state,edge-publisher,exhaustion,checkout,payments,orders-db)

> **The numbers to remember.** 25 buyers per seat, ~60 per ticket · ~300k naive position QPS vs ~50 shared-object origin req/s · admission ~100/s, capped at 25,000 concurrent buyers · ~97% of the queue told sold out within about 90 seconds.

#### Check your understanding
**Why is the seat lock itself the easy part of this design?** It is one conditional write settling two buyers in a microsecond, with no retry loop. The system's real difficulty is that 1.5 million browsers all want a live view of the same 60,000 seats, which is read volume no naive query pattern survives.

**Why does a per-user position endpoint fail even though each individual query is cheap?** The cost is in the multiplication, not any single query: 1.5 million clients polling every 5 seconds is roughly 300,000 queries a second purely to say wait, and that number grows linearly with audience size however cheap one query is.

**Why does a random sort key beat strict first-come-first-served here specifically?** Inventory is nominally exhausted within a fraction of a second of the on-sale opening, a window where only network latency varies and human reaction time plays no role at all, which turns FCFS into an auction on proximity to the edge that only a well-resourced bot can reliably win.

**Why must the admission bucket refill from completions rather than a clock?** A fixed schedule keeps admitting new buyers even if checkout slows down elsewhere, letting the number of buyers actually in flight drift past what the inventory supports, until every seat is held and freshly admitted users arrive to a fully grey map.

**Why does the design treat an early sold-out message as a feature rather than a failure?** Draining the full queue at a sustainable admission rate would take hours, while the inventory itself sells out in minutes, so continuously projecting the exhaustion point and telling the doomed majority quickly is the only honest option available.
### 50. Design a RAG System (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)
#### Understanding the problem
A RAG system answers natural-language questions about a company's own documents by retrieving the relevant passages and having a language model write a cited answer from only those passages, never surfacing anything the asker is not allowed to read.

Two things make this hard, and neither is the language model itself.

First, the model is fluent regardless of what it is given. Hand it the wrong passages and it writes a confident, well-cited, wrong answer, and nothing in a dashboard turns red to say so. Almost every real failure here is a retrieval failure wearing a generation costume.

Second, access control has to live inside the search, not after it. A permission check applied to results already chosen can hand a narrowly permissioned user zero usable passages out of a hundred retrieved, because none of the hundred were ever theirs to see.

> **What this is not.** It looks like the web search engine design: a query narrows an enormous corpus to a handful of results, and both live or die on ranking quality. The difference is what a bad result costs. Search returns links a user can judge in about a second, so a bad one costs a click. This returns an assertion the user cannot cheaply check, so a bad one costs their trust. Search relevance is verifiable by inspection, which is why search learns from click logs; semantic relevance is opaque, which is why this design needs a labelled set with span-level ground truth before it can improve at all.

#### Requirements and the numbers
**Functional.** Ingest heterogeneous sources incrementally. Chunk and embed. Hybrid retrieve with ACL enforcement. Rerank. Generate a streamed, cited answer, or abstain. Re-index on document or model change.

**Non-functional.** p95 time-to-first-token under 1.5 seconds, p95 retrieve-plus-rerank under 250ms, at 500 queries a second peak. Edit-to-searchable p50 under 2 minutes. Permission revocation effective within 60 seconds. Zero cross-ACL leaks.

The whole design is decided by four numbers, so derive them before drawing anything.

**How many chunks does the corpus become?** Roughly 50 million source documents, averaging around 10 chunks each once split: 50,000,000 × 10 ≈ **500 million chunks**.

**What does the vector index cost in memory, and why does the number type matter?** At full precision, 500M × 4KB ≈ 2TB. At int8, 500M × 1KB ≈ 500GB, plus roughly 135GB of graph overhead: **~635GB**, which is what forces sharding across multiple machines in the first place.

**Where does the compute bill actually go?** 500 queries/s × ~6,500 prompt tokens ≈ 3.3 million prefill tokens a second, needing roughly 220 accelerators for generation, against roughly 30 for reranking: generation runs **~8x the reranker fleet** and roughly 20x everything else combined.

**How much of the user-facing latency is retrieval?** Retrieval and reranking together land around 180ms, against a roughly 1.2-second time to first token: **retrieval is about 15% of latency and about 5% of the compute bill.**

> **The numbers to carry.** ~500M chunks from ~50M documents · vector index ~635GB, sharded · generation ~220 accelerators, ~8x the reranker fleet · retrieval + rerank ~180ms of a ~1.2s time to first token.

#### Retrieval and generation: two different systems
The design is really two systems meeting at a handful of stores. **Retrieval** runs continuously in the background, ingesting and indexing, and answers no question directly. **Generation** runs once per request, reads only what retrieval hands it, and never touches the source documents itself.

The entities:

- **Document**: one source item from a connector, parsed and normalised to text.
- **Chunk**: a roughly 512-token piece of a document, the actual unit that is embedded, indexed and retrieved.
- **ACL group**: a permission scope attached to every chunk, never to an individual reader.
- **Citation**: a pointer from a generated sentence back to the chunk it was grounded in.

```
POST /ask   body: { question, principal }
  -> SSE: { token } | { citations: [{ doc_id, char_span }] } | { no_answer: true }
```

#### High-level design
Follow one question from arrival to a streamed, cited answer.

[The hot path, question to answer](/diagram/rag-system?focus=query-api,hybrid,vector-index,lexical-index,reranker,assembler,generation,e7,e8,e9,e10,e12,e14,e15)

1. The **Query API** resolves the caller's permission groups and hands the embedded question to **Hybrid retrieval + RRF**.
2. **Hybrid retrieval + RRF** searches the **Vector index (HNSW)** for semantically similar chunks, filtered to the caller's groups.
3. In parallel, it searches the **Lexical index (BM25)** for literal term matches, under the same filter.
4. It fuses both ranked lists and hands the merged candidates to **Cross-encoder reranker**.
5. **Cross-encoder reranker** scores each candidate jointly with the question and passes the survivors to **Context assembly**.
6. **Context assembly** dedupes, drops expired chunks, and hands the best eight to **Prompt + LLM tier**.
7. **Prompt + LLM tier** streams a cited answer back through the **Query API**.

> **Why the flow is shaped this way.** Retrieval fans out to two independent indexes because dense and lexical retrieval fail on disjoint kinds of query, and merging two cheap rankings beats tuning one. The reranker sits between retrieval and generation because it is the only place an expensive, accurate model can afford to run, on a set small enough to justify its cost.

#### Hybrid retrieval, and why fusion beats a weighted sum
An embedding finds meaning. It cannot find an error code or a ticket id. What replaces it, and how do the two answers combine?

[Two retrievers, one fused list](/diagram/rag-system?focus=hybrid,vector-index,lexical-index,e8,e9)

**Bad: dense retrieval alone.** Excellent at topical similarity, and it has genuinely never seen most literal identifiers as meaningful tokens. A question like "why is JOB-4471 retrying" returns generic chunks about retry policy, because the embedding has no representation of what JOB-4471 is at all.

**Good: run both retrievers and combine their scores with a weighted sum.** This adds the lexical arm, which is real progress. It fails on scale mismatch: cosine similarity lives in a bounded range with a corpus-dependent distribution, BM25 is unbounded and depends on term rarity, so a weighted sum needs per-corpus tuning that silently breaks the moment the corpus mix shifts.

**Great: fuse by rank rather than by score, with reciprocal rank fusion.** Ignore the two scales entirely and use only each chunk's rank in each list: `score(c) = Σ 1/(60 + rank)`. A chunk ranked first by BM25 but fortieth by dense scores lower than a chunk ranked eighth by both, because agreement across two independent retrievers is stronger evidence than one spectacular rank paired with a bad one.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 195" role="img" aria-label="A chunk ranked eighth by both retrievers outscores one ranked first by BM25 but fortieth by dense, because reciprocal rank fusion rewards agreement over any single spectacular rank">
  <style>
    .bar{fill:none;stroke:currentColor;stroke-width:1.2}
    .fillacc{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.22;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.4}
    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    .sub{fill:currentColor;opacity:.8;font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
  </style>
  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="16">Chunk A: BM25 rank 1, dense rank 40</text>
  <rect class="bar" x="4" y="24" width="138" height="20" rx="4"/>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="60">1/61 + 1/100 ≈ 0.026</text>

  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="94">Chunk B: BM25 rank 8, dense rank 8</text>
  <rect class="bar fillacc" x="4" y="102" width="154" height="20" rx="4"/>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="138">2 × 1/68 ≈ 0.029, B wins</text>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="164">two moderate ranks that agree beat one spectacular</text>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="178">rank and one bad one</text>
</svg>
```

Without the lexical arm at all, questions naming an identifier the embedding model has never usefully seen are simply unanswerable, no matter how good the dense retriever is otherwise.

#### Access control inside the search, not after it
Every candidate a user cannot read must never occupy a slot meant for one they can. Where does that check actually have to run?

[Filtering before ranking, not after](/diagram/rag-system?focus=query-api,hybrid,vector-index,lexical-index,e7,e8,e9)

**Bad: retrieve the global top 100, then drop what the caller cannot read.** One line of code, and it collapses for exactly the users with the least access. A contractor who can read 0.1% of the corpus needs roughly a thousand-fold over-fetch to recover eight usable chunks, and no fixed `k` chosen in advance is correct for both them and an employee who can read everything.

**Good: over-fetch by a generous fixed multiple before filtering.** This buys headroom for moderately restricted users, and it still fails outright for anyone narrowly permissioned enough, and it leaks information regardless: result counts and latency both vary with how much was hidden, which is itself a signal about what exists.

**Great: evaluate the permission predicate inside the search itself.** The ACL check runs as a hard filter during the ANN graph traversal and the lexical query alike, so the top 100 candidates that come out are already 100 chunks the caller is entitled to read. A highly selective predicate still costs something, since a greedy graph walk can waste its budget on rejected nodes, so a small enough allowed set falls back to an exact brute-force scan instead.

That fallback matters because filtered graph search degrades exactly where it is most dangerous to degrade. A user in a twelve-person private space gets an exact scan over a few thousand chunks; a user in the all-company group gets the full filtered graph search over hundreds of millions. Neither path silently returns wrong results, only a slower one when the estimate is wrong.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="-4 -7 400 184" role="img" aria-label="Filtering after retrieval can leave a narrowly permissioned user with zero usable chunks from a hundred retrieved; filtering inside the search guarantees every candidate returned is already readable">
  <style>
    .allow{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.3;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.2}
    .deny{fill:none;stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.3;stroke-width:1}
    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    .sub{fill:currentColor;opacity:.8;font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
  </style>
  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="14">Post-filter: retrieve top 100, then drop unreadable</text>
  <g transform="translate(4,22)">
    <rect class="deny" x="0" y="0" width="384" height="18" rx="3"/>
    <rect class="allow" x="2" y="0" width="4" height="18" rx="1"/>
  </g>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="58">a contractor readable in 0.1% of the corpus keeps</text>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="74">roughly 0 of the 100 retrieved</text>

  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="106">Pre-filter: permission check runs inside the search</text>
  <g transform="translate(4,114)">
    <rect class="allow" x="0" y="0" width="384" height="18" rx="3"/>
  </g>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="150">every one of the 100 candidates returned was</text>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="166">already readable, whatever the caller's access</text>
</svg>
```

#### Scoring jointly, not separately
Dense and lexical retrieval both score a chunk in isolation from the question. What separates "about this topic" from "answers this question"?

[The cross-encoder pass](/diagram/rag-system?focus=hybrid,reranker,e10,e12)

**Bad: trust the fused retrieval rank as the final order.** A dense embedding of "how much parental leave do I get" sits closest to an HR page's introductory paragraph about leave in general, while the chunk actually containing the number often ranks well outside the top ten. The retriever found the topic, not the answer.

**Good: widen the candidate window and hope the answer surfaces somewhere in it.** More candidates do reach the prompt this way, and it trades one problem for another: a wider context dilutes the model's attention across more irrelevant text, which measurably lowers faithfulness rather than improving it.

**Great: run a cross-encoder over the top 100, scoring the question and each chunk jointly.** Every query token attends to every chunk token in one pass, roughly a thousand times more expensive per pair than a dot product between two independently computed vectors, which is exactly why it runs on a hundred candidates rather than five hundred million. That joint attention is what actually distinguishes topical relatedness from answering the question asked.

Ordering the survivors with the strongest chunks placed at both the start and the end of the prompt, rather than by raw score alone, is what keeps the model from ignoring a correct chunk buried in the middle of the context, a pattern models reliably exhibit regardless of how good the ranking underneath it is.

#### Chunking as a measured parameter
Every downstream stage depends on how the corpus was split before any of it ran. Why is chunk size a genuine trade-off rather than a default to pick once?

[Where the split happens](/diagram/rag-system?focus=chunker,chunk-store,e2,e3)

**Bad: split into very small, precise chunks.** Each vector represents one idea cleanly, so retrieval precision looks excellent in isolation. The retrieved text often lacks the surrounding sentence that makes it answerable at all, so the chunk containing "26 weeks" retrieves beautifully and never says what the 26 weeks are for.

**Good: split into large chunks that carry plenty of surrounding context.** Answerable once retrieved, and the embedding of a chunk spanning six unrelated ideas matches everything weakly and nothing strongly, so it stops reliably surfacing in the first place, and it burns the token budget after only a few chunks.

**Great: split on structural boundaries where the source has them, per source type.** Headings for wikis, whole tickets with top comments for tickets, function or class boundaries for code, section boundaries for PDFs, with a fixed-size fallback only where no structure exists. A benefits PDF split blindly at a fixed token count can cut a leave-entitlement table in half, separating the country column from the weeks column; splitting on the PDF's own section headings keeps the table intact.

The two curves that matter, retrieval precision and answer faithfulness, peak at different chunk sizes, and only the second one is the actual product. Storing a small chunk alongside a pointer to its parent section lets the assembler expand a winning chunk to its neighbours before prompting, recovering the answerability that a small chunk alone would have lost.

#### Answering "I don't know" on purpose
Two current, in-date documents disagree about a number. The retriever finds both. What should the system do?

[Where conflict and confidence are decided](/diagram/rag-system?focus=assembler,generation,e13,e14)

**Bad: always generate a confident answer from whatever was retrieved.** The model picks one of the two conflicting values essentially at random and cites it convincingly, which is worse than either an error or an outright refusal, because the citation makes a coin flip look verified.

**Good: filter by document date and hope the stale one drops out.** This closes the case where one document has genuinely expired, tagged with an `effective_to` in the past. It does nothing when both documents are still in date and simply disagree, which is the harder and more common version of the problem.

**Great: calibrate an abstention floor, and surface real conflicts rather than resolving them silently.** If the top rerank score falls below a floor calibrated so that roughly 95% of below-floor questions were genuinely unanswerable on the labelled set, the system returns its three best candidates as links rather than an invented answer. When surviving chunks still disagree after date filtering, the prompt instructs the model to cite both values explicitly rather than pick one.

This turns the worst possible failure, a confident wrong answer, into the second-best outcome, an honest "I don't know, here's what I found." The floor is tuned against the labelled set rather than intuition, and it will occasionally decline to answer a question the corpus genuinely does answer, which is the accepted cost of removing the far more damaging failure.

#### Where it breaks
| Layer | Failure | How the design handles it |
|---|---|---|
| ACL resolver | The resolver is unavailable, so retrieval cannot evaluate the permission predicate | Fail closed: refuse the query rather than serve unfiltered results, never falling back to allow-all |
| Vector index shard | One shard is down mid scatter-gather | Serve from a replica; if a whole shard set is unreachable, degrade to lexical-only with the response flagged, rather than silently answering from a fraction of the corpus |
| Embedding model | A query embedded with a new model version is compared against an old index | Model version is part of shard identity; a mismatched request is rejected rather than served, and cutover happens atomically behind a version flag |
| Reranker | The model server saturates and the rerank queue grows | Rerank depth adaptively drops from 100 toward 25 candidates under load, logged and alerted rather than degrading silently |
| Semantic cache | A near-duplicate query returns an answer for the wrong year or a negated question | A high similarity floor, mandatory bypass on years, numbers, negations and proper nouns, and a cache partitioned per permission group so a false hit can never also be a leak |
| Generation tier | The LLM endpoint is degraded or rate-limited | Fall back to a smaller model behind the same prompt contract; if generation is fully down, return the reranked chunks as a ranked list of links rather than an error page |

#### What this design does not solve
**Multi-hop questions fall outside single-shot retrieval entirely.** A question whose answer requires combining two chunks that are not similar to each other, and where neither alone contains the full answer, defeats a design built around one retrieval pass. Query decomposition or an agentic retrieve-decide-retrieve loop helps, and both roughly triple latency and cost while never reliably knowing when to stop, so this stays a genuine capability gap rather than a tuning problem.

**Production has no ground truth.** Everything that says the system is working comes from a labelled set the team wrote itself, which cannot cover the real distribution of questions, plus proxy signals like thumbs-down that are biased toward users who noticed they were misled. A confidently wrong answer to a question nobody anticipated produces no signal anywhere.

**The corpus can contradict itself with no authority to appeal to.** Two current, readable, in-date documents can simply disagree, and no amount of retrieval or reranking resolves that, because both are legitimate candidates on every measurable axis. The only real fix is editorial, a designated source of truth per topic, which is an organisational commitment the engineering design cannot substitute for.

#### Final design
Read it back through the numbers. Five hundred million chunks forcing a 635GB sharded vector index is what makes retrieval an infrastructure problem before it is ever a ranking one. An 8x gap between the generation fleet and the reranker fleet is what makes prefix caching and semantic caching worth building even though they touch the smaller half of the system's difficulty. And 180ms of retrieval inside a 1.2-second time to first token is what confirms the model was never the bottleneck, correctness was.

[The whole design](/diagram/rag-system?focus=connectors,chunker,embed,chunk-store,lexical-index,vector-index,query-api,hybrid,reranker,assembler,generation,eval)

> **The numbers to remember.** ~500M chunks, ~50M documents · vector index ~635GB, 6 shards · generation ~220 accelerators, ~8x the reranker fleet · retrieval + rerank ~180ms of a ~1.2s time to first token · full re-index on a model upgrade costs roughly a day end to end.

#### Check your understanding
**Why can a fluent, well-cited answer still be entirely wrong?** The generation model is only as good as the passages it was handed. If retrieval surfaces topically related but non-answering chunks, the model writes a confident answer grounded in the wrong evidence, and nothing about its fluency signals the mistake.

**Why does reciprocal rank fusion beat a weighted sum of dense and lexical scores?** The two scores live on incomparable scales, cosine similarity bounded and corpus-dependent, BM25 unbounded and rarity-dependent, so a weighted sum needs constant per-corpus retuning. Fusing by rank instead rewards agreement between two independent retrievers without ever needing to compare their raw scores.

**Why does filtering permissions after retrieval fail for narrowly permissioned users specifically?** A user who can read a small fraction of the corpus can have every one of a hundred retrieved candidates fall outside their access, since permission was never part of what got them retrieved in the first place. No fixed over-fetch factor chosen in advance works for both that user and someone who can read everything.

**Why is chunk size not something to set once at project start?** Retrieval precision and answer faithfulness peak at different chunk sizes, and both interact with whichever embedding model and reranker are in use. Changing either of those without re-measuring chunk size is one of the most common ways a RAG system quietly underperforms for months.

**Why does the system sometimes refuse to answer a question the corpus can genuinely answer?** The abstention floor is calibrated so that most below-floor questions really were unanswerable, which necessarily means a small number of genuinely answerable ones fall below it too. That cost is accepted deliberately, in exchange for removing the far more damaging failure of a confident, wrong, well-cited answer.
### 51. Design a Content Delivery Network (CDN)
#### Understanding the problem
A CDN serves a customer's content from a global fleet of caches, so a user gets bytes from a machine a few milliseconds away instead of from a distant origin. Serving a cache hit is an easy problem, solved by any competent proxy.

Two things make the rest of it hard.

First, one object now exists as thousands of independent copies across hundreds of datacentres. When the origin changes it, every one of those copies has to be corrected without the luxury of consensus and without any way to collect an acknowledgement from all of them.

Second, the freshness dial has a cliff at both ends. A long TTL serves wrong content for as long as it takes to expire. A short TTL means a popular object's expiry becomes a synchronised stampede, every cache asking the origin for the same bytes at once.

> **What this is not.** It looks like the distributed cache design: a tier of machines holding hot data in front of a slower store. The resemblance ends at ownership.
