A distributed cache sits next to the code that writes its origin, so invalidation is a delete issued by the writer at the moment of the write, cheap and roughly synchronous. Here the writer is the customer's own origin, which this system does not control, so it learns about changes by asking or by being told, and a lost entry that would cost one origin query in a distributed cache can, refilled against an origin sized for a sliver of total traffic, take a customer's whole site down.

#### Requirements and the numbers
**Functional.** Fetch and cache from customer origins. Route users to the nearest healthy edge. Configurable cache keys and TTLs. Purge by URL, tag or whole origin. TLS termination with customer certificates.

**Non-functional.** At least 95% request hit ratio and 90% byte hit ratio. p99 time to first byte under 50ms on an in-region hit. Purge reaching 99.9% of edge servers within 5 seconds. Loss of any single point of presence causes zero user-visible errors.

The whole design is decided by four numbers, so derive them before drawing anything.

**What does a hot object's expiry actually trigger?** At 5 million requests a second worldwide for one object, spread over 200 points of presence, against a 200ms origin fetch: roughly 25,000 requests a second per point of presence × 0.2s × 200 points of presence ≈ **1,000,000 concurrent origin requests** for a single URL the instant its TTL expires.

**What does one point of byte hit ratio cost?** At this scale, moving from 90% to 89% byte hit ratio adds enough origin egress to cost roughly **$420,000 a month**, purely from cache-key hygiene.

**How much does the tiered hierarchy collapse origin load?** Edge, regional mid-tier and origin shield fold **200 points of presence down to 20 regions down to 1** fetch per customer origin, cutting what would otherwise reach the origin by roughly 80%.

**How fast, and how completely, does a purge actually propagate?** A purge reaches **99.9% of roughly 13,000 edge servers within about 2 seconds**, which is a statement about the servers that answered, not a guarantee about the ones that did not.

> **The numbers to carry.** 1,000,000 concurrent origin requests at a hot expiry, collapsed to 1 · one byte-hit-ratio point ≈ $420k/month · 200 edges → 20 mid-tiers → 1 shield · purge reaches 99.9% of ~13,000 servers in ~2s.

#### Caching and correcting: two different problems
The design is really two problems that share a fleet of machines. **Caching** is well understood: fetch, store, serve, evict. **Correcting** thousands of unsupervised copies of somebody else's mutable data, with no consensus and no collectable acknowledgement, is the genuinely hard distributed systems problem this question is actually about.

The entities:

- **Object**: one cacheable response, identified by a cache key built from host, path and allowlisted parameters.
- **TTL**: how long a cached copy is trusted before it is considered stale.
- **Purge**: an explicit instruction telling caches to stop trusting an object before its TTL would have expired anyway.
- **Tag**: a label attached to many objects at once, so one purge can invalidate all of them without enumerating them.

```
GET  <object url>
  -> 200 body, X-Cache: HIT|MISS, Age: <seconds>

POST /purge   body: { url | tag | origin }
  -> { accepted: true, purge_id }   # eventually consistent, not a completion proof
```

#### High-level design
Follow one request from a client to whichever tier actually answers it.

[The hot path, request to origin](/diagram/cdn?focus=client,router,edge,coalesce,midtier,shield,origin,e1,e2,e3,e6,e7,e8,e9)

1. The **Client** connects, and **Anycast BGP + GeoDNS** delivers the packet to the nearest healthy point of presence.
2. That routes the connection to an **Edge PoP (x200)**, which terminates TLS and builds the cache key.
3. The **Edge PoP (x200)** checks the **Edge object cache** and, on a hit, answers directly with no upstream contact at all.
4. On a miss or a stale entry, the request goes to **Single-flight + SWR**, which coalesces duplicate fetches for the same key.
5. **Single-flight + SWR** forwards one fetch per key to the **Regional mid-tier (x20)**.
6. The **Regional mid-tier (x20)** forwards its own misses to the **Origin shield**.
7. The **Origin shield** issues one conditional fetch to the **Customer origin**, on behalf of everything behind it.

> **Why the flow is shaped this way.** Each tier exists to shrink the fan-out reaching the next one. The edge exists for latency; the mid-tier and shield exist purely to protect the origin, which is why they are allowed to add latency to a miss rather than being optimised for speed.

#### Coalescing a million-request stampede
A popular object's TTL expires at roughly the same instant on 200 points of presence. What stops that from becoming a million simultaneous origin requests?

[The coalescing cascade](/diagram/cdn?focus=coalesce,midtier,shield,e6,e7,e8,e9)

**Bad: let every request that misses go straight to the origin.** Correct, and at the scale a hot object's expiry produces, this is exactly the million-request stampede the numbers describe. The origin, normally seeing a tiny fraction of delivered bytes, is hit with a spike it was never provisioned for.

**Good: hold one global lock per key and make every request wait behind it.** This does collapse the fetch count to one, and it does so by making every waiting user pay the full round-trip latency of that one fetch, which turns a 12ms cache hit into a 270ms wait for everyone caught behind an expiry.

**Great: cascade several cheap coalescers, and serve stale while the real fetch runs in the background.** Single-flight inside each edge server takes the count down by roughly two orders of magnitude on its own. Consistent-hashing a key to one owning server per point of presence, then coalescing again at the mid-tier and again at the origin shield, folds the remaining fan-out down step by step: **1,000,000 → roughly 12,800 → 200 → 20 → 1**. Stale-while-revalidate means every one of those million waiting requests gets the old, still-useful copy immediately, while exactly one real fetch runs in the background.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="-4 0 400 215" role="img" aria-label="A million concurrent origin requests collapse through four coalescing stages to a single real fetch, log scale">
  <style>
    .bar{fill:none;stroke:currentColor;stroke-width:1.2}
    .fillacc{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.24;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.4}
    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    .sub{fill:currentColor;opacity:.8;font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
  </style>
  <rect class="bar" x="4" y="10" width="384" height="22" rx="4"/><text class="sub" x="10" y="25">requests wanting a fetch: 1,000,000</text>
  <rect class="bar" x="4" y="42" width="98" height="22" rx="4"/><text class="sub" x="10" y="57">per-server single-flight: ~12,800</text>
  <rect class="bar" x="4" y="74" width="33" height="22" rx="4"/><text class="sub" x="10" y="89">per-PoP key ownership: 200</text>
  <rect class="bar" x="4" y="106" width="10" height="22" rx="4"/><text class="sub" x="10" y="121">mid-tier coalescing: 20</text>
  <rect class="bar fillacc" x="4" y="138" width="2" height="22" rx="2"/><text class="lbl" x="10" y="153">origin shield: 1 fetch, ~270ms</text>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="188">every one of the million waiting requests is</text>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="204">served stale meanwhile, at zero added latency</text>
</svg>
```

#### Making invalidation unnecessary
Purging a change to thousands of machines is expensive and slow. What if most content never needed it?

[The escape from the TTL dial](/diagram/cdn?focus=cachekey,edge,e4)

**Bad: rely on a fixed TTL for everything, and accept the staleness window it implies.** Simple, and it means every content change is served wrong somewhere for up to the length of the TTL, with no way to correct it faster than that.

**Good: shorten the TTL and revalidate more often.** This narrows the staleness window and directly worsens the other cliff: a shorter TTL means more frequent expiries, and more frequent expiries mean more frequent stampedes on anything popular.

**Great: where the URL is owned, put a hash of the bytes in the filename and serve it immutable forever.** Changed content becomes a different object at a different address, so no cached copy is ever wrong, because nothing was ever mutated. A deploy becomes changing a short-lived pointer to the new hashed filename, concentrating the entire freshness problem into one small, easily refreshed reference instead of spreading it across millions of cached objects.

Purge remains the only lever for content whose URL is not owned, a customer's `/index.html`, an API response, a legal takedown, and there the honest guarantee is eventual consistency rather than instant correction. Content-hashed naming does not make purge cheaper; it removes the need for purge entirely on most of the bytes a CDN actually serves.

#### A broadcast nobody acknowledges
A purge has to reach roughly 13,000 machines across 200 datacentres, some of which are unreachable right now. What does a broadcast look like when nobody can collect an acknowledgement?

[The purge log and its offsets](/diagram/cdn?focus=purgelog,relay,edge,midtier,e11,e12,e13)

**Bad: push the purge synchronously and wait for every server to confirm.** This would give a real completion guarantee, and it is not available: some fraction of 13,000 machines across 200 datacentres will always be temporarily unreachable, so waiting for universal acknowledgement means the operation never reliably completes.

**Good: fire the purge out best-effort and move on.** Fast, and it silently loses the machines that were unreachable at the moment of the push, with no mechanism for them to ever catch up once they reconnect.

**Great: append the purge to a durable, replayable log, and let every point of presence track its own offset.** The control plane appends to the **Durable purge log**, fans out through 200 point-of-presence relays in the **Fan-out tree**, and each relay multicasts inside its own facility. A point of presence that was partitioned simply resumes reading from its last recorded offset once it reconnects, catching up on everything it missed without anyone re-sending it anything.

Two properties are what make this safe without acknowledgements at all: the operation is idempotent, so replaying it twice is identical to applying it once, and the log itself is the source of truth rather than any individual delivery. The honest guarantee stated out loud is "99.9% of servers within about two seconds, and a partitioned point of presence replays the log when it comes back", which is a statement about survivability, not a consistency proof.

#### Purging a tag without touching ten million objects
"Everything tagged `product-1234`" can match ten million objects scattered across 150 petabytes of disk. How does one purge reach all of them without scanning any of it?

[The generation counter](/diagram/cdn?focus=taggen,cachestore,e14,e15)

**Bad: enumerate every object carrying the tag and purge each one individually.** Correct, and finding ten million matching objects means scanning the index on every point of presence, minutes of work repeated 200 times for a single bulk invalidation.

**Good: maintain a per-tag list of object keys, so a purge only walks that list.** This avoids a full scan, and the list itself has to be kept correct as objects are added and evicted continuously, becoming its own large, contended piece of state that has to be replicated everywhere the objects are cached.

**Great: store the tag's generation at fetch time on every cached object, and purge by bumping one counter.** The **Tag generation table** holds one counter per tag, globally replicated. Purging a tag is a single, tiny write, roughly 40 bytes, pushed everywhere. On the next read, a server compares the generation stored on the cached object against the current generation for that tag, and any mismatch is treated as a miss.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 189" role="img" aria-label="Each cached object records the tag generation at fetch time; bumping the global counter for a tag makes every stale object miss on its next read, with no enumeration">
  <style>
    .box{fill:none;stroke:currentColor;stroke-width:1.2}
    .fillacc{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.22;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.4}
    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    .sub{fill:currentColor;opacity:.8;font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    text{dominant-baseline:middle;text-anchor:middle}
  </style>
  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="14" style="text-anchor:start">Objects, stamped with tag generation at fetch</text>
  <rect class="box" x="4" y="24" width="120" height="28" rx="5"/><text class="sub" x="64" y="40">obj A · gen 7</text>
  <rect class="box" x="132" y="24" width="120" height="28" rx="5"/><text class="sub" x="192" y="40">obj B · gen 7</text>
  <rect class="box" x="260" y="24" width="120" height="28" rx="5"/><text class="sub" x="320" y="40">obj C · gen 7</text>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="76" style="text-anchor:start">purge tag "product-1234": one counter bump,</text>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="92" style="text-anchor:start">~40B, pushed everywhere</text>
  <rect class="box fillacc" x="4" y="102" width="150" height="28" rx="5"/><text class="lbl" x="79" y="118">tag → gen 8</text>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="156" style="text-anchor:start">on next read: object gen 7 &lt; tag gen 8 →</text>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="172" style="text-anchor:start">treated as a miss, no scan, no enumeration</text>
</svg>
```

The cost is honesty rather than speed: a tag-purged object still occupies disk until it is next requested or evicted through the ordinary cache lifecycle, so this mechanism means the object will never be served again, not that it has been deleted, which matters for anything that must be physically removed rather than merely stopped from serving.

#### Routing users without waiting for DNS
A degraded point of presence needs traffic moved away from it fast. What actually decides which point of presence a user reaches?

[Anycast versus DNS steering](/diagram/cdn?focus=client,router,edge,e1,e2)

**Bad: give every point of presence its own address and steer entirely through DNS.** This is a real, defensible design, capable of capacity-aware and per-customer routing that anycast cannot express. Its weakness is how slowly it actually moves traffic: a stated TTL of 30 seconds does not mean 30 seconds, because a meaningful share of resolvers and client runtimes hold records for minutes to hours regardless of what the record says.

**Good: use a short DNS TTL and refresh it aggressively.** This narrows the gap somewhat, and it is still bounded by client behaviour the CDN does not control, so a drained point of presence can keep receiving traffic well past an incident's target resolution time.

**Great: announce the same address from every point of presence over BGP, and let internet routing itself deliver the packet.** Anycast means the internet's own convergence, not any client's cache, decides which point of presence a connection reaches. Withdrawing a route reconverges in seconds with no client-side state to wait out at all. GeoDNS sits on top, choosing between a handful of independently announced anycast rings, keeping a coarser steering knob for anything routing alone cannot express.

Anycast's price is that mid-flow reconvergence can land a packet on a point of presence with no state for that connection, returning a reset rather than continuing the stream. With typical CDN flows lasting a few seconds, that exposure window is small; a CDN whose flows last minutes, such as long downloads or held-open live streams, has the opposite exposure profile and should lean back toward DNS.

#### Where it breaks
| Layer | Failure | How the design handles it |
|---|---|---|
| Cache key | A config change removes a keyed header and personalised responses start being shared | Never-store rules on `Set-Cookie`, `Cache-Control: private` and authorization headers are enforced inside the cache engine itself, immune to any config change, treated as a security incident on detection |
| Edge cache | A software rollout corrupts on-disk entries | Per-object checksums treat a mismatch as a miss rather than serving corruption, and rollouts canary one point of presence at a time with automatic rollback on a hit-ratio drop |
| Mid-tier | A regional mid-tier is lost, and its points of presence lose their shield | Edges fail over to the next-nearest mid-tier at higher latency, and a per-origin fill token bucket at the shield prevents the origin absorbing the resulting spike |
| Purge control plane | Fan-out stalls, and stale content stays live past the target latency | The durable log's per-point-of-presence offsets mean any lagging point of presence replays automatically once it catches up, rather than needing to be told again |
| Origin | The origin returns errors or times out | Expired copies are served for a configured window while circuit-broken, and errors are negative-cached briefly so they cannot themselves stampede |
| Routing | A point of presence is up but its upstream transit has degraded | Automated health-based withdrawal of its anycast announcement reconverges traffic to neighbours within seconds |

#### What this design does not solve
**There is no safe setting for the TTL, and nothing here actually fixes that.** Every mechanism in this design works around the two-sided cliff rather than removing it. Stale-while-revalidate does not rescue the short end; it makes the staleness guaranteed by construction, since every expiry serves at least one stale response somewhere before the refresh completes. The honest description of a short TTL with a long stale-serve window is that content can be nearly as old as that whole window, not merely as old as the TTL suggests.

**Purge cannot be proven complete, and completing it does not mean deletion.** A reported acknowledgement count is a statement about the servers that answered, not about the whole fleet, and a partitioned point of presence keeps serving old bytes for as long as it stays disconnected, with no bound on how long that is. The tag-purge mechanism deliberately leaves bytes on disk and only stops serving them, so a legal takedown is not actually removed by the operation that was meant to remove it; that requires a separate, unbuilt deletion job with its own completion tracking.

**Nothing here is fast for content that genuinely must never be stale.** Routes that cannot tolerate any staleness, an inventory count, a live price, opt out of caching entirely and pay the full round-trip to the origin on every request. That is pure origin load with a CDN in front of it doing nothing but adding a hop, and it is the honest cost of a caching layer that cannot know when the source of truth changed without being told.

#### Final design
Read it back through the numbers. A million concurrent origin requests at one hot expiry is what makes cascading coalescers, not merely a bigger origin, the only workable answer. A $420,000-a-month price on one point of byte hit ratio is what makes cache-key hygiene a finance decision rather than a tuning one. A three-tier hierarchy collapsing 200 points of presence to one origin fetch is what keeps a customer's origin provisioned for a stable, small fraction of total traffic instead of a spiky, unbounded one. And a purge that reaches 99.9% of servers in two seconds, with no way to prove the rest, is what makes content-hashed immutable naming the real fix and purge the acknowledged fallback.

[The whole design](/diagram/cdn?focus=client,router,edge,coalesce,midtier,shield,origin,cachekey,cachestore,purgelog,relay,taggen)

> **The numbers to remember.** 1,000,000 concurrent origin requests at a hot expiry, collapsed to 1 · one byte-hit-ratio point ≈ $420k/month · 200 edges → 20 mid-tiers → 1 shield, origin sees ~2% of delivered bytes · purge reaches 99.9% of ~13,000 servers in ~2s, unbounded for a partitioned one.

#### Check your understanding
**Why does a single global lock per key fail to solve the thundering-herd problem properly, even though it collapses the fetch count to one?** It collapses the fetch, but every request stuck waiting behind that lock pays the full round-trip latency of the real fetch, turning a fast cache response into a slow one for everyone caught in the expiry window, which stale-while-revalidate avoids entirely.

**Why does content-hashing a filename remove the need for invalidation rather than merely make it cheaper?** Changed content becomes a different object at a different address, so no cached copy is ever incorrect, because nothing was ever mutated in place. There is nothing left to invalidate, only a small pointer left to update.

**Why can a purge broadcast never collect a completion acknowledgement from the whole fleet?** Some fraction of roughly 13,000 machines across 200 datacentres will always be temporarily unreachable at any given moment, so waiting for universal acknowledgement means the operation could never reliably finish at all.

**Why does purging a tag not require scanning the objects that carry it?** Every object records the tag's generation at fetch time, and a purge only bumps one small global counter. A mismatch between an object's stored generation and the tag's current one is treated as a miss the next time that object is read, with no enumeration ever required.

**Why does anycast move traffic away from a failing point of presence faster than DNS-based routing can?** Withdrawing a BGP route reconverges the internet's own routing within seconds and requires no client cooperation at all, while a DNS record's stated TTL is routinely ignored by resolvers and client runtimes that hold it far longer than advertised.
### 52. Design an Authentication & Authorization Service (SSO)
#### Understanding the problem
An SSO service registers users, authenticates them with passwords, MFA and enterprise federation, and issues tokens that every first-party service and third-party client can verify. Minting a token is the easy part.

Two things make this hard.

First, authentication and verification happen at wildly different rates. Logging in happens a few thousand times a second. Checking whether a token is still valid happens a few hundred thousand times a second, roughly a hundred times more often, and any design that puts a network call on that second path turns a small service into a hard dependency of everything on the platform.

Second, the token that makes verification cheap is the same thing that makes revocation hard. A self-contained signed credential is verifiable everywhere with no lookup at all, which is exactly why it is fast, and exactly why nothing can take it back once it is issued.

> **What this is not.** It looks like the CDN design: cache a decision everywhere, then invalidate it when the truth changes. The mechanisms genuinely rhyme, a TTL that bounds staleness plus a push for the urgent cases. Two things make the answers diverge. A CDN edge is allowed to miss, since a miss is just a fetch from origin, so correctness never depends on the cache being right. Token verification has no miss: every request carries a token that verifies locally, with no path back to the issuer to fall back on. And a stale cached image is cosmetic; a stale authorization is the breach, on the one machine, the attacker's, that this design can neither control nor reach.

#### Requirements and the numbers
**Functional.** Registration with breached-password screening. Password, TOTP, WebAuthn and enterprise-SAML login. OAuth 2.0 authorization-code with PKCE and OpenID Connect. Token issue, refresh, revoke and log-out-everywhere. Role and permission checks.

**Non-functional.** Token verification p99 under 1ms with zero network calls. Login p99 under 500ms of machine time. Revocation propagated within 1 second via the feed, bounded at 10 minutes by the access-token TTL. 99.99% availability.

The whole design is decided by four numbers, so derive them before drawing anything.

**What is the gap between logins and verifications?** Roughly 5,000 logins a second against roughly 500,000 token verifications a second: 500,000 ÷ 5,000 = **a 100x gap**.

**What does the deliberately slow password hash actually cost?** Argon2id at 75ms and 64MB per hash, times 5,000 logins a second: 5,000 × 75ms ≈ **375 dedicated cores** just for hashing.

**What does local verification cost compared with asking the issuer?** An Ed25519 signature check runs in roughly 40 microseconds, needing only about 20 cores across the whole fleet at 500,000/s. Checking with the issuer instead needs roughly **250 extra service instances** and adds about a millisecond to every API call on the platform.

**How small can a pushed revocation list actually stay?** At a realistic revocation rate and a 10-minute token lifetime, the live denylist holds roughly **350 entries, about 14KB**, small enough to replicate into every verifier's memory rather than looked up over the network.

> **The numbers to carry.** 100x more verifications than logins · argon2id ~375 cores at peak login · local verify ~20 cores fleet-wide vs introspection's ~250 extra instances · denylist ~350 entries, ~14KB, pushed everywhere.

#### Authentication and authorization: two different rates
The service is really two systems that happen to share an identity store. **Authentication** is slow, careful and stateful, and it happens a few thousand times a second. **Verification** is fast, stateless and happens roughly a hundred times more often, which is the single fact that decides almost every mechanism in the design.

The entities:

- **Access token**: a short-lived, self-contained, signed credential, verified locally by every service.
- **Refresh token**: a long-lived opaque handle, checked and rotated on every use, the real seat of revocable authority.
- **JTI**: a unique token identifier, the unit a denylist entry names.
- **`tokens_valid_after`**: a per-user timestamp compared against a token's issue time, capable of killing every token a user holds in one write.

```
POST /authorize          (front channel, browser redirect)
POST /token   body: { code, code_verifier }
  -> { access_token, id_token, refresh_token }
POST /token   body: { grant_type: refresh_token, refresh_token }
  -> new access + refresh pair
POST /revoke  body: { token | user_id }
GET  /.well-known/jwks.json -> { keys: [...] }
```

#### High-level design
Follow one login from a client to a token that resource services can verify without ever calling back.

[The hot path, login to verified request](/diagram/auth-service?focus=client,auth-service,identity-db,hashing-pool,mfa,token-mint,resource-services,e1,e2,e3,e4,e5,e8,e9)

1. The **Client app** submits credentials to the **Auth Service**.
2. The **Auth Service** looks up the identity in the **Identity DB**.
3. The **Auth Service** hands the password to the **argon2id hashing pool** for a deliberately slow comparison.
4. On success, the **argon2id hashing pool** passes control to the **MFA step**.
5. The **MFA step** hands off to **Token mint + rotation** once the second factor is satisfied.
6. **Token mint + rotation** signs the tokens and returns them to the **Client app**.
7. The **Client app** presents the access token to **Resource services** on every subsequent call.

> **Why the flow is shaped this way.** Authentication can afford to be slow because it happens rarely. Verification has to be nearly free because it happens constantly. Putting both behind the same synchronous interface would force the cheap, frequent path to pay the expensive, rare path's cost.

#### Two paths, a hundredfold apart
Every verified request could, in principle, ask the issuer whether the token is still good. Why does that principle break at this scale?

[Local verification versus asking the issuer](/diagram/auth-service?focus=auth-service,token-mint,resource-services,e8,e9)

**Bad: ask the issuer on every request.** Revocation becomes exact and immediate, because the source of truth is consulted every single time. At 500,000 verifications a second that is roughly 250 additional service instances and about a millisecond added to every API call on the platform, turning a service that used to handle a small fraction of that traffic into a hard synchronous dependency of everything.

**Good: hand out a self-contained signed credential with a long lifetime.** Verification becomes local and essentially free, and the cost is absolute rather than partial: nothing consults the issuer again until the credential expires on its own, so there is no revocation mechanism at all, only a long wait.

**Great: a self-contained token with a short lifetime, backed by a recallable handle behind it.** Verification stays local and fast. The long-lived authority moves into a refresh token, checked on every use, which happens once every several minutes per session rather than once per request, roughly a 300-fold reduction in lookup volume.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 180" role="img" aria-label="Logins run at roughly 5,000 a second; verifications run at roughly 500,000 a second, a hundredfold gap that decides where network calls are affordable">
  <style>
    .bar{fill:none;stroke:currentColor;stroke-width:1.2}
    .fillacc{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.22;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.4}
    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    .sub{fill:currentColor;opacity:.8;font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
  </style>
  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="16">Logins: ~5,000/s, can afford ~170ms + network</text>
  <rect class="bar" x="4" y="24" width="4" height="22" rx="2"/>
  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="76">Verifications: ~500,000/s, must be local</text>
  <rect class="bar fillacc" x="4" y="84" width="384" height="22" rx="4"/>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="128">a network call here is not a slower version of the</text>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="144">design, it is a different, unaffordable one</text>
</svg>
```

That distinction, not any property of tokens in general, is why local verification with a short lifetime wins here specifically: at a tenfold rather than hundredfold ratio, introspection's extra instances stop being a meaningful cost at all.

#### Buying revocation back in cheap pieces
A short-lived token bounds the worst case, but ten minutes is still ten minutes for an account that was just disabled. How do you claw back the rest without reintroducing a lookup on every request?

[The pushed denylist](/diagram/auth-service?focus=revocation-feed,resource-services,session-store,identity-db,e11,e12,e14)

**Bad: check a denylist over the network on every verification.** Correct, and at 500,000 requests a second that is roughly 15 storage nodes at full replication and half a millisecond added to every single request on the platform, for the sake of catching an event that happens a fraction of a percent of the time.

**Good: poll the denylist periodically instead of checking it live.** This removes the per-request network cost, and it trades it for a fixed staleness window equal to the poll interval, with no way to react faster than that interval without polling more often and paying the network cost back.

**Great: push a tiny denylist into every verifier's memory as revocations happen.** Because an entry only has to outlive an unexpired access token, the live list stays around 350 entries, roughly 14KB, small enough to replicate everywhere over a pub/sub feed rather than queried anywhere. A parallel `tokens_valid_after` timestamp per user rides the same feed, capable of invalidating every token a user holds with a single small write.

Pushing rather than pulling turns an unaffordable per-request cost into an affordable standing memory footprint. What it does not remove is the dependency itself: a verifier now carries a soft reliance on the feed being current, and the design has to decide explicitly what happens when that feed falls behind.

#### A stolen code is useless without the verifier
An authorization code travels through a browser redirect, exactly where it can be intercepted. How is it made worthless to anyone but the client that requested it?

[PKCE, front channel and back channel](/diagram/auth-service?focus=client,auth-service,e1)

**Bad: hand out a bare authorization code with no further check at redemption.** Anyone who intercepts the code off the redirect, through a malicious app registering the same URL scheme, a referrer header, or a shoulder-surfed address bar, can redeem it themselves.

**Good: require a client secret at redemption, as confidential server-side clients already do.** This works precisely where a secret can be kept safe, and a public client, a single-page app or a mobile app, cannot keep a secret at all; embedding one in shipped client code is not meaningfully different from having none.

**Great: bind the code to a value only the legitimate client ever held, using PKCE.** The client generates a random `code_verifier`, sends only its hash, the `code_challenge`, on the front channel during the redirect, and reveals the actual verifier only later, on the back channel, at token exchange. Whoever intercepts the code off the redirect never has the verifier and cannot derive it from the challenge, so the theft yields nothing redeemable.

A second presentation of an already-redeemed code is treated as evidence of exactly that kind of leak, not as an ordinary retry: the safe response is to revoke everything issued from it, since a legitimate client never needs to present a code twice.

#### Refresh rotation and catching the thief
The refresh token is the thing that actually carries long-lived authority. What happens the moment two different parties both try to use it?

[Rotation and reuse detection](/diagram/auth-service?focus=token-mint,session-store,e7)

**Bad: keep a refresh token valid and unchanging until it expires on its own.** Simple, and a copied token remains just as useful to whoever copied it as to the legitimate owner, indistinguishable for the entire remainder of its lifetime.

**Good: rotate the token on every use, issuing a fresh one each time.** This limits how long any single copy stays useful, and on its own it does not notice theft happening; an attacker who grabs a token and uses it before the legitimate client simply gets a valid new one, same as anyone else would.

**Great: rotate within a tracked family, and treat any reuse of an already-superseded token as proof of compromise.** Because a valid token is used exactly once, a second presentation of one that has already been rotated past means two parties are holding the same lineage. There is no way to tell attacker from legitimate client from that fact alone, so the safe response is to kill the entire family, forcing everyone holding any token in it to re-authenticate.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 217" role="img" aria-label="A stolen refresh token used after the legitimate client already rotated past it triggers reuse detection, killing the whole token family">
  <style>
    .box{fill:none;stroke:currentColor;stroke-width:1.2}
    .fillacc{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.24;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.4}
    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    .sub{fill:currentColor;opacity:.8;font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    text{dominant-baseline:middle;text-anchor:middle}
  </style>
  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="14" style="text-anchor:start">family_id F, legitimate client rotates normally</text>
  <rect class="box" x="4" y="24" width="120" height="26" rx="5"/><text class="sub" x="64" y="39">rotation 1 (used)</text>
  <rect class="box" x="132" y="24" width="120" height="26" rx="5"/><text class="sub" x="192" y="39">rotation 2 (used)</text>
  <rect class="box" x="260" y="24" width="120" height="26" rx="5"/><text class="sub" x="320" y="39">rotation 3 (now)</text>
  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="78" style="text-anchor:start">attacker replays the copied rotation 1 token</text>
  <rect class="box fillacc" x="4" y="88" width="180" height="28" rx="5"/><text class="sub" x="94" y="104">rotation 1 presented again</text>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="136" style="text-anchor:start">→ already superseded: family F killed,</text>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="152" style="text-anchor:start">both parties re-authenticate</text>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="184" style="text-anchor:start">a short grace window absorbs an honest client's</text>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="200" style="text-anchor:start">lost-response retry without treating it as reuse</text>
</svg>
```

A short grace window that accepts the immediately-previous token for a few seconds, returning the same reissued pair rather than rotating again, is what keeps an honest client's lost-response retry from being mistaken for an attack and logging out an innocent user.

#### Making the password hash expensive on purpose
A password comparison is one of the cheapest operations a service can run. Why does this design deliberately make it slow?

[The isolated hashing pool](/diagram/auth-service?focus=auth-service,hashing-pool,e3)

**Bad: hash passwords with a fast, general-purpose function.** Cheap to compute for a legitimate login, and just as cheap for an attacker running billions of guesses against a stolen hash offline, since a fast hash offers the attacker the same speed it offers the login path.

**Good: use a slow hash, but run it inline on the same request-handling threads as everything else.** This raises the cost of an offline guess, and it turns the login endpoint itself into an amplification weapon: a request costing 75ms of CPU and 64MB of memory, competing for the same resources as every other request the service handles, is a large amplification factor if a flood of login attempts shares that pool.

**Great: run a memory-hard hash, isolated in its own bounded pool, rate-limited ahead of the hash rather than after it.** Argon2id deliberately requires a large working memory per hash, which is what removes the advantage a GPU has over a general-purpose core. Running it on its own worker pool with bounded concurrency means a login flood saturates and gets shed at that pool specifically, rather than starving every other request the service handles.

At the peak login rate, this pool alone needs roughly 375 dedicated cores. That is a real, budgeted cost, not a rounding error, and it is exactly why the pool is isolated: a shared thread pool would let a login flood become a denial-of-service weapon against the rest of the service for free.

#### Where it breaks
| Layer | Failure | How the design handles it |
|---|---|---|
| Hashing pool | A login flood saturates the argon2id workers and queues grow | Rate limiting runs before the hash; bounded concurrency sheds excess logins with fast rejection rather than degrading everything else |
| Revocation feed | Pub/sub lag or a partition leaves verifiers with a stale denylist | Fail open with bounded staleness, since failing closed turns a feed partition into a total platform outage, strictly worse than briefly honouring a revoked token |
| JWKS distribution | The endpoint is down, or a verifier starts with a cold cache | A CDN with long stale-while-revalidate and a bootstrap key set baked into the image mean no verifier is ever left with zero usable keys |
| Session store | A shard loss drops refresh tokens and denylist entries for that range | Replication with automatic failover; on unrecoverable loss, affected users simply re-authenticate rather than the platform failing |
| Signing key | A private key is suspected compromised | Emergency rotation publishes a new key immediately and bumps `tokens_valid_after` platform-wide, accepting a global re-authentication wave that refresh tokens make survivable |
| Reuse detection | A flaky network makes a legitimate retry look like refresh-token reuse | A short idempotent grace window returns the same already-rotated pair instead of treating a duplicate retry as an attack |

#### What this design does not solve
**A bearer token is still a bearer token, so stealing a live session is not prevented.** Every mechanism here protects the credential exchange, PKCE protects the code, argon2id protects the stored password, WebAuthn removes the phishable secret, and none of it protects the token afterwards. An attacker who captures a valid token through XSS or an adversary-in-the-middle proxy holds a string indistinguishable from the real user until it expires. The genuine fix, sender-constrained tokens bound to a private key the attacker never obtains, needs client-side key handling in every SDK and is not in this baseline design.

**Failing open on the revocation feed means the one urgent mechanism is the one that fails first.** A verifier that has lost the feed keeps honouring a stale denylist, which is the correct availability trade but means the mechanism built specifically for cases that cannot wait for the TTL is exactly the one that silently stops working during an outage. The partial answer is requiring a synchronous check at genuinely high-consequence boundaries, drawn by hand rather than by any structural rule.

**A regional evacuation forces a re-authentication herd the login tier is not sized for.** Sessions are homed to a region deliberately, because globally replicated session state would let a rotation in one region race a replay in another and quietly defeat reuse detection during exactly the kind of event an attacker would pick. The cost is concentrated: losing a region means every session homed there must log in again, and draining that herd quickly would need many times the hashing capacity kept warm today.

#### Final design
Read it back through the numbers. A hundredfold gap between logins and verifications is what forces verification to be local and stateless while authentication stays slow and careful. A 375-core argon2id bill is what makes an isolated, rate-limited hashing pool non-negotiable rather than a nice-to-have. And a denylist that never grows past a few hundred entries is what makes pushing revocations into memory everywhere cheaper, by orders of magnitude, than looking them up over the network.

[The whole design](/diagram/auth-service?focus=client,auth-service,identity-db,hashing-pool,mfa,token-mint,session-store,kms,jwks,revocation-feed,resource-services,policy-engine)

> **The numbers to remember.** 100x more verifications than logins · argon2id ~75ms/64MB, ~375 cores at peak · local verify ~20 cores fleet-wide vs introspection's ~250 extra instances · denylist ~350 entries, ~14KB, pushed everywhere · revocation lands within ~1s when the feed is healthy, bounded at 10 minutes when it is not.

#### Check your understanding
**Why can't every resource service simply ask the auth service whether a token is still valid?** At roughly 500,000 verifications a second against 5,000 logins a second, that call would need on the order of 250 extra service instances and add about a millisecond to every request on the platform, converting a small service into a hard synchronous dependency of everything.

**Why does a self-contained signed token remove the ability to revoke it, and how does this design buy some of that back?** The token itself is the authority, verified locally with no lookup, so nothing consults the issuer again until it expires on its own. A short lifetime bounds the worst case, and a tiny pushed denylist plus a per-user timestamp handle the cases that cannot wait that long.

**Why is PKCE necessary even though the authorization code already travels over TLS?** The code can still be intercepted off the browser redirect through a malicious app registering the same URL scheme or through logging along the path. Binding the code to a verifier only the legitimate client holds makes an intercepted code worthless on its own.

**Why does presenting an already-rotated refresh token trigger killing the whole token family rather than just rejecting that one request?** A valid refresh token is used exactly once, so a second presentation proves two parties hold the same lineage, and there is no way to tell which one is the attacker. Revoking the whole family is the only response that is safe regardless of which side is legitimate.

**Why does the argon2id hashing pool run in isolation rather than alongside ordinary request handling?** Each hash deliberately costs about 75ms of CPU and 64MB of memory, so a request that cheap to send is expensive to serve. Isolating and rate-limiting that pool means a login flood exhausts only itself rather than starving every other request the service handles.
### 53. Design Trending Topics / Top-K in a Stream
#### Understanding the problem
Every social product has a box somewhere that says "trending". Behind it is a stream of events, a million a second at peak, each carrying a *key*: a hashtag, a phrase, a link. The job is to keep, continuously, the top 50 keys for the last 5 minutes, the last hour and the last day. For the world, and for each of about 200 geographies.

Two things make it harder than it sounds.

First, nobody registered the keys. A new hashtag is a string somebody typed a second ago. About 100 million distinct keys show up every day, and most are seen exactly once.

Second, "trending" does not mean "most". A term that runs at 10,000 mentions a minute every day is wallpaper. A term that usually runs at 10 a minute and just hit 500 is the story. So the answer has to be ranked by *surprise*, against each key's own normal.

> **What this is not.** It looks like ad-click aggregation, and the pipelines are cousins. The difference is the key space. Ads are ~5M ids that exist in a database before the first click, and the counts are billed, so that design is built around exactness. Here the keys are discovered from the data, nobody is invoiced, and there is no ground truth anywhere to reconcile against. That absence is what buys us the freedom to choose an error.

#### Requirements and the numbers
**Functional.** Ingest keyed events. Keep an approximate top 50 per (window, geo). Rank by deviation from each key's baseline. One vote per user per key. Resist coordinated inflation. Serve a precomputed list and a per-key drill-down.

**Non-functional.** 1M events/s peak. Published list at most ~10 s stale. Read p99 under 20 ms. Counting error at most 0.01% of window volume, 99.9% of the time. No per-key memory growth, because the key space is unbounded.

The whole design is decided by three numbers, so derive them before drawing anything.

**How many distinct keys per minute?** ~100M distinct keys a day, each active for about 20 minutes of it on average. 100M × 20 ÷ 1,440 ≈ **1.4M distinct keys per minute**.

**What would an exact map cost?** A hash-map entry is ~106 bytes once you count the string, the header, the count, the pointers and a 0.75 load factor. 1.4M × 106B ≈ 150MB per minute. A window that slides has to remember every minute's counts, so it knows what to subtract when a minute falls off the tail. A day therefore needs all 1,440 minute-maps resident: **~216GB per geography, ~40TB across 200**. Exact counting is not a tuning problem. It is off the table before we have chosen anything.

**What is the read load?** ~500M daily users opening the panel ~3 times. 1.5B loads a day ≈ 17k/s average, ~60k/s at peak. The read path has to be a single cache lookup.

> **The numbers to carry.** ~1.4M distinct keys/min · ~216GB per geo for an exact map · 1M events/s peak · ~60k reads/s peak against a 20 ms p99 · list ≤ 10 s stale.

#### Two problems in one pipeline
It helps to name the fact that this is two problems wearing one name. **Counting** a key space we cannot enumerate, and **deciding which counts are interesting**. They have different answers and different cost profiles. Counting has to survive a million events a second. Ranking runs once a minute over a few thousand candidates, where a database join is affordable.

The entities are simple:

- **Event** `{key, user_id, ts, geo}`, ~72 bytes.
- **Key**: the normalised string we count. Normalisation (lowercase, strip punctuation, collapse look-alike unicode) defines the key space, so it runs first.
- **Window**: 5m, 1h, 24h. Sliding, not tumbling.
- **Baseline**: what "normal" looks like for one key.
- **Trending list**: 50 entries per (geo, window), each with an estimated count and an error bound.

And the API is two reads and one internal write:

```
GET  /trending?window=5m|1h|24h&geo=GB-LND&limit=50
       → { as_of, items:[{ key, count_est, error_bound, rate_per_min, score, rank_delta }] }
GET  /trending/key/{key}?window=1h
       → { count_est, error_bound, baseline_rate, z_score, first_seen }
POST /events   (internal)  { key, user_id, ts, geo }
```

#### High-level design
Follow the numbered arrows. The write path runs from Ingest + normalise to the Top-K cache and never touches the read path.

[The hot path, ① to ⑦](/diagram/trending-topics?focus=e1,e2,e6,e7,e10,e13,e14)

1. **Ingest + normalise** turns a post into a key and appends it to the **Event stream**, partitioned by `hash(key)` so every occurrence of one key lands on the same shard.
2. One of 64 **Sketch workers** consumes its partition. It drops repeat `(user, key)` pairs through a Bloom filter, then counts the key in a fixed grid of counters.
3. The worker also offers the key to its **Per-shard top-500 heap**, the only place key strings are kept.
4. Once a minute the worker seals its grid into a 917KB tile and ships it to the **Merger**. The Merger adds the 64 tiles cell by cell and unions the heaps into ~32,000 candidates.
5. The Merger re-estimates every candidate against the merged grid, keeps the 500 largest, and hands them to the **Trend scorer**, which scores each against its **Baseline store** entry.
6. The scorer writes a 50-entry list per (geo, window) into the **Top-K cache** every 5 seconds.
7. The **Trending API** answers a panel load with one GET, ~2 ms.

> **Why the flow is shaped this way.** All the expensive work happens once a minute for everyone, not once per request. Two things are traded for that: the list lags reality by up to ~10 s, and nothing in the serving tier can answer "exactly how many".

#### Counting without a map
This is the mechanism everything else sits on, so take it apart properly. How do you count 1.4M distinct keys a minute, over a sliding day, in a fixed amount of memory?

[Where counting happens: the stream feeds the Sketch workers, which feed the heap](/diagram/trending-topics?focus=stream,sketch-worker,heap,e2,e6)

**Bad: a hash map per minute.** Exact, and what you would write first. It dies on the tail, not the head. Keys are discovered from the traffic and most are seen once, so a sliding day means holding 1,440 maps at once: ~216GB per geo. It only works when the key set is small or registered, which is the first question to ask.

**Good: Space-Saving, keep only as many keys as you have room for.** Fix *m* slots, each holding a key and a count. A monitored key increments. An unmonitored one evicts the smallest slot, inherits its count as a starting bid, and records how much of that count might not be its own. Memory is a constant you choose, the top-K falls out of the structure, and the error is total volume over slots. It is the strongest single-machine answer. Its weakness shows up in the next section: two Space-Saving summaries do not add together exactly.

**Great: a count-min sketch, plus a small heap of names.** Throw the keys away and keep only counters. A count-min sketch is a grid of *d* rows by *w* columns. To count a key, hash it once per row and add 1 to the cell that comes out in each row. To read a key, look at the same cells and take the *minimum*. Two grids of the same shape add together cell by cell, exactly, which is the property the rest of the design is built on.

**Why the minimum, and why the error is one-sided.** A cell holds the sum of increments from *every* key that hashed to it. So it contains your key's true count plus zero or more foreign contributions, and it can never be too low. Each row is an independent over-estimate. The minimum is the row where fewest other keys collided with yours.

Worked example. `#eclipse` truly occurred 41,000 times this minute, and its seven cells read `41,207 · 43,880 · 41,940 · 52,110 · 41,033 · 46,720 · 44,201`. The estimate is 41,033: 33 high, against a guaranteed bound of ~4,980. The mean (44,441) and the median (43,880) are both worse, because every sample is biased the same way. Only the minimum is an extremum of the contamination rather than an average of it.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 236" role="img" aria-label="Seven rows of counters; one key hashes to one cell per row; the estimate is the minimum">
  <style>
    .r{fill:none;stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.35;stroke-width:1.2}
    .c{fill:var(--accent)}
    .m{fill:currentColor;fill-opacity:.85}
    .t{font:12px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif;fill:currentColor;opacity:.8}
    .b{font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif;fill:currentColor}
  </style>
  <text class="b" x="8" y="16">#eclipse → 7 hashes → 7 cells</text>
  <g transform="translate(8,28)">
    <rect class="r" x="0" y="0" width="300" height="18" rx="3"/><rect class="c" x="47" y="0" width="10" height="18" rx="2"/><text class="t" x="308" y="13">41,207</text>
    <rect class="r" x="0" y="24" width="300" height="18" rx="3"/><rect class="c" x="161" y="24" width="10" height="18" rx="2"/><text class="t" x="308" y="37">43,880</text>
    <rect class="r" x="0" y="48" width="300" height="18" rx="3"/><rect class="c" x="105" y="48" width="10" height="18" rx="2"/><text class="t" x="308" y="61">41,940</text>
    <rect class="r" x="0" y="72" width="300" height="18" rx="3"/><rect class="c" x="252" y="72" width="10" height="18" rx="2"/><text class="t" x="308" y="85">52,110</text>
    <rect class="r" x="0" y="96" width="300" height="18" rx="3"/><rect class="m" x="192" y="96" width="10" height="18" rx="2"/><text class="b" x="308" y="109">41,033 ← min</text>
    <rect class="r" x="0" y="120" width="300" height="18" rx="3"/><rect class="c" x="22" y="120" width="10" height="18" rx="2"/><text class="t" x="308" y="133">46,720</text>
    <rect class="r" x="0" y="144" width="300" height="18" rx="3"/><rect class="c" x="274" y="144" width="10" height="18" rx="2"/><text class="t" x="308" y="157">44,201</text>
  </g>
  <text class="t" x="8" y="210">7 rows × 32,768 counters × 4 bytes = 917KB, whatever the key count</text>
  <text class="t" x="8" y="228">true 41,000 · every cell ≥ truth · min = 41,033 · bound ≈ 4,980</text>
</svg>
```

**Where the dimensions come from.** They are derived, not picked. *w* sets the size of the error: ε = e ÷ w. *d* sets the probability the bound holds: δ = e^−d. For ε = 0.01% we need w ≥ 27,183; round up to 32,768 so the modulo is a bit-mask, giving ε ≈ 8.3×10⁻⁵. For δ = 0.001, d = ⌈ln 1000⌉ = 7. On a 60M-event minute the bound is ε × N ≈ 4,980 counts, one-sided.

What does that mean where it is visible? The 50th key in a busy geo runs at roughly 82k a minute, so ~4,980 is about **6% relative error at rank 50**. Enough to reshuffle ranks 45 to 55 between refreshes, which is why the cache write applies hysteresis. Nowhere near enough to promote a tail key into the top 50.

> **The heap.** The grid can answer "how many times did #eclipse appear?" but not "which keys are big?", because a hash does not reverse. So each Sketch worker also keeps a bounded min-heap of the 500 largest keys it has seen, as strings, with their current estimates. The heap supplies names; the grid supplies counts. Why 500 and not 50 is the next section.

#### One list from 64 shards
Sixty-four workers each hold a grid and a heap. How do we get one global top 50 out of them without shipping the events?

[The merge: 64 tiles and 64 heaps become one grid and one candidate set](/diagram/trending-topics?focus=sketch-worker,heap,merger,e7,e8,e10)

**Bad: merge the shards' local top-50 lists.** The classic bug. A shard that happens to own three enormous keys pushes a 900k-count key down to rank 51 locally. A shard with only mid-weight traffic promotes a 40k key into its top 50. Merge the lists and the 900k key vanishes from the global answer with no error signal anywhere.

**Good: keep 10× K per shard.** Nominate 500 keys per shard rather than 50. The local cutoff is now far below the global one, so a globally big key is nominated somewhere. This is necessary, and it is why the heap is the size it is. On its own the ranking would still use per-shard counts.

**Great: merge the grids, then re-estimate every candidate.** Add the 64 tiles cell by cell: 64 × 229,376 ≈ 14.7M integer adds, ~20 ms. Union the heaps into ~32,000 candidate strings. Then read every candidate from the *merged* grid (32,000 × 7 = 224k probes, ~2 ms) and sort on those numbers. The candidate set is allowed to be lossy, because a key outside the top 500 on every one of 64 shards cannot plausibly be globally top 50 under a heavy-tailed distribution. The counts used to rank it are not allowed to be lossy, which is why the re-estimation is mandatory.

[Merging 64 shards: grids add, heaps only nominate](/diagram/trending-topics?figure=merge)

This is also why the stream is partitioned by `hash(key)`. Not for the counts, which merge correctly under any partitioning, but for *nomination*: a shard can only put a key in its heap if it has seen enough of it to believe it is heavy. The price is that a viral key at 200k events/s pins one worker. A skew monitor switches just that key to round-robin above 2× the median shard rate. At 1/64th of its volume it is still the biggest thing on every shard, so it is nominated everywhere.

> **The property everything rests on.** sketch(A) + sketch(B) = sketch(A ∪ B), cell by cell, exactly. Merging introduces no approximation because each cell is a plain sum. It is why 64 shards can be summed, why 60 minute tiles make an hour, and why a region can ship 917KB a minute instead of its 2.1TB a day of events. It is also why the tempting "conservative update" optimisation is banned: it makes cells path-dependent, and two such grids no longer sum to the grid of the union.

#### Windows that slide
The product ships three named windows. How do we maintain "the last hour" as the hour moves?

[The Merger pushes each minute tile into the Sketch ring](/diagram/trending-topics?focus=merger,ring,e9)

**Bad: recount the window every minute.** Replaying 60 minutes of events per geo per minute is 60× the ingest cost, and it needs the events resident. Nothing about it scales.

**Good: one exponentially decayed grid.** Multiply every cell by 0.98 each minute: a 34-minute half-life, one pass over 229k cells, no ring at all, 1.8MB per geo. It is the right answer when the dimension you multiply by is large (50,000 tenants), or when nobody needs a window with edges. Its cost here: it cannot answer "exactly the last 5 minutes", a past window cannot be recomputed, and the product's `rank_delta` needs crisp boundaries.

**Great: a ring of tiles, add the newest and subtract the oldest.** Keep the last 60 minute tiles and 24 hour tiles per geo. A 5-minute window is the sum of 5 tiles, an hour is 60, a day is 24 hour tiles. To slide, add the newest tile to the running window grid and subtract the one that just fell off the tail. Subtraction is safe because you are only ever removing increments you previously added, so no cell can go negative. 84 tiles × ~1.8MB ≈ 150MB per geo, 7.5% of a 2GB aggregator, against the 216GB an exact map would need.

[The ring of tiles: a window is a sum, sliding is add and subtract](/diagram/trending-topics?figure=ring)

#### Trending, not popular
We now have accurate-enough counts for ~500 candidates a minute. Which of them are *trending*?

[Scoring: the Trend scorer joins the Baseline store and applies the Abuse scorer's flags](/diagram/trending-topics?focus=scorer,baselines,abuse,e11,e12)

**Bad: rank by volume.** The same famous terms win every day. A term that is always enormous is background, not news. This is the entire difference between a trending panel and a leaderboard.

**Good: short window over long window.** Score = (count_5m ÷ 5) ÷ (count_24h ÷ 1,440). Two probes per candidate, no extra state, nothing to rebuild after an outage. It has one hole. A key born inside the window has a 24h count equal to its 5-minute count, so its ratio is exactly 288 whatever its size. A 500-count key ties a 500,000-count key at the top, and there is nowhere to put a prior. Keep it as the fallback for when the baseline store is down.

**Great: score against each key's own baseline.** The Baseline store keeps, per key, an EWMA of its rate and of its variance at a 7-day half-life. An EWMA is a running average that forgets the past on a half-life, so one spike does not become the new normal. For the top ~100k keys it also keeps a minute-of-day profile, because "coffee" is normal at 8am and strange at 3am. The score is z = (rate now − usual rate) ÷ usual spread.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 210" role="img" aria-label="Two keys: a famous one slightly above its normal scores low; a small one far above its normal scores high">
  <style>
    .bar{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.25;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.5}
    .bar2{fill:currentColor;fill-opacity:.12;stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.5;stroke-width:1.5}
    .line{stroke:currentColor;stroke-width:1.5;stroke-dasharray:4 3}
    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    .sub{fill:currentColor;opacity:.8;font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    text{dominant-baseline:middle}
  </style>
  <text class="lbl" x="8" y="14">#monday · usually 10,000/min, spread 1,500</text>
  <rect class="bar2" x="8" y="28" width="240" height="16" rx="3"/><text class="sub" x="256" y="36">normal 10,000</text>
  <rect class="bar" x="8" y="50" width="252" height="16" rx="3"/><text class="sub" x="268" y="58">now 10,500</text>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="80">z = (10,500 − 10,000) ÷ 1,500 = 0.33 · ignored</text>
  <text class="lbl" x="8" y="114">#eclipse · usually 10/min, spread 4</text>
  <rect class="bar2" x="8" y="128" width="3" height="16" rx="2"/><text class="sub" x="18" y="136">normal 10</text>
  <rect class="bar" x="8" y="150" width="120" height="16" rx="3"/><text class="sub" x="136" y="158">now 500</text>
  <text class="sub" x="8" y="180">z = (500 − 10) ÷ 4 = 122 · top of the list</text>
</svg>
```

**Cold start: the failure the great answer creates.** A brand-new key has no μ and no σ, so without guards anything new takes the top slot on a few hundred counts and holds it for one refresh. Three guards, used together. An absolute **floor** of 500 counts in 5 minutes to be eligible at all, which also keeps every ranked key well above the sketch's ~4,980 error band. A **prior** of μ₀ = 1/min, σ₀ = 2 so the score is finite. And an **age damper** of min(1, age_min ÷ 15), so a key must sustain its rate for a quarter of an hour before it can win. A genuinely explosive new key still reaches the top; it takes a few refreshes instead of one.

The Abuse scorer's flags are applied here, last, as a multiplier between 0 and 1. Never a deletion, so an override restores a key without touching any counts.

#### Keeping the read path cheap
~60k panel loads a second at peak, and the panel is on the first screen of every session. If it computed anything it would immediately be the most expensive query in the product.

[The materialised answer: the scorer writes the Top-K cache; the Trending API does one GET](/diagram/trending-topics?focus=scorer,cache,api,e13,e14)

So the scorer materialises the answer. 50 entries plus an `as_of` per (geo, window), rewritten every 5 seconds into the Top-K cache. 3 windows × 200 geos × ~5KB is ~3MB in total, 120 writes a second. The Trending API is a single GET, ~2 ms p99 against a 20 ms budget. It keeps a last-known-good copy of every list in process, so a Redis failover shows a slightly stale panel rather than an empty one. The geo fallback chain (metro → country → region → global) is resolved at write time, so a sparse metro never returns an empty list.

Two details live at this write. **Hysteresis**: a key must beat the rank-50 score by 10% to enter and fall 10% below it to leave, so the ~6% counting error cannot flicker the boundary. And every entry carries `count_est` with an `error_bound`, never a bare count, because a bare count would be a lie.

**The latency budget.** Seal and ship 64 tiles ~500 ms, merge ~20 ms, re-estimate ~2 ms, join 500 baselines ~5 ms, write ~1 ms. That is **~550 ms** from minute boundary to a fresh list, against a 10 s staleness target. Note where it goes: 500 of the 550 ms is sealing and shipping, none of it arithmetic. If the cycle ever had to be faster the answer would be staggered seals and incremental merging, not a faster merge.

#### Bots and brigades
Anything publicly ranked is a target. Three layers, each cheaper than the next attack it does not stop.

- **One vote per user per key.** A rotating 5-minute Bloom filter of `(user_id, key)` pairs in front of the counters, ~11MB per shard. Raw volume now means distinct participants. It prices out the single scripted account for the cost of a few memory probes. It also deletes ~1% of genuine pairs at a 1% false-positive rate, a loss that is uniform across keys and so leaves ranks alone.
- **Concentration signals.** The Abuse scorer reads the same stream off the counting path and scores candidates on network origin, account age and follow-graph density. It emits a multiplier between 0 and 1, never a deletion.
- **Soft suppression with a review queue.** A wrongly demoted key is still in the candidate set, so a human override restores it within minutes. Every decision writes an audit row. The override rate (target under 5%) is the only calibration signal there is, because there is no ground truth.

What this does not catch is in the "does not solve" section below.

#### Where it breaks
| Layer | Failure | How the design handles it |
|---|---|---|
| Ingest | A normalisation change splits `#Eclipse` from `#eclipse`; both halves fall off the list, no error anywhere | New normaliser shadow-runs for an hour; cutover only above 90% top-50 overlap |
| Stream | A viral key at 200k events/s pins one shard while 63 idle | Skew monitor round-robins just that key above 2× median; counts still merge, nomination survives |
| Sketch worker | Restart loses the in-flight minute | Merger publishes with the tiles it has, marked partial; the minute is replayed from the stream and merged late, because addition is order-independent |
| Merger | Tiles with different dimensions or hash seeds are summed after a rolling deploy: plausible, meaningless numbers | Every tile carries a version header; the Merger refuses to add across versions |
| Baseline store | Unavailable: no notion of normal | Fall back to the short/long ratio, serve with `degraded_scoring` |
| Cache | Eviction or failover empties a key | API serves its in-process last-known-good with `as_of`; the next 5 s tick refills |
| Ranking | ~6% error flickers keys 45–55 between refreshes | Hysteresis at the cache write, ±10% around the rank-50 score |

#### What this design does not solve
Three things stay open, and it is worth being able to say each one plainly.

**Nothing it publishes can be proved.** The grid returns an upper bound; the heap returns candidates some worker already believed were heavy. The honest fix, an exact recount over the ~500 published candidates from the Raw archive, is affordable and we would build it for a newsroom. It does not close the gap. It lands minutes later, over a slightly different event set, and it will disagree with the published estimate often enough to notice. So the design labels the two numbers instead of reconciling them.

**De-dup undercounts upstream of a structure that overcounts.** The clean one-sided guarantee holds over de-duplicated events, not over reality, and the ~1% the filter drops is not something we can measure. We state the guarantee that way and accept that the distinction is invisible downstream.

**Coordinated inflation by real accounts is made expensive, not prevented.** 10,000 aged, spread-out, human accounts look exactly like a grassroots event: regional concentration, dense follow clustering, a burst of new accounts created *because* of the event. Every threshold that catches one catches the other. The design makes the wrong decision cheap (soft demotion, minutes to override) rather than pretending it can tell them apart.

#### Final design
Read it back through the three numbers. 1.4M distinct keys a minute and a day that has to slide rule out the map and force the grid. 64 shards and one answer per geo force tiles and a Merger, and the Merger's exact addition is what makes windows, shards and regions all the same operation. Famous terms at 10,000 a minute every day force ranking by surprise against a baseline. And 60k reads a second force a precomputed list behind a single GET.

[The whole design](/diagram/trending-topics?focus=ingest,stream,sketch-worker,heap,merger,ring,scorer,baselines,abuse,cache,api,archive)

> **The numbers to remember.** 917KB per minute tile · ≤ ~5,000 over-count on a 60M-event minute · ~6.1% relative error at rank 50 · ~150MB ring vs ~216GB map · ~550 ms publish cycle vs 10 s SLO.

#### Check your understanding
**Why the minimum across rows, and not the mean or the median?** Every row's cell holds the true count plus non-negative contamination, so every sample is biased upward. Averaging averages the noise in. The minimum picks the least-collided row and is the only estimator that keeps est ≥ true.

**A key is 51st on every one of 64 shards. Do you lose it?** Only if you merge lists. Nominate 500 per shard, merge the grids, re-estimate every candidate against the merged grid, then sort. The candidate set may be lossy; the counts that rank it may not.

**A brand-new hashtag appears with no baseline. What score does it get?** Not infinity. It must clear 500 counts in 5 minutes, it is scored against the prior μ₀ = 1/min, σ₀ = 2, and its score is damped by min(1, age ÷ 15 min).

**Why is the grid 7 × 32,768 and not 3 × 1,000,000, which is more memory?** *w* sets the error size, *d* sets the probability the bound holds. Three rows gives δ = e⁻³ ≈ 5%: one estimate in twenty is outside the bound entirely, ~1,600 candidates a minute with no guarantee. And it costs 13× the memory.

**Two regions each count their own traffic. How do you produce one global list without shipping events?** Ship sealed tiles built with identical (d, w, seed) and sum them. ~917KB × 60 × 24 × 6 regions ≈ 8GB a day, against 2.1TB a day of events. Pin the seed and dimensions in every tile header; mismatched tiles still add and produce plausible garbage.
### 54. Design a CI/CD & Code Deployment System
#### Understanding the problem
A CI/CD system takes every commit an engineering organisation produces, builds and tests it on a shared farm, and pushes the resulting artifact into production across a large fleet, safely enough that a bad change can be undone in minutes.

Two things make this hard, and they are almost entirely unrelated.

First, the build side is a throughput problem. Thousands of commits a day, each expanding into a graph of jobs, have to run without the shared farm growing without bound, which means most of that work has to be avoided rather than executed.

Second, the deploy side is a risk problem. Rolling out a new binary is easy to undo, because the old one is still sitting right there. Rolling back a change to production data is not, and no amount of build-side cleverness touches that.

> **What this is not.** It looks like the job scheduler design: dispatch arbitrary work onto a fleet, retry it, fan it out. The two genuinely share a dispatch layer. Where they diverge is what the hard problem actually is. A scheduler's difficulty is knowing whether a run happened at all, since time is an input nobody produces and absence is silent. Here execution is the easy, deliberately avoided part, since most actions return from cache rather than run. The deploy half then inverts the question entirely: a scheduler that runs a job twice is fixed with an idempotency key, but a pipeline that puts a bad binary on ten thousand tasks is fixed by taking it back out, and whether that is even possible was decided weeks earlier by whoever wrote the migration.

#### Requirements and the numbers
**Functional.** Webhook-triggered pipelines. A declarative build DAG. Distributed build and test execution. Signed, provenance-tracked artifacts. Rolling, blue-green and canary deploys with automated analysis. One-click and automatic rollback. Feature flags. Deploy freezes.

**Non-functional.** p95 job queue wait under 30 seconds. p50 pipeline runtime under 10 minutes. Rollback p95 under 5 minutes from decision to fleet-wide. At least 99.9% pipeline control-plane availability. Zero long-lived secrets on any worker.

The whole design is decided by four numbers, so derive them before drawing anything.

**What does the action cache actually save?** At an 87% hit rate, a run executes roughly 5.5 worker-minutes instead of 24. Peak fleet size falls from roughly **14,300 workers to roughly 3,250**, a difference of about 44,000 vCPUs.

**How much traffic does a small canary actually see?** A flagship service at 10,000 requests a second gives a 1% canary about **100 requests a second**.

**How much evidence does detecting a regression need?** Catching a doubling of a 0.1% error rate at standard confidence and power needs roughly **23,000 requests per arm**, which at 100 requests a second takes about 4 minutes.

**How fast is rollback compared with a rebuild?** Replacing canary tasks with the pinned previous artifact digest takes about **45 seconds**, because nothing is rebuilt; the previous artifact already exists.

> **The numbers to carry.** 87% cache hit rate: ~3,250 workers vs ~14,300 uncached · 1% canary at flagship traffic sees ~100 req/s, needs ~23k requests/arm (~4 min) to catch a doubling · rollback to a pinned digest ~45s · merge-to-global for a standard service ~3h50m.

#### Building and deploying: two different systems joined by one object
The design is really two systems that share exactly one artefact. **Building** is a throughput problem, solved by caching and horizontal scaling. **Deploying** is a risk problem, solved by going slowly and measuring. The immutable, digest-addressed artifact each build produces is the only thing that connects them.

The entities:

- **Action**: one unit of build work, keyed by a hash of everything it declares as input.
- **Job**: a scheduled unit of work placed on an ephemeral worker.
- **Artifact**: an immutable, signed, digest-addressed build output.
- **Deploy**: pushing an artifact to some fraction of the fleet, distinct from releasing the behaviour it contains.
- **Migration**: a schema change, deliberately never a single atomic step.

```
POST /webhook  (source push/PR)         -> pipeline run created
GET  /runs/{id}                          -> { status, jobs[] }
POST /deploy   body:{ artifact_digest, service } -> { rollout_id }
POST /rollback body:{ service }          -> { status }   # ~45s, no rebuild
```

#### High-level design
Follow one commit from a webhook to production traffic.

[The hot path, commit to fleet](/diagram/cicd?focus=source-host,pipeline-controller,build-scheduler,worker-pool,action-cache,artifact-store,deploy-controller,rollout-ladder,fleet,e1,e3,e4,e6,e7,e8,e9,e10)

1. The **Source host** fires a webhook into the **Pipeline Controller** on every push or pull request.
2. The **Pipeline Controller** expands the pipeline spec at that exact commit into a DAG and hands jobs to the **Build Scheduler**.
3. The **Build Scheduler** matches each job's constraints to the **Ephemeral workers**.
4. Each **Ephemeral workers** instance checks the **Action cache + CAS** before running anything, and most actions return from there.
5. Novel output uploads to the **Artifact store**, content-addressed.
6. The **Artifact store** hands a pinned digest to the **Deploy Controller**.
7. The **Deploy Controller** starts the **Rollout ladder** at a small canary percentage.
8. The **Rollout ladder** widens exposure across the **Production fleet**, one rung at a time.

> **Why the flow is shaped this way.** Building and deploying are separate systems joined by one immutable object. The build side is solved by caching and horizontal workers; the deploy side is solved by slowness and measurement. Wiring them through a pinned artifact digest means the thing rolled back to is the exact thing that passed, never a rebuild that might differ.

#### Caching a build instead of running it
Most of the work a build graph describes has already been done before, on some earlier commit. How do you avoid redoing it without risking a wrong answer?

[The action cache](/diagram/cicd?focus=worker-pool,action-cache,e6)

**Bad: rebuild everything from source on every run.** Correct by construction, and it means the fleet's size scales directly with total build volume, with nothing at all reused between one run and the next.

**Good: key the cache on something loose, like a file path or a timestamp.** This catches some repeated work, and it is unsound the moment two different inputs happen to produce the same loose key, silently serving one build's output for another's inputs.

**Great: key every action by a hash of its complete declared inputs, and serve the result from a content-addressed store.** The key covers the command line, the environment, every input file's digest and the toolchain's digest, so two runs only ever share a cache entry when their inputs are provably identical. At an 87% hit rate, most actions return an answer in tens of milliseconds without executing anything at all.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 150" role="img" aria-label="At an 87 percent cache hit rate the fleet needs roughly 3,250 workers; at 70 percent it needs roughly 5,700; uncached it needs roughly 14,300">
  <style>
    .bar{fill:none;stroke:currentColor;stroke-width:1.2}
    .fillacc{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.22;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.4}
    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
  </style>
  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="14">Uncached: ~14,300 workers</text>
  <rect class="bar" x="4" y="22" width="384" height="22" rx="4"/>
  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="66">70% hit rate: ~5,700 workers</text>
  <rect class="bar" x="4" y="74" width="154" height="22" rx="4"/>
  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="118">87% hit rate: ~3,250 workers</text>
  <rect class="bar fillacc" x="4" y="126" width="88" height="10" rx="3"/>
</svg>
```

This is only safe under one precondition: hermeticity, meaning an action reads nothing it did not declare.
