An action that quietly reads something outside its declared inputs can produce different outputs for the same key, and the cache will serve one of them, silently, behind a build that reports green. A slow build is visible. A wrong cache hit is not, and it is exactly what propagates into production.

#### Comparing against a fair baseline
A canary running on new code is compared against the rest of the fleet still running the old one. What breaks if that comparison population was already running before the canary started?

[The restarted baseline](/diagram/cicd?focus=rollout-ladder,fleet,canary-analyser,e9,e10,e11)

**Bad: compare the canary against whichever tasks are already running the old version.** Simple, and those incumbent tasks have been up for hours or days, with warm JIT compilation, aged heap state and established connection pools that a freshly started canary task does not share, none of which has anything to do with the change being tested.

**Good: compare against a recent historical average for the old version instead of live tasks.** This removes the live-incumbent skew and introduces a different one: the average now reflects whatever traffic mix and system state happened to hold during that earlier window, not the conditions the canary is actually running under right now.

**Great: freshly restart an equal-sized baseline population on the old digest at the same moment the canary starts.** Both arms begin cold together, so JIT warm-up, heap age and connection-pool state affect both equally and cancel out of the comparison. What remains different between the two arms is the change itself.

Without this, the classic failure is a canary that reads 15% worse on tail latency and is actually fine: the difference was never the code, it was that one arm had been running longer than the other.

#### Bake time as a sample-size calculation
How long should a canary run before its result can be trusted?

[The statistics behind the wait](/diagram/cicd?focus=canary-analyser,fleet,e11,e12)

**Bad: wait a fixed, ritual amount of time regardless of traffic.** Easy to explain, and it is either far too short for a low-traffic service, where the sample collected in that window carries no statistical weight at all, or unnecessarily long for a high-traffic one that reached significance minutes ago.

**Good: watch the dashboards and use judgement about whether the numbers look stable.** More adaptive, and it substitutes a human's intuition for an actual confidence level, which means two people can reasonably disagree about the same graph and neither is being unreasonable.

**Great: compute the sample size the detection target actually requires, and bake for at least that long.** Detecting a 0.1% error rate doubling to 0.2% at standard confidence and power needs roughly 23,000 requests per arm. At 100 requests a second that is about 4 minutes, so a 10-minute rung leaves real margin.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 190" role="img" aria-label="Sample size needed grows with the inverse square of the effect size: catching a doubling needs about 23,000 requests per arm, but catching a 20 percent relative rise needs about 431,000">
  <style>
    .bar{fill:none;stroke:currentColor;stroke-width:1.2}
    .fillacc{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.22;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.4}
    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    .sub{fill:currentColor;opacity:.8;font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
  </style>
  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="14">Catch a doubling (0.1% → 0.2%):</text>
  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="30">~23,000 req/arm, ~4 min at 100 req/s</text>
  <rect class="bar fillacc" x="4" y="38" width="21" height="22" rx="4"/>
  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="96">Catch a 20% relative rise (0.1% → 0.12%):</text>
  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="112">~431,000 req/arm, ~72 min</text>
  <rect class="bar" x="4" y="120" width="384" height="22" rx="4"/>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="164">the same confidence level costs roughly 19x the</text>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="180">samples for a fivefold smaller effect</text>
</svg>
```

Smaller regressions get expensive to detect fast, because required sample size scales with the inverse square of the effect being measured. A low-traffic service's 1% canary may need many hours to reach the same confidence a flagship service reaches in minutes, which is a fact about the traffic, not a flaw in the gate.

#### Rollback is a lookup, not a rebuild
When a canary fails, how does the previous version come back so quickly?

[The pinned digest](/diagram/cicd?focus=artifact-store,deploy-controller,e8)

**Bad: rebuild the previous version from source on demand.** Correct in principle, and a rebuild is a full pipeline run, minutes at best, running at the exact moment speed matters most, with no guarantee the rebuild reproduces byte-for-byte what was actually running before.

**Good: keep the previous version's build logs and re-run the pipeline against the same commit.** Faster to locate than searching history from scratch, and it is still a build, with all of a build's variability and time cost, when the goal is restoring a known-good state as fast as possible.

**Great: retain the previous artifact itself, immutable and addressed by its own digest.** Rollback becomes pointing the fleet back at a digest that already exists in the artifact store, which is exactly the same mechanism that pushed the new version forward, just aimed the other way. Nothing is rebuilt, branched, or re-verified, because the artifact being restored already passed everything it needed to the first time.

That speed depends on retention being reference-counted against what is actually deployed, not purely time-based. Expiring the rollback target of a service nobody has redeployed in months silently deletes the recovery path, discovered only during the incident that needed it.

#### Expand/contract: keeping N and N-1 alive
A schema change and a code deploy both touch production. Why can the schema change never be part of the same step as the deploy?

[The migration that cannot be undone](/diagram/cicd?focus=schema-gate,deploy-controller,e2,e14)

**Bad: run the migration as part of the deploy, in a pre-deploy hook.** This is what most frameworks do by default, and it is fine right up until the migration is destructive. A dropped or renamed column means the previous binary, the one rollback would restore, now queries something that no longer exists, so a rollback attempt turns a bad deploy into a worse outage.

**Good: run the migration first, then wait a while before deploying the code that depends on it.** Better sequencing, and without an enforced boundary between the two, nothing stops a later migration from being destructive on its own, re-creating the exact same trap one step later.

**Great: expand before contracting, across separate deploys, gated in CI.** A rename becomes four deploys: add the new column and dual-write both, backfill in the background, flip reads to the new column while still writing both, and only weeks later, once nothing depends on the old shape, drop it. A **Schema lint gate** rejects any destructive statement whose expand phase is not already recorded as fully deployed.

[Four deploys expand a schema before contracting it](/diagram/cicd?figure=expand-contract)

#### Where it breaks
| Layer | Failure | How the design handles it |
|---|---|---|
| Action cache | A non-hermetic action produces a wrong cached output served to later builds | A nightly canary re-executes a sample of hits and diffs the output digests; any mismatch evicts the key's subtree and pages |
| Worker pool | A merge wave depletes the warm pool and queue wait breaches its SLO | Autoscaling on queue depth with a pre-booted buffer; low-priority jobs are shed first |
| Worker isolation | A malicious build step attempts to escape its sandbox or exfiltrate credentials | One microVM per job, destroyed after use; fork pull requests run on a credential-free pool entirely |
| Artifact store | A regional store degrades and deploys cannot fetch artifacts | Deploys block rather than proceed against a partial fleet; multi-region replication covers currently deployed artifacts |
| Canary analyser | The metrics pipeline lags or gaps, and the analyser has no data to score | Missing data is never treated as a pass; the rollout holds at its current rung and pages |
| Deploy controller | The controller crashes mid-rollout, leaving the fleet on mixed versions | Rollout state is a durable object, not controller memory, so a new leader resumes from the last recorded phase |

#### What this design does not solve
**A canary is only a real gate at the top of the traffic distribution.** Detecting a genuine regression needs tens of thousands of requests per arm, which a flagship service reaches in minutes and a median internal service, at a fraction of that traffic, might need many hours to reach at the same canary percentage. For most services, the honest protection is fast rollback and synthetic probes, not the canary, and treating every green canary verdict as equally meaningful is a mistake the numbers do not support.

**Rollback undoes the binary and never the effects it already emitted.** Expand/contract keeps the database in a state where the old code can still run, and a flag reverts a behaviour change in seconds, but neither takes back an email already sent, a payment already captured, or an event already consumed by forty downstream systems. A version that behaved wrongly for ten minutes before rollback cannot be rolled back in any sense the recipients of its effects would recognise.

**Hermeticity is verified statistically, not proven.** The whole cache depends on a property checked by sampling a small fraction of hits and re-executing them, which reliably catches an action that misbehaves often and is close to blind to one that misbehaves on exactly one specific input. Detection is also always after the fact: by the time a mismatch is caught, every artifact built from that poisoned key has already shipped.

#### Final design
Read it back through the numbers. An 87% cache hit rate cutting the fleet from roughly 14,300 workers to roughly 3,250 is what makes the whole build side affordable, provided hermeticity actually holds. A 100-request-a-second canary needing roughly 23,000 requests per arm to reach significance is what sets bake time as arithmetic rather than ritual. A 45-second rollback against an artifact that already exists is what makes code changes cheaply reversible. And a four-deploy expand/contract sequence is what keeps schema changes from turning that same rollback into a worse outage.

[The whole design](/diagram/cicd?focus=source-host,pipeline-controller,schema-gate,build-scheduler,worker-pool,action-cache,artifact-store,deploy-controller,rollout-ladder,canary-analyser,fleet,flag-service)

> **The numbers to remember.** 87% cache hit rate: ~3,250 workers vs ~14,300 uncached · 1% canary at flagship traffic needs ~23k requests/arm, ~4 min, to catch a doubling · rollback to a pinned digest ~45s · expand/contract spreads an irreversible change over four deploys and several weeks.

#### Check your understanding
**Why is hermeticity the precondition for the action cache rather than a nice-to-have?** An action that reads anything it did not declare can produce different outputs for the same cache key, and the cache will silently serve one of them behind a build that still reports green, propagating a wrong output straight into production.

**Why does the canary get compared against a freshly restarted baseline instead of the tasks already running the old version?** Long-running incumbents carry warm JIT state, aged heaps and established connection pools that a cold canary does not share, none of which reflects the actual change being tested. Restarting both arms together removes that skew from the comparison entirely.

**Why does a low-traffic service's canary provide much weaker protection than a flagship service's?** Detecting a given regression needs a fixed number of requests per arm regardless of the service, so a service with little traffic takes proportionally longer to gather that evidence, sometimes far longer than any rollout budget allows, leaving fast rollback as the real protection instead.

**Why is rolling back to a previous artifact fast while rolling back a database migration is not?** The previous artifact already exists, signed and immutable, so restoring it is a pointer change with nothing to rebuild or re-verify. A destructive schema change has already altered what data exists, so there is nothing equivalent to point back at.

**Why does a destructive migration have to wait until its expand phase has fully deployed before it is allowed to run?** Rollback restores a previous binary, and that binary can only run correctly if the schema it expects still exists. Contracting before the expand phase has fully rolled out removes something the rollback target still depends on, turning a routine rollback into a crash loop.
### 55. Design an Online Auction System
#### Understanding the problem
An online auction system runs millions of concurrent timed auctions, each with one seller, one item, a published deadline and a crowd of bidders, where proxy bids are resolved server-side and exactly one winner must be determined unambiguously at the close.

Two things make this hard.

First, a published deadline is not one instant, it is a value stored once in a database and read as N slightly different values across a fleet of API nodes, because ordinary clock skew between machines is larger than the gap between bids arriving near the close.

Second, most of an auction's activity is silence followed by a spike. A lot can sit quiet for days and then take a large share of its bids in the final ten seconds, because bidding late is a genuinely rational strategy: it denies an incumbent's proxy time to respond.

> **What this is not.** It looks like Ticketmaster: contention at a deadline, a crowd, money on the line. The two resolve it in opposite directions. Ticketmaster has tens of thousands of interchangeable seats and a deadline at the *start* of a sale, so its whole design throttles arrivals so the write path never sees the crowd. Here there is exactly one unit with no substitute, and the deadline is the *end*. Nothing can be queued for, because the only moment a bid is worth anything is right before the close, so the write path has to face the crowd directly rather than meter it away.

#### Requirements and the numbers
**Functional.** Create and schedule listings. Accept validated bids with proxy maxima. Enforce strict monotonic pricing. Anti-sniping extension. Deterministic close and winner determination. Real-time price updates to watchers. Settlement and fraud remediation.

**Non-functional.** Bid accept-or-reject p99 under 250ms end-to-end. Zero lost accepted bids and zero double-leaders, an absolute invariant. Close decisions unambiguous to the millisecond regardless of node clock skew. At least 5 million concurrent watchers.

The whole design is decided by four numbers, so derive them before drawing anything.

**How much bigger is watching than bidding?** Roughly 50 watchers per bidder, meaning a typical live lot carries **~1,500 watchers**, and a hot one carries **~15,000**.

**How extreme is the spike on a single hot item?** A top-1% lot's lifetime average is around 0.008 bids a second, and its final ten seconds run at roughly 40 bids a second: a **~5,000x spike on one row**.

**How much bigger is ordinary clock skew than the gap it has to resolve?** Ordinary NTP skew across a fleet runs **1 to 10ms**, while contested bids near a deadline can arrive only milliseconds apart, meaning the measurement error is comparable to or larger than the thing being measured.

**What does coalescing save on fan-out?** A naive broadcast from one hot item, one message per bid per watcher, would run at roughly 600,000 messages a second. Coalescing to at most 4 snapshots a second and fanning out per gateway node rather than per connection cuts that by **well over an order of magnitude**.

> **The numbers to carry.** ~50 watchers per bidder, up to ~15,000 on a hot lot · ~5,000x spike on a single hot row near close · clock skew 1-10ms against bids milliseconds apart · coalescing collapses a 600k msg/s broadcast to a handful of snapshots a second per node.

#### Bidding and watching: two shapes of traffic
The system is really two workloads that share only the number on the screen. **Bidding** is low-volume, high-consequence and strictly ordered. **Watching** is high-volume, low-consequence and tolerant of a lossy, coalesced broadcast. Forcing both through the same path would make one of them wrong.

The entities:

- **Auction**: one mutable row per item, holding price, leader, secret maximum, deadline and version.
- **Bid**: a submission carrying a maximum amount, appended to an ordered, immutable log.
- **Proxy maximum**: the secret ceiling a bidder authorised, resolved server-side, never displayed directly.
- **CLOSE event**: the deadline itself, ordered into the auction's own stream rather than compared against a clock.

```
POST /auctions/{id}/bids  body:{ max_amount, idempotency_key }
  -> { status: ACCEPTED|OUTBID, current_price, min_next_bid }
GET  /auctions/{id}       -> { current_price, high_bidder_masked, end_ts, bid_count }
WS   /auctions/{id}/watch -> coalesced snapshot, at most 4/s
```

#### High-level design
Follow one bid from a tap to a resolved price, and one price change to every watcher.

[The hot path, bid to fan-out](/diagram/online-auction?focus=bidder,bid-api,partition,resolver,auctions,bus,ws-gateway,watchers,e1,e2,e3,e4,e9,e10,e11)

1. The **Bidder app** submits a bid, carrying a maximum amount and an idempotency key, to the **Bid API tier**.
2. The **Bid API tier** routes it by `hash(auction_id)` to the one **Auction partition** that owns this item.
3. The **Auction partition** hands it to **Proxy resolve + CAS** for resolution against the current state.
4. **Proxy resolve + CAS** commits the new price, leader and maximum to **Auctions row** in one conditional write.
5. **Proxy resolve + CAS** publishes a coalesced price tick onto the **Price tick bus**.
6. The **Price tick bus** delivers one message per **WebSocket gateway** node, not per connection.
7. Each **WebSocket gateway** node fans the update out locally to its own **Watcher clients**.

> **Why the flow is shaped this way.** Bidding and watching have nothing in common except the number they both look at. Forcing them through one path would make the write path slow or the read path expensive. Routing the close event into the same stream as bids is the one deliberate coupling, because the deadline has to be ordered against them.

#### A deadline that isn't an instant
Two bidders tap at nearly the same moment, one just before the close and one just after. How does the system decide which is which, when every node's clock disagrees slightly with every other node's?

[Position instead of a clock comparison](/diagram/online-auction?focus=partition,close-scheduler,auctions,e6)

**Bad: have each API node compare its own clock to `end_ts` and decide locally.** This looks correct and is a different deadline on every node, because ordinary clock skew of a few milliseconds is comparable to the gap between two contested bids. One node's clock has drifted forward, accepts a bid; an adjacent node's has drifted back, rejects the identical timing. Two users, the same timing, different outcomes, and real money attached to the difference.

**Good: consult a single canonical clock service before accepting or rejecting.** This removes disagreement between nodes about what time it is, and it does not remove the underlying problem: a bid still has to travel to that clock service and back, and the comparison it makes is still a comparison against a moving target with network latency baked in.

**Great: stop comparing to a clock at all, and sequence the close into the auction's own ordered stream.** A `CLOSE` event is inserted into the same per-auction stream as the bids, or equivalently, every bid carries `AND state = 'OPEN'` and the close itself carries `WHERE state = 'OPEN'`. The store's own serialisation order becomes the sequencer. Whichever arrived first in that one ordered stream wins, and nothing anywhere ever measures wall-clock time to decide it.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 190" role="img" aria-label="Ordinary clock skew across nodes is comparable to the gap between two contested bids, so a wall-clock comparison cannot reliably order them; a single sequenced stream settles it by position instead">
  <style>
    .box{fill:none;stroke:currentColor;stroke-width:1.2}
    .fillacc{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.22;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.4}
    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    .sub{fill:currentColor;opacity:.8;font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
  </style>
  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="14">Node A: end_ts at T, bid at T-2ms → accepted</text>
  <rect class="box" x="4" y="22" width="384" height="14" rx="4"/>
  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="56">Node B: end_ts at T-6ms, same bid → rejected</text>
  <rect class="box" x="4" y="64" width="384" height="14" rx="4"/>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="98">the disagreement between nodes is bigger than</text>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="114">the gap the decision depends on</text>
  <rect class="fillacc" x="4" y="128" width="384" height="40" rx="4"/>
  <text class="lbl" x="10" y="146">Sequenced stream: position decides,</text>
  <text class="lbl" x="10" y="162">no clock read anywhere</text>
</svg>
```

#### One conditional write, never read-then-write
The obvious way to update a price is to read it, compute the new value, and write it back. Why does that lose bids silently?

[The version-fenced update](/diagram/online-auction?focus=partition,resolver,auctions,e3,e4)

**Bad: read the current price, compute the new one in application code, write it back.** Run this concurrently and it is a lost update: two bidders both read the same starting price, both compute their own new price, and the second write silently overwrites the first. The platform now shows one leader when two people validly bid, and one of them has been told they are winning when they never were.

**Good: hold a lock on the row for the duration of the whole read-compute-write sequence.** This closes the race, and it turns every contested row into a queue of lock waiters, which is exactly the shape that collapses under a genuine spike, since a lock held across a network round trip is far slower than the operation it protects.

**Great: a single conditional write, fenced on the version it read and the auction still being open.** One statement carries its own precondition, succeeding only if nothing else has moved the price since it was read. Zero rows affected means exactly one thing: someone else got there first, or the auction closed, and the safe response is to re-read and retry, never to silently raise the bidder's authorised maximum.

Routing every bid for one auction to a single owning writer, by hashing the auction id, sits underneath this and is worth stating precisely: the conditional write is correct with no routing at all. Routing exists purely so the conditional write almost never has to retry, which is a performance mechanism layered on top of a correctness mechanism that would work without it.

#### Resolving proxy maxima without ever revealing them
A bidder authorises a maximum they will pay, and the system bids only enough to keep them ahead. What happens the instant a stronger bidder arrives?

[The cascade, resolved atomically](/diagram/online-auction?focus=resolver,bid-log,e5)

**Bad: display the leading bidder's actual maximum once someone else challenges it.** This tells every subsequent bidder exactly what they need to beat, which defeats the entire point of a sealed proxy: nobody has any reason to bid their true value if the ceiling is visible, and the mechanism degenerates into ordinary incremental bidding.

**Good: reveal only that the challenger was outbid, without the number.** Better, and a determined bidder can still binary-search the hidden ceiling by submitting a sequence of strictly increasing probes and reading the displayed price after each one, converging on the secret maximum within one increment.

**Great: resolve the whole cascade in one in-memory step, commit atomically, and actively defend the secrecy.** A challenger's maximum is compared against the incumbent's hidden ceiling, the new displayed price is set to one increment above whichever is lower, and the entire result, price, leader, and new ceiling, lands in a single conditional write with two history rows appended. No observer ever sees an intermediate price, and a crash mid-cascade cannot leave the auction in a state nobody authorised.

Worked example, starting at £10: alice submits a max of £40 and leads at the £10 shown price. bob submits £30; his money clears the display but not alice's hidden £40, so the price becomes £31 and bob is outbid in the very response to his own bid. carol submits £60, genuinely beating alice's £40, and the price becomes £41, one increment above the ceiling she just beat.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 260" role="img" aria-label="Displayed price stays one increment above the second-highest hidden maximum; hidden ceilings never appear on screen until they are beaten">
  <style>
    .bar{fill:none;stroke:currentColor;stroke-width:1.2}
    .hidden{fill:currentColor;fill-opacity:.06;stroke:currentColor;stroke-opacity:.35;stroke-width:1;stroke-dasharray:3 3}
    .fillacc{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.26;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.4}
    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    .sub{fill:currentColor;opacity:.8;font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
  </style>
  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="14">alice max £40 (hidden)</text>
  <rect class="hidden" x="4" y="22" width="210" height="16" rx="3"/>
  <rect class="fillacc" x="4" y="22" width="52" height="16" rx="3"/>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="54">shown: £10, alice leads</text>

  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="82">bob max £30, clears £10 but not alice's £40</text>
  <rect class="hidden" x="4" y="90" width="210" height="16" rx="3"/>
  <rect class="fillacc" x="4" y="90" width="163" height="16" rx="3"/>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="122">shown: £31, alice still leads,</text>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="136">bob outbid instantly</text>

  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="166">carol max £60, genuinely beats alice's £40</text>
  <rect class="hidden" x="4" y="174" width="315" height="16" rx="3"/>
  <rect class="fillacc" x="4" y="174" width="216" height="16" rx="3"/>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="206">shown: £41, one increment above the ceiling</text>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="220">carol just beat; alice's £40 is now visible</text>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="234">only because she lost</text>
</svg>
```

This makes the whole mechanism approximately a second-price auction: the eventual winner pays one increment above the runner-up's true maximum, not their own, which only holds while maxima stay secret. Actively defending that secrecy, rate-limiting rapid successive bids from one account and never exposing an outbid delta, is what keeps the binary-search attack from working once someone tries it deliberately.

#### Choosing the closing rule out loud
A published end time is a promise. What should happen when a bid lands in the last few seconds?

[Where the deadline moves, or doesn't](/diagram/online-auction?focus=partition,auctions,close-scheduler,e4,e6)

**Bad: treat the published end time as fixed and give sniping no thought at all.** The auction simply ends when it says it will, and whoever's bid happens to land in the last window, network latency and reaction time rather than valuation, decides the outcome. That is a coherent choice, but only if it is a deliberate one.

**Good: pad the original end time with a fixed buffer up front, hoping it absorbs the rush.** This delays the same problem rather than removing it: whatever the new end time is, the final seconds before it still attract the same late-arriving spike, just at a slightly later clock reading.

**Great: extend the deadline dynamically whenever a bid lands close to it, capped.** An accepted bid inside the final window pushes `end_ts` forward and the extension repeats until a full quiet window passes with no bids, capped at a fixed number of extensions or an absolute time limit. Network latency stops deciding the winner because there is always another window to respond in, and the load spike flattens into a decaying tail instead of a wall.

This is a genuine product decision, not purely an engineering one. A hard close preserves a well-understood endgame and never risks an unbounded auction; auto-extension trades that predictability for reducing how much a bidder's connection speed determines the result. Both are defensible, and the choice belongs in the room with the product owner, stated explicitly rather than defaulted into.

#### Fifty watchers for every bidder
Most people looking at an auction are never going to bid on it. Why can't they just be told about every price change as it happens?

[Coalescing before the broadcast](/diagram/online-auction?focus=bus,ws-gateway,watchers,e9,e10,e11)

**Bad: push every price change to every watcher individually, as it happens.** Correct and immediate, and on a hot lot with thousands of watchers taking dozens of bids a second, this is hundreds of thousands of messages a second generated by one single item.

**Good: have watchers poll for the current price on a fixed interval instead.** This bounds the load per watcher predictably, and it wastes most of those requests on no change at all during quiet periods, while still lagging behind the real price during the exact bursts when watchers care most.

**Great: hold a persistent connection, coalesce updates to a fixed rate, and fan out per gateway node rather than per connection.** Price changes are coalesced to at most four snapshots a second regardless of how fast bids actually arrive. The message bus delivers exactly one update per gateway node, and each node fans that single update out locally to however many thousands of watchers it happens to be holding.

That per-node fan-out is what keeps the bus's own load independent of audience size: a lot with fifteen thousand watchers costs the bus the same handful of deliveries as one with fifteen, because the multiplication into individual connections happens locally at the edge, not centrally.

#### Where it breaks
| Layer | Failure | How the design handles it |
|---|---|---|
| Auction partition | The partition owner dies mid-bid, and ownership moves while bids are in flight | The new owner reads the row's version and the tail of the bid log before accepting writes; in-flight bids fail closed and clients retry with the same idempotency key |
| Auction row CAS | The conditional-write failure rate spikes, meaning routing is broken | Fall back to full serialisable isolation on the row while routing is repaired, never relaxing to a plain read-then-write |
| Close scheduler | A shard stalls, letting an auction blow past its end time and keep taking bids | An independent sweeper scans for overdue open auctions; the close is idempotent, so a double-fire is harmless |
| Clock / NTP | A node's clock drifts significantly | No node ever compares clocks to decide acceptance; drift only degrades the countdown display, never the actual close decision |
| Pub/sub bus | A bus partition goes down and watchers see a frozen price | Clients fall back to polling directly and the interface marks the price as reconnecting rather than showing a stale number as live |
| Settlement | The winner's payment declines after the auction has legally concluded | A defined aging window, reminders, then a second-chance offer to the runner-up at their own stored maximum, never a silent cancellation |

#### What this design does not solve
**The last-tap complaint does not actually go away, it only moves.** Auto-extension relocates the fairness boundary rather than removing it. At the extension cap, the auction ends hard, and the final moments of a long, capped bidding war have exactly the same latency-decides-the-winner problem the extension mechanism exists to fix, now with more money riding on it. Nothing short of trusting a client-attested timestamp closes this fully, and client time is trivially forgeable, so it is not an option.

**Shill detection is post-hoc, and remediation only repairs the accounting.** Every individual shill bid is, on its own, a perfectly valid bid; the pattern only becomes visible in months of accumulated graph structure. A ring can inflate a price for weeks before detection. Replaying the append-only log recomputes the price honest bidders would have reached and refunds the difference, but it cannot undo the fact that every other bidder valued their own bid against a price signal that was a lie for that entire period.

**Regional homing is a single point of failure, chosen deliberately.** An auction is written in exactly one region, because the single-writer invariant cannot survive a multi-master price row without becoming a lost-bid generator. Losing that region during a peak closing window means every auction ending inside the replication lag has to be suspended and extended rather than closed on time, which is correct for correctness and visibly unwelcome to every bidder watching a lot they have followed for days.

#### Final design
Read it back through the numbers. A clock skew of several milliseconds against bids that arrive only milliseconds apart is what forces the close to be a sequenced position in a log rather than a timestamp comparison. A ~5,000x spike on a single hot row is what forces one writer per auction and a version-fenced conditional write rather than any form of read-then-write. And a 50-to-1 gap between watchers and bidders is what forces coalesced, per-node fan-out instead of broadcasting every price change directly to every connection.

[The whole design](/diagram/online-auction?focus=bidder,bid-api,partition,resolver,auctions,bid-log,close-scheduler,close-timers,bus,ws-gateway,watchers,settlement)

> **The numbers to remember.** ~50 watchers per bidder, up to ~15,000 on a hot lot · ~5,000x spike on one row near close, from ~0.008 to ~40 bids/s · clock skew 1-10ms against bids milliseconds apart · coalescing collapses a 600k msg/s broadcast to a handful of deliveries a second per gateway node.

#### Check your understanding
**Why can't an auction's close be decided by comparing a node's local clock to the published end time?** Ordinary clock skew across a fleet of a few milliseconds is comparable to or larger than the gap between two genuinely contested bids, so different nodes can legitimately disagree about whether the same bid arrived in time.

**Why does a read-then-write price update lose bids silently rather than failing loudly?** Two concurrent updates both read the same starting price and independently compute a new one; the second write simply overwrites the first with no error, so the platform ends up showing one leader when two people validly bid, and there is nothing in that flow to notice the loss.

**Why must the proxy cascade commit in a single write rather than as a series of smaller updates?** Writing intermediate counter-bids separately lets an observer see a price that no bidder actually authorised, and a crash partway through would leave the auction in a state nobody agreed to. One atomic commit means every observer only ever sees a fully resolved result.

**Why does a bidder trying to binary-search the leader's hidden maximum eventually succeed regardless of any defence?** Once the leader is genuinely outbid, their true maximum is revealed by the resulting price itself; the defences only need to protect secrecy while the leader is still leading, not forever.

**Why does the message bus only need to deliver one update per gateway node rather than one per watcher?** Coalescing happens once, centrally, and each gateway node fans its single copy out to however many connections it happens to hold locally, so the bus's own load depends on the number of gateway nodes rather than the number of watchers.
### 56. Design a System to Push a Software Update to 500 Million Devices
#### Understanding the problem
Five hundred million devices are not yours: they are off, on cellular, out of battery, or running one of a dozen versions shipped over the last two years. The job is to get a signed update onto as many of them as possible, know how many actually took it, and be able to stop when something goes wrong.

Two things make this hard.

First, the headline number tempts the wrong instinct, sizing a CDN for peak load. The real free variable is time: the same total bytes are an ordinary commercial commitment spread over two weeks and a research problem compressed into six hours, with nothing about the payload changed at all.

Second, there is no undo. A device that has taken a bad build is gone until it voluntarily comes back and asks for something newer. Stopping a rollout only stops new devices from receiving it; it does nothing for the ones that already have.

> **What this is not.** It looks like the CI/CD design: ship one artifact to a large fleet on a widening ladder with automatic halt, the vocabulary is nearly identical. It inverts at the point that matters most. That fleet is owned, homogeneous, always on, and a bad canary is a one-minute restore to a pinned digest. This fleet belongs to other people, runs a dozen live versions, is mostly offline at any instant, and has no restore path at all. The other design spends its effort on detection speed, since being wrong is bounded by how fast recovery runs. This one spends its effort on blast radius, since being wrong here is permanent.

#### Requirements and the numbers
**Functional.** Generate and sign per-version deltas. Assign every device a stable cohort. Admit cohorts in bands under policy. Gate on device conditions. Deliver resumable, verifiable artifacts. Compare cohort health against a holdback and halt automatically.

**Non-functional.** The check-in path available at 99.99%, independently deployable from everything else. No band widens without a statistically meaningful signal. A bad build reaches no more than roughly 0.1% of the fleet before detection. The fleet never generates a synchronised request spike.

The whole design is decided by four numbers, so derive them before drawing anything.

**What is the total egress for one release?** Roughly 460 million reachable devices at a 25MB delta each: 460,000,000 × 25MB ≈ **11.5 petabytes**.

**How does the chosen duration change the required bandwidth?** 11.5PB over 14 days ≈ **76Gbps average, ~230Gbps at diurnal peak**. The same bytes over 24 hours ≈ **1.1Tbps**. Over 6 hours ≈ **4.3Tbps**. Nothing about the payload changed between those three numbers.

**What does jitter save on check-in load?** Every device checking in within the same synchronised minute would be 500,000,000 ÷ 60 ≈ **8.3 million requests a second**. Spread naturally across a day it is roughly **5,800 requests a second**, three orders of magnitude less.

**What does detecting a regression cost per rollout band?** At 0.1% of the fleet, **500,000 devices** are exposed before detection. At 5%, that is **25 million**.

> **The numbers to carry.** ~11.5PB egress per release · duration sets bandwidth: ~76Gbps over 14 days, ~1.1Tbps over 24h, ~4.3Tbps over 6h · jitter: ~5,800 req/s versus ~8.3M/s synchronised · detection cost 500k devices at 0.1%, 25M at 5%.

#### Control plane and data plane: tiny requests, huge bytes
The system is really two problems of opposite shape. The **control plane**, the rollout controller and check-in service, handles an enormous number of tiny requests and is the only channel that still reaches a device that has already been broken. The **data plane**, the artifact store behind a CDN, handles a trivial number of requests carrying enormous bytes, and is entirely replaceable.

The entities:

- **Delta artifact**: a signed, content-addressed diff from one source version to the target, small compared to a full build.
- **Cohort**: a stable, server-assigned bucket a device belongs to for the life of a rollout.
- **Band**: the widening slice of cohorts currently admitted to receive the update.
- **Holdback**: a permanent slice of the fleet that never receives the release, the only honest baseline for comparison.

```
POST /checkin  body:{ device_id, version, variant, region, token }
  -> {} | { url, digest, signature, not_before, conditions[], max_attempts }
POST /report   body:{ device_id, outcome }   # sent on the next check-in, not immediately
```

#### High-level design
Follow one device from a routine check-in to an applied update.

[The hot path, check-in to applied update](/diagram/fleet-update?focus=release-pipeline,artifact-store,cdn,checkin,update-client,device-fleet,rollout-state,e1,e2,e3,e4,e6,e7)

1. The **Release pipeline** produces a signed delta matrix, published into the **Signed artifact store**.
2. The **Signed artifact store** pre-positions the whole matrix, roughly 17GB, at every **CDN edge PoPs**.
3. The **Update client** on each device calls the **Check-in service** on a server-assigned, jittered schedule.
4. The **Check-in service** consults **Rollout state** and answers either nothing, or an artifact URL with a `not_before` time.
5. When conditions are met, the **Update client** fetches the delta from **CDN edge PoPs**.
6. The **Update client** verifies, stages and applies the update on the **500M devices** fleet.
7. The outcome is reported back on the device's next ordinary check-in, never immediately.

> **Why the flow is shaped this way.** The control plane and the data plane are kept independently deployable on purpose. The day the control plane is needed most, to halt a bad release, is often the day the data plane is under the heaviest load, and neither can be allowed to take the other down.

#### Bytes into a rate: choosing the rollout duration
The instinct is to size infrastructure for however many devices exist. What should actually be sized first?

[Duration as the capacity knob](/diagram/fleet-update?focus=release-pipeline,artifact-store,cdn,e1,e2)

**Bad: size a CDN for the theoretical peak of pushing the update to every device at once.** This treats 500 million as a load number to provision against, and it is the wrong reflex: the same total bytes, compressed into a shorter window, demand dramatically more instantaneous capacity for no benefit to a release that was never urgent in the first place.

**Good: pick a rollout duration that feels reasonably fast and see what bandwidth it implies.** An improvement, since duration is now at least a conscious input, and choosing it by feel rather than by what the release actually needs still risks committing to a number nobody can justify when asked why.

**Great: derive duration from the type of release, and let capacity fall out of it as arithmetic.** A routine release spread over 14 days needs roughly 76Gbps average, an ordinary commercial commitment. A genuine security emergency compressed into 24 hours needs roughly 1.1Tbps, a real but justifiable spend. The artifact set itself is small enough, roughly 17GB, that every edge point of presence holds the whole thing, so this was never a caching problem at all, only an egress one.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 170" role="img" aria-label="The same 11.5 petabytes of egress is roughly 76 gigabits a second over 14 days, 1.1 terabits a second over 24 hours, or 4.3 terabits a second over 6 hours">
  <style>
    .bar{fill:none;stroke:currentColor;stroke-width:1.2}
    .fillacc{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.24;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.4}
    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
  </style>
  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="16">14 days: ~76Gbps, an ordinary commitment</text>
  <rect class="bar fillacc" x="4" y="24" width="7" height="22" rx="3"/>
  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="76">24 hours: ~1.1Tbps, only for a genuine emergency</text>
  <rect class="bar" x="4" y="84" width="98" height="22" rx="3"/>
  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="136">6 hours: ~4.3Tbps, a research problem</text>
  <rect class="bar" x="4" y="144" width="384" height="10" rx="3"/>
</svg>
```

Delta size sits inside every one of these numbers linearly: halving the delta halves both the bill and the time at fixed bandwidth, which is why binary diffing is not a minor optimisation at this scale but one of the highest-leverage decisions in the whole design.

#### The herd lives in asking, not downloading
500 million devices each asking a small question sounds harmless. Why is it the part of the design most likely to fail first?

[Jitter, not the download](/diagram/fleet-update?focus=checkin,update-client,device-fleet,e6,e7)

**Bad: have every device check in on a fixed schedule, such as on the hour.** Innocuous for one device, and catastrophic in aggregate: the entire fleet asking within the same minute is roughly 8.3 million requests a second, three orders of magnitude above what the same population produces spread naturally across a day.

**Good: randomise the check-in time within a window, but keep everyone on roughly the same cadence.** This softens synchronisation somewhat, and a correlated event, a regional power cut, a carrier outage, a mass reboot, can still resynchronise a meaningful share of the fleet back onto overlapping windows.

**Great: full jitter, a server-assigned interval, and a smeared arrival time inside each rollout band.** Each device sleeps for a fully random duration up to its interval, not half the interval plus a smaller random component, which is the standard result from retry design and matters more here because it is the only thing that reliably re-spreads a fleet after a correlated wake-up. Within an admitted band, a `not_before` timestamp further smears when devices actually act, so admitting five million devices to a band does not mean five million requests at once.

95% of check-ins answer "nothing for you" in about 200 bytes with no database write at all, which is what keeps this path boring at scale, provided nothing correlates the asking.

#### Halt is not rollback
Stopping a rollout sounds like undoing it. What does "halt" actually do to a device that has already applied the update?

[The ladder as the only blast-radius control](/diagram/fleet-update?focus=rollout-controller,band-ladder,e9,e10)

**Bad: treat this like a server deployment, where a bad release is one restore away.** That intuition, correct everywhere else, is exactly backwards here. There is no previous artifact still running on the device to restore to; the device physically holds the new build, and nothing server-side can reach in and remove it.

**Good: a single global halt switch that stops the release entirely once triggered.** This does stop the bleeding at whatever scale it fires, and without a graduated ladder beneath it, the amount of damage already done by the time anyone pulls that switch is whatever fraction of the fleet happened to be admitted, which could already be a large one.

**Great: a banded ladder, 0.1% then 1% then 5% then 20% then 100%, each with soak time before the next band opens.** Halting at any rung stops further admission immediately; it changes nothing for devices already admitted, because that is the only lever that exists. The ladder's real job is making sure detection happens while the exposed population is still small: detecting a regression at 0.1% means owning 500,000 broken devices, and detecting it at 5% means owning 25 million.

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 170" role="img" aria-label="Devices exposed before detection grows from 500,000 at the 0.1 percent band to 25 million at the 5 percent band; halt only stops the next band from opening">
  <style>
    .bar{fill:none;stroke:currentColor;stroke-width:1.2}
    .fillacc{fill:var(--accent);fill-opacity:.24;stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:1.4}
    .lbl{fill:currentColor;font:600 12.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
    .sub{fill:currentColor;opacity:.8;font:11.5px system-ui,-apple-system,'Segoe UI',Roboto,sans-serif}
  </style>
  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="14">0.1% band, detected here: 500,000 already broken</text>
  <rect class="bar fillacc" x="4" y="22" width="4" height="22" rx="3"/>
  <text class="lbl" x="4" y="70">5% band, detected here: 25,000,000 already broken</text>
  <rect class="bar" x="4" y="78" width="184" height="22" rx="3"/>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="128">halt at either point stops the next band;</text>
  <text class="sub" x="4" y="144">neither point removes what already shipped</text>
</svg>
```

#### A holdback, or your halt is superstition
An updated cohort's crash rate moves. How do you know whether the new build caused that, or whether it was just a bad Monday?

[The permanent comparison group](/diagram/fleet-update?focus=health-analyser,holdback,telemetry,e12,e13,e14)

**Bad: compare the updated cohort's metrics against the same cohort's numbers from before the release.** Simple, and it compares against a different world: whatever else changed in the intervening time, network conditions, a third-party outage, a public holiday, is invisibly baked into the comparison and indistinguishable from anything the new build actually caused.

**Good: compare against a fleet-wide aggregate that includes both updated and not-yet-updated devices.** Closer to a fair comparison, and the aggregate itself shifts as the rollout proceeds, since more of it becomes updated devices over time, which contaminates the very baseline being used to judge them.

**Great: reserve a permanent holdback that never receives any release, and compare against it concurrently.** A fixed roughly 1% of the fleet stays on old software indefinitely, rotated between releases so no individual device is stranded forever. Comparing an admitted cohort against this concurrent, never-updated population controls for the day, the weather and every third-party outage at once, turning the halt decision into a statement with a confidence interval rather than a hunch read off a dashboard.

Without this holdback, every automatic halt is effectively a coin toss between a genuine regression and ordinary day-to-day noise, and a halt mechanism that fires on noise gets disabled by the people operating it, which is worse than never having built one.

#### The updater must never be broken by the update
Every one of these mechanisms depends on a device being able to check in and apply the next release. What happens if the update itself damages that ability?

[Protecting the last channel](/diagram/fleet-update?focus=update-client,device-fleet,e4,e5)

**Bad: ship the component that performs check-in and application in the same release train as the payload.** This is the natural default, and it means a bug in that one component can sever the device's only remaining path to receiving any future fix, leaving no mechanism left to reach it at all.

**Good: version-check the update client separately, but still ship it on the same cadence as everything else.** This adds a safety check, and it does not change the exposure: a broken updater still ships to however large a band was open at the time, on the same aggressive schedule as ordinary payload releases.

**Great: version the update client entirely separately, on its own slower, more conservative track, with minimal dependencies.** Every other component in this design is recoverable through the ladder and a forward release. The update client is the one component for which that recovery mechanism depends on the component working correctly, so it earns a stricter, slower release discipline than anything else in the system.

#### Where it breaks
| Layer | Failure | How the design handles it |
|---|---|---|
| Payload | The build is broken for one hardware variant only | Per-variant crash rate is compared against the holdback, not the fleet aggregate, so a variant-specific failure is not hidden inside a healthy-looking average |
| Rollout | The analyser halts on ordinary noise | Both effect size and statistical significance are required, since a halt that fires weekly on noise gets ignored, which is worse than no halt |
| Rollout | A band widens before enough usage time has passed to observe the metric | Minimum soak per band is expressed in device-usage-hours rather than wall-clock time |
| Distribution | An artifact is corrupted or truncated in transit | The device verifies the digest before applying anything, and refuses and re-requests with backoff rather than applying unverified bytes |
| Distribution | A cache miss storm hits the origin the moment a band opens | Artifacts are pre-positioned at every point of presence before any band opens, never fetched cold in response to release publish |
| Check-in | The fleet resynchronises after a correlated outage | Full jitter and a server-controlled interval mean the next wave spreads back out rather than staying correlated |
| Device | Conditions are never satisfied, and the device simply never updates | Conditions relax progressively with the age of the release, and success is reported as a percentile rather than claiming 100% |

#### What this design does not solve
**Who pays for the bytes is a product and regulatory question, not an engineering one.** On a metered connection, a user's own data allowance funds the download unless conditions gating explicitly excludes them, and no amount of system design settles whether that default is acceptable in a given region.

**A permanent, roughly 8% tail makes 100% an unreachable target.** Devices that are off, abandoned, or permanently on a throttled connection never take a given release inside any reasonable window. Someone has to define success as a percentile of active devices rather than a fraction of the whole fleet, or every release looks like a failure on a dashboard that was measuring the wrong thing.

**Whether a forced, hours-long update path should exist at all is unresolved on purpose.** The ability to compel most of the fleet to take a build within hours is invaluable during an active security incident and dangerous on any other day. If it is built, it needs deliberate, audited controls; the decision to build it before it is needed, or refuse to build it at all, is a governance choice the architecture cannot make on its own.

#### Final design
Read it back through the numbers. 11.5 petabytes of egress is what turns the question from "how big a CDN" into "how long can this take", since duration is what sets the required bandwidth rather than the other way round. A three-order-of-magnitude gap between jittered and synchronised check-in load is what makes the control plane, not the download, the part most likely to fail. And a detection cost that grows from 500,000 devices to 25 million between the first two rungs of the ladder is what makes the banded rollout, with a genuine concurrent holdback behind it, the entire safety mechanism this design has.

[The whole design](/diagram/fleet-update?focus=release-pipeline,artifact-store,cdn,update-client,device-fleet,checkin,rollout-controller,band-ladder,rollout-state,telemetry,health-analyser,holdback)

> **The numbers to remember.** ~11.5PB egress per release · ~76Gbps over 14 days, ~1.1Tbps over 24h · jitter: ~5,800 req/s vs ~8.3M/s synchronised · ladder detection cost: 500k devices at 0.1%, 25M at 5% · a permanent ~1% holdback is what makes any halt decision a statement rather than a guess.

#### Check your understanding
**Why is sizing infrastructure for 500 million devices the wrong first move?** The same total egress can be an ordinary commercial commitment or an extraordinary one depending purely on how long the rollout is allowed to take. Duration is the actual design variable; capacity is simply what falls out of choosing it.

**Why does full jitter matter more here than in most systems that use it?** A correlated event, a regional outage, a mass reboot, can resynchronise a meaningful share of five hundred million devices at once. Full jitter is what reliably spreads that population back out afterwards, rather than merely softening synchronisation under ordinary conditions.

**Why does halting a rollout at 5% leave 25 million devices on a bad build rather than fixing them?** Halting only stops new devices from being admitted into the release. There is no mechanism to reach into a device that already applied the update and remove it; the only path back is a new release that the device has to voluntarily come and collect on its own next check-in.

**Why is comparing an updated cohort against last week's numbers not good enough to trigger an automatic halt?** Crash rate, battery drain and engagement all shift for reasons unrelated to any particular build, so a historical comparison conflates the new release with everything else that changed in the meantime. Only a concurrent, never-updated holdback controls for those confounders.

**Why does the update client need its own, slower release track separate from the payload it delivers?** It is the one component whose failure removes the device's only remaining path to receiving any future fix at all. Every other part of this system is recoverable through a forward release; a broken updater is not, because nothing can reach the device to deliver that fix.
